events.title: Traditional foundation of Rome
events.summary: Varro's foundation date for Rome, 21 April (the Parilia) 753 BC, fixed by Atticus and Varro in the late Republic; Fabius Pictor gave 748/747, Cincius Alimentus 729/728, Timaeus 814/813 (the same year as Carthage).

events.title: Numa Pompilius and the religious calendar
events.summary: Tradition credits the Sabine king Numa (r. 715-673) with the pontiffs, flamines, Vestals, Salii, the twelve-month calendar adding January and February, and the temple of Janus whose closed doors signified peace.

events.title: Destruction of Alba Longa under Tullus Hostilius
events.summary: Traditionally under Tullus Hostilius (r. 673-642) Rome fought Alba Longa, the duel of the Horatii and Curiatii decided the war, and the Alban dictator Mettius Fufetius was torn apart by chariots for treachery; Alba was razed and its people moved to the Caelian.

events.title: Draining and paving of the Forum; the Cloaca Maxima
events.summary: Tradition assigns the drainage of the Forum valley by the Cloaca Maxima to the Tarquins; archaeology shows the Forum was landfilled and given its first pebble pavement c. 625-600 BC, the moment Rome becomes recognisably urban.

events.title: Reforms attributed to Servius Tullius
events.summary: Servius Tullius (trad. r. 578-535) is credited with the first census, the five property classes and 193 centuries of the comitia centuriata, the four urban tribes, and a city wall; the census allegedly counted 80,000 men (Fabius Pictor in Livy).

events.title: Battle of Alalia (Sardinian Sea)
events.summary: Sixty Phocaean penteconters from Alalia in Corsica met a combined fleet of 60 Carthaginian and 60 Etruscan (Caeretan) ships; the Phocaeans won a 'Cadmean victory', lost 40 ships, and abandoned Corsica for Rhegium and then Elea.

battle.significance: Phocaean victory in name but they abandoned Corsica; Etruscans secured Corsica, Carthage Sardinia. The Greek third side (Phocaeans of Alalia) is not a polity in this dataset.

events.title: Croton destroys Sybaris
events.summary: Croton, led in the field by the Olympic wrestler Milo, routed the army of Sybaris at the river Traeis and then razed the richest Greek city in Italy, reportedly diverting the Crathis over its ruins.

battle.significance: Removed the dominant city of Magna Graecia and redistributed power along the Ionian coast.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus
events.summary: The great triad temple of Jupiter, Juno and Minerva on the Capitol, begun by the Tarquins, was dedicated on the Ides of September in the first year of the Republic by the consul M. Horatius Pulvillus.

events.title: Expulsion of the Tarquins and end of the monarchy
events.summary: After Sextus Tarquinius raped Lucretia, L. Junius Brutus and L. Tarquinius Collatinus led an aristocratic coup that expelled Tarquinius Superbus, then besieging Ardea, and replaced the king with two annual magistrates.

events.title: First annual magistrates of the Republic
events.summary: The Fasti list five consuls in 509 (Brutus, Collatinus, Sp. Lucretius Tricipitinus, P. Valerius Publicola, M. Horatius Pulvillus), an overcrowding that betrays later reconstruction of the year.

events.title: First treaty between Rome and Carthage
events.summary: Polybius transcribed from bronze tablets in the treasury of the aediles a treaty of the first consuls: Romans and allies were not to sail beyond the Fair Promontory except under duress, trade in Libya and Sardinia only before a herald or scribe, and Carthage was not to harm Ardea, Antium, Laurentum, Circeii, Tarracina or any Latin city subject to Rome.

events.title: Battle of the Silva Arsia
events.summary: Veii and Tarquinii, supporting the exiled Tarquins, fought the new Republic in the Arsian wood; Brutus and Arruns Tarquinius killed each other in a cavalry duel, and a divine voice (Silvanus) proclaimed that the Etruscans had lost one man more.
events.locName: Silva Arsia, between Rome and Veii (unlocated)

sides.losses: 11,301 (one more than the Romans, per the divine voice)

battle.significance: Legendary first victory of the Republic and death of Brutus.

events.title: Lex Valeria de provocatione (509)
events.summary: Publicola is said to have carried a law granting citizens the right of appeal (provocatio) to the people against a magistrate's capital sentence, and to have lowered the fasces before the assembly.

events.title: Royalist conspiracy and the execution of Brutus' sons
events.summary: Envoys of the exiled Tarquins, sent to reclaim the royal property, recruited young nobles of the Vitellii and Aquilii, among them Titus and Tiberius, sons of the consul Brutus; a slave, Vindicius, betrayed the plot and Brutus watched his own sons scourged and beheaded.

events.title: Creation of the rex sacrorum
events.summary: To perform the sacrifices that only a king could offer, the Republic created a 'king of sacred things' (rex sacrorum or sacrificulus), first held by Manius Papirius, and made him subordinate to the pontifex maximus so that the title could never again carry power.

events.title: Collatinus forced into exile
events.summary: Because he bore the hated name Tarquinius, the consul L. Tarquinius Collatinus, Lucretia's husband, was persuaded by Brutus to resign; he withdrew to Lavinium with his property and a law of Brutus exiled the whole Tarquin gens.

events.title: The Tarquins' field becomes the Campus Martius
events.summary: The royal estate between the city and the Tiber was consecrated to Mars; the grain standing on it, sacrilegious to eat, was thrown into the river, where it lodged in the shallows and, according to the legend, formed the Tiber Island.

events.title: Valerius demolishes his house on the Velia
events.summary: When rumours spread that P. Valerius, sole consul after Brutus' death, was building a fortress-house on the Velia to make himself king, he had it pulled down in a single night, rebuilt below the hill, and lowered his fasces before the assembly; hence the name Publicola, 'friend of the people'.

events.title: Treasury placed under the quaestors
events.summary: Plutarch credits Publicola with making the Temple of Saturn the state treasury (aerarium Saturni) and letting the people elect two quaestors to manage it, the first being P. Veturius and M. Minucius.

events.title: Lars Porsenna's attack on Rome
events.summary: Lars Porsenna of Clusium seized the Janiculum and blockaded Rome; Roman legend tells of Horatius Cocles holding the Sublician bridge, Mucius Scaevola burning his hand in Porsenna's brazier, and the escape of the hostage Cloelia, after which Porsenna made peace in admiration.

battle.significance: Roman tradition claims a moral victory; Tacitus and Pliny imply Rome capitulated. Porsenna's peace returned the Septem Pagi to Veii and took hostages.

events.title: Census of 508: 130,000 citizens
events.summary: Dionysius records a census of 130,000 adult male citizens in the consulship of Valerius and Lucretius, the first of a series of early figures that grow implausibly large.

events.title: Sabine war and the first ovation
events.summary: In 505 the consuls M. Valerius Volusus and P. Postumius Tubertus defeated the Sabines; fighting resumed in 504 (Publicola's last triumph) and 503, when Postumius Tubertus entered the city 'ovans', the first recorded ovation, crowned with myrtle rather than laurel.

events.title: Battle of Aricia
events.summary: A Latin army reinforced by Aristodemus of Cumae defeated and killed Arruns, son of Porsenna, beneath the walls of Aricia, breaking Clusine power in Latium; Etruscan survivors fled to Rome and settled in the Vicus Tuscus.

battle.significance: Ends Clusine control of Latium and launches Aristodemus' tyranny at Cumae.

events.title: Migration of Attus Clausus and the Claudii
events.summary: The Sabine noble Attus Clausus of Regillum migrated to Rome with a large following (5,000 clients in Dionysius), was enrolled as a patrician as Appius Claudius, and received land beyond the Anio that became the tribus Claudia.

events.title: Death and public funeral of Publicola
events.summary: P. Valerius Publicola, four times consul, died so poor that he was buried at public expense, and the matrons mourned him for a year as they had Brutus; his descendants kept the rare right of burial inside the city at the foot of the Velia.

events.title: Siege and destruction of Suessa Pometia
events.summary: The Latin colonies of Pometia and Cora went over to the Aurunci in 503; after a sortie burned the Roman siege works and wounded a consul, Pometia was taken in 502, its leaders beheaded, the population sold and the town razed.

battle.significance: Removed a Volscian-Auruncan foothold on the edge of the Alban hills; the episode illustrates the instability of the Pontine borderland.

events.title: First dictator: Titus Larcius
events.summary: Facing a threat from the Latins and Sabines, Rome appointed its first dictator, T. Larcius (Livy 2.18 gives 501 or 498 depending on his sources), with Sp. Cassius as master of the horse.

events.title: Lapis Satricanus inscription
events.summary: A dedication to Mars (Mamars) by 'the companions (suodales) of Poplios Valesios' reused in the foundations of the temple of Mater Matuta at Satricum, found in 1977 and dated c. 500.

events.title: Pyrgi tablets: Thefarie Velianas' dedication
events.summary: Three gold tablets (two Etruscan, one Phoenician) found in 1964 at the sanctuary of Pyrgi, Caere's port, record the dedication of a shrine to Uni-Astarte by Thefarie Velianas, ruler (Phoenician 'king over Kysry') of Caere, c. 500.

events.title: Pre-monetary bronze: aes rude and the libral as
events.summary: For two centuries after 509 Rome had no coins: payments, fines and dowries were made in bronze weighed on a balance (aes rude, shapeless lumps), reckoned in asses of a Roman pound, while older fines were expressed in sheep and oxen.

events.title: Aes signatum 'ramo secco' currency bars
events.summary: Cast bronze bars marked with a 'dry branch' (ramo secco) or fishbone pattern circulated in Etruria, Emilia and Umbria between the 6th and 4th centuries, usually broken into fragments and weighed; they are Etruscan, not Roman, the ancestors of the later Roman aes signatum.

events.title: Latin dedication of the grove of Diana at Aricia
events.summary: Cato recorded that Egerius Baevius of Tusculum, as dictator Latinus, dedicated the grove of Diana at Aricia on behalf of Tusculum, Aricia, Lanuvium, Laurentum, Cora, Tibur, Pometia and Ardea; Rome is not on the list.

events.title: Commercial treaties between Carthage and the Etruscans
events.summary: Aristotle cites the Etruscans and Carthaginians as peoples bound by agreements on imports, conventions against wrongdoing and written alliances, yet not forming one state; the Pyrgi tablets and the joint fleet at Alalia confirm a long Etrusco-Punic partnership.

events.title: Crustumerium taken; Praeneste joins Rome
events.summary: In 499 Rome besieged Fidenae and captured Crustumerium, a Latin town on the Via Salaria, while Praeneste broke with the Latins and went over to Rome, on the eve of the war that ended at Lake Regillus.

events.title: Census under the first dictator: 150,700
events.summary: Dionysius says the first dictator, T. Larcius, held a census which found 150,700 men of military age; Livy dates Larcius' dictatorship to 501.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Saturn
events.summary: The temple of Saturn at the foot of the Capitol was dedicated on 17 December (the Saturnalia) in 497 according to Livy (others gave 498 or 501); it later housed the aerarium, the state treasury.

events.title: Battle of Lake Regillus
events.summary: The dictator A. Postumius Albus defeated the Latin League, led by Octavius Mamilius of Tusculum with the aged Tarquinius Superbus, near Lake Regillus; Castor and Pollux reportedly fought for Rome and watered their horses at the Juturna spring in the Forum.
events.locName: Lake Regillus (probably Pantano Secco near Frascati)

battle.significance: Ends Tarquin's hopes of restoration; leads to the Foedus Cassianum of 493 on terms of equality.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Mercury
events.summary: The temple of Mercury by the Circus Maximus was dedicated on the Ides of May 495; when the consuls quarrelled over who should dedicate it, the people gave the honour to the senior centurion M. Laetorius, who also founded a guild of merchants (collegium mercatorum).

events.title: Death of Tarquinius Superbus at Cumae
events.summary: The last king died in exile at Cumae at the court of the tyrant Aristodemus; Livy notes that news of his death prompted the patricians to begin oppressing the plebs.

events.title: Colonists sent to Signia
events.summary: Livy reports that Signia, founded by Tarquinius Superbus, received a fresh draft of colonists in 495 to hold the Monti Lepini against the Volsci.

events.title: Twenty-one tribes
events.summary: Livy notes under 495 that 'twenty-one tribes were made at Rome': four urban tribes inherited from Servius Tullius and seventeen rustic tribes, most named after patrician gentes, plus the Clustumina; the number did not rise again until 387.

events.title: Volscian and Auruncan war of 495
events.summary: With the plebs refusing the levy, the consul P. Servilius won recruits by an edict protecting debtors' property while they served, defeated the Volsci and sacked Suessa Pometia, and then routed an Auruncan army near Aricia.

battle.significance: Cleared the Alban approaches; set the stage for the debt crisis of 494.

events.title: The old centurion and the debt riots of 495
events.summary: An aged former centurion, his farm burned in the Sabine war and himself enslaved for debt, burst into the Forum showing battle scars on his chest and the marks of the lash on his back; the crowd rioted and the plebs refused to serve.

events.title: First Secession of the Plebs and creation of the tribunate
events.summary: Plebeian soldiers crushed by debt bondage (nexum) refused to fight and withdrew to the Mons Sacer (or the Aventine, per Piso); they returned after Menenius Agrippa's fable of the belly and the limbs, having won sacrosanct tribunes of the plebs to protect them.
events.locName: Mons Sacer (by the Anio, 3 Roman miles from Rome)

events.title: Dictatorship of Manius Valerius (494)
events.summary: Facing Sabine, Aequian and Volscian attacks and a plebs that would not enlist, the Senate named the popular Manius Valerius dictator; he raised ten legions, triumphed over the Sabines, but resigned when the Senate refused the debt relief he had promised the soldiers.

events.title: Colonists sent to Velitrae
events.summary: Velitrae, a Volscian town on the southern slopes of the Alban hills, was taken in 494 and received Roman colonists, reinforced in 492 after plague emptied it; it repeatedly revolted and was harshly punished in 338.

events.title: Foedus Cassianum
events.summary: Sp. Cassius concluded a treaty of perpetual peace and mutual defence between Rome and the Latin League: equal shares of booty, alternating command, and no aid to each other's enemies.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera
events.summary: Sp. Cassius dedicated the temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera on the Aventine, vowed by A. Postumius during a famine in 496; it became the religious centre of the plebs, seat of the plebeian aediles and archive of plebiscites and senatus consulta.
events.locName: Aventine slope above the Circus Maximus

events.title: Capture of Corioli
events.summary: During the consul Postumus Cominius' attack on the Volscian town of Corioli, the young patrician Gnaeus Marcius forced his way through the gate and took the town, earning the cognomen Coriolanus.

sides.strength: town garrison and relief army from Antium

battle.significance: Source of the Coriolanus legend.

events.title: Plebeian aediles created
events.summary: Alongside the first tribunes the plebs elected two aediles, assistants of the tribunes based at the Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera, who kept the plebeian archives and later the copies of senatus consulta.
events.locName: Temple of Ceres, near the Aventine

events.title: Census of 493: 110,000
events.summary: After the Foedus Cassianum Dionysius records a census of slightly over 110,000 citizens.

events.title: Famine and grain embassies of 492
events.summary: After the secession left fields unsown, Rome sent grain buyers to Etruria, Cumae (where Aristodemus seized their ships) and Sicily, where 'the tyrant' supplied corn; in 491 Coriolanus allegedly proposed withholding it unless the tribunate was abolished.

events.title: Colony at Norba
events.summary: A colony was sent to Norba, on the edge of the Monti Lepini overlooking the Pontine plain, as a citadel against the Volsci.

events.title: Lex Icilia protecting tribunes' speech
events.summary: Dionysius reports a law carried by the tribune Sp. Icilius forbidding anyone to interrupt or contradict a tribune addressing the plebs, on pain of a fine or death.

events.title: Trial and exile of Coriolanus
events.summary: When grain sent from Sicily arrived during the famine, Cn. Marcius Coriolanus urged the Senate to sell it dear unless the plebs gave up the tribunate; the tribunes indicted him, he refused to appear, was condemned in absence and fled to the Volsci.

events.title: The Roman Games repeated after Titus Latinius' dream
events.summary: A master had a slave flogged through the Circus before the procession of the Ludi Romani; Jupiter told the farmer T. Latinius in a dream that the 'leading dancer' displeased him; when Latinius delayed, his son died and he was paralysed, until he told the Senate and walked home cured, and the games were held again.

events.title: Assassination of Aristodemus of Cumae
events.summary: Aristodemus 'the Effeminate', tyrant of Cumae and host of the exiled Tarquinius Superbus, was murdered by the sons of the aristocrats he had killed, ending the tyranny some years after Tarquin's death.

events.title: Anaxilas of Rhegium seizes Zancle and renames it Messana
events.summary: Anaxilas, tyrant of Rhegium (c. 494-476), encouraged Samian and Milesian refugees from the Ionian revolt to seize Zancle, then expelled them and resettled the city, renaming it Messana after his family's Messenian origin; for a generation he controlled both sides of the Strait.

events.title: Coriolanus leads the Volsci against Rome
events.summary: Exiled after a tribunician prosecution, Coriolanus joined the Volscian leader Attius Tullius of Antium and led a Volscian army that took a string of Latin towns and camped at the Fossae Cluiliae, five miles from Rome, until his mother Veturia and wife Volumnia persuaded him to withdraw.
events.locName: Fossae Cluiliae, 5 miles from Rome on the Via Latina

events.title: Treaty with the Hernici
events.summary: Sp. Cassius in his third consulship brought the Hernici of the Sacco valley into the Roman-Latin alliance on the same terms as the Latins, taking two-thirds of their land according to Livy.

events.title: Temple of Fortuna Muliebris
events.summary: Where Veturia, Volumnia and the matrons turned back Coriolanus, the Senate founded a shrine of Women's Fortune, whose first priestess was Valeria; its statue was said to have spoken, and only women married once (univirae) could touch it.
events.locName: Fourth milestone of the Via Latina

events.title: Agrarian proposal and execution of Spurius Cassius
events.summary: Sp. Cassius, three times consul, proposed distributing public land to plebs and Latins in 486; next year he was condemned for aiming at kingship (adfectatio regni) and executed, by the quaestors or by his own father, and his house razed.

events.title: Gelon makes Syracuse his capital
events.summary: Gelon, tyrant of Gela, intervened when the Syracusan landowners (gamoroi) were expelled by the demos and their serfs; he took the city, left Gela to his brother Hiero, and turned Syracuse into the greatest city of the Greek West by transplanting the populations of Camarina, Gela and Megara Hyblaea.

events.title: Seven years of Fabian consuls
events.summary: From 485 to 479 a Fabius held one of the two consulships every year: Quintus (485, 482), Caeso (484, 481, 479) and Marcus (483, 480), an aristocratic dominance unparalleled in the Fasti, ended by the clan's private war against Veii.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Castor
events.summary: The son of the dictator Postumius dedicated the temple of Castor (and Pollux) in the Forum beside the spring of Juturna, fulfilling his father's vow at Lake Regillus.

events.title: Execution of the Vestal Oppia
events.summary: Amid prodigies and war with Veii and the Volsci, the soothsayers declared that rites were being improperly performed; the Vestal Oppia (Opimia in Dionysius) was convicted of unchastity and put to death.

events.title: Battle of Himera
events.summary: Gelon of Syracuse and Theron of Acragas annihilated a large Carthaginian expedition under Hamilcar the Magonid at Himera; Greek tradition placed it on the same day as Salamis (Herodotus) or Thermopylae (Diodorus).

sides.losses: army destroyed; Hamilcar killed or self-immolated

battle.significance: Halts Carthaginian expansion in Sicily for 70 years; Syracusan hegemony under the Deinomenids.

events.title: Theron builds the Olympieion of Acragas with Carthaginian prisoners
events.summary: After Himera Theron of Acragas set thousands of Carthaginian prisoners to work on public projects: the vast Temple of Olympian Zeus, c. 113 by 56 m with giant telamon figures, the city's drains (named phaeaces after their architect Phaeax) and an artificial fishpond.

events.title: Peace terms after Himera and the Damareteion
events.summary: After Himera Carthage obtained peace from Gelon for 2,000 talents of silver and the building of two temples where copies of the treaty would be kept; Gelon's wife Damarete, who had interceded for the Carthaginians, received a gold crown of 100 talents.

events.title: Battle before Veii and the soldiers' oath (480)
events.summary: Soldiers who had refused to win victories for unpopular consuls were stung by Etruscan taunts and swore an oath, led by the centurion M. Flavoleius, to return victorious; Rome won, but the former consul Q. Fabius and the consul Cn. Manlius were killed and M. Fabius declined the triumph.

sides.losses: heavy; a consul and an ex-consul killed

battle.significance: Costly victory; prelude to the Fabian expedition and the Cremera disaster.

events.title: Disaster of the Fabii at the Cremera
events.summary: The gens Fabia undertook the war against Veii as a private enterprise, garrisoning a fort on the Cremera with 306 Fabii and their clients; they were ambushed and all killed, leaving a single boy to continue the line.
events.locName: River Cremera (Fosso della Valchetta) near Veii

battle.significance: Veii seizes the Janiculum briefly; war ends with a 40-year truce in 474.

events.title: Hiero I refounds Catana as Aetna
events.summary: Hiero expelled the citizens of Catana and Naxos and settled 10,000 new colonists (half Syracusans, half Peloponnesians) at Catana, renamed Aetna, with his son Deinomenes as its king; Pindar's First Pythian and Aeschylus' 'Women of Aetna' celebrated the foundation.

events.title: Veientes occupy the Janiculum
events.summary: Exploiting the Cremera disaster, the Veientes seized the Janiculum and crossed the Tiber; after fights at the Temple of Spes and the Colline Gate they were dislodged in 476, though the consul Sp. Servilius nearly lost his army attacking the hill.

battle.significance: Restored Rome's hold on the Tiber crossing.

events.title: Trial of Titus Menenius for the Cremera
events.summary: The tribunes Q. Considius and T. Genucius prosecuted the consul of 477, T. Menenius, son of Agrippa, for failing to relieve the Fabii at the Cremera; he was fined 2,000 asses and died soon after; in 475 Sp. Servilius was acquitted on a similar charge.

events.title: Naval battle of Cumae
events.summary: Hiero I of Syracuse, answering an appeal from Cumae, destroyed an Etruscan fleet off Cumae, ending Etruscan naval dominance in the Tyrrhenian and isolating the Etruscan cities of Campania.

battle.significance: End of Etruscan sea power in the southern Tyrrhenian.

events.title: Forty-year truce with Veii
events.summary: The first Veientine war ended with a 40-year truce (indutiae), a typical early Roman instrument; Veii paid grain and money.

events.title: Census of 474: 103,000
events.summary: Dionysius gives slightly over 103,000 citizens at the lustrum of 474, the year of the forty-year truce with Veii.

events.title: Iapygians annihilate the Tarentines and Rhegines
events.summary: The Iapygians (Messapians) inflicted on Tarentum and its Rhegine allies what Herodotus called the greatest slaughter of Greeks he knew; 3,000 Rhegines fell, and the losses among the Tarentine nobility led to a democratic constitution at Tarentum.

battle.significance: Worst Greek defeat in Italy before the 4th century; produced the Tarentine democracy.

events.title: Murder of the tribune Gnaeus Genucius
events.summary: The tribune Cn. Genucius indicted the consuls of 474 for not appointing the agrarian commission; on the morning of the trial he was found dead in his house, and the frightened tribunes dropped the case, while the consuls pressed the levy.

events.title: The Vestal Urbinia buried alive
events.summary: During a plague that struck women and unborn children, the Vestal Urbinia was convicted of unchastity and buried alive; one of her lovers killed himself and the other was scourged in the Forum and executed.
events.locName: Campus Sceleratus, by the Colline Gate

events.title: Lex Publilia Voleronis
events.summary: The tribune Volero Publilius, a former centurion who had resisted being enrolled as a common soldier, carried a law that tribunes be elected by an assembly organised by tribes rather than curiae.

events.title: Trial and death of Appius Claudius (cos. 471)
events.summary: Appius Claudius, the consul of 471 who had fought the lex Publilia and decimated his army, was prosecuted by the tribunes M. Duillius and Cn. Siccius for obstructing the agrarian law; he died before judgement, by illness or suicide, and his son delivered his funeral eulogy over tribunician protests.

events.title: Tomb of the Diver at Poseidonia
events.summary: A cist tomb of c. 480-470 found in 1968 near Poseidonia bears the only surviving Greek figured wall painting of its date: symposiasts on the walls and, on the lid, a young man diving from a platform into water.

events.title: T. Quinctius takes Antium
events.summary: The consul T. Quinctius Capitolinus defeated the Volsci and captured Antium, their chief port, in 468; the city was colonised the next year but soon reverted to Volscian control.

battle.significance: Gave Rome a temporary foothold on the Volscian coast.

events.title: Colony at Antium (467)
events.summary: To deflect agrarian agitation the Senate sent a colony to Antium under three commissioners (T. Quinctius, A. Verginius, P. Furius); so few Romans enrolled that Volscians were admitted to fill the lists.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Semo Sancus Dius Fidius
events.summary: The temple of the oath-god Semo Sancus Dius Fidius on the Quirinal, begun by the Tarquins, was dedicated by Sp. Postumius on 5 June 466; it held the archaic treaty with Gabii written on an ox-hide shield.

events.title: Fall of the Deinomenid tyranny at Syracuse
events.summary: Thrasybulus, who succeeded his brother Hiero I in 467, was expelled within a year by a general rising; Syracuse became a democracy, instituting a festival of Zeus Eleutherios, and the tyrannies at Acragas and elsewhere also collapsed.

events.title: Census of 465: 104,714 citizens
events.summary: Livy records a lustrum in 465 counting 104,714 citizens (some manuscripts 124,214), 'besides orphans and widows'.

events.title: Plague of 463
events.summary: A pestilence struck Rome and its allies, killing both consuls (L. Aebutius and P. Servilius) or one of them, many senators and a large part of the population; the Aequi and Volsci exploited the paralysis.

events.title: Terentilius Harsa demands written limits on consular power
events.summary: The tribune C. Terentilius Harsa proposed a five-man commission to write down the limits of consular imperium, so that consuls could no longer use their power as they pleased; patrician resistance kept the bill blocked for nearly a decade, until the plebs won the decemvirate of 451.

events.title: Trial of Caeso Quinctius and the first sureties
events.summary: Caeso Quinctius, son of Cincinnatus and leader of the young patricians who drove tribunes from the Forum, was accused on capital charges; ten sureties (vades) pledged 3,000 asses each for his appearance, the first such bail recorded at Rome, but he fled to Etruria and his father sold his estate to pay.

events.title: Rain of flesh
events.summary: Among the prodigies of 461 Livy records that flesh rained from the sky, birds snatching pieces in mid-air and the rest lying on the ground for days without rotting; the Sibylline Books were consulted.

events.title: Ducetius and the Sicel league
events.summary: The Sicel leader Ducetius united the native towns of eastern Sicily into a league, founded new cities at Menaenum and Palike, and fought Syracuse and Acragas; defeated in 450, he threw himself as a suppliant on the altars of Syracuse, was exiled to Corinth, returned to found Kale Akte, and died in 440.
events.locName: Palike, near the sanctuary of the Palici

events.title: Appius Herdonius seizes the Capitol
events.summary: The Sabine Appius Herdonius with c. 2,500 exiles and slaves occupied the Capitol by night, calling on slaves to rise; the Romans, with help from a Tusculan army under L. Mamilius, retook it after several days, but the consul P. Valerius was killed in the assault.

events.title: Census of 459: 117,319 citizens
events.summary: Livy gives 117,319 citizens counted at the lustrum of 459.

events.title: Cincinnatus' dictatorship and the battle of Mount Algidus
events.summary: When the Aequi under Gracchus Cloelius trapped the consul L. Minucius in the Algidus pass, envoys found L. Quinctius Cincinnatus ploughing his four-iugera farm across the Tiber; named dictator, he relieved Minucius, sent the Aequi under the yoke, and resigned after sixteen days.

sides.strength: relief army from the city plus Minucius' trapped consular army

sides.losses: surrendered and sent under the yoke

battle.significance: Legendary model of the citizen-dictator; one of many Algidus engagements.

events.title: Tribunes of the plebs increased to ten
events.summary: The number of plebeian tribunes was raised to ten, two from each of the five classes according to one tradition; the number remained ten thereafter.

events.title: Lex Icilia de Aventino publicando
events.summary: The tribune L. Icilius carried a law distributing the Aventine, then public land outside the pomerium, to plebeians for houses; several families could share one building plot by floors.

events.title: Lex Aternia Tarpeia on fines
events.summary: A consular law set the maximum fine a magistrate could impose at two sheep and thirty oxen, values later converted to bronze (10 asses per sheep, 100 per ox) by the lex Iulia Papiria of 430.

events.title: Embassy to Greece to study the laws of Solon
events.summary: Three envoys (Sp. Postumius Albus, A. Manlius, P. Sulpicius Camerinus) were reportedly sent to Athens and other Greek cities to copy the laws of Solon before codification; they returned in 452.

events.title: Syracusan fleet raids Etruria, Elba and Corsica
events.summary: Syracuse sent the admiral Phayllus against 'Tyrrhenian pirates'; when he took bribes and was exiled, Apelles followed with 60 triremes, ravaged the Etruscan coast and Corsica, seized Elba and returned with many captives.

battle.significance: Further reduced Etruscan control of the Tyrrhenian Sea.

events.title: Plague of 453
events.summary: A pestilence killed the consul Sex. Quinctilius, the flamen Quirinalis Ser. Cornelius and the augur C. Horatius Pulvillus, and many of the poor; the codification debate paused while the embassy to Greece was away.

events.title: First Decemvirate
events.summary: Consulship and tribunate were suspended and ten patrician decemviri legibus scribundis, headed by Appius Claudius, governed with full powers and drafted ten tables of law.

events.title: The Law of the Twelve Tables
events.summary: Rome's first written code, ten tables drafted in 451 and two more in 450, was set up in bronze (or wood) in the Forum: Livy called it 'the fount of all public and private law', and Cicero learned it by heart as a schoolboy.

events.title: The Second Decemvirate
events.summary: Appius Claudius had himself re-elected with nine new colleagues, including several of plebeian name; the board added two tables, among them the ban on intermarriage between patricians and plebeians, and then refused to lay down office when its year ended.

events.title: Anti-Pythagorean risings in Magna Graecia
events.summary: Around the mid-5th century popular risings destroyed the Pythagorean political clubs that dominated Croton and other Italiote cities; the meeting house in Croton was burned with its members inside, and survivors such as Philolaus fled to Greece.

events.title: Verginia, the fall of the decemvirs and the Second Secession
events.summary: The second decemvirate became a tyranny; when Appius Claudius tried to claim the plebeian girl Verginia as a slave, her father killed her in the Forum, the armies mutinied and the plebs seceded to the Aventine and the Mons Sacer until the decemvirs abdicated.

events.title: Leges Valeriae Horatiae
events.summary: The consuls of 449 carried laws making plebiscites binding on the whole people, renewing provocatio and forbidding magistracies without appeal, and confirming the sacrosanctity of tribunes and plebeian aediles.

events.title: Murder of Lucius Siccius Dentatus
events.summary: L. Siccius Dentatus, the plebeian 'Roman Achilles' with 45 wounds in front, eight single combats and 14 civic crowns, was sent by the decemvirs to choose a campsite and murdered by the soldiers escorting him; his body was found among dead escorts with no enemy slain.

events.title: First triumph voted by the people against the Senate
events.summary: After L. Valerius defeated the Aequi and Volsci and M. Horatius the Sabines, the Senate refused them triumphs; the tribune L. Icilius carried a vote of the people granting both, the first triumph celebrated by popular decision without senatorial authority.

events.title: Prosecution of the decemvirs
events.summary: Verginius, now tribune, prosecuted Appius Claudius, who appealed to the people under the provocatio he had denied others; imprisoned before trial, he killed himself, as did Sp. Oppius; the other decemvirs went into exile and their property was confiscated.

events.title: Lex Trebonia on tribunician elections
events.summary: When only five tribunes were elected in 448 and they co-opted two patricians, the tribune L. Trebonius carried a law that the presiding tribune must continue the election until all ten places were filled by vote, outlawing co-optation.

events.title: Quaestors first elected by the people
events.summary: Tacitus records that quaestors, previously appointed by the kings and then the consuls, were first elected by the people 63 years after the expulsion of the Tarquins (c. 447), when Valerius Potitus and Aemilius Mamercus held the office.

events.title: The Roman people award themselves disputed land
events.summary: Asked to arbitrate a boundary dispute between Ardea and Aricia, the Roman assembly, prompted by the old soldier P. Scaptius, voted the land to Rome; Livy calls it a disgraceful verdict that the senate tried in vain to stop.

events.title: Aequian and Volscian raid to the Esquiline Gate
events.summary: Exploiting civil strife, the Aequi and Volsci raided up to the Esquiline Gate; T. Quinctius Capitolinus, consul for the fourth time, rallied the plebs with a famous speech and with Agrippa Furius defeated the invaders.
events.locName: Between Rome and the Alban hills

battle.significance: Removed an immediate threat to Rome.

events.title: Lex Canuleia: intermarriage between patricians and plebeians
events.summary: The tribune C. Canuleius carried a plebiscite repealing the ban on conubium between patricians and plebeians that the second decemvirate had added to the Twelve Tables.

events.title: First military tribunes with consular power
events.summary: In 444 three tribuni militum consulari potestate replaced the consuls; in about 50 of the years from 444 to 367 the state was headed by colleges of three, four or six consular tribunes rather than two consuls.

events.title: Panhellenic foundation of Thurii
events.summary: Athens organised a panhellenic colony near the site of Sybaris, led by Lampon and Xenocritus; Protagoras is said to have drafted its laws, Hippodamus of Miletus may have planned it on a grid, and Herodotus and the orator Lysias became citizens.

events.title: Treaty with Ardea and the linen books
events.summary: After the first consular tribunes abdicated as improperly elected, the suffect consuls L. Papirius Mugillanus and L. Sempronius Atratinus renewed the treaty with Ardea; Licinius Macer later found their names both in the treaty and in the 'linen books' (libri lintei) kept in the temple of Juno Moneta.

events.title: Creation of the censorship
events.summary: Two censors, L. Papirius Mugillanus and L. Sempronius Atratinus, were elected to take the census, a task the consuls (or consular tribunes) no longer had time for; the office grew to control the roll of the Senate and public contracts.

events.title: Colony at Ardea
events.summary: A Latin colony was planted at the Rutulian city of Ardea to protect it after a civil conflict between its nobles and plebs had drawn in the Volsci.

events.title: Spurius Maelius and the famine of 440-439
events.summary: During a famine the rich plebeian knight Sp. Maelius distributed grain he had bought in Etruria; accused of seeking kingship, he was summoned by the dictator Cincinnatus and killed by the master of horse C. Servilius Ahala; his house was razed (the Aequimaelium).

events.title: Formation of the Campanian people
events.summary: Diodorus notes under 438 that 'the nation of the Campanians was formed, named for the fertility of the plain': Oscan-speaking newcomers from the Samnite hills organised a federal people centred on Capua, a prelude to seizing Etruscan Capua (423) and Greek Cumae (421).

events.title: Fidenae defects and murders Rome's envoys
events.summary: Fidenae, a Roman colony on the Tiber, defected to Lars Tolumnius of Veii and killed four Roman envoys, C. Fulcinius, Cloelius Tullus, Sp. Antius and L. Roscius, at Tolumnius' prompting; Rome set up their statues on the Rostra.

events.title: Fidenae revolts; Cossus wins the spolia opima
events.summary: Fidenae, a Roman colony on the Tiber, defected to Lars Tolumnius of Veii and murdered four Roman envoys; in the ensuing battle the military tribune A. Cornelius Cossus killed Tolumnius and dedicated his armour to Jupiter Feretrius, the second spolia opima after Romulus.
events.locName: Fidenae, on the Tiber north of Rome

battle.significance: Second of three spolia opima in Roman history.

events.title: Plague and famine of 436-433
events.summary: Repeated pestilence afflicted Rome from 436; in 433 the Temple of Apollo Medicus was vowed 'for the health of the people', and grain was bought in Etruria, the Pomptine plain, Cumae and Sicily.

events.title: Construction of the Villa Publica
events.summary: The censors C. Furius Pacilus and M. Geganius Macerinus approved the Villa Publica on the Campus Martius and held the first census there.

events.title: Etruscan league refuses aid to Veii
events.summary: Veii and Falerii sent envoys to the council of the twelve Etruscan peoples at the sanctuary of Voltumna; the league refused to make their war its own, the first of several such refusals that left Veii isolated.

events.title: Lex Aemilia limits the censorship to 18 months
events.summary: The dictator Mam. Aemilius Mamercinus carried a law cutting the censors' tenure from five years to eighteen months; the censors in office took revenge by removing him from his tribe and rating him an aerarius taxed at eight times his assessment.

events.title: Tarentum and Thurii found Heraclea
events.summary: After fighting over the Siritis, Tarentum and Thurii jointly founded Heraclea near the old Ionian colony of Siris; Tarentum soon dominated it, and it became the meeting place of the Italiote League.

events.title: First law against electoral canvassing
events.summary: To stop patricians from using conspicuous canvassing against plebeian candidates for the consular tribunate, the tribunes carried a law forbidding candidates to whiten their togas with chalk.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Apollo Medicus
events.summary: Vowed during the plague of 433, the temple of Apollo the Healer in the Prata Flaminia was dedicated by the consul Cn. Iulius in 431, the first Roman temple of a purely Greek god.

events.title: Battle of Mount Algidus (431)
events.summary: The dictator A. Postumius Tubertus decisively defeated a combined Aequian and Volscian army on the Algidus; the victory, unlike earlier Algidus stories, marks a real turning point after which the Aequi ceased to threaten Latium.

sides.strength: dictator's army with Latin and Hernican contingents

battle.significance: End of the Aequian threat to the Alban Hills; beginning of Roman counter-offensive in the Volscian and Aequian hills.

events.title: Postumius Tubertus and the execution of his son
events.summary: A story told that the dictator A. Postumius Tubertus, victor at Mount Algidus, had his son beheaded for leaving his post to fight, even though he won; Livy rejects it, but 'imperia Postumiana' became a proverb for pitiless discipline.

events.title: Leontini's appeal and the first Athenian intervention in Sicily
events.summary: Leontini, at war with Syracuse, sent the orator Gorgias to Athens, which dispatched Laches with twenty ships in 427; the Congress of Gela (424), where Hermocrates urged 'Sicily for the Sicilians', ended the war.

events.title: Capture and destruction of Fidenae
events.summary: After Fidenae revolted again with Veii, the dictator Mam. Aemilius defeated the Veientines and Fidenates (who attacked with burning torches) and took Fidenae through a tunnel; it was sacked and the population sold.

sides.strength: dictator Mam. Aemilius Mamercinus with master of horse A. Cornelius Cossus

battle.significance: Rome secures the lower Tiber and the Via Salaria.

events.title: Samnite highlanders seize Etruscan Capua
events.summary: Oscan-speaking Samnite settlers, admitted as partners, massacred the Etruscan inhabitants of Capua in a night attack (Livy, 423), creating the Oscan Campanian people; Diodorus dates the formation of the Campanian nation to 438.

events.title: Sextus Tempanius saves the army against the Volsci
events.summary: When the consul C. Sempronius Atratinus' army was being beaten by the Volsci, the cavalry decurion Sextus Tempanius had his troopers dismount and fight on foot, restoring the line; both armies withdrew believing themselves defeated.

battle.significance: Indecisive; led to the prosecution of the consul.

events.title: Campanians capture Greek Cumae
events.summary: The new Oscan masters of Capua stormed Cumae, the oldest Greek colony in the west and Rome's former refuge for Tarquin; Cumae became an Oscan town and Greek civic life in Campania contracted to Neapolis.

events.title: Quaestorship doubled and opened to plebeians
events.summary: The number of quaestors rose from two to four, two to accompany the consuls in war, and plebeians became eligible; the first plebeian quaestors were elected in 409.

events.title: Trial of the Vestal Postumia
events.summary: The Vestal Postumia was tried for unchastity because of her elegant dress and too-free wit; she was acquitted, and the pontifex maximus ordered her to abstain from jokes and to dress with more holiness than elegance.

events.title: Colony at Labici
events.summary: After Labici joined the Aequi and was captured, 1,500 Roman colonists were sent there, each receiving two iugera.

events.title: Agrarian bill of Maecilius and Metilius
events.summary: The tribunes Sp. Maecilius and M. Metilius proposed that land taken from enemies be distributed man by man; the patricians defeated it by persuading other tribunes to veto, a tactic Livy credits to Ap. Claudius.

events.title: Athenian siege of Syracuse
events.summary: Athens sent 134 triremes and over 5,000 hoplites against Syracuse in 415, reinforced in 413 by Demosthenes; the Spartan Gylippus and the Syracusan Hermocrates organised resistance, and the Athenian army was destroyed in the retreat to the Assinarus, with survivors sent to the quarries.

sides.strength: c. 200 triremes and over 40,000 men in total, 415-413
sides.losses: almost entire force killed or enslaved

battle.significance: Made Syracuse the dominant power of the Greek West; Etruscan contingents fought on the Athenian side.

events.title: Soldiers stone the consular tribune M. Postumius
events.summary: After capturing the Aequian town of Bolae, the consular tribune M. Postumius Regillensis denied his soldiers the promised booty and threatened them; they stoned him to death, the first Roman commander killed by his own army.

events.title: Velthur Spurinna's Sicilian expedition (Elogia Tarquiniensia)
events.summary: Latin honorific inscriptions set up in the 1st century AD at Tarquinii by the Spurinnae recall an ancestor, Velthur Spurinna, who as praetor led an army to Sicily, 'the first of all Etruscans to cross the sea with an army'; most scholars link this to the Athenian siege of Syracuse.

events.title: Plague and famine of 412-411
events.summary: A plague in 412 left the fields untilled and in 411 Rome faced famine; envoys bought grain in Etruria, while the Samnites now holding Cumae refused to sell and Sicilian rulers sent aid.

events.title: Lucanians capture Poseidonia
events.summary: Around 410 Oscan-speaking Lucanians took the Greek city of Poseidonia; Aristoxenus wrote that its citizens became barbarians, keeping only one Greek festival at which they gathered to lament their lost language and customs.

events.title: First plebeian quaestors
events.summary: In the first election after the quaestorship was opened to plebeians in 421, three of the four places went to plebeians, Q. Silius, P. Aelius and P. Pupius; patricians reacted by obstructing the elections of the following year.

events.title: Carthage destroys Selinus
events.summary: Answering an appeal from Segesta, Hannibal son of Gisco, grandson of the Hamilcar killed at Himera, landed with a huge army, battered Selinus with siege towers and rams and took it after nine days, killing some 16,000 and enslaving 5,000.

battle.significance: Carthage's return to Sicily after 70 years; start of the great Punic-Syracusan wars.

events.title: Hannibal avenges his grandfather at Himera
events.summary: After Selinus, Hannibal stormed Himera, razed it and sacrificed 3,000 prisoners at the place where his grandfather Hamilcar had died in 480; in 407 Carthage founded Thermae Himeraeae nearby.

battle.significance: Erased the site of the Carthaginian defeat of 480.

events.title: Capture of Anxur (Tarracina)
events.summary: The consular tribune N. Fabius Ambustus took the Volscian coastal stronghold of Anxur by a feint, opening the coast road south toward Campania.

sides.strength: army of the consular tribune N. Fabius Ambustus

battle.significance: Rome reaches the southern edge of the Pontine plain.

events.title: Introduction of military pay (stipendium)
events.summary: The Senate decreed that soldiers should be paid from public funds, financed by a property tax (tributum), so that a long winter siege of Veii became possible.

events.title: Siege and sack of Acragas
events.summary: Hannibal and Himilco besieged Acragas, the richest city of Sicily, for eight months; Hannibal died of plague in camp, Himilco sacrificed a child to Baal Hammon and cut Syracusan supply convoys, and the starving Acragantines evacuated to Gela before the city was sacked.

battle.significance: Brought Carthage to the borders of Syracusan territory and triggered the tyranny of Dionysius.

events.title: Siege and fall of Veii
events.summary: Rome besieged Veii, its great Etruscan neighbour 15 km up the Cremera, traditionally for ten years; in 396 the dictator M. Furius Camillus took the city through a tunnel, called out its goddess Juno Regina by evocatio, sold the inhabitants and annexed its territory, nearly doubling the ager Romanus.

sides.strength: Roman army with Latin and Hernican allies; volunteers flocked for booty

sides.losses: city sacked; survivors sold into slavery

battle.significance: Doubles Roman territory and manpower; the first great conquest and the model for later expansion.

events.title: Dionysius I becomes tyrant of Syracuse
events.summary: After the fall of Acragas a young clerk, Dionysius, denounced the generals in the assembly, was elected one of the new generals and then sole general with full powers (strategos autokrator), obtained a bodyguard of 600 at Leontini, and ruled Syracuse for 38 years.

events.title: Treaty of 405 between Carthage and Dionysius
events.summary: With plague in his army, Himilco made peace: Carthage kept the Elymians and Sicans; Selinus, Acragas, Himera, Gela and Camarina became unwalled tributaries; Leontini, Messana and the Sicels were declared autonomous; and Syracuse was left subject to Dionysius.

events.title: Six consular tribunes for the first time
events.summary: For the first time six military tribunes with consular power were elected in 405, the number that became standard for the colleges of the Veientine and post-Gallic years.

events.title: Campanian mercenaries seize Entella
events.summary: Campanian mercenaries discharged after the Carthaginian war were admitted to the Elymian town of Entella, then killed its men and married their wives, keeping the city.

events.title: Censors tax bachelors
events.summary: The censors M. Furius Camillus and M. Postumius Albinus are said to have imposed a tax (aes uxorium) on men who reached old age unmarried, and to have compelled bachelors to marry the widows of men killed in the Veientine war.

events.title: Volunteers serve on their own horses; cavalry pay
events.summary: When a Veientine sortie burned the Roman siege works, citizens rated in the equestrian census but without a public horse volunteered to serve on their own mounts; the Senate thanked them and fixed pay for them, the first cavalry pay.

events.title: Veii elects a king and is shunned by the Etruscan league
events.summary: Tired of annual elections, the Veientes chose a king; the Etruscans resented him because, defeated in an election for the federal priesthood, he had withdrawn his performers from the sacred games, and the league resolved not to help Veii while he reigned.

events.title: The quarrel of Sergius and Verginius and the loss of the camp
events.summary: Capenates and Faliscans attacked the Roman lines at Veii while the Veientes sallied; the consular tribune M'. Sergius refused to call for help from his personal enemy L. Verginius in the next sector, and the camp was lost; both were forced to resign early and in 401 were fined 10,000 asses each.

battle.significance: Setback in the siege; showed the weakness of the collegiate consular tribunate.

events.title: Solar eclipse 'around the 350th year from the foundation'
events.summary: Cicero quotes Ennius: 'on the Nones of June the moon and night covered the sun', about the 350th year from the foundation, and says the pontifical annals calculated earlier eclipses back from it; the eclipse of 21 June 400 BC fits.

events.title: First plebeian consular tribune
events.summary: P. Licinius Calvus became the first plebeian elected military tribune with consular power; in 399 plebeians held five of six places.

events.title: The Senones settle the Adriatic coast
events.summary: Polybius names the Senones as the last Gallic people to cross the Alps, settling the coastal strip from the Utens (Montone) to the Aesis (Esino) south of Ariminum, the 'ager Gallicus' from which they raided Etruria and Rome.
events.locName: Ager Gallicus, between the Utens and the Aesis

events.title: The Chimera of Arezzo
events.summary: A large bronze chimera, made around 400-380 and inscribed 'tinścvil' (gift to Tinia), was discovered at Arezzo in 1553 and is the masterpiece of Etruscan bronze casting.

events.title: The Mars of Todi
events.summary: A life-size bronze warrior of c. 400, found at Todi in 1835 and now in the Vatican, carries an inscription in Umbrian written in Etruscan script recording that Ahal Trutitis, a man with a Celtic name, gave it as a gift.

events.title: First lectisternium
events.summary: During a plague after a harsh winter the duoviri sacris faciundis, on the authority of the Sibylline Books, held Rome's first lectisternium: for eight days images of Apollo and Latona, Hercules and Diana, Mercury and Neptune reclined on couches before banquets.

events.title: The Alban Lake prodigy and emissarium
events.summary: When Lake Albano rose to an unprecedented level without rain, a captured Veientine haruspex and the Delphic oracle declared Veii would not fall until its water was drawn off; Rome cut a drainage tunnel.

events.title: Dionysius I destroys Motya
events.summary: Dionysius I of Syracuse besieged and stormed the Punic island-city of Motya in western Sicily using a mole, six-storey siege towers and the newly invented arrow-firing catapult (gastraphetes/oxybeles).

sides.losses: city destroyed; inhabitants massacred or enslaved

battle.significance: First use of torsion-free catapults in a siege; leads to the founding of Lilybaeum.

events.title: Himilco's siege of Syracuse and its collapse
events.summary: In revenge for Motya, Himilco destroyed Messana and besieged Syracuse by land and sea, but plague broke out in his camp in the marshes; Dionysius attacked by land and sea and burned the fleet, and Himilco bribed him with 300 talents to escape with the Carthaginian citizens, abandoning his mercenaries.

sides.losses: fleet burned, army destroyed by plague

battle.significance: Saved Syracuse and established Dionysius as master of eastern Sicily.

events.title: Gauls destroy Etruscan Melpum
events.summary: Cornelius Nepos, quoted by Pliny, said that Melpum, a city 'outstanding in wealth' in the Po valley, was destroyed by the Insubres, Boii and Senones on the same day that Camillus took Veii.

battle.significance: Marks the end of Etruscan rule in Lombardy.

events.title: Camillus restores the temple of Mater Matuta
events.summary: Before the assault on Veii the dictator Camillus vowed to restore the temple of Mater Matuta, founded by Servius Tullius, and to build one for Juno Regina; he dedicated the restored Mater Matuta after the victory.

events.title: Capena sues for peace
events.summary: After two years of devastation of their fields, the Capenates, Veii's allies, surrendered and received peace; their territory, including the great sanctuary of Feronia (Lucus Feroniae), came under Roman control.

events.title: Golden bowl to Delphi intercepted by Liparaean pirates
events.summary: Roman envoys carrying a gold bowl to Apollo at Delphi from the Veientine spoils were captured by ships of Lipara; the chief magistrate Timasitheus released them and escorted them to Delphi, and Rome granted him public hospitality.

events.title: Surrender of Falerii and the schoolmaster
events.summary: Besieging the Faliscan capital Falerii, Camillus refused the offer of a schoolmaster who brought him the children of its leading men, and had the boys whip the traitor back to the city; moved by this fides, the Faliscans surrendered.

sides.losses: surrendered; paid soldiers' pay for the year

battle.significance: Ends the Veientine war's Faliscan front.

events.title: Colony at Circeii
events.summary: Diodorus records a colony sent to Circeii in 393, a promontory town on the Volscian coast first claimed by Tarquinius Superbus; it was named in the Carthage treaty of 509 as a city subject to Rome.

events.title: No more replacement censors
events.summary: When the censor C. Julius died in office and M. Cornelius was chosen to replace him, Rome was captured by the Gauls within the lustrum; thereafter a censor whose colleague died had to resign, and no suffect censor was ever appointed again.

events.title: Italiote League against Dionysius and the Lucanians
events.summary: Threatened by Dionysius I from the south and the Lucanians from the north, the Greek cities of Italy formed an alliance with a common council, pledging that any city that failed to help a member attacked by the Lucanians would have its generals executed.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Juno Regina on the Aventine
events.summary: Camillus dedicated on the Aventine the temple of Juno Regina, whose cult statue had been 'invited' from Veii by evocatio in 396; a young soldier allegedly asked the statue if it wished to go to Rome and it nodded.

events.title: Census before the Gallic sack: 152,573 free persons
events.summary: Pliny reports that at the time Rome paid the Gauls their ransom, a census had counted 152,573 free persons.

events.title: Gauls besiege Clusium
events.summary: The Senones under Brennus crossed the Apennines and besieged Clusium; Roman envoys, three sons of M. Fabius Ambustus, violated the law of nations by fighting in the Clusine ranks, one killing a Gallic chief, and Rome refused to surrender them.

events.title: War with Volsinii and Salpinum; twenty-year truce
events.summary: Volsinii and Salpinum raided Roman territory during a famine in 392; in 391 the Romans routed them, taking 8,000 prisoners, and granted a twenty-year truce on condition that they return the booty and pay the Roman army for a year.

events.title: Exile of Camillus
events.summary: Accused by the tribune L. Apuleius over the distribution of the Veientine booty, Camillus went into exile at Ardea, praying that the ungrateful city might soon need him; he was condemned in absence to a fine of 15,000 asses.

events.title: The voice of Aius Locutius
events.summary: The plebeian M. Caedicius reported that in the silence of night on the Nova Via, above the shrine of Vesta, a voice louder than human had warned that the Gauls were coming; he was ignored because of his low rank, and after the sack the Senate built an altar to Aius Locutius, 'the Speaker who Spoke'.

events.title: Battle of the Allia
events.summary: A Gallic war band of Senones under Brennus routed the Roman army at the Allia stream, 11 Roman miles north of Rome, on 18 July; most survivors fled to Veii rather than Rome, leaving the city undefended.
events.locName: Allia stream at its confluence with the Tiber, near Crustumerium

sides.losses: heavy; most survivors fled to Veii

battle.significance: Leaves Rome open to capture; the greatest humiliation of early Roman history and a lasting Roman fear of Gauls (metus Gallicus).

events.title: Gallic sack of Rome and siege of the Capitol
events.summary: The Gauls entered undefended Rome three days after the Allia, massacred the old senators sitting in their curule chairs, and besieged the Capitol for seven months; after Juno's geese warned M. Manlius of a night assault, the defenders bought them off with 1,000 pounds of gold.

sides.strength: garrison of the Capitol (men of military age)

sides.losses: disease in the summer heat (Livy); Gauls left with ransom

battle.significance: Only capture of Rome by a foreign enemy until 410 AD. Roman recovery was rapid: within a generation Rome dominated southern Etruria and Latium.

events.title: Massilia helps pay Rome's ransom
events.summary: Justin's epitome of Trogus, himself of Gallic descent, says the Massiliots declared public mourning on hearing that Rome had been taken by the Gauls and collected public and private gold and silver toward the ransom; Rome rewarded them with immunity from duties, a seat among the senators at the games and a treaty on equal terms.

events.title: The Gallic sack in contemporary Greek writers
events.summary: The capture of Rome was the first Roman event noticed by Greek writers: Heraclides Ponticus wrote that an army from the Hyperboreans had taken 'a Greek city called Rhome', Aristotle knew it had been taken by Celts and saved by a certain Lucius, and Pliny says Theopompus mentioned only that the city was captured by Gauls.

events.title: Battle of the Elleporus
events.summary: Dionysius I of Syracuse, allied with the Lucanians, crushed the army of the Italiote League under Heloris on the river Elleporus near Caulonia, then released 10,000 prisoners without ransom and broke up the league.

battle.significance: Syracusan hegemony over southern Italy; the Italiote League's centre shifts to Tarentum.

events.title: Rejection of the move to Veii and rebuilding of Rome
events.summary: Tribunes proposed moving the population to empty Veii; Camillus' speech and an omen (a centurion's 'Standard-bearer, plant the standard; here we shall best remain') kept Rome on its site, and the city was rebuilt in haste with state-supplied tiles and free quarrying.

events.title: Battle of Maecium
events.summary: Camillus as dictator relieved a Roman army surrounded by Volsci at Maecium near Lanuvium, burned the Volscian camp and subdued the Volsci after 70 years of war; he then defeated the Aequi at Bolae and the Etruscans at Sutrium, triumphing three times in one year.

sides.strength: Volscian army with Latin and Hernican volunteers

battle.significance: Rome reasserts itself after the sack.

events.title: Lucanians crush the Thurians near Laus
events.summary: A Thurian army of 14,000 foot and 1,000 horse invading Lucania was trapped in a plain near Laus and lost about 10,000 men; survivors who swam out to the fleet of Leptines, Dionysius' brother, were ransomed, and Leptines brokered a peace, for which Dionysius removed him from command.

battle.significance: Exposed the military weakness of the Italiote League.

events.title: Camillus recovers Sutrium in a day
events.summary: When the Etruscans seized Sutrium, a Roman ally on the edge of the Ciminian forest, Camillus arrived the same day the townspeople had surrendered and retook it, catching the Etruscans scattered and plundering.

battle.significance: Secured Rome's frontier towns against Etruria after the sack.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Mars outside the Porta Capena
events.summary: The temple of Mars vowed during the Gallic war was dedicated by the duumvir sacris faciundis T. Quinctius on 1 June 388 beside the road later paved as the Via Appia; it became the starting point of the cavalry parade (transvectio equitum) of 15 July.
events.locName: Via Appia, first to second milestone

events.title: Four new tribes on Veientine land
events.summary: The territory of Veii, Capena and Falerii was organised into four new rural tribes, Stellatina, Tromentina, Sabatina and Arnensis, bringing the total to 25.

events.title: Dionysius I takes Rhegium
events.summary: After razing Caulonia (389) and Hipponion (388) and giving their land to his ally Locri, Dionysius besieged Rhegium for eleven months until famine forced surrender; the general Phyton was tortured and drowned, and citizens who could not pay a mina ransom were sold.

battle.significance: Gave Dionysius control of both sides of the Strait; synchronised by Polybius with the Gallic sack of Rome.

events.title: Colony at Satricum
events.summary: Two thousand Roman citizens were sent to Satricum, each with two and a half iugera, but the site was repeatedly lost to the Volsci and Latins and burned in 377 and 346.

events.title: Dionysius' Adriatic colonies
events.summary: Dionysius I extended Syracusan power into the Adriatic, founding Lissus on the Illyrian coast, helping Parian settlers establish Pharos (385/384) and Syracuse's colony at Issa, and allying with Illyrian chiefs to restore the Molossian king Alcetas in Epirus.

events.title: Trial and execution of M. Manlius Capitolinus
events.summary: M. Manlius, the saviour of the Capitol, championed indebted plebeians, paying off a centurion's debt with his own money; accused of aiming at kingship, he was condemned and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock, and the gens Manlia banned the praenomen Marcus.

events.title: Dionysius I sacks the sanctuary of Pyrgi
events.summary: A Syracusan fleet of 60 triremes under Dionysius I raided Pyrgi, port of Caere, looting at least 1,000 talents from the temple of Leucothea/Ilithyia and defeating a Caeretan relief force.

events.title: Latin colonies at Sutrium and Nepet
events.summary: Sutrium and Nepet, 'the gates of Etruria' on the edge of the Ciminian hills, were made Latin colonies to guard the newly won Veientine territory.

events.title: Latin colony at Setia
events.summary: Velleius dates a colony at Setia, on the Lepini hills above the Pontine plain, to the year after Sutrium, and Livy records its reinforcement in 379; the town was famous later for its wine, Augustus' favourite.

events.title: Tusculum incorporated with Roman citizenship
events.summary: When Camillus marched on Tusculum for aiding the Volsci, the town met him with open gates and business as usual; Rome granted it full citizenship, making Tusculum the first municipium.

events.title: Camillus and L. Furius at Satricum
events.summary: The aged Camillus, consular tribune for the sixth time, shared command against the Volsci and Praenestines with the young L. Furius Medullinus, whose rash attack nearly lost the battle; Camillus rallied the army and won, and generously chose Furius as his colleague for the next operation.

battle.significance: Restored Roman control of the Pontine edge; led to Tusculum's incorporation.

events.title: Battle at the Allia against Praeneste
events.summary: Praeneste, leading the rebel Latins, marched to the Allia hoping the ill-omened site would unnerve Rome; the dictator T. Quinctius Cincinnatus Capitolinus routed them, took eight towns subject to Praeneste and brought back a statue of Jupiter Imperator.

battle.significance: Breaks the Praenestine-led Latin revolt of the 380s.

events.title: Construction of the 'Servian' Wall
events.summary: The censors let contracts for a stone wall of squared tufa blocks enclosing c. 426 hectares and about 11 km of circuit, the largest city wall in Italy at the time.

events.title: Fabia, the lictor's rod, and the origins of the Licinian agitation
events.summary: Livy tells that the younger daughter of the patrician M. Fabius Ambustus, married to the plebeian C. Licinius Stolo, was startled when a lictor rapped at her sister's door to announce the return of her husband, a consular tribune; her sister's laughter at her ignorance hurt her, and her father helped Licinius seek the consulship for plebeians.

events.title: Battles of Cabala and Cronium
events.summary: Dionysius I won a great victory at Cabala, killing the Carthaginian general Mago, but at Cronium Mago's young son Himilco destroyed his army, killing his brother Leptines and some 14,000 men; peace fixed the frontier at the river Halycus and Dionysius paid 1,000 talents.

battle.significance: Fixed the Halycus boundary between Carthaginian and Greek Sicily.

events.title: The 'anarchy' of 375-371
events.summary: Livy says the tribunes Licinius and Sextius, re-elected every year, blocked the election of curule magistrates for five years ('solitudo magistratuum'), leaving only plebeian officers.

events.title: Temple of Juno Lucina on the Esquiline
events.summary: Pliny records that the temple of Juno Lucina, goddess of childbirth, was built in the 379th year of the city (375 BC) in a grove on the Esquiline, and that a lotus tree there was older than the temple.

events.title: Dionysius allies with the Gauls and sends Celtic mercenaries to Greece
events.summary: Justin says the Gauls who had burned Rome sent envoys to Dionysius offering alliance; Xenophon records that in 369 and 368 Dionysius sent Sparta triremes carrying Celtic and Iberian mercenaries, who impressed the Greeks with their skirmishing horsemen.

events.title: Gallic incursion to the Alban Hills
events.summary: Livy has Camillus, in his fifth dictatorship at about 80, defeat Gauls in the Alban territory; Polybius says that thirty years after the sack the Gauls came to Alba and the Romans, surprised, did not dare meet them.

events.title: Licinio-Sextian laws
events.summary: After ten years of agitation the tribunes C. Licinius Stolo and L. Sextius Lateranus carried three laws: one consulship to be open to (or reserved for) a plebeian, interest already paid to be deducted from debt principal with the rest payable in three years, and no one to hold more than 500 iugera of public land.

events.title: Camillus' vow of a Temple of Concord
events.summary: Ovid and Plutarch say Camillus vowed a temple to Concordia to mark the reconciliation of the orders in 367; Livy is silent.

events.title: Death of Dionysius I
events.summary: Dionysius I died in 367 after 38 years in power, soon after his tragedy 'The Ransom of Hector' won first prize at the Lenaea in Athens; one tradition says he died after a celebratory feast, another that doctors gave him a fatal sleeping draught at the request of his son and successor Dionysius II.

events.title: Plato in Syracuse
events.summary: Invited by Dion, Plato came to Syracuse in 367 to educate the young Dionysius II as a philosopher-ruler; the experiment collapsed when Dion was exiled, and a third visit in 361 ended with Plato a virtual prisoner until Archytas of Tarentum sent a ship to fetch him.

events.title: Archytas governs Tarentum
events.summary: The Pythagorean mathematician Archytas was elected general of Tarentum seven times, against a law limiting the office to one year, and was said never to have been defeated; under him Tarentum led the Italiote League at the height of its prosperity.

events.title: First praetor and curule aediles; first plebeian consul
events.summary: In 366 L. Sextius took office as the first plebeian consul, while the patricians secured a new magistracy, the praetor, with imperium for jurisdiction, and two curule aediles, initially patrician only.

events.title: Plague, death of Camillus, and the first stage performances
events.summary: A plague in 365-363 killed Camillus among many; to appease the gods Rome held a second lectisternium and, for the first time, stage performances by Etruscan ludiones dancing to the pipe, the origin of Roman drama in Livy's famous sketch.

events.title: Dictator appointed to drive the nail
events.summary: When the plague of 365-363 would not abate, elders recalled that a pestilence had once ended when a dictator drove a nail; L. Manlius Capitolinus Imperiosus was named dictator clavi figendi causa, but he tried to use the office to raise an army and was forced to resign.
events.locName: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Capitol

events.title: Defeat by the Hernici; first plebeian consul to command killed
events.summary: L. Genucius, the first plebeian consul to conduct a war under his own auspices, was ambushed and killed by the rebel Hernici; patricians cried that the gods had punished the plebeian auspices.

battle.significance: Ammunition for patrician arguments against plebeian auspices.

events.title: Young Manlius forces a tribune to drop his father's prosecution
events.summary: The tribune M. Pomponius indicted the ex-dictator L. Manlius for his harsh levy and for banishing his slow-spoken son Titus to the countryside; Titus went to the tribune's house at dawn with a dagger and made him swear to drop the case.

events.title: Marcus Curtius leaps into the chasm
events.summary: A chasm opened in the Forum and the seers declared it would close only if Rome's greatest strength were thrown in; the young M. Curtius, saying that Rome's strength was arms and valour, rode fully armed into the gulf, which closed over him.

events.title: Military tribunes of the legions first elected
events.summary: For the first time six of the military tribunes of the legions were chosen by popular vote instead of being appointed by the commanders; young T. Manlius came second in the poll.

events.title: Duel of Manlius Torquatus at the Anio bridge
events.summary: With Gallic and Roman armies facing each other across the Anio, a giant Gaul challenged any Roman to single combat; the young T. Manlius killed him, took his torque and earned the cognomen Torquatus.

battle.significance: Founding legend of the Manlii Torquati.

events.title: Gauls defeated before the Colline Gate
events.summary: A Gallic war band, operating from the territory of Tibur with Tiburtine support, advanced to the Colline Gate; the dictator Q. Servilius Ahala fought them in sight of the walls, the families watching from the ramparts, and drove them back toward Tibur.

battle.significance: Ended the Gallic threat of 361-360; exposed Tibur's hostility.

events.title: Battle of Pedum against the Gauls
events.summary: The dictator C. Sulpicius Peticus defeated a Gallic army near Pedum after a long delay, using camp followers mounted on mules as a mock cavalry to frighten the Gauls; he dedicated gold from the spoils on the Capitol.

battle.significance: Restores Roman prestige in Latium.

events.title: Renewal of the treaty with the Latins and Hernici
events.summary: Under pressure from the Gauls the Latins renewed their alliance with Rome and sent troops 'in accordance with the treaty'; the Hernici were forced back into alliance after their revolt.

events.title: Tribus Pomptina and Publilia created
events.summary: Two new tribes were formed on conquered Volscian land in the Pontine plain (Pomptina) and Hernican land (Publilia), making 27.

events.title: Tarquinii sacrifices 307 Roman prisoners
events.summary: The army of Tarquinii defeated the consul C. Fabius and sacrificed 307 Roman prisoners in its forum; in 354 Rome retaliated by flogging and beheading 358 noble Tarquinienses in the Roman Forum.

events.title: Lex Poetelia against canvassing
events.summary: The tribune C. Poetelius, on the Senate's authority, carried the first statute against ambitus aimed at 'new men' who toured markets and rural gathering places to canvass.

events.title: Lex Manlia de vicesima manumissionum
events.summary: The consul Cn. Manlius had his soldiers in camp at Sutrium vote, by tribes, a 5% tax on the value of manumitted slaves; the tribunes then made it a capital offence to convene an assembly away from Rome.

events.title: Lex Duilia Menenia: interest capped at one-twelfth
events.summary: A tribunician law fixed the maximum rate of interest at one-twelfth (fenus unciarium), probably 8 1/3 % a year (or per ten-month year); in 347 it was halved to semunciarium.

events.title: Dion expels Dionysius II
events.summary: Dion, Plato's friend and Dionysius II's uncle, sailed from Zacynthus with about 800 mercenaries, landed at Carthaginian Heraclea Minoa, and entered Syracuse to popular acclaim while the tyrant was in Italy; Ortygia held out until 355, and Dion was murdered in 354 by Callippus, an Athenian of the Academy.

events.title: First plebeian dictator
events.summary: C. Marcius Rutilus became the first plebeian dictator, named his own plebeian master of horse, and defeated the Etruscans who had raided to the salt-works at the Tiber mouth; the people voted him a triumph over senatorial objections.

events.title: Emergence of the Bruttii
events.summary: Diodorus dates to 356 the formation of the Bruttii in the toe of Italy, a people he describes as runaway slaves and herdsmen of the Lucanians, who took Terina, Hipponium and other Greek towns.

events.title: Dionysius II tyrant of Locri
events.summary: Expelled from Syracuse, Dionysius II made his mother's city Locri his base and ruled it as tyrant for about ten years; when he returned to Syracuse in 346 the Locrians drove out his garrison and took a horrific revenge on his wife and daughters.

events.title: First treaty between Rome and the Samnites
events.summary: Livy and Diodorus record a treaty of friendship (foedus) between Rome and the Samnite League in 354, probably fixing the Liris valley as the boundary between their spheres.

events.title: Roman revenge on Tarquinian prisoners
events.summary: In revenge for the 307 Romans sacrificed at Tarquinii in 358, Rome had 358 of the noblest Tarquinian prisoners scourged and beheaded in the Forum; the rest of the captives were killed on the battlefield.

events.title: Hundred-year truce with Caere
events.summary: Caere, having joined Tarquinii, sued for peace and in memory of its help in 390 received a hundred-year truce.

events.title: Five-man debt commission (quinqueviri mensarii)
events.summary: Five commissioners set up tables in the Forum and settled debts by advancing state money against security or by valuing property for transfer to creditors.

events.title: First plebeian censor
events.summary: C. Marcius Rutilus was elected the first plebeian censor despite patrician opposition; Tarquinii and Falerii received 40-year truces the same year.

events.title: Forty-year truces with Tarquinii and Falerii
events.summary: After Roman armies ravaged their territory, Tarquinii and the Faliscans obtained forty-year truces, ending the war begun in 358.

events.title: Popillius Laenas defeats the Gauls
events.summary: With his colleague ill, the plebeian consul M. Popillius Laenas led four legions against a large Gallic force camped in Latium, was wounded in the shoulder by a javelin while leading from the front, and won; the Gauls withdrew to the Alban hills for the winter.

battle.significance: Plebeian consular victory; pushed the Gauls into the hills.

events.title: The Boii take Felsina
events.summary: In the mid-4th century the Boii overran Felsina, the leading Etruscan city north of the Apennines, which Pliny calls 'chief of Etruria'; Celtic graves appear at Bologna, Marzabotto and Monte Bibele as Etruscan communities were absorbed or displaced.

events.title: Valerius Corvus and the raven: battle against the Gauls
events.summary: In the Pomptine territory the military tribune M. Valerius fought a Gallic champion; a raven landed on his helmet and attacked the Gaul's face, and Valerius (henceforth Corvus) won; the consul L. Furius Camillus then routed the Gauls, who scattered to Apulia.

sides.strength: consular army of L. Furius Camillus

battle.significance: End of the series of 4th-century Gallic raids on Latium.

events.title: Greek fleet raids the coast of Latium
events.summary: A Greek fleet harried the Laurentine coast and the mouth of the Tiber, skirmishing with the Gauls who also roamed the region; Livy guesses the ships came from Syracusan tyrants.

events.title: Second treaty between Rome and Carthage
events.summary: A new treaty, in which Tyre and Utica joined Carthage, extended the forbidden zone to Mastia Tarseion in Spain and banned Romans from trading or founding cities in Sardinia and Libya, while Carthage might raid Latin towns not subject to Rome but must hand them over to Rome.

events.title: Interest halved and debts rescheduled
