events.summary: Ten years after the Duilian-Menenian law capped interest at one-twelfth (8 1/3 percent a year by the usual interpretation), the rate was halved to one twenty-fourth and debts made payable in instalments over four years.

events.title: Valerius Corvus burns Satricum
events.summary: When Antium rebuilt Satricum and stirred up the Latins, the consul M. Valerius Corvus defeated the Volsci, stormed the town, sold 4,000 prisoners and burned it, sparing only the temple of Mater Matuta.

battle.significance: Destroyed a Volscian base in the Pontine plain.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Juno Moneta
events.summary: Vowed in 345 by the dictator L. Furius Camillus during a war with the Aurunci, the temple of Juno Moneta was dedicated on 1 June 344 on the Arx, on the site of the razed house of M. Manlius Capitolinus; the Roman mint later operated beside it, giving 'moneta' and so 'money'.

events.title: Rain of stones and a festival dictator
events.summary: A rain of stones and daylight darkness led the Senate to consult the Sibylline Books, and P. Valerius Publicola was named dictator to establish a day of religious observance, with a supplication that involved not only Rome but neighbouring peoples.

events.title: Timoleon lands in Sicily and takes Syracuse
events.summary: Answering an appeal from Syracusan exiles, Corinth sent Timoleon with ten ships and about 1,200 mercenaries; he slipped past the Carthaginian fleet at Rhegium, defeated the tyrant Hicetas at Adranum, received the surrender of Dionysius II in Ortygia, and saw the Carthaginian general Mago abandon the harbour.

events.title: Capua surrenders itself to Rome
events.summary: Attacked by the Samnites after Capua aided the Sidicini of Teanum, the Campanians appealed to Rome; when the Senate refused to break its treaty with the Samnites, the envoys made an unconditional deditio of Capua and its people, obliging Rome to defend its new property.

events.title: Battle of Mount Gaurus
events.summary: The consul M. Valerius Corvus defeated the Samnites in a hard-fought battle at Mount Gaurus above Cumae, the first battle between Rome and the Samnites.

battle.significance: First Roman-Samnite battle; secures Campania.

events.title: Decius Mus saves the army near Saticula
events.summary: The consul A. Cornelius Cossus' army was trapped in a valley near Saticula; the military tribune P. Decius Mus seized a height with a detachment, drew off the Samnites and broke out at night, enabling a Roman victory.

battle.significance: Makes the reputation of Decius Mus.

events.title: Battle of Suessula
events.summary: Valerius Corvus surprised and destroyed the Samnite camp near Suessula; Livy claims 40,000 shields were collected and Carthage sent congratulations and a 25-pound gold crown for the Capitol.

battle.significance: Ends the active campaigning of the First Samnite War.

events.title: Carthage congratulates Rome with a golden crown
events.summary: After Rome's victories over the Samnites at Mount Gaurus and Suessula, a Carthaginian embassy brought congratulations and a golden crown of 25 pounds for the shrine of Jupiter on the Capitol.

events.title: Mutiny of the Campanian garrison and the Genucian laws
events.summary: Roman troops wintering in Campania plotted to seize Capua and marched on Rome; the dictator Valerius Corvus reconciled them, and the tribune L. Genucius carried laws banning interest, forbidding re-election to the same office within ten years and holding two offices at once, and allowing both consuls to be plebeian.

events.title: Peace and renewal of the Samnite treaty
events.summary: Rome renewed its 354 treaty with the Samnites and left them free to attack the Sidicini, effectively abandoning the cause for which it had fought; the Latins and Campanians, alarmed, prepared for war against Rome.

events.title: Battle of Vesuvius (Veseris)
events.summary: The consuls T. Manlius Torquatus and P. Decius Mus defeated the Latins and Campanians near Mount Vesuvius on the road to Veseris; when the Roman left wavered, Decius devoted himself and the enemy to the gods of the underworld and charged to his death.
events.locName: Near the foot of Vesuvius, road to Veseris

sides.strength: two consular armies with Samnite allies (Livy)
sides.losses: heavy on the left; consul Decius killed

battle.significance: Breaks the Latin-Campanian coalition and decides the Latin War.

events.title: Battle of Trifanum
events.summary: Torquatus caught the regrouped Latins and Campanians at Trifanum between Sinuessa and Minturnae and crushed them; the Latins surrendered and Campanian land (the ager Falernus) was confiscated.

battle.significance: Final field battle of the Latin War's first phase; ager Falernus annexed.

events.title: Loyal Campanian knights receive Roman citizenship
events.summary: Because 1,600 Campanian cavalrymen had refused to join the Latin revolt, Rome granted them citizenship and imposed on the Campanian people an annual payment to each, recorded on a bronze tablet set up in the temple of Castor at Rome.

events.title: Emergence of the manipular legion
events.summary: During the 4th century the Roman army abandoned the phalanx and the round hoplite shield (clipeus) for the oblong scutum and a flexible line of maniples arranged in three ranks of hastati, principes and triarii, a change the ancients linked to the introduction of pay and to lessons learned from the Samnites.

events.title: Leges Publiliae Philonis
events.summary: The plebeian dictator Q. Publilius Philo carried three laws: plebiscites to bind all citizens, the patrician senators' approval (patrum auctoritas) of centuriate laws to be given in advance, and one censor to be plebeian.

events.title: Battle of the Crimissus
events.summary: Timoleon of Corinth with about 12,000 men surprised a large Carthaginian army crossing the river Crimissus in western Sicily during a thunderstorm and destroyed it, including the 2,500-strong Sacred Band of Carthaginian citizens.
events.locName: River Crimissus, western Sicily (Belice or Freddo?)

sides.losses: 10,000 killed, 15,000 captured including the Sacred Band (Diodorus)

battle.significance: Halycus frontier; Greek revival in Sicily under Timoleon.

events.title: Publilius Philo defeats the Latins on the Fenectane plains
events.summary: The plebeian consul Q. Publilius Philo routed the Latins on the Fenectane plains and triumphed, while his colleague Ti. Aemilius besieged Pedum without success.

battle.significance: Advanced the reduction of Latium.

events.title: Battles of Pedum and the Astura
events.summary: The consul L. Furius Camillus defeated the last Latin army (Tiburtines, Praenestines, Veliterni, Lanuvini, Antiates) at Pedum while his colleague C. Maenius destroyed the Antiates and Lanuvini at the river Astura; both triumphed and received equestrian statues in the Forum.

sides.strength: two consular armies (L. Furius Camillus, C. Maenius)

battle.significance: End of the Latin League as an independent power.

events.title: The settlement of 338: dissolution of the Latin League
events.summary: Rome dissolved the Latin League and dealt with each community separately: Lanuvium, Aricia, Nomentum and Pedum received full citizenship, Tusculum's was confirmed, Velitrae was punished, Antium became a citizen colony, Tibur and Praeneste remained allies minus land, and Capua, Fundi, Formiae, Cumae and Suessula received citizenship without the vote.

events.title: The Rostra adorned with the beaks of Antium's ships
events.summary: The Antiate warships were burned or taken to Rome's dockyards, and their bronze beaks (rostra) were fixed to the speaker's platform in the Comitium, which thereafter took the name Rostra; a column was raised to C. Maenius.

events.title: Citizen colony at Antium
events.summary: Antium received a garrison colony of Roman citizens (colonia maritima) while the Antiates were enrolled as citizens; in 317 they asked Rome for patroni to give them laws.

events.title: The castrum of Ostia
events.summary: Roman tradition credited King Ancus Marcius with founding Ostia for its salt pans, but the earliest structure found is a rectangular fort (castrum) of about 194 by 126 m with walls of Fidenae tufa, dated by most archaeologists to the second half of the 4th century, a citizen garrison colony guarding the river mouth.

events.title: Archidamus III of Sparta killed at Manduria
events.summary: Archidamus III, king of Sparta, called in by Tarentum against the Messapians and Lucanians, was killed with his army before Manduria, by tradition on the same day as the battle of Chaeronea; his body was never recovered for burial.

battle.significance: Ended the first Spartan intervention in Italy.

events.title: Timoleon's resettlement of Greek Sicily
events.summary: After the Crimissus and peace with Carthage, Timoleon expelled or executed the remaining tyrants (Hicetas, Mamercus of Catana), invited settlers from Greece (Plutarch claims 60,000), refounded Acragas and Gela, gave Syracuse a moderate constitution, and retired, blind, to die honoured in 337/336.
events.locName: Syracuse and the Sicilian Greek cities

events.title: Vestal Minucia buried alive; first plebeian praetor
events.summary: The Vestal Minucia, suspected for her elegant dress and convicted on a slave's evidence, was buried alive at the Campus Sceleratus by the Colline gate; the same year Q. Publilius Philo became the first plebeian praetor.
events.locName: Campus Sceleratus, by the Porta Collina

events.title: The Aurunci refound themselves at Suessa
events.summary: Attacked by the Sidicini while Rome delayed help, the Aurunci abandoned their old town and fortified Suessa, which took the name Aurunca; the Sidicini destroyed the deserted city.

events.title: Latin colony at Cales
events.summary: After the Ausonian town of Cales was captured, 2,500 colonists were sent there, the first Latin colony founded after 338 and the first planted beyond Latium, controlling the route from Latium into northern Campania.

events.title: Alexander of Epirus campaigns in southern Italy
events.summary: Invited by Tarentum against the Lucanians and Messapians, Alexander the Molossian, uncle of Alexander the Great, campaigned from Apulia to Bruttium, took Heraclea, Sipontum, Consentia and Terina, and made a treaty of friendship with Rome (332).

events.title: The 'dictator years' of the Varronian fasti
events.summary: The Fasti Capitolini insert four years (333, 324, 309, 301) in which a dictator and master of horse held office without consuls; Livy and the other annalists know nothing of them.

events.title: Tribus Maecia and Scaptia created
events.summary: Two new tribes on land confiscated from Latin cities in 338 brought the total to 29; the people of Acerrae received citizenship without vote.

events.title: Peace treaty with the Gauls
events.summary: Polybius records that after thirteen quiet years the Gauls, seeing Rome's growing power, made a formal peace, which they kept for thirty years until a new movement of Transalpine Gauls.

events.title: The great poisoning trial of 331
events.summary: After many prominent men died of an apparent disease, a slave woman told the curule aedile Q. Fabius Maximus that matrons were brewing poisons; twenty were caught, two patrician women drank their own potions and died, and 170 were ultimately convicted.

events.title: Death of Alexander of Epirus at Pandosia
events.summary: Alexander the Molossian, warned by Dodona to beware Pandosia and the Acheron (which he took to mean the places in Epirus), was trapped by Lucanians and Bruttians at the Italian Pandosia and killed crossing the river Acheron by a Lucanian exile.

battle.significance: Ends the first Epirote intervention in Italy.

events.title: Paintings of the François Tomb at Vulci
events.summary: In a chamber tomb painted around 340-310 for Vel Saties of Vulci, Achilles sacrificing Trojan prisoners faces a scene in which Macstrna frees Caile Vipinas while companions kill rival chieftains of Volsinii, Sovana and Rome, including 'Cneve Tarchunies Rumach', Gnaeus Tarquinius of Rome.

events.title: The Ficoroni cista: 'Novios Plautios made me at Rome'
events.summary: A bronze toilet casket from a Praenestine tomb, engraved with the Argonauts at the spring of the Bebryces where Pollux has bound King Amycus, carries the Latin inscription 'Novios Plautios med Romai fecid / Dindia Macolnia fileai dedit': made at Rome by Novius Plautius, given by Dindia Macolnia to her daughter.

events.title: Capture of Privernum
events.summary: Privernum, led by Vitruvius Vaccus of Fundi, revolted and was taken; when asked what punishment they deserved, a Privernate envoy replied 'what those deserve who think themselves worthy of liberty', and the Senate granted citizenship. A citizen colony of 300 was sent to Tarracina.

sides.strength: two consular armies (L. Aemilius Mamercinus, C. Plautius Decianus)

battle.significance: Last Volscian revolt.

events.title: Citizen colony at Tarracina
events.summary: After the fall of Privernum, 300 Roman citizens were settled at the Volscian port of Anxur, renamed Tarracina, each receiving two iugera, to hold the coastal road between the Pontine marshes and the mountains.

events.title: Latin colony at Fregellae
events.summary: Rome planted a Latin colony at Fregellae on the east bank of the Liris, on land the Samnites regarded as theirs, a provocation that helped cause the Second Samnite War.

events.title: Siege of Neapolis and the first prorogation of command
events.summary: Q. Publilius Philo besieged Palaepolis and Neapolis, held by Samnite and Nolan garrisons; his command was extended into 326 'pro consule', the first prorogation of imperium, and the city was betrayed by the Greek leaders Charilaus and Nymphius.

battle.significance: First promagistracy; Neapolis becomes a Roman ally.

events.title: Lex Poetelia Papiria: abolition of nexum
events.summary: After the moneylender L. Papirius flogged the debt-bondsman C. Publilius for refusing his advances, public outrage led to a law abolishing nexum: debtors could no longer pledge their persons, and creditors' claims lay against property, not bodies.

events.title: First coins in Rome's name: the ROMAION bronzes
events.summary: Bronze coins with a head of Apollo and a man-headed bull, of Neapolitan type but with the Greek legend ROMAION ('of the Romans'), are the earliest coins issued in Rome's name; Crawford dated them to c. 326, the year of the Neapolitan treaty.

events.title: Alliance with the Lucanians and Apulians
events.summary: At the outbreak of the Second Samnite War the Lucanians and Apulians, with whom Rome had had no dealings, offered alliance; the Tarentines then turned the Lucanians against Rome by sending young men who showed fake wounds as Roman atrocities.

events.title: Battle of Imbrinium: Papirius Cursor and Fabius Rullianus
events.summary: While the dictator L. Papirius Cursor was in Rome renewing auspices, his master of horse Q. Fabius Rullianus attacked the Samnites at Imbrinium against orders and won; Papirius demanded his execution, and only the pleas of the army, Fabius' father and the people saved him.

battle.significance: Constitutional drama of dictatorial imperium.

events.title: War with the Vestini
events.summary: When the Vestini joined the Samnites, the consul D. Junius Brutus Scaeva ravaged their land and stormed the towns of Cutina and Cingilia, giving the booty to his soldiers.

battle.significance: First Roman campaign in the central Apennines.

events.title: Alleged Roman embassy to Alexander the Great
events.summary: Arrian reports, citing Aristus and Asclepiades, that a Roman embassy reached Alexander at Babylon in 323 and that he foretold Rome's greatness; Arrian himself doubts it, noting that no Roman writer mentions it.

events.title: The Samnites surrender the body of Brutulus Papius
events.summary: After a heavy defeat the Samnites blamed the war on their noble Brutulus Papius and voted to surrender him; he killed himself, and they sent his body and goods to Rome with the Roman prisoners, but Rome rejected the peace terms.

events.title: The Caudine Forks
events.summary: Deceived by Samnite soldiers disguised as shepherds into believing Luceria was under siege, the consuls T. Veturius Calvinus and Sp. Postumius Albinus marched through the Caudine pass, found both ends blocked, and surrendered their whole army to Gavius Pontius; the Romans passed under the yoke and gave 600 equites as hostages.
events.locName: Caudine Forks (Valle Caudina, between Arpaia and Montesarchio)

battle.significance: Greatest Roman humiliation of the Samnite wars; five-year peace; spur to Roman military reorganisation and the Via Appia strategy.

events.title: Recapture of Luceria (320)
events.summary: Livy has L. Papirius Cursor besiege and take Luceria, recover the 600 hostages and send 7,000 Samnites under the yoke in revenge for Caudium; Livy himself was unsure whether Papirius or Q. Aulius was in command.

battle.significance: Patriotic revenge narrative; likely doublet.

events.title: Rome repudiates the Caudine peace
events.summary: On the proposal of Sp. Postumius himself, the Senate declared the Caudine agreement a personal pledge (sponsio) not binding on the people and had the fetials hand over the consuls and other guarantors, naked and bound, to the Samnites; Postumius kicked the fetial, declaring himself a Samnite so that Rome would have a just war, and Gavius Pontius refused to accept them.

events.title: Tarentum tries to dictate peace
events.summary: Tarentine envoys reached the armies in Apulia and announced that Tarentum would make war on whichever side refused to stop fighting; Papirius Cursor took the auspices, declared them favourable and attacked, dismissing the envoys.

events.title: Prefects for Capua; tribes Oufentina and Falerna
events.summary: Rome sent praefecti to Capua at the Campanians' request to give them laws, created the tribes Oufentina and Falerna (31 in all), and made alliances with Teanum Apulum and Canusium in Apulia.

events.title: Lex Ovinia: censors choose the Senate
events.summary: A tribunician law of Ovinius transferred the choice of senators from the consuls to the censors, who were to enrol 'the best men of every rank', in practice ex-magistrates; the Senate thus became a body of former office-holders with life membership.

events.title: Teanum Apulum and Canusium submit
events.summary: The Teates of Apulia obtained a treaty, Canusium gave hostages after its land was ravaged, and in 317 Forentum was taken; Rome now held a ring of allies around Samnium from Apulia, while in the same year prefects were first sent to Capua.

events.title: Agathocles seizes power in Syracuse
events.summary: Agathocles, son of a potter from Thermae, twice exiled, returned with the backing of the Carthaginian general Hamilcar, led his troops in a massacre of about 4,000 members of the oligarchic Six Hundred and their supporters, drove 6,000 into exile, and was elected general with full powers.

events.title: Q. Aemilius Barbula storms Nerulum
events.summary: The consul Q. Aemilius Barbula took the Lucanian town of Nerulum by storm, a sign that Rome's war against Samnium already reached into Lucania.

battle.significance: Roman reach into Lucania.

events.title: Battle of Lautulae
events.summary: The dictator Q. Fabius Rullianus fought the Samnites at the Lautulae pass between Tarracina and Fundi; his master of horse Q. Aulius Cerretanus was killed, and Diodorus states plainly that the Romans were defeated, while Livy calls it indecisive.
events.locName: Lautulae pass (Monte S. Biagio, near Terracina)

battle.significance: Samnites break into Latium; Campanian and Auruncan defections.

events.title: Fall of Saticula
events.summary: After a long siege begun in 316 by the dictator L. Aemilius, Saticula, a Samnite town on the edge of the Campanian plain, fell to the dictator Q. Fabius in 315, while the Samnites took Plistica in retaliation.

battle.significance: Prepared the colony of 313.

events.title: Destruction of the Ausones
events.summary: The three Ausonian towns of Ausona, Minturnae and Vescia, which had joined the Samnites after Lautulae, were betrayed by young nobles and stormed at night; Livy says the Ausonian people were wiped out ('deleta Ausonum gens').

battle.significance: Annihilation of the Ausones; Liris corridor secured.

events.title: Latin colony at Luceria
events.summary: Captured Luceria received 2,500 Latin colonists, a bastion in northern Apulia behind Samnium, after the Senate debated destroying the town altogether.

events.title: Recapture of Sora
events.summary: Sora, which had killed its Roman colonists and gone over to the Samnites, was retaken in 314 when a deserter led ten soldiers up to the citadel at night; 225 ringleaders were taken to Rome, scourged and beheaded in the Forum.

battle.significance: Reopened the Liris corridor.

events.title: Acrotatus of Sparta at Acragas
events.summary: Acragas, Gela and Messana, allied against Agathocles, called in Acrotatus son of the Spartan king Cleomenes II as general; he proved luxurious and murderous, killing the exile leader Sosistratus at a banquet, and was stoned and driven out, after which Carthage brokered a peace that left Agathocles master of eastern Sicily.

events.title: Colonies at Suessa Aurunca, Pontiae, Saticula and Interamna
events.summary: Latin colonies were founded at Suessa Aurunca and on the island of Pontiae (313), at Saticula (313) and at Interamna Lirenas (312), consolidating the Liris-Volturnus corridor; Fregellae was refounded.

events.title: Capture of Nola
events.summary: Nola, the Oscan-Greek city east of Vesuvius that had sent its garrison to Palaepolis in 327, was taken in 313, by the dictator C. Poetelius according to most of Livy's sources; Atina and Calatia were taken in the same campaign.

battle.significance: Secured eastern Campania.

events.title: Censorship of Appius Claudius Caecus
events.summary: Appius Claudius as censor enrolled sons of freedmen in the Senate, distributed the landless (humiles) across all tribes, built the Via Appia and Aqua Appia without senatorial approval, transferred the cult at the Ara Maxima from the gens Potitia to public slaves, and kept office beyond the 18-month limit.

events.title: Construction of the Via Appia
events.summary: Appius Claudius built the first great Roman highway, the Via Appia, 132 Roman miles from the Porta Capena to Capua, driving straight across the Alban Hills and the Pontine marshes (the 19-mile 'decennovium' stretch).

events.title: Construction of the Aqua Appia
events.summary: Rome's first aqueduct, built by Appius Claudius with his colleague C. Plautius (who found the springs, hence 'Venox'), ran 11,190 paces (c. 16.5 km), almost entirely underground, from springs off the Via Praenestina to the Forum Boarium.

events.title: The cult of the Ara Maxima made public
events.summary: The censor Appius Claudius persuaded the Potitii, hereditary priests of Hercules at the Ara Maxima with the Pinarii, to teach the rites to public slaves; within a year all twelve families of the Potitii, thirty adult men, were dead, and Appius later went blind, which pious tradition read as punishment.

events.title: Duoviri navales and elected military tribunes
events.summary: Plebiscites created two naval officers (duoviri navales) to equip and repair a fleet, and provided for 16 military tribunes for four legions to be elected by the people (lex Atilia Marcia).

events.title: Battle of the Himeras river (Ecnomus)
events.summary: Hamilcar son of Gisgo defeated Agathocles of Syracuse near Gela at the Himeras river below the hill of Ecnomus; most Sicilian cities defected and Carthage besieged Syracuse.

battle.significance: Carthage besieges Syracuse; Agathocles invades Africa.

events.title: Etruscan siege of Sutrium
events.summary: With the end of the 40-year truce with Tarquinii, all the Etruscan cities except Arretium attacked the Roman colony at Sutrium; the consul Q. Aemilius Barbula and then Q. Fabius Rullianus defeated them before the walls.

battle.significance: Relief of the gateway colony of Etruria.

events.title: The flute-players' strike
events.summary: Forbidden by the censors to hold their customary feast in the temple of Jupiter, the guild of flute-players, indispensable at every sacrifice, left for Tibur; the Tiburtines got them drunk at a banquet and carted them back to Rome asleep, and their feasting rights were restored, with three days of masked revelry each June.

events.title: C. Junius Bubulcus takes Cluviae and Bovianum
events.summary: The consul C. Junius Bubulcus retook Cluviae, where the Samnites had tortured a Roman garrison to death, and sacked Bovianum, the chief town of the Pentri; escaping an ambush in a mountain pass, he vowed a temple to Salus.

battle.significance: Raid into the Pentrian heartland.

events.title: Agathocles invades Africa
events.summary: Blockaded in Syracuse, Agathocles slipped out with 60 ships and 14,000 men, landed on Cape Bon, burned his ships, and carried the war to Carthage's own territory for four years; a total solar eclipse on 15 August 310 BC occurred during the crossing.

events.title: The eclipse of Agathocles' crossing
events.summary: As Agathocles' fleet slipped out of blockaded Syracuse for Africa, a total solar eclipse turned day into night and stars appeared everywhere; Agathocles told his frightened men it portended disaster for the enemy.

events.title: Fabius Rullianus crosses the Ciminian forest
events.summary: Q. Fabius Rullianus, after sending his brother, who had been educated at Caere and spoke Etruscan, to scout disguised as a shepherd, led his army through the dense Ciminian forest, until then 'more impassable than the forests of Germany were lately', and ravaged the untouched lands of central Etruria.

events.title: Battle near Perusia
events.summary: Fabius defeated the Etruscan army near Perusia after crossing the Ciminian hills; Perusia, Cortona and Arretium, the leading cities of northern Etruria, asked for peace and received a 30-year truce.

battle.significance: Thirty-year truce with the northern Etruscan cities.

events.title: First battle of Lake Vadimon
events.summary: The Etruscans, having raised an army under a lex sacrata (each man choosing a comrade), fought Rome at Lake Vadimon in the Tiber valley; Livy says it was the bloodiest Etruscan battle yet and broke the 'ancient wealth' of the Etruscans.
events.locName: Lake Vadimon (Laghetto di Bassano, near Orte)

sides.strength: Etruscan League army under lex sacrata

battle.significance: Breaks Etruscan League resistance; truces follow in 308.

events.title: Battle of White Tunis
events.summary: Agathocles with about 13,500 men defeated a much larger Carthaginian citizen army under Hanno and Bomilcar near Tunis; Hanno fell and Bomilcar, contemplating a coup, withdrew.

battle.significance: Agathocles establishes himself in Africa.

events.title: Treaties with Camerinum and Ocriculum
events.summary: Scouting beyond the Ciminian forest in 310, Fabius' brother reached the Umbrian Camertes, who offered alliance and received a treaty on equal terms; in 308 Ocriculum, on the Tiber, also obtained a treaty.

events.title: First recorded Roman naval landing
events.summary: P. Cornelius, put in charge of the coast by the Senate, landed a naval force at Pompeii and ravaged the territory of Nuceria Alfaterna; on the way back, laden with booty, the raiders were attacked by country people and lost some men.

battle.significance: First Roman amphibious raid.

events.title: The first Roman silver: the Mars/horse-head didrachm
events.summary: Rome's first silver coin, a didrachm of Greek weight (c. 7.3 g) showing a bearded helmeted Mars and a horse's head with the legend ROMANO, was struck in Campania, most likely at Neapolis; Burnett dates it c. 310-300, perhaps to pay for the Via Appia, while Crawford placed it c. 280-276.

events.title: Hamilcar's night assault on Syracuse
events.summary: While Agathocles campaigned in Africa, the Carthaginian general Hamilcar attempted a night assault on Syracuse by the Euryalus; the column fell into confusion, Hamilcar was captured, tortured and killed, and his head was sent to Agathocles, who displayed it before the Carthaginian camp.

battle.significance: Relieved Syracuse while Agathocles was in Africa.

events.title: Papirius Cursor and the gilded shields
events.summary: The dictator L. Papirius Cursor defeated a Samnite army arrayed in two divisions, one with gilded shields and multicoloured tunics, the other with silvered shields and white; the gilded shields decorated the bankers' shops in the Forum, and the Campanians dressed their gladiators in the captured Samnite armour, origin of the 'Samnite' gladiator.

sides.strength: two divisions, gilded and silvered shields

battle.significance: Restored Roman fortunes in Samnium after 310.

events.title: Agathocles murders Ophellas
events.summary: Ophellas, Ptolemy's governor of Cyrene, marched a great army with Athenian colonists and their families across the Syrtis to join Agathocles, who had promised him Africa; on arrival Agathocles killed him and took over his troops.

events.title: Bomilcar's attempted tyranny at Carthage
events.summary: In the crisis of Agathocles' invasion the Carthaginian general Bomilcar tried to make himself tyrant, leading troops into the city; the citizens fought from the rooftops, his men surrendered under an amnesty, and Bomilcar was crucified in the agora.

events.title: Battle of Mevania
events.summary: When the Umbrians boasted they would march on Rome, Q. Fabius Rullianus hurried from Samnium to Mevania and attacked them before they could deploy; most of the Umbrian peoples surrendered.

battle.significance: Ended Umbrian resistance for a decade.

events.title: Censors build roads through the countryside
events.summary: The censors C. Junius Bubulcus and M. Valerius Maximus let contracts at public expense for roads through the fields, and Junius contracted the temple of Salus he had vowed; the Via Valeria toward Tibur and the Apennines is often attributed to Valerius.
events.locName: Roads east of Rome toward Tibur

events.title: Agathocles abandons his army in Africa
events.summary: After his son Archagathus' defeats in the interior, Agathocles fled secretly back to Sicily; the abandoned army killed his sons Archagathus and Heraclides and made terms with Carthage, and Agathocles massacred the soldiers' relatives in Syracuse.

events.title: Hernican revolt and citizenship for Anagnia
events.summary: Anagnia led the Hernici in revolt after Hernican volunteers were captured among Samnites; the consul Q. Marcius Tremulus crushed them, and Anagnia and others received citizenship without vote while the loyal Aletrium, Verulae and Ferentinum kept their autonomy and conubium by choice.

events.title: Third treaty between Rome and Carthage (the 'Philinus treaty')
events.summary: Livy records a third renewal of the Carthage treaty in 306; the pro-Carthaginian historian Philinus claimed a treaty by which Romans were to keep out of Sicily and Carthaginians out of Italy, which would make Rome's crossing to Messana in 264 a breach.

events.title: Beginnings of Roman-Rhodian friendship
events.summary: Polybius says that by 167 Rhodes had cooperated with Rome for almost 140 years without a formal alliance, implying informal friendship from c. 306, perhaps tied to trade and anti-piracy interests.

events.title: Battle of Bovianum
events.summary: Both consuls, L. Postumius Megellus and Ti. Minucius Augurinus, invaded Samnium; the Samnite commander Statius Gellius was captured, Bovianum (capital of the Pentri) was taken, and the Samnites sued for peace.

battle.significance: Ends the Second Samnite War.

events.title: End of the Second Samnite War
events.summary: The Samnites made peace and the old treaty was renewed; Rome emerged in control of Campania, the Liris valley and northern Apulia, with a girdle of colonies around Samnium.

events.title: Annihilation of the Aequi
events.summary: After the Aequi refused Roman citizenship, the consuls P. Sempronius Sophus and P. Sulpicius Saverrio stormed 31 of their towns in 50 days, burning most and nearly exterminating the people.
events.locName: Aequian highlands (upper Anio and Turano valleys)

battle.significance: End of the Aequi as a people.

events.title: Gnaeus Flavius publishes the legal formulas and calendar
events.summary: Cn. Flavius, son of a freedman and secretary to Appius Claudius, published the forms of legal action (legis actiones, the 'ius Flavianum') and posted the calendar of court days in the Forum, ending pontifical monopoly of legal knowledge; elected curule aedile, he dedicated a bronze shrine of Concord in the Graecostasis.

events.title: Censorship of Q. Fabius Rullianus: urban tribes and the transvectio
events.summary: The censor Q. Fabius Rullianus confined the 'forensis turba' of freedmen and landless to the four urban tribes, reversing Appius Claudius, and instituted the annual parade of the equites on 15 July (transvectio equitum); for this he earned the cognomen Maximus.

events.title: Treaties with the Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini, Frentani and Vestini
events.summary: After the annihilation of the Aequi, the Marrucini, Marsi, Paeligni and Frentani sent envoys seeking peace and friendship and received treaties; the Vestini followed in 302.

events.title: Agathocles calls himself king
events.summary: Following Antigonus, Demetrius, Ptolemy, Seleucus and Cassander, who had assumed the royal title in 306-305, Agathocles began to style himself king (basileus), though he did not wear a diadem; his coins now read 'of King Agathocles'.

events.title: Expedition of Cleonymus of Sparta
events.summary: Tarentum hired the Spartan prince Cleonymus against the Lucanians and Romans; he took Metapontum and campaigned among the Sallentini, was driven off by Roman forces according to Livy, then sailed up the Adriatic and was defeated by the Patavini near the Brenta.

events.title: Treaty with Tarentum: the Lacinian promontory clause
events.summary: Appian refers to 'ancient treaties' forbidding Roman ships to sail beyond the Lacinian promontory (Capo Colonna near Croton) into the Gulf of Tarentum; Rome's breach of this in 282 provoked the Tarentine attack.

events.title: Latin colonies at Sora and Alba Fucens
events.summary: Rome sent 4,000 colonists to Sora on the upper Liris and 6,000 to Alba Fucens beside the Fucine lake in former Aequian land; Carseoli followed (302 per Velleius, 298 per Livy).

events.title: Latin colony at Carseoli and the Marsic war
events.summary: A colony was voted for Carseoli in the former Aequian land in 302, and 4,000 colonists were sent in 298; when the Marsi resisted, the dictator M. Valerius Maximus defeated them and took Milionia, Plestina and Fresilia.

events.title: Rome restores the Cilnii at Arretium
events.summary: When the people of Arretium rose to expel the powerful Cilnii family, Rome intervened; the dictator M. Valerius Maximus fought the Etruscans after his master of horse was ambushed, though Livy reports another version in which the Cilnii were simply reconciled with the plebs without war.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Salus; Fabius Pictor's paintings
events.summary: C. Junius Bubulcus, who had vowed a temple to Salus as consul in 311 and contracted it as censor in 307, dedicated it as dictator in 302; its walls were painted by C. Fabius, who took the cognomen Pictor, the first Roman noble known as a painter.

events.title: Lex Ogulnia: plebeians admitted to the priestly colleges
events.summary: The tribunes Q. and Cn. Ogulnius carried a law raising the pontiffs from four to eight and the augurs from four to nine, the new places reserved for plebeians.

events.title: Lex Valeria de provocatione (300)
events.summary: The consul M. Valerius Corvus carried a law forbidding magistrates to flog or execute a citizen who appealed to the people; Livy calls it the third such law, 'always brought by the same family'.

events.title: First barbers arrive from Sicily
events.summary: Varro records that barbers first came to Italy from Sicily in 300, brought by P. Titinius Mena; before then Romans went unshaven, as the long-bearded statues of the early Republic showed.

events.title: Statues of Pythagoras and Alcibiades in the Comitium
events.summary: During the Samnite wars Apollo of Delphi told the Romans to set up statues of the bravest and the wisest of the Greeks in a busy place; they chose Alcibiades and Pythagoras and placed them at the corners of the Comitium, where they stood until Sulla rebuilt the Senate house.

events.title: Demetrius Poliorcetes complains of Antiate pirates
events.summary: Strabo records that Alexander, and later Demetrius Poliorcetes, sent back to Rome captured pirates from Antium, Demetrius remarking that it was wrong for the masters of Italy to send out pirates and to honour the Dioscuri in their Forum while allowing raids on the gods' own homeland.

events.title: Colony at Narnia; last tribes of the century
events.summary: After a long siege of the Umbrian town of Nequinum, Rome refounded it as the Latin colony of Narnia on a cliff above the Nar gorge, and created the tribes Aniensis and Teretina (33 in all).

events.title: Agathocles seizes Corcyra
events.summary: Agathocles broke Cassander's siege of Corcyra, took the island for himself, and later gave it as dowry when his daughter Lanassa married Pyrrhus of Epirus; Lanassa then left Pyrrhus and offered herself and the island to Demetrius Poliorcetes.

events.title: Transalpine Gauls raid Etruria and Roman territory
events.summary: A new wave of Transalpine Gauls was bought off by the Cisalpine Celts and joined the Etruscans in a raid on Roman territory; they returned home with booty, quarrelled over it and destroyed most of their own army.

events.title: Treaty with the Picentes
events.summary: Envoys of the Picentes warned Rome that the Samnites were seeking their alliance and obtained a treaty of friendship.

events.title: Alliance with the Lucanians; outbreak of the Third Samnite War
events.summary: Lucanian envoys asked Rome for protection against a Samnite invasion and gave hostages; Rome ordered the Samnites out of Lucania, they refused, and the fetials declared war.

events.title: Campaign of L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus
events.summary: The epitaph on Scipio Barbatus' sarcophagus in the Tomb of the Scipios claims he 'took Taurasia and Cisauna in Samnium, subdued all Lucania and brought back hostages'; Livy instead places the consul of 298 in Etruria fighting near Volaterrae.

events.title: Battle near Volaterrae
events.summary: L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus fought the Etruscans near Volaterrae until nightfall; the Etruscans withdrew from their camp by night, leaving Rome the field, and the consul ravaged Etruscan territory.

battle.significance: Drawn battle claimed as a victory.

events.title: Battle near Tifernum
events.summary: Q. Fabius Rullianus, consul for the fourth time, defeated a Samnite army that had tried to ambush him in a valley near Tifernum, while his colleague P. Decius Mus beat the Apulians at Maleventum.

battle.significance: Roman pressure on central Samnium.

events.title: Appius Claudius Caecus vows the Temple of Bellona
events.summary: In a battle against Etruscans and Samnites Appius Claudius vowed a temple to Bellona, later built near the Circus Flaminius outside the pomerium; its anniversary was 3 June.

events.title: Gellius Egnatius forms the anti-Roman coalition
events.summary: The Samnite leader Gellius Egnatius led an army north through the Apennines into Etruria and organised a grand coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls against Rome.

events.title: The Ogulnii set up the she-wolf and twins
events.summary: The curule aediles Cn. and Q. Ogulnius, using fines from moneylenders, set up statues of the infant Romulus and Remus under the she-wolf at the Ficus Ruminalis, placed bronze thresholds and vessels on the Capitol, and paved the road from the Porta Capena to the temple of Mars.
events.locName: Ficus Ruminalis by the Lupercal, Rome

events.title: Citizen colonies at Minturnae and Sinuessa
events.summary: Two small coastal citizen colonies of 300 families each were planted at Minturnae on the Liris mouth and at Sinuessa on the Massic coast, in former Ausonian land, though recruits were hard to find.

events.title: Volumnius surprises the Samnite raiders on the Volturnus
events.summary: Samnite bands plundering the Falernian and Campanian plains were caught by L. Volumnius as they withdrew laden with booty; he killed many, freed 7,400 prisoners and captured the Samnite general Staius Minatius.

battle.significance: Protected Campania; led to the colonies of 296.

events.title: Destruction of a Roman legion near Camerinum
events.summary: Before Sentinum, the Senones (with Samnites) annihilated a Roman legion under the propraetor L. Cornelius Scipio; Polybius places it near Camerinum, Livy near Clusium, and Livy notes some sources said the Gauls rode off with heads on their spears and hanging from their horses' chests.

sides.strength: one legion under L. Cornelius Scipio

battle.significance: Prelude to Sentinum.

events.title: Battle of Sentinum
events.summary: At Sentinum in Umbria the consuls Q. Fabius Rullianus and P. Decius Mus, with four legions and as many allies, defeated the Samnites under Gellius Egnatius and the Senonian Gauls; when Gallic chariots broke the Roman left, Decius devoted himself like his father, and the line held.

battle.significance: Decisive battle for the mastery of Italy; collapse of the Samnite-Gallic-Etruscan coalition.

events.title: Temple of Venus Obsequens built from fines on adulteresses
events.summary: Q. Fabius Gurges as curule aedile fined matrons convicted of adultery (stuprum) and used the money to build a temple of Venus Obsequens near the Circus Maximus, Rome's first temple of Venus.

events.title: Fabius vows a temple to Jupiter Victor at Sentinum
events.summary: In the crisis of Sentinum Q. Fabius Rullianus vowed a temple and the enemy's spoils to Jupiter Victor; the temple, probably on the Palatine, is attested later.

events.title: Agathocles in southern Italy
events.summary: Agathocles took Croton by a ruse, allied with the Iapygians and Peucetians, to whom he gave pirate ships, and campaigned against the Bruttii, capturing Hipponion and building a harbour there.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Victoria on the Palatine
events.summary: L. Postumius Megellus dedicated the temple of Victory on the Palatine, built as aedile from fines; in 204 the black stone of Magna Mater was housed there until her own temple was ready next door.

events.title: Battle near Luceria and the vow to Jupiter Stator
events.summary: The consul M. Atilius Regulus, his camp attacked and his army giving way near Luceria, vowed a temple to Jupiter Stator, 'the Stayer'; the line held and the Samnites were defeated, 7,800 prisoners being sent under the yoke.

battle.significance: Restored Roman control of northern Apulia.

events.title: Postumius Megellus takes Rusellae
events.summary: The consul L. Postumius Megellus stormed the Etruscan city of Rusellae, taking over 2,000 prisoners.

battle.significance: Broke Etruscan resistance after Sentinum.

events.title: Forty-year truces with Volsinii, Perusia and Arretium
events.summary: Volsinii, Perusia and Arretium sued for peace and obtained forty-year truces, each paying 500,000 asses; Postumius Megellus triumphed although the Senate refused, defying even the tribunes.

events.title: Battle of Aquilonia
events.summary: The consul L. Papirius Cursor (son of the dictator) crushed the Samnite 'linen legion' at Aquilonia, while his colleague Sp. Carvilius took Cominium; the Samnites had sworn its 16,000 picked men by gruesome oaths in a linen-roofed enclosure, executing those who refused.

battle.significance: Final great field battle of the Samnite wars.

events.title: Temple of Quirinus and Rome's first sundial
events.summary: L. Papirius Cursor dedicated the temple of Quirinus vowed by his father and decorated it with Samnite spoils; Pliny, citing Fabius Vestalis, says he set up the first sundial in Rome there.

events.title: Census of 293: 262,321 citizens
events.summary: Livy records 262,321 citizens counted in the census of 293, the first of the mid-Republican figures generally treated as broadly reliable (adult males, including cives sine suffragio).

events.title: Carvilius' colossal Jupiter on the Capitol
events.summary: From the breastplates, greaves and helmets of the Samnites killed at Aquilonia and Cominium, the consul Sp. Carvilius had a colossal bronze Jupiter cast for the Capitol, so large that it could be seen from the temple of Jupiter Latiaris on the Alban Mount; from the filings he made a statue of himself to stand at its feet.

events.title: Temple of Fors Fortuna across the Tiber
events.summary: Sp. Carvilius built a temple of Fors Fortuna from Samnite spoils near the older shrine attributed to Servius Tullius, on the right bank of the Tiber.

events.title: Aesculapius brought from Epidaurus to the Tiber Island
events.summary: After a three-year plague and consultation of the Sibylline Books (293), envoys under Q. Ogulnius sailed to Epidaurus; a sacred snake boarded their ship and, at Rome, slipped overboard onto the Tiber Island, where a temple to Aesculapius was dedicated on 1 January.

events.title: Execution of Gavius Pontius
events.summary: Q. Fabius Gurges, after a defeat retrieved with help from his father Rullianus as legate, beat the Samnites and led the captured C. Pontius in his triumph; Pontius, probably the Caudine victor (or his son), was then beheaded.

events.title: Latin colony at Venusia
events.summary: Rome founded at Venusia, on the border of Samnium, Apulia and Lucania, a Latin colony that Dionysius says numbered 20,000 colonists, the largest ever, splitting the Samnites from their southern neighbours.

events.title: Postumius Megellus fined for using soldiers on his estate
events.summary: In his third consulship L. Postumius Megellus used 2,000 soldiers to clear woodland on his own estate and arrogantly overrode his colleague; after his term he was prosecuted and heavily fined.

events.title: Manius Curius conquers the Sabines and Praetuttii
events.summary: The consul M'. Curius Dentatus overran the Sabine country and the Praetuttii to the Adriatic in a single campaign; the Sabines received citizenship without vote (full citizenship in 268), and Rome's territory now crossed Italy from sea to sea.

events.title: Curius drains the Lacus Velinus (Cascata delle Marmore)
events.summary: Curius Dentatus cut a channel through the travertine sill at Marmore to drain the Lacus Velinus near Reate into the Nar, creating the artificial waterfalls still known as the Cascata delle Marmore and reclaiming the plain of Rosea.

events.title: The Esquiline historical painting (Fabius and Fannius)
events.summary: A fragment of fresco from a tomb on the Esquiline, painted in the early 3rd century, shows registers of battle and parley scenes with figures labelled Q. Fabius and M. Fannius, probably commemorating a Samnite war episode; it is the oldest surviving Roman historical painting.

events.title: Lex Maenia: patrician approval given before elections
events.summary: A lex Maenia, of uncertain early 3rd-century date, required the patrician senators to give their sanction (auctoritas patrum) to elections in advance, extending to electoral assemblies the rule that the lex Publilia of 339 had applied to legislation.

events.title: Creation of the tresviri capitales
events.summary: The Periochae note that 'tresviri capitales were then created for the first time': three junior officials who ran the prison, supervised executions, policed the city at night and judged petty cases involving slaves and the poor at the Maenian column.

events.title: Latin colony at Hadria
events.summary: Hadria (Atri) in Praetuttian territory was made a Latin colony near the Adriatic, consolidating Curius' conquests; Castrum Novum on the coast may date from the same years.

events.title: Beginnings of Roman coinage: aes grave and the tresviri monetales
events.summary: The board of three moneyers (tresviri aere argento auro flando feriundo) is traditionally dated c. 289, around the time Rome began casting heavy bronze coins (aes grave) on a libral standard, after centuries of using raw bronze by weight (aes rude) and cast bars (aes signatum).
events.locName: Rome (mint by the temple of Juno Moneta, Arx)

events.title: Census of 289: about 272,000
events.summary: The Periochae record a lustrum with about 272,000 citizens counted in the late 290s or 289, the first census after the Third Samnite War.

events.title: Death of Agathocles
events.summary: Agathocles died in 289 aged about 72, possibly poisoned at the instigation of his grandson Archagathus; before dying he restored 'democracy' to the Syracusans, refusing to name a successor, and his Campanian mercenaries were dismissed, to seize Messana as the Mamertines.

events.title: Mamertines seize Messana
events.summary: Campanian mercenaries discharged after Agathocles' death, calling themselves Mamertini ('sons of Mars'), were admitted to Messana as guests, massacred or expelled the men, took their wives and property, and made the city a base for raiding north-east Sicily.
tags: road to the First Punic War

events.title: Lex Hortensia and the last secession of the plebs
events.summary: After a debt crisis drove the plebs to secede to the Janiculum, the plebeian dictator Q. Hortensius carried a law making plebiscites binding on the whole Roman people without further sanction; the concilium plebis became Rome's main legislative body.
tags: end of the Struggle of the Orders

events.title: Lex Aquilia on wrongful damage
events.summary: A plebiscite carried by the tribune Aquilius, which Byzantine tradition dates to the secession of 287, laid down liability for wrongfully killing another's slave or four-footed herd animal (the highest value it had in the past year), for an accessory creditor's fraud, and for burning, breaking or spoiling (urere, frangere, rumpere) any other property (the value in the next thirty days).

events.title: Thurii appeals to Rome; statue of the tribune Aelius
events.summary: Attacked repeatedly by the Lucanians under Sthenius Statilius, the Greek city of Thurii turned to Rome rather than Tarentum; the tribune C. Aelius carried a measure against the Lucanian leader, and the grateful Thurians honoured him with a statue and a golden crown in Rome.

events.title: Battle of Arretium
events.summary: Senones, joined by Etruscans, besieged Rome's ally Arretium; the relieving army was destroyed and the praetor (or consul) L. Caecilius Metellus Denter killed with 13,000 men. Roman envoys sent to the Senones about prisoners were murdered.

battle.significance: Provokes the Roman destruction of the Senones.

events.title: Expulsion of the Senones; colony at Sena Gallica
events.summary: Rome invaded the ager Gallicus, killed or expelled the Senones, and planted a citizen colony at Sena Gallica on the Adriatic coast, the first Roman colony on Gallic land.
events.locName: Sena Gallica (Senigallia) and the ager Gallicus

events.title: Second battle of Lake Vadimon
events.summary: Alarmed by the fate of the Senones, the Boii joined the Etruscans and marched on Rome; the consul P. Cornelius Dolabella annihilated them at Lake Vadimon, where, Polybius says, most of the Etruscans were cut down and very few Boii escaped.

sides.losses: most Etruscans killed; few Boii escaped

battle.significance: Ends the last Etruscan-Gallic coalition.

events.title: Battle near Populonia
events.summary: The Boii, with Etruscans, raised another army of young men the following year and were defeated again; they then sued for peace, which they kept for 45 years.

sides.strength: consular army of Q. Aemilius Papus

battle.significance: Peace with the Boii for 45 years.

events.title: Fabricius relieves Thurii
events.summary: Thurii, besieged by the Lucanians and Bruttians, appealed to Rome rather than Tarentum; the consul C. Fabricius Luscinus defeated the besiegers, and Rome garrisoned Thurii, Locri, Rhegium and Croton.

battle.significance: Rome intervenes among the Italiote Greeks.

events.title: Tarentum attacks a Roman squadron and insults Rome's envoy
events.summary: Ten Roman ships under the duumvir L. Valerius sailed into the Gulf of Tarentum; the Tarentines, watching in their theatre, attacked, sank four and killed the commander, then expelled the Roman garrison from Thurii. When L. Postumius Megellus came to demand redress, his Greek was mocked and a drunk soiled his toga; he said the stain would be washed out in blood.

events.title: Roman garrisons in Thurii, Locri, Croton and Rhegium
events.summary: After Fabricius relieved Thurii, several Greek cities of the south received Roman garrisons against the Lucanians and Bruttii: Thurii, Locri, Croton and Rhegium, the last held by a legion of 4,000 Campanians under Decius Vibellius.

events.title: Phintias of Acragas moves Gela to a new city
events.summary: Phintias, tyrant of Acragas, destroyed Gela and moved its population to a new city he named after himself at the mouth of the Himeras, modern Licata.

events.title: Tarentum invites Pyrrhus
events.summary: Facing the consul L. Aemilius Barbula's army, Tarentum and its Italian allies invited Pyrrhus of Epirus, offering a combined force of 350,000 foot and 20,000 horse (a boast); Pyrrhus sent Milo ahead with 3,000 men to garrison the citadel.

events.title: Aemilius Barbula ravages the Tarentine territory
events.summary: The consul L. Aemilius Barbula, sent from Samnium against Tarentum, defeated a Tarentine army and ravaged the land while offering peace; when Pyrrhus' advance guard under Milo arrived, he withdrew along the coast, shielding his column from attacks by ships with Tarentine prisoners placed on the seaward side.

battle.significance: Opening campaign of the Pyrrhic war.

events.title: The Campanian legion seizes Rhegium
events.summary: A Roman garrison of 4,000 Campanian citizen-soldiers under Decius Vibellius, sent to protect Rhegium against Pyrrhus, imitated the Mamertines across the strait, massacred or expelled the men and took the city for themselves.

events.title: Battle of Heraclea
events.summary: Pyrrhus defeated the consul P. Valerius Laevinus on the plain between Heraclea and Pandosia by the river Siris; the Roman cavalry and legions held the phalanx through seven charges until Pyrrhus' 20 elephants, never seen before by Romans, panicked the horses.
events.locName: Plain of the Siris near Heraclea (Policoro)

sides.strength: c. 25,000-30,000 including 20 elephants, Macedonian phalanx, Thessalian cavalry, Tarentines

battle.significance: First clash of legion and Hellenistic phalanx; first Roman encounter with war elephants.

events.title: Pyrrhus marches on Rome
events.summary: After Heraclea, Pyrrhus advanced through Campania (failing to take Capua and Neapolis) up the Via Latina to Anagnia or Praeneste, perhaps within 60 km of Rome, but finding Laevinus reinforced and Coruncanius' army back from Etruria, he withdrew to winter in Tarentum.

events.title: Cineas' embassy and the speech of Appius Claudius
events.summary: Pyrrhus sent his Thessalian orator Cineas to Rome with gifts and offers of peace if Rome left the Italiote Greeks free; as the Senate wavered, the old, blind Appius Claudius Caecus had himself carried to the Curia and declared Rome would not negotiate while a foreign army stood in Italy.

events.title: Coruncanius triumphs over Volsinii and Vulci
events.summary: While Pyrrhus invaded the south, the consul Ti. Coruncanius defeated the Etruscan cities of Volsinii and Vulci, triumphing in 280; Vulci lost its coastal territory, where the Latin colony of Cosa was founded in 273.

events.title: Census of 280 and the first plebeian lustrum
events.summary: The censors of 280 counted 287,222 citizens, and Cn. Domitius Calvinus Maximus became the first plebeian censor to perform the lustrum, the purificatory sacrifice that closed the census.

events.title: Fabricius' embassy to Pyrrhus
events.summary: After Heraclea, C. Fabricius went to Pyrrhus to negotiate the return of prisoners; the king offered him gold and, the next day, tried to frighten him with an elephant trumpeting behind a curtain, but Fabricius was unmoved by either, and Pyrrhus let the prisoners go home on parole for the Saturnalia.

events.title: Battle of Ausculum
events.summary: Pyrrhus fought the consuls P. Sulpicius Saverrio and P. Decius Mus over two days in rough ground near Ausculum in Apulia; on the second day he forced a battle on the plain and won, but at such cost that he reportedly said 'one more such victory and we are finished', the origin of 'Pyrrhic victory'.

sides.strength: four legions plus allies, c. 40,000 (consuls P. Sulpicius Saverrio and P. Decius Mus)

battle.significance: The proverbial 'Pyrrhic victory'; Pyrrhus turns to Sicily.

events.title: Fourth treaty between Rome and Carthage (against Pyrrhus)
events.summary: A Carthaginian admiral, Mago, arrived at Ostia with 120 ships to offer help; the resulting treaty, quoted by Polybius, renewed the earlier ones and provided that if either made an alliance with Pyrrhus it should reserve the right to help the other, with Carthage supplying ships for transport and combat but no obligation for crews to fight on land against their will.

events.title: The Gauls invade Greece and attack Delphi
events.summary: A great Celtic migration killed Ptolemy Keraunos of Macedon in 279; one army under a Brennus forced Thermopylae and attacked Delphi, where it was repulsed by the Aetolians and Phocians in snow and earthquakes, and Brennus killed himself; other bands crossed to Asia in 278 to become the Galatians.

events.title: Temple of Summanus
events.summary: When the terracotta Summanus on the roof of the Capitoline temple was struck by lightning and its head was lost, the haruspices found it in the Tiber; a temple of Summanus, god of nocturnal thunder, was dedicated by the Circus Maximus on 20 June, 'when Pyrrhus was feared'.

events.title: Fabricius returns Pyrrhus' would-be poisoner
events.summary: Pyrrhus' physician (named Nicias or Cineas in some sources) offered the consul Fabricius to poison the king; Fabricius sent him back to Pyrrhus with a letter, and Pyrrhus released his Roman prisoners without ransom.

events.title: Pyrrhus crosses to Sicily
events.summary: Invited by Syracuse, Acragas and Leontini against Carthage, which was besieging Syracuse, Pyrrhus left Milo in Tarentum and sailed with c. 8,000 foot and elephants from Locri to Tauromenium and Catana, lifted the siege of Syracuse and was hailed hegemon and king of Sicily.

events.title: The privileged treaty with Heraclea
events.summary: In 278 Heraclea in Lucania broke with Pyrrhus and concluded a treaty with Rome, negotiated by Fabricius, that Cicero called 'almost unique' in its favourable terms; the city valued it so highly that in 89 it hesitated to exchange it for Roman citizenship.

events.title: Pyrrhus storms Eryx
events.summary: Pyrrhus stormed the Carthaginian mountain stronghold of Eryx, being himself first onto the walls in Homeric style, and celebrated games to Heracles as he had vowed; Panormus also fell.

battle.significance: Carthage reduced to Lilybaeum.

events.title: Pyrrhus fails before Lilybaeum
events.summary: Carthage, supplied by sea, offered Pyrrhus money and ships for peace; he demanded they evacuate Sicily entirely, then failed in a two-month siege of the impregnable sea-fortress of Lilybaeum.

battle.significance: Turning point of Pyrrhus' Sicilian venture.

events.title: Roman defeat in the Cranita hills
events.summary: With Pyrrhus in Sicily, the consuls P. Cornelius Rufinus and C. Junius Bubulcus invaded Samnium; the Samnites withdrew to the wooded Cranita hills, and a Roman assault up through the thickets was beaten back with heavy losses, after which the consuls quarrelled and divided their armies.

battle.significance: Showed continued Samnite resilience in the Pyrrhic war.

events.title: Rufinus takes Croton by a ruse
events.summary: P. Cornelius Rufinus sent a false deserter to Croton to report that he was withdrawing; Pyrrhus' general Nicomachus left with his garrison for Locri, and Rufinus seized the city; Locri then massacred its Epirote garrison and returned to Rome.

battle.significance: Deprived Pyrrhus of key Italiote allies.

events.title: Naval battle in the Strait of Messina
events.summary: Recalled by his Italian allies, Pyrrhus sailed back to Italy and was attacked in the strait by a Carthaginian fleet, losing many ships; landing, he was harassed by 10,000 Mamertines, then took Locri and plundered the treasury of Persephone to pay his troops.

sides.losses: many ships sunk or disabled (Plutarch: 70 ruined)

battle.significance: Pyrrhus returns to Italy weakened.

events.title: Pyrrhus plunders the treasure of Persephone at Locri
events.summary: Returning from Sicily short of money, Pyrrhus punished Locri for going over to Rome and took the sacred treasure of Persephone's temple; the ships carrying it were wrecked and the treasure washed ashore, and Pyrrhus restored it in fear of the goddess.

events.title: Plague among women and cattle
events.summary: A pestilence struck pregnant women and livestock, causing stillbirths and the deaths of mothers and calves, so that Orosius says the Romans feared their stock would fail.

events.title: Battle of Beneventum (Maleventum)
events.summary: Pyrrhus attempted a night march to surprise the consul M'. Curius Dentatus near Maleventum, but lost his way in wooded hills and arrived at dawn exhausted; Curius drove back his troops and stampeded elephants into his own lines, and Pyrrhus abandoned Italy.

sides.strength: c. 20,000-25,000 with elephants and Samnite allies

battle.significance: Ends Pyrrhus' Italian venture; Rome becomes master of southern Italy.

events.title: Census of 275 and the expulsion of Rufinus
events.summary: The census of 275 counted 271,224 citizens, down from 287,222 in 280/279; the censor C. Fabricius Luscinus expelled the twice-consul P. Cornelius Rufinus from the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate.

events.title: Hiero elected general at Syracuse
events.summary: After Pyrrhus left Sicily the Syracusan army, camped at Mergane, chose Hiero and Artemidorus as generals; Hiero entered the city, reconciled the factions, married the daughter of the leading citizen Leptines, and rid himself of his unruly mercenaries by sending them against the Mamertines without support.

events.title: Curius' triumph and the first elephants in Rome
events.summary: M'. Curius Dentatus triumphed over the Samnites and Pyrrhus with a procession that showed Rome for the first time gold, purple, Greek statues and paintings, and four captured elephants with their towers.

events.title: Curius sells a draft-dodger
events.summary: When a citizen failed to answer the levy against Pyrrhus, the consul Curius had his property sold, and when he appealed to the tribunes, sold the man himself, saying that the state had no need of a citizen who would not obey.

events.title: Locri's coin of Roma crowned by Faith
events.summary: A silver stater of Locri shows a seated goddess labelled ROMA being crowned by a standing figure labelled PISTIS (Good Faith), with a head of Zeus on the obverse: the earliest known image of personified Roma, struck when Locri returned to the Roman alliance after Pyrrhus.

events.title: Aes signatum: the elephant and sow bar
events.summary: Among the cast bronze bars of about five Roman pounds (c. 1.6 kg) issued by Rome in the 3rd century, one type shows an elephant on one side and a sow on the other, generally linked to the Pyrrhic war; other types show an eagle and Pegasus with the legend ROMANOM.

events.title: Vestals Sextilia and Caparronia condemned
events.summary: During the Pyrrhic war the Vestal Sextilia was convicted of unchastity and buried alive; in 266 the Vestal Caparronia hanged herself before trial, and her lover and the slave who abetted them were executed.

events.title: Ptolemy II establishes friendship with Rome
events.summary: Impressed by Rome's defeat of Pyrrhus, Ptolemy II Philadelphus sent an embassy to Rome and a treaty of friendship (amicitia) was made; Rome returned an embassy of Q. Fabius Gurges, N. Fabius Pictor and Q. Ogulnius, who refused Ptolemy's personal gifts and deposited them in the treasury.

events.title: Latin colonies at Paestum and Cosa; Caere punished
events.summary: Rome founded Latin colonies at Paestum (Greek Poseidonia, long ruled by Lucanians) and at Cosa on the Etruscan coast, on territory taken from Vulci; Caere lost half its territory after an abortive revolt.

events.title: Death of Pyrrhus at Argos
events.summary: After a failed attack on Sparta, Pyrrhus fought his way into Argos at night; in the street fighting an old woman threw a roof tile from a housetop, stunning him, and a soldier of Antigonus Gonatas beheaded him.

events.title: Surrender of Tarentum
events.summary: Besieged by L. Papirius Cursor and with a Carthaginian fleet appearing off the harbour, Pyrrhus' general Milo surrendered the citadel of Tarentum to Rome in exchange for safe passage; Tarentum's walls were demolished, its ships and arms surrendered, and it became a Roman ally.

sides.strength: Epirote garrison under Milo and Tarentines

battle.significance: End of the Pyrrhic War; Rome master of Magna Graecia.

events.title: Final submission of Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttians
events.summary: Campaigns of 273-272 against the peoples who had joined Pyrrhus ended with triumphs over the Samnites, Lucanians and Bruttians; the Bruttians lost half the Sila forest with its timber and pitch, and the Samnite League was broken up into separate treaty states.

events.title: Construction of the Anio Vetus aqueduct
events.summary: The censors M'. Curius Dentatus and L. Papirius Praetextatus let the contract for Rome's second aqueduct, financed from the spoils of Pyrrhus, drawing water from the Anio above Tibur along a winding course of 43 Roman miles (c. 64 km), almost all underground.

events.title: Temple of Consus on the Aventine
events.summary: L. Papirius Cursor, victor at Tarentum in 272, dedicated a temple to Consus on the Aventine and had himself painted in it wearing triumphal dress.

events.title: Recapture of Rhegium and punishment of the Campanian legion
events.summary: Rome, with grain and troops supplied by Hiero of Syracuse, besieged and stormed Rhegium; the 300 surviving mutineers of the Campanian legion were taken to Rome, flogged and beheaded in the Forum in batches of fifty, and the city was restored to the surviving Rhegines.

sides.strength: consular army (Cn. Cornelius Blasio?) with Syracusan supplies
Campanian legion, c. 4,000 at the outset

battle.significance: Rome shows fides to Greek allies; cooperation with Hiero.

events.title: Battle of the Longanus river; Hiero becomes king
events.summary: Hiero, general of Syracuse, decisively defeated the Mamertines on the Longanus river near Mylae, captured their leaders, and was acclaimed king (basileus) by the Syracusans; the Mamertines appealed for help, first to a Carthaginian garrison and then to Rome.

battle.significance: Hiero becomes king; Mamertine appeals lead to the First Punic War.

tags: road to the First Punic War

events.title: First Roman silver coinage at Rome (Pliny's 269)
events.summary: Pliny says the Roman people first struck silver in 269, five years before the First Punic War; numismatists reinterpret this as the didrachm with Hercules / she-wolf and twins and the legend ROMANO, among the Romano-Campanian series, rather than the denarius (introduced c. 211).

events.title: Conquest of Picenum: battle during an earthquake
events.summary: The consuls P. Sempronius Sophus and Ap. Claudius Russus defeated the Picentes near Asculum (Ascoli Piceno); when an earthquake shook the field, Sempronius vowed a temple to Tellus (Earth), and the battle was won.

battle.significance: Annexation of Picenum.

events.title: Latin colonies at Ariminum and Beneventum; Sabines enfranchised
events.summary: Ariminum (Rimini) on the Adriatic, Rome's northern bastion against the Gauls of the Po valley, and Beneventum, renamed from Maleventum, in the heart of Samnium, became Latin colonies; the Sabines received full citizenship.

events.title: Temple of Tellus vowed during the earthquake
events.summary: When the earth shook during the battle against the Picentes, the consul P. Sempronius Sophus vowed a temple to Tellus, Mother Earth; it was built on the Carinae on the site of the house of Sp. Cassius, razed in 485.

events.title: Quaestors increased to eight; Sallentine war
events.summary: The number of quaestors was doubled to eight, the new 'quaestores classici' (or Italici) stationed in Italy, at Ostia, Cales and elsewhere, to manage fleet levies and relations with the allies; the same year Rome campaigned against the Sallentini and Messapians whose chief port, Brundisium, came under Roman control.

events.title: Temple of Pales vowed in the Sallentine war
events.summary: In the war against the Sallentini, which brought Brundisium into Rome's hands, the consul M. Atilius Regulus vowed a temple to Pales, the shepherds' deity whose festival, the Parilia of 21 April, was the birthday of Rome.

events.title: Rome hands over young nobles who struck the envoys of Apollonia
events.summary: Two young Romans of senatorial family, Q. Fabius and Cn. Apronius, insulted and struck envoys from Apollonia in Illyria; the Senate handed them over to the Apolloniates, who released them unharmed.

events.title: Subjugation of the Umbrian Sarsinates
events.summary: The consuls of 266 celebrated triumphs over the Sarsinates of the upper Savio valley (birthplace of Plautus), completing the reduction of Umbria.

events.title: Destruction of Volsinii
events.summary: The aristocrats of Volsinii, overthrown by their freedmen or slaves who had taken power, appealed to Rome; M. Fulvius Flaccus besieged and took the city, razed it, moved the population to a new site by Lake Bolsena, and carried off some 2,000 bronze statues.

sides.strength: consular army of M. Fulvius Flaccus
sides.losses: consul Q. Fabius Gurges died of wounds in 265

sides.strength: city held by former slaves or freedmen

battle.significance: End of Etruscan independence; transfer of the Fanum Voltumnae's prestige to Rome.

events.title: Census of 265: 292,234 citizens; ban on iterating the censorship
events.summary: The lustrum of 265 counted 292,234 citizens; C. Marcius Rutilus, censor for the second time, rebuked the people for re-electing him and carried a law forbidding anyone to hold the censorship twice, earning the cognomen Censorinus.

events.title: The Mamertine appeal and the Roman vote for war
events.summary: The Mamertines, Campanian ex-mercenaries holding Messana and pressed by Hiero II of Syracuse, appealed to both Carthage and Rome. The Senate could not decide; the people, encouraged by the consuls with promises of plunder, voted to accept the Mamertines into alliance, beginning Rome's first war outside Italy.

events.title: Battle of Messana
events.summary: Appius Claudius Caudex ran the Carthaginian blockade of the Straits by night and defeated first Hiero and then the Carthaginian army besieging Messana, breaking their improvised alliance. It was the first Roman army ever to fight outside Italy.

battle.significance: Opened Sicily to Roman armies and broke the Syracusan-Carthaginian coalition; within a year Hiero changed sides.

events.title: First gladiatorial games at Rome
events.summary: Decimus Junius Brutus Pera and his brother staged three pairs of gladiators in the Forum Boarium at the funeral of their father, the first recorded munus in Rome.

events.title: Latin colonies at Firmum and Castrum Novum; Aesernia (263)
events.summary: Rome planted colonies at Firmum and Castrum Novum in Picenum (264) to hold the newly conquered Picentes, and a Latin colony at Aesernia in Samnium (263).
events.note: Castrum Novum's location (Giulianova) is the standard identification; Velleius' dates are the only explicit evidence.

events.title: Temple of Vortumnus on the Aventine
events.summary: Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, consul 264, triumphed over Volsinii on 1 November 264 and built a temple on the Aventine to Vortumnus, the chief god of the Volsinians, whom he had 'called out' (evocatio) before the sack. A painting of Flaccus in triumphal dress decorated the temple.

events.title: Alliance with Hiero II; Messalla's sundial
events.summary: After the consul Manius Valerius Maximus marched on Syracuse with four legions, Hiero II made peace, returned prisoners, paid 100 talents and became Rome's loyal ally for the rest of his long life (to 215). Valerius took the cognomen Messalla from Messana.

events.title: Siege of Agrigentum
events.summary: Both consuls besieged Agrigentum, the main Carthaginian base in Sicily, for about seven months, defeated Hanno's relief army and stormed the town after Hannibal son of Gisco broke out at night. The 25,000 inhabitants were sold into slavery.

sides.losses: heavy losses from disease and fighting; Diodorus gives 30,000 foot and 540 horse (implausible)

sides.strength: garrison c. 50,000 (Diodorus) plus Hanno's 50,000 foot, 6,000 horse, 60 elephants

battle.significance: First great Roman success in Sicily; Polybius treats it as the point at which Rome resolved on the conquest of the whole island and the creation of a navy.

events.title: Rome builds its first battle fleet
events.summary: Rome built 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes, reportedly in sixty days, copying a Carthaginian quinquereme that had run aground. Rowers were trained on benches set up on land.

events.title: Battle of the Lipari Islands
events.summary: The consul Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio sailed into Lipara harbour with 17 ships hoping for a betrayal, was trapped by Boodes with 20 Carthaginian ships, and was captured with his whole squadron. The disaster earned him the nickname Asina ('she-ass').

battle.significance: Humiliating opening for the new Roman navy, quickly reversed at Mylae.

events.title: Battle of Mylae
events.summary: Gaius Duilius defeated a Carthaginian fleet of 130 ships under Hannibal son of Gisco off Mylae, using the corvus boarding bridge to turn sea battle into infantry combat. It was Rome's first naval victory.

sides.losses: c. 50 ships captured or sunk (Polybius); the restored Duilius inscription claims 31 captured and 13 sunk

battle.significance: Proved that Rome could beat Carthage at sea and made Duilius a hero; the corvus dominated the next four years of naval war.

events.title: Duilius' naval triumph and the Columna Rostrata
events.summary: Duilius celebrated the first Roman naval triumph and was honoured with a column decorated with the rams of captured ships in the Forum, and with the lifelong privilege of being escorted home from dinners by a torch-bearer and a flute player.

events.title: Battle of Thermae
events.summary: Hamilcar, the Carthaginian commander in Sicily, caught a force of Roman allies separated from the main army near Thermae and killed 4,000-6,000 of them.

battle.significance: Limited, but checked Roman expansion along the north coast.

events.title: Duilius relieves Segesta and storms Macella
events.summary: After Mylae, Duilius landed in Sicily, raised the Carthaginian siege of Segesta, an Elymian city which had joined Rome claiming Trojan kinship, and took Macella by storm. His inscription on the Columna Rostrata lists both successes before the naval victory.

events.title: Duilius' temple of Janus in the Forum Holitorium
events.summary: From the spoils of Mylae, Gaius Duilius built a temple of Janus near the Theatre of Marcellus in the vegetable market. Tiberius restored it in AD 17. It is usually identified with one of the three Republican temples incorporated in the church of San Nicola in Carcere.

events.title: Lucius Scipio takes Aleria in Corsica
events.summary: The consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio captured Aleria in Corsica and campaigned against Carthaginian bases in Sardinia. His epitaph in the Tomb of the Scipios boasts 'hec cepit Corsica Aleriaque urbe' and records that he dedicated a temple to the Tempestates (Storms) in thanks for surviving a storm.

events.title: Temple of the Tempestates vowed after a storm off Corsica
events.summary: Lucius Cornelius Scipio, consul 259, caught in a storm during his Corsican campaign, vowed a temple to the Weather Goddesses and built it near the Porta Capena. His epitaph in the Tomb of the Scipios records that he took Corsica and Aleria and 'gave a temple to the Tempestates, deservedly'.

events.title: Battle of Sulci
events.summary: The consul Gaius Sulpicius Paterculus defeated the Carthaginian fleet off Sulci in Sardinia. The Carthaginian admiral Hannibal son of Gisco, victor of Lipara and loser at Mylae, was crucified by his own surviving officers.

battle.significance: Ended Hannibal son of Gisco's career and weakened Carthage's hold on Sardinia.

events.title: Calpurnius Flamma's 300 at Camarina
events.summary: When the consul Atilius Calatinus led his army into a defile near Camarina and was trapped, the military tribune Marcus Calpurnius Flamma led 300 volunteers to seize a hill and draw the enemy, allowing the army to escape. Flamma alone survived, found alive under the corpses.

sides.strength: 300 volunteers as rearguard of a consular army

battle.significance: Saved a consular army; became a celebrated exemplum of devotio-like sacrifice.

events.title: Calatinus takes Hippana, Mytistratus, Camarina and Enna
events.summary: The consul Aulus Atilius Calatinus cleared central and southern Sicily: he stormed Hippana, took Mytistratus (which had resisted for seven months in 260) and sold its people, besieged Camarina with siege engines borrowed from Hiero and sold the inhabitants, and captured Enna by treachery.

events.title: Battle of Tyndaris
events.summary: The consul Gaius Atilius Regulus Serranus, rushing ahead with ten ships, was nearly overwhelmed off Tyndaris but the main Roman fleet came up and sank 8 and captured 10 Carthaginian ships.

battle.significance: Indecisive in strategic terms but encouraged Rome to plan an invasion of Africa.

events.title: Battle of Cape Ecnomus
events.summary: Off the south coast of Sicily the consuls Lucius Manlius Vulso and Marcus Atilius Regulus, carrying an army to invade Africa, fought the Carthaginian fleet of Hamilcar and Hanno. Polybius says 330 Roman ships against 350, perhaps the largest naval battle of antiquity by number of men.

sides.strength: 350 ships, c. 150,000 men (Polybius) under Hamilcar and Hanno

battle.significance: Opened the way for the first Roman invasion of Africa.

events.title: Roman landing at Aspis (Clupea)
events.summary: The Roman army landed at Aspis on the Cape Bon peninsula, took the town and ravaged the rich estates of the Carthaginian hinterland, taking more than 20,000 slaves. On Senate orders Manlius sailed home with most of the fleet, leaving Regulus with 15,000 foot and 500 horse.

events.title: Battle of Adys
