events.summary: Regulus defeated a Carthaginian army under Hasdrubal, Bostar and Hamilcar that had unwisely camped on a hill near Adys, where its cavalry and elephants were useless. Regulus then occupied Tunes, within sight of Carthage.

battle.significance: Brought Carthage to the brink of capitulation in 256.

events.title: Regulus' peace terms rejected
events.summary: Regulus, wanting to finish the war before his successor arrived, offered Carthage terms so harsh (evacuation of Sicily and Sardinia, a fleet available to Rome, war indemnity) that the Carthaginians preferred to fight on.

events.title: Regulus' army and the serpent of the Bagradas
events.summary: Roman tradition held that Regulus' army, camped on the Bagradas, had to kill with siege artillery a serpent 120 feet long that was carrying off soldiers who went for water; its skin and jaws were displayed in a temple at Rome until the Numantine War.

events.title: Fleet destroyed in a storm off Camarina
events.summary: Returning from Africa the Roman fleet, against the advice of its pilots, sailed along the exposed south coast of Sicily in the season of the Orion and Dog Star gales and was wrecked off Camarina: Polybius says only 80 of 364 ships survived.

events.title: Battle of Tunes (Bagradas plain)
events.summary: The Spartan mercenary Xanthippus retrained the Carthaginian army and offered battle on open ground with 12,000 foot, 4,000 cavalry and about 100 elephants. Regulus' army was trampled and enveloped; only about 2,000 men escaped to Aspis and Regulus was captured with 500 others.

sides.losses: all but c. 2,000 killed or captured; 500 captured with Regulus

battle.significance: Ended the African invasion; Rome would not return to Africa until Scipio in 204.

events.title: Battle of Cape Hermaeum
events.summary: A Roman fleet of 350 ships under the consuls Servius Fulvius Paetinus Nobilior and Marcus Aemilius Paullus, sent to evacuate the survivors at Aspis, defeated a Carthaginian fleet of 200 off Cape Bon and captured 114 ships with their crews.

battle.significance: A great victory immediately thrown away by the storm off Camarina.

events.title: Capture of Panormus
events.summary: A new Roman fleet of 220 ships, built in three months, carried the consuls Aulus Atilius Calatinus and Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina to Panormus, which they stormed. 14,000 inhabitants ransomed themselves at two minae each; 13,000 were sold.

battle.significance: Gave Rome the chief port of north-western Sicily.

events.title: Second storm disaster off Cape Palinurus
events.summary: Returning from a raid on the African coast, the Roman fleet was caught by a storm off Cape Palinurus in Lucania and lost about 150 ships. The Senate for a time limited the navy to 60 ships to guard the coasts.

events.title: Censors degrade 400 equites
events.summary: The censors Manius Valerius Maximus and Publius Sempronius Sophus deprived 400 equites of their public horses for refusing orders to work on fortifications in Sicily, and reduced them to aerarii.

events.title: Aurelius Cotta takes Thermae and Lipara
events.summary: The consul Gaius Aurelius Cotta captured Thermae Himeraeae and the Carthaginian naval base of Lipara, using ships borrowed from Hiero. When his kinsman Publius Aurelius Pecuniola let the siege works at Lipara be burned in his absence, Cotta had him flogged and reduced to the ranks.

sides.strength: consular army with borrowed Syracusan ships

battle.significance: Removed the last Carthaginian naval base north of Sicily.

events.title: Battle of Panormus
events.summary: Lucius Caecilius Metellus, holding Panormus, provoked Hasdrubal's army to the walls, then had light troops shower the elephants with missiles from the ditch. The maddened beasts turned on their own lines, and a sally completed the rout. Many elephants were captured.

sides.strength: a consular army, perhaps 2 legions and allies
army under Hasdrubal with c. 100-140 elephants

battle.significance: Last major land battle of the war in Sicily; confined Carthage to Lilybaeum and Drepana.

events.title: Metellus' triumph with captured elephants
events.summary: Metellus shipped the captured elephants across the Straits on rafts made of jars and paraded them in his triumph; they were then killed with javelins in the Circus Maximus. The elephant became a hereditary emblem on coins of the Caecilii Metelli.

events.title: Embassy and death of Regulus
events.summary: According to Roman tradition the captive Regulus was sent to Rome on parole to negotiate an exchange of prisoners, advised the Senate to refuse, kept his oath by returning to Carthage, and was tortured to death.

events.title: Siege of Lilybaeum
events.summary: Rome besieged Lilybaeum, the strongest Carthaginian fortress in Sicily, by land and sea from 250 until the end of the war. The garrison under Himilco held out, supplied by blockade runners such as Hannibal 'the Rhodian', whose fast quadrireme ran in and out of the harbour in daylight until it was captured.

sides.strength: both consular armies in 250 (110,000 by Diodorus, impossible) and a fleet of 200

battle.significance: Tied down Roman forces for nine years; the town surrendered only under the peace of 241.

events.title: Alexon the Achaean foils a mercenary plot at Lilybaeum
events.summary: Early in the siege of Lilybaeum, mercenary officers of the garrison agreed to betray the city to the Romans. Alexon, an Achaean who had already saved Agrigentum from a similar betrayal, warned the commander Himilco, who won the troops back with promises of pay before the conspirators could act.

events.title: Greek mercenaries burn the Roman siege works at Lilybaeum
events.summary: When a violent wind sprang up, some Greek mercenaries of the Lilybaeum garrison suggested a night sortie; they fired the Roman towers, rams and penthouses from upwind, and the smoke and flames blinded the defenders. Rome gave up storming the city and settled for a blockade by land, which lasted to the end of the war.

battle.significance: Turned the siege of Lilybaeum from assault to a nine-year blockade.

events.title: Hannibal the Rhodian runs the blockade of Lilybaeum
events.summary: A Carthaginian noble known as the Rhodian repeatedly sailed his fast ship through the shoals into Lilybaeum and out again by daylight, challenging the Roman fleet to catch him. The Romans eventually blocked the channel with a mole, captured a four-banker that ran aground, used it to catch the Rhodian, and later copied his ship for their final fleet.

battle.significance: Supplied the model for the quinqueremes built in 242.

events.title: Battle of Drepana
events.summary: The consul Publius Claudius Pulcher attempted a surprise attack on the Carthaginian fleet in Drepana harbour. Adherbal slipped out, caught the Romans strung out against the shore and destroyed the fleet: 93 Roman ships were taken and only about 30 escaped with Claudius.

battle.significance: Destroyed Roman naval power for the time being; combined with the storm at Phintias it left Rome almost without a fleet until 242.

events.title: Trial of Claudius Pulcher and the dictatorship of Claudius Glicia
events.summary: Recalled after Drepana, Claudius Pulcher mocked the order to appoint a dictator by naming his freedman clerk Marcus Claudius Glicia, who was forced to resign. Prosecuted for perduellio by tribunes, Claudius was fined 120,000 asses. In 246 his sister Claudia, jostled by the crowd at the games, wished her brother were alive to lose another fleet and thin the mob; she was fined by the aediles.

events.title: Battle of Phintias and the storm off Pachynus
events.summary: Carthalo attacked a Roman supply convoy of about 120 warships and 800 transports under the consul Lucius Junius Pullus near Phintias, then manoeuvred so that a southerly gale struck the Romans on the lee shore near Camarina and Pachynus. Almost the entire fleet was wrecked.

sides.strength: c. 120 warships, 800 transports under L. Junius Pullus

battle.significance: Left Rome with almost no fleet for six years.

events.title: Atilius Calatinus, first dictator to command outside Italy
events.summary: After the Glicia fiasco Aulus Atilius Calatinus was named dictator and led an army to Sicily, the first time a dictator commanded outside Italy.

events.title: First Ludi Tarentini (Secular Games)
events.summary: Amid war disasters and portents, the Sibylline Books prescribed nocturnal sacrifices to Dis Pater and Proserpina at the Tarentum in the Campus Martius, to be repeated every hundred years. Varro regarded this as the first celebration of the Ludi Saeculares.

events.title: Junius Pullus seizes Mount Eryx
events.summary: After losing his convoy, the consul Lucius Junius Pullus surprised the summit of Mount Eryx with its famous temple of Aphrodite and the town halfway down, establishing a post that would watch Drepana and later sandwich Hamilcar Barca's force on the mountain.

events.title: Hamilcar Barca at Heircte
events.summary: Hamilcar Barca took command in Sicily and seized Heircte, a fortified height near Panormus with its own anchorage, from which he raided the Italian coast as far as Cumae and harried Roman forces for three years.

events.title: Maritime colonies at Alsium (247) and Fregenae (245)
events.summary: Two small citizen colonies of about 300 families each were planted on the Etruscan coast west of Rome to guard against Carthaginian raids such as those launched by Hamilcar from Sicily.

events.title: Hamilcar Barca raids Locri and Bruttium
events.summary: On taking command in 247, Hamilcar Barca opened with a seaborne raid on the coast of Italy around Locri and Bruttium before seizing Heircte near Panormus. Carthaginian raids continued to reach as far as Cumae in the following years.

events.title: Hanno the Great takes Hecatompylus (Theveste)
events.summary: While Hamilcar fought in Sicily, Carthage's African expansionists under Hanno pushed into the interior and took Hecatompylus, 'the city of a hundred gates', usually identified with Theveste. Diodorus says Hanno took 3,000 hostages and spared the city when its elders came out as suppliants.

events.title: Census of 247: 241,212 citizens
events.summary: The censors of 247 registered 241,212 citizens, against 297,797 at the lustrum of 252. The fall of over 50,000 reflects the slaughter of Ecnomus, Tunes, Drepana and especially the fleet disasters off Camarina and Palinurus, in which the rowers and marines drowned by the tens of thousands.

events.title: Trial of Claudia for insulting the Roman people
events.summary: Claudia, sister of Publius Claudius Pulcher (the loser of Drepana), was jostled by the crowd leaving the games and said she wished her brother were alive to lose another fleet and thin out the mob. The plebeian aediles Gaius Fundanius and Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus fined her 25,000 asses of heavy bronze.

events.title: Latin colony at Brundisium
events.summary: A Latin colony was founded at Brundisium, the best harbour of the Adriatic coast and the future gateway to Greece and the East.

events.title: Hamilcar holds Eryx
events.summary: Hamilcar seized the town of Eryx halfway up the mountain, between a Roman garrison on the summit (holding the temple of Venus Erycina) and a Roman army at its foot. Besieger and besieged at once, he held the position for three years until ordered to make peace.

sides.strength: garrison on summit and army at foot

battle.significance: Hamilcar was undefeated in Sicily, a fact central to Barcid pride and resentment after 241.

events.title: Citizens fund a new fleet
events.summary: With the treasury exhausted, wealthy Romans singly or in groups of two or three each undertook to build and equip a quinquereme, to be repaid only if the war was won. Some 200 ships were built on the model of the Rhodian's captured blockade runner.

events.title: Creation of the second praetorship (praetor peregrinus)
events.summary: A second praetor was created, who came to deal with legal cases involving foreigners (inter peregrinos), leaving the praetor urbanus for citizens. The new office also supplied an additional holder of imperium for war.

events.title: Lutatius Catulus seizes the harbour of Drepana
events.summary: With 200 new quinqueremes, the consul Gaius Lutatius Catulus occupied the harbour of Drepana and the anchorages near Lilybaeum in summer 242, cutting the Carthaginian garrisons and Hamilcar's army on Eryx off by sea. Wounded in the thigh while assaulting Drepana, he spent the winter training his crews.

battle.significance: Forced Carthage to send a relief fleet, leading to the Aegates.

events.title: Battle of the Aegates Islands
events.summary: Gaius Lutatius Catulus and the praetor Quintus Valerius Falto, with 200 newly built quinqueremes, intercepted a hastily manned Carthaginian relief fleet under Hanno west of Sicily as it tried to reach Hamilcar at Eryx. The heavily laden Punic ships were routed: 50 sunk and 70 captured with nearly 10,000 men. Carthage sued for peace.

battle.significance: Decided the First Punic War.

events.title: Triumphs of Lutatius Catulus and Valerius Falto
events.summary: The Fasti record naval triumphs over the Carthaginians for the consul Gaius Lutatius Catulus on 4 October 241 and for the praetor Quintus Valerius Falto on 6 October. Falto had claimed the victory because the consul was lying wounded; the dispute was decided in Catulus' favour by a formal wager (sponsio) judged by Atilius Calatinus.

events.title: Treaty of Lutatius
events.summary: Carthage agreed to evacuate Sicily, not to make war on Hiero or his allies, return all Roman prisoners without ransom and pay 2,200 Euboic talents over twenty years. The Roman assembly rejected Lutatius' draft; a commission of ten raised the indemnity to 3,200 talents, 1,000 at once and the rest in ten years, and added the islands between Sicily and Italy.

events.title: Revolt and destruction of Falerii
events.summary: The Falisci rebelled immediately after the war and were crushed in six days by both consuls. Half their territory was confiscated and the hill town (Falerii Veteres, Civita Castellana) was abandoned for a new, less defensible site in the plain, Falerii Novi, whose walls still stand.

battle.significance: Last revolt of an Etruscan-area community for a century; the relocation of Falerii is archaeologically visible.

events.note: The Falisci are not separately listed as a polity; they appear here under rome as rebel allies.

events.title: Creation of the last two tribes: Velina and Quirina
events.summary: The censors created the tribus Velina and Quirina for citizens settled in Picenum and the Sabine country, bringing the number of tribes to 35. No further tribes were ever created; later citizens were enrolled in existing ones.

events.title: Reform of the comitia centuriata
events.summary: Between the First and Second Punic Wars the centuriate assembly was reorganised to align its centuries with the 35 tribes: each tribe supplied two centuries (seniores, iuniores) of each of five property classes. The first class lost its outright majority, and the right of the prerogative century passed to a century chosen by lot.

events.title: Outbreak of the Mercenary (Truceless) War
events.summary: About 20,000 mercenaries evacuated from Sicily mutinied at Sicca over arrears of pay. Led by Spendius, a runaway Campanian slave, and Mathos, a Libyan, they seized the Carthaginian envoy Gisco and raised the Libyan countryside, beginning a savage three-year war that nearly destroyed Carthage.

events.title: Lutatius Catulus builds a temple of Juturna
events.summary: Gaius Lutatius Catulus, victor of the Aegates, dedicated a temple to the nymph Juturna in the Campus Martius. It is often identified with Temple A of the Largo Argentina, though some scholars prefer to give that temple to Feronia or to Lutatius Catulus' later kinsman.

events.title: Latin colony at Spoletium
events.summary: Rome founded a Latin colony at Spoletium in Umbria, on the route that the Via Flaminia would later follow. In 217, after Trasimene, it repulsed Hannibal's assault; the Porta Fuga was later said to commemorate his flight.

events.title: Hanno the Great fails to relieve Utica
events.summary: Hanno, commanding Carthage's army against the rebel mercenaries besieging Utica, routed them with his elephants and seized their camp, but then let his men disperse; the rebels rallied and retook the camp. Carthage replaced him with Hamilcar Barca.

battle.significance: Discredited Hanno and brought Hamilcar back to command.

events.title: Battle of the Bagradas
events.summary: Hamilcar Barca, with 10,000 men and 70 elephants, slipped out of the blockaded isthmus of Carthage by crossing the Bagradas mouth when wind piled sand across it, then drew the rebels under Spendius into an attack by feigning retreat, wheeled about and killed some 6,000.
events.locName: Mouth of the Bagradas near Utica

battle.significance: First major Carthaginian success of the Mercenary War.

events.title: First Latin play at the Ludi Romani
events.summary: At the Ludi Romani of 240, the year after the victory over Carthage, Livius Andronicus, a Greek from Tarentum, staged the first Latin play adapted from a Greek original. Cicero and Gellius, following Atticus and Varro, date the start of Roman literature to this production.

events.title: Torture of Gesco and the Carthaginian prisoners
events.summary: To make reconciliation with Carthage impossible after Hamilcar's offers of clemency drew men away, Spendius, Autaritus and Mathos had Gesco and about 700 Carthaginian prisoners mutilated, their limbs broken, and thrown alive into a ditch. Polybius calls the war that followed 'truceless' (aspondos).

events.title: Rome refuses Utica and helps Carthage against the rebels
events.summary: Despite a quarrel over 500 Italian traders arrested for supplying the rebels, Rome kept faith with the treaty of 241: it returned the remaining Carthaginian prisoners of war without ransom, banned trade with the rebels while allowing it with Carthage, let Hiero supply Carthage, and refused offers of surrender from Utica and from the mercenaries in Sardinia.

events.title: Battle of the Saw
events.summary: Hamilcar Barca trapped a rebel army of some 40,000 under Spendius in a saw-shaped range of hills, the Prion, starved it into cannibalism and annihilated it after seizing its leaders at a parley.

sides.strength: c. 10,000 plus Numidian allies under Naravas

battle.significance: Broke the rebellion; restored Hamilcar's political dominance at Carthage.

events.title: Rome seizes Sardinia
events.summary: When mercenaries in Sardinia revolted and invited Rome in, Rome accepted. Carthage prepared to reconquer the island; Rome declared war, and exhausted Carthage surrendered Sardinia and paid an additional 1,200 talents (238/237).

events.title: Institution of the Floralia; Clivus Publicius
events.summary: The plebeian aediles Lucius and Marcus Publicius Malleolus used fines from graziers who had encroached on public land to found a temple of Flora near the Circus Maximus and to build the Clivus Publicius up the Aventine. The Ludi Florales became annual in 173.

events.title: Final defeat and execution of Mathos
events.summary: Reconciled by their senate, Hamilcar and Hanno jointly brought Mathos' remaining army to a pitched battle in the east of Carthaginian Africa and destroyed it. Mathos was led through Carthage in a triumph of torture; Utica and Hippo Acra surrendered soon after, ending the war after three years and four months.

battle.significance: Ended the Mercenary War; Carthage free to turn to Spain.

events.title: First Roman campaigns against the Ligurians
events.summary: From 238 consuls campaigned against the Ligurians of the northern Apennines, partly to protect Pisae and the coastal route to Spain. Publius Cornelius Lentulus Caudinus triumphed over them in 236 and Quintus Fabius Maximus, in his first consulship, in 233, vowing a temple to Honos.

events.title: Hamilcar Barca goes to Spain; Hannibal's oath
events.summary: Hamilcar sailed to Gades and began building a Carthaginian dominion in southern Spain, rich in silver mines and manpower. Before leaving he made his nine-year-old son Hannibal swear on an altar never to be a friend of the Romans.

events.title: Boii and Transalpine Gauls march on Ariminum
events.summary: A new generation of Boii, Polybius says, invited Gauls from beyond the Alps and advanced on Ariminum. A Roman army marched out, but the Boian rank and file, distrusting the newcomers, killed their own kings Atis and Galatus and fought the Transalpines, so the invasion collapsed without a battle with Rome.

events.title: Temple of Janus closed
events.summary: The consul Titus Manlius Torquatus closed the doors of the temple of Janus, signifying that Rome was at peace, for the first time since King Numa. The peace lasted only months.

events.title: Naevius stages his first play
events.summary: Gnaeus Naevius, a Campanian veteran of the First Punic War, produced his first drama in 235. He wrote comedies and tragedies on Greek models, invented the fabula praetexta on Roman subjects (Clastidium, on Marcellus' victory of 222), and in old age composed the Bellum Punicum, the first Latin epic on Roman history.

events.title: Wars in Sardinia and Corsica
events.summary: Rome spent five years subduing the interior of its new islands. Titus Manlius Torquatus triumphed over the Sardinians in 235 and closed the temple of Janus; Spurius Carvilius triumphed in 234; Manius Pomponius Matho in 233 hunted Sardinian fugitives in the mountains with dogs brought from Italy; Papirius Maso fought in Corsica in 231.

events.title: Census of 234: 270,713 citizens
events.summary: The census of 234 recorded 270,713 citizens, a recovery from 241,212 in 247 and 260,000 in 241 as the generation lost at sea was replaced and the new tribes Velina and Quirina were filled.

events.title: Fabius Maximus' temple of Honos
events.summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus dedicated a temple to Honos (the deified idea of military honour) outside the Porta Capena from his Ligurian spoils. Marcellus later sought to add Virtus to the same building, provoking the pontifical ruling that one cella could not serve two deities.

events.title: Lex Flaminia de agro Gallico viritim dividundo
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Flaminius, against strong senatorial opposition, carried a plebiscite distributing the ager Gallicus (land taken from the Senones in 283) in individual allotments to Roman citizens rather than founding colonies.

events.title: First triumph on the Alban Mount
events.summary: Refused a triumph by the Senate for his Corsican campaign, the consul Gaius Papirius Maso held one on his own authority on the Alban Mount, wearing a myrtle crown instead of laurel. The precedent was followed by Marcellus in 211 and others.

events.title: Murder of a Roman envoy by the Illyrians
events.summary: Responding to Italian traders' complaints of Illyrian piracy, Rome sent Gaius and Lucius Coruncanius to Queen Teuta, regent of the Ardiaean kingdom. Polybius says Teuta replied that it was not the custom of Illyrian kings to stop their subjects plundering at sea; one envoy spoke insolently and was murdered on the way home.

events.title: Spurius Carvilius Ruga and the first divorce
events.summary: Roman antiquarians dated the first divorce at Rome to around 230: Spurius Carvilius Ruga dismissed his much-loved wife because she bore him no children, after the censors had required citizens to swear that they married to beget children. The case prompted the first legal arrangements for the return of dowries (cautiones rei uxoriae).

events.title: Death of Hamilcar Barca
events.summary: Hamilcar drowned while retreating across a river during the siege of Helice, according to Diodorus by the treachery of the Oretani king. His son-in-law Hasdrubal the Fair succeeded to the command.

events.title: Battle of Paxos
events.summary: An Illyrian fleet with Acarnanian allies defeated the combined fleet of the Achaean and Aetolian Leagues off the island of Paxos. The Illyrians lashed their lembi together in fours to snare the enemy ships, then boarded. Corcyra surrendered to Demetrius of Pharos.

sides.losses: 4 quadriremes and a quinquereme lost; Margos of Caryneia killed

battle.significance: Showed the Greek leagues could not check Illyrian sea power; Rome intervened weeks later.

events.title: First Roman army crosses the Adriatic
events.summary: The consul Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus with 200 ships and Aulus Postumius Albinus with 20,000 foot and 2,000 horse crossed to Illyria. Demetrius of Pharos betrayed Corcyra to them; Apollonia, Epidamnus and the Parthini and Atintani surrendered into Roman fides, and the siege of Issa was raised.

events.title: Peace with Teuta and Roman embassies to Greece
events.summary: Teuta agreed to pay tribute, give up most of Illyria to Demetrius and others, and not sail south of Lissus with more than two lembi, and those unarmed. Rome sent envoys to the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues to explain its actions; Corinth admitted Romans to the Isthmian Games.

events.title: Gauls and Greeks buried alive in the Forum Boarium
events.summary: On the instruction of the Sibylline Books, a Gallic man and woman and a Greek man and woman were buried alive in the Forum Boarium to avert a prophecy that Gauls and Greeks would occupy Rome. The rite was repeated after Cannae (216) and in 114/113.

events.title: Two new praetors for Sicily and Sardinia-Corsica
events.summary: The number of praetors was raised from two to four so that annual magistrates could govern Sicily and Sardinia-Corsica. Gaius Flaminius was the first praetor in Sicily and Marcus Valerius in Sardinia. This is usually taken as the formal beginning of the Roman province system.

events.title: Hasdrubal founds New Carthage
events.summary: Hasdrubal the Fair founded Qart Hadasht ('New City', Carthago Nova) on a superb defensible harbour in south-east Spain, near silver mines that employed 40,000 workers in Polybius' day. He married an Iberian princess and was acclaimed as general by the Spanish peoples.

events.title: The Ebro Treaty
events.summary: Worried by the Gallic threat, Rome sent envoys to Hasdrubal, who undertook not to cross the Iber (Ebro) under arms. Nothing was said of the rest of Spain.

events.title: Earthquake at Rhodes; fall of the Colossus
events.summary: A great earthquake threw down the Colossus of Rhodes, the walls and the dockyards. Polybius lists the gifts that poured in from Hiero and Gelon of Syracuse, Ptolemy III, Antigonus Doson, Seleucus III and others, and comments that the Rhodians turned disaster into profit by their skill in appeals.

events.title: Battle of Faesulae
events.summary: A huge Gallic army of Boii, Insubres and Gaesatae from beyond the Alps (Polybius: 50,000 foot, 20,000 horse and chariots) invaded Etruria, plundering towards Rome. Near Faesulae, pretending to retreat at night, it ambushed a Roman praetorian army and killed 6,000.

sides.strength: praetor's army of Etruscans and Sabines

battle.significance: Deepest Gallic penetration since 390; heightened Roman panic.

events.title: Rome's manpower register of 225
events.summary: In alarm at the Gallic invasion, Rome and its allies drew up lists of men capable of bearing arms. Polybius, probably from Fabius Pictor who served in the war, gives a total of over 700,000 foot and 70,000 horse.

events.title: Battle of Telamon
events.summary: Retreating along the Etruscan coast, the Gallic army was caught between the consul Gaius Atilius Regulus, who had just landed at Pisa from Sardinia, and Lucius Aemilius Papus following behind. Fighting back to back, the Gauls were annihilated: 40,000 killed and 10,000 captured, including the king Concolitanus. Aneroestes fled and killed himself.

sides.strength: two consular armies, c. 40,000 under C. Atilius Regulus and L. Aemilius Papus
c. 50,000-70,000 Boii, Insubres, Taurisci and Gaesatae

battle.significance: Ended the last great Gallic invasion of peninsular Italy and opened the conquest of the Po valley.

events.title: The quadrigatus silver and the oath-scene gold
events.summary: In the years before and during the early Second Punic War Rome struck a silver didrachm showing a Janus head and Jupiter in a four-horse chariot (the quadrigatus), with the legend ROMA, alongside rare gold staters and half-staters showing two warriors swearing an oath over a pig. The quadrigatus was steadily debased and abandoned when the denarius was introduced.

events.title: Boii submit
events.summary: The consuls Quintus Fulvius Flaccus and Titus Manlius Torquatus invaded Boian territory, the first Roman army to campaign north of the Apennines in strength, and forced the Boii to submit.

events.title: Flaminius defeats the Insubres
events.summary: The consuls Gaius Flaminius and Publius Furius Philus crossed the Po and defeated the Insubres. The military tribunes ordered the front ranks to use their thrusting spears to absorb the first Gallic sword blows before closing with swords. Flaminius, who had ignored a Senate letter recalling him over bad omens, triumphed by popular vote.

sides.strength: two consular armies with Cenomani allies

battle.significance: First major Roman victory north of the Po.

events.title: Battle of Clastidium
events.summary: While his colleague Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio besieged Acerrae, the consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus led cavalry to relieve Clastidium, besieged by Insubres and Gaesatae. He killed the Gallic king Viridomarus in single combat and dedicated his armour to Jupiter Feretrius, the third and last spolia opima of the Republic.

battle.significance: Broke the Insubrian resistance; made Marcellus a heroic figure.

events.title: Capture of Mediolanum and submission of the Insubres
events.summary: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus captured Acerrae and then Mediolanum, the chief town of the Insubres, who surrendered. Within four years Rome planted colonies at Placentia and Cremona to hold the line of the Po.

battle.significance: Completed the first conquest of the Insubres, undone by Hannibal's arrival in 218.

events.title: Battle of Sellasia
events.summary: Antigonus III Doson, leading Macedonians, Achaeans and the Hellenic Symmachy (about 28,000 foot and 1,200 horse), defeated Cleomenes III of Sparta (about 20,000) on the hills of Euas and Olympus north of Sparta. The young Philopoemen distinguished himself by charging without orders. Sparta was occupied for the first time in its history.

battle.significance: Restored Macedonian hegemony in the Peloponnese, which Philip V inherited.

events.title: First Istrian War
events.summary: The consuls Marcus Minucius Rufus and Publius Cornelius Scipio Asina subdued the Istrians, accused of piracy against Roman grain ships.

events.title: Assassination of Hasdrubal; Hannibal takes command
events.summary: Hasdrubal the Fair was killed at night in his house by a Celt with a private grievance (Livy: a slave avenging his master). The army acclaimed the 25-year-old Hannibal as general, confirmed by the assembly at Carthage.

events.title: Hannibal's first campaigns: the Olcades
events.summary: In his first season of command Hannibal attacked the Olcades in central Spain, stormed their chief town (Polybius' Althaea, Livy's Cartala) and wintered at New Carthage with his army well paid. In 220 he struck at the Vaccaei, taking Helmantica and Arbucala, and won at the Tagus on the way back.

events.title: Censorship of Flaminius: Via Flaminia and Circus Flaminius
events.summary: As censor, Gaius Flaminius built the Via Flaminia from Rome across the Apennines to Ariminum and the Circus Flaminius in the Campus Martius, where the Ludi Plebeii were held. He also restricted freedmen to the four urban tribes.
events.locName: Circus Flaminius, Rome / Via Flaminia to Ariminum

events.title: Battle of the Tagus
events.summary: Returning from a raid deep into the territory of the Vaccaei (taking Helmantica and Arbucala), Hannibal was attacked at the Tagus by the Carpetani with Olcades and Vaccaei. He let them begin to cross the river and slaughtered them in the water with cavalry and elephants.

battle.significance: Secured Hannibal's base in central Iberia before the war with Rome.

events.title: Defeat of the satrap Molon
events.summary: Antiochus III, king since 223, marched against Molon, satrap of Media, who had defeated two royal armies and taken Seleucia on the Tigris. In the battle near Apollonia Molon's left wing defected to the king at the first contact; Molon killed himself. Antiochus then purged his minister Hermeias.

battle.significance: Secured the eastern satrapies for the young Antiochus III.

events.title: War of Rhodes and Byzantium over the Bosporus tolls
events.summary: Byzantium, paying tribute to the Gauls of Tylis, imposed a toll on ships passing the Bosporus. Rhodes, speaking for the Aegean trading cities, went to war in alliance with Prusias I of Bithynia; within a year Byzantium gave way and abolished the dues.

events.title: Ludi Plebeii first attested
events.summary: The Plebeian Games, held in November and organised by the plebeian aediles, are first securely attested in the 210s; a late tradition connects them with Gaius Flaminius and his circus of 220. Livy records them being repeated (instauratio) for ritual faults in 216 and 213.

events.title: Siege of Saguntum
events.summary: Hannibal besieged Saguntum, an Iberian town south of the Ebro in friendship with Rome, and took it by storm after eight months. Rome, which had sent envoys but no help, treated the attack as the casus belli of the Second Punic War.

battle.significance: Precipitated war with Rome; supplied Hannibal's war chest.

events.title: Second Illyrian War: Dimale and Pharos
events.summary: Demetrius of Pharos had sailed beyond Lissus with 50 lembi and raided the Aegean. The consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Marcus Livius Salinator took his fortress of Dimale in seven days, then captured Pharos by landing a decoy force in the harbour while the main army hid in a wooded hollow. Demetrius fled to Philip V.

battle.significance: Ended Demetrius' bid for Adriatic power; pushed him into Philip V's camp, a link in the chain to the First Macedonian War.

events.title: Archagathus, the first Greek doctor at Rome
events.summary: According to Cassius Hemina, the Peloponnesian doctor Archagathus came to Rome in 219, was granted citizenship and a surgery bought at public expense at the Compitum Acilium. His enthusiasm for cutting and cautery soon earned him the name 'carnifex' (butcher).

events.title: Roman embassy to Carthage and declaration of war
events.summary: A Roman embassy headed by Quintus Fabius demanded the surrender of Hannibal. When the Carthaginian senate defended Hannibal, Fabius held up a fold of his toga and said it held peace or war; told to give whichever he chose, he let it fall and declared war.

events.title: Colonies of Placentia and Cremona; the Boian revolt
events.summary: Rome founded two Latin colonies of 6,000 settlers each at Placentia and Cremona on the Po. Hearing of Hannibal's approach the Boii and Insubres rose, drove the colonists to Mutina, seized the three land commissioners at a parley, and twice ambushed the praetor Lucius Manlius Vulso, whose army took refuge at Tannetum.

events.title: Crossing of the Rhône
events.summary: Hannibal forced the crossing of the Rhône against the Volcae, sending Hanno son of Bomilcar upstream to cross at night and attack the defenders from behind. Thirty-seven elephants were ferried on earth-covered rafts. Publius Scipio, landing at Massalia, arrived three days too late.

battle.significance: Opened the route to the Alps; Scipio's decision to send his army to Spain anyway shaped the whole war.

events.title: Hannibal crosses the Alps
events.summary: In about fifteen days in October-November 218 Hannibal took his army over the Alps, fighting off ambushes by Alpine tribes, losing men and animals on icy paths, and cutting a new track where a landslide had destroyed the road. He descended into the territory of the Taurini with 20,000 foot and 6,000 horse, according to his own inscription at Cape Lacinium.
events.locName: Alpine pass (Col du Clapier, Mont Cenis, Traversette or Little St Bernard)

events.title: Battle of Cissa
events.summary: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio, landing at Emporiae with the Roman army sent from the Rhône, defeated the Carthaginian commander north of the Ebro, Hanno, near Cissa, capturing him and the Ilergetan chief Indibilis.

battle.significance: Gave Rome a foothold north of the Ebro.

events.title: Battle of the Ticinus
events.summary: In the first clash in Italy, Hannibal's Numidian and Spanish cavalry routed Publius Cornelius Scipio's cavalry and light troops near the Ticinus. Scipio was badly wounded and, by the most famous account, rescued by his 17-year-old son, the future Africanus.

battle.significance: Exposed Roman cavalry inferiority; brought Gallic support to Hannibal.

events.title: Battle of the Trebia
events.summary: On a snowy morning around the winter solstice, Hannibal's Numidians lured the consul Tiberius Sempronius Longus across the icy, swollen Trebia before breakfast. Hannibal's cavalry and elephants routed the Roman wings while his brother Mago burst from an ambush in a watercourse onto the Roman rear. Only 10,000 Romans cut their way through the centre to Placentia.

sides.losses: perhaps 20,000-30,000 killed or captured; 10,000 broke out

battle.significance: First great Roman defeat of the war; brought the whole Po valley over to Hannibal.

events.title: Lex Claudia de nave senatorum
events.summary: The tribune Quintus Claudius carried a plebiscite forbidding senators and their sons to own seagoing ships of more than 300 amphorae capacity, enough to ship produce from their estates but not to engage in large-scale trade. Livy says only Gaius Flaminius among senators supported it, which won him popularity and senatorial hatred.

events.title: Clastidium and its granary betrayed to Hannibal
events.summary: Short of supplies after the Ticinus, Hannibal obtained Clastidium, a Roman supply base south of the Po, when its commander Dasius of Brundisium handed it over for 400 gold pieces. Hannibal treated the garrison well to advertise his mildness towards Rome's allies.

events.title: Hannibal storms Victumulae
events.summary: In the winter after the Trebia, Hannibal was wounded in an attack on a Roman trading post near Placentia, then stormed Victumulae, a fortified market town that had armed the local population against him, and sacked it.

events.title: Prodigies and expiations of winter 218/217
events.summary: After the Trebia, Livy lists a cascade of portents: a six-month-old child shouted 'Io triumphe' in the vegetable market, an ox climbed to the third storey of a house, phantom ships shone in the sky, the temple of Hope was struck by lightning. The Senate ordered a lustration of the city, a lectisternium for Juventas and a supplication at the temple of Hercules.

events.title: Condemnation of Livius Salinator
events.summary: Marcus Livius Salinator, consul 219 and victor in the Second Illyrian War, was convicted by the people of unfair division of the booty. All the tribes except the Maecia voted against him; he withdrew to his estates for years before returning to win the Metaurus in 207 and, as censor in 204, to punish the 34 tribes.

events.title: Battle of Lake Trasimene
events.summary: Hannibal concealed his army in the hills above the narrow north shore of Lake Trasimene and, on a misty morning, ambushed the column of the consul Gaius Flaminius as it marched into the defile. About 15,000 Romans died, many driven into the lake; Flaminius was killed by an Insubrian horseman. It was the largest ambush in Roman history.

sides.losses: c. 15,000 killed, 15,000 captured (Polybius); Livy (from Fabius Pictor) 15,000 killed, 10,000 scattered

battle.significance: Opened central Italy to Hannibal and led to the dictatorship of Fabius.

events.title: Battle of Raphia
events.summary: Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III near Raphia on the Egyptian-Syrian border in one of the largest battles of the Hellenistic age, ending the Fourth Syrian War and saving Coele-Syria for Egypt. Antiochus' Indian elephants beat Ptolemy's smaller African ones, but Ptolemy's phalanx, with 20,000 newly trained Egyptians, won the centre.

battle.significance: Preserved Ptolemaic Coele-Syria for 17 years, but arming native Egyptians destabilised the dynasty; Antiochus turned east to his anabasis.

events.title: Peace of Naupactus and the 'cloud in the west'
events.summary: Philip V ended the Social War against the Aetolians at Naupactus. Polybius has the Aetolian Agelaus warn the Greeks that whoever won the war in Italy would turn east, a 'cloud rising in the west'; Polybius makes this moment, when the affairs of Italy, Africa and Greece became intertwined (symploke), the true start of his universal history.

events.title: Fabius Maximus dictator: the strategy of delay
events.summary: After Trasimene the people elected Quintus Fabius Maximus dictator, the first dictator since 249 to take the field. He refused battle and shadowed Hannibal through the hills, harassing foragers. The strategy was deeply unpopular and earned him the nickname Cunctator ('Delayer'), later a title of honour.

events.title: Religious response to Trasimene
events.summary: On Fabius' advice the Sibylline Books were consulted: Rome vowed a ver sacrum (all animals born in one spring), Ludi Magni, and temples to Venus Erycina and Mens, and held a Greek-style lectisternium with the twelve great gods on six couches.

events.title: Escape from the Ager Falernus
events.summary: Hannibal ravaged the rich Falernian plain of Campania to provoke Fabius, who then blocked the passes out. At night Hannibal tied torches to the horns of 2,000 oxen and drove them up a ridge; the Roman guard on the pass rushed to the lights and the army slipped through.

battle.significance: Humiliated Fabius and strengthened the critics of delay.

events.title: Lex Metilia and the battle of Gerunium
events.summary: After a small success near Gerunium, the master of horse Marcus Minucius Rufus was given imperium equal to the dictator Fabius by a plebiscite of the tribune Metilius, an unprecedented step. Minucius then took half the army, was lured into an ambush and was saved only by Fabius' intervention, after which he placed himself again under Fabius' command.

sides.strength: half the Roman army, rescued by the other half
unknown, with 500 horse and 5,000 foot in ambush

battle.significance: Seemed to vindicate Fabius; confirmed Hannibal's mastery of ambush.

events.title: Naval battle at the mouth of the Ebro
events.summary: Gnaeus Scipio, with 35 Roman and Massaliot ships, surprised the Carthaginian fleet of 40 ships under Himilco at the mouth of the Ebro and captured 25, giving Rome command of the Spanish coast.

battle.significance: Gave Rome control of the sea off Spain; Publius Scipio soon joined his brother with reinforcements.

events.title: The Spanish hostages at Saguntum
events.summary: Publius Scipio joined his brother in Spain with 20 ships and 8,000 men; the brothers crossed the Ebro and camped near Saguntum, where Hannibal had left the hostages of the Iberian peoples. A Spanish noble, Abilyx, persuaded the Carthaginian commander Bostar to release them to him, then handed them to the Scipios, who sent them home and won over many tribes.

events.title: Destruction of Centenius' cavalry near Lake Plestina
events.summary: Days after Trasimene, 4,000 cavalry sent ahead by the consul Servilius Geminus under the propraetor Gaius Centenius were intercepted by Maharbal in the Umbrian uplands; half were killed and the rest surrendered the next day.

battle.significance: Stripped the remaining consular army of its cavalry and deepened the panic after Trasimene.

events.title: Servilius Geminus' naval raid on Africa
events.summary: With 120 ships, the consul Servilius Geminus sailed round Sardinia and Corsica to Africa, extracted 10 talents from the island of Cercina, ravaged Meninx (Djerba), and lost about 1,000 men to an ambush on the African mainland before returning via Lilybaeum.

events.title: Lex Flaminia minus solvendi
events.summary: Festus records a lex Flaminia 'minus solvendi' of 217 by which debts expressed in the old heavy bronze could be settled with lighter coin, a measure tied to the reduction of the as during the war (Pliny puts the uncial as in Fabius' dictatorship of 217).

events.title: Temple of Concordia on the Arx
events.summary: The praetor Lucius Manlius had vowed a temple to Concord during a mutiny of his troops in Gaul in 218; it was dedicated on the Arx on 5 February 216 by duumviri appointed for the purpose.

events.title: Battle of Cannae
events.summary: On the plain by the Aufidus, Hannibal's thin crescent of Gauls and Spaniards drew the massed Roman infantry forward while his African veterans on either side turned inwards and his cavalry, having routed the Roman horse, struck the Roman rear. The largest army Rome had ever fielded was surrounded and destroyed. The consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus, the previous year's consul Servilius Geminus, Minucius Rufus and some 80 senators were among the dead.

sides.strength: c. 80,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry (Polybius); modern estimates 50,000-86,000

battle.significance: The archetypal battle of annihilation. It triggered the defection of Capua, much of the south and (soon) Syracuse and Macedon, yet Rome refused to negotiate and won the war of attrition.

events.title: Rome after Cannae
events.summary: Rome responded to Cannae with mobilisation and expiation: Quintus Fabius Pictor was sent to consult Delphi; two Vestals, Opimia and Floronia, convicted of unchastity, died (one buried alive); a Gallic and a Greek couple were again buried alive in the Forum Boarium; 8,000 slaves bought by the state were armed as volones; the Senate refused to ransom the prisoners held by Hannibal.

events.title: Two dictators at once: Fabius Buteo refills the Senate
events.summary: With Cannae having killed so many senators and no censors in office, Marcus Fabius Buteo, the senior ex-censor, was named a second dictator, sole purpose to revise the Senate, while Junius Pera held the military dictatorship. Buteo enrolled 177 new senators by strict seniority of office and valour, then resigned the same day.

events.title: Defection of Capua
events.summary: Capua, the second city of Italy, went over to Hannibal on the promise that it would remain self-governing and become the leading city of Italy. Arpi, Salapia, most of the Samnites, the Lucanians and the Bruttians also defected in 216-215.

events.title: First battle of Nola
events.summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus, holding Nola, sallied from three gates and repulsed Hannibal's assault, the first check Hannibal suffered after Cannae. Livy says 2,800 Carthaginians fell for fewer than 500 Romans.

battle.significance: Morale-restoring success; made Marcellus 'the sword of Rome' beside Fabius 'the shield' (Posidonius in Plutarch).

events.title: Ambush in the Litana forest
events.summary: The consul-designate Lucius Postumius Albinus, marching through the Litana forest in Boian territory, was ambushed when the Boii, having sawn through the trees along the road, toppled them onto his column. His army of 25,000 was destroyed; his gilded skull became a libation cup in a Boian temple.

sides.strength: 2 legions and allies, 25,000 (Livy) under L. Postumius Albinus

battle.significance: Ended Roman operations in Cisalpine Gaul for years.

events.title: Siege of Casilinum
events.summary: A garrison of about 500 Praenestines and 460 Perusians held the Volturnus crossing at Casilinum against Hannibal through the winter of 216/215, eating leather and roots. Livy and Pliny say a mouse sold for 200 denarii. Starved out, the survivors were allowed to ransom themselves.

battle.significance: Tied Hannibal down for months; became an exemplum of allied loyalty.

events.title: Lex Minucia: the three public bankers
events.summary: Amid the post-Cannae financial crisis, the tribune Marcus Minucius carried a law creating three public bankers (triumviri mensarii), who managed state payments and loans; the board was enlarged to five in 214. Livy calls it a measure forced by 'scarcity of money'.

events.title: The Senate refuses to ransom the Cannae prisoners
events.summary: Hannibal sent ten of the 8,000 Romans captured at Cannae to Rome with Carthalo to negotiate a ransom of three minae a head (Polybius; Livy gives 300 quadrigati for a foot soldier). After a debate in which Titus Manlius Torquatus spoke against, the Senate refused; Hannibal sold most of the prisoners into slavery.

events.title: The legions of Cannae banished to Sicily
events.summary: The survivors of Cannae, organised into two legions, were sent to garrison Sicily and forbidden to return to Italy or be discharged until the war was over. Twice denied pardon by the Senate, they fought under Marcellus at Syracuse and finally redeemed themselves with Scipio in Africa.

events.title: Siege of Petelia
events.summary: The small Bruttian town of Petelia refused to join Hannibal after Cannae and held out for eleven months against Himilco and the Bruttians, eating leather, bark and grass, after Rome told its envoys it could not help. It finally surrendered in 215; Rome later rewarded the survivors.

battle.significance: A celebrated example of loyalty among Rome's allies.

events.title: Lex Oppia
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Oppius carried a sumptuary law forbidding any woman to possess more than half an ounce of gold, to wear multi-coloured clothing or to ride in a carriage in Rome or within a mile of it except for religious festivals.

events.title: Treaty between Hannibal and Philip V
events.summary: Philip V sent Xenophanes of Athens to Hannibal and concluded an alliance. Polybius preserves the oath text, sworn before Zeus, Hera, Apollo, the daimon of Carthage, Heracles, Iolaus and other gods: mutual help, and if Rome made peace it must give up Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus, Pharos, Dimale, the Parthini and Atintania, and restore Demetrius of Pharos' friends.

events.title: Death of Hiero II; Syracuse turns to Carthage
events.summary: Hiero II died at over ninety after 54 years of rule, his loyalty to Rome unshaken. His fifteen-year-old grandson Hieronymus switched to Carthage, was assassinated in 214 at Leontini, and in the turmoil the pro-Carthaginian Hippocrates and Epicydes, Syracusans born in Carthage, seized power.

events.title: Battle of Dertosa (Ibera)
events.summary: The Scipio brothers defeated Hasdrubal Barca near Ibera on the Ebro as he prepared to march to Italy. Hasdrubal used Hannibal's Cannae formation, but his weak Spanish centre broke first and the battle was a rout.

battle.significance: Stopped Hasdrubal's first attempt to join Hannibal.

events.title: Hampsicora's revolt in Sardinia
events.summary: Sardinian chieftains under Hampsicora rose with Carthaginian help. Titus Manlius Torquatus defeated them and a Carthaginian force under Hasdrubal the Bald near Cornus; Hampsicora's son Hiostus was killed and Hampsicora took his own life.

sides.strength: c. 22,000 foot, 1,200 horse under T. Manlius Torquatus
Sardinians and a Carthaginian expeditionary force

battle.significance: Kept Sardinia, a grain source, in Roman hands.

events.title: Temples of Mens and Venus Erycina on the Capitol
events.summary: Vowed after Trasimene on the advice of the Sibylline Books, temples to Mens (Right Thinking) and to Venus of Eryx were dedicated on the Capitol in 215, Mens by Titus Otacilius Crassus and Venus Erycina by Quintus Fabius Maximus. The Sicilian goddess of the mountain held by Rome in the First Punic War became a Roman state cult.

events.title: Massacre at Hamae and the defence of Cumae
events.summary: The Campanians planned to seize Cumae during a joint nocturnal festival at Hamae. Warned, the consul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus fell on their camp at midnight and killed some 2,000, including their commander Marius Alfius. Hannibal then besieged Gracchus in Cumae but was beaten off.

battle.significance: Kept Cumae and its harbour for Rome.

events.title: Second battle of Nola
events.summary: Marcellus again repulsed Hannibal outside Nola. Livy reports 5,000 Carthaginians killed against fewer than 1,000 Romans, figures most scholars doubt; the substance is that Hannibal failed to win Nola, which remained a Roman base for the rest of the war.

battle.significance: Kept Nola Roman.

events.title: Bruttians take Croton; Locri defects
events.summary: The Bruttians, now Hannibal's allies, besieged Croton, a shadow of its old size with fewer than 20,000 citizens; Hanno negotiated its surrender and the Greek citizens moved to Locri, which had itself gone over to Carthage. Rhegium alone of the Greek cities of the toe stayed Roman.

events.title: Relief of Iliturgi and Intibili
events.summary: After Ibera, Livy says the Scipios relieved Iliturgi, besieged by three Carthaginian armies, killing 16,000, and then won again at Intibili. The figures and perhaps the battles derive from the inflated annalist Valerius Antias.

events.title: Battle of Beneventum and the freeing of the volones
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, commanding legions largely of slave volunteers (volones), defeated Hanno near Beneventum after promising freedom to any who brought back an enemy head. He freed them all on the field; the feast that followed was painted on the walls of the temple of Libertas on the Aventine.

battle.significance: Showed that slave soldiers could fight; Livy's moralising set-piece on Roman freedom.

events.title: Philip V's failure at Apollonia
events.summary: Philip V sailed into the Adriatic with 120 lembi, took Oricum and besieged Apollonia. The praetor Marcus Valerius Laevinus retook Oricum and sent Quintus Naevius Crista into Apollonia, who surprised Philip's camp at night. Philip burned his ships at the mouth of the Aous and retreated overland, half-naked.

sides.strength: 2,000 men under Q. Naevius Crista plus fleet

battle.significance: Ended Philip's hopes of crossing to Italy.

events.title: Third battle of Nola
events.summary: For the third time Hannibal tried to take Nola and was checked by Marcellus in an indecisive engagement; Claudius Nero's cavalry, sent round to take Hannibal in the rear, failed to arrive in time.

battle.significance: Third failure before Nola.

events.title: Fabius and Marcellus recapture Casilinum
events.summary: Casilinum, which Hannibal had taken in 215 after a heroic defence, was retaken by Fabius Maximus and Marcellus; the 2,000 Campanian and 700 Carthaginian defenders were allowed to leave under truce, but Marcellus' troops cut down many as they came out.

events.title: Assassination of Hieronymus and the Syracusan revolution
events.summary: Hieronymus, king of Syracuse at fifteen, was murdered at Leontini by conspirators. In Syracuse the people restored a republic, then massacred the royal family, including Hiero's daughters Damarata and Heraclia and Heraclia's young daughters. Hippocrates and Epicydes won the generalship and broke with Rome.

events.title: Marcellus storms Leontini
events.summary: Marcellus took Leontini, held by Hippocrates, at the first assault and beheaded some 2,000 Roman deserters found there. Hippocrates and Epicydes spread the story at Syracuse that the Romans had massacred the townspeople, which swung Syracuse decisively against Rome.

events.title: Massacre at Henna
events.summary: Fearing that the people of Henna would betray the town to Carthage, the Roman commander Lucius Pinarius summoned an assembly in the theatre and had his soldiers kill the unarmed citizens. Marcellus condoned the act, and the sacrilege at the sanctuary town of Ceres turned more Sicilians against Rome.

events.title: Censors punish the defeatists of Cannae
events.summary: The censors Marcus Atilius Regulus and Publius Furius Philus degraded Lucius Caecilius Metellus, who after Cannae had talked of abandoning Italy, together with prisoners who had broken their oath to return, and about 2,000 young men who had dodged service, sending the latter to Sicily to serve with the Cannae legions.

events.title: Siege of Sardis and the death of Achaeus
events.summary: Antiochus III besieged his rebel cousin Achaeus in Sardis; the lower city fell in 215/4 when a Cretan, Lagoras, saw vultures perched on an unguarded cliff and led an escalade there. Achaeus held the citadel until the Cretan Bolis, pretending to rescue him for Sosibius, betrayed him in 213. He was mutilated and crucified.

battle.significance: Restored Seleucid control of Asia Minor, freeing Antiochus for his eastern anabasis.

events.title: Battles of Munda and Auringis
events.summary: Livy records victories of the Scipios over Hasdrubal Barca and Mago near Munda and Auringis in southern Spain, with Gnaeus Scipio wounded in the thigh. The scale and even the location of these battles are suspect, but the Scipios were active in the south by this date.

events.title: Siege of Syracuse
events.summary: Marcellus and Appius Claudius Pulcher besieged Syracuse by land and sea. Archimedes' engines, catapults graded for range, cranes that lifted ships by the bow and dropped them, and the 'claw', repelled every assault. Marcellus settled for a blockade and in 212, during a festival of Artemis, scaled a weakly guarded stretch of the Epipolae walls. The island citadel of Ortygia fell later that year; Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier in the sack.

sides.strength: city militia, mercenaries and Carthaginian reinforcements under Himilco

battle.significance: Removed the last independent Greek power in Sicily and made the whole island Roman; began the flood of Greek art into Rome.

events.title: Recapture of Arpi
events.summary: The consul Quintus Fabius Maximus, son of the Cunctator, entered Arpi at night in a rainstorm that drowned the noise of his men scaling the walls. The townsmen, after negotiating, turned on the 5,000-strong Carthaginian garrison; the Spaniards among it changed sides, and the rest were allowed to go to Hannibal.

battle.significance: First major Roman recovery of a defected Apulian city.

events.title: The Scipios ally with Syphax
events.summary: The Scipio brothers sent three centurions to Syphax, king of the Masaesylii, who was at war with Carthage; one, Quintus Statorius, stayed to train Syphax's footsoldiers in Roman fashion. Carthage replied by allying with Gala of the Massylii, whose son Masinissa defeated Syphax.

events.title: Himilco lands in Sicily and takes Agrigentum
events.summary: Carthage sent Himilco with 25,000 foot, 3,000 horse and 12 elephants, who landed at Heraclea Minoa and recaptured Agrigentum. Many Sicilian towns, including Murgantia with its Roman grain store, went over to Carthage, and Rome's grip on the island briefly depended on the siege lines at Syracuse.

events.title: Battle of Acrillae
events.summary: Marching back to Syracuse after failing to save Agrigentum, Marcellus surprised Hippocrates' 10,000 foot and 500 horse building a camp near Acrillae and routed them, killing or capturing about 8,000.

battle.significance: Prevented a junction of the Syracusan field army with Himilco.

events.title: Philip V captures Lissus
events.summary: Having burned his fleet at the mouth of the Aous after Laevinus' night attack in 214, Philip V marched overland and in a skilful operation took the citadel of Acrolissus and then Lissus, giving Macedon an outlet on the Adriatic north of the Roman protectorate.

battle.significance: Gave Philip a base on the Adriatic and alarmed Rome.

events.title: Death of Aratus of Sicyon
events.summary: Aratus, seventeen times general of the Achaean League, died in 213, believing himself poisoned by Philip V, whom he had criticised over the outrage at Messene and the seduction of his daughter-in-law. Sicyon buried him as a hero inside the city.

events.title: Institution of the Ludi Apollinares
events.summary: Following the prophecies of the seer Marcius (carmina Marciana), which were said to have predicted Cannae, the Senate instituted games for Apollo to drive the enemy from Italy. They became annual in 208, held in July.

events.title: Tarentum betrayed to Hannibal
events.summary: Young Tarentine nobles, angered by the execution of Tarentine hostages who had tried to escape from Rome, let Hannibal into the city at night. The Roman garrison under Marcus Livius held the citadel for the next three years, and with it the harbour mouth.

battle.significance: Hannibal's greatest gain in the south, but he never took the citadel.

events.title: Fraud of the war contractors
events.summary: Contractors supplying the armies in Spain under a state guarantee against loss at sea sank old hulks loaded with worthless goods and claimed compensation. When tribunes prosecuted the ringleader Marcus Postumius of Pyrgi, the publicani rioted in the assembly; he and others went into exile.

events.title: Battle of the Silarus
events.summary: Marcus Centenius Paenula, an ex-centurion who boasted he could beat Hannibal and was given 8,000 men, gathered as many volunteers and attacked Hannibal in Lucania. Fewer than 1,000 escaped.

battle.significance: Minor, but illustrates Roman overconfidence and the Senate's willingness to try anyone.

events.title: First battle of Herdonia
events.summary: Hannibal surprised the praetor Gnaeus Fulvius Flaccus near Herdonia in Apulia; of 18,000 Romans barely 2,000 escaped. Fulvius, accused of fleeing first, was later prosecuted and went into exile.

sides.strength: c. 18,000 under praetor Cn. Fulvius Flaccus

battle.significance: Another Roman disaster; Hannibal's last great field victory in open battle against a large army.

events.title: Anabasis of Antiochus III
events.summary: Antiochus III led a seven-year expedition to the eastern satrapies, forcing Armenia, Parthia under Arsaces II and the Graeco-Bactrian king Euthydemus (after a two-year siege of Bactra) to acknowledge his supremacy, and renewing friendship with the Indian king Sophagasenus. He returned in 205/204 with 150 elephants and the title Megas, 'the Great'.

events.title: Plague destroys the Carthaginian army at Syracuse
events.summary: In late summer and autumn 212 an epidemic, favoured by the marshes around the Anapus, struck both armies outside Syracuse. The Romans, quartered in the city and on higher ground, suffered less; the Carthaginian and Sicilian forces of Himilco and Hippocrates were destroyed and both commanders died.

events.title: Death of Archimedes
events.summary: When Achradina fell in 212, Archimedes, aged about 75, was killed by a Roman soldier despite Marcellus' order to spare him. Plutarch gives three versions: he was absorbed in a geometrical diagram and refused to come; he asked for time to finish a proof; he was carrying instruments a soldier took for gold. Marcellus honoured his relatives.

events.title: Fulvius Flaccus storms Hanno's camp near Beneventum
events.summary: Hanno had gathered grain near Beneventum to revictual Capua, but the Campanians came to collect it with too few wagons. The consul Quintus Fulvius Flaccus stormed the camp; Livy claims 6,000 killed and 7,000 captured with all the grain.

battle.significance: Doomed Capua to starvation before the siege began.

events.title: Death of Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus in Lucania
events.summary: The proconsul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, victor of Beneventum, was lured into an ambush by Flavus, a Lucanian leader who had turned to Hannibal, and killed fighting. Hannibal gave his body an honourable funeral; his slave-volunteer legions dispersed.

events.title: Metapontum, Thurii and Heraclea join Hannibal
events.summary: After the fall of Tarentum, Metapontum, whose garrison had been withdrawn to the Tarentine citadel, joined Hannibal, followed by Thurii (angry at Rome's execution of its hostages) and Heraclea. Hannibal now held almost the whole Greek coast of the Gulf of Tarentum.

events.title: Scipios recapture Saguntum
events.summary: The Scipio brothers retook Saguntum, eight years after Hannibal's sack, expelled the Carthaginian garrison, restored surviving Saguntines and punished the Turdetani who had provoked the original war. Livy places it in 214, but most historians date it to 212.

events.title: Siege and fall of Capua
events.summary: Three Roman armies surrounded Capua with a double line of works. Hannibal failed to break the siege and marched on Rome to draw the besiegers off; they stayed. Capua surrendered in 211. Twenty-seven senators led by Vibius Virrius poisoned themselves at a last banquet; the proconsul Quintus Fulvius Flaccus executed 53 others. Capua lost its civic institutions and its land became ager publicus.

sides.strength: Campanian forces and a Carthaginian garrison

battle.significance: Decisive turning point in Italy; Hannibal's inability to protect his allies became plain.

events.title: Hannibal at the gates
events.summary: Hannibal marched on Rome and camped by the Anio three miles from the city; he rode with cavalry up to the Colline Gate. Two consular armies plus the troops from Capua faced him and he withdrew. Livy says the land on which he was camped was sold at auction in Rome at full price during his stay.

events.title: Battle of the Upper Baetis: death of the Scipios
events.summary: The Scipio brothers divided their forces to attack three Carthaginian armies. Publius was overwhelmed near Castulo by Mago and Hasdrubal son of Gisco, joined by Numidian cavalry under the young Masinissa; 29 days later Gnaeus, deserted by his 20,000 Celtiberian mercenaries, was killed near Ilorci. Rome lost all of Spain south of the Ebro.

sides.losses: both commanders and most of both armies

battle.significance: Collapse of Roman Spain; led to the appointment of the younger Scipio in 210.

events.title: Introduction of the denarius
events.summary: At the height of the war crisis Rome reformed its coinage, introducing the silver denarius (originally about 4.5 g, tariffed at 10 asses), with the quinarius and sestertius, a gold coinage and the victoriatus. The denarius became the standard silver coin of Rome for 450 years.

events.title: Roman-Aetolian alliance
events.summary: Marcus Valerius Laevinus allied Rome with the Aetolian League against Philip V. The terms divided the spoils: captured cities and land would go to the Aetolians, movable property and captives to the Romans. Neither party could make a separate peace.

events.title: Marcellus' ovation and the Syracusan spoils
events.summary: Denied a full triumph because his army remained in Sicily, Marcellus triumphed on the Alban Mount and celebrated an ovation in Rome, displaying paintings, statues and the riches of Syracuse. Livy says this began the Roman craze for Greek art and the despoiling of sacred and profane buildings alike.

events.title: Trial and exile of Gnaeus Fulvius Flaccus
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Sempronius Blaesus prosecuted the praetor of 212 for losing his army at Herdonia through negligence and running away. When the charge was turned into a capital one before the comitia centuriata, Fulvius went into exile at Tarquinii, which the people confirmed.

events.title: Hasdrubal escapes at the Black Stones
events.summary: Gaius Claudius Nero, sent to Spain with 12,000 men after the deaths of the Scipios, trapped Hasdrubal Barca in a pass at the Black Stones. Hasdrubal opened negotiations to evacuate Spain, spun them out over several days and slipped his army away under cover of mist.
events.locName: Lapides Atri, between Iliturgi and Mentissa

events.title: Lucius Marcius rallies the remnants in Spain
events.summary: After the deaths of the Scipios, the Roman survivors north of the Ebro elected a young equestrian officer, Lucius Marcius Septimus, as their commander. He beat off Hasdrubal son of Gisco and, Livy says, stormed two Carthaginian camps. His self-styled title 'propraetor' in a dispatch to the Senate offended the fathers.

events.title: Arson in the Forum
events.summary: On the eve of the Quinquatrus in March 210 fires broke out at several points around the Forum, destroying the Lautumiae, the fish market, the Atrium Regium and the old shops; the temple of Vesta was saved with difficulty. A slave named Manus denounced the Calavii, young Campanian nobles avenging their city, and was freed with 20,000 asses.

events.title: Scipio given the Spanish command as a privatus
events.summary: When no experienced commander would take the Spanish command, the people elected the 25-year-old Publius Cornelius Scipio, who had held only the aedileship, as proconsul with imperium. It was the first grant of consular imperium to a man who had never been consul or praetor.

events.title: Second battle of Herdonia
events.summary: Hannibal destroyed the army of the proconsul Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus near Herdonia; Fulvius and eleven military tribunes were killed. Hannibal then burned Herdonia and moved its people to Metapontum and Thurii, a sign that he could no longer defend his Apulian allies.

sides.strength: c. 2 legions under Cn. Fulvius Centumalus

battle.significance: Tactical victory but strategic retreat: Hannibal was abandoning the cities he could not hold.

events.title: The sack of Aegina
events.summary: The Roman fleet under Publius Sulpicius Galba, with Aetolian allies, captured Aegina and enslaved its people. Under the treaty of 211 the island went to the Aetolians, who sold it to Attalus I of Pergamon for 30 talents.

battle.significance: Brought Pergamon an Aegean base and cemented its alliance with Rome.

events.title: Laevinus and the Aetolians take Anticyra
events.summary: Under the Roman-Aetolian treaty, Marcus Valerius Laevinus took Anticyra in Phocis and handed the town to the Aetolians while the Romans kept the movable property and the people, the first application of the treaty's grim division of spoils.

events.title: Battle of Numistro
events.summary: Marcellus, consul for the fourth time, followed Hannibal into Lucania after the second Herdonia and fought him near Numistro from the third hour until nightfall without result. Hannibal withdrew towards Apulia at night and Marcellus followed.

battle.significance: Showed Rome could again face Hannibal in the open after the Herdonia disasters.

events.title: Naval battle of Sapriportis
events.summary: A Roman squadron of 20 ships under Decimus Quinctius, bringing supplies to the besieged citadel of Tarentum, was met 15 miles from the city by an equal Tarentine fleet under Democrates. Quinctius was killed when his flagship was boarded and the Romans lost most of their ships.

battle.significance: Tightened the blockade of the Roman garrison in the citadel of Tarentum.

events.title: Salapia betrayed to Marcellus
events.summary: Blattius, a leading man of Salapia, negotiated with Marcellus to hand over the town despite his rival Dasius, the leader of the Carthaginian party. The 500 Numidian cavalry of the garrison, Hannibal's best, died fighting almost to a man, a loss Livy calls greater than the town.

events.title: Fall of Agrigentum and the end of the war in Sicily
events.summary: The consul Marcus Valerius Laevinus secured Agrigentum when Muttines, the Libyphoenician cavalry commander slighted by the Carthaginian general Hanno, opened a gate to the Romans. The leading citizens were beheaded and the rest sold. Some forty towns then surrendered, twenty were betrayed and six stormed, and Laevinus set Sicily to growing grain for Rome.

sides.losses: city taken; leaders escaped by sea

battle.significance: Ended Carthaginian resistance in Sicily; the island became Rome's granary for the rest of the war.

events.title: The Syracusans accuse Marcellus before the Senate
events.summary: Syracusan envoys complained to the Senate about the sack of their city. Marcellus answered them in person and withdrew; the Senate upheld his acts but promised to look after Syracuse. The Syracusans then threw themselves at his feet and took him as their patron, a role his descendants held into Cicero's day.

events.title: Senators give their gold and silver to the state
events.summary: With the treasury empty and the people refusing a new levy of rowers, the consul Laevinus proposed that senators lead by handing over their gold, silver and bronze, keeping only rings, a bulla for each son, a salt cellar and a dish for the gods. Equestrians and plebeians followed, and the contributions were entered in public accounts for repayment.

events.title: Roman embassy to Ptolemy IV
events.summary: With Italian agriculture ruined and grain prices extreme, Rome sent an embassy to Alexandria to renew friendship with Ptolemy IV and Arsinoe, bringing a toga, purple tunic and ivory chair for the king and an embroidered robe for the queen, and appealed for grain.

events.title: Philip V besieges Echinus
events.summary: Philip besieged the Aetolian-held town of Echinus on the Malian Gulf with siege towers and mines. Publius Sulpicius Galba with the Roman fleet and the Aetolian general Dorimachus tried to relieve it but were beaten off, and the town surrendered.

sides.strength: garrison, with Roman and Aetolian relief

battle.significance: Showed the limits of the Roman-Aetolian alliance against Philip on land.

events.title: Twelve Latin colonies refuse troops
events.summary: Twelve of the thirty Latin colonies (Ardea, Nepete, Sutrium, Alba, Carseoli, Sora, Suessa, Circeii, Setia, Cales, Narnia and Interamna) told the consuls they had neither men nor money left. The other eighteen, led by Fregellae, declared their loyalty and the Senate thanked them publicly.

events.title: The sacred reserve of gold opened
events.summary: The state opened the sanctius aerarium, the reserve built from the 5 percent tax on manumissions (vicesima libertatis) since 357, and drew out about 4,000 pounds of gold to pay for the war.

events.title: Capture of New Carthage
events.summary: Scipio marched from the Ebro to New Carthage in a week and stormed the Punic capital of Spain in a single day. While the walls were assaulted from the isthmus, a picked force waded across the lagoon at ebb, which Scipio had told his men Neptune had promised him, and climbed the undefended north wall.

sides.strength: c. 1,000 soldiers under Mago plus 2,000 armed citizens

battle.significance: Gave Scipio the enemy's base, treasury and hostages, and won over many Iberian peoples.

events.title: Fabius recaptures Tarentum
events.summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus, consul for the fifth time, recovered Tarentum through the treachery of the Bruttian garrison commander, who was in love with the sister of one of Fabius' soldiers. 30,000 Tarentines were enslaved and 3,000 talents of gold and silver taken; but Fabius left the statues of the gods, saying 'let us leave the Tarentines their angry gods'.

sides.strength: consular army and the citadel garrison

battle.significance: Hannibal arrived too late; his grip on the south was weakening.

events.title: Battle of Canusium
events.summary: Marcellus caught up with Hannibal near Canusium. On the first day the Romans were worsted; Marcellus berated his men, and on the second day, with the disgraced cohorts in front, they drove Hannibal back with elephants turned by javelins and fire. Livy claims 8,000 Carthaginians and 3,000 Romans killed; Marcellus' army was so mauled it spent the summer in Venusia.

sides.losses: c. 2,700 on day one, c. 3,000 on day two (Livy)

battle.significance: Pinned Hannibal while Fabius recovered Tarentum.

events.title: Gaius Valerius Flaccus forced to become flamen Dialis
events.summary: The pontifex maximus Publius Licinius Crassus compelled the dissolute young Gaius Valerius Flaccus to be inaugurated as priest of Jupiter. The office reformed him, and he then claimed the old right of the flamen Dialis to a seat in the Senate, which had lapsed; the tribunes upheld his claim.

events.title: Philip V defeats the Aetolians near Lamia
events.summary: Philip V twice defeated the Aetolians under Pyrrhias, supported by 1,000 Romans and Pergamene troops sent by Attalus, near Lamia, driving them into the town with heavy losses. Peace talks mediated by Ptolemy IV, Rhodes, Chios and Athens followed but failed.

battle.significance: Kept the Aetolians on the defensive.

events.title: Battle of Baecula
events.summary: Scipio attacked Hasdrubal Barca on a two-level plateau near Baecula, pinning him with light troops in front while he and Laelius led the heavy infantry up both flanks. Hasdrubal, judging the position lost, withdrew with his elephants, treasury and most of his army and marched for Italy.
events.locName: Baecula (Cerro de las Albahacas, Santo Tomé, Jaén?)

battle.significance: Tactical success but failed to prevent Hasdrubal's march to Italy, which ended at the Metaurus.

events.title: Death of Marcellus
events.summary: The consuls Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Titus Quinctius Crispinus rode out with 220 horsemen to reconnoitre a hill between their camps near Venusia and were ambushed by Numidians. Marcellus, aged about sixty and consul for the fifth time, was killed; Crispinus died of his wounds.

sides.losses: Marcellus killed, Crispinus mortally wounded, c. 40 killed

battle.significance: Both consuls lost in one year, a unique Roman calamity.

events.title: Galba and Attalus take Oreus; Philip surprises Attalus at Opus
events.summary: The Roman fleet under Galba and Attalus I took Oreus in Euboea through the treachery of its commander. When Attalus then sacked Opus in Locris, Philip arrived by forced marches and nearly caught him; Attalus escaped to his ships and soon went home to face Prusias of Bithynia.

events.title: Livius Andronicus' hymn to Juno and the guild of poets
events.summary: After prodigies, the pontiffs ordered 27 maidens to process through the city singing a hymn to Juno Regina composed by Livius Andronicus. In his honour the state recognised a college of writers and actors (scribae et histriones) meeting at the temple of Minerva on the Aventine.

events.title: Battle of Grumentum
events.summary: The consul Gaius Claudius Nero fought an inconclusive but bloody action against Hannibal near Grumentum in Lucania, keeping him in the south as Hasdrubal descended into Italy.

battle.significance: Pinned Hannibal in the south.

events.title: Battle of the Metaurus
events.summary: Capturing Hasdrubal's dispatch to Hannibal, the consul Gaius Claudius Nero secretly marched 7,000 picked men from Apulia to join his colleague Marcus Livius Salinator at Sena Gallica, about 400 km in six or seven days. Hasdrubal, realising from the double trumpet call that two consuls faced him, tried to withdraw, was caught at the Metaurus and killed with most of his army.
events.locName: River Metaurus (near Fossombrone or San Silvestro?)

sides.strength: c. 30,000 incl. Gauls, Ligurians and 10 elephants
sides.losses: c. 10,000 killed (Polybius); 56,000 killed and 5,400 captured (Livy, absurd)

battle.significance: Decisive: Hannibal withdrew into Bruttium and never again threatened central Italy.

events.title: Triumph of Livius Salinator; Nero rides behind
events.summary: For the Metaurus, Marcus Livius Salinator triumphed in a chariot because the battle had been fought in his province, while his colleague Claudius Nero, whose march had won it, followed on horseback without his soldiers. Livy says the crowd's applause went to Nero.

events.title: Battle of Mantinea
