events.summary: Philopoemen, general of the Achaean League, whose army he had re-equipped in Macedonian style, defeated the Spartan tyrant Machanidas outside Mantinea, killing him with his own hand at a ditch; some 4,000 Spartans fell. Polybius, Philopoemen's admirer, describes the battle in detail.

sides.strength: Spartan army and mercenaries under Machanidas

battle.significance: Made the Achaean League an independent military power; Machanidas was succeeded by Nabis.

events.title: Silanus defeats Hanno and Mago in Celtiberia
events.summary: Scipio's lieutenant Marcus Junius Silanus surprised the new Carthaginian general Hanno and Mago Barca while they were recruiting in Celtiberia. The 9,000 Celtiberian recruits were scattered; Hanno was captured, while Mago escaped with the cavalry to Gades.

battle.significance: Prevented Carthage from rebuilding its Spanish army with Celtiberian levies.

events.title: Lucius Scipio takes Orongis
events.summary: Scipio's brother Lucius stormed Orongis, a rich town in the mining district of the Maesesses, where Hasdrubal son of Gisco had based himself. Only about 90 Romans fell; Scipio praised the capture as equal to New Carthage.

events.title: Battle of Ilipa
events.summary: After days of drawn-up armies facing each other with the same dispositions, Scipio suddenly reversed his line one dawn, placing his Roman legions on the wings and his unreliable Spanish allies in the centre, and attacked before the enemy had eaten. His wings executed a complex wheeling manoeuvre and crushed the Carthaginian flanks while the Libyan centre stood idle. Carthaginian power in Spain collapsed.

battle.significance: Ended Carthaginian rule in Spain; Gades surrendered later that year.

events.title: Mutiny at Sucro and the Ilergetan revolt
events.summary: While Scipio lay ill, 8,000 Roman soldiers at Sucro, unpaid and idle, mutinied and drove out their tribunes. Scipio paid them, summoned them to New Carthage, and executed the 35 ringleaders while the rest stood surrounded by loyal troops. Indibilis and Mandonius of the Ilergetes, who had rebelled on news of his illness, were crushed; Indibilis was killed in a renewed revolt in 205.

events.title: Founding of Italica
events.summary: After Ilipa, Scipio settled wounded veterans at a town he named Italica near the Baetis, the first Roman settlement in Spain and, centuries later, the home town of the families of Trajan and Hadrian.

events.title: Surrender of Gades; Mago to the Balearics
events.summary: Mago Barca, ordered to take his fleet to Italy, failed in a raid on New Carthage, found Gades closed to him, and sailed for the Balearics, where he wintered at the harbour on Minorca that still bears his name (Portus Magonis, Mahón). Gades surrendered to Rome on terms that made it a federate ally (foedus Gaditanum).

events.title: Aetolians make a separate peace with Philip
events.summary: Abandoned by Rome, which sent no forces after 208, and having seen Philip sack their federal sanctuary at Thermum a second time (207), the Aetolians made peace with Philip on his terms. Rome regarded this as a breach of the 211 treaty, a grievance it remembered.

events.title: Destruction of Iliturgi
events.summary: Iliturgi had betrayed Roman refugees after the defeat of the Scipios in 211. In 206 Scipio stormed it; the soldiers, Livy says, killed everyone including women and infants, and burned the town. Castulo then surrendered without a fight.

battle.significance: Exemplary punishment for the betrayal of 211.

events.title: Mass suicide at Astapa
events.summary: When Lucius Marcius besieged the pro-Carthaginian town of Astapa, its men piled their women, children and valuables in the forum, set guards to burn them, and sallied to die fighting. The guards fired the pyre and threw themselves in; the Romans found only ashes.

battle.significance: One of the most notorious episodes of the Spanish war.

events.title: Funeral games for the Scipios at New Carthage
events.summary: Scipio held games at New Carthage for his father and uncle. The gladiators were volunteers, not slaves, and included two Spanish cousins, Corbis and Orsua, who settled a dispute over a chieftainship by single combat; Corbis won.

events.title: Scipio and Hasdrubal dine with Syphax
events.summary: Scipio crossed to Africa with two quinqueremes to win Syphax, arriving at Siga at the same moment as Hasdrubal son of Gisco, who had escaped from Spain. Syphax entertained both on the same couch; Hasdrubal, Livy says, judged Scipio more formidable in conversation than in battle.

events.title: Masinissa goes over to Rome
events.summary: After Ilipa, the Massylian prince Masinissa, who had fought for Carthage in Spain since 212, met Silanus and then Scipio secretly and pledged himself to Rome. Losing his father's kingdom to Syphax soon afterwards, he spent 205 as a fugitive in the mountains until Scipio landed in Africa.

events.title: The fire of Vesta goes out
events.summary: The sacred fire in the temple of Vesta went out through the negligence of the Vestal on watch. The pontifex maximus had her scourged and the Senate ordered expiation with full-grown victims and a supplication at the temple.

events.title: Peace of Phoenice
events.summary: Rome and Philip V ended the First Macedonian War at Phoenice in Epirus. Rome kept the Parthini, Dimale, Bargullum and Eugenium; Philip kept Atintania. Each side listed allies (adscripti) included in the peace.

events.title: Mago lands at Genua
events.summary: Mago sailed from Minorca with about 12,000 foot and 2,000 horse, took Genua and tried to raise the Ligurians and Gauls against Rome. Two years of manoeuvres in the north tied down several Roman armies.

events.title: First Cretan War
events.summary: Encouraged by Philip V's agent Dicaearchus, Cretan cities, especially Hierapytna, waged a pirate war on Rhodes and the Cyclades. Rhodes and its allies eventually defeated them, but the war absorbed Rhodian strength just as Philip expanded in the Aegean.

events.title: Hannibal's inscription at the temple of Juno Lacinia
events.summary: Before leaving Italy, Hannibal set up a bronze tablet in Punic and Greek at the temple of Hera (Juno) Lacinia recording his deeds and the strength of his army. Polybius read it and used its figures, for example the 20,000 foot and 6,000 horse with which Hannibal reached Italy.

events.title: Final defeat and death of Indibilis
events.summary: Scipio's departure encouraged Indibilis of the Ilergetes and Mandonius to rise again. The proconsuls Lucius Lentulus and Lucius Manlius Acidinus crushed their army; Indibilis was killed and the Spaniards surrendered Mandonius and other leaders for execution.

battle.significance: Ended the Ilergetan revolts; northern Spain stayed under Roman control.

events.title: The Etruscan and Umbrian contributions to Scipio's fleet
events.summary: Denied a levy by a reluctant Senate, Scipio raised volunteers and accepted gifts from allies: Caere grain, Populonia iron, Tarquinii sailcloth, Volaterrae ship fittings and grain, Arretium 3,000 shields, 3,000 helmets, 50,000 javelins and pikes, Perusia, Clusium and Rusellae fir timber. Thirty ships were built 45 days after the timber was cut.

events.title: Temple of Honos and Virtus dedicated
events.summary: Marcus Marcellus, son of the hero, dedicated the double temple of Honos and Virtus at the Porta Capena, vowed by his father at Clastidium (222). The pontiffs had ruled that one cella could not house two gods, so Virtus received her own shrine; the temple became a museum of Syracusan art.

events.title: The great revolt of the Thebaid
events.summary: In the last years of Ptolemy IV native Egyptian pharaohs, Haronnophris and then Chaonnophris, ruled the Thebaid from Thebes for some twenty years with priestly support. Ptolemaic forces regained the south only in 186, when Chaonnophris was defeated near Syene.

events.title: Arrival of the Magna Mater
events.summary: Following a Sibylline oracle that a foreign enemy would be driven from Italy if the Idaean Mother were brought to Rome, an embassy obtained from Attalus I the black meteoric stone of Cybele from Pessinus (or Pergamon). It was received at Ostia in April 204 by Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica, chosen as the best man in Rome, and carried by matrons to the temple of Victoria on the Palatine.

events.title: Recapture of Locri and the Pleminius scandal
events.summary: Scipio recovered Locri in 205 and left Quintus Pleminius in command. Pleminius and his troops plundered the treasury of Persephone's temple and committed atrocities; when two tribunes flogged him, he had them tortured to death. A Locrian embassy complained to the Senate in 204.

events.title: Lex Cincia de donis et muneribus
events.summary: The tribune Marcus Cincius Alimentus carried a law forbidding advocates to accept fees or gifts for pleading cases and restricting large gifts generally except between close kin. Cato spoke for it in his youth.

events.title: Censorship of Claudius Nero and Livius Salinator
events.summary: The victors of the Metaurus, bitter personal enemies, held the censorship together. Each removed the other's public horse; Livius made aerarii of 34 of the 35 tribes for having first condemned and then elected him. A new tax on salt earned Livius the mocking cognomen Salinator.

events.title: Cato brings Ennius to Rome
events.summary: Marcus Porcius Cato, returning from his quaestorship in Sicily and Africa by way of Sardinia, brought to Rome the Oscan-speaking, Greek-educated poet Quintus Ennius, who had been serving there as a centurion.

events.title: Scipio lands in Africa; siege of Utica
events.summary: Scipio sailed from Lilybaeum with perhaps 25,000-35,000 men, including the disgraced legions of Cannae, and landed near the Fair Promontory west of Carthage. Masinissa joined him with a few hundred horsemen. A Carthaginian cavalry force under Hanno was destroyed, but a 40-day siege of Utica failed and Scipio wintered on a headland, the Castra Cornelia.

events.title: Cavalry battle near Salaeca
events.summary: Soon after landing, Scipio used Masinissa, who feigned retreat with a small force, to draw the Carthaginian cavalry under Hanno son of Hamilcar into an ambush near the tower of Salaeca. Hanno was killed with about 1,000 of his men and some 2,000 were captured.

battle.significance: Gave Scipio freedom to ravage the Carthaginian countryside.

events.title: Battle near Croton
events.summary: The consul Publius Sempronius Tuditanus fought Hannibal near Croton; Livy reports a defeat with 1,200 Roman dead and then a victory the next day with the help of the proconsul Licinius Crassus, killing 4,000. One of the last pitched actions of Hannibal in Italy.

battle.significance: Kept Hannibal confined to Bruttium.

events.title: Burning of the camps
events.summary: While pretending to negotiate peace, Scipio sent spies disguised as slaves into the camps of Syphax and Hasdrubal son of Gisco near Utica. One night Laelius and Masinissa set fire to Syphax's camp of reed huts; as the Carthaginians ran out unarmed to help, Scipio fired their camp too. The two armies were destroyed.

battle.significance: Destroyed the field armies of Carthage and Syphax at one stroke.

events.title: The secret pact of Philip V and Antiochus III
events.summary: After the death of Ptolemy IV left a child king in Egypt, Philip V and Antiochus III allegedly agreed to divide the Ptolemaic overseas possessions between them. Antiochus attacked Coele-Syria; Philip seized Ptolemaic and independent cities in the Aegean and the Straits.

events.title: Battle of the Great Plains
events.summary: Hasdrubal and Syphax raised a new army, stiffened by 4,000 newly arrived Celtiberian mercenaries, on the Great Plains of the Bagradas. Scipio's Roman and Italian cavalry and Masinissa's Numidians routed both wings; the Celtiberians, with no hope of pardon, died fighting where they stood.

battle.significance: Led Carthage to recall Hannibal and Mago.

events.title: Capture of Syphax; Sophonisba
events.summary: Laelius and Masinissa pursued Syphax into his kingdom and defeated him; his horse was wounded and he was captured. Cirta opened its gates. Masinissa married Syphax's wife Sophonisba, daughter of Hasdrubal son of Gisco, but when Scipio demanded her surrender as a captive, Masinissa sent her poison, which she drank.

battle.significance: Removed Carthage's chief African ally and made Masinissa master of Numidia.

events.title: Mago defeated in Insubrian territory
events.summary: The praetor Publius Quinctilius Varus and the proconsul Marcus Cornelius Cethegus defeated Mago's army in Insubrian territory. Mago, wounded in the thigh, withdrew to the Ligurian coast and sailed for Africa on the recall order, dying of his wound off Sardinia.

sides.strength: 4 legions under P. Quinctilius Varus and M. Cornelius Cethegus

battle.significance: Ended the Carthaginian presence in northern Italy.

events.title: Hannibal leaves Italy
events.summary: Recalled to defend Carthage, Hannibal sailed from Croton in autumn 203 after fifteen years in Italy, landing at Leptis Minor. Before leaving he set up at the temple of Hera Lacinia a bronze tablet in Punic and Greek recording his deeds and army numbers, which Polybius read.

events.title: Naval battle off Utica
events.summary: While Scipio was at Tunis after the Great Plains, the Carthaginian fleet sailed against his warships beached before Utica. Scipio lashed his transports four deep into a floating wall to protect them; the Carthaginians, attacking with grapnels, towed off about 60 transports but failed to destroy the fleet.

sides.strength: warships behind a line of transports

battle.significance: Carthage's last notable naval effort of the war.

events.title: Fall of Agathocles in Alexandria
events.summary: Agathocles, who with Sosibius had concealed Ptolemy IV's death and had Queen Arsinoe III murdered to rule for the child Ptolemy V, was overthrown when the Macedonian guard and the Alexandrian crowd rose under Tlepolemus. Agathocles, his sister Agathoclea and their mother were torn to pieces in the stadium.

events.title: Battle of Zama
events.summary: In the final battle of the war, Scipio arranged his maniples in columns with lanes through which Hannibal's 80 elephants were funnelled harmlessly. Laelius and Masinissa drove off the Carthaginian cavalry. The Roman infantry broke Hannibal's first two lines; the decisive struggle with his third line of Italian veterans was ended when the Roman and Numidian cavalry returned and fell on its rear.

sides.strength: c. 29,000 Romans and Italians plus Masinissa's 6,000 foot and 4,000 horse

sides.losses: c. 20,000 killed and as many captured (Polybius)

battle.significance: Ended the Second Punic War and Carthage's career as a great power.

events.title: The armistice broken
events.summary: During an armistice while a Carthaginian embassy was in Rome, a Roman supply convoy was driven ashore by a storm in the Gulf of Carthage and the Carthaginians seized it. When Roman envoys protested, their ship was attacked on the way back. Scipio resumed the war.

events.title: Battle of Chios
events.summary: Philip V's fleet was badly mauled off Chios by the combined fleets of Rhodes and Attalus I. Polybius says Philip lost 92 decked ships and 70 lembi, and 9,000 men, far more than his enemies; Attalus was nearly captured. Philip claimed victory because he held the field.

sides.losses: 92 decked ships and 70 lembi lost; 3,000 Macedonians and 6,000 rowers killed (Polybius)

battle.significance: Weakened Macedonian sea power and provoked the appeal to Rome.

events.title: Peace treaty ending the Second Punic War
events.summary: Carthage kept its African territory within the 'Phoenician trenches' and its own laws, but surrendered all warships except ten triremes, all elephants, and all prisoners and deserters; paid 10,000 talents over fifty years; gave 100 hostages chosen by Scipio; agreed to wage no war outside Africa and none in Africa without Roman permission; and restored to Masinissa all that had belonged to him or his ancestors.

events.title: Scipio's triumph; the cognomen Africanus
events.summary: Scipio returned and celebrated a magnificent triumph, depositing 123,000 pounds of silver in the treasury and giving each soldier 400 asses. He was the first Roman general to take a cognomen from a conquered land, Africanus, whether given by his soldiers, his friends or popular favour.

events.title: Battle of Lade
events.summary: In the same campaign as Chios, Philip V defeated the Rhodian fleet off the island of Lade near Miletus. The Milesians crowned Philip and his admiral Heraclides, and Philip went on to plunder Caria, where in winter 201/200 the Rhodian and Pergamene fleets blockaded him in Bargylia.

battle.significance: Encouraged Rhodes and Pergamon to appeal to Rome.

events.title: Antiochus III takes Gaza
events.summary: Opening the Fifth Syrian War, Antiochus III besieged and took Gaza, whose loyalty to the Ptolemies Polybius praises. The fall of Gaza opened the road to Egypt and prompted the Ptolemaic counter-offensive under Scopas.

battle.significance: Opened the Fifth Syrian War.

events.title: Battle of Panium
events.summary: Antiochus III decisively defeated the Ptolemaic army under the Aetolian mercenary general Scopas at Panium near the sources of the Jordan, using elephants and cataphract cavalry led by his son Antiochus. Coele-Syria and Judaea passed permanently to the Seleucids.

battle.significance: Ended a century of Ptolemaic rule in Coele-Syria and Judaea.

events.title: Rome votes for war with Philip
events.summary: The consul Publius Sulpicius Galba proposed war against Philip V. The comitia centuriata, war-weary after 17 years against Hannibal, rejected it almost unanimously; after a speech by Sulpicius warning that Philip would otherwise invade Italy like Pyrrhus, a second vote approved it. The young envoy Marcus Aemilius Lepidus delivered the ultimatum to Philip at the siege of Abydos.

events.title: Siege of Abydos
events.summary: Philip V besieged Abydos on the Hellespont. When the walls were breached, the citizens resolved to kill their women and children and burn their property if the city fell; their magistrates surrendered instead, but the populace carried out the mass suicide when Philip entered. Philip gave them three days to die.

sides.strength: citizens of Abydos with Rhodian and Pergamene help

battle.significance: Gave Philip the Straits, but sealed his reputation for savagery in Greek opinion.

events.title: Athens declares war on Philip; Attica ravaged
events.summary: After two Acarnanian youths were executed for straying into the Eleusinian Mysteries, Acarnania and Philip attacked Attica. Athens declared war, abolished the two tribes named after Antigonus and Demetrius and ordered the destruction of all Antigonid statues and inscriptions. Philip ravaged the Attic countryside, burning the Academy, the Lyceum and the sanctuaries and tombs around the city.

events.title: Battle of Cremona
events.summary: Insubres, Boii and Cenomani, led by a Carthaginian officer named Hamilcar who had stayed in Italy, sacked Placentia and besieged Cremona. The praetor Lucius Furius Purpureo crushed them; Hamilcar was killed. Livy claims 35,000 Gauls killed or captured.

sides.strength: praetorian army under L. Furius Purpureo

battle.significance: Opened the final Roman conquest of Cisalpine Gaul.

events.title: Plautus' Stichus at the Plebeian Games
events.summary: The surviving production notice (didascalia) of Plautus' Stichus dates its staging to the Ludi Plebeii of 200, with music by Marcipor, slave of Oppius, and adapted from Menander's Adelphoi. It is one of only two Plautine plays with a secure date; the other is the Pseudolus of 191.

events.title: Fabius Pictor writes the first Roman history
events.summary: Around 200 the senator Quintus Fabius Pictor, a veteran of the Gallic war of 225 and envoy to Delphi after Cannae, wrote a history of Rome in Greek from Aeneas and Romulus to his own day, aimed largely at Greek readers. It was the foundation of the Roman annalistic tradition.

events.title: Battle of Ottolobus
events.summary: Publius Sulpicius Galba, invading Macedonia from Illyria, won a cavalry and light infantry action near Ottolobus in Lyncestis; Philip V was nearly caught when his horse was killed and survived only because a guardsman gave him his own. Galba then took Pelium and retired to Apollonia.

battle.significance: First Roman success of the war, but without strategic result.

events.title: Claudius Centho raids Chalcis
events.summary: A Roman squadron under Gaius Claudius Centho, sent to help Athens, surprised Chalcis at dawn, burned the Macedonian arsenal and granaries, freed prisoners held there and destroyed the royal statues before withdrawing. Philip, arriving too late, marched on Athens in revenge.

events.title: Philip V at the gates of Athens
events.summary: Philip attacked Athens at dawn and fought a cavalry battle at the Dipylon, then, unable to take the city, ravaged Attica, destroying the Academy, the Lyceum, shrines and tombs. Athens answered by abolishing the honours of the Antigonids and cursing Philip and his ancestors.

battle.significance: Turned Greek opinion against Philip.

events.title: Ovation of Lucius Cornelius Lentulus
events.summary: Lucius Cornelius Lentulus, who had held command in Spain without holding a magistracy (as a privatus cum imperio), asked for a triumph. The Senate replied that no one had triumphed who had not held office as dictator, consul or praetor and allowed only an ovation; a tribune's veto was overcome.

events.title: Public land in lieu of repayment: the trientabula
events.summary: The creditors who had lent to the state in 210 were due their third instalment in 200, but the treasury needed money for the Macedonian war. The Senate offered them public land within 50 miles of Rome at a nominal rent of one as per iugerum, redeemable for cash later; the land was called trientabulum because it stood for a third of the debt.

events.title: Scopas surrenders at Sidon
events.summary: After Panium, Scopas shut himself up in Sidon with 10,000 men. Blockaded by Antiochus III and starving, he surrendered and was allowed to leave without arms; Antiochus then took the rest of Phoenicia, Judaea, where Jerusalem welcomed him, and Coele-Syria.

battle.significance: Completed the Seleucid conquest of Coele-Syria.

events.title: Battle of the Aous
events.summary: Philip V held the narrow gorge of the Aous (Aoi Stena) for weeks against the new consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus. A shepherd sent by the pro-Roman Epirote chief Charops guided 4,000 Romans over the mountains in three nights to a height above the Macedonian camp; attacked from front and rear, Philip abandoned the pass with the loss of 2,000 men.
events.locName: Aoi Stena, gorge of the Aous (Vjosë) near Këlcyrë

battle.significance: Opened Thessaly to the Romans and brought the Achaeans over to Rome.

events.title: Conference of Nicaea
events.summary: Flamininus and Philip negotiated on the shore of the Malian Gulf near Nicaea, Philip speaking from the prow of his ship. Flamininus arranged that the matter be referred to the Senate, where his friends ensured negotiations would fail if his command was prorogued, or succeed if he was to be replaced. It was prorogued.

events.title: The Leges Porciae on provocatio
events.summary: One or more laws proposed by members of the Porcian gens extended the citizen's right of appeal (provocatio) against magistrates, in particular protecting Roman citizens from flogging, including outside Rome and in military contexts.

events.title: The Achaean League joins Rome
events.summary: At a stormy assembly at Sicyon, the Achaean strategos Aristaenus persuaded the League to abandon its long alliance with Macedon and join Rome. Some cities, including Dyme, Megalopolis and Argos, walked out; Argos then handed itself to Philip, who gave it to Nabis of Sparta.

events.title: Siege of Atrax
events.summary: Flamininus breached the walls of Atrax, but the Macedonian garrison formed a phalanx in the breach and the legionaries could not shift it; a siege tower stuck in the rubble. Flamininus abandoned the siege, an episode Livy uses to show the phalanx's strength on a narrow front.

battle.significance: Rare example of the phalanx beating legionaries in the breach.

events.title: Capture of Eretria
events.summary: The combined fleets of Lucius Quinctius Flamininus, Attalus I and Rhodes besieged Eretria; the Macedonian garrison surrendered the citadel. Livy notes that few gold and silver objects but many statues, paintings and old works of art were taken, an early sign of Rome's appetite for Greek art.

events.title: Flamininus takes Elatea
events.summary: After the Aous, Flamininus overran Phocis and stormed Elatea, which he then used as his winter base, while his diplomats won over the Achaean League at Sicyon.

events.title: Battle of Cynoscephalae
events.summary: On the misty 'Dog's Head' hills of Thessaly, an encounter battle between Flamininus and Philip V developed piecemeal. Philip's right wing phalanx charged downhill and pushed back the Roman left; Flamininus attacked the Macedonian left as it was still deploying, using elephants, and broke it. An unnamed military tribune then took 20 maniples from the victorious Roman right and attacked the rear of the Macedonian right phalanx, which collapsed. Macedonian soldiers raising their sarissas in surrender were cut down by Romans who did not understand the signal.

sides.strength: c. 26,000 incl. 6,000 Aetolians and Athamanians, 20 elephants

battle.significance: Ended the Second Macedonian War; Polybius' showcase for the superiority of the legion over the phalanx.

events.title: Two Spanish provinces and six praetors
events.summary: The number of praetors was raised to six so that two could be sent annually to govern Hispania Citerior (the east coast north of New Carthage) and Hispania Ulterior (the Baetis valley), with boundaries fixed by the praetors of that year.

events.title: Revolt in Spain; death of Sempronius Tuditanus
events.summary: Most of southern and eastern Spain rose against Roman rule, the Turdetani under the chieftain Culchas and the cities of Malaca and Sexi among them. The praetor of Citerior, Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus, was defeated and died of his wounds.

events.title: Battle of the Mincius
events.summary: The consul Gaius Cornelius Cethegus defeated the Insubres and Cenomani on the Mincius after secretly persuading the Cenomani to change sides during the battle. The Carthaginian Hamilcar was captured (in one version) and Cethegus triumphed.

sides.strength: consular army under C. Cornelius Cethegus

battle.significance: Broke the Insubrian coalition; the Cenomani became loyal allies.

events.title: Death of Attalus I
events.summary: Attalus I, aged 72, collapsed with a stroke while addressing the Boeotian assembly at Thebes in spring 197 in support of Rome, and was carried home to Pergamon to die. He had founded the dynasty's royal title by defeating the Galatians and had made Pergamon Rome's indispensable eastern ally. His son Eumenes II succeeded.

events.title: The Memphis decree (Rosetta Stone)
events.summary: On 27 March 196 a synod of Egyptian priests at Memphis decreed honours for Ptolemy V on the first anniversary of his coronation, in thanks for tax remissions, temple gifts and the suppression of rebels at Lycopolis. Copies were set up in temples in hieroglyphic, demotic and Greek; one, found at Rashid in 1799, made possible Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs.

events.title: Flamininus proclaims the freedom of the Greeks
events.summary: At the Isthmian Games of 196, a herald announced that the Senate and Flamininus declared free, ungarrisoned, untaxed and governed by their own laws the Greek peoples formerly subject to Philip. The crowd's shouts were so loud, Plutarch says, that crows flying overhead fell stunned into the stadium.

events.title: Conference of Lysimachia
events.summary: Roman commissioners met Antiochus III at Lysimachia in Thrace, which he was rebuilding, and told him to keep his hands off the autonomous cities of Asia and out of Europe. Antiochus replied that Asia was none of Rome's business, any more than he meddled in Italy, and that Thrace was his by inheritance from Seleucus I's victory over Lysimachus.

events.title: Creation of the tresviri epulones
events.summary: A law of the tribune Gaius Licinius Lucullus created a new priestly college of three epulones to organise the sacred banquet (epulum Iovis) at the Ludi Romani and Plebeii, relieving the overburdened pontiffs. It became one of the four great colleges (later septemviri).

events.title: Battle of Turda
events.summary: The praetor Quintus Minucius Thermus defeated the Spanish chiefs Budares and Baesadines near the town of Turda, claiming 12,000 enemy dead and the capture of Budares, part of the suppression of the great Spanish revolt of 197.

events.title: Marcellus defeats the Insubres and takes Comum
events.summary: The consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus, after a reverse at the hands of the Boii, crossed the Po and defeated the Insubres and the people of Comum, taking 28 strongholds, and triumphed. His colleague Furius Purpurio worked with him in the Boian country.

battle.significance: Broke Insubrian resistance north of the Po.

events.title: Repeal of the Lex Oppia
events.summary: Two tribunes, Marcus Fundanius and Lucius Valerius, proposed repealing the wartime Lex Oppia. Roman women filled the streets and the approaches to the Forum to lobby men for repeal, the first recorded women's demonstration in Rome. The consul Cato spoke against; the law was repealed.

events.title: Cato in Spain: the battle of Emporiae
events.summary: The consul Cato landed at Emporiae with two legions, sent away his ships to force his men to fight, and defeated a large Iberian army in a dawn attack, using his reserve to break the enemy centre. He then disarmed the tribes north of the Ebro and, by sending sealed letters to all cities to be opened the same day, had their walls demolished simultaneously.

sides.strength: 2 legions, allies and Spanish auxiliaries, c. 25,000

battle.significance: Pacified north-east Spain; Cato triumphed in 194.

events.title: War against Nabis: siege of Sparta
events.summary: A Panhellenic coalition led by Flamininus, with Achaeans, Macedonians, Rhodians and Pergamenes, took Gythium and attacked Sparta itself. Nabis, whose revolutionary regime had freed helots and redistributed land, sued for peace: he kept Sparta but surrendered Argos and the coastal towns, his fleet and hostages.

battle.significance: Freed Argos but left Nabis in power.

events.title: Hannibal's suffeteship and flight
events.summary: Elected suffete in 196, Hannibal broke the power of the oligarchic court of 104 judges by making membership annual and reformed the state finances so that the Roman indemnity could be paid without extra taxes. His enemies denounced him at Rome for plotting with Antiochus; when a Roman embassy arrived in 195 he fled by night to Tyre and then to Antiochus at Ephesus.

events.title: Valerius Flaccus defeats the Boii near the Litana forest
events.summary: The consul Lucius Valerius Flaccus, Cato's colleague, defeated the Boii near the Litana forest where Postumius' army had been destroyed in 216, reportedly killing 8,000, and spent the rest of the year rebuilding Placentia and Cremona.

events.title: Cato disarms Hispania Citerior
events.summary: After Emporiae, Cato sent sealed letters to the communities north of the Ebro ordering them to demolish their walls on the same day; most complied for fear that each was the only one ordered. He also organised the silver and iron mines for revenue, and boasted that he had taken more towns than he had spent days in Spain.

events.title: The sacred spring fulfilled
events.summary: The ver sacrum vowed in 217 after Trasimene, the dedication to Jupiter of all livestock born in one spring, was finally performed in 195. The pontifex maximus Licinius Crassus declared it improperly done, and it was repeated in 194, covering animals born between 1 March and 30 April.

events.title: Eight citizen colonies on the coasts of southern Italy
events.summary: Rome planted eight citizen colonies of 300 families each at Puteoli, Volturnum, Liternum, Salernum, Buxentum, Sipontum, Tempsa and Croton, on land confiscated from communities that had sided with Hannibal.

events.title: Flamininus' triumph and Roman withdrawal from Greece
events.summary: Flamininus evacuated the last Roman garrisons from Greece, including Acrocorinth, Chalcis and Demetrias, and celebrated a three-day triumph displaying Macedonian armour, bronze and marble statues, silver and gold, including 14,514 gold coins called Philippei. Freed Roman captives sold as slaves in Greece after Cannae, ransomed by the Achaeans, marched behind his chariot with shaved heads.

events.title: Senators given separate seats at the games
events.summary: At the Ludi Romani of 194, on the order of the censors Sextus Aelius Paetus and Gaius Cornelius Cethegus (supported, it was said, by Scipio Africanus in his second consulship), the curule aediles reserved separate seats for senators. Livy reports popular resentment and Africanus' later regret.

events.title: Temples of Juno Sospita, Faunus and Fortuna Primigenia dedicated
events.summary: In 194 Gaius Cornelius Cethegus dedicated the temple of Juno Sospita in the vegetable market, vowed at the Mincius; plebeian aediles dedicated a temple of Faunus on the Tiber island from fines on graziers; and a temple of Fortuna Primigenia, vowed by Sempronius Tuditanus in 204 and modelled on the cult of Praeneste, was dedicated on the Quirinal.
events.locName: Forum Holitorium, Tiber Island and Quirinal, Rome

events.title: Triumph of Cato over Spain
events.summary: Cato triumphed over Hispania Citerior, displaying 25,000 pounds of silver bullion, 123,000 bigati, 540 pounds of Oscan silver and 1,400 pounds of gold, and gave each soldier 270 asses. He then served as a legate under others, refusing to rest on his triumph.

events.title: Scipio Nasica defeats the Lusitanians near Ilipa
events.summary: The praetor Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica intercepted a Lusitanian raiding army returning laden with booty from Ulterior near Ilipa and defeated it, claiming 12,000 killed and recovering the plunder.

events.title: Lex Sempronia extends usury limits to allies
events.summary: Because Roman creditors evaded the limits on interest by lending through Latin and Italian allies not bound by Roman law, a plebiscite of the tribune Marcus Sempronius Tuditanus applied Roman laws on loans to dealings with allies.

events.title: Emporium and Porticus Aemilia
events.summary: The curule aediles Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Aemilius Paullus built an emporium on the Tiber below the Aventine and a vast portico outside the Porta Trigemina; the Porticus Aemilia was rebuilt in concrete in 174, one of the earliest large concrete structures.

events.title: Battle of Mutina
events.summary: The consul Lucius Cornelius Merula fought a hard battle against the Boii near Mutina, claiming 14,000 Gauls killed. His legates accused him of letting the enemy escape and blocked his triumph.

sides.strength: consular army under L. Cornelius Merula

battle.significance: Part of the grinding final war against the Boii.

events.title: Latin colonies at Copia (Thurii) and Vibo Valentia
events.summary: Rome founded Latin colonies at Thurii, renamed Copia (193), and at Hipponium, renamed Vibo Valentia (192), in the Bruttian south, the last Latin colonies in southern Italy.

events.title: Marriage of Ptolemy V and Cleopatra I
events.summary: In the winter of 194/3, sealing the peace that ended the Fifth Syrian War, Antiochus III married his daughter Cleopatra to Ptolemy V at Raphia. Ptolemaic courtiers later claimed the dowry included the revenues or even the possession of Coele-Syria, a claim that fuelled the Sixth Syrian War.

events.title: Ligurians besiege Pisae
events.summary: A Ligurian army of 40,000, Livy says, ravaged the territory of Luna and besieged Pisae. The consul Quintus Minucius Thermus held the city in 193 and in 192 defeated the Ligurians near Pisae, killing 9,000, the start of four years of command against them.

events.title: Fulvius Nobilior at Toletum
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Fulvius Nobilior defeated a coalition of Vaccaei, Vettones and Celtiberians near Toletum and captured their king Hilermus; in 192 he stormed Toletum itself, the first Roman advance onto the Meseta.

battle.significance: First Roman push into the central Meseta.

events.title: The conversation of Hannibal and Scipio at Ephesus
events.summary: When Roman envoys, among them Publius Villius Tappulus and perhaps Scipio Africanus, came to Antiochus' court in 193, the Romans conferred with Hannibal. Tradition reported that Scipio asked who was the greatest general: Hannibal answered Alexander, then Pyrrhus, then himself, and added that had he beaten Scipio he would have put himself first.

events.title: Tiber floods and the fire of 192
events.summary: In 193 the Tiber flooded twice, destroying two bridges and many buildings around the Porta Flumentana; a landslide fell from the Capitol onto the Vicus Iugarius. In 192 a fire burned the buildings along the Tiber for two days, and there were twelve floods in the year.

events.title: Antiochus III lands at Demetrias
events.summary: Invited by the Aetolians, who named him their commander and 'liberator of Greece', Antiochus crossed to Demetrias in autumn 192 with only 10,000 foot, 500 horse and 6 elephants. Rome declared war. Antiochus wintered at Chalcis, where he married a young Chalcidian woman, which Roman tradition mocked as idleness.

events.title: Murder of Nabis; Sparta joins the Achaean League
events.summary: The Aetolians, seeking to seize Sparta as a base for Antiochus, sent Alexamenus with 1,000 men as 'allies'; he murdered Nabis during a review. The Spartans rose and killed the Aetolians, and Philopoemen brought Sparta into the Achaean League.

events.title: Temple of Veiovis on the Capitol
events.summary: Quintus Marcius Ralla dedicated a temple of Veiovis between the two summits of the Capitol, vowed by Lucius Furius Purpurio in his Gallic battle of 200. Its later rebuilding survives beneath the Tabularium.

events.title: Philopoemen defeats Nabis near Gythium
events.summary: Philopoemen, whose naval attempt to relieve Gythium failed when his old flagship broke up, ambushed Nabis' army in rough country near Mount Barbosthenes, killing many and pursuing the tyrant to Sparta. The Romans, preoccupied with Antiochus, imposed a truce.

battle.significance: Weakened Nabis shortly before his murder by the Aetolians.

events.title: Battle of Thermopylae
events.summary: Antiochus fortified the pass of Thermopylae against the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio, leaving Aetolians to hold the mountain paths. Cato, as a legate, led a force by night over the heights of Callidromus, surprised the Aetolian guard and appeared above Antiochus' camp. The Seleucid army broke; Antiochus fled to Chalcis with 500 men and sailed for Asia.

sides.losses: almost the whole army, according to Livy

battle.significance: Drove Antiochus out of Europe after a single campaign.

events.title: Dedication of the temple of Magna Mater
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Junius Brutus dedicated the temple of the Great Mother on the Palatine, thirteen years after the goddess's arrival. Plautus' comedy Pseudolus was staged at the dedication games, as its production notice (didascalia) records.

events.title: Battle of Corycus
events.summary: The Roman fleet of Gaius Livius Salinator, with Eumenes II of Pergamon, defeated the Seleucid admiral Polyxenidas off Cape Corycus near Erythrae, sinking 10 and capturing 13 ships.

battle.significance: Gave the allies the initiative in the Aegean.

events.title: Siege of Heraclea Trachinia
events.summary: After Thermopylae, Acilius Glabrio besieged and stormed the Aetolian stronghold of Heraclea near Mount Oeta, then besieged Naupactus until Flamininus arranged a truce.

battle.significance: Forced the Aetolians to negotiate.

events.title: The Aetolians and the meaning of deditio
events.summary: Aetolian envoys led by Phaeneas agreed to entrust themselves to the 'faith of the Romans' (in fidem). When Acilius then demanded the surrender of individuals and threatened to put the envoys in chains, Phaeneas protested that this was not Greek custom. Acilius replied that by Roman usage those who gave themselves into Roman fides were at Rome's absolute disposal.

events.title: Final defeat of the Boii
events.summary: The consul Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica defeated the Boii in a great battle and forced their surrender, confiscating half their territory for Roman colonists. Livy claims 28,000 Boii killed. Nasica's triumph, opposed by a tribune, was granted; its spoils included 1,471 gold torques.

battle.significance: Completed the Roman conquest of Cisalpine Gaul south of the Po.

events.title: Antiochus III winters at Chalcis and marries
events.summary: Antiochus, aged about fifty, spent the winter of 192/1 at Chalcis, where he married a young Chalcidian, daughter of Cleoptolemus, whom he named Euboea. Polybius and Livy made the wedding festivities the symbol of the king's lost momentum before Thermopylae.

events.title: Lex Acilia on intercalation
events.summary: Macrobius, citing Varro, says that the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio carried a law in 191 giving the pontiffs discretion over intercalation. The Roman calendar was then badly out of step with the seasons, as the eclipse reported by Livy for 190 shows.

events.title: Plautus' Pseudolus at the dedication of the Magna Mater temple
events.summary: The didascalia of the Pseudolus records its production at the Ludi Megalenses of 191, the games celebrating the dedication of the Magna Mater's temple on the Palatine, with the urban praetor Marcus Junius Brutus presiding. The play, about a scheming slave, was performed on a temporary stage in front of the temple.

events.title: Temple of Juventas dedicated
events.summary: Gaius Licinius Lucullus dedicated a temple of Juventas (Youth) at the Circus Maximus, vowed by Marcus Livius Salinator on the day of the Metaurus sixteen years earlier.

events.title: Siege of Naupactus
events.summary: After Heraclea, Acilius Glabrio besieged the Aetolians in Naupactus for two months. Flamininus, worried that the Achaeans and Philip were gaining at Aetolian expense, walked up to the walls, was recognised and arranged a truce to let the Aetolians send envoys to Rome.

events.title: Carthage offers to pay its indemnity at once
events.summary: Ten years after Zama, Carthaginian envoys offered to pay the remaining 40 annual instalments of the war indemnity immediately, and to supply grain and a fleet for the war against Antiochus. Rome took the grain but refused the lump sum, preferring the annual tribute as a mark of Carthage's subjection.

events.title: Battle of the Eurymedon (Side)
events.summary: A Rhodian fleet under Eudamus defeated the Seleucid Phoenician fleet commanded by Hannibal and Apollonius off Side in Pamphylia. It was Hannibal's only recorded naval command, and his defeat prevented the Phoenician squadrons from joining the main Seleucid fleet.

battle.significance: Kept the Phoenician fleet out of the Aegean.

events.title: Battle of Myonessus
events.summary: The Roman praetor Lucius Aemilius Regillus with Rhodian allies defeated Polyxenidas off Myonessus near Teos. The Rhodian fire-pots, braziers slung on poles from the bows, were decisive. The Seleucids lost 42 ships, and Antiochus abandoned Lysimachia, leaving the Hellespont open.

sides.strength: 58 Roman and 22 Rhodian ships under L. Aemilius Regillus

battle.significance: Gave Rome command of the Aegean and allowed the Scipios to cross into Asia unopposed.

events.title: Antiochus' peace offer and Africanus' son
events.summary: As the Scipios crossed into Asia, Antiochus offered to pay half the Roman war costs and abandon Lampsacus, Smyrna and Alexandria Troas, and offered Africanus, through the envoy Heraclides, the return without ransom of his captured son. Africanus refused to treat but advised Antiochus not to fight. The king returned the son anyway.

events.title: Battle of Magnesia
events.summary: On the plain near Magnesia-ad-Sipylum, Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus effectively in command while Africanus lay ill at Elaea, defeated Antiochus III's huge multi-ethnic army. Eumenes II's light troops stampeded the scythed chariots back into the Seleucid left, and his cavalry broke it. Antiochus' cataphracts on the right routed a Roman legion and charged to the Roman camp, but too late; the Seleucid phalanx, attacked on all sides and disordered by its own panicking elephants, was destroyed.

sides.strength: c. 30,000 (4 legions and allies, Pergamenes, Achaeans) plus 16 African elephants
c. 72,000 (Livy) with 54 Indian elephants and scythed chariots
sides.losses: 50,000 foot, 3,000 horse killed, 1,400 captured (Livy; probably inflated)

battle.significance: Destroyed Seleucid power west of the Taurus and made Rome the arbiter of the whole Hellenistic world.

events.title: The eclipse that dates the Roman calendar
events.summary: Livy reports that during the Ludi Apollinares, on the fifth day before the Ides of Quinctilis (11 July by the Roman calendar) of 190, the sun was darkened as the moon passed in front of it. Astronomical tables identify this as the partial eclipse of 14 March 190 BC (Julian), showing the Roman calendar about four months ahead of the solar year.

events.title: Polyxenidas destroys the Rhodian squadron at Panormus
events.summary: Polyxenidas, himself a Rhodian exile, lured the Rhodian admiral Pausistratus with a pretended offer to betray the Seleucid fleet, then caught his 36 ships at Panormus. Pausistratus died fighting; only seven ships escaped by using fire pots slung on poles.
events.locName: Panormus, on the coast near Ephesus/Samos

battle.significance: The fire-pot device used by the survivors became a Rhodian speciality.

events.title: Siege and sack of Phocaea
events.summary: The praetor Aemilius Regillus besieged Phocaea, which had gone over to Antiochus; after Myonessus it surrendered on terms, but the Roman soldiers sacked it anyway. Regillus restored the town and its laws.

events.title: Aemilius Paullus defeated at Lyco
events.summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus, the future victor of Pydna, then propraetor in Ulterior, was routed by the Lusitanians near Lyco in Bastetania, losing 6,000 men, and only just held his camp. He recovered and won a large victory in 189.

battle.significance: A rare defeat for Paullus.

events.title: Placentia and Cremona reinforced
events.summary: The two Latin colonies on the Po, depleted by war and Gallic attacks, petitioned for new settlers; the Senate sent 6,000 families to be divided between them. The following year a new colony was founded at Bononia.

events.title: Decree of Aemilius Paullus at Lascuta
events.summary: On 19 January 189 Lucius Aemilius Paullus, as propraetor in Hispania Ulterior, decreed that the 'slaves of the Hastenses' living in the Turris Lascutana should be free and keep the land and town they held, as long as the Roman people and Senate wished.
events.locName: Turris Lascutana (near Alcalá de los Gazules)

events.title: Triumph of Lucius Scipio Asiaticus
events.summary: On the last day of February 189 Lucius Cornelius Scipio triumphed over Antiochus, displaying 224 military standards, 134 town models, 1,231 ivory tusks, 234 gold crowns, 137,420 pounds of silver, 224,000 Attic tetradrachms and 140,000 gold Philippics, and took the cognomen Asiaticus (Asiagenes in the Fasti).

events.title: Siege of Ambracia
events.summary: The consul Marcus Fulvius Nobilior besieged Ambracia, formerly Pyrrhus' capital. When the Romans dug a mine, the defenders countermined and drove them out by filling the tunnel with smoke from burning feathers blown with a bellows. The city surrendered on terms; Fulvius removed its statues and paintings, including statues of the Muses, which he set up in his temple of Hercules Musarum in Rome.

battle.significance: Forced the Aetolians to accept peace.

events.title: Peace with the Aetolian League: the maiestas clause
events.summary: The Aetolians made peace on harsh terms: an indemnity of 500 talents, surrender of hostages and of the cities taken by Rome since 192, and the obligation to 'preserve the empire and majesty of the Roman people' and to have the same friends and enemies. It was the first Roman treaty with a Greek state to contain the maiestas clause.

events.title: Manlius Vulso's Galatian war: Mount Olympus
events.summary: Without clear authorisation from the Senate, the consul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso marched against the Galatians, Antiochus' allies. He stormed the Tolistobogii on their refuge of Mount Olympus with massed slingers and archers, then defeated the Tectosages on Mount Magaba near Ancyra. Livy claims 40,000 captives.

battle.significance: Crushed Galatian raiding power and handed Eumenes a secure kingdom; brought vast booty to Rome.

events.title: Latin colony at Bononia
events.summary: A Latin colony of 3,000 settlers was founded at Bononia (Bologna) on land taken from the Boii; cavalrymen received 70 iugera, others 50.

events.title: Battle of Mount Magaba
events.summary: Having stormed the Tolistobogii on Mount Olympus, Manlius Vulso marched on the Tectosages and Trocmi gathered on Mount Magaba near Ancyra. Roman missile troops again drove the Galatians from their hill position, and their camp and families were captured. The Galatians sued for peace.

battle.significance: Broke Galatian power in western Anatolia for a generation.

events.title: Siege of Same in Cephallenia
events.summary: After the Aetolian peace, Same in Cephallenia, which had surrendered, rose again fearing deportation. Marcus Fulvius Nobilior besieged it for four months; slingers from Aegium, Patrae and Dyme helped. When it fell the inhabitants were sold into slavery.

battle.significance: Last act of the Aetolian war.

events.title: Acilius Glabrio withdraws from the censorship race
events.summary: Manius Acilius Glabrio, victor of Thermopylae and a new man, stood for the censorship of 189 with lavish gifts to voters. Two tribunes accused him of keeping royal booty from Antiochus' camp, and Cato, his former legate, testified that vessels he had seen in the camp were missing from the triumph. Glabrio withdrew and the prosecution was dropped.

events.title: Census of 189: 258,318 citizens
events.summary: The censors Titus Flamininus and Marcus Claudius Marcellus registered 258,318 citizens, nearly double the figure of 209 (137,108) and well up on 194 (143,704), and for the first time registered the people of Campanian towns, whose census had been taken at Capua. They chose Scipio Africanus princeps senatus for the third time.

events.title: Treaty of Apamea
events.summary: Antiochus III gave up all territory west of the Taurus, paid 15,000 talents (the largest indemnity in ancient history), surrendered his elephants and all warships but ten, which were not to sail west of Cape Sarpedon, and gave 20 hostages including his son Antiochus. He also had to hand over Hannibal and other enemies of Rome, who escaped.

events.title: Full citizenship for Formiae, Fundi and Arpinum
events.summary: A tribunician law gave Formiae, Fundi and Arpinum, communities of citizens without the vote (cives sine suffragio), full voting citizenship, enrolling them in the tribes Aemilia and Cornelia. Arpinum later produced Marius and Cicero.

events.title: Philopoemen razes the walls of Sparta
events.summary: After Spartan exiles attacked Las, Philopoemen marched on Sparta. At Compasion some 80 (Polybius) or 350 (Aristocrates) Spartans were killed or executed; Sparta's walls were pulled down, its mercenaries and Nabis' new citizens expelled or sold, and the laws of Lycurgus abolished in favour of Achaean institutions.

events.title: Thracians ambush Manlius Vulso's army
events.summary: Marching home overland from Asia with the Galatian booty, Manlius Vulso's column was attacked by some 10,000 Thracians of the Asti, Caeni and others in a wooded defile. The baggage train was plundered and Quintus Minucius Thermus was among the dead.

battle.significance: Fuelled the opposition to Vulso's triumph.

events.title: Death of Antiochus III
events.summary: Short of money for the Apamea indemnity, Antiochus III attempted to plunder the treasury of the temple of Bel in Elymais and was killed by the local population. His son Seleucus IV succeeded.

events.title: The trials of the Scipios
events.summary: Cato and the tribunes Quintus and Quintus Petillius demanded an account of 500 talents received from Antiochus. Africanus tore up his brother's account books in the Senate. Later, prosecuted himself, he reminded the people that it was the anniversary of Zama and led them up to the Capitol to give thanks, leaving the accusers alone. He withdrew to his villa at Liternum. Lucius Scipio was condemned to a fine; the tribune Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, though an enemy, vetoed his imprisonment.

events.title: Manlius Vulso's triumph and 'the origin of foreign luxury'
events.summary: Gnaeus Manlius Vulso, after a fight in the Senate over his unauthorised Galatian war, triumphed with Asiatic booty. Livy says his army introduced to Rome bronze dining couches, costly coverlets and tapestries, one-legged tables, female lute and harp players at dinners, and cooks, who rose from the cheapest of slaves to the most valued.

events.title: Via Aemilia
events.summary: The consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus built a road from Ariminum to Placentia along the foot of the Apennines, binding the newly conquered Po plain to Rome. His colleague Gaius Flaminius built a road from Bononia across the Apennines to Arretium.

events.title: Twelve thousand Latins sent home
events.summary: Envoys of the Latin allies complained that their citizens had migrated to Rome and been registered there, draining their manpower for the allied levies. The praetor Quintus Terentius Culleo traced those registered at Rome since 204 and sent 12,000 back to their communities.

events.title: Triumph of Fulvius Nobilior and the Muses of Ambracia
events.summary: Marcus Fulvius Nobilior triumphed over the Aetolians and Cephallenia, carrying 785 bronze and 230 marble statues from Ambracia. He installed the statues of the Nine Muses in a temple of Hercules of the Muses (Hercules Musarum) in the Campus Martius and placed there a calendar with commentary (Fasti). Ennius, who had accompanied him, celebrated the campaign in his Ambracia.

events.title: Lepidus and Flaminius subdue the Friniates and Apuani
events.summary: The consuls of 187, Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Gaius Flaminius (son of the consul of 217), campaigned in the Apennines, forcing the Friniates and some Apuani down from their mountain strongholds into the plains. Flaminius built a road from Bononia to Arretium; Lepidus the Via Aemilia.

events.title: The Bacchanalia affair
events.summary: Alerted by the courtesan Hispala Faecenia and her young lover Publius Aebutius, the consul Spurius Postumius Albinus revealed to the Senate a secret Bacchic cult accused of nocturnal orgies, forged wills and murders. A special inquiry pursued it across Italy: over 7,000 people were said to be implicated, and many were executed. The Senate's decree permitted Bacchic worship only with its permission, in groups of no more than five, with no common fund or male priests.
events.locName: Rome and Italy (copy found at Tiriolo, Calabria)

events.title: First athletic contests and wild-beast hunt at Rome
events.summary: Marcus Fulvius Nobilior celebrated votive games for his Aetolian victory lasting ten days, at which Rome saw for the first time Greek athletic contests and a venatio, a hunt of lions and panthers. Many Greek actors came to honour him.

events.title: The Saltus Marcius disaster
events.summary: The consul Quintus Marcius Philippus pursued the Apuani into a narrow wooded pass where they ambushed him, killing about 4,000 men and taking three standards of the second legion and eleven allied ones. The place, Livy says, was afterwards called the Saltus Marcius.

battle.significance: The worst Roman defeat in the Ligurian wars.

events.title: Deserted colonies of Sipontum and Buxentum resettled
events.summary: The consul Spurius Postumius, travelling through Italy during the Bacchanalia inquiry, found that the citizen colonies of Sipontum and Buxentum, founded in 194, had been deserted by their settlers. New colonists were enrolled in 186 and sent out the following year.

events.title: Transalpine Gauls settle near the site of Aquileia
events.summary: About 12,000 armed Transalpine Gauls crossed into Venetia and began building a town near the future Aquileia without asking permission. After embassies across the Alps, the Romans disarmed them in 183 and sent them back, and the Senate decided to plant a Latin colony there.

events.title: War of Eumenes II and Prusias I; Hannibal's snake jars
events.summary: Prusias I of Bithynia fought Eumenes II over disputed borderland, with Hannibal as his admiral. Nepos tells how Hannibal had jars filled with snakes thrown onto Pergamene decks to throw the crews into panic. A Roman embassy under Flamininus imposed peace in 183, and Hannibal's surrender was demanded.

battle.significance: Hannibal's last victory.

events.title: Battle of the Tagus
events.summary: After a defeat in 186, the praetors Gaius Calpurnius Piso and Lucius Quinctius Crispinus forced a crossing of the Tagus against Carpetani and Celtiberians and won a large victory, claiming 35,000 enemy dead. Both triumphed in 184.

battle.significance: Secured the Tagus line before the First Celtiberian War.

events.title: Conspiracy of the Apulian herdsmen
events.summary: The praetor Lucius Postumius, sent to Tarentum, investigated a 'great conspiracy of shepherds' who had made the roads and pasturelands unsafe, and condemned about 7,000 men; many escaped. He also continued the Bacchanalian inquiry in the south.

events.title: Censorship of Cato
events.summary: Cato and Lucius Valerius Flaccus held the most famous censorship in Roman history. Cato expelled seven senators, among them the ex-consul Lucius Quinctius Flamininus for killing a Gallic noble at a banquet to amuse a boy lover, took the public horse from Lucius Scipio Asiaticus, assessed luxury goods, slaves and carriages at ten times their value and taxed them, cut off private pipes illegally drawing public water, demolished buildings encroaching on public land, and let public contracts at harsh prices.

events.title: Basilica Porcia, the first basilica in Rome
events.summary: Cato as censor bought two houses and four shops by the Curia and built the Basilica Porcia, the first known basilica in Rome, a covered hall for business and courts. The tribunes of the plebs later used it as their headquarters. It burned with the Curia in 52 BC.

events.title: The massacre at Maronea
events.summary: When a Roman commission ordered Philip V to withdraw his garrisons from the Thracian coast, his agent Onomastus and the officer Cassander let Thracians into Maronea at night to massacre the anti-Macedonian citizens. Rome demanded Onomastus and Cassander; Philip sent only Cassander, who died on the way, it was said by poison.

events.title: Ennius receives Roman citizenship
events.summary: Quintus Fulvius Nobilior, son of Ennius' patron and one of the commissioners founding the citizen colonies of Potentia and Pisaurum, enrolled Ennius as a colonist, giving him Roman citizenship. Ennius commemorated it: 'nos sumus Romani qui fuimus ante Rudini' ('We are Romans, who were once men of Rudiae').

events.title: Death of Plautus
events.summary: Cicero dates the death of Titus Maccius Plautus, the Umbrian from Sarsina whose 21 surviving comedies (the canon Varro accepted) are the oldest complete works of Latin literature, to the censorship of Cato in 184. His adaptations of Greek New Comedy filled the expanding Roman festival calendar from about 205.

events.title: Death of Scipio Africanus
events.summary: Scipio Africanus died in voluntary exile at his villa at Liternum, aged about 52. He reportedly asked to be buried there rather than in ungrateful Rome; Valerius Maximus quotes the epitaph 'Ingrata patria, ne ossa quidem mea habes'.

events.title: Death of Hannibal
events.summary: After Apamea Hannibal fled via Crete (where, Nepos says, he hid his treasure in amphorae filled with lead) to Armenia and then to Prusias I of Bithynia, for whom he won a naval battle against Eumenes by hurling jars of snakes onto the enemy ships. When Flamininus came as envoy and Prusias agreed to surrender him, Hannibal took poison at Libyssa, saying, according to Livy, 'let us relieve the Romans of their long anxiety'.

events.title: Death of Philopoemen
events.summary: The seventy-year-old Achaean general Philopoemen, 'the last of the Greeks', was captured by rebel Messenians and forced to drink poison in prison. The young Polybius carried his funeral urn in the procession to Megalopolis.

events.title: Colonies of Parma, Mutina and Saturnia; Potentia and Pisaurum
events.summary: A burst of colonisation in the north and on the Adriatic: citizen colonies at Potentia and Pisaurum (184), Parma and Mutina with 2,000 settlers each and Saturnia (183), and Graviscae (181). Unlike earlier Latin colonies these were citizen colonies with substantial allotments.

events.title: War of Pharnaces I against Eumenes II
events.summary: Pharnaces I of Pontus seized Sinope in 183 and pushed into Galatia and Paphlagonia, fighting Eumenes II, Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia and Prusias II. Repeated Roman embassies failed until, in 179, a peace dictated in Rome's shadow forced Pharnaces to give up his conquests except Sinope, which became the Pontic capital.

events.title: Lycortas captures Messene and avenges Philopoemen
events.summary: After the Messenian rebels executed Philopoemen in 183, his successor Lycortas besieged Messene, forced its surrender and compelled the ringleaders to kill themselves. Philopoemen's ashes were carried to Megalopolis in a solemn procession in which the young Polybius carried the urn.

events.title: Lex Orchia sumptuaria
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Orchius carried, with Senate backing, the first of the second-century sumptuary laws, limiting the number of guests at dinner parties. Cato spoke for it; the lex Fannia of 161 and lex Didia of 143 extended its restrictions to expenditure and to all Italy.

events.title: Founding of Aquileia
events.summary: A Latin colony of 3,000 infantry families was founded at Aquileia at the head of the Adriatic to block Gallic migrations and Istrian raids; it was reinforced with 1,500 more families in 169. It was the last Latin colony founded in Italy and grew into one of the great cities of the Empire.

events.title: Discovery and burning of the 'Books of Numa'
events.summary: Workmen digging on land of the scribe Lucius Petillius at the foot of the Janiculum found two stone chests, one inscribed as the coffin of King Numa, the other containing books on pontifical law in Latin and on Pythagorean philosophy in Greek. The urban praetor judged them subversive of religion and, with the Senate's approval, burned them in the Comitium.

events.title: Lex Cornelia Baebia de ambitu
events.summary: The consuls Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus carried the first known law against electoral bribery (ambitus), reflecting the escalating cost of competition for office. A related Lex Baebia provided for four and six praetors in alternate years, but was soon abandoned.

events.title: Battle of Aebura
events.summary: In the First Celtiberian War the praetor Quintus Fulvius Flaccus defeated a Celtiberian army near Aebura in Carpetania and in 180 fought his way through an ambush at the Manlian Pass. Livy claims 23,000 enemy killed at Aebura.

sides.strength: praetorian army under Q. Fulvius Flaccus

battle.significance: Opened the way for Gracchus' settlement.

events.title: Aemilius Paullus defeats the Ingauni
events.summary: The proconsul Lucius Aemilius Paullus, besieged in his camp by the Ingauni Ligurians during a sham truce, broke out and routed them, killing 15,000 and capturing 2,500. The Ingauni surrendered hostages and 32 pirate ships were taken. Paullus triumphed in 181.

battle.significance: Ended Ingaunian piracy on the coast route to Massalia.

events.title: Temple of Pietas and the first gilded statue
events.summary: Manius Acilius Glabrio, son of the victor of Thermopylae, dedicated the temple of Pietas in the vegetable market vowed by his father, and set up a gilded equestrian statue of his father, the first gilded statue in Italy.

events.title: Temple of Venus Erycina outside the Colline Gate
events.summary: Lucius Porcius Licinus dedicated a second temple of Venus of Eryx, vowed by his father in the Ligurian war of 184, outside the Colline Gate. Modelled on the Sicilian sanctuary, it became associated with prostitutes, who celebrated the goddess on 23 April.

events.title: Citizen colony at Graviscae
events.summary: A citizen colony of 300 families, each receiving five iugera, was founded at Graviscae, the old port of Tarquinii and site of a Greek emporium sanctuary, on the unhealthy Etruscan coast.

events.title: Lex Baebia on the number of praetors
events.summary: A law of the consul Marcus Baebius Tamphilus provided that four and six praetors be elected in alternate years, to reduce competition for the consulship. It was soon disregarded, and six praetors were elected annually from 177.

events.title: Lex Villia Annalis
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Villius carried a law fixing the minimum ages at which each magistracy could be held. It probably also required an interval of two years (biennium) between curule offices and made the praetorship a prerequisite for the consulship, regularising the cursus honorum.

events.title: Pestilence and poisoning trials
events.summary: A severe epidemic struck Rome and Italy between 182 and 180, killing a consul (Gaius Calpurnius Piso), a pontifex maximus and many others. Suspicion of poisoning led to special inquiries; Livy says 3,000 were condemned in 180, among them Piso's widow Hostilia, accused of poisoning her husband to make her son consul.

events.title: Deportation of the Apuan Ligurians to Samnium
events.summary: After years of Ligurian warfare, the proconsuls Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus forcibly moved 40,000 Apuan Ligurians with their women and children to public land in Samnium, giving them 150,000 sesterces for equipment. Another 7,000 followed. The deportees formed two communities, the Ligures Baebiani and Ligures Corneliani.
events.locName: Samnium (Ligures Baebiani, Macchia di Circello) from the Apuan Alps

events.title: Fulvius Flaccus fights his way through the Manlian pass
events.summary: Leaving Spain with his veterans, the praetor Quintus Fulvius Flaccus was ambushed by Celtiberians in the Manlian pass. The Roman column, fighting in the defile, beat off the attackers, killing 17,000 by Livy's figures. Flaccus vowed a temple to Fortuna Equestris after his cavalry broke the enemy wedge.

battle.significance: Closed the First Celtiberian War's fighting season before Gracchus arrived.

events.title: Callicrates before the Senate
events.summary: Sent by the Achaean League to defend its independent handling of the Spartan exiles, Callicrates instead advised the Senate to support its friends in every Greek state and to make clear that its wishes must be obeyed. Polybius dates the beginning of Greek political degeneration under Rome from this speech.

events.title: Philip V executes his son Demetrius
events.summary: Philip V's younger son Demetrius, former hostage and favourite of the Senate, was accused by his brother Perseus of plotting to flee to Rome and seize the throne with Roman help. After a forged letter purporting to come from Flamininus was produced, Philip had him poisoned in 180. Philip is said to have died the next year in remorse.

events.title: Latin colony at Luca
events.summary: Livy reports that the Pisans offered land for a Latin colony and that triumvirs led settlers to Luca in 180, on land taken from the Ligurians; Velleius dates Luca to 177. The colony guarded the Serchio valley route into the Apuan mountains.

events.title: Temples of Juno Regina, Diana and the Lares Permarini
events.summary: In December 179 Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, as censor, dedicated the temples of Juno Regina and Diana in the Circus Flaminius, vowed in his Ligurian war of 187, with games, and the temple of the Lares Permarini in the Campus Martius was dedicated with an inscription recording Regillus' naval victory over Antiochus.

events.title: Tiberius Gracchus' settlement of Celtiberia
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus (father of the Gracchi), praetor in Citerior 180-178, combined victories with negotiation. His treaties fixed tribute and military service obligations, settled landless Celtiberians, forbade the founding of new fortified towns, and founded Gracchurris on the upper Ebro. The peace held for 25 years.

events.title: Censorship of Lepidus and Nobilior: Basilica Aemilia and Pons Aemilius
events.summary: The censors Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Marcus Fulvius Nobilior, publicly reconciled from bitter enmity at the Senate's urging, built the Basilica Aemilia et Fulvia on the north side of the Forum, a fish market, a harbour and the piers of the first stone bridge over the Tiber, the Pons Aemilius, whose arches were completed in 142. They also reorganised voting in the tribal assembly by region, status and class.

events.title: Death of Philip V; accession of Perseus
events.summary: Philip V, who had rebuilt Macedonian strength since 196, died at Amphipolis in 179, haunted, as the tradition has it, by the execution in 180 of his pro-Roman younger son Demetrius on charges brought by his elder son Perseus, supported by a letter from Flamininus later said to be forged. Perseus succeeded and renewed the treaty with Rome.

events.title: Gracchus founds Gracchurris
events.summary: After taking Complega and a string of Celtiberian towns, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus founded Gracchurris on the site of the native town of Ilurcis in the upper Ebro valley, the first Roman town named after its founder. His colleague in Ulterior, Lucius Postumius Albinus, campaigned against the Vaccaei.

events.title: Second Istrian War: siege of Nesactium
events.summary: After the Istrians captured a Roman camp at the Timavus in 178 (its garrison was found drunk on the captured wine when retaken), the consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher besieged Nesactium and took it by diverting the river that supplied it. King Aepulo and the defenders killed their families and themselves. Istria submitted.

sides.strength: consular army under C. Claudius Pulcher

battle.significance: Ended Istrian independence.

events.title: Gracchus' war in Sardinia: 'Sardi venales'
events.summary: The consul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus crushed a rising of the Ilienses and Balari in Sardinia in 177-176, killing or capturing 80,000 according to the tablet he dedicated in the temple of Mater Matuta. So many captives were sold that 'Sardi venales' ('Sardinians for sale', i.e. cheap goods) became a proverb.

battle.significance: Broke Sardinian resistance for a generation; flooded the slave market.

events.title: Citizen colony at Luna
events.summary: A citizen colony of 2,000 settlers was founded at Luna on land taken from the Ligurians at the mouth of the Magra; it later became famous for the white marble of the nearby Apuan quarries (Carrara).

events.title: Lex Claudia de sociis and the second expulsion of Latins
events.summary: On the complaints of Latin and allied envoys, the consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher carried a law requiring Latins registered at Rome since 189 to return home by 1 November. Livy describes the tricks used to gain citizenship, such as selling sons as slaves to a Roman who then freed them, and fictitious manumissions.

events.title: Ligurians capture Mutina
events.summary: In 177 the Ligurians surprised the new citizen colony of Mutina and killed its settlers. The consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher, back from Istria, retook it in three days in 176, killing 8,000 Ligurians.

battle.significance: Restored the Aemilian road colonies.

events.title: Death of the consul Petillius on Mons Letum
events.summary: The consul Quintus Petillius Spurinus attacked Ligurians holding Mons Letum and the heights of Ballista. Having said in his speech that he would 'take Letum' that day, he was killed by a javelin while rallying his men. The army took the hill; the omen of 'Letum' (death) was much remarked.

battle.significance: A consul killed in action, rare in this period.

events.title: Triumph of Gracchus and the Sardinian tablet
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus triumphed over Sardinia in 175 and dedicated in the temple of Mater Matuta a tablet in the shape of the island with pictures of the battles, recording that under his command over 80,000 of the enemy had been killed or captured. So many Sardinian slaves were sold that 'Sardi venales' became a proverb for cheap goods.
events.locName: Temple of Mater Matuta, Forum Boarium

events.title: Murder of Seleucus IV; Antiochus IV seizes the throne
events.summary: Seleucus IV was murdered by his chief minister Heliodorus. His brother Antiochus, just released from Rome as a hostage in exchange for Seleucus' son Demetrius and living in Athens, was escorted home by Eumenes II and Attalus, expelled Heliodorus and took the throne as Antiochus IV, at first as co-regent with Seleucus' infant son.

events.title: Censorship of Fulvius Flaccus and Postumius Albinus
events.summary: The censors of 174 expelled nine senators, including Flaccus' own brother, and let contracts for the first paving of Rome's streets with flint (silex), gravel surfaces outside the city, the paving of the Clivus Capitolinus, a stepped approach from the Tiber to the emporium, and works in colonies such as Calatia, Auximum and Pisaurum. The census counted 269,015 citizens.

events.title: Pestilence of 174
events.summary: A severe epidemic struck Rome in 174, after cattle disease the year before. Livy says corpses lay unburied in the streets, the undertakers (Libitinarii) could not cope, and slaves and the poor died in great numbers; a praetor and several priests were among the dead.

events.title: Expulsion of two Epicurean philosophers
events.summary: In the consulship of Lucius Postumius, two Epicureans, Alcaeus and Philiscus, were expelled from Rome for corrupting the young with the doctrine of pleasure.

events.title: The Statellates affair
events.summary: The consul Marcus Popillius Laenas attacked the Ligurian Statellates, who had never fought Rome, and after they surrendered sold 10,000 of them into slavery. The Senate ordered their freedom and restitution; Popillius defied it. In 172 the tribunes passed a Lex Marcia for an inquiry, but Popillius' brother, the new consul, obstructed it and the case collapsed.

events.title: The marble tiles of Juno Lacinia
events.summary: To roof his temple of Fortuna Equestris in Rome, the censor Quintus Fulvius Flaccus had half the marble roof tiles stripped from the temple of Juno Lacinia near Croton, the most venerated sanctuary of Magna Graecia. The Senate condemned the sacrilege and ordered the tiles returned, but no one could be found to replace them and they were left in the temple precinct.
events.locName: Temple of Hera Lacinia, near Croton

events.title: Postumius Albinus burdens Praeneste
events.summary: The consul Lucius Postumius Albinus, offended because Praeneste had once neglected him as a private visitor, wrote ahead demanding that its magistrates meet him, provide lodging at public expense and furnish pack animals for his departure. Livy notes that no magistrate before him had imposed any charge on the allies, and that the precedent spread.

events.title: Locust plague in Apulia
events.summary: Swarms of locusts from the sea covered Apulia. The praetor-elect Gnaeus Sicinius was sent with full imperium and gathered a great crowd of men to collect and destroy them, which took a long time.

events.title: Temple of Fortuna Equestris
events.summary: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus dedicated the temple of Fortuna Equestris that he had vowed in Spain in 180, celebrating four days of scenic and one day of circus games. By the reign of Tiberius the temple had disappeared.
events.locName: Near the Theatre of Pompey, Rome

events.title: Both consuls plebeian for the first time
events.summary: Gaius Popillius Laenas and Publius Aelius Ligus were elected consuls for 172, the first time both consuls were plebeians. The Fasti Capitolini note 'ambo primi de plebe'. The Licinio-Sextian requirement that one consul be plebeian (367) had never been matched by a rule requiring a patrician.

events.title: Eumenes' denunciation of Perseus and the attack at Delphi
events.summary: Eumenes II came to Rome in person and denounced Perseus to the Senate for war preparations, his marriage alliance with the Seleucids and his intrigues in Greece. On his way home he was nearly killed by a rockfall at Delphi engineered, it was said, by Perseus' agents. The Senate decided on war.

events.title: Marcius Philippus' embassy and the 'new wisdom'
events.summary: Roman envoys led by Quintus Marcius Philippus met Perseus by the Peneus and induced him to accept a truce and send envoys to Rome, while Rome completed its mobilisation. Livy reports that older senators condemned this 'new wisdom' as unworthy of Roman good faith, which had once forewarned even enemies like Pyrrhus.

events.title: Carteia, the first Latin colony outside Italy
events.summary: More than 4,000 men, sons of Roman soldiers and Spanish women, who as children of unions without conubium had no citizenship, petitioned the Senate for a town. They were settled at Carteia near the Strait of Gibraltar as a Latin colony 'of freedmen' (libertinorum), together with the existing inhabitants who wished to join.

events.title: Spanish envoys accuse Roman governors
events.summary: Envoys from both Spanish provinces complained to the Senate of the greed of Roman magistrates. The praetor appointed panels of five senatorial recuperatores for each case, and patrons for the Spaniards, among them Cato, Aemilius Paullus and Scipio Nasica. One ex-governor was acquitted and two, Publius Furius Philus and Marcus Matienus, went into exile before verdict.

events.title: Battle of Callinicus
events.summary: Perseus caught the consul Publius Licinius Crassus' cavalry and light troops near the hill of Callinicus outside Larissa and routed them, but did not commit his phalanx to exploit the victory. He then offered peace on the terms of his father's treaty; the Romans, true to their custom of never negotiating after a defeat, refused.

sides.strength: cavalry and light infantry of P. Licinius Crassus' army
sides.losses: c. 200 cavalry and 2,000 infantry killed, 600 captured (Livy)

battle.significance: Perseus' only major victory; his failure to follow it up and Rome's refusal to negotiate set the pattern of the war.
