events.summary: The consul Lucius Calpurnius Bestia, with Scaurus on his staff, invaded Numidia and then quickly accepted Jugurtha's surrender on easy terms: 30 elephants, cattle, horses and a little silver. The tribune Gaius Memmius denounced the deal as bought, leading to Jugurtha's summons to Rome.

events.title: Capitulation of Aulus Albinus at Suthul
events.summary: Aulus Postumius Albinus, left in command by his brother the consul, marched in midwinter to seize Jugurtha's treasury at Suthul. A night attack, helped by bribed centurions and auxiliaries, broke his camp; the army passed under the yoke and agreed to leave Numidia within ten days.

sides.losses: camp taken, army sent under the yoke

battle.significance: The low point of the war; discredited the senatorial leadership at Rome.

events.note: Suthul is sometimes identified with Calama (Guelma).

events.title: The Mamilian commission
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Mamilius Limetanus established a special court, with equestrian juries, to try those who had taken Jugurtha's money. It condemned Opimius, Bestia, Spurius Albinus, Gaius Cato and the priest Gaius Sulpicius Galba. Scaurus, himself implicated, contrived to be one of the three presiding commissioners.

events.title: Battle of the Muthul
events.summary: Jugurtha ambushed Quintus Caecilius Metellus' column from a scrub-covered ridge parallel to its march. After a long day's fighting the Romans drove off the Numidian infantry while Publius Rutilius Rufus defeated Bomilcar's elephants, killing or capturing all 44.

sides.strength: consular army of perhaps 2 legions plus allies

battle.significance: Tactical Roman success that did not end the war; Jugurtha turned to guerrilla warfare.

events.title: Failed siege of Zama
events.summary: Metellus besieged Zama to force Jugurtha to battle but failed to take it and withdrew to winter quarters. Over the winter the garrison at Vaga was massacred in a rising, and its commander Turpilius, a friend of Metellus, was executed.

battle.significance: Showed the limits of siege warfare against a mobile enemy.

events.title: Scaurus builds the Pons Mulvius and Via Aemilia Scauri
events.summary: As censor Marcus Aemilius Scaurus rebuilt the Milvian Bridge over the Tiber in stone and built the Via Aemilia Scauri along the Tyrrhenian coast from Pisa via Vada to Dertona. The bridge's piers still carry traffic.

events.title: Silanus defeated by the Cimbri
events.summary: The consul Marcus Junius Silanus refused the Cimbri's request for land in exchange for military service and was defeated somewhere in southern Gaul, the second Roman army beaten by the migrants. He was tried and acquitted in 104.

battle.significance: Confirmed that the Cimbri could beat Roman armies in the open field.

events.title: Minucius Rufus defeats the Scordisci
events.summary: Marcus Minucius Rufus, consul 110 and proconsul of Macedonia, defeated the Scordisci and Thracian Bessi, many drowning in the frozen Hebrus. With the spoils of his triumph (106) he built the Porticus Minucia on the Campus Martius, later used for grain distributions.

events.title: Siege of Thala
events.summary: Metellus marched across waterless country, carrying water in skins on pack animals, and took Jugurtha's treasure town Thala after a 40-day siege. Jugurtha escaped with his children and much of the treasure; Roman deserters inside burned themselves in the palace.

battle.significance: Showed Rome could reach Jugurtha's strongholds; prompted Bocchus of Mauretania to join Jugurtha.

events.title: Marius elected consul for 107
events.summary: Gaius Marius, a novus homo from Arpinum and Metellus' legate, returned to Rome against his commander's wishes, campaigned on Metellus' slowness and was elected consul. A tribunician law then gave him the Numidian command, overriding the senate's decision to prorogue Metellus.

events.title: Marius enrols the capite censi
events.summary: Raising reinforcements for Numidia, Marius enrolled volunteers from the proletarii (capite censi, those assessed by head count) rather than conscripting from the property classes. Sallust says he did it to court popularity or because the poor had nothing to lose.

events.title: Defeat of Cassius Longinus by the Tigurini
events.summary: The consul Lucius Cassius Longinus, Marius' colleague, was killed with his legate Lucius Piso in an ambush by the Tigurini, a Helvetian canton, led by the young Divico. The legate Gaius Popillius Laenas saved the survivors by surrendering half the baggage and sending the army under the yoke.
events.locName: territory of the Nitiobriges, near Agen

sides.losses: consul and legate killed; army under the yoke

battle.significance: Another consular army lost; the Volcae Tectosages of Tolosa defected.

events.note: Orosius places it near Burdigala; Livy's Periocha says in the territory of the Nitiobriges (Agen).

events.title: Marius takes Capsa
events.summary: Marius marched for days across desert, driving cattle for food and water, and stormed Capsa at dawn. Though it surrendered, the town was burned, its adult men killed and the rest sold, the booty divided among the troops.

battle.significance: Bold deep raid that demonstrated no Numidian town was beyond reach.

events.title: Lex Coelia tabellaria
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Coelius Caldus extended the secret ballot to trials for perduellio (treason) before the people, completing the series of ballot laws begun in 139. He had been determined to convict Gaius Popillius Laenas for the surrender of his army to the Tigurini.

events.title: Births of Cicero and Pompey
events.summary: Marcus Tullius Cicero was born at Arpinum on 3 January 106 to an equestrian family; Gnaeus Pompeius, son of the Picene grandee Pompeius Strabo, was born on 29 September of the same year, sharing the consular year of Atilius Serranus and Servilius Caepio.

events.title: Capture of the fort on the Mulucha
events.summary: On the far western border of Numidia Marius besieged a fort on a sheer rock holding a royal treasury. A Ligurian auxiliary, climbing to gather snails, found a route up the back; a small party with trumpeters scaled it and panicked the defenders.

battle.significance: Deprived Jugurtha of treasure on the Mauretanian border, pressuring Bocchus.

events.title: Battles near Cirta
events.summary: Returning east to winter quarters, Marius' army was attacked at dusk by Jugurtha and Bocchus combined and held a pair of hills through the night; a dawn sally routed the Africans. A few days later a second battle near Cirta, with Sulla commanding the cavalry, ended in another Roman victory.

sides.strength: large combined Numidian and Moorish cavalry and infantry

battle.significance: Broke the Numidian-Mauretanian alliance militarily and led Bocchus to betray Jugurtha.

events.title: Lex Servilia Caepionis
events.summary: The consul Quintus Servilius Caepio carried a law restoring senators to the extortion juries, alone or alongside equites. Crassus the orator's speech for it (attacking equestrian juries) was a celebrated model. It was reversed within a few years by Glaucia's law.

events.title: The gold of Tolosa
events.summary: Caepio occupied Tolosa, whose Volcae Tectosages had joined the Cimbri, and seized temple treasures and sacred lakes of bullion that Posidonius put at 15,000 talents. The convoy sent to Massalia was ambushed and the treasure vanished; Caepio was widely suspected, and 'having Tolosan gold' became a proverb for ill-gotten wealth that brings ruin.

events.title: Battle of Arausio
events.summary: The proconsul Quintus Servilius Caepio and the consul Gnaeus Mallius Maximus, refusing to coordinate because Caepio despised the novus homo Mallius, were destroyed one after the other by the Cimbri and Teutones under Boiorix. It was Rome's worst defeat since Cannae.

sides.strength: two consular armies, perhaps 10 legions with allies
migrating host of Cimbri, Teutones and allies

battle.significance: Opened Italy to invasion; produced Marius' five consecutive consulships and the army reforms associated with them.

events.title: Rutilius Rufus introduces gladiatorial weapons drill
events.summary: After Arausio the consul Publius Rutilius Rufus, raising emergency levies, brought in instructors from the gladiatorial school of Gaius Aurelius Scaurus to teach recruits swordsmanship. Marius chose Rutilius' trained troops over his own for the Cimbric campaign.

events.title: Bocchus hands Jugurtha to Sulla
events.summary: After months of secret negotiation, Bocchus of Mauretania lured Jugurtha to a meeting and handed him in chains to Marius' quaestor, Lucius Cornelius Sulla, ending the war. Bocchus received the western part of Numidia.

events.title: Marius' Numidian triumph and death of Jugurtha
events.summary: Marius celebrated his triumph over Jugurtha on the day he entered his second consulship, then entered the senate still in triumphal dress, a breach of custom. Jugurtha was thrown naked into the Tullianum; Plutarch has him exclaim how cold the Romans' bath was before he starved six days later.

events.title: Marius' five consecutive consulships
events.summary: From 104 to 100 Marius held the consulship every year, his second to sixth, in defiance of the rule requiring ten years between tenures. The Cimbri obligingly wandered off to Spain in 104-103, giving him two years to train a new army in Transalpine Gaul.

events.title: Lex Domitia de sacerdotiis
events.summary: The tribune Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, angry at not being co-opted into the pontifical college, carried a law that vacancies in the major priestly colleges be filled by a vote of 17 of the 35 tribes from candidates nominated by the college. Sulla repealed it; Labienus restored it in 63, enabling Caesar's election as pontifex maximus.

events.title: Outbreak of the Second Sicilian Slave War
events.summary: When the senate, needing troops against the Cimbri, ordered governors to free allied citizens enslaved for debt by publicani, the praetor of Sicily, Licinius Nerva, freed 800 and then stopped under pressure from owners. Slaves rose, choosing as king Salvius, who took the name Tryphon and built a capital at Triocala, while Athenion, a Cilician, led a rising in the west.

events.title: Marius digs the Fossa Mariana
events.summary: While waiting for the Cimbri and Teutones to return from Spain, Marius had his army dig a canal from the Rhône delta to the sea near Fos, bypassing silted mouths so that supply ships could reach his camp. He later gave the canal and its tolls to Massalia.

events.title: Battle of Scirthaea
events.summary: The praetor Lucius Licinius Lucullus with some 17,000 men defeated Tryphon's slave army near Scirthaea but failed to take Triocala and was later convicted, allegedly for destroying his own siege works to spite his successor.

battle.significance: Checked but did not end the revolt.

events.title: Saturninus' first tribunate and the lex Appuleia de maiestate
events.summary: As tribune in 103 Lucius Appuleius Saturninus carried land grants of 100 iugera in Africa for Marius' veterans and a law creating the crime of diminishing the majesty of the Roman people (maiestas minuta), tried by an equestrian court. It was aimed at incompetent nobles like Caepio and Mallius.

events.title: Saturninus' land law for Marius' veterans
events.summary: In his first tribunate Lucius Appuleius Saturninus allotted 100 iugera each in Africa to Marius' Jugurthine veterans, the first settlement of a general's soldiers by tribunician law. The colonists were settled around Thibaris, Uchi Maius and Thuburnica, whose inscriptions later honoured Marius.

events.title: Battle of Aquae Sextiae
events.summary: Marius destroyed the Teutones and Ambrones near Aquae Sextiae. A skirmish at a stream between water-carriers drew in the Ambrones, who were beaten; two days later the Teutones attacked uphill into Marius' line while Claudius Marcellus with 3,000 men fell on their rear.
events.locName: plain below Mont Sainte-Victoire, near Aquae Sextiae

battle.significance: Annihilated the Teutones and removed the western half of the migratory threat to Italy.

events.title: Catulus abandons the Alpine passes
events.summary: The consul Quintus Lutatius Catulus, guarding the Brenner route against the Cimbri, fell back from the Atiso (Adige) when his men panicked; a detachment's fort beyond the river held out and was released by the Cimbri on oath. The Cimbri overran Transpadane Italy that winter.

events.title: Marcus Antonius' command against the pirates
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Antonius, grandfather of the triumvir, received a special command against the pirates of Cilicia, operating from Side and Athens; his fleet was hauled across the Isthmus of Corinth. He triumphed in 100, and Cilicia became a praetorian provincia in the sense of a task.

events.title: Battle of Vercellae (Campi Raudii)
events.summary: Marius and the proconsul Quintus Lutatius Catulus, whose army had retreated from the Adige before the Cimbri in 102, annihilated the Cimbri on the Raudine Plain in the July heat. King Boiorix died fighting; the Cimbrian women killed their children and themselves at the wagon laager.

battle.significance: Ended the Cimbric threat; made Marius the first man in Rome and his veterans a political force.

events.title: Marius' Temple of Honos and Virtus
events.summary: From the spoils of the Cimbri and Teutones, Marius built a temple of Honour and Virtue, probably on the Velia or Capitoline, deliberately kept low so as not to obstruct the augurs' view. Cicero's recall in 57 was voted by the Senate meeting there.

events.title: Birth of Gaius Julius Caesar
events.summary: Gaius Julius Caesar was born on 12 or 13 July, probably in 100, to a patrician family of modest recent success whose aunt Julia had married Marius. The family lived in the Subura.

events.title: Law on the pirates (lex de provinciis praetoriis)
events.summary: A Roman law of c. 101/100, preserved in Greek translation on inscriptions from Delphi and Cnidus, ordered the consul to write to the kings of Cyprus, Egypt, Cyrene and Syria to deny harbour to pirates, assigned Cilicia as a praetorian command and laid down rules for governors of Macedonia.

events.title: Manius Aquillius ends the Second Servile War
events.summary: The consul of 101, Manius Aquillius, Marius' colleague, killed Athenion in single combat and stamped out the revolt by 100. A thousand captives sent to Rome to fight beasts in the arena killed one another instead, the last stabbing himself.

battle.significance: Ended the revolt; Aquillius was later prosecuted for extortion and acquitted after baring his battle scars.

events.title: The crisis of 100: Saturninus, Glaucia and the second senatus consultum ultimum
events.summary: Saturninus, tribune again with Marius consul for the sixth time, carried colonies and land for veterans with violence, and required senators to swear to obey his agrarian law. When his gangs killed the consular candidate Gaius Memmius, the senate passed the senatus consultum ultimum and Marius besieged his own allies on the Capitol, cutting the water. They surrendered, were locked in the Curia Hostilia, and a mob tore off the roof tiles and stoned them to death.

events.title: Murder of Gaius Memmius at the consular elections
events.summary: During the elections for 99, Gaius Memmius, the former tribune who had attacked Jugurtha's patrons, was clubbed to death in the Campus Martius by men linked to Saturninus and Glaucia, who feared he would beat Glaucia to the consulship. The killing turned Marius and the equites against his former allies.

events.title: Recall of Metellus Numidicus
events.summary: After a campaign led by his son, who earned the name Pius for it, Metellus Numidicus was recalled from exile by a tribune's law. Marius left Rome for a tour of Asia rather than witness his return.

events.title: Lex Caecilia Didia
events.summary: The consuls Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos and Titus Didius required a gap of three market days (trinundinum) between publication of a bill and the vote and forbade omnibus bills (leges saturae) that bundled unrelated measures. In 91 it was used to annul Drusus' laws.

events.title: Senate bans human sacrifice
events.summary: In the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus and Publius Licinius Crassus a senatus consultum forbade human sacrifice, a generation after the burial alive of Gauls and Greeks in the Forum Boarium in 114/113. Pliny says the rite had been performed publicly 'even in our own time'.

events.title: Ptolemy Apion bequeaths Cyrene to Rome
events.summary: Ptolemy Apion, king of Cyrene, left his kingdom to Rome. The senate accepted the royal lands but left the cities free; Cyrenaica was organised as a province only in 74, and joined to Crete in 67.

events.title: Sulla meets the Parthian envoy Orobazus
events.summary: As governor of Cilicia, after restoring Ariobarzanes to the throne of Cappadocia, Sulla received the first Parthian embassy to Rome on the Euphrates. He placed himself on the central chair between the Parthian Orobazus and Ariobarzanes, and the Parthian king later executed Orobazus for accepting the humiliation.

events.title: Lex Licinia Mucia
events.summary: The consuls Lucius Licinius Crassus and Quintus Mucius Scaevola established a court to expel from the citizen rolls Italians who had passed themselves off as Romans. Asconius calls it the chief cause of the Social War, so thoroughly did it alienate the Italian leadership.

events.title: Sulla installs Ariobarzanes in Cappadocia
events.summary: After Mithridates and Nicomedes III of Bithynia had both put pretenders on the Cappadocian throne, the Senate let the Cappadocians choose a king; they chose Ariobarzanes I. Sulla, governing Cilicia, installed him with a small force, driving out Gordius and Armenian troops.

events.title: Scaevola's model governorship of Asia
events.summary: Quintus Mucius Scaevola, with Rutilius Rufus as legate, governed Asia with conspicuous honesty, curbing the publicani. His edict became a model that Cicero adopted in Cilicia in 51, and the Asians founded a festival in his honour, the Mucia.

events.title: Condemnation of Rutilius Rufus
events.summary: Publius Rutilius Rufus, the upright consular and former legate in Asia, was convicted of extortion by an equestrian jury in revenge for checking the publicani. He went into exile among the provincials he had supposedly robbed, at Mytilene and Smyrna, where they honoured him, and wrote memoirs; he refused Sulla's later invitation to return.

events.title: Censors' edict against the Latin rhetoricians
events.summary: The censors Crassus the orator and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus condemned the new schools teaching rhetoric in Latin as contrary to ancestral custom. Teaching oratory in Latin rather than Greek threatened the elite's monopoly of political education.

events.title: Tribunate and murder of Marcus Livius Drusus
events.summary: Marcus Livius Drusus, son of Gaius Gracchus' opponent, proposed to enrol 300 equites in the senate and return the juries to it, to found colonies, cheapen grain and, finally, to give citizenship to the Italians. The consul Philippus had his laws annulled on technical grounds, and in the autumn Drusus was stabbed in the atrium of his house.

events.title: Massacre of the Romans at Asculum
events.summary: Learning that Asculum was exchanging hostages with neighbouring peoples, the proconsul Quintus Servilius rebuked the town at a festival; the Asculans killed him, his legate Fonteius and every Roman in the town. It was the signal for the Social War.

events.title: Battle of the Tolenus
events.summary: The consul Publius Rutilius Lupus, ignoring the advice of his legate Marius, crossed the Tolenus and was ambushed by the Marsi under Vettius Scato; Rutilius and 8,000 men were killed. Marius, crossing elsewhere, took the Marsic camp.

battle.significance: Worst Roman defeat of the war's first year; contributed to the concession of the lex Julia.

events.title: The Italian confederation founds 'Italia' at Corfinium
events.summary: The Marsi, Paeligni, Vestini, Marrucini, Picentes, Frentani, Hirpini, Samnites, Lucanians and others formed a state with its capital at Corfinium, renamed Italia, a senate of 500, two consuls (Quintus Poppaedius Silo for the Marsic group, Gaius Papius Mutilus for the Samnite) and twelve praetors. It struck its own silver with the legend ITALIA and in Oscan VITELIU, some showing the Italian bull goring the Roman wolf.

events.title: Lex Julia de civitate
events.summary: The consul Lucius Julius Caesar carried a law granting citizenship to Latins and to allied communities that had stayed loyal or laid down arms, and allowing commanders to enfranchise individuals for valour. It peeled Etruria and Umbria away from the revolt.

events.title: Lex Varia and the treason trials of 90
events.summary: The tribune Quintus Varius Hybrida set up a special court, staffed by equestrian jurors, to try those who had encouraged the allies to revolt. It struck at the friends of Drusus: Gaius Aurelius Cotta went into exile, Lucius Memmius and others were condemned. Varius himself was condemned under his own law in 89.

events.title: Vettius Scato defeats Perperna
events.summary: Early in 90 the Roman legate Gaius Perperna lost 4,000 men and most of his weapons to the Marsic-Paelignian commander Publius Vettius Scato. The consul Rutilius Lupus stripped him of his command and transferred his remaining troops to Marius.

battle.significance: One of a string of Italian successes in the first campaigning season.

events.title: Vettius Scato defeats the consul Lucius Caesar
events.summary: The consul Lucius Julius Caesar, commanding the southern front, was defeated by Vettius Scato with the loss of 2,000 men; Venafrum was then betrayed to the Samnite Marius Egnatius, who destroyed two Roman cohorts there.

battle.significance: Opened the Volturnus corridor to the Samnites.

events.title: Siege of Aesernia
events.summary: The Latin colony of Aesernia, held by Lucius Cornelius Scipio and Lucius Acilius (who escaped dressed as slaves), was blockaded by the Samnites through 90 and surrendered from starvation late in the year. It became a rebel stronghold and, in 89/88, the seat of the Italian government after Corfinium.

battle.significance: Gave the insurgents a fortified base in the heart of Samnium.

events.title: Papius Mutilus invades Campania
events.summary: The Samnite commander Gaius Papius Mutilus took Nola by betrayal, executing Roman officers who refused to join him, then captured Stabiae, Minturnae, Salernum and Liternum and enrolled their slaves and prisoners. He besieged Acerrae, the key to Capua.

events.title: Siege of Acerrae and Lucius Caesar's victory
events.summary: Lucius Julius Caesar, reinforced by 10,000 Gauls and Numidian horse, held Acerrae against Papius Mutilus and in a sortie killed some 6,000 Samnites, the first real Roman success of the war. The news let Romans in the city put off the military cloak (sagum).

sides.strength: consular army with Gallic and Numidian auxiliaries

battle.significance: Restored morale in Rome; the Numidian cavalry deserted after Mutilus paraded a captured son of Jugurtha, Oxyntas.

events.title: Poppaedius Silo ambushes Servilius Caepio
events.summary: Quintus Servilius Caepio, sharing command of Rutilius' army with Marius, was lured into an ambush by Quintus Poppaedius Silo, who came over as a pretended deserter with his own sons as hostages and two lumps of gilded lead as treasure. Caepio and most of his force were killed.
events.locName: Marsic territory near the Fucine Lake

battle.significance: Left Marius in sole command of the northern army.

events.title: Marius defeats the Marsi and Marrucini
events.summary: After Rutilius' death Marius, cautious and refusing battle until he chose his ground, defeated the Marsi and Marrucini in a battle in which the Marrucine commander Herius Asinius fell; with Sulla's help some 6,000 rebels were killed. He was nevertheless criticised as slow and resigned the command at year's end.

battle.significance: Stabilised the northern front.

events.title: Pompeius Strabo besieged at Firmum
events.summary: Defeated by the Picene and Marsic commanders Titus Lafrenius, Gaius Vidacilius and Publius Ventidius near Mount Falernus, Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo shut himself up in Firmum. Relieved by Sulpicius, he broke out, killed Lafrenius and drove the rebels back into Asculum.

battle.significance: Opened the siege of Asculum, epicentre of the revolt.

events.title: Etruria and Umbria waver
events.summary: Late in 90 there were risings or threats of revolt among the Umbrians and Etruscans, put down by Aulus Plotius and Lucius Porcius Cato. The danger was a main reason for the lex Julia's offer of citizenship to communities that had stayed loyal or laid down arms.

events.title: Coinage of the Italian insurgents
events.summary: The confederates struck denarii on the Roman standard with Oscan or Latin legends, ITALIA or VITELIU, a helmeted Italia, scenes of eight warriors swearing an oath over a sow, and the Sabellian bull goring the Roman wolf. Issuing generals' names (C. PAAPI, Q. SILO) appear in Oscan.

events.title: Sulla destroys Stabiae
events.summary: Sulla, legate in Campania, captured Stabiae on the day before the Kalends of May 89 (29 or 30 April, depending on the calendar reckoning), as Pliny records, and razed it; it survived only as a village of villas, later buried by Vesuvius in AD 79. He went on to besiege Pompeii and Herculaneum.

battle.significance: Began the reconquest of the Bay of Naples.

events.title: Pompeius Strabo enfranchises the Spanish horsemen at Asculum
events.summary: A bronze tablet records that on 17 November 89, in camp before Asculum, Pompeius Strabo granted citizenship 'for valour' to thirty horsemen of the turma Salluitana from the Ebro valley, under the lex Julia. His council (consilium) listed on it includes his son Gnaeus Pompeius (the future Magnus) and the young Lucius Sergius Catilina.

events.title: Lex Plautia Papiria
events.summary: The tribunes Marcus Plautius Silvanus and Gaius Papirius Carbo offered citizenship to any man enrolled as a citizen of an allied community who was domiciled in Italy and registered with a praetor at Rome within sixty days. With the lex Julia it effectively enfranchised Italy south of the Po.

events.title: Lex Pompeia on the Transpadanes
events.summary: The consul Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo gave Latin rights to the communities north of the Po, so their magistrates became Roman citizens. Full citizenship for the Transpadanes became a popularis cause (Crassus as censor in 65, Caesar) until Caesar granted it in 49.

events.title: Siege of Asculum
events.summary: Pompeius Strabo besieged Asculum from 90, defeated a relief army of the Italians outside the walls and took the town in late 89, executing its leaders. The Italian commander Judacilius poisoned himself on a pyre in a temple.

sides.strength: Picentes and allies; relief army allegedly 75,000

battle.significance: Crushed the revolt in Picenum and gave Strabo a triumph (25 December 89).

events.title: Sulla takes Aeclanum and Bovianum
events.summary: Sulla, legate in the south, burned the wooden walls of the Hirpinian town of Aeclanum and sacked it, prompting the Hirpini to submit; he then beat Papius Mutilus and stormed Bovianum, the insurgents' later capital. Earlier at Nola he had won the grass crown (corona graminea), the rarest of Roman military honours.

battle.significance: Broke the southern insurgency and made Sulla's name; elected consul for 88.

events.title: Murder of the praetor Asellio and the debt crisis
events.summary: With credit collapsing in wartime, the urban praetor Aulus Sempronius Asellio allowed debtors to invoke ancient laws against usury. Creditors murdered him while he sacrificed at the temple of Castor, and no one was convicted.

events.title: Battle of the Amnias
events.summary: Mithridates' generals Archelaus and Neoptolemus routed Nicomedes IV of Bithynia, whom the Roman envoy Manius Aquillius had pushed into raiding Pontus. Aquillius' own forces were then scattered and Mithridates overran Bithynia and Asia.

sides.losses: camp and much of the army lost

sides.strength: Pontic advance force with scythed chariots

battle.significance: Opened Asia to Mithridates and began the First Mithridatic War.

events.title: Death of the consul Lucius Porcius Cato at the Fucine Lake
events.summary: The consul Lucius Porcius Cato, after successes against the Marsi, was killed attacking their camp near the Fucine Lake; Orosius says he was struck down by the son of Marius in the confusion. He was the second consul killed in the war.

battle.significance: Left Pompeius Strabo as sole consul in the field.

events.title: Siege of Pompeii
events.summary: Sulla besieged Pompeii, whose walls still show the impact craters of ballista stones and lead sling bullets; painted Oscan notices (eituns inscriptions) directing defenders to their posts survive on house walls. The town submitted and later received a colony of Sulla's veterans (80).

sides.strength: garrison and Lucius Cluentius' relieving army

battle.significance: Archaeologically the best-documented siege of the war.

events.title: Sulla defeats Cluentius before Nola
events.summary: Attacked while besieging Pompeii by the Samnite Lucius Cluentius, Sulla drove him back to the walls of Nola and, according to Appian, killed 20,000 of his men, including Cluentius. His army awarded him the grass crown (corona graminea), the highest Roman military honour.

battle.significance: Made Sulla's reputation and his consulship for 88.

events.title: Surrender of the Marsi, Vestini and Paeligni
events.summary: During 89 the northern peoples gave up: the Vestini and Marrucini to Servius Sulpicius Galba, the Marsi to Cinna and Caecilius Pius, the Paeligni after the fall of Asculum. The rebel capital moved from Corfinium to Aesernia.

events.title: Lex Papiria reduces the as to half an ounce
events.summary: A lex Papiria, usually dated 91 or 89, reduced the bronze as to the semuncial standard (half an ounce). Bronze was scarcely struck after the 80s until the Augustan reform; the Social War economy ran on denarii, which were minted in record quantities.
events.locName: Mint at the Temple of Juno Moneta

events.title: Nicomedes IV raids Pontus at Roman instigation
events.summary: Pressed by the legate Manius Aquillius and Roman creditors to whom he owed vast sums, Nicomedes IV of Bithynia raided Pontic territory as far as Amastris. Mithridates protested to Rome through his envoy Pelopidas, was rebuffed, and occupied Cappadocia, beginning the First Mithridatic War.

events.title: The Asiatic Vespers
events.summary: On secret orders from Mithridates, issued at Ephesus, the cities of Asia on an appointed day killed all resident Romans and Italians, men, women, children and freedmen. Ancient totals are 80,000 (Valerius Maximus, Memnon) or 150,000 (Plutarch).
events.locName: Ephesus and the cities of Asia

events.title: Execution of Manius Aquillius with molten gold
events.summary: Handed over by Mytilene, the consular Manius Aquillius was paraded on a donkey and executed at Pergamon by having molten gold poured down his throat, a comment on Roman greed.

events.title: Mithridates' siege of Rhodes
events.summary: Rhodes, a refuge for Romans from Asia, beat off Mithridates' fleet and a siege that culminated in a night assault with a huge sambuca mounted on two ships, which collapsed. Mithridates withdrew.

battle.significance: Kept a naval base loyal to Rome in the Aegean.

events.title: The laws of Publius Sulpicius Rufus
events.summary: The tribune Publius Sulpicius Rufus, once a friend of Drusus, carried laws distributing the new Italian citizens and freedmen across all 35 tribes, recalling exiles, expelling senators with debts above 2,000 denarii, and transferring the Mithridatic command from the consul Sulla to Marius. He used an armed following of 3,000 he called his anti-senate.

events.title: Sulla's first march on Rome
events.summary: Sulla persuaded his six legions at Nola that Marius would take them away and raise a different army for the lucrative eastern war, and led them on Rome. All his officers except one quaestor refused to follow. He fought his way in through the Esquiline with fire-arrows, declared Marius, Sulpicius and ten others public enemies, and passed laws curbing the tribunate.

events.title: Flight of Marius: Minturnae and the ruins of Carthage
events.summary: Marius fled along the coast and hid neck-deep in the marshes of Minturnae, where he was caught and condemned. The Cimbrian slave sent to kill him dropped his sword, reportedly at Marius' cry, 'Man, do you dare to kill Gaius Marius?', and the townsfolk let him go. He reached Africa, where he told the governor's messenger to report that he had seen Marius sitting among the ruins of Carthage.

events.title: Death of Poppaedius Silo
events.summary: Silo, who had retaken Bovianum and entered it in triumph, was killed in battle against the praetor Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius in Apulia, ending effective resistance outside Samnium and Lucania.

battle.significance: Effectively ended the confederation as a military power.

events.title: Murder of the consul Quintus Pompeius Rufus
events.summary: Sent to take over Pompeius Strabo's army in Picenum after Sulla's march on Rome, the consul Quintus Pompeius Rufus was killed by Strabo's soldiers while sacrificing, almost certainly with Strabo's connivance. Strabo resumed command.

events.title: Mithridates overruns Roman Asia
events.summary: After routing Nicomedes on the Amnias and the Roman forces at Protopachium, Mithridates swept through Phrygia, Mysia and Ionia almost unopposed. Cities opened their gates and cancelled debts; Lucius Cassius fled to Rhodes, Oppius was surrendered at Laodicea, and Aquillius was handed over at Mytilene. Mithridates made Pergamon and then Ephesus his capital.

events.title: Sack of Delos
events.summary: The Pontic general Archelaus (or Menophanes, in Pausanias' version) seized Delos, where Italian merchants had dominated the slave and luxury trade since it became a free port in 166. Some 20,000 people, mainly Italians, were reportedly killed and the island's treasures sent to Athens. A second pirate sack in 69 completed its decline.

battle.significance: Ended Delos as the hub of the Aegean slave trade.

events.title: Aristion brings Athens over to Mithridates
events.summary: The Peripatetic philosopher Athenion (called Aristion by most sources), returning from an embassy to Mithridates, persuaded the Athenian assembly to abandon Rome, became general with tyrannical powers, and admitted Archelaus' troops. Athenian silver tetradrachms of 87/86 bear Mithridates' star-and-crescent badge.

events.title: Bellum Octavianum: Cinna expelled from Rome
events.summary: The consul Lucius Cornelius Cinna revived Sulpicius' tribal distribution and was driven from Rome by his colleague Gnaeus Octavius in a battle in the Forum; the senate deposed him from the consulship. Cinna rallied the army at Nola and the new citizens, and Marius returned from Africa.

events.title: Marius and Cinna besiege Rome
events.summary: Marius took Ostia and cut the grain supply while Cinna, Carbo and Sertorius ringed the city. Pompeius Strabo fought an inconclusive battle at the Colline Gate and then died, by lightning according to one tradition, by plague according to another; plague also killed thousands in Octavius' camp. The senate surrendered.

sides.losses: heavy losses to plague and desertion

battle.significance: Delivered Rome to the Marian-Cinnan regime for four years.

events.title: Marian massacres in Rome
events.summary: Marius' entry was followed by five days of killings: the consul Octavius was beheaded on his curule chair on the Janiculum and his head was the first consul's displayed on the rostra; the orator Marcus Antonius, Crassus' father and brother, Lucius and Gaius Julius Caesar were killed; Catulus suffocated himself with charcoal fumes; the flamen Dialis Merula opened his veins.

events.title: Death of Pompeius Strabo
events.summary: Pompeius Strabo, who had played both sides while Cinna and the Senate fought for Rome, died in his camp outside the Colline Gate, according to tradition struck by lightning or of the plague then raging in the camps. The populace dragged his body from its bier.

events.title: Bruttius Sura holds Greece for Rome
events.summary: Quintus Bruttius Sura, legate of the governor of Macedonia, defeated a Pontic fleet off Sciathus and fought Archelaus and Aristion for three days near Chaeronea before Sulla's arrival ordered him back to Macedonia. Plutarch says these fights checked the Pontic advance into Thessaly.

events.title: Sulla requisitions the treasures of Delphi, Olympia and Epidaurus
events.summary: Short of money and cut off from Rome, which was in the hands of his enemies, Sulla seized the dedications of Delphi, Olympia and Epidaurus to pay his army before Athens. When the Delphic envoy reported hearing Apollo's lyre sound from the sanctuary, Sulla replied that it meant the god was pleased to give.

events.title: Suicides of Merula and Catulus
events.summary: When Marius and Cinna took Rome, the flamen Dialis Lucius Cornelius Merula, who had replaced Cinna as consul, opened his veins at the altar of Jupiter, leaving a note that he had first removed his priestly cap. Quintus Lutatius Catulus, victor of Vercellae, shut himself in a freshly plastered room and suffocated himself with charcoal fumes.

events.title: Death of Marius in his seventh consulship
events.summary: Gaius Marius, consul for the seventh time with Cinna, without any election, died after seventeen days in office, aged about seventy, of pleurisy after heavy drinking, haunted, Plutarch says, by dreams of the Mithridatic command he had wanted.

events.title: Sulla's siege and sack of Athens and the Piraeus
events.summary: Sulla besieged Athens, held by Mithridates' partisan the tyrant Aristion, and the Piraeus, held by Archelaus, from 87. He cut down the groves of the Academy and the Lyceum for siege timber and requisitioned the treasures of Delphi, Olympia and Epidaurus. Athens was stormed by night on 1 March 86 near the Heptachalcon; the Piraeus fell soon after and Philo's arsenal was burned.

sides.strength: Pontic garrison of the Piraeus and Aristion's Athenians
sides.losses: many killed; Archelaus escaped by sea

battle.significance: Destroyed Mithridates' foothold in Greece and gave Sulla a base for the field campaign.

events.title: Lex Valeria on debts
events.summary: The suffect consul Lucius Valerius Flaccus, Marius' replacement, carried a law cancelling three quarters of all debts, repayment of one quarter (a quadrans) being deemed full settlement. Velleius called it a most disgraceful law.

events.title: Battle of Chaeronea
events.summary: Sulla, with under 17,000 men, defeated Archelaus' far larger Pontic army. Local men guided a detachment to dislodge the enemy from Mount Thurium; Sulla's front ranks stood behind stakes and laughed at the scythed chariots, calling for more as at the races; the phalanx was then ground down.

sides.losses: most of the army; c. 10,000 escaped

battle.significance: Destroyed the Pontic army in Greece and ended Mithridates' hopes of holding Europe.

events.title: Battle of Orchomenus
events.summary: Archelaus, reinforced by 80,000 men under Dorylaus, met Sulla on the plain of Orchomenus, where Sulla dug trenches to neutralise the Pontic cavalry. When his line wavered Sulla seized a standard and ran at the enemy, shouting that if anyone asked where they had abandoned their general they should say Orchomenus. The Pontic camp was stormed on the second day.

battle.significance: Second annihilation of Mithridates' European army; led to negotiations at Delium and Dardanus.

events.title: Fimbria murders the consul Flaccus
events.summary: The Cinnan government sent the consul Lucius Valerius Flaccus east with two legions to fight Mithridates and, if possible, to supersede Sulla. His legate Gaius Flavius Fimbria stirred the troops to mutiny and had Flaccus killed at Nicomedia, then took command.

events.title: Mithridates deports the people of Chios
events.summary: Suspecting Chios of Roman sympathies after a Chian ship rammed his flagship off Rhodes, Mithridates demanded 2,000 talents, then declared the payment short, and had his general Zenobius deport the population to the Black Sea in chains. Pontic ships carrying them were intercepted at Heraclea, which returned the Chians home.

events.title: Mithridates massacres the Galatian tetrarchs
events.summary: Fearing the Galatians would join Rome, Mithridates invited sixty Galatian nobles with their families to a banquet at Pergamon and had them killed; one, Deiotarus, escaped and led the Galatian revolt that drove Pontic garrisons out of the country. Deiotarus became Rome's most loyal client in Anatolia.

events.title: The Asian cities turn against Mithridates
events.summary: After Chaeronea, Ephesus rose against Mithridates' governor Zenobius and decreed war on the king; Tralles, Hypaepa, Metropolis, Sardis and Colophon followed. Mithridates answered with a counter-programme of freeing slaves, cancelling debts and granting citizenship to resident aliens in cities that stayed loyal. The Ephesian decree survives on stone.

events.title: The coinage edict of Marius Gratidianus
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Marius Gratidianus issued an edict on testing denarii, to drive out plated forgeries in a debased wartime currency. It made him so popular that statues of him were set up in every district with candles and incense; Sulla's men tortured him to death at the tomb of Catulus in 82.

events.title: Battle of the Rhyndacus (Miletopolis)
events.summary: Fimbria defeated Mithridates' son, also called Mithridates, near the Rhyndacus and nearly trapped the king himself at Pitane, but Lucullus, commanding Sulla's fleet, refused to cooperate with a Marian general. Fimbria then sacked Ilium, boasting he had done in eleven days what took Agamemnon ten years.

sides.strength: 2 legions (later the Valerian or Fimbrian legions)

battle.significance: Pressed Mithridates to accept Sulla's terms quickly; illustrates the three-cornered nature of the war.

events.title: Peace of Dardanus
events.summary: Sulla and Mithridates met at Dardanus. Mithridates gave up Asia, Bithynia, Paphlagonia and Cappadocia, surrendered 70 or 80 warships, paid 2,000 or 3,000 talents, and was recognised as a friend and ally of Rome. The peace was never ratified by the senate.

events.title: Lucullus' naval victory off Tenedos
events.summary: Sulla's quaestor Lucius Licinius Lucullus, who had spent the winter collecting ships from Cyprus, Phoenicia, Rhodes and Pamphylia, defeated a Pontic fleet under Neoptolemus near Lectum and Tenedos. He then refused Fimbria's request to blockade Mithridates at Pitane, letting the king escape by sea to Mytilene.

battle.significance: Gave Sulla command of the Aegean for the crossing to Asia.

events.title: Fimbria sacks Ilium
events.summary: Gaius Flavius Fimbria, having taken over Flaccus' army, besieged Ilium, which wished to surrender to Sulla, took it after eleven days and destroyed it, boasting that he had done in eleven days what Agamemnon needed ten years for. A citizen replied that the Trojans then had had Hector.

battle.significance: A Roman army destroying the mother city of Rome's own legend; Sulla later rebuilt and freed it.

events.title: Suicide of Fimbria
events.summary: Sulla, after the peace of Dardanus, marched against Fimbria near Thyatira; Fimbria's men deserted to him, and Fimbria, after a failed attempt to have Sulla assassinated, killed himself in the temple of Asclepius at Pergamon. His two legions, the Valeriani, were left in Asia and served Lucullus for years.

events.title: The Rhetorica ad Herennium
events.summary: The earliest complete Latin handbook of rhetoric, dedicated to one Gaius Herennius, was written in the 80s by an author with popularis sympathies; its examples come from the Social War and the 90s. Long attributed to Cicero, it was the standard medieval rhetorical textbook and contains the classic account of the 'memory palace'.

events.title: Sulla's fine on Asia
events.summary: Sulla assembled the Asian cities at Ephesus and imposed 20,000 talents, five years' arrears of tax plus war costs, while billeting his army on households that had to pay each soldier 16 drachmas a day. The cities borrowed from Roman lenders at ruinous rates; by 70 the debt had grown to 120,000 talents, which Lucullus reduced.

events.title: Cinna killed by his troops at Ancona
events.summary: Preparing to meet Sulla in the Balkans rather than Italy, Cinna, consul for the fourth successive year, tried to ship his army across the Adriatic from Ancona. The troops mutinied and killed him. Carbo remained sole consul for the rest of the year.

events.title: Sulla's imperatorial gold
events.summary: Sulla's eastern mint struck the first substantial Roman gold coinage since the Second Punic War: aurei and denarii naming him IMPER ITERVM with trophies, jug and lituus, and his quaestor Manlius Torquatus' issue showing Sulla in a triumphal quadriga crowned by Victory. They paid the army that was about to invade Italy.

events.title: New citizens distributed through all thirty-five tribes
events.summary: The Cinnan regime gave effect to Sulpicius' programme: a decree of the Senate distributed the enfranchised Italians and freedmen among all thirty-five tribes rather than confining them to a few. The censors of 86 had registered only 463,000 citizens, showing how incomplete enrolment of the new citizens still was.

events.title: Burning of the Capitoline temple
events.summary: The temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus burned down, by accident or arson, and with it the Sibylline Books. The cause was never discovered. Sulla undertook the rebuilding, which Catulus completed and dedicated in 69; a new collection of oracles was assembled from Erythrae, Samos and elsewhere.
events.locName: Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Capitol

events.title: Sulla lands at Brundisium
events.summary: In spring 83 Sulla crossed from Dyrrachium with five legions, about 40,000 men, his soldiers swearing to stay with him and not to plunder Italy. Brundisium opened its gates and was rewarded with exemption from customs. Metellus Pius, Crassus and the 23-year-old Pompey, who had raised three legions from his father's clients in Picenum on his own authority, joined him.

events.title: Battle of Mount Tifata
events.summary: Sulla defeated the consul Gaius Norbanus near Mount Tifata above Capua; Appian has 6,000 of Norbanus' men killed against 70 Sullans. Sulla dedicated land to Diana Tifatina in thanks. Shortly afterwards the army of the other consul, Scipio Asiagenus, defected to Sulla wholesale at Teanum.

battle.significance: First victory of the war; the defection at Teanum showed the Cinnan armies' brittle loyalty.

events.title: Murena raids Pontus: the Second Mithridatic War begins
events.summary: Lucius Licinius Murena, left by Sulla in Asia with Fimbria's legions, claimed Mithridates was arming and raided Pontic Cappadocia, plundering the rich temple-town of Comana. The Senate's envoy Calidius ordered him to stop, but in 82 he invaded again and was defeated on the Halys.

events.title: The army of the consul Scipio goes over to Sulla near Teanum
events.summary: Encamped near Teanum Sidicinum, the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus negotiated with Sulla; during a truce Sulla's soldiers fraternised with Scipio's and the whole consular army defected. Scipio, captured in his tent with his son, was released. Carbo said he had to fight a fox and a lion in Sulla, and the fox gave more trouble.

events.title: Pompey raises a private army in Picenum
events.summary: Gnaeus Pompeius, aged twenty-three and holding no office, raised three legions from his father's clients in Picenum, set up his tribunal at Auximum, drove out the Carbonian recruiting officers and defeated three enemy commanders before joining Sulla, who saluted him as imperator.

events.title: Sertorius leaves for Spain
events.summary: Despairing of the Marian leadership, Quintus Sertorius took up his province of Hither Spain late in 83, raising troops and paying the passes of the Pyrenean tribes for passage. Expelled in 81 by Gaius Annius, he fled to Mauretania before the Lusitanians called him back in 80.

events.title: Battle of the Colline Gate
events.summary: A Samnite and Lucanian army under Pontius Telesinus and Marcus Lamponius, trying to relieve Praeneste, swung against Rome itself. Sulla arrived in the afternoon and attacked at once; his left wing broke and he barely escaped death, but Crassus routed the enemy on the right. Fighting went on into the night. Telesinus was found dying with an expression of victory on his face.

sides.losses: c. 50,000 dead on both sides; 6,000-8,000 prisoners massacred

battle.significance: Decided the civil war; Sulla became master of Rome.

events.note: The Samnite army is listed under italia_socii as well as mariani: it fought for the Marians but as a continuation of the Italian insurgency.

events.title: Battle of Sacriportus
events.summary: The 26-year-old consul Gaius Marius the Younger was routed by Sulla at Sacriportus after five of his cohorts defected; Appian gives 20,000 killed and 8,000 captured. Marius fled into Praeneste, but first sent orders to Rome for the praetor Brutus Damasippus to murder leading senators, including the pontifex maximus Scaevola, killed at the temple of Vesta.

battle.significance: Opened the road to Rome and trapped the younger Marius in Praeneste.

events.title: Siege of Praeneste
events.summary: Quintus Lucretius Ofella blockaded the younger Marius in Praeneste through 82; every relief attempt by Carbo, the Samnites and Lucanians failed. After the Colline Gate the town surrendered; Marius, trying to escape through a tunnel, killed himself. Sulla had the men of Praeneste, some 12,000, massacred and later settled a veteran colony there.

battle.significance: Its fall, after the Colline Gate, ended organised Marian resistance in Italy.

events.title: Battle of Faventia
events.summary: Carbo and Norbanus attacked Metellus Pius' camp at Faventia late in the day with tired troops and were defeated with 10,000 killed and 6,000 deserting. Carbo soon abandoned Italy for Africa; Norbanus fled to Rhodes and killed himself.

battle.significance: Collapsed the Marian position in the north.

events.title: The Sullan proscriptions
events.summary: Sulla posted lists of men whom anyone could kill with impunity; the killer received two talents (12,000 denarii), the property was auctioned, and the sons and grandsons of the proscribed were barred from office. Totals reported range from 520 to 4,700 names, including some 40 senators and 1,600 equites in the first lists according to Appian.

events.title: Sulla named dictator to write laws and restore the state
events.summary: With both consuls dead, the interrex Lucius Valerius Flaccus carried a law (lex Valeria) appointing Sulla dictator legibus scribundis et rei publicae constituendae, without time limit, and ratifying all his acts. The dictatorship had been dormant for 120 years.

events.title: Pompey in Sicily and Africa; 'Magnus'
events.summary: Sulla sent Pompey with propraetorian imperium to Sicily, where he captured Carbo on Cossyra and had him executed at Lilybaeum, and then to Africa, where in forty days he destroyed Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and the Numidian king Hiarbas. Sulla greeted him as Magnus, and Pompey demanded and got a triumph though he had held no magistracy.

events.title: Battle of the Halys: the Second Mithridatic War
events.summary: Lucius Licinius Murena, Sulla's legate in Asia, raided Pontus without authority in 83-82. Mithridates crushed him at the Halys; Sulla sent Aulus Gabinius to order Murena to stop and reconciled the two kings. Murena still celebrated a triumph.

battle.significance: Ended the Second Mithridatic War with the Dardanus terms restored.

events.title: Battles around Clusium
events.summary: In the northern theatre Sulla fought Carbo near Clusium in a day-long indecisive battle, while Pompey and Crassus defeated Carbo's lieutenant Carrinas near Spoletium. Carbo, losing hope after Faventia and the defection of his lieutenants, fled to Africa.

battle.significance: Pinned Carbo's main army while Praeneste was besieged.

events.title: Damasippus' massacre of senators
events.summary: On orders sent by the besieged younger Marius, the praetor Lucius Junius Brutus Damasippus summoned the Senate and had leading suspected Sullan sympathisers killed in the Curia Hostilia, including the pontifex maximus Quintus Mucius Scaevola, cut down at the entrance to the temple of Vesta, and the ex-praetor Papirius Carbo Arvina.

events.title: Pompey's African triumph
events.summary: Pompey, still an eques who had held no magistracy, extorted from Sulla a triumph for his African victories over Domitius Ahenobarbus and King Iarbas, celebrated on 12 March. His chariot, drawn by elephants, could not pass through the triumphal gate and he had to switch to horses.

events.title: Sulla's legislation
events.summary: Sulla doubled the senate to about 600 by adding equites, raised the quaestors to 20 with automatic entry into the senate, increased praetors to 8, fixed minimum ages and intervals for office (lex annalis), returned the juries to senators, set up standing criminal courts, and gutted the tribunate: tribunes kept only the right to protect individuals, needed senatorial approval for bills, and were barred from further office.

events.title: Sullan veteran colonies
events.summary: Sulla settled his veterans, Appian says 23 legions or 120,000 men, on land confiscated from hostile communities in Etruria, Latium, Campania and Samnium. Pompeii became Colonia Cornelia Veneria Pompeianorum; Faesulae, Arretium, Volaterrae, Praeneste and Clusium were punished.

events.title: Caesar refuses to divorce Cinna's daughter
events.summary: Ordered by Sulla to divorce Cornelia, Cinna's daughter, the eighteen-year-old Julius Caesar refused, lost his priesthood and his wife's dowry, and went into hiding in Sabine country, bribing his way past patrols while sick with fever. Sulla relented at the pleas of the Vestals and Caesar's relatives, warning that there were many Mariuses in him.

events.title: Cicero's first surviving speech: Pro Quinctio
events.summary: Cicero, aged twenty-five, defended Publius Quinctius in a civil suit over a Gallic partnership against Sextus Naevius, a crier backed by the great orator Hortensius and by powerful Sullan connections. The speech is the earliest surviving Ciceronian oration.

events.title: Fall of Mytilene; Caesar's civic crown
events.summary: Marcus Minucius Thermus captured Mytilene, which had handed Manius Aquillius to Mithridates and held out since. The 20-year-old Julius Caesar, serving on his staff, won the civic crown (corona civica) for saving a citizen's life, having earlier been sent to Nicomedes IV of Bithynia to fetch a fleet, a mission that fed lifelong gossip.

battle.significance: Last act of the Mithridatic rebellion in Asia.

events.title: Cicero defends Sextus Roscius of Ameria
events.summary: In his first criminal case, the 26-year-old Cicero defended Sextus Roscius on a charge of parricide trumped up by men who had entered Roscius' father on the proscription lists after his death and bought his estate cheaply through Sulla's freedman Chrysogonus. Roscius was acquitted.

events.title: Sertorius returns to Spain at the Lusitanians' invitation
events.summary: Quintus Sertorius, the last Marian commander, expelled from Spain in 81, had fought in Mauretania and dug at Tingis into the giant grave of Antaeus. Invited by the Lusitanians, he crossed back in 80 with 2,600 Romans and 700 Africans and built a Romano-Iberian state that defied Rome for eight years.

events.title: Battle of the Baetis
events.summary: Soon after landing, Sertorius defeated the governor of Further Spain, Lucius Fufidius, on the Baetis, killing 2,000 Romans. With Hirtuleius' victory over Domitius Calvinus on the Anas in 79/78, it convinced the senate to send Metellus Pius and then Pompey.

battle.significance: Established Sertorius in the peninsula.

events.title: Sertorius defeats Cotta off Mellaria
events.summary: Returning from Mauretania with Lusitanian support, Sertorius beat Sulla's legate Aurelius Cotta in a sea battle in the Strait near Mellaria, then crossed into Spain and defeated the governor Fufidius on the Baetis.

battle.significance: Let Sertorius establish himself in Lusitania.

events.title: Murder of Ptolemy XI and accession of Ptolemy XII
events.summary: Ptolemy XI Alexander II, installed by Sulla, murdered his co-ruler and stepmother Berenice III after nineteen days and was lynched by the Alexandrians. They chose an illegitimate son of Ptolemy IX, Ptolemy XII 'Neos Dionysos', nicknamed Auletes (the flute-player). Rumour said Alexander II, or his predecessor Alexander I, had bequeathed Egypt to Rome.

events.title: Sulla retires to private life
events.summary: Having laid down the dictatorship and held a consulship in 80, Sulla declined a further term, dismissed his lictors and walked in the Forum as a private citizen, offering to account for his actions to anyone who asked. He retired to his estate near Puteoli to write his memoirs.

events.title: Cicero studies in Athens and Rhodes
events.summary: Partly for his health and partly, Plutarch suggests, to avoid Sulla after the Roscius case, Cicero spent two years in Athens, Asia and Rhodes, hearing Antiochus of Ascalon, the Epicurean Zeno, and the rhetorician Apollonius Molon, who taught him to restrain his strained, full-voiced delivery. Posidonius was also among his teachers.

events.title: Death and funeral of Sulla
events.summary: Sulla died at his villa near Puteoli aged sixty, of a haemorrhage after a fit of rage in which he had a local magistrate strangled. Against the consul Lepidus, Catulus and Pompey secured a state funeral: his body was carried through Italy and cremated in the Campus Martius, the first Cornelius to be burned rather than buried, and the women of Rome gave spices enough to model him and a lictor in frankincense.
events.locName: Puteoli, Campania; funeral in the Campus Martius

events.title: Revolt of Lepidus
events.summary: The consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus campaigned to undo Sulla's settlement, restoring the grain dole and promising to return confiscated land and the tribunes' powers. Sent to suppress a rising of dispossessed farmers at Faesulae, he joined them, and in 77 marched on Rome demanding a second consulship.

events.title: Sertorius relieves Lacobriga
events.summary: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius besieged the Lusitanian town of Lacobriga, expecting it to fall within days for lack of water; Sertorius smuggled in 2,000 skins of water, evacuated non-combatants and ambushed Metellus' foraging legion, forcing him to withdraw.

battle.significance: Typical of Sertorius' guerrilla success against Metellus' heavy columns.

events.title: Rising at Faesulae
events.summary: Dispossessed farmers at Faesulae in Etruria attacked the Sullan veterans settled on their land and killed several. The Senate sent both consuls, Lepidus and Catulus, to deal with it; Lepidus took the side of the rebels, the prelude to his revolt.

events.title: Servilius Vatia's war in Cilicia and Isauria
events.summary: Publius Servilius Vatia, proconsul of Cilicia, won a sea battle against the pirates, took the strongholds of the pirate chief Zenicetes on Mount Olympus in Lycia, and was the first Roman to lead an army over the Taurus, capturing Isaura by diverting its water supply. He earned the cognomen Isauricus.

events.title: Catulus builds the Tabularium
events.summary: Quintus Lutatius Catulus, as consul of 78, built a massive record office on the slope of the Capitol above the Forum, whose arcaded façade of Gabine stone and tufa still forms the base of the Palazzo Senatorio. The identification with the state archive rests on an inscription naming Catulus' substructio et tabularium.

events.title: Defeat of Lepidus outside Rome
events.summary: Under the senatus consultum ultimum, the proconsul Quintus Lutatius Catulus defeated Lepidus' army near the Milvian Bridge. Pompey besieged Lepidus' lieutenant Marcus Junius Brutus (father of the assassin) in Mutina; Brutus surrendered and was killed on Pompey's orders. Lepidus, beaten again near Cosa, fled to Sardinia and died there.
events.locName: Milvian Bridge and Campus Martius, Rome

battle.significance: Ended the Lepidan revolt; Pompey used his army as leverage to obtain the Spanish command.

events.title: Pompey receives the Spanish command as a private citizen
events.summary: With both consuls unwilling, the senate gave Pompey, who had held no magistracy, proconsular imperium against Sertorius. Philippus quipped that he was sent not pro consule but pro consulibus, in place of both consuls. He marched by a new route over the Alps (via the Mont Genèvre).

events.title: Pompey besieges Brutus at Mutina
events.summary: Marching against the Lepidan forces in Cisalpine Gaul, Pompey besieged Marcus Junius Brutus, father of the tyrannicide, in Mutina. Brutus surrendered and was killed the next day at Regium Lepidi by Pompey's agent Geminius, an act later held against Pompey.

battle.significance: Ended the Lepidan threat in the north.

events.title: Pompey opens a new road over the Alps
events.summary: On his way to Spain Pompey cut a new route through the Cottian Alps, probably over the Mont Genèvre, fighting the mountain tribes. In his letter of 75 he boasted that he had opened a road different from Hannibal's and more convenient for Rome. He wintered among the Vocontii and Gallic tribes he later settled.

events.title: Sertorius' school for the children of Spanish nobles
events.summary: Sertorius gathered the sons of the leading Spanish families at Osca (Huesca), dressed them in the toga praetexta, and had them taught Greek and Latin by Roman teachers. It was a civilising gesture and a means of holding hostages; Perperna's faction later used it as a grievance.

events.title: Siege of Lauro
events.summary: Pompey's first campaign in Spain ended in humiliation: trying to relieve Lauro, he was outmanoeuvred by Sertorius, who ambushed his foragers and a relieving legion, killing perhaps 10,000, and burned the town before Pompey's eyes.

battle.significance: Pompey's worst defeat; taught him caution in Spain.

events.title: Battle of Italica
events.summary: Metellus Pius defeated Sertorius' best lieutenant, Lucius Hirtuleius, near Italica, holding his centre back while his wings enveloped the enemy. It secured the south for the Sullan side.

battle.significance: Turned the war in Further Spain.

events.title: Battle of the Sucro
events.summary: Pompey, eager to win before Metellus arrived, attacked Sertorius late in the day. Sertorius broke Pompey's wing and Pompey, wounded, escaped only by abandoning his richly caparisoned horse; Afranius beat the other wing. Metellus' approach made Sertorius withdraw.

battle.significance: Drawn battle that brought Metellus and Pompey together.

events.title: Battle of Saguntum (Segontia)
events.summary: A hard-fought battle in which Metellus was wounded and Pompey's brother-in-law and quaestor Memmius killed ended with Sertorius withdrawing to Clunia. That winter Pompey wrote to the senate threatening to bring his starving army back to Italy unless supplied.

battle.significance: Sertorius lost the initiative and the war became one of sieges and attrition.

events.title: Treaty between Sertorius and Mithridates
events.summary: Mithridates offered Sertorius 3,000 talents and 40 ships in exchange for recognition of his claims and Roman officers to train his army. Sertorius conceded Bithynia and Cappadocia but refused to give up the province of Asia, and sent Marcus Marius with troops to Pontus.

events.title: Caesar captured by pirates
events.summary: Sailing to Rhodes to study rhetoric with Apollonius Molon, the 25-year-old Caesar was captured by Cilician pirates. He laughed at their ransom of 20 talents and told them to ask 50, spent 38 days among them, joking that he would crucify them; when freed he raised ships at Miletus, captured them and did exactly that.

events.title: Lex Aurelia restores the tribunes' career
events.summary: The consul Gaius Aurelius Cotta, after grain riots, carried a law allowing former tribunes to stand for higher office, the first breach in Sulla's restrictions on the tribunate.

events.title: Pompey destroys Herennius and Perperna at Valentia
events.summary: Early in 75 Pompey defeated Sertorius' lieutenants Gaius Herennius and Marcus Perperna outside Valentia, killing 10,000 and Herennius, and sacked the city. Archaeologists have found the skeletons of executed and mutilated men in a destruction layer dated to this event.

battle.significance: Opened the east coast to Pompey.

events.title: Pompey's letter to the Senate
events.summary: Short of pay and grain after the campaigns of 75, Pompey wrote to the Senate threatening that unless supplies arrived his army, and with it the Spanish war, would cross into Italy. The consul Lucius Lucullus, eager to keep Pompey in Spain and away from the Mithridatic command, ensured money was sent.

events.title: Cicero quaestor at Lilybaeum
events.summary: As quaestor in western Sicily, Cicero shipped grain to Rome during a shortage and won the Sicilians' trust; on his tour he rediscovered Archimedes' overgrown tomb near Syracuse by its sphere and cylinder. Returning, he found that Rome had barely noticed his absence, a lesson he says he never forgot.

events.title: Nicomedes IV bequeaths Bithynia to Rome
events.summary: Nicomedes IV died late in 75 or early 74, leaving Bithynia to Rome. Its annexation put Roman power at the Bosporus and on Pontus' doorstep; Mithridates claimed a son of Nicomedes was the true heir and invaded.

events.title: Antonius' command against the pirates and defeat by Crete
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Antonius, father of the triumvir, received an unlimited command (imperium infinitum) over the coasts against the pirates. After requisitioning heavily in Sicily and Greece, he attacked Crete and was defeated at sea near Cydonia; his captured men were hung from the ships' rigging. He died soon after, mocked with the cognomen Creticus.

events.title: Cyrene organised as a province
events.summary: Twenty-two years after Ptolemy Apion's bequest, the Senate sent the quaestor Publius Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus to administer Cyrenaica as a province, largely to exploit the royal lands and secure grain during the shortage of the 70s.

events.title: The iudicium Iunianum: bribed jurors in the Oppianicus case
events.summary: A senatorial jury under Gaius Junius condemned Statius Albius Oppianicus for attempting to poison his stepson Aulus Cluentius; it emerged that both sides had bribed jurors, and that one juror, Staienus, had pocketed the money. The scandal became the standing proof that senatorial juries could be bought, fuel for the jury reform of 70.

events.title: Siege of Calagurris
events.summary: Sertorius relieved Calagurris in 74 against Pompey and Metellus; after his death the town held out against Pompey's legate Lucius Afranius until 72, its starving defenders reduced to eating their women and children. 'Calagurritan hunger' became proverbial.

battle.significance: Last major resistance of the Sertorian war.

events.title: Pompey's repulse at Pallantia
events.summary: Pompey besieged the Vaccaean stronghold of Pallantia and had undermined its timber walls when Sertorius arrived; Pompey burned his works and retreated to join Metellus. It was one of several Sertorian successes in 74 that kept the war going despite his dwindling base.

battle.significance: Checked Pompey's advance into the Meseta.

events.title: Battle of Chalcedon
events.summary: Mithridates overran Bithynia and trapped the consul Marcus Aurelius Cotta in Chalcedon, defeating him on land and destroying his fleet in the harbour after breaking its chain.

sides.losses: several thousand killed; much of the fleet lost

battle.significance: Gave Mithridates command of the Propontis and opened the way to Cyzicus.

events.title: Siege of Cyzicus
events.summary: Mithridates besieged Cyzicus with a vast army and fleet, using towers, rams and a 100-cubit siege tower on ships. Lucullus, rather than attack, occupied the heights behind the besiegers and cut their supply. Winter, famine and plague destroyed the Pontic army; Mithridates escaped by sea and his retreating columns were cut down at the Aesepus and Granicus.

sides.losses: most of the army, to famine, disease and pursuit

battle.significance: Destroyed Mithridates' great army without a pitched battle; the turning point of the war's first phase.

events.title: Murder of Sertorius and the end of the Sertorian War
events.summary: Increasingly suspicious and harsh, Sertorius was stabbed at a banquet at Osca by Perperna and other Roman officers. Pompey defeated Perperna in his first battle, and when Perperna offered letters from leading men in Rome inviting Sertorius to Italy, Pompey burned them unread and had him executed.

events.title: Gladiators break out of Capua: the Spartacus revolt
events.summary: About 70 gladiators from the training school of Gnaeus Lentulus Batiatus at Capua broke out with kitchen knives and spits, seized a wagon of gladiatorial weapons and took refuge on Vesuvius. Their leaders were the Thracian Spartacus and the Gauls Crixus and Oenomaus.

events.title: Battle of Mount Vesuvius
events.summary: The praetor Gaius Claudius Glaber blockaded the rebels on Vesuvius with 3,000 hastily raised men. The slaves wove ladders from wild vines, climbed down the cliffs behind him and stormed his camp. A second praetor, Publius Varinius, was then beaten, losing his lictors and his horse.

sides.strength: a few hundred to a few thousand

battle.significance: Turned a breakout into a war; fugitive slaves and rural poor flocked to Spartacus.

events.title: Lex Terentia Cassia frumentaria
events.summary: The consuls Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus and Gaius Cassius Longinus restored subsidised grain distributions, abolished by Sulla, at five modii a month for some 40,000 citizens, financed by compulsory purchases of Sicilian grain. Verres was among the governors who administered the purchases.

events.title: Licinius Macer's campaign for the tribunate
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Licinius Macer, also a historian of early Rome, agitated for the restoration of the tribunes' powers removed by Sulla, urging the plebs to refuse military service. Sallust gives him a fiery speech. He was convicted of extortion in 66, with Cicero presiding, and killed himself.

events.title: Spartacus defeats the praetor Varinius
events.summary: After escaping the blockade of Vesuvius, Spartacus defeated the praetor Publius Varinius and his legates Furius and Cossinius in a series of engagements in Campania and Lucania, capturing Varinius' lictors and horse. His army swelled with herdsmen and runaways to tens of thousands.

sides.strength: several thousand rising to tens of thousands

battle.significance: Turned the breakout into a full-scale slave war.

events.title: Lucullus destroys the retreating Pontic army on the Aesepus and Granicus
events.summary: Starved out at Cyzicus, Mithridates' army retreated west; Lucullus caught one column in snow at the Rhyndacus and another at the crossing of the Aesepus and Granicus, killing or capturing tens of thousands. The king escaped by sea and lost much of his fleet in a storm.

battle.significance: Destroyed the invasion army of 74.

events.title: Naval battle off Lemnos
events.summary: Lucullus' fleet caught and destroyed a Pontic squadron under Marcus Marius, the officer sent by Sertorius, off Lemnos. Marius was captured and executed: Lucullus would not let a Roman senator be paraded as a prisoner.

sides.strength: 13 ships destroyed at the first encounter, the rest beached

battle.significance: Ended Pontic naval power in the Aegean and the Sertorian connection.

events.title: Battle of Cabira
events.summary: Lucullus invaded Pontus and confronted Mithridates at Cabira. After cavalry skirmishing, his legates destroyed a Pontic supply column in a defile; panic swept the royal camp and the army disintegrated. Mithridates fled to Tigranes of Armenia, escaping because Roman troops stopped to fight over a mule loaded with gold.

battle.significance: Lost Mithridates his kingdom; Pontus was occupied over the next two years.

events.title: Battle of Mount Garganus
events.summary: Crixus, who had separated from Spartacus with a contingent of Gauls and Germans, was destroyed near Mount Garganus by the consul Lucius Gellius Publicola's praetor Quintus Arrius. Spartacus later honoured Crixus with gladiatorial combats between 300 Roman prisoners.

battle.significance: Split and weakened the slave army.

events.title: Spartacus defeats both consuls
events.summary: Marching north, Spartacus defeated the consuls Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus and Lucius Gellius Publicola in turn, and then the proconsul of Cisalpine Gaul, Gaius Cassius Longinus, near Mutina. Instead of crossing the Alps he turned back south.

sides.strength: two consular armies, then c. 10,000 under Cassius

battle.significance: The high point of the revolt; Rome had lost two consular armies to slaves.

events.title: Spartacus defeats Cassius Longinus at Mutina
events.summary: Marching north toward the Alps after beating both consuls, Spartacus routed the proconsul of Cisalpine Gaul, Gaius Cassius Longinus, near Mutina. Instead of crossing the Alps he turned back south, for reasons the sources do not agree on.

battle.significance: Left the road out of Italy open.

events.title: Pompey defeats and executes Perperna
events.summary: Perperna, who had murdered Sertorius and taken command, was drawn into an ambush and routed by Pompey. Captured hiding in a thicket, he offered Sertorius' correspondence with leading senators; Pompey burned the letters unread and had him executed.

battle.significance: Ended organised Sertorian resistance.

events.title: Crassus revives decimation
events.summary: After his legate Mummius disobeyed orders and lost two legions to Spartacus, Crassus revived the ancient punishment of decimation, executing one man in ten of the 500 who had fled first, before the whole army.

events.title: Battle of the Silarus: death of Spartacus
events.summary: Penned into Bruttium behind a 300-stade ditch and wall Crassus dug across the peninsula, and betrayed by Cilician pirates who took his money but never brought ships, Spartacus broke out on a snowy night. After his Gallic contingent under Castus and Gannicus was destroyed, he turned to fight. He killed his horse before the battle, saying that if he won he would have plenty, and if he lost he would not need one; he died trying to reach Crassus, and his body was never found.

battle.significance: Ended the last great slave war of antiquity.

events.title: Six thousand crucified along the Via Appia
events.summary: Crassus crucified the 6,000 prisoners from Spartacus' army along the Via Appia from Capua to Rome, roughly one cross every 30 to 40 metres for 200 km. It was a deliberate message to Italy's slaves.
events.locName: Via Appia between Capua and Rome

events.title: Lucullus' debt relief in Asia
events.summary: Finding the Asian cities crushed by the 120,000 talents their Sullan fine had grown into through Roman moneylending, Lucullus capped interest at 12 per cent a year, cancelled interest beyond the principal and limited creditors to a quarter of a debtor's income. The debts were cleared in four years.

events.title: Cotta's siege and sack of Heraclea Pontica
events.summary: Marcus Aurelius Cotta besieged Heraclea, which had admitted a Pontic garrison, for two years; it fell by betrayal in 70 and was plundered and burned, Cotta taking the statue of Heracles from the agora. The Senate later restored the Heracleots' freedom and Cotta was expelled from the Senate for embezzlement.

sides.strength: Cotta's army and fleet of Triarius

battle.significance: Memnon's local history gives an unusual civic view of the war.

events.title: Lucullus takes Amisus
events.summary: After a siege of nearly two years, Lucullus stormed Amisus, whose Pontic commander Callimachus fired the city as he fled; Lucullus tried in vain to save it, wept at the destruction, and then rebuilt it and restored its freedom. Among the captives was the grammarian Tyrannion, later Cicero's librarian.

battle.significance: Completed the conquest of coastal Pontus.

events.title: Appius Claudius demands Mithridates from Tigranes
events.summary: Lucullus sent his brother-in-law Appius Claudius Pulcher to Antioch to demand that Tigranes II surrender his father-in-law Mithridates. Appius addressed the 'King of Kings' simply as king, won over several of his vassals, and was refused, making war with Armenia inevitable.

events.title: Crassus destroys the Gallic and German breakaway force
events.summary: After breaking through Crassus' line in Bruttium, Spartacus' army split again; a group of Gauls and Germans under Castus and Gannicus encamped by a Lucanian lake near Mount Cantenna was attacked by Crassus, who killed 12,300 of them, all, Plutarch says, with their wounds in front.

battle.significance: Preceded the final battle on the Silarus.

events.title: Crassus walls off the toe of Italy
events.summary: When Spartacus, cheated by Cilician pirates who had promised to ferry him to Sicily, was trapped in Bruttium, Crassus dug a ditch and wall some 300 stadia (c. 55 km) long across the isthmus. Spartacus broke through on a snowy night by filling a section of the ditch with earth, timber and corpses.

events.title: Pompey's trophy on the Pyrenees
events.summary: On his return from Spain Pompey set up a monumental trophy on the summit of the Pyrenean pass at Panissars, recording that he had brought 876 towns from the Alps to the borders of Further Spain under Roman control. Its foundations were identified in 1984 at Col de Panissars.

events.title: The trial of Verres
events.summary: Cicero prosecuted Gaius Verres for plundering Sicily as governor (73-71), outflanking the defence of the leading orator Quintus Hortensius, which aimed to drag the trial into 69 when friendly magistrates would preside. Cicero skipped the usual long speech, presented witnesses at once, and Verres went into exile after the first hearing.

events.title: Birth of Virgil
events.summary: Publius Vergilius Maro was born on 15 October 70 at Andes near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul, then still without full citizenship, to a family of modest landowners. He was educated at Cremona, Milan and Rome, then with the Epicurean Siro at Naples.

events.title: First consulship of Pompey and Crassus; tribunate restored
events.summary: Pompey, aged 35 and never yet a senator, and Crassus, both with armies outside the city, were elected consuls for 70. They restored the tribunes' full powers (lex Pompeia Licinia), dismantling the core of Sulla's settlement, and revived the censorship, whose holders expelled 64 senators.

events.title: Lex Aurelia iudiciaria
