events.summary: The praetor Lucius Aurelius Cotta ended a fifty-year fight over the juries with a compromise: panels were to be drawn equally from senators, equites and tribuni aerarii (a census class just below the equites).

events.title: Census of 70: 910,000 citizens
events.summary: The censors Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus and Lucius Gellius Poplicola, the first since 86, registered 910,000 citizens, roughly double the previous count, as the enfranchised Italians were at last enrolled. They also expelled 64 senators, including Gaius Antonius Hybrida and Publius Lentulus Sura.

events.title: Lex Plautia recalls the Lepidans
events.summary: A tribune Plautius carried a law recalling those who had followed Lepidus and later Sertorius. Caesar, then a young senator, spoke for it because it would restore his brother-in-law Lucius Cornelius Cinna.

events.title: Battle of Tigranocerta
events.summary: Lucullus, with perhaps 12,000 legionaries and 3,000 cavalry, routed the immense army Tigranes brought to relieve his new capital. Tigranes famously said the Romans were too many for an embassy and too few for an army. Lucullus led his men uphill against the flank of the armoured cataphracts and told them to strike at their thighs and legs, the only exposed parts; the whole host collapsed.

battle.significance: Destroyed Armenian military prestige; the first Roman victory over cataphract cavalry.

events.title: Metellus conquers Crete
events.summary: After Marcus Antonius (father of the triumvir) had been defeated by the Cretans in 72/71 and mockingly called Creticus, the proconsul Quintus Caecilius Metellus systematically besieged the Cretan cities. When the Cretans offered surrender to Pompey instead, Pompey's legate fought Metellus' troops, an unedifying clash of Roman commands. Crete became a province.

events.title: Caesar's funeral speeches for Julia and Cornelia
events.summary: As quaestor Caesar delivered the funeral oration for his aunt Julia, Marius' widow, tracing her descent from King Ancus Marcius and from Venus, and displayed Marius' images in the procession for the first time since Sulla. He then praised his young wife Cornelia, an unusual honour for a young woman.

events.title: Catulus dedicates the rebuilt Capitoline temple
events.summary: Quintus Lutatius Catulus dedicated the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, rebuilt after the fire of 83 with columns Sulla had taken from the Olympieion at Athens. Catulus' name on the pediment was resented by Caesar, who tried as praetor in 62 to transfer the dedication to Pompey.

events.title: Battle of the Arsanias and the mutiny of Lucullus' army
events.summary: Marching on the old Armenian capital Artaxata, Lucullus again beat Tigranes and Mithridates at the Arsanias, but early snow and the troops' refusal to go on forced him to turn south. He took Nisibis in winter 68/67, but his army, led in agitation by his brother-in-law Publius Clodius, mutinied; the Fimbrian veterans, in the East since 86, demanded discharge.

battle.significance: Last major victory of Lucullus; the campaign stalled as his soldiers turned against him.

events.title: Lucullus takes Nisibis
events.summary: Turning south after the mutinous retreat from Artaxata, Lucullus stormed Nisibis in Mygdonia on a stormy night in autumn 68, capturing Tigranes' brother Gouras and the engineer Callimachus. It was his last success: the army wintered there, and Clodius stirred the troops against him.

battle.significance: Last Roman gain under Lucullus.

events.title: Pirates burn the fleet at Ostia
events.summary: Pirates entered the harbour of Ostia, burned a consular fleet and kidnapped two praetors with their lictors, as well as relatives of Marcus Antonius Creticus. Grain shipments to Rome were disrupted and prices soared, preparing opinion for the lex Gabinia.

events.title: Manilius' law on freedmen's votes
events.summary: Immediately on entering office on 10 December 67, the tribune Gaius Manilius carried a law distributing freedmen among all tribes; amid violence on the Capitol it was annulled by the Senate the next day. He then turned to his successful bill giving Pompey the war against Mithridates.

events.title: Battle of Zela (67 BC)
events.summary: While Lucullus' army was paralysed, Mithridates returned to Pontus and destroyed the legate Gaius Valerius Triarius' army at Zela, killing 7,000 men, including 24 military tribunes and 150 centurions, the worst Roman losses of the war. Mithridates was wounded in the thigh and below the eye.

battle.significance: Restored Mithridates in Pontus and ended Lucullus' command.

events.title: Lex Gabinia: Pompey's command against the pirates
events.summary: The tribune Aulus Gabinius carried a law giving one man of consular rank, obviously Pompey, a three-year command over the whole Mediterranean and its coasts to 50 miles inland, with imperium equal to the governors', 15 (later 24) legates of praetorian rank, 500 ships, 120,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry and 6,000 talents. The price of grain at Rome fell the day it passed.

events.title: Battle of Coracesium
events.summary: After clearing the western Mediterranean in 40 days, Pompey trapped the pirates' main fleet off Coracesium in Rough Cilicia, defeated it and besieged their strongholds, which surrendered. The whole campaign took three months.

sides.strength: 60 ships in the final squadron of a 500-ship command

battle.significance: Ended large-scale piracy in the Mediterranean for a generation.

events.title: Lex Roscia theatralis
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Roscius Otho reserved the first fourteen rows in the theatre behind the senators for equites. The privilege was hissed by the crowd for years; Cicero calmed a riot about it in 63.

events.title: Lex Calpurnia de ambitu
events.summary: The consul Gaius Calpurnius Piso, under pressure from the tribune Gaius Cornelius, carried a law against electoral bribery that disqualified the convicted from office for life and expelled them from the Senate. Under it Publius Autronius Paetus and Publius Sulla lost the consulships they had won for 65.

events.title: Lex Cornelia binds praetors to their edicts
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Cornelius carried a law that praetors must administer justice according to the edict they published at the start of the year, ending ad hoc favours. It was a milestone in the development of the praetorian edict into a stable body of law.

events.title: Pompey and Metellus quarrel over Crete
events.summary: The Cretan cities, besieged by Quintus Caecilius Metellus, offered their surrender to Pompey, whose lex Gabinia gave him authority over all coasts. Pompey sent his legate Lucius Octavius, who fought alongside the Cretans against Metellus' troops at Lappa and Hierapytna. Metellus ignored him and completed the conquest.

events.title: Hasmonean civil war: Hyrcanus II against Aristobulus II
events.summary: On the death of Queen Salome Alexandra, her younger son Aristobulus II defeated his brother Hyrcanus II near Jericho and took the kingship and high priesthood. The Idumaean Antipater persuaded Hyrcanus to flee to the Nabataean king Aretas III, who besieged Aristobulus in the Temple at Jerusalem.

events.title: Lex Manilia: Pompey given the war against Mithridates
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Manilius transferred the provinces of Bithynia and Cilicia and the war against Mithridates and Tigranes from Lucullus and Glabrio to Pompey, who was still in the East after the pirate war, with power to make war and peace. Cicero, praetor and eyeing the consulship, spoke for it in his first political speech; so did Caesar.

events.title: Battle of the Lycus
events.summary: Pompey cornered Mithridates' army in a valley near the Lycus and attacked at night. The moon low behind the Romans threw their shadows far ahead, so the Pontic archers shot short. The royal army was destroyed; Mithridates escaped with a handful of riders, including his concubine Hypsicratea dressed as a man.
events.locName: near Dasteira, later Nicopolis, Lesser Armenia

sides.losses: c. 10,000 killed and the rest captured or scattered

battle.significance: Destroyed Mithridates' last field army.

events.title: Tigranes submits to Pompey at Artaxata
events.summary: Facing his rebellious son, the younger Tigranes, backed by Parthia and Pompey, the old king walked into Pompey's camp and laid his diadem at his feet. Pompey gave it back: Tigranes kept Armenia proper, paid 6,000 talents, and lost Syria, Cilicia and Sophene. The son, who wanted more, was taken to Rome in chains.

events.title: The so-called first Catilinarian conspiracy
events.summary: After the consuls-elect for 65, Publius Autronius Paetus and Publius Cornelius Sulla, were convicted of bribery, stories circulated that they, Catiline and Gnaeus Piso planned to murder the new consuls on 1 January 65; later hostile writers added Crassus and Caesar as backers.

events.title: Pompey and Lucullus meet at Danala
events.summary: Pompey and Lucullus met at Danala in Galatia; the courtesies, with both lictors' fasces wreathed in laurel, turned to recriminations, Lucullus calling Pompey a vulture who came to feed on others' kills. Pompey annulled Lucullus' arrangements and took all but 1,600 of his soldiers.

events.title: Pompey's agreement with Phraates III
events.summary: Pompey renewed friendship with the Parthian king Phraates III, encouraging him to attack Tigranes, but later treated him with contempt, refusing him the title King of Kings and sending Afranius to occupy Gordyene, which Phraates claimed. The Euphrates boundary agreed with Sulla in 96 became ambiguous.

events.title: Mithridates escapes to Colchis and the Bosporus
events.summary: Defeated at night near Dasteira on the Lycus, Mithridates, refused asylum by Tigranes, fled through Colchis, wintered at Dioscurias, and in 65 passed along the Caucasian coast through the lands of the Heniochi and Achaei to the Cimmerian Bosporus, where his son Machares killed himself.

events.title: Birth of Horace
events.summary: Quintus Horatius Flaccus was born on 8 December 65 at Venusia in Apulia, son of a freedman who worked as a coactor (auction agent) and gave him a costly education at Rome and Athens.

events.title: Battle of the Abas
events.summary: After defeating the Iberians of King Artoces at the Pelorus river, Pompey met the Albanian king Oroeses on the Abas. He hid his infantry behind his cavalry, which feigned retreat, drawing the Albanians onto the legions. Plutarch says women's shields and buskins found among the dead were taken for those of Amazons.

battle.significance: Brought Albania and Iberia into Rome's orbit; the farthest point of Roman arms in the Caucasus under the Republic.

events.title: Caesar's aedileship and the trophies of Marius
events.summary: As curule aedile Caesar gave lavish games with 320 pairs of gladiators in silvered armour, eclipsing his colleague Bibulus, and overnight re-erected the trophies of Marius' victories on the Capitol, which Sulla had pulled down. Catulus denounced him for attacking the state with siege engines rather than sappers.

events.title: Lightning strikes the Capitol: the prodigies of 65
events.summary: Lightning struck the Capitol, melting statues of the gods and bronze law tablets and striking the gilded statue of the she-wolf with Romulus and Remus. The haruspices ordered games and a larger statue of Jupiter facing east, which took two years to make.

events.title: Pompey defeats the Iberians of the Caucasus
events.summary: Pursuing Mithridates, Pompey invaded Iberia (Kartli), defeated King Artoces on the Pelorus river after the king burned the bridge over the Cyrus, and took his children as hostages. Pompey turned back before reaching the Caspian, allegedly three days' march away, deterred by snakes and terrain.

battle.significance: Brought Roman arms to the Caucasus for the first time.

events.title: Crassus' censorship and the Egyptian plan
events.summary: Censor with Catulus, Marcus Licinius Crassus proposed to annex Egypt under Alexander's supposed will and to enrol the Transpadanes as citizens. Catulus blocked both, the censors resigned without completing the census, and Caesar, as aedile, was linked to the Egyptian scheme.

events.title: Lex Papia expels non-citizens
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Papius carried a law expelling non-citizens from Rome and setting up a court to try false claims to citizenship. In 62 the poet Archias, protégé of the Luculli, was prosecuted under it and defended by Cicero.

events.title: Scaurus lifts the siege of Jerusalem
events.summary: Pompey's quaestor Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, arriving in Syria, accepted 400 talents from Aristobulus II and ordered Aretas III to raise the siege of Jerusalem; Aristobulus defeated the retreating Nabataeans and Hyrcanus at Papyron. Both brothers then courted Pompey.

events.title: Pompey annexes Syria and ends the Seleucid kingdom
events.summary: Pompey deposed Antiochus XIII Asiaticus, saying he would not give Syria to a king who could not defend it against Arabs and Jews, and made it a Roman province. The Seleucid dynasty, founded in 312, ended.

events.title: Senate dissolves the collegia
events.summary: A senatus consultum abolished most collegia (neighbourhood and trade associations) and banned the Compitalia games, which they organised, as instruments of political violence. Clodius restored them by law in 58.

events.title: Cicero's consular campaign: the Commentariolum and In toga candida
events.summary: Cicero's canvass for 63 is documented by the Commentariolum petitionis, a handbook of electioneering addressed to him under the name of his brother Quintus, and by his speech In toga candida against his rivals Catiline and Gaius Antonius, preserved in fragments with Asconius' commentary. He topped the poll as a novus homo.

events.title: Birth of Gaius Octavius, the future Augustus
events.summary: Gaius Octavius was born at a house called Ox Heads on the Palatine, son of an equestrian-turned-senator from Velitrae and of Atia, daughter of Caesar's sister Julia. Suetonius records that the senator Nigidius Figulus, hearing the hour of birth, declared that the master of the world had been born.

events.title: Senatus consultum ultimum of 63
events.summary: After Crassus brought Cicero anonymous letters at night warning of a massacre, and news came that the Sullan veteran Gaius Manlius was raising an army at Faesulae, the senate passed the ultimate decree. Manlius took up arms on 27 October.

events.title: Pro Murena: Cicero defends the consul-elect
events.summary: In the middle of the Catilinarian crisis Cicero, with Hortensius and Crassus, defended the consul-elect Lucius Licinius Murena against an ambitus charge brought by the defeated candidate Servius Sulpicius Rufus and Cato. Cicero teased Cato's Stoicism and Sulpicius' legal pedantry; Murena was acquitted.

events.title: The First Catilinarian: 'Quo usque tandem'
events.summary: The day after a failed attempt to murder him at his house, Cicero denounced Catiline to his face in the temple of Jupiter Stator: 'How long, Catiline, will you abuse our patience?' Senators shifted away from the bench where Catiline sat. He left Rome that night for Manlius' camp and was declared a public enemy.

events.title: Arrest at the Milvian Bridge: the Allobroges' evidence
events.summary: Envoys of the Allobroges, in Rome to complain of debt and provincial oppression, were approached by the conspirators and informed their patron, who told Cicero. They played along, obtained sealed letters from Publius Cornelius Lentulus Sura and others, and were arrested by prearrangement at the Milvian Bridge in the night of 2-3 December. The letters were opened in the senate the next day.

events.title: Execution of the Catilinarian conspirators
events.summary: In the senate in the temple of Concord the consul-designate Silanus proposed death; Caesar, praetor-designate, proposed life imprisonment in Italian towns and confiscation, warning of the precedent; Cato's speech swung the house to death. Cicero personally escorted Lentulus Sura, Cethegus, Statilius, Gabinius Capito and Caeparius to the Tullianum where they were strangled, then announced to the crowd: 'vixerunt', they have lived.
events.locName: Temple of Concord and the Tullianum, Rome

events.title: Pompey's siege of Jerusalem
events.summary: Called in to arbitrate between the Hasmonean brothers Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, Pompey arrested Aristobulus, whose followers held the Temple. After a three-month siege with engines brought from Tyre, the Romans stormed it, Josephus says on a fast day, and 12,000 Jews died. Pompey entered the Holy of Holies, found it empty of any image, and left the treasure untouched.

battle.significance: Ended Hasmonean independence; Judaea became a Roman dependency.

events.title: Death of Mithridates VI
events.summary: Planning, it was said, to march around the Black Sea and invade Italy through the Danube lands, Mithridates faced a revolt by his son Pharnaces and his army. He took poison, but his body, long immunised by daily doses, resisted it; he had his Gallic bodyguard Bituitus kill him with the sword.

events.title: Pompey's eastern settlement
events.summary: Pompey reorganised the East: new provinces of Bithynia-Pontus and Syria, an enlarged Cilicia, a ring of client kings (Deiotarus in Galatia, Ariobarzanes in Cappadocia, Antiochus of Commagene, Pharnaces in the Bosporus, Hyrcanus in Judaea, Tigranes in Armenia) and dozens of new or refounded cities. His settlement held, with modifications, into the Principate.

events.title: Cicero defeats the Rullan land bill
events.summary: The tribune Publius Servilius Rullus proposed a ten-man commission with praetorian powers for five years to sell public land abroad and buy land in Italy, including the rich ager Campanus, for settlers. On his first day as consul Cicero attacked it in the senate and then, unusually, before the people, and Rullus withdrew it.

events.title: Trial of Gaius Rabirius for the murder of Saturninus
events.summary: The tribune Titus Labienus, with Caesar as one of the judges, revived an archaic treason procedure (perduellio) against the elderly senator Gaius Rabirius for killing Saturninus 37 years before, to challenge the legitimacy of the senatus consultum ultimum. Cicero defended him; when the people seemed about to condemn him, the praetor Metellus Celer struck the red flag on the Janiculum, an ancient signal of enemy attack, dissolving the assembly.

events.title: Caesar elected pontifex maximus
events.summary: After Metellus Pius died, Caesar, aged 37 and only an ex-aedile, beat the senior consulars Catulus and Servilius Isauricus for the chief priesthood in a popular election revived by Labienus' law. He told his mother as he left that he would return as pontifex maximus or not at all.

events.title: The consulship of Cicero
events.summary: Marcus Tullius Cicero, the first novus homo consul in thirty years, defeated a land bill, defended Rabirius and Murena, and suppressed Catiline's conspiracy, executing five conspirators without trial on 5 December. He was hailed as father of his country (pater patriae) and never stopped reminding Rome of it.

events.title: Lex Labiena restores election of priests
events.summary: The tribune Titus Labienus restored the Domitian system of electing members of the major priestly colleges by seventeen tribes chosen by lot, which Sulla had abolished. It made possible Caesar's election as pontifex maximus later that year.

events.title: Battle of Pistoria
events.summary: Trying to escape over the Apennines to Gaul, Catiline was trapped between Metellus Celer's army to the north and Gaius Antonius', commanded on the day by Marcus Petreius because Antonius claimed gout. His 3,000 remaining men fought to the death; Catiline was found far in advance of his line among enemy bodies, still breathing.

sides.strength: Antonius' army under Petreius, perhaps 3 legions

battle.significance: Ended the Catilinarian rising.

events.title: The Bona Dea scandal
events.summary: At the women-only rites of the Bona Dea held in the house of the pontifex maximus Caesar, Publius Clodius Pulcher was discovered disguised as a female musician, allegedly to meet Caesar's wife Pompeia. Caesar divorced her, saying his wife must be above suspicion. At the trial for sacrilege in 61 Cicero demolished Clodius' alibi, but the jury acquitted him 31 to 25, bribed, Cicero says, with Crassus' money.

events.title: Pompey lands at Brundisium and disbands his army
events.summary: Returning from the East with an undefeated army, Pompey landed at Brundisium in December 62 and, against widespread fear that he would repeat Sulla, dismissed his soldiers to their homes until his triumph. He then found he could not get his eastern settlement ratified or land for his veterans.

events.title: Construction of the Pons Fabricius
events.summary: Lucius Fabricius, curator of roads, built the stone bridge linking the Campus Martius to the Tiber Island; inscriptions on both arches record his name and its approval by the consuls of 21 BC. It is the oldest Roman bridge still in use in its original form.

events.title: Scaurus' expedition against the Nabataeans
events.summary: Pompey had marched toward Petra in 63 when news of Mithridates' death turned him back; his legate Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, governing Syria, invaded Nabataea and, through Antipater's mediation, accepted 300 talents from Aretas III. Scaurus celebrated it on coins as aedile in 58 showing Aretas kneeling beside a camel.

events.title: Metellus Nepos and Caesar suspended from office
events.summary: The tribune Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos, Pompey's agent, proposed recalling Pompey to restore order with his army. Cato and Quintus Minucius Thermus vetoed it and violence broke out in the Forum; the Senate suspended Nepos and the praetor Caesar, who backed him. Nepos fled to Pompey; Caesar was reinstated after dismissing his lictors.

events.title: Cicero's Pro Archia
events.summary: Cicero defended the citizenship of the Syrian Greek poet Aulus Licinius Archias, client of the Luculli, prosecuted under the lex Papia, and turned the speech into a celebration of literature and humane learning. Archias had promised an epic on Cicero's consulship.

events.title: Pompey visits Posidonius at Rhodes
events.summary: On his way home Pompey called on the Stoic philosopher-historian Posidonius at Rhodes, ordering his lictors not to knock at the door and lowering his fasces before the philosopher. Posidonius, though in pain from gout, lectured him on the theme that only the good is honourable.

events.title: Clodius acquitted of sacrilege
events.summary: Tried before a specially constituted court for profaning the Bona Dea rites, Publius Clodius claimed to have been at Interamna that night; Cicero destroyed his alibi by testifying that Clodius had visited him in Rome. The jury acquitted 31 to 25, bought, said Cicero, with money from Crassus.

events.title: Pompey's third triumph
events.summary: Having disbanded his army at Brundisium in December 62, confounding fears of a Sullan coup, Pompey celebrated over two days, 28-29 September, a triumph over Mithridates, Tigranes, the pirates and fourteen nations. The second day was his 45th birthday. Placards boasted that he had triumphed over all three continents.

events.title: Caesar's propraetorship in Further Spain
events.summary: Released by his creditors only when Crassus stood surety for 830 talents, Caesar campaigned against the Lusitanians and Callaeci, sailing to Brigantium in the far north-west, and was hailed imperator. He returned in 60 and gave up his triumph to stand for the consulship when the senate, led by Cato, refused to let him stand in absentia.

events.title: Ariovistus defeats the Aedui at Magetobriga
events.summary: The Sequani and Arverni, rivals of the Aedui, hired the Suebic king Ariovistus with some 15,000 Germans; at Magetobriga (or Admagetobriga) he crushed the Aedui, who lost their nobility and hostages. Ariovistus then seized a third of the Sequani's land and settled 120,000 Germans in Gaul. The Aeduan druid Diviciacus went to Rome to plead for help.

battle.significance: Created the pretext for Caesar's intervention in 58.

events.title: Revolt of the Allobroges under Catugnatus
events.summary: Despite their loyalty during the Catilinarian affair, the debt-burdened Allobroges rose under Catugnatus and attacked Narbonese towns. The governor Gaius Pomptinus defeated them at Solonium in 61; he had to wait until 54 for his triumph.

events.title: Pompey buys the consulship for Afranius
events.summary: Pompey had his legate Lucius Afranius elected consul for 60 by open bribery, distributing money from his own gardens; the Senate passed decrees allowing magistrates' houses to be searched. Afranius proved, said Cicero, a consul whose only skill was dancing.

events.title: Formation of the 'First Triumvirate'
events.summary: Caesar, consul-elect for 59, brought together Pompey, frustrated by the senate's refusal to ratify his acta and give land to his veterans, and Crassus, who wanted relief for the tax-farmers of Asia who had overbid their contract. The three agreed that nothing should happen in the state that displeased any of them. Varro called the alliance the three-headed monster.

events.title: Caesar forgoes his triumph to stand for the consulship
events.summary: Returning from Further Spain in summer 60, Caesar asked permission to stand for the consulship in absence so that he could keep his imperium and celebrate a triumph. Cato talked the request out until sunset on the last day, and Caesar crossed the pomerium, giving up the triumph.

events.title: Defeat of the Flavian land bill
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Flavius proposed land for Pompey's veterans, to be funded from the eastern revenues; the consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer opposed it so vehemently that Flavius imprisoned him, and Celer had the wall of the prison broken to summon the Senate to his cell. Pompey dropped the bill.

events.title: Bribery on both sides in the elections for 59
events.summary: To match Caesar's alliance with the rich Lucius Lucceius, the optimates funded Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus with a common chest; even Cato, Suetonius says, admitted the bribery was in the public interest. Caesar and Bibulus were elected.

events.title: Burebista's Dacian kingdom
events.summary: The Getic-Dacian king Burebista, advised by the high priest Decaeneus, united the Dacians, destroyed the Boii and Taurisci on the middle Danube (c. 60), and sacked the Greek cities of the Black Sea from Olbia to Apollonia. Strabo credits him with 200,000 warriors; Caesar planned a war against him before his death, and Burebista was murdered about the same time.

events.title: Frescoes of the Villa of the Mysteries
events.summary: In a suburban villa outside Pompeii's Herculaneum Gate, a room was painted in the Second Style around 60 with a continuous megalographic frieze of near life-size figures in a Dionysiac ritual: a reading boy, a flagellation, a winged figure, a bride's toilette. It is the most celebrated surviving Roman wall-painting of the Republic.

events.title: Caesar's first consulship
events.summary: Backed by Pompey's veterans and Crassus' money, Caesar forced through land laws, the ratification of Pompey's eastern settlement, a one-third rebate on the Asian tax contract, a comprehensive extortion law and recognition of Ptolemy XII as king, for which Ptolemy paid Caesar and Pompey 6,000 talents. His colleague Bibulus, pelted with dung and his fasces broken, shut himself at home and declared he was watching the sky for omens, which in religious law invalidated every assembly held that year.

events.title: Lex Julia agraria and the Campanian law
events.summary: Caesar's first land law distributed remaining public land and land bought from willing sellers to Pompey's veterans and the poor, with a twenty-man commission; senators had to swear to obey it, and Cato and Metellus Celer gave way only at the last moment. A second law in May distributed the ager Campanus, the last great block of Italian public land, to 20,000 fathers of three or more children.

events.title: Lex Vatinia: Caesar's Gallic command
events.summary: The tribune Publius Vatinius carried a law giving Caesar Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum for five years, to 1 March 54, with three legions. The senate, on Pompey's motion, added Transalpine Gaul and a fourth legion when its governor-designate Metellus Celer died.

events.title: Lex Julia de repetundis
events.summary: Caesar's extortion law, over 100 chapters long, regulated governors' requisitions, gifts, and accounts, and remained the basis of Roman law on provincial misgovernment into the imperial period. Cicero called it an excellent law even while attacking its author.

events.title: Caesar remits a third of the Asian tax contract
events.summary: Caesar, as consul, carried a law remitting a third of the price the publicani had bid for the taxes of Asia, which Crassus and his equestrian allies had been pressing for since 61 and Cato had blocked. Caesar warned the contractors not to bid so recklessly again.

events.title: Ptolemy XII recognised as friend and ally
events.summary: A law of Caesar recognised Ptolemy XII Auletes as king and 'friend and ally of the Roman people', in return for a promised 6,000 talents to Caesar and Pompey, roughly a year's revenue of Egypt. Auletes borrowed the money from the Roman banker Gaius Rabirius Postumus.

events.title: Ariovistus declared king and friend
events.summary: In Caesar's consulship the Senate gave Ariovistus, who now dominated eastern Gaul, the titles 'king and friend' of the Roman people, with gifts. A year later Caesar would cite his own generosity as proof of Ariovistus' ingratitude.

events.title: Bibulus watches the skies
events.summary: After being driven from the Forum with a basket of dung tipped over his head, his fasces broken, Caesar's colleague Marcus Bibulus withdrew to his house for the rest of 59 and announced that he was watching the heavens for omens, technically invalidating every assembly. Wags dated documents to the consulship 'of Julius and Caesar'.

events.title: The Vettius affair
events.summary: The informer Lucius Vettius claimed a plot by young optimates, including Curio, Brutus and Lucius Lentulus, to murder Pompey, then changed his list, adding Lucullus and Cicero's son-in-law. He was found strangled in prison. Cicero suspected Caesar had staged it.

events.title: Clodius transfers to the plebs
events.summary: To become eligible for the tribunate, the patrician Publius Clodius Pulcher had himself adopted by a plebeian, Publius Fonteius, who was younger than he; Caesar as pontifex maximus presided and Pompey took the auspices, within hours of Cicero's complaints in a speech in court. Fonteius emancipated him at once.

events.title: Publication of the acta of Senate and people
events.summary: One of Caesar's first acts as consul was to have the proceedings of the Senate and of the people published daily. The acta diurna, posted publicly and copied for readers in the provinces, continued under the Principate (without the Senate's debates, which Augustus suppressed) as a kind of official gazette.

events.title: Pompey marries Caesar's daughter Julia
events.summary: In April or May 59 Julia, aged about seventeen and already betrothed to Servilius Caepio, married Pompey, aged forty-seven; Caepio was compensated with Pompey's daughter. The marriage, by all accounts affectionate, sealed the alliance, and Caesar married Calpurnia, daughter of Lucius Calpurnius Piso, consul designate for 58.

events.title: Cicero's Pro Flacco
events.summary: Cicero defended Lucius Valerius Flaccus, his praetor of 63, on charges of extortion in Asia. The speech's attacks on Greek witnesses and on the Jews of Rome, whose gold for the Temple Flaccus had confiscated, preserve important evidence for Jewish communities in Asia and Rome. Flaccus was acquitted.

events.title: Lex Clodia de capite civis and the exile of Cicero
events.summary: Clodius carried a law outlawing anyone who had executed a citizen without trial. Cicero, abandoned by Pompey, left Rome in March before it passed; a second law named him, banished him 400 miles and confiscated his property. His Palatine house was demolished and Clodius dedicated a shrine of Liberty on the site.
events.locName: Rome; Cicero's house on the Palatine

events.title: Caesar blocks the Helvetii at Geneva
events.summary: The Helvetii, having burned their twelve towns and four hundred villages, set out on 28 March 58 to cross through the Roman province at Geneva. Caesar hurried from Rome, broke the Rhône bridge, stalled their envoys, and fortified the left bank with a wall and ditch nineteen Roman miles long, forcing them to take the route through Sequanian territory.

events.title: Battle of the Arar
events.summary: The Helvetii, 368,000 people by Caesar's count, began migrating west on 28 March 58. Blocked at Geneva by Caesar's 19-mile wall along the Rhône, they took the route through Sequanian territory. Caesar caught the Tigurini canton still on the east bank of the Saône after three quarters had crossed, and cut them to pieces with three legions.

battle.significance: Opening blow of the Gallic Wars; justified by Caesar as both defensive and revenge for 107.

events.title: Battle of Bibracte
events.summary: When Caesar turned aside toward the Aeduan capital Bibracte for grain, the Helvetii attacked him. He sent away his horse and his officers', so that all shared the danger equally, and fought uphill against the Helvetian phalanx, then faced about when the Boii and Tulingi struck his flank. The fight at the wagon laager lasted into the night.

sides.losses: considerable (Caesar spent three days burying the dead)

battle.significance: Destroyed the Helvetian migration; made Caesar the arbiter of central Gaul.

events.title: Battle against Ariovistus
events.summary: Ariovistus, king of the Suebi, whom the Sequani had invited into Gaul and whom Caesar himself as consul had had declared a friend of the Roman people, now ruled much of Alsace. After a panic in the Roman camp at Vesontio, where officers made their wills, Caesar marched against him and forced a battle before the new moon that, according to captives, German seeresses said was required for victory. Publius Crassus' cavalry reserve rescued the wavering left; the Germans fled to the Rhine.

sides.strength: seven peoples including Harudes, Marcomanni, Triboci, Vangiones, Nemetes, Sedusii and Suebi

battle.significance: Expelled the Suebi from Gaul and set the Rhine as Rome's de facto frontier.

events.title: The laws of Clodius: free grain and the collegia
events.summary: Publius Clodius Pulcher, a patrician who had himself adopted into a plebeian family in 59 with Caesar presiding as pontifex maximus, carried as tribune a law making the monthly grain ration free, and restored the neighbourhood associations (collegia) banned in 64. Cicero says the grain cost a fifth of state revenue.

events.title: Cato annexes Cyprus
events.summary: Clodius had Cyprus annexed from its Ptolemaic king, brother of Ptolemy XII, and sent Cato to carry out the confiscation, removing him from Rome. The king poisoned himself; Cato auctioned the royal treasures and brought back nearly 7,000 talents, keeping meticulous accounts that were then lost in a shipwreck and a fire.

events.title: Panic at Vesontio
events.summary: At Vesontio (Besançon), where Caesar seized the Sequani's main town and supply base, tales of the Germans' size and ferocity caused panic; officers wrote their wills and soldiers threatened mutiny. Caesar shamed them by announcing he would march with the Tenth legion alone, which then became his favourite.

events.title: Clodius destroys Cicero's house and builds a shrine to Liberty
events.summary: After Cicero's flight, Clodius had his Palatine house, bought from Crassus for 3.5 million sesterces, demolished and dedicated part of the site to Libertas, with a statue said to be a Greek courtesan's from Tanagra. Cicero's villas at Tusculum and Formiae were also plundered.

events.title: Ptolemy XII expelled from Alexandria
events.summary: Driven out by Alexandrians angry at taxes and at his acquiescence in the loss of Cyprus, Ptolemy XII travelled to Rome via Rhodes, where Cato advised him to go home. In Rome he lived at Pompey's Alban villa and spent borrowed money to buy his restoration, while his daughter Berenice IV took the throne.

events.title: Senate destroys altars of Isis
events.summary: The Senate repeatedly ordered the private altars of Isis and Sarapis on the Capitol destroyed (58, 53, 50 and 48); in 50 the consul Lucius Aemilius Paullus took an axe to a temple door himself when workmen refused. In 43 the triumvirs reversed policy and voted a public temple of Isis and Sarapis.

events.title: Recall of Cicero
events.summary: With Pompey now hostile to Clodius, and the tribunes Milo and Sestius fighting Clodius' gangs in the streets, the centuriate assembly voted Cicero's recall. He landed at Brundisium on his daughter's birthday and entered Rome on 4 September to a hero's welcome.

events.title: Cicero recovers his house: De domo sua
events.summary: Returning from exile on 4 September 57, Cicero argued before the pontifical college on 29 September that Clodius' consecration of his house site was invalid because Clodius' adoption and tribunate were unlawful. The pontiffs found for him and the Senate voted compensation, but Clodius' gangs attacked the builders.

events.title: Pompey takes charge of the grain supply
events.summary: Amid a grain shortage blamed on Clodius' free distributions, Cicero proposed and a consular law gave Pompey charge of the grain supply (cura annonae) for five years with proconsular imperium and 15 legates. It was another great command, and it made Pompey indispensable.

events.title: Battle of the Axona
events.summary: The Belgae, allegedly 300,000 strong, gathered against Caesar, who was guided and supplied by the Remi. Caesar fortified a camp on the Aisne with long flanking trenches and drove off Belgic attempts to cross the river. Short of food, the coalition dispersed, and the Suessiones, Bellovaci and Ambiani submitted one by one.

battle.significance: Broke up the Belgic coalition without a pitched battle.

events.title: Battle of the Sabis
events.summary: The Nervii, with the Atrebates and Viromandui, burst out of woods across the Sabis while the legions were still digging camp. The Roman army fought in disconnected blocks; the Twelfth and Seventh legions were nearly overrun, all but one centurion of the Twelfth's fourth cohort dead. Caesar snatched a shield and went to the front line; Labienus sent the Tenth back across the river and the Nervii were annihilated.

battle.significance: Destroyed the most formidable Belgic people; northern Gaul submitted.

events.title: Siege of the Atuatuci
events.summary: The Atuatuci, descendants of the Cimbri and Teutones left behind in 102, laughed at Caesar's siege tower until it moved; they surrendered, threw some arms over the wall, and attacked at night with the weapons they had hidden. Caesar sold the whole population, 53,000 people by the purchasers' count.

battle.significance: Completed the Belgic campaign.

events.title: Battle of Octodurus
events.summary: Servius Sulpicius Galba, sent with the Twelfth legion to open the Great St Bernard route, was attacked in his half-built winter camp at Octodurus by the Seduni and Veragri. A desperate sortie routed them, but Galba abandoned the valley.

battle.significance: Showed the Alpine route could not yet be held.

events.title: Murder of the Alexandrian envoys
events.summary: An embassy of a hundred Alexandrians led by the philosopher Dio came to Rome to argue against Ptolemy XII's restoration; agents of the king killed many of them at Puteoli and Dio himself in Rome. Marcus Caelius Rufus was later prosecuted for involvement, which Cicero rebutted in Pro Caelio.

events.title: Street war of Clodius and Milo
events.summary: From late 57 the armed bands of Clodius, now aedile-designate, and of the tribune Titus Annius Milo, backed by Pompey and the optimates, fought for control of the streets. In November Clodius' men attacked Cicero's builders, set fire to Quintus Cicero's house and assaulted Cicero on the Sacred Way; Milo obstructed Clodius' election by watching for omens.

events.title: Belgic siege of Bibrax
events.summary: The combined Belgic army attacked Bibrax, a town of the Remi, with the Gallic siege method of surrounding the walls and showering them with stones before undermining the gates under a testudo. Caesar sent Numidian, Cretan and Balearic missile troops at night and the siege was lifted.

battle.significance: Prelude to the standoff on the Axona.

events.title: Surrender of the Suessiones and Bellovaci
events.summary: After the Belgic coalition dispersed, Caesar marched on Noviodunum of the Suessiones, whose inhabitants surrendered in terror at the sight of his siege towers and vineae; the Bellovaci gave up at Bratuspantium at the intercession of Diviciacus, and the Ambiani followed.

battle.significance: Broke the southern Belgae before the campaign against the Nervii.

events.title: Publius Crassus receives the submission of Armorica
events.summary: With a single legion Publius Crassus, Caesar's young legate and son of the triumvir, received the submission of the Veneti, Venelli, Osismi, Coriosolites, Esuvii, Aulerci and Redones. Caesar announced all Gaul pacified; the Veneti revolted the following winter by seizing Crassus' requisitioning officers.

events.title: Pro Sestio: 'cum dignitate otium'
events.summary: Defending the tribune Publius Sestius on a charge of violence brought by Clodian supporters, Cicero delivered a manifesto for a broad 'party of the best' (optimates), all honest and propertied citizens united for peace with dignity. Sestius was acquitted unanimously.

events.title: The meeting at Luca
events.summary: After meeting Crassus at Ravenna, Caesar met Pompey at Luca, the southernmost town of his province, and renewed the alliance: Pompey and Crassus would be consuls in 55 and receive five-year commands; Caesar's command would be extended. Plutarch says 200 senators and 120 lictors gathered there.

events.title: Pro Caelio
events.summary: Marcus Caelius Rufus, Cicero's former pupil, was prosecuted for violence, including the murder of the Alexandrian envoy Dio and an attempt to poison Clodia Metelli, during the Megalensian games. Cicero turned the case into a demolition of Clodia, 'the Medea of the Palatine', and won an acquittal.

events.title: Naval battle against the Veneti
events.summary: The Veneti, the seafaring people of southern Brittany, detained Roman officers requisitioning grain. Decimus Brutus brought a fleet of galleys built on the Loire against their tall oak sailing ships with leather sails. The Romans cut the enemy halyards with sickles on poles, the wind died, and the immobilised Venetic fleet was boarded ship by ship while Caesar watched from the cliffs.

sides.strength: galley fleet and Gallic allied ships

battle.significance: Rome's first Atlantic naval battle; secured Armorica and opened the Channel.

events.title: The Sibylline oracle on the king of Egypt
events.summary: In January 56 the tribune Gaius Cato produced a Sibylline oracle, leaked from the quindecimviri, forbidding Rome to restore the king of Egypt 'with a multitude'. It blocked the commission to Publius Lentulus Spinther and Pompey alike, until Gabinius acted without authority in 55.

events.title: De provinciis consularibus: Cicero's palinode
events.summary: After the meeting at Luca, Cicero spoke in the Senate for keeping Caesar in Gaul and for recalling his own enemies Piso from Macedonia and Gabinius from Syria. He privately called the speech his palinode, his recantation, and stopped resisting the dynasts.

events.title: Publius Crassus conquers Aquitania
events.summary: With twelve cohorts and cavalry, Publius Crassus defeated the Sotiates, besieging their town against mining countermines (the Aquitani were skilled copper miners), and accepted the surrender of Adiatuanus and his 600 devoted followers (soldurii). He then stormed the camp of an Aquitanian and Cantabrian army advised by veterans of Sertorius.

battle.significance: Brought south-western Gaul under Roman control.

events.title: Sabinus defeats Viridovix
events.summary: Quintus Titurius Sabinus, with three legions among the Venelli of the Cotentin, feigned fear and had a Gallic auxiliary 'desert' to report him ready to flee; the Gauls under Viridovix charged uphill at his camp, exhausted, and were routed.

battle.significance: Secured Normandy while Caesar fought the Veneti.

events.title: Caesar's late campaign against the Morini and Menapii
events.summary: At the end of 56 Caesar marched against the Morini and Menapii on the Channel coast, who withdrew into forests and marshes; he began cutting down woods to reach them but autumn rains forced him into winter quarters.

events.title: Caesar's first expedition to Britain
events.summary: Late in the season, with two legions, Caesar crossed from the land of the Morini. Finding armed Britons on the cliffs at Dover, he coasted to an open beach; the legionaries hesitated in the surf until the eagle-bearer of the Tenth leapt into the sea. A storm at full moon wrecked many ships, the Seventh was ambushed while foraging, and Caesar left after a few weeks with token hostages.

sides.strength: 2 legions (7th and 10th), cavalry failed to arrive

battle.significance: Propaganda triumph more than conquest: Rome's first military contact with Britain.

events.title: The tribune Ateius curses Crassus' departure
events.summary: As Crassus left Rome in November 55 for Syria and the war with Parthia, the tribune Gaius Ateius Capito tried to arrest him, then at the city gate lit a brazier and pronounced dire curses invoking strange gods. After Carrhae the censor Appius Claudius expelled Ateius from the Senate for falsifying the auspices.

events.title: Second consulship of Pompey and Crassus; lex Trebonia
events.summary: Elected after violent delays, Pompey and Crassus had the tribune Gaius Trebonius carry a law giving Pompey both Spains and Crassus Syria for five years, and then themselves passed a law extending Caesar's Gallic command for five years. Cato, protesting, was dragged from the Forum.

events.title: Dedication of the Theatre of Pompey
events.summary: Pompey dedicated Rome's first permanent stone theatre, with a temple of Venus Victrix at the top of the cavea so that the seats could be described as steps to a shrine, a great portico garden, and a meeting hall (curia) in which the senate could gather. At the inaugural games 500 lions and some 18 elephants were killed.

events.title: Gabinius restores Ptolemy XII
events.summary: Defying a Sibylline oracle and the senate, Aulus Gabinius, governor of Syria, marched into Egypt and restored Ptolemy XII Auletes, allegedly for 10,000 talents. His young cavalry commander Mark Antony distinguished himself at Pelusium. Gabinius was convicted of extortion in 54 and exiled; his troops, the Gabiniani, stayed in Alexandria as royal guards.

events.title: Massacre of the Usipetes and Tencteri
events.summary: Two German peoples driven from their lands by the Suebi crossed the lower Rhine, 430,000 souls by Caesar's figure. While their chiefs were in his camp negotiating, Caesar detained them and attacked the leaderless camp, slaughtering men, women and children, who were driven into the rivers. Caesar reports no Roman dead.
events.locName: near the confluence of the Meuse and Rhine

battle.significance: Atrocity that provoked an attempt to prosecute Caesar; ended German crossings for a time.

events.title: Caesar bridges the Rhine
events.summary: To show the Germans that Rome could cross at will, Caesar built a timber trestle bridge over the Rhine in ten days, describing its piles, driven at an angle against the current, and its braces in a famous technical passage. He spent eighteen days on the east bank burning Sugambrian villages and then destroyed the bridge.

events.title: The elephants at Pompey's games
events.summary: At the games for the dedication of his theatre Pompey staged five days of beast hunts with some 500 lions, 410 leopards and the first rhinoceros and lynx seen at Rome, and on the last day twenty elephants fought Gaetulian hunters. When the wounded elephants seemed to plead for mercy the crowd turned against Pompey and cursed him.

events.title: Lex Licinia de sodaliciis
events.summary: Crassus, as consul, carried a law against the use of organised clubs (sodalicia) to canvass and bribe tribes, with an unusual procedure in which the prosecutor named four tribes and the defendant rejected one to form the jury. Cicero's Pro Plancio (54) was delivered under it.

events.title: Lucretius' De rerum natura
events.summary: Titus Lucretius Carus' didactic poem in six books expounds Epicurean physics in Latin hexameters: atoms and void, the mortality of the soul, the origins of the world, civilisation, disease. Cicero wrote to his brother in February 54 that it had 'many flashes of genius, yet much art'. Jerome's later story that a love-potion drove Lucretius mad is now generally rejected.

events.title: Cicero's De oratore
events.summary: Cicero's three-book dialogue on the ideal orator, set in 91 at the villa of Lucius Licinius Crassus in the days before his death, presents Crassus and Marcus Antonius debating whether the orator needs universal learning. Written in the political sidelines after Luca, it is his first great dialogue.

events.title: Second expedition to Britain: Cassivellaunus
events.summary: In 54 Caesar crossed with five legions, 2,000 cavalry and some 800 ships, beat off the British war leader Cassivellaunus' chariot tactics, forced the Thames at a staked ford and stormed his oppidum. The Trinovantes, whose prince Mandubracius had fled to Caesar, defected; Caesar imposed tribute and took hostages before a revolt in Gaul called him back.
events.locName: Thames crossing and the oppidum of Cassivellaunus

sides.strength: allied British tribes, 4,000 charioteers kept after the main battle

battle.significance: Created the first Roman client relationships in Britain, used by Claudius in 43.

events.title: Death of Julia
events.summary: Julia, Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife, died in childbirth in late summer 54; the child died days later. The people insisted on burying her in the Campus Martius. Ancient writers saw the loss of the personal bond between the two men as the beginning of the break; Pompey declined Caesar's offer of another marriage alliance and married Cornelia, daughter of Metellus Scipio, in 52.
events.locName: Rome; buried in the Campus Martius

events.title: Destruction of Sabinus and Cotta at Atuatuca
events.summary: Ambiorix, king of the Eburones, persuaded Quintus Titurius Sabinus that a general Gallic rising and German invasion were coming, and offered safe passage. Overruling Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta, Sabinus marched his legion and five cohorts out of their winter camp and into an ambush in a wooded valley two miles away. Sabinus was killed while negotiating, Cotta fighting; the survivors killed themselves in the camp that night.

battle.significance: Triggered the rising of the Nervii and Treveri in 54-53 and Caesar's war of extermination against the Eburones.

events.title: Siege of Quintus Cicero's camp
events.summary: The Nervii and their allies besieged Quintus Cicero's legion, building a rampart and towers Roman-style and firing the thatched huts with red-hot clay sling bullets. A Gallic slave smuggled out a message; Caesar sent a letter in Greek tied to a javelin, which stuck in a tower for two days, and relieved the camp with 7,000 men, routing 60,000.
events.locName: winter camp in the territory of the Nervii

battle.significance: Saved the army in northern Gaul after Atuatuca.

events.title: Crassus' first campaign in Mesopotamia
events.summary: Crassus crossed the Euphrates at Zeugma in 54, received the submission of Greek cities such as Ichnae, Nicephorium and Carrhae, stormed Zenodotium after it killed a hundred of his soldiers, and was saluted imperator. He then withdrew to winter in Syria, leaving garrisons, which Plutarch and Dio judge a fatal loss of momentum.

events.title: Crassus plunders the Temple at Jerusalem
events.summary: Wintering in Syria, Crassus collected funds for his campaign, including the 2,000 talents in the Temple treasury at Jerusalem that Pompey had left untouched, and a golden beam the priest Eleazar gave him on oath that he would take nothing more. He also stripped the temple of Atargatis at Hierapolis.

events.title: The electoral scandal of 54
events.summary: The consular candidates Gaius Memmius and Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus made a pact with the consuls of 54 promising them, in return for support, either three augurs and two ex-consuls to swear falsely to a lex curiata and a senatus consultum on their provinces, or 400,000 sesterces each. Memmius, encouraged by Pompey, read the contract aloud in the Senate. Interest rates doubled from 4 to 8 per cent a month on the eve of the elections.

events.title: The trials of Gabinius
events.summary: Returning from Syria after restoring Ptolemy XII without authority, Aulus Gabinius was acquitted of treason (maiestas) in October 54 amid suspicion of bribery, but then convicted of extortion, with Cicero, under pressure from Pompey, defending his old enemy. Gabinius went into exile; the 10,000 talents he was said to have received from Ptolemy could not be recovered.

events.title: Pro Rabirio Postumo
events.summary: Cicero defended the banker Gaius Rabirius Postumus, who had lent Ptolemy XII the money for his recognition and restoration and then served as the king's finance minister (dioiketes) in Alexandria, wearing Greek dress, before being imprisoned and fleeing. He was charged with receiving part of Gabinius' bribes.

events.title: The Tiber flood of 54
events.summary: A great flood of the Tiber in autumn 54 inundated low-lying parts of Rome and destroyed houses and goods; popular opinion blamed it on the gods' anger at Gabinius' acquittal, and Cicero quoted Homer on Zeus flooding the land of unjust judges.

events.title: Caesar buys land for a new forum
events.summary: Through his agents Cicero and Oppius, Caesar bought private property north-west of the Forum Romanum for a new forum at a cost of 60 million sesterces, rising to 100 million according to Suetonius. The same year Lucius Aemilius Paullus began rebuilding the Basilica Aemilia with Caesar's money and the Basilica Julia was begun on the site of the Basilica Sempronia.

events.title: Labienus kills Indutiomarus
events.summary: Indutiomarus, leader of the Treveri, gathered the Gauls against Labienus' winter camp among the Remi after Atuatuca; Labienus secretly brought in cavalry, offered a reward for Indutiomarus alone, and his horsemen caught and beheaded him at a river ford.

battle.significance: Calmed the north-east for the winter of 54/53.

events.title: The poems of Catullus
events.summary: Gaius Valerius Catullus of Verona, who died young about 54, left a book of 116 poems: short lyrics in Greek metres, epigrams and longer learned pieces including a miniature epic on Peleus and Thetis. His affair with 'Lesbia', usually identified with Clodia Metelli, and his abuse of Caesar and Mamurra made him the voice of the neoteric poets.

events.title: Brutus' LIBERTAS denarius
events.summary: As moneyer about 54, Marcus Junius Brutus struck denarii showing the head of Libertas and, on the reverse, his ancestor Lucius Junius Brutus, the first consul, walking between lictors; another type paired the founder with Servilius Ahala, killer of the would-be tyrant Maelius. The ancestry Brutus advertised was quoted at him by those urging him to kill Caesar.

events.title: Battle of Carrhae
events.summary: Crassus invaded Mesopotamia with seven legions, rejecting Artavasdes of Armenia's advice to come through the hills, and was led into open steppe by the Osrhoene chieftain Abgar (Plutarch's Ariamnes). The Parthian general Surena, with 1,000 cataphracts and 9,000 horse archers resupplied with arrows from a camel train, pinned the Roman square. Publius Crassus' breakout ended with his head on a lance; the army retreated to Carrhae by night, abandoning 4,000 wounded.

battle.significance: Rome's worst defeat in the East; ended the triumvirate's balance and made Parthia Rome's great eastern rival for 270 years.

events.title: Death of Crassus at the parley
events.summary: Retreating from Carrhae toward the Armenian hills, Crassus was forced by his mutinous soldiers to accept Surena's offer of a parley. In a scuffle over the horse brought for him, Crassus and his officers were killed. His head and hand were sent to King Orodes.

events.title: No consuls until July: the interregnum of 53
events.summary: Because of bribery scandals, tribunician obstruction and calls for Pompey's dictatorship, no consuls were elected for 53 until July, when Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus and Marcus Valerius Messalla Rufus were finally chosen under a succession of interreges. Violence prevented elections for 52 as well.

events.title: Labienus defeats the Treveri
events.summary: Labienus, facing the Treveri across a river with 25 cohorts, pretended to retreat in panic so that the Gauls crossed to attack on bad ground, then turned and routed them before German reinforcements arrived. Power among the Treveri passed to Caesar's ally Cingetorix.

battle.significance: Secured the Moselle region before Caesar's Rhine crossing.

events.title: Caesar's second Rhine bridge
events.summary: To punish the Suebi for aiding the Treveri, Caesar built a second timber bridge over the Rhine a little upstream of the first, probably near Neuwied or Urmitz. The Suebi withdrew into the forest of Bacenis and Caesar returned after a few days, demolishing the end of the bridge and leaving a tower and garrison.

events.title: Sugambrian raid on Atuatuca
events.summary: While Caesar ravaged the Eburones, 2,000 Sugambrian horsemen crossed the Rhine to plunder, learned that Caesar's baggage was at Atuatuca under Quintus Cicero, and nearly stormed the camp, destroying two cohorts of recruits caught foraging. The centurion Publius Sextius Baculus, sick in his tent, held the gate.

battle.significance: Caesar's own lesson on the dangers of dispersing troops.

events.title: Caesar executes Acco at Durocortorum
events.summary: At a council of Gaul at Durocortorum (Reims) in autumn 53, Caesar tried the Senonian leader Acco for conspiracy and had him flogged to death 'in the ancestral manner'. The execution of a Gallic noble horrified the Gallic aristocracy and helped spark the general revolt of 52.

events.title: Crassus' head and Euripides' Bacchae
events.summary: When Surena's messenger arrived at the Armenian court, where Orodes was celebrating a marriage alliance with Artavasdes II, a performance of Euripides' Bacchae was under way. The actor Jason of Tralles took Crassus' head and sang Agave's lines over it as if it were Pentheus'. Surena meanwhile staged a mock triumph at Seleucia with a Roman captive dressed as Crassus.

events.title: Murder of Clodius and the burning of the Curia
events.summary: Clodius, riding back to Rome, met Milo's larger armed retinue on the Via Appia near Bovillae. A brawl started between the slaves; Clodius was wounded and carried into an inn, and Milo had him dragged out and killed. Next day the Clodian mob carried the body into the Curia Hostilia and cremated it on a pyre of benches and records, burning down the senate house and the Basilica Porcia.

events.title: Massacre at Cenabum and the rising of Vercingetorix
events.summary: The Carnutes killed the Roman traders at Cenabum, among them Caesar's grain agent Gaius Fufius Cita. The news was shouted from field to field and reached the Arverni, 160 miles away, by the end of the first watch. There the young noble Vercingetorix, expelled from Gergovia by his uncle, raised an army, was proclaimed king and became leader of a pan-Gallic rising.

events.title: The trial of Milo: Pro Milone
events.summary: Tried under Pompey's new law on violence before a court ringed by Pompey's soldiers, Milo was convicted 38 to 13. Cicero, unnerved by the soldiers and the Clodian crowd, delivered his defence badly; he later published the polished Pro Milone, arguing Clodius' death was lawful self-defence. Milo, in exile at Massilia, said that if Cicero had spoken that way he would not be eating such good mullets.

events.title: Siege of Alesia
events.summary: After a failed cavalry attack on Caesar's column, Vercingetorix shut himself and 80,000 men in Alesia. Caesar enclosed it with a 11-mile inner line and a 14-mile outer line of ditches, ramparts, towers and booby traps, the stimuli, lilia and cippi. A relief army that Caesar puts at 250,000 foot and 8,000 horse attacked from outside while Vercingetorix attacked from within; the final assault fell on a weak camp on the north side, where Caesar himself, recognisable by his red cloak, led the reserve and German cavalry took the attackers in the rear.

sides.strength: c. 10 legions plus German cavalry and auxiliaries, perhaps 60,000-70,000
80,000 besieged; relief 250,000 foot, 8,000 horse (Caesar's figures, inflated)

battle.significance: Decided the conquest of Gaul.

events.title: Pompey sole consul
events.summary: With no consuls elected for 52 and the city in chaos, the senate under a senatus consultum ultimum had Pompey named consul without a colleague, on the motion of Bibulus seconded by Cato, as the lesser evil to a dictatorship. Pompey brought in troops, passed laws on violence and bribery, and imposed a five-year gap between magistracy and provincial command.

events.title: Siege of Avaricum
events.summary: Vercingetorix ordered a scorched-earth policy, but the Bituriges begged him to spare Avaricum, their finest town. Caesar's men, starving on short rations, built a siege terrace 330 feet wide and 80 feet high in 25 days. In a rainstorm they stormed the wall; Caesar says of 40,000 inside barely 800 escaped.

battle.significance: Fed Caesar's army; strengthened Vercingetorix's authority, since he had urged burning the town.

events.title: Battle of Gergovia
events.summary: Caesar besieged Vercingetorix in the Arvernian hill town of Gergovia. An assault meant to seize outlying camps ran out of control up to the walls; the legionaries, deaf to the recall, were thrown back with 46 centurions and nearly 700 men killed. It was Caesar's only clear defeat by Vercingetorix, and the Aedui defected.

battle.significance: Caesar's most serious reverse in Gaul; brought the Aedui into the revolt.

events.title: Battle of Lutetia
events.summary: Labienus, with four legions, faced the Parisii and Senones under the old commander Camulogenus near Lutetia. He crossed the Seine at night by deception, defeated Camulogenus, who was killed, and rejoined Caesar.

battle.significance: Allowed Caesar to reunite his army before Alesia.

events.title: The law of the ten tribunes
events.summary: With Pompey's backing all ten tribunes carried a law permitting Caesar to stand for a second consulship in absence, so that he could pass directly from his Gallic command to office without becoming a private citizen exposed to prosecution. Pompey's subsequent lex de iure magistratuum seemed to cancel it, and he added a clause exempting Caesar by hand after it was engraved.

events.title: Lex Pompeia de provinciis: the five-year interval
events.summary: Following a senatus consultum of 53, Pompey's law required a five-year gap between holding a consulship or praetorship and a provincial command, filling the gap in the meantime with ex-magistrates who had not yet governed. It ended the link between office and immediate provincial enrichment that drove bribery, and forced men like Cicero and Bibulus to govern in 51.

events.title: Caesar crosses the Cevennes in winter
events.summary: Hearing that Lucterius of the Cadurci was threatening the province, Caesar secured Narbo and then had his men clear six feet of snow to cross the Cevennes into Arvernian territory, forcing Vercingetorix to turn back to defend his home. Caesar then rode with a small escort through Aeduan country to join his legions.

events.title: Vellaunodunum, Cenabum and Noviodunum
events.summary: In a rapid winter march Caesar took the Senonian town of Vellaunodunum in two days, burned Cenabum in revenge for the massacre of Roman traders, and was accepting the surrender of Noviodunum of the Bituriges when Vercingetorix's cavalry appeared; the townsmen took up arms again until Caesar's German horse drove the Gauls off.

battle.significance: Led Vercingetorix to adopt a scorched-earth strategy.

events.title: Litaviccus leads the Aedui into revolt
events.summary: During the siege of Gergovia the Aeduan noble Litaviccus, bribed by the Arverni, led 10,000 Aeduan infantry marching to join Caesar into revolt by claiming Caesar had murdered their leaders. Caesar intercepted them with four legions, showing them the 'murdered' Eporedorix and Viridomarus alive; Litaviccus fled to Gergovia. The Aedui defected anyway after Caesar's repulse.

events.title: Council of Bibracte confirms Vercingetorix
events.summary: After the Aedui seized Noviodunum with Caesar's hostages, treasury and remounts, a council of all Gaul at Bibracte confirmed Vercingetorix as supreme commander, to the chagrin of the Aeduan leaders. Only the Remi, Lingones and Treveri stayed away. Vercingetorix demanded 15,000 cavalry.

events.title: The cavalry battle before Alesia
events.summary: As Caesar marched toward the province through the land of the Lingones, Vercingetorix attacked his column with his cavalry, whose leaders had sworn not to return home unless they rode twice through the Roman army. Caesar's German horsemen routed them, and Vercingetorix fell back to Alesia.

sides.strength: army on the march, German cavalry

battle.significance: Turned the campaign: Vercingetorix shut himself in Alesia.

events.title: Pompey marries Cornelia, daughter of Metellus Scipio
events.summary: Declining Caesar's offer of his great-niece Octavia, Pompey married Cornelia, widow of Publius Crassus and daughter of Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio, and made her father his colleague as consul for the last five months of 52. The marriage marked his realignment with the optimates.

events.title: Siege of Uxellodunum
events.summary: The last Gallic holdouts under Drappes and Lucterius held the hill fort of Uxellodunum. Caesar cut off their water by tunnelling to divert the spring; the defenders, believing the gods had dried it up, surrendered. Caesar had the hands of every man who had borne arms cut off and dispersed them as a warning, his clemency being known, says Hirtius, so that the punishment would not be blamed on cruelty.

battle.significance: Ended organised resistance in Gaul.

events.title: Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War
events.summary: Caesar's seven books on the Gallic War, written as plain 'notes' (commentarii) in the third person, probably drew on his annual dispatches to the senate and were in circulation by 51-50; Hirtius added an eighth. Cicero praised their unadorned elegance; Asinius Pollio thought them careless and too credulous of officers' reports and that Caesar would have revised them.

events.title: Parthian invasion of Syria repulsed by Cassius
events.summary: The king's son Pacorus and the general Osaces invaded Syria. Cassius, quaestor of Crassus now in charge of the province, held Antioch and ambushed the Parthians near Antigonea; Osaces was mortally wounded. Cicero, governor of neighbouring Cilicia, marched to the Taurus passes, then besieged the mountain fort of Pindenissum for 57 days and was hailed imperator.

sides.strength: Parthian army under Pacorus and Osaces

battle.significance: Saved Syria; ended the immediate Parthian threat after Carrhae.

events.title: Siege of Lemonum
events.summary: Dumnacus of the Andes besieged Duratius, a pro-Roman leader of the Pictones, in Lemonum (Poitiers); Caninius Rebilus and Gaius Fabius relieved the town and caught Dumnacus' army crossing the Loire, killing 12,000. Survivors under Drappes and Lucterius fled south to Uxellodunum.

sides.strength: two legions under Caninius, 25 cohorts under Fabius

battle.significance: Dispersed the last western coalition.

events.title: Campaign against the Bellovaci
events.summary: The Bellovaci under Correus and the Atrebatian Commius held a fortified hill against Caesar and four legions; when Caesar built a causeway and siege works, they escaped behind a screen of burning bundles and staged an ambush in which Correus refused to surrender and was killed.

events.title: Cicero takes Pindenissum
events.summary: As proconsul of Cilicia, Cicero campaigned against the 'Free Cilicians' of the Amanus, was hailed imperator by his troops near Issus, and besieged the mountain town of Pindenissum for 57 days with siege towers and mantlets, selling its people as slaves on the Saturnalia. He spent the next years seeking a triumph for it.

sides.strength: two weak legions and allied troops

battle.significance: Cicero's only military command.

events.title: Marcellus flogs a citizen of Novum Comum
events.summary: To deny the validity of the Latin rights and citizenship Caesar had given the Transpadane colony of Novum Comum, the consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus had a former magistrate of Comum flogged and told him to show his scars to Caesar. Cicero thought it outrageous; the man would have been immune as a citizen.

events.title: Cicero publishes De re publica
events.summary: Cicero's six-book dialogue on the best constitution, set in 129 at the house of Scipio Aemilianus, argued that Rome's mixed constitution was the best and imagined a rector or princeps guiding the state; it ended with the Dream of Scipio. It was a success on publication; most of it was lost until Angelo Mai found a palimpsest in the Vatican in 1819.

events.title: Death of Ptolemy XII; Cleopatra VII and Ptolemy XIII succeed
events.summary: Ptolemy XII died early in 51, leaving his kingdom by will to his eldest surviving daughter Cleopatra, about eighteen, and elder son Ptolemy XIII, about ten, under the guardianship of the Roman people; a copy of the will was sent to Rome and lodged with Pompey. Within two years the boy's regents Pothinus and Achillas had driven Cleopatra out.

events.title: Curio's motion: 370 votes to 22
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Scribonius Curio, whose enormous debts Caesar had quietly paid, blocked every attempt to recall Caesar unless Pompey also gave up his army. On 1 December 50 the senate voted 370 to 22 for both men to disarm. The consul Gaius Marcellus dissolved the session and, with the consuls-elect, went to Pompey and handed him a sword to defend the state.

events.title: Curio goes over to Caesar
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Scribonius Curio, elected as an opponent of Caesar, swung to Caesar early in 50, allegedly after Caesar paid his debts of 60 million sesterces (some say 10 million). He then vetoed every attempt to name a successor to Caesar, proposing instead that Caesar and Pompey both give up their armies.

events.title: Pompey's illness at Naples and the prayers of Italy
events.summary: When Pompey fell seriously ill at Naples in 50, the towns of Italy held public prayers and celebrations for his recovery. Plutarch says the enthusiasm misled him into believing that he had only to stamp his foot to raise armies throughout Italy.

events.title: Caesar surrenders two legions for a Parthian war
events.summary: The Senate decreed that Caesar and Pompey each provide one legion for the Parthian war; Pompey asked for the return of the legion he had lent Caesar in 53, so Caesar lost two. He paid each soldier 250 denarii. The legions were kept in Italy at Capua, and Caesar's partisans treated it as proof of bad faith.

events.title: The severe censorship of Appius Claudius
events.summary: Appius Claudius Pulcher, censor with Lucius Calpurnius Piso, struck many senators and equites off the rolls for debt or misconduct, among them the historian Sallust, thereby driving several into Caesar's camp. His fellow censor Piso, Caesar's father-in-law, blocked the expulsion of Curio.

events.title: Philodemus and the library at Herculaneum
events.summary: The Epicurean philosopher Philodemus of Gadara lived under the patronage of Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus, whose villa at Herculaneum, buried in AD 79, has yielded some 1,800 carbonised papyrus rolls, largely Philodemus' own works on poetry, music, rhetoric, anger and death. Cicero mocked the relationship in In Pisonem.

events.title: Labienus deserts Caesar
events.summary: Within days of the Rubicon, Titus Labienus, Caesar's ablest legate throughout the Gallic War, went over to Pompey, a fellow Picene to whom he probably owed his early career. Caesar sent his baggage after him. Labienus became the most implacable of the Pompeian commanders and died at Munda.

events.title: Caesar's march down the Adriatic
events.summary: From Ariminum Caesar's advance guard occupied Pisaurum, Fanum and Ancona, while Antony took Arretium; Iguvium and Auximum, Pompey's home country, opened their gates, and Pompey's recruiting officers fled. By early February Caesar had the whole Adriatic coast and the loyal veterans of the Eighth and Twelfth legions had joined him.

events.title: Senatus consultum ultimum against Caesar
events.summary: After Caesar's letter proposing that both commanders disarm was read on 1 January, the senate on 7 January passed the ultimate decree. The Caesarian tribunes Mark Antony and Quintus Cassius, threatened, fled to Caesar disguised as slaves, giving him a cause: the violation of tribunician sacrosanctity.

events.title: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
events.summary: With only the Thirteenth legion, 5,000 foot and 300 horse, Caesar crossed the stream marking the boundary of his province into Italy, an act of war against the state. Suetonius has him say 'iacta alea est', the die is cast; Plutarch (via Pollio) says he quoted Menander in Greek.

events.title: Siege of Corfinium
events.summary: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, Caesar's designated successor in Gaul, made a stand at Corfinium with 30 cohorts against Pompey's advice. After seven days his own troops handed him over. Caesar released Domitius and the senators with him and enrolled the soldiers, proclaiming a new way of conquering by mercy and generosity.

sides.strength: 6 legions by the end of the siege

battle.significance: Showcase of clementia; Pompey abandoned Italy.

events.title: Pompey abandons Italy
events.summary: Pompey shipped his army from Brundisium to Dyrrachium, slipping out on 17 March despite Caesar's attempt to close the harbour mouth with moles and rafts. His strategy was to gather the resources of the East and starve Italy; Cicero thought it a Sullan plan and was appalled.

events.title: Caesar takes the treasury
events.summary: In Rome Caesar forced open the state treasury in the temple of Saturn, including the sacred reserve kept against Gallic invasion, which he declared obsolete since he had conquered the Gauls. When the tribune Lucius Metellus barred the way, Caesar told him it was harder to say than to do that he would kill him.

events.title: Battle of the Bagradas: death of Curio
events.summary: Curio, sent to seize Africa with legions that had surrendered at Corfinium, beat the Pompeian Attius Varus near Utica, then, deceived by a report that King Juba had withdrawn, rushed his tired army into the ambush of Juba's general Saburra on the Bagradas. Curio refused to escape, saying he could not face Caesar having lost the army entrusted to him, and died fighting.

sides.strength: Numidian cavalry and infantry under Saburra

battle.significance: Left Africa in Pompeian hands until 46.

events.title: Campaign of Ilerda
events.summary: Pompey's legates Afranius and Petreius held Ilerda with five legions and many auxiliaries. A flood swept away Caesar's bridges over the Sicoris and nearly starved him; he built light coracles like those he had seen in Britain and restored his communications. When the Pompeians tried to slip away to the Ebro, Caesar headed them off, cut them from water and forced their surrender without a pitched battle on 2 August.

sides.losses: c. 70 in the worst skirmish; light overall

sides.strength: 5 legions and c. 80 cohorts of Spanish auxiliaries under Afranius and Petreius

battle.significance: Secured the West for Caesar within six months of the Rubicon.

events.title: Siege of Massilia
events.summary: Massilia shut its gates to Caesar and admitted Domitius Ahenobarbus. Gaius Trebonius besieged it by land with a huge terrace and a six-storey brick tower, while Decimus Brutus' hastily built fleet won two naval battles. Starving and plague-stricken, the city surrendered when Caesar returned from Spain; it kept nominal freedom but lost its fleet, treasury and most of its territory.

battle.significance: Ended Massilia's independent power, six centuries old.

events.title: Caesar's first dictatorship and the enfranchisement of the Transpadanes
events.summary: Named dictator to hold elections, Caesar held office for eleven days in late 49, had himself elected consul for 48, eased debts by valuing property at pre-war prices, recalled most exiles except Milo, and gave citizenship to the Transpadanes (lex Roscia), completing the enfranchisement of Italy to the Alps.

events.title: Disaster at Curicta: Antonius surrenders in Illyricum
events.summary: Caesar's legate Gaius Antonius, the triumvir's brother, was blockaded on the island of Curicta (Krk) by the Pompeian admirals Marcus Octavius and Lucius Scribonius Libo after Dolabella's fleet was destroyed; he surrendered with fifteen cohorts. One raft of Opitergine troops chose mass suicide rather than surrender.

battle.significance: Gave the Pompeians the Adriatic and delayed Caesar's crossing to Epirus.

events.title: Naval battles off Massilia
events.summary: During the siege of Massilia, Decimus Brutus with twelve hastily built ships beat the Massiliot fleet, reinforced by Domitius Ahenobarbus, in June, and won again in July off Tauroeis against a combined Massiliot and Pompeian fleet under Lucius Nasidius, whose squadron fled.

battle.significance: Isolated Massilia from the sea.

events.title: Mutiny of the Ninth legion at Placentia
events.summary: Returning from Spain, the Ninth legion mutinied at Placentia, demanding the donative Caesar had promised and discharge. Caesar threatened decimation, then executed twelve ringleaders chosen by lot from the 120 most guilty, one of whom proved to have been absent.

events.title: Curio's victory at Utica
events.summary: Landing in Africa with two of Domitius' surrendered legions, Curio defeated the Pompeian Publius Attius Varus outside Utica, the troops of whose camp reportedly wavered over whether to change sides. Varus fled into Utica, and Curio, misinformed that Juba was far away, marched to the Bagradas.

battle.significance: Prelude to Curio's destruction on the Bagradas.

events.title: Varro surrenders Further Spain
