events.summary: After Ilerda, Marcus Terentius Varro, Pompey's legate in Further Spain and Rome's greatest scholar, tried to hold Gades, but Corduba and the towns declared for Caesar and one of his two legions deserted. He surrendered his last legion and the treasury at Corduba. Caesar placed Quintus Cassius Longinus in charge.

events.title: Caesar's debt settlement
events.summary: Faced with a collapse of credit and demands for cancellation of debts (novae tabulae), Caesar as dictator ordered property to be valued at pre-war prices and handed to creditors at that valuation, banned the hoarding of more than 60,000 sesterces in cash, and later deducted interest already paid from principal, cutting debts by about a quarter.

events.title: Pompeians kill Aristobulus II and his son Alexander
events.summary: Caesar freed Aristobulus II, Pompey's captive, to raise Judaea against the Pompeians, but partisans of Pompey poisoned him; his son Alexander was beheaded at Antioch on Pompey's orders by Metellus Scipio. Their deaths left Hyrcanus and Antipater free to side with Caesar.

events.title: Caesar's elephant denarius
events.summary: Caesar's first military coinage of the civil war, struck in vast quantities from 49, shows an elephant trampling a serpent or dragon over the name CAESAR, and on the reverse the pontifical implements. It was minted from the treasury he had seized and is the commonest denarius of the period.

events.title: Caesar crosses to Epirus in midwinter
events.summary: With shipping for only seven legions (some 15,000 men) and 500 cavalry, Caesar sailed from Brundisium on 4 January 48 by the unreformed calendar, slipping past Bibulus' fleet of over 100 ships to land at Palaeste on the Ceraunian coast. He took Oricum and Apollonia, but Bibulus burned 30 returning transports and blockaded the rest at Brundisium.

events.title: Antony brings the second wave to Nymphaeum
events.summary: After months of waiting, Antony crossed with four legions and 800 cavalry in late March or April, chased by the Pompeian Coponius' Rhodian squadron, which a shift in the wind wrecked on the rocks. He landed at Nymphaeum north of Lissus and joined Caesar despite Pompey's attempt to intercept him.

events.title: Battle of Dyrrhachium
events.summary: Caesar, having crossed in January past Bibulus' fleet and been joined by Antony in April, tried to blockade Pompey's larger army against the sea with 17 miles of earthworks. His men ate bread made from a root called chara; the centurion Scaeva's shield took 120 holes holding a fort. Informed by two Allobrogian deserters of a gap at the southern end, Pompey broke through; Caesar's counterattack collapsed in panic and he lost 960 men and 32 officers.

battle.significance: Pompey's victory broke the blockade but his failure to pursue let Caesar regroup.

events.title: Battle of Pharsalus
events.summary: Pompey, with about 45,000 infantry and 7,000 cavalry, planned for Labienus' massed cavalry to sweep around Caesar's right while his infantry stood still to receive the charge. Caesar, with 22,000 infantry and 1,000 cavalry, had secretly formed a fourth line of six cohorts behind his right, which routed the cavalry, thrusting their pila at the riders' faces, and then rolled up Pompey's left. Pompey left the field for his camp and then fled.
events.locName: plain of Pharsalus, near the Enipeus, Thessaly

battle.significance: Decided the civil war in the East; the old senatorial government never recovered.

events.title: Murder of Pompey at Pelusium
events.summary: Pompey sought refuge with the court of Ptolemy XIII, whose father he had helped restore. The king's advisers Pothinus, Achillas and Theodotus decided a dead Pompey was safer; as he was rowed ashore he was stabbed by Achillas and the former Roman centurion Lucius Septimius in sight of his wife Cornelia. He was killed on or about the eve of his 58th birthday.

events.title: The Alexandrian War: Caesar besieged in the palace
events.summary: Caesar, with only 3,200 infantry and 800 cavalry, tried to arbitrate between Ptolemy XIII and his sister Cleopatra VII, who had herself smuggled into the palace. The king's general Achillas and then Arsinoe's eunuch Ganymedes besieged him in the royal quarter for months; Ganymedes pumped seawater into the palace cisterns, and in a fight on the Pharos causeway Caesar had to swim for it, holding his papers above the water.

sides.losses: considerable; 400 killed at the Pharos mole alone

sides.strength: c. 20,000 under Achillas incl. the Gabiniani

battle.significance: Put Cleopatra on the throne; delayed Caesar's return for nine months while the Pompeians regrouped in Africa.

events.title: Cleopatra comes to Caesar
events.summary: Expelled by her brother's regents and encamped near Pelusium, Cleopatra had herself brought by boat to the palace at night by the Sicilian Apollodorus, concealed, Plutarch says, in a bedding sack. Caesar, who had come to arbitrate under Ptolemy XII's will, sided with her and summoned both siblings.

events.title: Battle of Nicopolis
events.summary: Pharnaces II, son of Mithridates, exploited the civil war to reconquer Pontus. Caesar's legate Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, with one Roman legion, a scratch legion from Pontus and Deiotarus' two legions trained in the Roman manner, was defeated near Nicopolis.

battle.significance: Gave Pharnaces Pontus and drew Caesar to Asia in 47.

events.title: The risings of Caelius and Milo
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Caelius Rufus, frustrated by Caesar's moderate debt policy, proposed remission of rents and debts and, when deposed by the Senate, joined the exiled Milo, who returned to raise gladiators and herdsmen in southern Italy. Milo was killed besieging Compsa, and Caelius near Thurii.

events.title: Caesar sacks Gomphi
events.summary: Retreating into Thessaly after Dyrrhachium, Caesar found Gomphi had closed its gates on news of his defeat; he stormed it in a few hours and gave it to his starving soldiers to plunder, after which Metropolis and other Thessalian towns submitted. Appian describes the army's drunken march out of Gomphi.

battle.significance: Restored morale and supplies before Pharsalus.

events.title: Revolt against Quintus Cassius in Further Spain
events.summary: Quintus Cassius Longinus, Caesar's governor of Further Spain, provoked a conspiracy of provincials at Corduba, was wounded, and then faced the mutiny of two legions under the quaestor Marcellus. Lepidus from Hither Spain mediated; Cassius drowned at the mouth of the Ebro on his way home with his loot.

events.title: Caesar burns the Alexandrian fleet and part of the city
events.summary: To prevent Achillas' forces seizing the 72 warships in the harbour, Caesar set them on fire; the blaze spread to the docks and warehouses. Later writers (Seneca, Plutarch, Dio, Gellius) say that 40,000 books or the Great Library itself burned, though Caesar and Strabo, who used the Museum's resources around 25 BC, are silent.

events.title: Battle of the Nile
events.summary: Relieved by an army of Syrian and Jewish allies under Mithridates of Pergamon and Antipater, Caesar marched up the Delta and stormed Ptolemy XIII's fortified camp. The young king drowned when his overloaded boat sank; his body was identified by his golden armour. Alexandria surrendered and Cleopatra was made queen with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV.

sides.strength: Caesar's legions plus Mithridates of Pergamon's relief army

battle.significance: Ended the Alexandrian War.

events.title: Battle of Zela: veni, vidi, vici
events.summary: Five days after arriving, while his men were entrenching on a hill facing Pharnaces' position, Caesar was attacked uphill by the king's army with scythed chariots. The veteran Sixth legion, reduced to under 1,000 men, broke the attack on the right and the Pontic army was routed within four hours.

battle.significance: Restored Roman control of Asia Minor in a single afternoon.

events.title: Mutiny of the Tenth legion
events.summary: Veterans in Campania, led by the Tenth, mutinied demanding discharge and their promised rewards, killed two ex-praetors sent to them and marched on Rome. Caesar faced them in the Campus Martius, granted discharge at once and addressed them as 'Quirites', citizens, instead of soldiers. Shamed, they begged to be taken to Africa.

events.title: Battle of the Heptastadion: Caesar swims for his life
events.summary: Fighting for the mole (Heptastadion) linking Pharos to the city, Caesar's men were routed by an Egyptian counterattack; the overcrowded boat Caesar boarded capsized and he swam to safety, holding papers above the water and, Suetonius adds, dragging his general's cloak in his teeth. About 400 legionaries and many sailors died.

sides.strength: detachments of the 13th legion and marines

battle.significance: Left Caesar confined until the relief army arrived.

events.title: Mithridates of Pergamon storms Pelusium
events.summary: A relief army raised in Syria and Cilicia by Mithridates of Pergamon, reinforced by 3,000 Jewish troops under Antipater and Arabs and Nabataeans, stormed Pelusium in a single day and marched up the Delta, defeating an Egyptian force near the 'Camp of the Jews' and joining Caesar for the Battle of the Nile.

sides.strength: Syrian, Cilician, Jewish and Arab troops

battle.significance: Turned the Alexandrian War.

events.title: Caesar and Cleopatra on the Nile
events.summary: After the Battle of the Nile, Caesar made Cleopatra co-ruler with her younger brother Ptolemy XIV, gave Cyprus back to Egypt, and, according to Suetonius and Appian, cruised up the Nile with her in the royal barge with 400 ships nearly to Ethiopia before his soldiers protested. Their son Ptolemy Caesar (Caesarion) was born in June 47.

events.title: Caesar's settlement of Judaea
events.summary: Caesar confirmed Hyrcanus II as high priest and ethnarch, made Antipater a Roman citizen exempt from taxes and procurator of Judaea, permitted the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls, restored Joppa, and granted the Jews exemption from military service and other privileges that Josephus records from a series of decrees.

events.title: Dolabella's debt agitation
events.summary: The tribune Publius Cornelius Dolabella, Cicero's son-in-law, proposed cancellation of debts and rents in Caesar's absence; his rival Trebellius opposed him, and their gangs fought in the Forum. Antony, as Master of Horse, sent in troops, killing 800 people. Caesar's return settled the matter with limited rent relief.

events.title: Varro's Antiquities
events.summary: Marcus Terentius Varro dedicated the forty-one books of his Antiquitates rerum humanarum et divinarum, the last sixteen on Roman religion, to Caesar as pontifex maximus. Lost except for fragments, mainly through Augustine's City of God, it was the foundation of all later knowledge of Roman religious institutions.

events.title: Battle of Ruspina
events.summary: Landing in Africa with only part of his army, Caesar (who stumbled on the beach and turned it into an omen with 'I hold you, Africa') was caught foraging near Ruspina by Labienus' Numidian cavalry and light infantry and surrounded. He extended his line and had alternate cohorts face about, broke out and fell back to camp at nightfall as Petreius arrived.

sides.strength: Numidian cavalry and light infantry, c. 10,000+

battle.significance: Caesar narrowly escaped disaster in the first weeks of the African campaign.

events.title: Suicide of Cato at Utica
events.summary: Commanding Utica, Cato organised the escape of those who wished to flee, refused to seek Caesar's pardon, read Plato's Phaedo on the immortality of the soul twice, and stabbed himself. His physicians bandaged the wound; when he came to, he tore it open and died.

events.title: Battle of Thapsus
events.summary: Caesar besieged Thapsus to force Metellus Scipio and King Juba to battle on a narrow strip between lagoon and sea. Before he gave the signal his veterans charged; slingers and archers stampeded Scipio's elephants, which the Fifth legion met on foot, and the Pompeian army collapsed. Caesar's soldiers butchered men trying to surrender.

sides.strength: c. 10 legions with veterans of the 5th, 9th, 10th, 13th and 14th
c. 10 Roman legions, Numidian forces, 60 elephants

battle.significance: Destroyed the Pompeian army in Africa; Numidia annexed as Africa Nova.

events.title: Caesar's quadruple triumph
events.summary: Caesar celebrated four triumphs within a month, over Gaul, Egypt, Pontus and Africa (officially over Juba). Vercingetorix, held six years, was executed afterwards; Arsinoe, Cleopatra's sister, was paraded but spared; the infant Juba II walked in the procession. His soldiers sang that Caesar had subdued the Gauls and Nicomedes had subdued Caesar, and warned citizens to lock up their wives because the bald adulterer was back.

events.title: Dedication of the Forum Iulium and Temple of Venus Genetrix
events.summary: On 26 September 46, the last day of his triumphal games, Caesar dedicated his new forum, unfinished, with the temple of Venus Genetrix that he had vowed at Pharsalus. The temple contained a statue of Venus by Arcesilaus, paintings of Ajax and Medea by Timomachus, cabinets of engraved gems, a British pearl corselet, and a gilded statue of Cleopatra beside the goddess.

events.title: The Julian calendar
events.summary: As pontifex maximus Caesar, advised by the Alexandrian astronomer Sosigenes, replaced the lunisolar Republican calendar, which through neglected intercalation had drifted nearly three months ahead of the seasons, with a solar year of 365 days and a leap day every fourth year. To realign it, 46 was given 445 days, adding an intercalary month after February and two extra months between November and December; the new calendar began on 1 January 45.

events.title: Caesar's colonies and the refoundation of Carthage and Corinth
events.summary: Caesar settled some 80,000 citizens, veterans and urban poor, in colonies overseas, including refoundations of Corinth (Laus Iulia Corinthiensis) and Carthage, both destroyed in 146, and Urso in Spain, whose charter (lex coloniae Genetivae Iuliae) survives on bronze tablets. Freedmen were allowed to hold office in some colonies.

events.title: Manoeuvres and battle at Uzitta
events.summary: For weeks Caesar and Metellus Scipio, joined by Juba with elephants, faced each other before Uzitta south of Ruspina, building lines of fortifications; a cavalry and infantry clash in which Labienus was nearly trapped was inconclusive. Caesar trained his men to fight elephants with animals imported from Italy.

battle.significance: A war of position before Thapsus.

events.title: Sittius takes Cirta; Numidia becomes Africa Nova
events.summary: While Caesar fought Scipio, the Campanian adventurer Publius Sittius and King Bocchus II of Mauretania invaded Juba's kingdom and took Cirta, forcing Juba to divide his forces. After Thapsus Caesar annexed most of Numidia as the province of Africa Nova under Sallust as governor and gave Sittius' men the territory of Cirta.

events.title: Sittius destroys Metellus Scipio's flight at Hippo Regius
events.summary: After Thapsus, Metellus Scipio fled by sea for Spain; storms drove his ships into Hippo Regius, where Sittius' fleet overwhelmed them. Scipio stabbed himself and threw himself overboard, telling those who asked for the general: 'The general is well.'

battle.significance: Ended the career of the Pompeian commander-in-chief.

events.title: Suicide pact of Juba and Petreius at Zama
events.summary: Refused entry by his own city of Zama, where he had built a pyre to burn his family and treasure, King Juba I and the Pompeian legate Marcus Petreius fought a duel so as to die honourably; Petreius was killed, and Juba had a slave kill him.

events.title: Caesar cuts the grain dole
events.summary: Caesar ordered a street-by-street census of grain recipients through the landlords of tenement blocks, reducing the number from 320,000 to 150,000 and filling vacancies by lot from those not registered. He also sent 80,000 poor citizens to overseas colonies.

events.title: Caesar's laws of 46: provinces, juries and luxury
events.summary: Caesar limited praetorian governorships to one year and consular to two, removed the tribuni aerarii from juries, dissolved most collegia except ancient ones and Jewish synagogues, raised penalties for violence and treason, and passed a sumptuary law policed by inspectors in the markets.

events.title: Pro Marcello: Cicero breaks his silence
events.summary: When Caesar, at the Senate's plea, pardoned his bitter enemy Marcus Claudius Marcellus, consul of 51, Cicero broke a long silence with a speech of thanks that urged Caesar to heal the state's wounds. Marcellus was murdered at Piraeus on his way home in 45. Pro Ligario followed in the same autumn.

events.title: Cleopatra in Rome
events.summary: Cleopatra, with Ptolemy XIV and probably Caesarion, came to Rome in 46 and lived in Caesar's gardens across the Tiber, where she was formally recognised as a friend and ally. Cicero, who met her about books she had promised him, wrote 'I hate the queen'. She left soon after the Ides of March.

events.title: Laberius and Publilius Syrus: the mime contest
events.summary: At Caesar's games the elderly equestrian mime-writer Decimus Laberius was induced to act in his own mime, losing caste, and lamented in a prologue that he left home a knight and would return an actor; Caesar then gave the prize to the Syrian freedman Publilius, whose collection of moral one-line maxims (sententiae) became a school text.

events.title: Revolt of Caecilius Bassus in Syria
events.summary: Quintus Caecilius Bassus, a Pompeian survivor of Pharsalus, engineered the murder of Caesar's governor of Syria, Sextus Julius Caesar, at Tyre, won over his legion, and held out at Apamea for three years with Arab and Parthian help against Antistius Vetus and Statius Murcus. His troops joined Cassius in 43.

events.title: Caesar's gold: the aurei of Hirtius
events.summary: In 46 Caesar's praetor Aulus Hirtius struck large issues of aurei (C CAESAR COS TER / A HIRTIVS PR) at 40 to the Roman pound, from the gold of Gaul and the civil war, to pay the triumphal donatives of 5,000 denarii a soldier. It made the aureus, worth 25 denarii, a regular denomination for the first time.

events.title: Cicero's Brutus: a history of Roman oratory
events.summary: In early 46 Cicero wrote the Brutus, a dialogue with Brutus and Atticus surveying some two hundred Roman orators from the earliest times to Hortensius, who had just died, and himself. It is the first history of Latin literature and contains Cicero's account of his own training. The Orator followed later that year.

events.title: Battle of Munda
events.summary: In Spain Pompey's sons Gnaeus and Sextus and Labienus raised 13 legions. At Munda they took a strong hillside position; Caesar attacked and for hours the issue hung in the balance, Caesar saying afterwards that he had often fought for victory but this time for his life. When Bogud of Mauretania's cavalry threatened the Pompeian camp, Labienus pulled five cohorts back to cover it; the movement was taken for retreat and the line broke.

battle.significance: Last major battle of Caesar's civil war.

events.title: Death of Gnaeus Pompeius the Younger
events.summary: Wounded at Munda, Gnaeus Pompeius fled to Carteia, was abandoned when his fleet was destroyed by Caesar's admiral Didius, and was hunted down near Lauro, where he was killed hiding in a cave. His head was exhibited at Hispalis on 12 April.

events.title: Caesar's Spanish triumph
events.summary: In October 45 Caesar triumphed over Spain, a triumph over fellow citizens that offended many; when the tribune Pontius Aquila remained seated as the chariot passed, Caesar mocked him for days. Caesar's legates Fabius Maximus and Pedius were also given triumphs, and Fabius died in office on 31 December, his consular place filled for a few hours by Caninius Rebilus.

events.title: Pro rege Deiotaro
events.summary: In November 45 Cicero defended the Galatian king Deiotarus, accused by his grandson of having plotted to murder Caesar when Caesar was his guest in 47, before Caesar in his own house; it was the first Roman trial held in a private house. No verdict is recorded.

events.title: Caesar dines with Cicero at Puteoli
events.summary: On 19 December 45 Caesar, with 2,000 soldiers, visited Cicero's villa near Puteoli, took a bath and an emetic, dined well and talked of literature, not politics. Cicero wrote to Atticus that it was not the sort of guest to whom one says 'come again when you are passing'.

events.title: Siege of Ategua
events.summary: Caesar opened his Spanish campaign by besieging Ategua, a Pompeian depot east of Corduba, in midwinter. Gnaeus Pompeius failed to relieve it; the garrison commander massacred pro-Caesarian citizens before the town surrendered on 19 February. The anonymous Bellum Hispaniense gives vivid details of sling bullets and burning fascines.

battle.significance: Opened the road to Munda.

events.title: Caesar storms Corduba and Munda
events.summary: After Munda, Caesar's legate Fabius Maximus besieged Munda town, walled, the Bellum Hispaniense says, with enemy corpses and shields, while Caesar stormed Corduba, where factions fought inside; 22,000 were killed. Hispalis and Urso were taken soon after.

battle.significance: Ended organised resistance in Baetica.

events.title: Cicero's philosophical burst
events.summary: After the death of his daughter Tullia in February 45, Cicero retreated to his villas and in about eighteen months wrote a Consolatio, the Hortensius, Academica, De finibus, Tusculan Disputations, De natura deorum, De divinatione, De fato, Cato Maior de senectute, Laelius de amicitia, Topica and De officiis: a Latin encyclopaedia of Hellenistic philosophy.

events.title: The pamphlet war over Cato
events.summary: After Cato's suicide, Cicero wrote a eulogy, Cato, and Brutus another; Hirtius replied with a critique, and Caesar, during the Munda campaign, wrote two books of Anticato attacking Cato's character, alleging he had sifted his brother's ashes for gold. The exchange made Cato a martyr of the Republic.

events.title: The Tabula Heracleensis: Caesarian municipal regulations
events.summary: A bronze tablet found at Heraclea in Lucania in 1732 preserves regulations, probably from a lex Iulia of about 45, on road maintenance and wheeled traffic in Rome (banned by day except for building and religious purposes), the grain dole register, and the qualifications for municipal councillors in Italy.

events.title: Caesar dictator for life
events.summary: Already dictator for ten years from 46, by mid-February 44 Caesar took the title dictator perpetuo, struck on coins (RRC 480). Honours piled up: the title parens patriae, a statue among the kings on the Capitol, a gilded chair, the renaming of Quinctilis as Iulius, a temple to his Clemency, and a flamen of his own. When the senate came to him at the temple of Venus Genetrix, he did not rise.

events.title: The Lupercalia: Antony offers Caesar a diadem
events.summary: At the Lupercalia the consul Mark Antony, running near-naked as a Lupercus, offered Caesar, seated on the Rostra in triumphal dress, a royal diadem. Caesar refused it; the crowd cheered; Antony offered it again, and again it was refused, and Caesar had it sent to Jupiter on the Capitol. The fasti were made to record that the consul had offered kingship at the people's bidding and Caesar had refused.

events.title: The Ides of March: assassination of Caesar
events.summary: Three days before he was to leave for a war against Parthia with 16 legions and 10,000 cavalry, Caesar was stabbed to death at a meeting of the senate in the curia of Pompey's theatre complex by more than 60 conspirators led by Marcus Brutus, Gaius Cassius and Decimus Brutus. Trebonius detained Antony outside; Tillius Cimber pulled at Caesar's toga; Casca struck first. He received 23 wounds, of which, his physician judged, only the second, in the chest, was fatal, and fell at the foot of Pompey's statue.

events.title: The amnesty in the temple of Tellus
events.summary: Two days after the murder the consul Antony convened the senate. On Cicero's motion, citing the Athenian amnesty of 403, the assassins were granted immunity, while all Caesar's acts and appointments were confirmed, since half the senators owed their offices or provinces to them. The liberators came down from the Capitol, with Antony's and Lepidus' sons as hostages, and dined with Antony and Lepidus.

events.title: Caesar's will and funeral
events.summary: Caesar's will, opened at Antony's house, adopted his great-nephew Gaius Octavius as son and heir to three quarters of his estate, left his gardens across the Tiber to the people and 300 sesterces to every citizen, and named Decimus Brutus, one of the assassins, as a secondary heir. At the funeral Antony's speech and the display of the bloodied toga, perhaps with a wax effigy showing the wounds, turned the crowd: they cremated the body in the Forum on a pyre of benches and set off to burn the conspirators' houses.

events.title: The lynching of the poet Helvius Cinna
events.summary: At Caesar's funeral the crowd, inflamed by Antony's speech, took the tribune and poet Gaius Helvius Cinna, a friend of Caesar, for the praetor Lucius Cornelius Cinna, who had praised the assassins, and tore him to pieces, carrying his head on a spear.

events.title: Octavian accepts Caesar's inheritance
events.summary: The 18-year-old Gaius Octavius, studying at Apollonia, crossed to Italy against his family's advice, accepted the adoption and took the name Gaius Julius Caesar. When Antony stalled over handing over Caesar's funds, he paid Caesar's legacies to the people from his own and borrowed money and courted Caesar's veterans.

events.title: The comet of 44 BC (sidus Iulium)
events.summary: During the games Octavian gave in late July in honour of Caesar's victories, a bright comet was seen for seven days. Octavian proclaimed it Caesar's soul received among the gods, set a star on the head of his statue and put it on his coins; he privately took it as his own sign, according to his memoirs quoted by Pliny.
events.locName: Rome, during the Ludi Victoriae Caesaris

events.title: The Ludi Apollinares of Brutus
events.summary: Brutus, as urban praetor, paid for lavish Games of Apollo in July 44 but dared not attend; he had hoped that a performance of Accius' Tereus would win applause for the Liberators. Octavian then staged Games for Caesar's Victory, during which the comet appeared.

events.title: Cicero's Philippics
events.summary: On 2 September 44 Cicero delivered the first of fourteen speeches against Antony, which he named after Demosthenes' speeches against Philip of Macedon. The Second Philippic, a pamphlet never delivered, savaged Antony's private life. Through the winter of 44-43 Cicero led the senate in backing Octavian and Decimus Brutus against Antony.

events.title: The Martia and Fourth legions defect to Octavian
events.summary: Antony brought four Macedonian legions to Brundisium, where he executed centurions of the Martia for insubordination; Octavian, who had raised 3,000 veterans in Campania on his own authority, outbid him with 500 denarii a man. The Legio Martia and Legio IV went over to Octavian at Alba Fucens, and Cicero hailed the boy in the Senate.

events.title: Charter of the Colonia Genetiva Iulia at Urso
events.summary: Bronze tablets found at Osuna in Andalusia in 1870-71 preserve much of the charter given to Caesar's colony of Urso, drafted on Caesar's instructions and passed under Antony after his death: rules for magistrates, priesthoods, games, militia, and the admission of freedmen to the council.

events.title: Caesar's portrait on the coinage
events.summary: Early in 44 the moneyers of the year, among them Marcus Mettius and Publius Sepullius Macer, struck denarii with Caesar's laureate (later veiled) head and the legend CAESAR DICT QVART, then CAESAR DICT PERPETVO, the first portrait of a living Roman on the city coinage. The change of title on the dies lets numismatists date issues within weeks of the Ides.

events.title: Caesar's planned Getic and Parthian war
events.summary: Caesar planned to leave Rome on 18 March 44 for a three-year war, first against Burebista's Dacians and then against Parthia to avenge Crassus, with sixteen legions and 10,000 cavalry; Octavius and Agrippa were sent ahead to Apollonia to join the army. A Sibylline oracle that only a king could conquer Parthia fed rumours that Caesar would be named king outside Italy.

events.title: Antony takes the treasure in the temple of Ops
events.summary: Antony took possession of Caesar's papers and of 700 million sesterces Caesar had deposited in the temple of Ops for his campaigns, using both to buy support; Cicero accused him of forging decrees in Caesar's name and selling privileges, such as citizenship for all Sicilians and the restoration of Deiotarus.
events.locName: Temple of Ops, Capitol or Forum

events.title: Lex Antonia abolishes the dictatorship
events.summary: Early in the period after the Ides, Antony carried a law abolishing the dictatorship forever, a popular gesture of reconciliation. The office was never revived; Augustus refused it in 22 BC when the people tried to force it on him.

events.title: Cicero's De officiis
events.summary: In autumn 44, between the Second and later Philippics, Cicero wrote De officiis for his son, then studying in Athens: three books on duties, adapting the Stoic Panaetius, arguing that the honourable and the useful never conflict and that Caesar's tyranny was the supreme example of crime passing for utility.

events.title: Battle of Forum Gallorum
events.summary: Antony, besieging Decimus Brutus in Mutina, ambushed the consul Pansa's army of recruits marching to join Hirtius and Octavian. The veteran Martian legion fought him to a standstill in the marshes; Pansa was mortally wounded. Late in the day Hirtius arrived with fresh troops and routed Antony's exhausted army.

sides.strength: Pansa's 4 recruit legions, Martian legion and Hirtius' relief

battle.significance: Checked Antony but cost the senate one consul.

events.title: Battle of Mutina
events.summary: A week later Hirtius and Octavian attacked Antony's siege lines; Hirtius was killed inside Antony's camp, but Antony abandoned the siege and retreated over the Alps. Pansa died of his wounds. Rumour said Octavian had both consuls killed; the senate voted Decimus Brutus the command and snubbed Octavian.

sides.strength: Hirtius' and Octavian's armies, Decimus Brutus' garrison

battle.significance: Senatorial victory that collapsed within months; left Octavian with the only intact army in Italy.

events.title: Lepidus joins Antony at Forum Iulii
events.summary: Antony, retreating from Mutina, crossed the Alps to Narbonensis. On 29 May 43, after the soldiers of Lepidus, governor of Narbonensis and Nearer Spain, fraternised with Antony's at the Pons Argenteus, Lepidus joined him, writing to the Senate that his troops had compelled him. The Senate declared him a public enemy.

events.title: Lex Pedia: the assassins condemned
events.summary: Octavian's colleague and cousin Quintus Pedius carried a law setting up a court to try Caesar's murderers in absence; all were condemned and outlawed, including Sextus Pompey, who had not been involved. The same month a lex curiata confirmed Octavian's adoption as Caesar's son.

events.title: Octavian marches on Rome and becomes consul
events.summary: When the senate refused him a consulship, Octavian, aged nineteen, marched on Rome with eight legions; a centurion delegation had told the senate, patting his sword, that this would make him consul. He was elected on 19 August with his cousin Quintus Pedius; a lex curiata ratified his adoption, and the lex Pedia set up a court that condemned Caesar's assassins in absence.

events.title: The meeting at Bononia
events.summary: Antony, Lepidus and Octavian met for two days on a small river island near Bononia, guarded by their armies, and agreed to form a legal triumvirate for five years, divide the western provinces, take vengeance on Caesar's murderers and proscribe their enemies. Octavian was betrothed to Antony's stepdaughter Clodia.
events.locName: island in a river near Bononia (Bologna)

events.title: Plancus founds Lugdunum
events.summary: Lucius Munatius Plancus, governor of Gallia Comata, founded the colony of Lugdunum (Lyon) on the hill of Fourvière above the confluence of Rhône and Saône, on Senate's orders, for Roman refugees expelled from Vienna by the Allobroges. It became the capital of the Three Gauls and seat of the imperial mint.

events.title: The triumviral proscriptions
events.summary: The triumvirs posted lists of men to be killed and their property confiscated, to raise money for the war against Brutus and Cassius as much as for revenge: Appian gives some 300 senators and 2,000 equites. Bounties were 100,000 sesterces for a free killer, 40,000 and freedom for a slave. Each triumvir sacrificed relatives: Antony's uncle Lucius Caesar, Lepidus' brother Paullus.

events.title: Lex Titia: the Second Triumvirate
events.summary: The tribune Publius Titius carried a law, passed the day it was proposed, making Antony, Lepidus and Octavian triumviri rei publicae constituendae, three men for restoring the state, with consular power for five years to 31 December 38, the right to appoint magistrates and to issue binding edicts. Antony took the Gauls, Lepidus Spain and Narbonensis, Octavian Africa, Sicily and Sardinia.

events.title: Murder of Cicero
events.summary: Proscribed at Antony's insistence, Cicero dithered between flight and staying, and was overtaken near his villa at Formiae by a squad under the centurion Herennius and the tribune Popillius Laenas, whom he had once defended. He leaned out of his litter and offered his neck. His head and the hands that wrote the Philippics were nailed to the Rostra; Dio says Fulvia pierced the tongue with her hairpin.

events.title: The cold years after Caesar's death
events.summary: Ancient writers report a dimmed sun, failed harvests and famine in the years after Caesar's murder. Greenland ice cores show that a huge eruption of the Okmok volcano in Alaska in early 43, following an Etna eruption in 44, made 43-42 among the coldest years in the northern hemisphere of the last 2,500 years; Egyptian Nile floods also failed.
events.locName: Italy and the Mediterranean (eruption site: Okmok volcano, Aleutians)

events.title: Dolabella murders Trebonius at Smyrna
events.summary: Publius Cornelius Dolabella, on his way to Syria, entered Smyrna by night, seized Gaius Trebonius, proconsul of Asia and one of the conspirators, tortured him for two days and beheaded him, the first of the assassins to die. The Senate declared Dolabella a public enemy.

events.title: Cassius besieges Dolabella at Laodicea
events.summary: Cassius, who had taken over all eight legions in Syria, besieged Dolabella in Laodicea-on-Sea; the city was betrayed and Dolabella had a soldier kill him. Cassius then fined Laodicea and Tarsus heavily.

battle.significance: Made Cassius master of the East.

events.title: Death of Decimus Brutus
events.summary: Deserted by his legions after Plancus joined Antony, Decimus Brutus tried to reach Macedonia through the Alps and Illyricum disguised as a Gaul, but was captured by a Gallic chieftain, Camilus, and killed on Antony's orders. He had been the first conspirator to be honoured and the first to fall in the field.

events.title: Deification of Julius Caesar
events.summary: The senate and people declared Caesar a god, Divus Iulius, and voted a temple on the site of his cremation. His statue could no longer be carried in family funerals; his birthday became a festival. Octavian became divi filius, son of a god.

events.title: Murcus and Ahenobarbus destroy the triumviral convoy
events.summary: On the day of the first battle of Philippi the Liberators' admirals Statius Murcus and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus intercepted Domitius Calvinus' convoy bringing two legions, including the Martia, across the Adriatic, and destroyed it; many soldiers burned with their ships. News arrived too late to stop Brutus giving battle again.

battle.significance: A victory that could have starved the triumvirs had Brutus waited.

events.title: First Battle of Philippi
events.summary: Brutus and Cassius held strong camps astride the Via Egnatia with the sea at their backs; Antony built a causeway through the marsh to outflank Cassius. When Cassius attacked the works, Antony stormed Cassius' camp; meanwhile Brutus' men overran Octavian's camp, the sick Octavian having been carried out, he later said, because of his doctor's dream. Cassius, short-sighted and misinformed that Brutus too had lost, had his freedman Pindarus kill him.

battle.significance: Each side took one camp; Cassius' death left Brutus in sole command.

events.title: Second Battle of Philippi
events.summary: Three weeks later, with his officers restless and his supply secure but his men deserting, Brutus offered battle. After hard fighting Antony's legions broke his line. Brutus fell on his sword held by his friend Strato. Antony covered the body with his own purple cloak; Octavian, says Suetonius, sent the head to Rome to be thrown at the feet of Caesar's statue.

battle.significance: Ended republican resistance; Antony became the dominant figure in the Roman world.

events.title: Siege of Xanthus
events.summary: Raising money and troops in the East, Brutus besieged Xanthus, whose citizens refused to pay. When the Romans broke in, the Xanthians burned their city and killed themselves and their families, as their ancestors had done before the Persians in 546. Cassius meanwhile took Rhodes, extracting 8,500 talents.

battle.significance: Showed the ruthless fund-raising of the liberators in Asia.

events.note: Xanthus is listed under the generic 'rome' polity as a free Lycian city in the Roman orbit.

events.title: The EID MAR denarius of Brutus
events.summary: Brutus' moneyer Lucius Plaetorius Cestianus struck a denarius showing Brutus' head and, on the reverse, a cap of liberty between two daggers with the legend EID MAR. Dio describes it, and it is the most famous coin of antiquity; fewer than a hundred silver examples and three gold aurei are known.
events.locName: travelling mint of Brutus, Macedonia or Asia

events.title: Cassius takes Rhodes
events.summary: Rhodes refused to join the Liberators; Cassius defeated its fleet twice off Myndus and Cnidus, blockaded the city and took it without a fight, executing fifty leaders, stripping the temples and confiscating 8,500 talents. Brutus meanwhile sacked Xanthus in Lycia.

sides.strength: fleet of c. 80 ships and army

battle.significance: Funded the Liberators' campaign.

events.title: Plancus rebuilds the Temple of Saturn
events.summary: Lucius Munatius Plancus rebuilt the Temple of Saturn in the Forum, seat of the state treasury, from spoils of an Alpine campaign, as recorded on an inscription. The eight Ionic columns standing today belong to a fourth-century restoration on Plancus' podium.

events.title: Cleopatra meets Antony at Tarsus
events.summary: Summoned to answer for help allegedly given to Cassius, Cleopatra sailed up the Cydnus to Tarsus in a gilded barge with purple sails and silver oars, dressed as Aphrodite, and invited Antony to dine. At her request he had her sister Arsinoe dragged from the temple of Artemis at Ephesus and killed, and spent the winter of 41-40 with her in Alexandria.

events.title: Antony in Ephesus: the levy on Asia
events.summary: Entering Ephesus as the new Dionysus, Antony demanded that the cities of Asia pay in one year the tribute of nine (then reduced to two years' worth payable in two), to pay the 170,000 men of the triumviral armies. He rewarded cities that had resisted the Liberators, such as Laodicea and Tarsus, and summoned Cleopatra to Tarsus.

events.title: Confiscations for the veterans in Italy
events.summary: Octavian, charged with settling some 40,000 or more veterans of Philippi, confiscated land from eighteen Italian cities, among them Cremona, Mantua, Beneventum and Capua, and many smaller properties. The dispossessed thronged to Rome, Octavian was stoned in the theatre, and Lucius Antonius and Fulvia championed the victims, leading to the Perusine War.

events.title: Antony has Arsinoe IV killed at Ephesus
events.summary: At Cleopatra's request Antony had her younger sister Arsinoe IV, who had led the Alexandrians against Caesar and walked in his triumph of 46 before being allowed into sanctuary at the temple of Artemis at Ephesus, dragged from the temple and killed. An octagonal tomb in Ephesus containing a young woman's skeleton has been proposed, contentiously, as hers.

events.title: Sallust's Catiline and Jugurtha
events.summary: Retired from politics after his African governorship, Sallust wrote the Bellum Catilinae (c. 42-41) and Bellum Iugurthinum (c. 41-40), monographs in an archaic, abrupt style modelled on Thucydides and Cato, analysing Rome's decline through ambition and avarice after the fall of Carthage. His Histories (78-67 onward) survive only in fragments and speeches.

events.title: Siege of Perusia
events.summary: The consul Lucius Antonius, Antony's brother, and Fulvia, Antony's wife, championed Italian landowners dispossessed for Octavian's veteran settlements. Octavian, Agrippa and Salvidienus Rufus penned Lucius in Perusia and starved it through the winter of 41-40. Lucius surrendered and was spared; the town was burned.

battle.significance: Gave Octavian control of Italy and the western legions.

events.title: Treaty of Brundisium
events.summary: Antony returned to Italy and was refused entry at Brundisium; the soldiers of both sides refused to fight. Mediated by Maecenas, Pollio and Cocceius Nerva, the triumvirs divided the empire at Scodra in Illyricum, Antony taking the East and Octavian the West, Lepidus keeping Africa. Antony married Octavian's widowed sister Octavia.

events.title: Parthian invasion of Syria and Asia Minor
events.summary: The Parthian prince Pacorus and Quintus Labienus, son of Caesar's general and once Brutus' envoy to Parthia, overran Syria, killing its governor Decidius Saxa. Labienus swept through Asia Minor to Caria, styling himself imperator Parthicus on his coins. Pacorus took Jerusalem and installed the Hasmonean Antigonus as king; Herod fled to Rome, where the senate, at Antony's and Octavian's request, named him king of Judaea.

events.title: The Senate names Herod king of Judaea
events.summary: Fleeing the Parthian-backed Antigonus, Herod, son of Antipater, sailed via Alexandria and Rhodes to Rome in winter 40. Antony and Octavian sponsored him in the Senate, which declared him king of Judaea; the consuls led him to the Capitol to sacrifice. He then had to conquer his kingdom.

events.title: Parthians install Antigonus in Jerusalem
events.summary: With the Parthian invasion, the Hasmonean Antigonus, son of Aristobulus II, promised Pacorus 1,000 talents and 500 women to be made king. The Parthians took Jerusalem, captured Hyrcanus II and Phasael by treachery; Phasael killed himself and Antigonus cut off Hyrcanus' ears to disqualify him from the high priesthood.

events.title: Death of Fulvia at Sicyon
events.summary: Fulvia, who had raised troops for the Perusine War and, according to Martial's epigram from Augustus, provoked Octavian's verse insults, fled to Greece after Perusia; Antony met her at Athens coldly and she died of illness at Sicyon. Her death smoothed the reconciliation at Brundisium.

events.title: Downfall of Salvidienus Rufus
events.summary: At Brundisium Antony revealed that Quintus Salvidienus Rufus, Octavian's boyhood friend and commander in Gaul with eleven legions, had offered to defect. Octavian summoned him to Rome, where the Senate declared him a public enemy; he was executed or killed himself. Agrippa took his place as Octavian's marshal.

events.title: Antony marries Octavia
events.summary: To seal the Treaty of Brundisium, Antony married Octavian's elder sister Octavia, recently widowed by Gaius Marcellus, with the Senate waiving the ten-month mourning period. Coins of Antony at Ephesus showed both their portraits, the first living Roman woman on coinage.

events.title: Sextus Pompey's Neptune coinage
events.summary: Sextus Pompey's Sicilian mint struck denarii proclaiming him 'son of Neptune' and praefectus classis et orae maritimae, with Neptune standing on a ship's prow, the monster Scylla, the Pharos of Messana, and the Catanaean brothers carrying their parents from Etna's lava, an emblem of Sextus' cognomen Pius.

events.title: Octavian's DIVI IVLI F coinage
events.summary: From about 40 Octavian's gold and silver styled him CAESAR DIVI F or IMP CAESAR DIVI IVLI F, pairing his bearded portrait (mourning for Caesar) with the head of the deified Caesar or the star of the comet. 'Imperator' used as a praenomen was his invention.

events.title: Quintus Labienus Parthicus Imperator
events.summary: Quintus Labienus, son of Caesar's legate and envoy of the Liberators to Parthia, led the Parthian invasion of Roman Asia in 40 and struck aurei and denarii with his own portrait and a saddled Parthian horse, styling himself Q LABIENVS PARTHICVS IMP, 'the Parthian' in the sense of conqueror of, or with, the Parthians.

events.title: Treaty of Misenum
events.summary: Starved by Sextus Pompey's blockade, Italy forced the triumvirs to negotiate. Sextus was granted Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and the Peloponnese for five years, a future consulship and augurate, and an amnesty for the proscribed who had fled to him (except Caesar's murderers). The parties celebrated with banquets aboard Sextus' flagship.

events.title: Battle of the Cilician Gates and Mount Amanus
events.summary: Antony's legate Publius Ventidius Bassus, a muleteer's son once paraded as a child captive in Pompeius Strabo's triumph, surprised Quintus Labienus in the Taurus and defeated the Parthian cavalry that attacked his hill camp; Labienus fled and was killed. Ventidius then beat the Parthian Pharnapates at the Amanus pass and recovered Syria.

sides.strength: Parthian cavalry and Labienus' Roman troops

battle.significance: Expelled the Parthians from Asia Minor and Syria.

events.title: Virgil's Eclogues
events.summary: Virgil's ten pastoral poems, composed about 42-39 under the patronage of Pollio and modelled on Theocritus, transpose Greek bucolic into the Italian countryside of the confiscations. The Fourth Eclogue, addressed to Pollio as consul in 40, prophesies the birth of a child who will bring back the golden age.

events.title: Pollio founds the first public library
events.summary: From the spoils of his campaign against the Parthini in Illyricum, Gaius Asinius Pollio restored the Atrium Libertatis and installed in it the first public library in Rome, with Greek and Latin sections and portraits of authors, including the living Varro. Caesar's plan for a library under Varro's direction had died with him.

events.title: Antony and Octavia in Athens
events.summary: Wintering in Athens in 39/38 with Octavia, Antony played the Greek gentleman, attended lectures, and was hailed as the New Dionysus; Octavia was honoured as Athena Polias. Seneca the Elder reports the jest that Antony agreed to marry Athena but demanded a dowry of 1,000 talents.

events.title: Octavian marries Livia
events.summary: Octavian divorced Scribonia, Sextus Pompey's kinswoman, on the day she bore his only child Julia, and married Livia Drusilla, six months pregnant by her husband Tiberius Claudius Nero, who gave her away at the wedding. The marriage, which lasted 51 years, allied him with the Claudii.

events.title: Battle of Gindarus
events.summary: Pacorus invaded Syria again. Ventidius, having fed him false information about his route, waited on high ground near Gindarus; the Parthian cavalry charged uphill into slingers and legionaries and Pacorus was killed. His head was sent round the cities of Syria.

battle.significance: Avenged Carrhae in Roman eyes; killed Parthia's heir.

events.title: Naval battle off Cumae and the storm of Scyllaeum
events.summary: Sextus' freedman admiral Menas defected to Octavian with Sardinia. In the war that followed Sextus' admiral Menecrates was killed in a sea fight off Cumae, but Octavian was beaten in the straits of Messina and a storm off Scyllaeum wrecked most of his fleet. Octavian had to start again.

battle.significance: Sextus kept control of the sea; Octavian turned to Agrippa to build a new navy.

events.title: Menodorus surrenders Sardinia to Octavian
events.summary: Menodorus (or Menas), Sextus Pompey's freedman admiral, handed over Sardinia and Corsica, three legions and sixty ships to Octavian, who made him an equestrian. Octavian treated it as Sextus breaking the Treaty of Misenum, and war resumed. Menodorus changed sides twice more.

events.title: Agrippa in Gaul and across the Rhine
events.summary: As governor of Gaul, Agrippa suppressed a rising in Aquitania and became the second Roman to cross the Rhine with an army; he resettled the Ubii, at their request, on the left bank, the origin of the Oppidum Ubiorum (Cologne). He declined a triumph because of Octavian's recent naval defeats.
events.locName: Rhine at the land of the Ubii

events.title: Antony besieges Samosata
events.summary: After Ventidius' victory at Gindarus, Antony took over the siege of Antiochus I of Commagene in Samosata, which had sheltered Parthian fugitives; it dragged on, and he settled for 300 talents. Ventidius, suspected of having taken bribes from Antiochus, returned to Rome to triumph over the Parthians, the first Roman to do so.

battle.significance: Ended with a payment instead of a capture.

events.title: Treaty of Tarentum
events.summary: Through Octavia's mediation the triumvirs renewed their powers for a further five years, to the end of 33. Antony gave Octavian 120 ships for the war against Sextus in return for a promise of 20,000 legionaries for Parthia, which Octavian never delivered. Antony returned east and soon after formally acknowledged his twins by Cleopatra.

events.title: Herod and Sosius take Jerusalem
events.summary: With Antony's governor Gaius Sosius and Roman legions, Herod besieged Antigonus in Jerusalem and took it after five months. The Roman troops massacred the population until Herod bought them off. Antigonus, the last Hasmonean king, was sent to Antony and beheaded at Antioch.

sides.strength: Sosius' legions and Herod's army, c. 11 legions per Josephus

battle.significance: Ended the Hasmonean dynasty; inaugurated Herodian Judaea.

events.title: Agrippa builds the Portus Julius
events.summary: Preparing for the decisive war against Sextus Pompey, Agrippa cut channels to join Lake Lucrinus and Lake Avernus to the sea near Puteoli, creating a sheltered naval base where 20,000 freed slaves were trained as rowers through the winter of 37/36. Tunnels through the hills, including the Grotta di Cocceio, connected it to Cumae.

events.title: Antony executes Antigonus
events.summary: After Herod and Sosius took Jerusalem, the last Hasmonean king, Antigonus, was sent in chains to Antony at Antioch and, at Herod's request, beheaded, the first king Rome executed with the axe, says Dio. Herod's rule in Judaea now began in earnest.

events.title: Varro's Res rusticae
events.summary: At eighty, Marcus Terentius Varro wrote three books of dialogues on agriculture, livestock and villa husbandry (including aviaries and fishponds) for his wife Fundania, who had bought a farm. It is the main source for the slave-run estate economy of late Republican Italy, with figures on yields, staff and prices.

events.title: Phraates IV murders his father; Monaeses defects
events.summary: Phraates IV succeeded the grieving Orodes II, whom he then murdered along with his brothers. The noble Monaeses fled to Antony, who promised him three Syrian cities and planned an invasion around his knowledge, but Monaeses was lured home by Phraates, possibly as a double agent.

events.title: Battle of Mylae (36 BC)
events.summary: Agrippa, with the new fleet he had trained in the Portus Julius, a harbour he created in 37 by cutting Lake Avernus and Lake Lucrinus through to the sea, defeated Sextus' admiral Papias off Mylae. Days later Octavian, landing near Tauromenium, was routed at sea by Sextus and barely escaped.

battle.significance: Agrippa's first sea victory; prelude to Naulochus.

events.title: Lepidus deposed
events.summary: Lepidus, who had brought 14 legions from Africa and received the surrender of Sextus' army, claimed Sicily for himself. Octavian walked into his camp almost alone and the legions deserted to him. Lepidus, in mourning clothes, begged for mercy; he was stripped of his triumviral power but allowed to keep the office of pontifex maximus and lived under guard at Circeii until 13 or 12 BC.

events.title: Battle of Naulochus
events.summary: Some 300 ships a side met off Naulochus. Agrippa's heavier ships used the harpax, a grapnel fired from a catapult and reeled in by winch, to drag enemy ships alongside for boarding. Sextus lost 28 ships sunk and almost all the rest captured, burned or run ashore, escaping with 17 to the East. Agrippa received a naval crown, a golden wreath decorated with ships' prows.

battle.significance: Destroyed Sextus' sea power; ended the last Pompeian resistance.

events.title: Antony's Parthian campaign and the siege of Phraaspa
events.summary: Antony invaded Media Atropatene through Armenia with 16 legions and perhaps 100,000 men, leaving his siege train of 300 wagons with two legions under Oppius Statianus. The Parthian king Phraates IV and the Median king destroyed the train and its escort while Artavasdes of Armenia withdrew his cavalry. Unable to take Phraaspa without engines, Antony retreated in October across mountains in 27 days and 18 battles.

sides.strength: 16 legions, 10,000 Gallic and Spanish horse, allies; c. 100,000 (Plutarch)
sides.losses: c. 24,000 in the retreat plus c. 8,000 on the march home; 10,000 with the siege train

battle.significance: Antony's military reputation was badly damaged; the East was not conquered.

events.title: Octavian's defeat off Tauromenium
events.summary: In August 36 Octavian ferried three legions to Tauromenium, then was caught by Sextus Pompey's fleet and lost most of his ships; he escaped to the mainland almost alone and contemplated suicide. Cornificius' stranded legions marched across Sicily under constant attack to join Agrippa at Mylae.

battle.significance: Octavian's lowest point in the war; Agrippa's Naulochus followed within weeks.

events.title: Destruction of Antony's siege train
events.summary: Antony, hurrying ahead to besiege Phraaspa, left his siege engines, carried on 300 wagons including an 80-foot ram, under Oppius Statianus with two legions. Parthian and Median cavalry annihilated the column, killing 10,000 men and burning the engines; Artavasdes of Armenia then took his cavalry home.

battle.significance: Doomed the siege of Phraaspa.

events.title: Octavian receives tribunician sacrosanctity
events.summary: After Naulochus the Senate voted Octavian an ovation, a golden statue on the Rostra, the right to wear the laurel at all times, and the sacrosanctity of a tribune; Octavian announced the remission of arrears of taxes and promised to restore the Republic once Antony returned from Parthia.

events.title: Octavian's house on the Palatine
events.summary: Octavian bought the house of the orator Hortensius on the Palatine and adjacent properties; after lightning struck part of it he declared the site public and vowed a temple to Apollo there. The modest-looking rooms, with Second Style paintings such as the 'Room of the Masks', were excavated from 1961 onward.

events.title: Octavian's Illyrian war: the siege of Metulum
events.summary: To give his legions work and himself military glory, Octavian campaigned in Illyricum in 35-33. At Metulum, capital of the Iapydes, he was wounded when a siege bridge collapsed; the defenders burned the town and themselves. He took Siscia on the Save and later recovered standards lost by Gabinius in 48.

battle.significance: Gave Octavian a military record to set against Antony's.

events.title: Execution of Sextus Pompey at Miletus
events.summary: Fleeing to Asia after Naulochus, Sextus Pompey tried to raise forces and negotiate with both Antony and the Parthians; captured by Antony's general Marcus Titius, he was executed at Miletus. Responsibility was disputed between Antony and his governor Plancus. Titius was later hissed out of Pompey's theatre.

events.title: Octavian takes Siscia
events.summary: Campaigning against the Pannonians, Octavian besieged Siscia (Sisak) at the confluence of the Colapis and Savus with a river fleet, took it after thirty days, and made it a base with twenty-five cohorts under Fufius Geminus, a forward post for later wars on the Danube.

battle.significance: Opened the Sava valley route toward the Danube.

events.title: Horace's first book of Satires
events.summary: Horace, a freedman's son who had fought for Brutus at Philippi and was introduced to Maecenas by Virgil and Varius in 38, published his first book of Satires about 35, including the Journey to Brundisium with Maecenas on a diplomatic mission to Antony in 37 and the 'Bore' satire. Maecenas gave him a Sabine farm about 33.

events.title: The Donations of Alexandria
events.summary: After capturing Artavasdes of Armenia, Antony staged a triumph-like procession in Alexandria and then, on silver thrones in the gymnasium, proclaimed Cleopatra Queen of Kings and Caesarion, as Caesar's true son, King of Kings. Alexander Helios was given Armenia, Media and Parthia (yet to be conquered), Cleopatra Selene Cyrenaica and Libya, and the infant Ptolemy Philadelphus Phoenicia, Syria and Cilicia.

events.title: Octavian wounded at Setovia
events.summary: In the Dalmatian campaign of 34 Octavian was wounded in the knee besieging Setovia; Promona and Synodium had already fallen. The Dalmatae surrendered in 33, returning the standards taken from Gabinius in 48, which Octavian displayed in the Porticus Octaviae.

battle.significance: Completed Octavian's reconquest of the Dalmatian coast.

events.title: Antony seizes Artavasdes of Armenia
events.summary: Blaming Artavasdes II for the failure of 36, Antony invited him to a meeting at Nicopolis, arrested him with his family and his treasure, occupied Armenia, and took the king in silver chains to Alexandria, where he paraded him in a triumphal procession before Cleopatra.

events.title: Cornelius Nepos' Lives
events.summary: Cornelius Nepos of Cisalpine Gaul, friend of Catullus, Cicero and Atticus, published his De viris illustribus, biographies comparing foreign and Roman generals, kings and historians, the earliest surviving Latin biographies. Only the book on foreign generals and the lives of Cato and Atticus survive; Atticus' life was revised after his death in 32.

events.title: Agrippa's aedileship
events.summary: Though a former consul, Agrippa took the junior office of aedile and spent lavishly on the city: he repaired the aqueducts and built the Aqua Julia, sailed through the Cloaca Maxima on a boat after cleaning it, set up 700 basins and 105 fountains, and provided free baths, barbers, oil and lotteries. It was a campaign to win the urban plebs for Octavian.

events.title: The rupture of 32: Antony's will and the oath of Italy
events.summary: When the consuls Sosius and Ahenobarbus attacked Octavian in the senate, he came with armed men; the consuls and over 300 senators fled to Antony. Antony divorced Octavia. Plancus and Titius defected and revealed Antony's will, which Octavian seized illegally from the Vestals and read to the senate: it recognised Caesarion, left legacies to Cleopatra's children and asked for burial in Alexandria.

events.title: War declared on Cleopatra
events.summary: Octavian had war declared on Cleopatra alone, not Antony, to frame the coming civil war as a foreign war. He performed the archaic fetial rite himself, hurling a bloodied spear into a plot of 'enemy' ground by the temple of Bellona. Antony was stripped of his consulship for 31 and his powers.

events.title: Denarii of Antony and Cleopatra
events.summary: A denarius struck about 32, probably at Antioch or Alexandria, shows Antony with ARMENIA DEVICTA and Cleopatra with the legend CLEOPATRAE REGINAE REGVM FILIORVM REGVM, 'of Cleopatra, Queen of Kings and of her sons who are kings'. It is the only Roman silver coin of a foreign queen with a Latin legend.

events.title: Antony's legionary denarii
events.summary: To pay his army and fleet before Actium, Antony struck a vast issue of debased denarii showing a galley and a legionary eagle between standards with the name of each legion, LEG II to LEG XXIII plus the praetorian cohorts and the speculatores. They circulated for over two centuries; Marcus Aurelius restruck the type in 168.

events.title: The consuls flee to Antony
events.summary: The consuls of 32, Antony's partisans Gaius Sosius and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, attacked Octavian in the Senate; Octavian appeared with an armed escort, and the consuls and some 300 senators left Rome for Antony at Ephesus. Octavian let them go and summoned the Senate to hear his charges.

events.title: Battle of Actium
events.summary: Antony and Cleopatra's fleet, bottled up in the Ambracian Gulf through summer by Agrippa's blockade and weakened by disease and desertion, came out to break through. After hours of fighting, Cleopatra's squadron of 60 ships hoisted sail and fled through a gap with the war chest; Antony followed in a fast ship. The rest of the fleet fought on and was burned or surrendered; the land army of 19 legions surrendered a week later.
events.locName: mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, off Actium

sides.strength: c. 400 ships (lighter), 8 legions embarked or ashore
c. 230 warships incl. 60 Egyptian, 19 legions ashore
sides.losses: c. 5,000 killed; fleet and army surrendered

battle.significance: Decided the last civil war of the Republic.

events.title: Agrippa seizes Methone and the Greek coast
events.summary: Early in 31 Agrippa crossed with part of the fleet, stormed Methone in the south-western Peloponnese, where the exiled king Bogud of Mauretania was killed, then took Leucas, Patrae and Corinth, cutting Antony's grain route from Egypt and leaving his army at Actium hungry and stricken by disease.

events.title: Ahenobarbus deserts Antony
events.summary: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, Antony's most distinguished Roman supporter and an enemy of Cleopatra, rowed across to Octavian's camp shortly before Actium, already ill with fever; Antony sent his baggage and servants after him. He died within days.

events.title: Herod's Nabataean war and the earthquake
events.summary: Sent by Antony against the Nabataean king Malichus instead of to Actium, Herod was defeated at Canatha, then, after a severe earthquake in spring 31 killed some 30,000 in Judaea (and damaged Qumran), won a victory near Philadelphia (Amman). Absence from Actium let him change sides cleanly.

battle.significance: Kept Herod out of Actium.

events.title: Fall of Alexandria and death of Antony
events.summary: Octavian advanced on Egypt from Syria while Cornelius Gallus came from Cyrene. Antony won a cavalry skirmish near the hippodrome on 31 July, but the next day his fleet and cavalry went over to Octavian. Told falsely that Cleopatra was dead, he stabbed himself and was hauled up into her mausoleum to die in her arms. 1 August became a holiday at Rome.

sides.strength: remnant forces; fleet and cavalry defected

battle.significance: Ended the war and the Ptolemaic dynasty.

events.title: Death of Cleopatra
events.summary: Learning that Octavian meant to lead her in his triumph, Cleopatra VII, last Ptolemaic ruler and the last Hellenistic monarch of note, killed herself with her maids Iras and Charmion, probably about 10 or 12 August. The asp brought in a basket of figs is the version Plutarch reports along with others; he admits no one knew the truth, and poison is equally possible.

events.title: Annexation of Egypt
events.summary: Egypt became a Roman possession under an equestrian prefect answerable to Octavian; senators and leading equites were forbidden to enter it without his permission. Its first prefect, the poet-soldier Gaius Cornelius Gallus, crushed a revolt in the Thebaid and boasted of it on a trilingual stele at Philae (29), and fell from favour and killed himself in 26.

events.title: Herod meets Octavian at Rhodes
events.summary: Having executed the aged Hyrcanus II as a possible rival, Herod went to Octavian at Rhodes in spring 30, laid aside his diadem, and declared that he had been loyal to Antony and would be as loyal to his new master. Octavian restored his crown and later enlarged his kingdom with Jericho, Gaza and coastal cities.

events.title: Cornelius Gallus takes Paraetonium
events.summary: While Octavian approached Egypt from Syria, Gaius Cornelius Gallus, with Antony's former African legions, seized Paraetonium (Mersa Matruh) and repulsed Antony's attack, during which Gallus drowned out Antony's appeals to the troops with trumpets and destroyed his ships with a harbour chain.

battle.significance: Closed the western approach to Alexandria.

events.title: Death of Caesarion
events.summary: Cleopatra had sent Caesarion, then seventeen, with treasure toward the Red Sea and India; his tutor Rhodon persuaded him to return, and Octavian, advised by the philosopher Areius that 'too many Caesars is not good', had him killed. Antony's elder son Antyllus was dragged from Caesar's statue and executed.

events.title: Diodorus completes his Bibliotheca
events.summary: Diodorus of Agyrium in Sicily completed his forty-book universal history, from mythical times to Caesar's Gallic War, about 30 after some thirty years of work including a visit to Egypt in 60-56, where he saw a Roman lynched for killing a cat. Books 1-5 and 11-20 survive, preserving lost sources such as Posidonius on the Sicilian slave wars.

events.title: The doors of Janus closed
events.summary: On 11 January 29 the Senate decreed that the doors of the shrine of Janus Geminus be closed, signalling that Rome was at peace on land and sea, for only the third time in Roman history after Numa and 235 BC. Augustus would close them twice more.

events.title: The trilingual stele of Cornelius Gallus at Philae
events.summary: The first prefect of Egypt, the poet Gaius Cornelius Gallus, crushed a revolt in the Thebaid, received Meroitic envoys and placed a client ruler over the Triakontaschoinos south of Aswan, recording his deeds in Latin, Greek and hieroglyphs on a stele at Philae dated 16 April 29, boasting that he had taken his army further than any before him.

events.title: Octavian's triple triumph
events.summary: On 13, 14 and 15 August Octavian triumphed over Illyricum, Actium and Egypt; in the Egyptian procession Cleopatra's effigy with the asp and her children Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene were displayed. He dedicated the temple of the Deified Julius on 18 August, its speakers' platform adorned with rams from Actium, and the rebuilt senate house, the Curia Julia, with an altar and statue of Victory, on 28 August. The doors of the temple of Janus had been closed earlier that year, signalling peace throughout the empire for the first time since 235.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Divus Iulius
events.summary: On 18 August 29, during his triple triumph celebrations, Octavian dedicated the Temple of the Deified Julius at the east end of the Forum, on the spot where Caesar's body was burned, its podium decorated with the bronze rams of ships captured at Actium (the Rostra Iulia).

events.title: Dedication of the Curia Iulia
events.summary: On 28 August 29 Octavian dedicated the new Senate house begun by Caesar in 44 to replace Faustus Sulla's curia, which had been demolished after the fire at Clodius' funeral pyre. He placed in it the statue and altar of Victory from Tarentum, decorated with Egyptian spoils; the altar's removal in 382 became a great pagan-Christian controversy.

events.title: Marcus Crassus denied the spolia opima
events.summary: Marcus Licinius Crassus, grandson of the triumvir and proconsul of Macedonia, killed Deldo, king of the Bastarnae, with his own hands and claimed the right to dedicate the spolia opima to Jupiter Feretrius, the rarest honour in Roman arms. He was refused, it seems because he did not hold independent command; Livy reports that Augustus produced the linen corslet of Cossus proving that only a consul could claim it.

events.title: Amphitheatre of Statilius Taurus
events.summary: Titus Statilius Taurus, Octavian's general, built Rome's first permanent stone amphitheatre on the Campus Martius from the spoils of his African triumph (34) and dedicated it with gladiatorial games in 29. It burned in the fire of AD 64 and was replaced by the Colosseum.

events.title: Virgil's Georgics read to Octavian
events.summary: Returning from the East in summer 29, Octavian rested at Atella, where Virgil and Maecenas read him the newly finished Georgics over four days, Maecenas taking over when Virgil's voice failed. The four-book poem on farming, trees, livestock and bees had taken seven years and is dedicated to Maecenas.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine
events.summary: On 9 October 28 Octavian dedicated the Temple of Apollo next to his house on the Palatine, vowed in 36 against Sextus Pompey on land struck by lightning. Its porticoes of yellow Numidian marble held statues of the fifty Danaids, and its libraries of Greek and Latin literature; the Sibylline Books were later moved to the temple's base.

events.title: Census of 28 and the restoration of laws
events.summary: As consuls with Agrippa, Octavian held the first census in 42 years, registering 4,063,000 citizens, and purged the senate, removing perhaps 190 members. He annulled the illegal measures of the triumviral period by edict from the end of 28, and an aureus of that year proclaims that he restored to the Roman people their laws and rights.

events.title: AEGYPTO CAPTA coinage
events.summary: Aurei and denarii of 28 show Octavian's head with a crocodile and the legend AEGYPTO CAPTA, proclaiming the conquest of Egypt, while the cistophori of Ephesus of the same year call him 'champion of the liberty of the Roman people' (LIBERTATIS P R VINDEX). The two messages, conquest abroad and restoration at home, frame the settlement of 27.

events.title: Octavian begins his Mausoleum
events.summary: In 28 Octavian began a huge circular tomb, 87 metres across, on the northern Campus Martius, with public gardens around it. Built during the war with Antony, it was a pointed contrast with Antony's reported wish to be buried in Alexandria. Marcellus was the first to be buried there in 23.

events.title: Division of the provinces between princeps and Senate
events.summary: The settlement of 27 BC divided provinces into those of the princeps (Hispania Tarraconensis and Lusitania, the Gauls, Syria, Cyprus and Egypt) and 'public' provinces assigned by lot to proconsuls (Africa, Asia, Achaea, Macedonia, Illyricum, Crete-Cyrene, Bithynia-Pontus, Sardinia, Baetica, Sicily).

events.title: First constitutional settlement; Octavian becomes Augustus
events.summary: On 13 January 27 BC Octavian announced to the Senate that he was transferring the res publica to the Senate and people; the Senate begged him to retain a large provincial command, and on 16 January voted him the name Augustus, the oak-leaf corona civica over his door, laurels on his doorposts and a golden shield (clupeus virtutis) in the Curia.

events.title: Octavian receives the name Augustus
events.summary: Three days later, on the motion of Lucius Munatius Plancus, the senate gave Octavian the name Augustus, 'the revered one', with associations of augury and sanctity. He had considered Romulus but rejected it for its overtones of kingship and fratricide. The date is conventionally taken as the end of the Republic and the start of the Principate.

events.title: Triumph of Marcus Licinius Crassus and the spolia opima controversy
events.summary: Crassus, grandson of the triumvir, triumphed 'ex Thraecia et Geteis' after campaigns of 29-28 BC in which he killed Deldo, king of the Bastarnae, with his own hand. His claim to dedicate the spolia opima in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius was blocked on the ground that he had not fought under his own auspices.

events.title: Augustus holds a census of the Gauls at Narbo
events.summary: On his way to Spain Augustus convened an assembly at Narbo and ordered a census of the Three Gauls, the first systematic registration of persons and property for tribute in the lands conquered by Caesar.

events.title: Livy begins Ab Urbe Condita
events.summary: Between about 27 and 25 BC Livy of Patavium published the first pentad of his 142-book history of Rome from the foundation, which he went on writing until his death in AD 17.

events.title: Battle of Vellica
events.summary: Opening victory of Augustus's Cantabrian campaign, fought 'under the walls of Vellica' after the Cantabri descended from their hill forts to meet the Roman columns.
events.locName: Vellica, near Aguilar de Campoo (Monte Cildá?)

sides.strength: Several legions in three columns (numbers unknown)

sides.losses: heavy; survivors fled to Mons Vindius

battle.significance: Broke Cantabrian field resistance and drove them into hill-top refuges that the Romans then blockaded.

events.title: Siege of Aracillum
events.summary: Cantabrian stronghold besieged by the Roman columns in 26 BC and taken after a long resistance; it became the type-site for Roman siege archaeology in the Cantabrian war.

sides.strength: Probably more than one legion with auxiliaries

battle.significance: Consolidated the Roman hold on the upper Besaya valley, the main north-south route through Cantabria.

events.title: Downfall and suicide of Cornelius Gallus
events.summary: Gaius Cornelius Gallus, poet, friend of Virgil and first prefect of Egypt, was renounced by Augustus for boastful self-promotion and indiscreet talk; after the Senate voted his condemnation and exile he killed himself.

events.title: Augustus campaigns in Cantabria and convalesces at Tarraco
events.summary: Augustus took personal command against the Cantabri in 26 BC, operating from Segisama, but fell ill and withdrew to Tarraco, where he spent the winter of 26/25 and entered his eighth and ninth consulships.

events.title: Siege of Marib (Marsiaba)
events.summary: Climax of Aelius Gallus's expedition to Arabia Felix: the Roman army besieged the Sabaean capital for six days and withdrew for lack of water, two days' march from the 'land of aromatics'.

sides.strength: c. 10,000 at the start, much reduced by disease
sides.losses: few in battle; many to disease

battle.significance: Ended Roman ambitions to conquer the incense lands; no Roman army returned to South Arabia.

events.title: Siege of Lancia
events.summary: The Astures, descending in three columns along the Astura (Esla) to attack Roman camps, were betrayed by the Brigaecini; Publius Carisius pre-empted them and besieged the survivors in Lancia, which he took but spared.

sides.strength: Army of Lusitania (legions V Alaudae and X Gemina probable)

battle.significance: Broke Asturian resistance in the plains; Augustus closed the temple of Janus for the second time.

events.title: Destruction of the Salassi and foundation of Augusta Praetoria
events.summary: Aulus Terentius Varro Murena crushed the Salassi of the Val d'Aosta, who had controlled the Alpine passes and gold-washing for generations; 36,000 were sold at auction at Eporedia, and the colony of Augusta Praetoria was founded with 3,000 praetorian veterans.

events.title: Foundation of Augusta Emerita
events.summary: Publius Carisius settled discharged veterans (emeriti) of legions V Alaudae and X Gemina on the Anas (Guadiana), creating the colony that became capital of Lusitania.

events.title: Annexation of Galatia
events.summary: When king Amyntas was killed fighting the Homonadenses of the Taurus, Augustus did not appoint a successor but turned his large kingdom (Galatia, Lycaonia, Pisidia, parts of Pamphylia) into a province under a legate at Ancyra.

events.title: Agrippa dedicates the first Pantheon
events.summary: Marcus Agrippa completed the Pantheon on the Campus Martius as part of a complex with the Saepta Julia (dedicated 26 BC) and the Baths of Agrippa. The inscription still on Hadrian's rebuilding, M. AGRIPPA L.F. COS. TERTIUM FECIT, refers to his third consulship in 27 BC.

events.title: Janus closed for the second time under Augustus
events.summary: After the supposed end of the Cantabrian war Augustus closed the doors of Janus Geminus in 25 BC, the second of the three closings of his reign (29 BC, 25 BC and a third of uncertain date).

events.title: Marriage of Julia and Marcellus
events.summary: Augustus married his only child Julia, aged fourteen, to his nephew Marcus Claudius Marcellus in 25 BC, while he himself was still in Spain; Agrippa presided in his stead.

events.title: Juba II made king of Mauretania
events.summary: In 25 BC Augustus gave the vacant kingdom of Mauretania, together with parts of Gaetulia, to Juba II, son of the Juba who died at Thapsus, and married him to Cleopatra Selene, daughter of Antony and Cleopatra.

events.title: Vitruvius dedicates De Architectura to Augustus
events.summary: Around 30-22 BC the military engineer Vitruvius dedicated his ten books On Architecture to Augustus, the only complete architectural treatise to survive from antiquity.

events.title: Battle of Pselchis
events.summary: Gaius Petronius, prefect of Egypt, routed a Kushite army three times his size near Pselchis (Dakka) in Lower Nubia, reversing the Kushite capture of Syene, Elephantine and Philae.

battle.significance: Restored the southern frontier of Egypt and led to the peace of Samos.

events.title: Second constitutional settlement: tribunicia potestas and imperium maius
events.summary: After a near-fatal illness (when he handed his signet ring to Agrippa and state papers to his consular colleague Piso), Augustus resigned the consulship on 1 July 23 BC and received instead the tribunician power for life, numbered annually, and a proconsular imperium overriding that of governors in all provinces.

events.title: Conspiracy of Fannius Caepio and Murena
events.summary: Following the trial of Marcus Primus, governor of Macedonia, who claimed he had attacked the Odrysians on Augustus's or Marcellus's orders, a plot against Augustus was alleged; Fannius Caepio and a Murena (probably Varro Murena, Primus's advocate) were condemned in absence and killed.

events.title: Death of Marcellus
events.summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus, Augustus's nephew and son-in-law (married to Julia in 25 BC) and presumed heir, died at Baiae aged 19, the first to be buried in the Mausoleum of Augustus.

events.title: Augustan reform of the base-metal coinage
events.summary: Around 23 BC the mint at Rome resumed production under the tresviri monetales and introduced a new token coinage: brass (orichalcum) sestertii and dupondii and copper asses and quadrantes, alongside the gold aureus and silver denarius.
