events.title: Horace publishes Odes I-III
events.summary: In 23 BC Horace issued the three books of Carmina, 88 poems adapting Alcaeus, Sappho and other Greek lyric metres to Latin, dedicated to Maecenas.

events.title: Augustus's near-fatal illness
events.summary: In 23 BC Augustus fell so ill that he handed his state papers to his consular colleague Calpurnius Piso and his signet ring to Agrippa, not to Marcellus; he was saved by the cold-water treatment of his physician Antonius Musa.

events.title: Tiber floods of the Augustan age
events.summary: Cassius Dio records the Tiber flooding the low-lying city in 27 BC (read as a portent of Octavian's greatness), 23 BC and 22 BC, when the Pons Sublicius was carried away and the flood combined with plague and famine.

events.title: Augustus refuses the dictatorship and takes the cura annonae
events.summary: During famine, plague and floods in 23-22 BC the Roman crowd tried to force the dictatorship and a perpetual consulship on Augustus. He knelt and bared his breast in refusal but accepted charge of the grain supply, ending the shortage within days at his own expense.

events.title: Augustus's tour of Sicily, Greece and the East
events.summary: From late 22 to 19 BC Augustus toured Sicily, Greece, Asia, Bithynia and Syria, wintering twice on Samos, reorganising cities and client kingdoms and negotiating the return of the standards from Parthia.

events.title: Marriage of Julia and Agrippa
events.summary: In 21 BC Augustus married the widowed Julia to Agrippa, who divorced Octavia's daughter Marcella to make way; the marriage produced Gaius, Lucius, Julia the Younger, Agrippina the Elder and Agrippa Postumus.

events.title: Return of the Parthian standards
events.summary: Under threat of Tiberius's army in Armenia and Augustus's presence in Syria, Phraates IV returned the standards and surviving prisoners taken from Crassus at Carrhae (53 BC), from Decidius Saxa (40 BC) and from Antony (36 BC). The diplomatic success was trumpeted as a military victory.

events.title: Peace of Samos with Kush
events.summary: Kushite envoys, escorted by Petronius's officers to Augustus wintering on Samos, obtained everything they asked, including remission of the tribute Petronius had imposed.

events.title: Herod begins rebuilding the Jerusalem Temple
events.summary: In the eighteenth year of his reign (20/19 BC) Herod began the reconstruction of the Second Temple, doubling the Temple Mount platform with vast retaining walls (including the Western Wall) to about 144,000 square metres.

events.title: Tiberius crowns Tigranes III in Armenia
events.summary: In 20 BC the 22-year-old Tiberius led an army into Armenia, where the anti-Roman king Artaxias II had been murdered by his own nobles, and set the Roman-educated Tigranes III on the throne.

events.title: Indian embassy and the self-immolation of Zarmanochegas at Athens
events.summary: An embassy from an Indian king (named Porus or Pandion in the sources) reached Augustus on Samos in 20 BC; one member, the ascetic Zarmanochegas of Bargosa, burned himself alive at Athens after being initiated into the Mysteries.

events.title: Augustus grants the ius respondendi
events.summary: According to the jurist Pomponius, Augustus was the first to give selected jurists the right to give legal opinions (responsa) "by his authority", tying private legal expertise to the princeps.

events.title: Triumph of Cornelius Balbus over the Garamantes
events.summary: Lucius Cornelius Balbus the Younger, proconsul of Africa, triumphed over the Garamantes after capturing their capital Garama in the Fezzan. He was the first man born outside Italy (at Gades) to triumph, and the last person outside the imperial family ever to do so.

events.title: Agrippa opens the Aqua Virgo
events.summary: Agrippa's aqueduct, about 21 km long and almost entirely underground, brought spring water to the Campus Martius to supply his baths. It still feeds the Trevi Fountain.

events.title: Death of Virgil
events.summary: Publius Vergilius Maro died at Brundisium after falling ill in Greece, where he had met Augustus at Athens. He asked that the unfinished Aeneid be burned; Augustus ordered Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca to publish it without additions.

events.title: Execution of Egnatius Rufus
events.summary: Marcus Egnatius Rufus, who had won popularity as aedile by running a private fire brigade of his slaves, tried to stand for the consulship of 19 BC illegally; when the consul Sentius Saturninus refused his candidacy he was accused of plotting against Augustus and executed.

events.title: Agrippa ends the Cantabrian War
events.summary: A last revolt by Cantabrian slaves who had escaped from Roman owners and killed them was crushed by Agrippa, who had to overcome his own soldiers' reluctance; virtually all men of military age were killed and the rest forced from their mountains into the plains.

events.title: The Aeneid published by Varius and Tucca
events.summary: Virgil died at Brundisium in September 19 BC with the Aeneid unrevised and asked for it to be burned; Augustus overruled him and had Lucius Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca publish it with minimal editing, leaving the half-lines in place.

events.title: Lex Julia de maritandis ordinibus and Lex Julia de adulteriis coercendis
events.summary: Augustus used his tribunician power to carry laws penalising celibacy and childlessness among the propertied classes and making adultery a public crime tried before a standing court (quaestio).

events.title: Lectio senatus of 18 BC
events.summary: Augustus purged the Senate from about 800 to 600 members after a chaotic system of co-optation failed; Suetonius says he presided wearing a breastplate under his toga and a sword, with ten senators around his chair.

events.title: Lex Julia de ambitu and sumptuary law of 18 BC
events.summary: Alongside the marriage legislation of 18 BC Augustus passed a law against electoral bribery, barring offenders from office for five years, and a sumptuary law restricting spending on banquets.

events.title: Secular Games of 17 BC
events.summary: Augustus and Agrippa, as magistri of the quindecimviri sacris faciundis, celebrated the Ludi Saeculares over three nights and days (31 May-3 June), proclaiming the beginning of a new age. Horace's Carmen Saeculare was sung by 27 boys and 27 girls on the Palatine and the Capitol.

events.title: Augustus adopts Gaius and Lucius
events.summary: Soon after the birth of Lucius in 17 BC Augustus adopted both of Agrippa and Julia's sons by a symbolic sale (per assem et libram), making his grandsons his own heirs as Gaius Julius Caesar and Lucius Julius Caesar.

events.title: Clades Lolliana
events.summary: The Sugambri, Usipetes and Tencteri crucified Roman traders in their territory, crossed the Rhine, ambushed Roman cavalry and routed the legate Marcus Lollius, capturing the eagle of legio V Alaudae.

sides.losses: Unknown; the eagle of V Alaudae captured

battle.significance: Triggered the Augustan offensive into Germany and Augustus's three-year stay in Gaul.

events.title: Augustus in Gaul and the Licinus scandal
events.summary: After the Lollian disaster Augustus spent 16-13 BC in Gaul, organising the three Gallic provinces and the campaigns into the Alps and Germany, while the freedman procurator Licinus enriched himself by inventing a fourteen-month year for tax purposes.

events.title: Drusus and Tiberius conquer the Raeti and Vindelici
events.summary: In a pincer campaign Drusus advanced from Italy up the Adige valley and over the Alps while Tiberius came from Gaul, fought a naval battle on Lake Constance and joined his brother near the source of the Danube, subduing the Raeti and Vindelici in a single summer.

events.title: Incorporation of Noricum
events.summary: The Celtic kingdom of Noricum, long a trading partner of Rome, was absorbed in 16-15 BC after the Norici joined Pannonians in raiding Istria; it was governed by an equestrian prefect and from Claudius as a procuratorial province.

events.title: Agrippa visits Herod and Jerusalem
events.summary: During his eastern command Agrippa visited Herod in 15 BC, saw Caesarea, Sebaste and the fortresses, and offered a hecatomb at the Temple; the next year in Ionia he confirmed the right of the Jews of Asia to send temple money to Jerusalem.

events.title: Imperial mint opened at Lugdunum
events.summary: From about 15 BC the main imperial mint for gold and silver was at Lugdunum, which struck the aurei and denarii that paid the Rhine armies; from about 10 BC it also struck the copper asses with the Altar of Lugdunum reverse.

events.title: Agrippa settles the Bosporan Kingdom
events.summary: Agrippa brought a fleet to Sinope to dislodge the usurper Scribonius from the Bosporan throne and installed Polemon I of Pontus as king, married to the Bosporan queen Dynamis.

events.title: Ara Pacis Augustae
events.summary: The Senate voted the Altar of Augustan Peace on 4 July 13 BC to mark Augustus's return from Gaul and Spain; it was dedicated on 30 January 9 BC, Livia's birthday, on the Campus Martius beside the Via Flaminia.
events.locName: Campus Martius, Rome (original site under Palazzo Fiano)

events.title: Dedication of the Theatre of Marcellus
events.summary: Augustus dedicated the stone theatre begun by Julius Caesar near the Circus Flaminius in the name of his dead nephew Marcellus; it held perhaps 11,000-20,000 spectators.

events.title: Augustus fixes terms of military service
events.summary: In 13 BC Augustus fixed service at 16 years for legionaries and 12 for praetorians, with a fixed cash discharge payment instead of land, ending the late-Republican scramble for veteran settlements.

events.title: Theatre and Crypta of Balbus dedicated
events.summary: Lucius Cornelius Balbus, the last private citizen to triumph (19 BC), dedicated his stone theatre in the southern Campus Martius in 13 BC, during a Tiber flood that forced him to reach it by boat.

events.title: Lucius Calpurnius Piso's Thracian war
events.summary: In 13 BC the Bessi, led by Vologaeses, a priest of Dionysus, killed the Odrysian client king Rhescuporis and drove his uncle Rhoemetalces into the Chersonese; Lucius Calpurnius Piso, brought from Pamphylia, needed three campaigns (13-11 BC) to suppress them and won triumphal ornaments.

events.title: Death of Agrippa
events.summary: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa died in Campania shortly after returning from Pannonia, aged about 51. Augustus delivered the funeral oration and buried him in his own Mausoleum.

events.title: Augustus becomes pontifex maximus
events.summary: On the death of the former triumvir Lepidus, who had kept the chief pontificate in exile at Circeii since 36 BC, Augustus was elected pontifex maximus by a crowd that Res Gestae claims was larger than any ever seen in Rome.

events.title: Altar of Rome and Augustus at Lugdunum
events.summary: Drusus dedicated an altar of Rome and Augustus at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône outside Lugdunum, where delegates of the sixty civitates of the Three Gauls met each year on 1 August under an elected Gallic priest.

events.title: Drusus digs the Fossa Drusiana
events.summary: In preparation for his first German campaign in 12 BC Drusus cut a canal linking the Rhine to the IJssel (Flevo lake), allowing his fleet to reach the North Sea through the territory of the friendly Frisii.

events.title: Pyramid of Gaius Cestius
events.summary: The 36 m marble-faced pyramid tomb of Gaius Cestius Epulo, praetor and septemvir epulonum, was completed in 330 days before 12 BC, as its inscription and the naming of Agrippa among his heirs show.

events.title: Battle of Arbalo
events.summary: Returning from the Weser in 11 BC, Drusus's army was trapped by the Germans in a narrow defile at Arbalo and nearly destroyed, but the overconfident attackers came to close quarters in disorder and were beaten.

battle.significance: Allowed Drusus to extricate his army and fortify the Lippe line.

events.title: Tiberius forced to marry Julia
events.summary: After Agrippa's death Augustus made Tiberius divorce Vipsania Agrippina, whom he loved and who had borne him Drusus the Younger, and marry the widowed Julia in 11 BC.

events.title: Herod inaugurates Caesarea Maritima
events.summary: In 10 or 9 BC Herod dedicated Caesarea, built over twelve years on the site of Strato's Tower, with the great artificial harbour Sebastos and a temple of Roma and Augustus facing the sea.

events.title: Augustus erects Egyptian obelisks in Rome; the Horologium
events.summary: In 10 BC Augustus set up two obelisks from Heliopolis, one on the spina of the Circus Maximus and one in the Campus Martius as the pointer of a huge meridian or sundial, both dedicated to the Sun "Aegypto in potestatem populi Romani redacta".

events.title: Death of Drusus the Elder
events.summary: After reaching the Elbe, Drusus was injured when his horse fell on his leg and died about 30 days later in his summer camp, aged 29. Tiberius rode some 200 miles in a day and a night from Ticinum to reach him before he died.

events.title: Tiberius deports 40,000 Sugambri across the Rhine
events.summary: Succeeding his dead brother in Germany, Tiberius forced the Sugambri to submit; their envoys, including leading nobles, were arrested and killed themselves, and some 40,000 Sugambri and Suebi were transplanted to the left bank of the Rhine.

events.title: Sextilis renamed Augustus; calendar error corrected
events.summary: A senatus consultum renamed the month Sextilis 'Augustus' because Augustus had begun his first consulship and conquered Egypt in it. Augustus also corrected the Julian calendar, which the pontiffs had misapplied by intercalating every third year instead of every fourth.

events.title: Deaths of Maecenas and Horace
events.summary: Maecenas died in 8 BC leaving his property, including the Esquiline gardens, to Augustus; Horace died fifty-nine days later and was buried beside him on the Esquiline.

events.title: Census of 8 BC: 4,233,000 citizens
events.summary: Augustus, acting alone with consular power, closed the second census of his reign in 8 BC with 4,233,000 Roman citizens registered, against 4,063,000 in 28 BC and 4,937,000 in AD 14.

events.title: Division of Rome into 14 regions and the vici
events.summary: Augustus reorganised the city of Rome into fourteen regiones subdivided into vici (265 by AD 73), each under four annually elected vicomagistri, mostly freedmen, who tended the crossroads shrines of the Lares Augusti and the Genius of Augustus.

events.title: Edicts of Augustus at Cyrene
events.summary: A marble stele found in the agora of Cyrene in 1926 preserves five edicts of Augustus (7/6-4 BC) regulating juries, citizen privileges and provincial justice in this senatorial province, ending with the senatus consultum Calvisianum on extortion trials.

events.title: Porticus of Livia dedicated
events.summary: In 7 BC Livia and Tiberius dedicated the Porticus Liviae on the Oppian, built on the site of the vast house of Vedius Pollio, which Augustus had inherited and razed as an example against luxury.

events.title: Herod executes his sons Alexander and Aristobulus
events.summary: After years of court intrigue Herod, with Augustus's permission and after a hearing before a council at Berytus, had his sons by the Hasmonean Mariamme strangled at Sebaste in 7 BC; in 4 BC, five days before his own death, he executed his eldest son Antipater.

events.title: Agrippa's world map displayed in the Porticus Vipsania
events.summary: The world map compiled from Agrippa's commentaries was set up after his death in the Porticus Vipsania, completed by his sister Vipsania Polla and Augustus around 7 BC.

events.title: Tropaeum Alpium at La Turbie
events.summary: The Senate and people erected a monumental trophy on the Via Julia Augusta above Monaco, recording that under Augustus's leadership and auspices all the Alpine peoples from the Adriatic to the Tyrrhenian had been brought under Roman rule; 45 peoples are named.

events.title: Tiberius withdraws to Rhodes
events.summary: Just after receiving the tribunician power for five years and a mission to Armenia, Tiberius insisted on retiring to Rhodes, where he spent nearly eight years as a private scholar, alienated from Augustus.

events.title: Birth of Jesus of Nazareth
events.summary: Jesus was probably born a few years before the death of Herod the Great in 4 BC, conventionally c. 6-4 BC; the birth narratives of Matthew and Luke place it at Bethlehem but disagree on most details.

events.title: Gaius and Lucius Caesar hailed principes iuventutis
events.summary: Augustus held his twelfth and thirteenth consulships (5 and 2 BC) to introduce his adopted sons to public life. Each was designated consul at fourteen to take office five years later, and the equestrian order hailed each as princeps iuventutis with silver shields and spears.

events.title: Quirinius's war against the Homonadenses
events.summary: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, probably as legate of Galatia or Syria, reduced the Homonadenses of the Taurus, who had killed king Amyntas, starving out 44 strongholds and settling 4,000 captives in nearby towns; he received triumphal ornaments.

events.title: Death of Herod and partition of his kingdom
events.summary: Herod died at Jericho in spring 4 BC, after executing three of his sons. Augustus largely confirmed his will: Archelaus became ethnarch of Judaea, Samaria and Idumaea, Herod Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, and Philip tetrarch of the north-eastern territories.

events.title: Roman town at Waldgirmes on the Lahn
events.summary: A civilian Roman town with stone-founded forum and basilica was laid out around 4 BC at Lahnau-Waldgirmes, 100 km east of the Rhine, and abandoned peacefully around AD 9. It is the clearest archaeological proof that a province of Germania was being built.

events.title: Augustus hailed Pater Patriae
events.summary: On 5 February 2 BC the Senate, equites and whole people, on a motion by Valerius Messalla Corvinus, saluted Augustus as Father of his Country; he answered in tears that his prayers were fulfilled.

events.title: Dedication of the Forum of Augustus and Temple of Mars Ultor
events.summary: Augustus dedicated his forum, built on private land bought from war booty, with the temple of Mars the Avenger vowed at Philippi. Its colonnades held statues of Aeneas, Romulus, the Julian ancestors and the 'summi viri' of the Republic with elogia.

events.title: Exile of Julia, daughter of Augustus
events.summary: Augustus denounced his daughter Julia to the Senate by letter for adulteries and sent her to the island of Pandateria; her mother Scribonia went with her. Iullus Antonius, son of Mark Antony, was forced to suicide, and other noble lovers were exiled.

events.title: Lex Fufia Caninia and Lex Aelia Sentia
events.summary: Two laws restricted manumission: the lex Fufia Caninia (2 BC) capped the number of slaves freed by will on a sliding scale to a maximum of 100; the lex Aelia Sentia (AD 4) required a master to be 20 and the slave 30 for a formal manumission conferring citizenship, unless justified before a council.

events.title: Augustus's naumachia and the Aqua Alsietina
events.summary: For the dedication of the Temple of Mars Ultor in 2 BC Augustus staged a sea battle of Athenians against Persians, with 30 rams and 3,000 men besides rowers, in a basin 1,800 by 1,200 feet dug across the Tiber.

events.title: Ovid publishes the Ars Amatoria
events.summary: Around 2 BC to AD 2 Ovid issued the Ars Amatoria, a mock-didactic manual of seduction in three books, which he later named as one of the two causes ("carmen et error") of his relegation to Tomis in AD 8.

events.title: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus crosses the Elbe
events.summary: As legate of Illyricum and then of Germany, Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus (cos. 16 BC) resettled wandering Hermunduri, crossed the Elbe unopposed some time between 7 BC and AD 1, set up an altar to Augustus on its far bank and built the causeway roads called pontes longi across the marshes between the Rhine and Ems.

events.title: Death of Lucius Caesar
events.summary: Lucius Caesar, Augustus's younger adopted son, died at Massilia of a sudden illness while on his way to the Spanish armies, aged 18.

events.title: Gaius Caesar meets Phraataces on the Euphrates
events.summary: Augustus's grandson and heir met the Parthian king Phraataces (Phraates V) on an island in the Euphrates; the Parthian renounced claims to Armenia, and the two dined on each bank in turn.

events.title: Tiberius returns from Rhodes
events.summary: With Gaius Caesar's consent and Livia's pleading, Tiberius was allowed to return from his seven-year retirement on Rhodes in AD 2, on condition that he take no part in public affairs; he lived in the Gardens of Maecenas.

events.title: Siege of Artagira; Gaius Caesar wounded
events.summary: Gaius Caesar, sent to settle Armenia, was treacherously wounded on 9 September AD 3 by Addon, commander of the fortress of Artagira, during a parley; the fort was taken after a long siege, but Gaius never recovered and died in Lycia in February AD 4.

battle.significance: Victory cost Augustus his heir.

events.title: Death of Gaius Caesar
events.summary: Gaius Caesar, wounded by treachery at the siege of Artagira in Armenia on 9 September AD 3, lost heart, asked to retire to private life, and died at Limyra in Lycia on his way back to Italy, aged 23.

events.title: Augustus adopts Tiberius and Agrippa Postumus
events.summary: Augustus adopted Tiberius, saying 'I do this for the sake of the state', and on the same day his last grandson Agrippa Postumus. Tiberius in turn was required to adopt his nephew Germanicus, though he had a son of his own, Drusus.

events.title: Tiberius's immensum bellum in Germany
events.summary: Tiberius's campaigns of AD 4-5 subdued the Cananefates, Chattuarii, Bructeri and Cherusci, wintered the army at the source of the Lippe, then crushed the Langobardi and reached the Elbe, where a fleet that had sailed round from the Rhine through the North Sea met the army.

events.title: Augustus pardons the conspirator Cinna
events.summary: Seneca and Dio tell how Augustus, on Livia's advice, pardoned Gnaeus Cornelius Cinna Magnus, Pompey's grandson, who had plotted to kill him, and made him consul the next year (AD 5).

events.title: Maison Carree at Nemausus dedicated to Gaius and Lucius
events.summary: The best-preserved Roman temple anywhere, the Maison Carree at Nemausus, carried a bronze inscription (reconstructed from its nail holes in 1758) dedicating it to Gaius and Lucius Caesar as consuls designate and principes iuventutis, so c. AD 2-4.

events.title: Military service extended to twenty years
events.summary: In AD 5 legionary service was raised to 20 years (with a further five sub vexillo as veterans) and praetorian service to 16, with discharge bounties of 12,000 sesterces for legionaries and 20,000 for praetorians.

events.title: Lex Valeria Cornelia and the destinatio centuries
events.summary: A law of AD 5 created ten new voting centuries of senators and equestrians, named after Gaius and Lucius Caesar, whose preliminary vote (destinatio) on consular and praetorian candidates guided the full Centuriate Assembly.

events.title: Creation of the aerarium militare
events.summary: Augustus created a military treasury to pay discharge bonuses to veterans, endowing it with 170 million sesterces of his own money and funding it permanently from a new 5% tax on inheritances (vicesima hereditatium) and a 1% sales tax.

events.title: Judaea becomes a Roman province; census of Quirinius
events.summary: After Jewish and Samaritan complaints against Archelaus, Augustus deposed him and exiled him to Vienne in Gaul; Judaea, Samaria and Idumaea were placed under an equestrian prefect, Coponius, while Quirinius, legate of Syria, took a census for tribute.

events.title: Creation of the vigiles
events.summary: After a serious fire Augustus established seven cohorts of vigiles, recruited from freedmen, each responsible for two of the fourteen regions, under an equestrian praefectus vigilum. They fought fires and patrolled the streets at night.

events.title: Outbreak of the Great Illyrian Revolt
events.summary: As Tiberius advanced from Carnuntum with twelve legions to attack Maroboduus's Marcomannic kingdom in Bohemia, the Daesitiates of Dalmatia, mustered as auxiliaries, rose under Bato, and the Breuci of Pannonia under another Bato and Pinnes marched on Sirmium. Tiberius had to abandon the Bohemian war and make peace with Maroboduus.

events.title: Battle near Sirmium
events.summary: Aulus Caecina Severus, governor of Moesia, marched to save Sirmium and defeated the Breuci near the city, but with heavy losses, and soon had to return to Moesia to repel Dacian and Sarmatian raids.

battle.significance: Saved Sirmium for Rome in the first weeks of the revolt.

events.title: Famine and unrest at Rome in AD 6
events.summary: A severe grain shortage in AD 6 led Augustus to expel gladiators, slaves for sale and most foreigners (except doctors and teachers) to beyond the hundredth milestone, double the grain dole and appoint two consulars as grain commissioners.

events.title: Cossus Cornelius Lentulus's Gaetulian war
events.summary: Around AD 6 the proconsul of Africa Cossus Cornelius Lentulus defeated the Gaetuli and Musulamii, who had attacked the territory of Juba II and Roman Africa, earning triumphal ornaments and the cognomen Gaetulicus for his son.

events.title: Tiberius's planned pincer attack on Maroboduus
events.summary: In AD 6 Tiberius prepared a two-pronged invasion of Maroboduus's Marcomannic kingdom in Bohemia, with Sentius Saturninus advancing from the Rhine through the Hercynian forest and Tiberius from Carnuntum, using twelve legions; the outbreak of the Pannonian-Dalmatian revolt forced him to abandon it within days of contact.

events.title: Judas the Galilean and the census revolt
events.summary: When Quirinius registered Judaea for tribute in AD 6, Judas of Gamala (the Galilean) and the Pharisee Saddok called on Jews to refuse it, teaching that God alone was master; Josephus calls the movement a "fourth philosophy" and blames it for the later revolt.

events.title: The rival law schools of Labeo and Capito
events.summary: Under Augustus the jurists Marcus Antistius Labeo, a republican who refused the consulship, and Gaius Ateius Capito, a loyalist consul of AD 5, founded the two schools later called Proculians (after Proculus) and Sabinians (after Masurius Sabinus and Cassius Longinus).

events.title: Battle of the Volcaean Marshes
events.summary: Caecina Severus and Plautius Silvanus, bringing five legions with auxiliaries and Thracian cavalry from the east to join Tiberius, were ambushed by the two Batos near the Volcaean marshes; the cavalry and auxiliaries broke but the legions rallied and won.
events.locName: Volcaean marshes, between the Sava and Drava (near Cibalae?)

battle.significance: Allowed the eastern army to join Tiberius at Siscia, concentrating overwhelming Roman forces.

events.title: Exile of Agrippa Postumus
events.summary: Augustus disowned his last grandson, Agrippa Postumus, for his 'savage' and unmanageable character, banishing him first to Surrentum and then, by senatorial decree, permanently to the island of Planasia under military guard.

events.title: Surrender of the Breuci at the Bathinus river
events.summary: Worn down by famine and Tiberius's devastation, the Pannonians laid down their arms at the river Bathinus. The Breucian Bato, who had betrayed his colleague Pinnes to the Romans and been rewarded, was captured and executed soon after by the Daesitiate Bato.

events.title: Relegation of Ovid to Tomis
events.summary: Augustus relegated the poet Ovid by personal edict to Tomis on the Black Sea, for 'a poem and a mistake' (carmen et error). The poem was the Ars Amatoria; the mistake has never been identified.

events.title: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest (Varian Disaster)
events.summary: Publius Quinctilius Varus, leading legions XVII, XVIII and XIX with auxiliaries and a long baggage train to winter quarters, was lured by the Cheruscan Arminius, a Roman citizen and equestrian commanding auxiliaries, into a multi-day running fight in forest and bog where the army was annihilated.

sides.strength: 3 legions, 3 alae, 6 cohorts: c. 15,000-20,000 soldiers plus camp followers
Cherusci, Bructeri, Marsi, Chatti and others; unknown

battle.significance: Ended Augustus's attempt to make Germany between Rhine and Elbe a province; fixed the Rhine as the frontier and became a founding myth of German nationalism (Hermannsdenkmal, 1875).

events.title: Siege of Aliso
events.summary: After the Varian disaster the Germans besieged the Lippe fortress of Aliso. Its commander, the camp prefect Lucius Caedicius, held out until supplies failed, then broke out on a stormy night with soldiers, women and children and reached the Rhine.

battle.significance: The breakout preserved a remnant and denied the Germans a second triumph.

events.title: Siege of Raetinium
events.summary: Germanicus besieged the Dalmatian stronghold of Raetinium; the defenders set fire to the outer town as the Romans broke in, trapping many attackers, and withdrew to the citadel, which later fell.

battle.significance: Part of the methodical reduction of the Dalmatian hill-forts in AD 9.

events.title: Siege of Andetrium and surrender of Bato
events.summary: Tiberius besieged the Daesitiate Bato in the rock fortress of Andetrium near Salona. Bato negotiated his own surrender; the garrison fought on and was stormed, ending the Great Illyrian Revolt.

battle.significance: Ended the most dangerous revolt of Augustus's reign.

events.title: Lex Papia Poppaea
events.summary: The consuls Marcus Papius Mutilus and Quintus Poppaeus Secundus, both themselves unmarried and childless as Dio wryly notes, carried a law revising the Augustan marriage legislation of 18 BC, refining the incentives for parenthood and the inheritance penalties for the unmarried and childless.

events.title: Tiberius dedicates the Temple of Concord
events.summary: On 16 January AD 10 Tiberius dedicated the rebuilt Temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol in his own name and that of his dead brother Drusus, paid for from German spoils.

events.title: Senatus consultum Silanianum
events.summary: A decree of the Senate of AD 10 provided that if a master was murdered at home, all the slaves under the same roof were to be tortured and executed, a rule applied with full rigour in the Pedanius Secundus case of AD 61.

events.title: Tiberius and Germanicus restore the Rhine frontier
events.summary: After the Varian disaster Tiberius took command on the Rhine (AD 10-12), raised the garrison to eight legions and made cautious incursions across the river with Germanicus, avoiding battle and taking no unnecessary risks.

events.title: Tiberius's Pannonian and Dalmatian triumph
events.summary: Tiberius celebrated his postponed triumph over the Pannonians and Dalmatians; before mounting the Capitol he dismounted and knelt before Augustus. He spared the rebel leader Bato and gave him a residence at Ravenna.

events.title: Death of Augustus
events.summary: Augustus died at Nola, in the room where his father had died, aged 75, after a journey to Campania and Beneventum with Tiberius. Suetonius gives his last words to friends as asking whether he had played the comedy of life well, and to Livia: 'Livia, live mindful of our marriage, and farewell.'

events.title: Mutinies of the Pannonian and German legions
events.summary: On news of Augustus's death the three Pannonian legions and the four legions of the lower Rhine mutinied, demanding service limited to 16 years, a denarius a day in pay and discharge bonuses in cash in camp. Drusus quelled the Pannonian mutiny, Germanicus the German one.
events.locName: Ara Ubiorum (Cologne) and Pannonian summer camp

events.title: Deification of Augustus
events.summary: The Senate voted Augustus divine honours as Divus Augustus, with a temple, priests and a new sodality of the sodales Augustales; Livia became his priestess and was adopted into the Julian family as Julia Augusta.

events.title: Accession of Tiberius
events.summary: Already holding tribunician power and proconsular imperium, Tiberius gave the watchword to the praetorians at once on Augustus's death, but in the Senate staged a long show of reluctance before accepting the position, likening it to holding a wolf by the ears.

events.title: Lunar eclipse ends the Pannonian mutiny
events.summary: During the mutiny of the three Pannonian legions in September AD 14, a total lunar eclipse on the night of 26/27 September terrified the soldiers, who banged bronze and blew trumpets to help the moon, and Drusus's agents used their fear to break the revolt.
events.locName: summer camp of the Pannonian legions

events.title: Germanicus's massacre of the Marsi
events.summary: To channel the guilt of the mutiny, Germanicus led 12,000 legionaries, 26 auxiliary cohorts and 8 alae across the Rhine and fell on the Marsi during a nocturnal festival, killing without distinction of age or sex over fifty miles and razing their most famous shrine, of the goddess Tanfana.
events.locName: Territory of the Marsi, between Lippe and Ruhr

battle.significance: First act of the campaigns of revenge for Varus.

events.title: Res Gestae Divi Augusti
events.summary: Augustus's own account of his achievements, completed in his 76th year and deposited with his will at the house of the Vestal Virgins, was inscribed on bronze pillars before his Mausoleum. Copies survive at Ancyra (Latin and Greek), Apollonia and Antioch in Pisidia.
events.locName: Temple of Rome and Augustus, Ancyra (best surviving copy)

events.title: Murder of Agrippa Postumus
events.summary: Augustus's last surviving grandson was killed on Planasia by a centurion immediately after Augustus's death: 'the first crime of the new principate', in Tacitus's phrase. Tiberius denied responsibility; the order may have come from Augustus, Livia or Sallustius Crispus.

events.title: Elections transferred from the people to the Senate
events.summary: In the first year of Tiberius the election of magistrates passed effectively from the popular assemblies to the Senate, which drew up lists that the comitia merely ratified. Tacitus says the people, apart from idle murmurs, did not complain.

events.title: Augustus's last census: 4,937,000 citizens
events.summary: Augustus and Tiberius completed a census and lustrum in AD 14, registering 4,937,000 citizens, just before Augustus left Rome for the last time; a snake was seen in the Campus Martius during the closing ceremony, read later as an omen of his death.

events.title: Battle of Pontes Longi
events.summary: Returning from the Varian battlefield across the causeways called 'long bridges' through the moors, Caecina's four legions were caught by Arminius in a marsh and nearly suffered Varus's fate; they were saved when the Germans, against Arminius's advice, assaulted the fortified camp and were routed by a sally.
events.locName: Pontes longi, moors between Ems and Rhine

battle.significance: A narrow escape that revealed the vulnerability of Roman columns in the north German plain.

events.title: Germanicus buries the dead of the Varian disaster
events.summary: In summer AD 15 Germanicus reached the site of Varus's defeat, where Caecina had gone ahead to bridge the marshes, and buried the bones of the three legions six years after the battle, laying the first turf of the tumulus himself.

events.title: Recovery of the eagles lost with Varus
events.summary: Of the three eagles lost in AD 9, Lucius Stertinius recovered that of the XIX legion from the Bructeri in AD 15, Germanicus's forces took a second from the Marsi in AD 16 after a traitor revealed where it was buried, and Publius Gabinius Secundus took the third from the Chauci in AD 41, earning the cognomen Chaucius.

events.title: Tiber flood and the first curators of the riverbed
events.summary: A great flood in AD 15 led Tiberius to appoint a permanent five-man board of senators, the curatores riparum et alvei Tiberis, and the Senate debated diverting tributaries such as the Chiana and Nar; the towns of the upper valley protested and nothing was done.

events.title: Battle of Idistaviso
events.summary: On a plain called Idistaviso between the Weser and the hills, Germanicus's eight legions and auxiliaries crushed Arminius's Cherusci in a set-piece battle; the Germans were driven into the river and forest and slaughtered over ten miles.
events.locName: Idistaviso, on the Weser near Minden or Rinteln

sides.strength: 8 legions with auxiliaries, Batavian cavalry and archers: c. 70,000

battle.significance: Avenged Varus in the field but did not destroy Arminius's power.

events.title: Battle of the Angrivarian Wall
events.summary: Weeks after Idistaviso, the Germans made a stand behind the boundary earthwork between the Angrivarii and Cherusci; Germanicus stormed it with slingers and artillery, fought bareheaded so as to be recognised, and ordered that no prisoners be taken.

battle.significance: Last major Roman battle in free Germany for two centuries before Maximinus Thrax's campaign (the Harzhorn, c. 235).

events.title: Trial of Libo Drusus
events.summary: Marcus Scribonius Libo Drusus, a young noble related to Pompey and the Julii, was accused of plotting revolution on the evidence of consultations with astrologers, magicians and dream-interpreters; he committed suicide during the trial, and his estate was divided among the accusers.

events.title: Clemens, the false Agrippa Postumus
events.summary: Clemens, a slave of the murdered Agrippa Postumus, sailed to Cosa intending to rescue his master, and on finding him dead impersonated him, gathering a large following in Italy and Gaul in AD 16 until Tiberius had him kidnapped by agents and secretly executed.

events.title: Storm wrecks Germanicus's fleet in the North Sea
events.summary: Returning from the campaign of AD 16 by the Ems, Germanicus's fleet of a thousand ships was scattered by a storm; many ships were lost, horses and baggage thrown overboard, and some vessels driven to Britain, whose rulers sent back the men.
events.locName: North Sea off the Ems estuary

events.title: Triumph of Germanicus
events.summary: Germanicus triumphed over the Cherusci, Chatti, Angrivarii and other peoples as far as the Elbe, with his five children in the chariot. Among the captives was Thusnelda, Arminius's wife, with their three-year-old son Thumelicus, born in captivity.

events.title: Annexation of Cappadocia and Commagene
events.summary: King Archelaus of Cappadocia, summoned to Rome and accused before the Senate, died there; Tiberius annexed his kingdom under an equestrian procurator. Commagene, after the death of Antiochus III, was attached to Syria in the same year.

events.title: Great earthquake in Asia
events.summary: In one night an earthquake destroyed twelve cities of Asia, Sardis worst of all. Tiberius gave Sardis 10 million sesterces and remitted the tribute of the affected cities for five years.

events.title: Tiberius halves the sales tax; fortunes of the Augustan taxes
events.summary: In AD 17, using the new revenues of Cappadocia, Tiberius halved the 1% sales tax (centesima rerum venalium) that Augustus had imposed alongside the 5% inheritance tax to fund veteran bounties, the first direct burdens on Roman citizens in Italy since 167 BC.

events.title: Furius Camillus defeats Tacfarinas
events.summary: In AD 17 the proconsul Marcus Furius Camillus, with a single legion and auxiliaries, defeated Tacfarinas, a deserter from the Roman auxilia who had organised the Musulamii and Moors on Roman lines, and received the triumphal ornaments.

battle.significance: First Roman success against Tacfarinas; triumphal ornaments.

events.title: Germanicus in the East and his visit to Egypt
events.summary: Germanicus crowned Zeno, son of Polemon of Pontus, as Artaxias III of Armenia at Artaxata in 18, organised Cappadocia and Commagene, and in early 19 toured Egypt, sailing up the Nile to Thebes and Syene, without the emperor's permission that Augustus required of senators.

events.title: Strabo completes his Geography
events.summary: Strabo of Amaseia, a Greek from a Pontic family loyal to Rome, completed his 17-book Geography, the fullest surviving description of the Augustan world, in the early years of Tiberius (after AD 18 and before c. 23).

events.title: Germanicus crowns Artaxias III of Armenia
events.summary: In AD 18 Germanicus crowned Zeno, son of Polemon I of Pontus, as king of Armenia at Artaxata under the name Artaxias, to the acclaim of the Armenian nobles who liked his native habits of hunting and feasting.

events.title: Death of Germanicus
events.summary: Germanicus died at Epidaphne near Antioch, aged 33, convinced that Piso and Plancina had poisoned him. Remains of human bodies, spells and lead tablets inscribed with his name were found hidden in his house.

events.title: Senatorial honours for Germanicus (Tabula Siarensis and Tabula Hebana)
events.summary: The Senate decreed posthumous honours for Germanicus in December 19, including marble arches in the Circus Flaminius, on the Rhine near Drusus's cenotaph at Mainz, and on Mount Amanus in Syria. Bronze copies found in Spain (Tabula Siarensis, 1982) and Etruria (Tabula Hebana, 1947) preserve the decree and the resulting law.

events.title: Expulsion of Jews and worshippers of Isis from Rome
events.summary: A senatus consultum banished Egyptian and Jewish rites from Rome; 4,000 freedmen 'tainted with that superstition' were drafted to Sardinia to fight bandits, and the rest ordered to leave Italy unless they renounced their rites.

events.title: Rhescuporis murders Cotys of Thrace
events.summary: After the death of Rhoemetalces I (AD 12) Augustus divided Thrace between his brother Rhescuporis and his son Cotys; in 19 Rhescuporis seized Cotys at a banquet and murdered him, was lured to Rome by Pomponius Flaccus, tried before the Senate and exiled to Alexandria, where he was killed.

events.title: Fall of Maroboduus
events.summary: Weakened by his defeat by Arminius in AD 17, Maroboduus was driven out in 19 by Catualda, a Gothonian noble with Roman encouragement; he crossed into Noricum and lived for eighteen years as a pensioner in Ravenna, dying in 37.

events.title: Lex Junia Norbana and the Junian Latins
events.summary: The Lex Junia, probably the consular law of Marcus Junius Silanus and Lucius Norbanus Balbus in AD 19, gave slaves freed informally the status of Latini Iuniani: free during life but unable to make a will, so that their property reverted to their former master on death.

events.title: Herod Antipas founds Tiberias
events.summary: Around AD 19 the tetrarch Herod Antipas built Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee as his new capital in honour of the emperor, settling it partly by compulsion, because the site lay over tombs and was ritually impure.

events.title: Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls at Lugdunum
events.summary: In AD 19 Gaius Julius Rufus, priest of Rome and Augustus at the Altar of the Three Gauls, built the amphitheatre beside the federal sanctuary at Condate, as its dedicatory inscription records.

events.title: Trial of Piso and the Senatus Consultum de Cn. Pisone patre
events.summary: Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso, accused of poisoning Germanicus and of attempting to retake his province by force after being dismissed, was tried before the Senate and killed himself before the verdict. The Senate's resulting decree, dated 10 December 20, survives in several bronze copies from Baetica.
events.locName: Rome (copies found at El Tejar, Seville)

events.title: Apronius decimates a cohort; Helvius wins the civic crown
events.summary: When a cohort fled before Tacfarinas in AD 20, the proconsul Lucius Apronius revived the old punishment of decimation, clubbing every tenth man to death; soon after, a detachment of 500 veterans routed Tacfarinas at Thala, where the common soldier Helvius Rufus won the corona civica.

battle.significance: Revived decimation and the civic crown of Helvius Rufus.

events.title: Revolt of Florus and Sacrovir; battle near Augustodunum
events.summary: Indebted Gallic notables rose under the Treveran Julius Florus and the Aeduan Julius Sacrovir, both Roman citizens. Florus was defeated in the Ardennes by a fellow-Treveran; Sacrovir seized Augustodunum and its schools of noble youths, but his army was crushed by Gaius Silius twelve miles from the city.

sides.strength: 2 legions of upper Germany with auxiliaries

battle.significance: The last significant revolt in central Gaul until 68-70.

events.title: Death of Arminius
events.summary: Arminius, after defeating his rival Maroboduus in 17 and seeing him expelled to Roman exile, was killed by his own kinsmen for aspiring to kingship, aged 37, after twelve years of power.

events.title: Senate decrees a ten-day interval before executions
events.summary: After the knight Clutorius Priscus was condemned and executed on the same day in AD 21 for composing a poem anticipating the death of Drusus, Tiberius had the Senate decree that its sentences should not be registered at the treasury, and so executed, for ten days.

events.title: Junius Blaesus's campaign against Tacfarinas
events.summary: When Tacfarinas demanded land and threatened endless war, Tiberius sent Quintus Junius Blaesus, Sejanus's uncle, who in AD 22-23 broke the revolt into small mobile columns and kept his troops in winter forts, capturing Tacfarinas's brother.

events.title: Drusus the Younger receives tribunician power
events.summary: In AD 22 Tiberius asked the Senate to give his son Drusus the tribunician power, the "title of the highest rank", marking him unmistakably as heir.

events.title: Death of Drusus the Younger
events.summary: Tiberius's only son and designated successor, who had held the tribunician power since 22, died apparently of illness. Eight years later Sejanus's divorced wife Apicata revealed that Drusus had been poisoned by Sejanus and Drusus's wife Livilla, using the eunuch Lygdus.

events.title: Sejanus concentrates the praetorians in the Castra Praetoria
events.summary: The praetorian prefect Lucius Aelius Sejanus brought the praetorian cohorts, previously billeted in and around Rome, into a single fortified camp on the north-eastern edge of the city, making them a concentrated political force.

events.title: Battle of Auzea and death of Tacfarinas
events.summary: Publius Cornelius Dolabella, with help from king Ptolemy of Mauretania, located Tacfarinas's camp beside the half-ruined fort of Auzea, surrounded it with light columns and attacked at dawn, killing Tacfarinas, who threw himself on the Roman weapons, and ending the seven-year war.

sides.strength: Legio III Augusta, auxiliaries and Mauretanian cavalry

battle.significance: Ended the longest guerrilla war of Tiberius's reign.

events.title: Trial of Cremutius Cordus
events.summary: The historian Aulus Cremutius Cordus was prosecuted by clients of Sejanus for having praised Brutus and called Cassius 'the last of the Romans' in his histories. After a defiant speech he starved himself to death, and the Senate ordered his books burned.

events.title: Revolt of the Thracian hill tribes
events.summary: Thracian mountain peoples, refusing to supply recruits to Roman units and serve far from home, rebelled against the client king Rhoemetalces II; Gaius Poppaeus Sabinus, governor of Moesia, blockaded them in a fortress on the Haemus until thirst and disease forced surrender.

events.title: Tiberius withdraws from Rome to Capri
events.summary: Tiberius left Rome for Campania in 26 and in 27 settled on Capri, never to return to the city; he governed by letter, leaving Sejanus as the indispensable intermediary.

events.title: Smyrna wins the provincial temple of Tiberius
events.summary: In AD 26 eleven cities of Asia competed before the Senate for the honour of building a temple to Tiberius, Livia and the Senate voted in 23; the Senate chose Smyrna after hearing delegates cite their ancient loyalty, while Tiberius declined a similar request from Hispania Ulterior in 25.

events.title: Pilate brings the standards into Jerusalem
events.summary: Soon after his arrival as prefect of Judaea (26), Pontius Pilate sent troops into Jerusalem by night with standards bearing the emperor's image; crowds besieged him at Caesarea for five days and bared their necks to his soldiers rather than accept them, and Pilate withdrew the standards.

events.title: Collapse of the amphitheatre at Fidenae
events.summary: A wooden amphitheatre built on poor foundations by a freedman named Atilius, to profit from gladiatorial shows, collapsed at Fidenae near Rome during a crowded spectacle. Tacitus gives 50,000 killed or injured, Suetonius 20,000 killed.

events.title: Fire on the Caelian Hill
events.summary: A fire in AD 27, soon after the Fidenae disaster, burned the Caelian Hill; Tiberius compensated owners, and a statue of him in the house of the senator Junius that survived was hailed as a sign of divine favour, so that the Senate proposed renaming the hill Mons Augustus.

events.title: Revolt of the Frisii and battle of Baduhenna Wood
events.summary: The Frisii, whose tribute of ox-hides had been arbitrarily redefined by the primipilaris Olennius as hides of aurochs size, hanged the Roman soldiers collecting it and besieged the fort of Flevum. In the relief operations under Lucius Apronius, 900 Romans were cut down in the sacred wood of Baduhenna.

sides.strength: Vexillations of the lower German legions and auxiliaries
sides.losses: c. 1,300 (900 in the wood, 400 at Cruptorix's villa)

battle.significance: Showed the cost of arbitrary tribute and the weakness of Rome's hold beyond the Rhine delta.

events.title: Public ministry of Jesus in Galilee and Judaea
events.summary: After his baptism by John, Jesus of Nazareth preached the coming kingdom of God, mainly in the Galilean villages around Capernaum, gathered twelve disciples and acquired a reputation as healer and exorcist, over a period of one to three years ending with his execution at Jerusalem c. 30 or 33.
events.locName: Capernaum and the Sea of Galilee

events.title: Death of Livia
events.summary: Livia (Julia Augusta) died aged 86. Tiberius did not attend the funeral, vetoed her deification and ignored her will; her great-grandson Gaius (Caligula), aged 17, delivered the eulogy.

events.title: Destruction of Agrippina the Elder and her sons
events.summary: A letter from Tiberius denounced Agrippina and her eldest son Nero Caesar; she was exiled to Pandateria and he to Pontia, where he died in 31. Her second son Drusus Caesar was imprisoned in the palace and starved to death in 33; Agrippina starved herself on 18 October 33, two years to the day after Sejanus's fall.

events.title: Pilate's aqueduct and the massacre of protesters
events.summary: Pilate used the Temple treasury (the korban) to build an aqueduct to Jerusalem; when crowds protested during one of his visits, he had soldiers in civilian dress mingle with them and beat them with clubs, killing many.

events.title: Execution of John the Baptist
events.summary: Herod Antipas imprisoned the popular preacher John the Baptist at Machaerus and executed him, probably c. 28-30; Josephus says Antipas feared he would raise a revolt, while the gospels blame John's condemnation of Antipas's marriage to Herodias.

events.title: Crucifixion of Jesus of Nazareth
events.summary: Jesus of Nazareth, a Galilean Jewish preacher and healer, was crucified in Jerusalem around Passover on the order of the prefect Pontius Pilate. Tacitus, the only pagan author to mention it explicitly, records that 'Christus, the author of the name, was executed by the procurator Pontius Pilatus in the reign of Tiberius'.

events.title: Velleius Paterculus publishes his history
events.summary: In AD 30 Velleius Paterculus, an equestrian officer who had served under Tiberius in Germany and Pannonia, dedicated a two-book summary of Roman history to Marcus Vinicius, consul that year.

events.title: Arrest of Asinius Gallus
events.summary: In AD 30 Gaius Asinius Gallus, son of Asinius Pollio and husband of Tiberius's first wife Vipsania, was condemned in absentia while dining as Tiberius's guest on Capri, and kept in solitary confinement for three years until he starved to death in 33.

events.title: Fall of Sejanus
events.summary: At the height of his power, consul with Tiberius and betrothed into the imperial family, Sejanus was destroyed by a long letter from Capri read to the Senate. The new praetorian prefect Macro had secured the guard, and Sejanus was executed the same day and his body thrown down the Gemonian stairs.

events.title: Valerius Maximus publishes Memorable Deeds and Sayings
events.summary: About AD 31 Valerius Maximus dedicated to Tiberius nine books of Memorable Deeds and Sayings, nearly a thousand moral exempla arranged by theme, Roman and foreign, for use by orators.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Bel at Palmyra
events.summary: The great Temple of Bel at Palmyra was dedicated on 6 Nisan (April) AD 32, according to a bilingual dedication, marking the city's rise as the hinge of caravan trade between Roman Syria and the Parthian Euphrates.

events.title: Credit crisis of AD 33
events.summary: Prosecutions under a neglected Caesarian law requiring creditors to invest a share of their capital in Italian land triggered a scramble to call in loans, a collapse of land prices and a liquidity crisis in Rome. Tiberius made 100 million sesterces available through banks as three-year interest-free loans secured on land worth double.

events.title: The phoenix reported in Egypt
events.summary: Tacitus records that in the consulship of Paullus Fabius and Lucius Vitellius (AD 34) the phoenix appeared in Egypt after a long interval, prompting learned debate about the length of its cycle (500 or 1,461 years).

events.title: Conversion of Paul on the road to Damascus
events.summary: Saul of Tarsus, a Pharisee who had persecuted the followers of Jesus, experienced a vision of the risen Christ near Damascus around AD 33-36, and became the most important missionary of the early movement.

events.title: Martyrdom of Stephen
events.summary: Stephen, a leader of the Greek-speaking ("Hellenist") followers of Jesus in Jerusalem, was stoned after a speech attacking the Temple, around AD 34; Acts presents Saul as approving witness.

events.title: Tiberius's Armenian and Parthian intervention
events.summary: When Artabanus II put his son Arsaces on the Armenian throne in 35, Tiberius sent the Arsacid hostage Tiridates III to claim Parthia and backed Mithridates, brother of Pharasmanes I of Iberia, for Armenia; Iberian and Alan forces took Artaxata and defeated the Parthians while Lucius Vitellius advanced from Syria.

events.title: Fire on the Aventine and around the Circus
events.summary: In AD 36 a fire destroyed the part of the Circus Maximus next to the Aventine and the buildings on the hill; Tiberius paid owners 100 million sesterces, and four men married to his granddaughters assessed claims.

events.title: Aretas IV destroys the army of Herod Antipas
events.summary: Aretas IV of Nabataea, whose daughter Antipas had divorced to marry Herodias, and who disputed the border district of Gamalitis, destroyed Antipas's army c. 36; Tiberius ordered Vitellius to take Aretas dead or alive, but the campaign was abandoned on news of Tiberius's death.

battle.significance: Humiliation of Antipas; Roman punitive expedition aborted.

events.title: Pilate removed after the Samaritan massacre
events.summary: In 36 Pilate's cavalry and infantry attacked an armed crowd of Samaritans who had gathered at Tirathana to follow a prophet up Mount Gerizim to find sacred vessels buried by Moses; the Samaritan council complained to Vitellius, legate of Syria, who sent Pilate to Rome to answer to Tiberius.

events.title: Death of Tiberius
events.summary: Tiberius died at the villa of Lucullus at Misenum, aged 77. Tacitus reports that when he unexpectedly revived after being thought dead, Macro had him smothered with bedclothes; Suetonius gives versions blaming Caligula.

events.title: Accession of Gaius (Caligula)
events.summary: The Senate conferred all the powers of the principate on the 24-year-old Gaius in a single session, setting aside Tiberius's will that had made Gemellus co-heir. He entered Rome on 28 March to wild popular enthusiasm as the son of Germanicus.

events.title: Caligula's illness and the first purges
events.summary: In October 37 Gaius fell gravely ill; after recovering he forced Tiberius Gemellus to kill himself, then destroyed his father-in-law Marcus Junius Silanus and Macro, the prefect who had helped him to power.

events.title: Vitellius and Artabanus meet on the Euphrates
events.summary: Lucius Vitellius and Artabanus II met on a bridge over the Euphrates in 36/37, settling the Armenian conflict; Artabanus paid homage to the images of the emperor and sent his son Darius as a hostage to Rome.

events.title: Caligula dedicates the Temple of Divus Augustus
events.summary: The temple of the deified Augustus, begun by Tiberius and Livia, was dedicated by Caligula in 37 with two days of races and the slaughter of 400 bears and 400 African beasts.
events.locName: between the Palatine and the Forum (site not located)

events.title: Caligula makes Agrippa I a king
events.summary: On his accession in 37 Caligula freed his friend Agrippa, grandson of Herod, imprisoned by Tiberius for wishing aloud for Gaius's succession, gave him a gold chain equal in weight to his iron one and made him king of the former tetrarchy of Philip (Batanaea, Trachonitis, Gaulanitis).
events.locName: Caesarea Philippi and the tetrarchy of Philip

events.title: Caligula brings the Vatican obelisk to Rome
events.summary: Caligula had an uninscribed 25 m obelisk shipped from the Forum Iulium at Alexandria in a giant ship and set up on the spina of his private circus in the Vatican gardens.
events.locName: Circus of Gaius and Nero, Vatican

events.title: Death and deification of Drusilla
events.summary: Gaius's favourite sister Julia Drusilla died; on 23 September 38 the Senate consecrated her as Diva Drusilla, the first Roman woman to be deified.

events.title: Anti-Jewish riots in Alexandria
events.summary: After the Jewish king Agrippa I passed through Alexandria and was mocked by a Greek mob dressing up a madman named Carabas as a king, the prefect Avillius Flaccus allowed images of the emperor to be placed in synagogues, declared Jews foreigners and confined them to one quarter, where many were killed.

events.title: Caligula's popular measures: elections, accounts and tax relief
events.summary: In his first year Caligula published the imperial accounts as Augustus had done, restored elections to the popular assemblies, abolished the 0.5% sales tax in Italy, recalled exiles and allowed the banned works of Cremutius Cordus, Labienus and Cassius Severus to circulate.

events.title: Caligula's reshuffle of eastern client kingdoms
events.summary: In 38 Caligula restored Commagene, a province since 17, to Antiochus IV with a hundred million sesterces of back revenue, gave Pontus to Polemon II, Lesser Armenia to Cotys and part of Thrace to Rhoemetalces III, the sons of Antonia Tryphaena who had been raised with him.

events.title: Conspiracy of Gaetulicus and Lepidus
events.summary: Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Gaetulicus, commander of upper Germany for ten years, and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, Drusilla's widower, were executed for an alleged plot; Gaius's sisters Agrippina and Livilla were exiled, Agrippina made to carry Lepidus's ashes to Rome.

events.title: Caligula's German and British expedition
events.summary: Gaius spent the winter of 39/40 on the Rhine and the Channel coast, staged punitive raids across the Rhine, accepted the surrender of the British prince Adminius, and, according to Suetonius, ordered his troops drawn up on the shore to gather seashells as 'spoils of the Ocean'.

events.title: Exile of Herod Antipas
events.summary: Urged by Herodias to seek the royal title granted to her brother Agrippa, Antipas sailed to Caligula in 39, but Agrippa's letters accused him of conspiring with Sejanus and Artabanus and of storing arms for 70,000 men; Caligula exiled him to Gaul and gave his tetrarchy to Agrippa.

events.title: Philo leads the Alexandrian Jewish embassy to Caligula
events.summary: After the riots of 38 the Jews of Alexandria sent five envoys led by the philosopher Philo to Caligula, while the Greeks sent Apion and Isidorus; the emperor received them in 40 while inspecting the Esquiline gardens, mocked them for not eating pork and dismissed them as "unfortunate rather than wicked" for not believing him a god.
events.locName: Rome and Puteoli; audience in the Gardens of Maecenas and Lamia

events.title: Caligula's bridge of boats from Baiae to Puteoli
events.summary: In 39 Caligula built a 3.6-mile pontoon bridge of merchant ships across the bay from Baiae to the mole of Puteoli, paved like the Appian Way, and rode across it in Alexander's breastplate on two successive days.

events.title: Caligula separates the African legion from the proconsul
events.summary: In 39 Caligula, distrusting the proconsul of Africa Lucius Calpurnius Piso, gave command of the legion III Augusta to an imperial legate, ending the last case of a senatorial proconsul commanding a legion.

events.title: Murder of Ptolemy and annexation of Mauretania
events.summary: Gaius summoned his cousin Ptolemy, king of Mauretania and grandson of Antony and Cleopatra, and had him killed, allegedly because his purple cloak drew admiration at the games or because of his wealth. The kingdom was annexed, provoking a revolt led by Ptolemy's freedman Aedemon.

events.title: Caligula's statue for the Jerusalem Temple
events.summary: After Jews of Jamnia tore down an altar erected to the emperor by local Greeks, Gaius ordered the legate of Syria, Publius Petronius, to install a colossal statue of himself as Zeus in the Temple of Jerusalem. Petronius delayed in the face of mass non-violent protest; Agrippa I interceded; Gaius's death ended the crisis.

events.title: Caligula's ships on Lake Nemi
events.summary: Caligula had two enormous ships, about 70 and 73 m long, built on the small volcanic lake of Nemi beside the sanctuary of Diana, floating palaces with marble floors, bronze fittings, lead pipes and possibly a shrine.

events.title: Assassination of Caligula
events.summary: During the Palatine Games, Gaius was stabbed to death in a covered passage of the palace by the praetorian tribune Cassius Chaerea, whom he had repeatedly mocked with obscene watchwords, together with Cornelius Sabinus and other officers. His wife Caesonia and infant daughter were killed soon after.

events.title: Accession of Claudius
events.summary: Found hiding in the palace after Caligula's murder, the 50-year-old Claudius was taken to the praetorian camp and acclaimed emperor, while the Senate debated restoring the Republic. He promised each praetorian 15,000 sesterces, the first emperor, as Suetonius says, to buy the soldiers' loyalty.

events.title: Claudius's letter to the Alexandrians
events.summary: A papyrus copy (P.Lond. VI 1912), published by the prefect Lucius Aemilius Rectus on 10 November 41, preserves Claudius's reply to Alexandrian embassies: he declines a temple and high priest for himself, and orders Greeks to stop molesting Jews and Jews not to seek more privileges or bring in co-religionists from Syria and Egypt.

events.title: Seneca relegated to Corsica
events.summary: In 41 Messalina procured the condemnation of Caligula's sister Julia Livilla for adultery with Seneca; Livilla was exiled and killed, and Seneca spent eight years relegated on Corsica until Agrippina recalled him in 49 to tutor Nero.

events.title: Revolt of Aedemon and the conquest of Mauretania
events.summary: After Caligula's murder of king Ptolemy (40), the royal freedman Aedemon raised Mauretania in revolt; Roman forces needed until 42-44 to suppress it, after which Claudius organised the kingdom as two procuratorial provinces, Caesariensis and Tingitana.

events.title: Revolt of Scribonianus in Dalmatia
events.summary: Lucius Arruntius Camillus Scribonianus, legate of Dalmatia, wrote to Claudius ordering him to abdicate; within five days his two legions, VII and XI, deserted him when their eagles could not be decorated or pulled from the ground, and he was killed.

events.title: Claudius begins the harbour of Portus
events.summary: To secure Rome's grain supply, Claudius began an artificial harbour two miles north of Ostia, with two curving moles and a lighthouse built on the sunken hull of the giant ship that had brought Caligula's Vatican obelisk from Egypt.

events.title: Suetonius Paullinus crosses the Atlas
events.summary: In 42 Gaius Suetonius Paullinus, as legate in Mauretania, became the first Roman commander to cross the Atlas, marching ten days beyond the range to the river Ger through black dust deserts and forests full of elephants and snakes.

events.title: Battle of the Medway
events.summary: A two-day battle at a river crossing, generally identified with the Medway, in which Plautius's army defeated the British forces of Togodumnus and Caratacus. 'Celtic' auxiliaries (probably Batavians) swam the river in full armour and maimed the chariot horses, while Vespasian and his brother Sabinus forced a crossing.

battle.significance: Opened south-east Britain to Roman conquest.

events.title: Claudius in Britain; fall of Camulodunum
events.summary: Summoned by Plautius, Claudius crossed to Britain with praetorians and elephants, led the advance on the Catuvellaunian capital Camulodunum and received the submission of British kings, staying only sixteen days.

events.title: Claudian invasion of Britain
events.summary: Aulus Plautius led four legions and auxiliaries across the Channel to Britain, ostensibly to restore the exiled Atrebatic king Verica. After a mutiny of troops reluctant to cross the Ocean, the army sailed in three divisions and landed unopposed.

events.title: Annexation of Lycia
events.summary: After civic strife in which Romans were killed, Claudius ended the freedom of the Lycian League and made Lycia a province, later joined with Pamphylia.

events.title: Death of Agrippa I; Judaea returns to procurators
events.summary: Herod Agrippa I, whom Claudius had made king of all his grandfather Herod's territory in 41, collapsed during games at Caesarea after being hailed as a god and died days later. Judaea reverted to direct Roman rule under procurators, beginning with Cuspius Fadus.

events.title: Storming of Maiden Castle
events.summary: The great Durotrigan hillfort in Dorset is traditionally identified as one of the more than twenty oppida taken by Vespasian and legio II Augusta. Mortimer Wheeler's excavations of 1934-37 found a 'war cemetery' of about 38 burials at the east gate, including a skeleton with an iron ballista bolt in its spine.

sides.losses: unknown; perhaps a few dozen dead

battle.significance: Iconic, though archaeologically overstated, image of the Roman conquest of the south-west.

events.title: Agrippa I executes James son of Zebedee
events.summary: Shortly before his death in 44, Agrippa I had the apostle James, son of Zebedee, beheaded and imprisoned Peter, who escaped; Acts presents Agrippa's sudden death at Caesarea as divine punishment.

events.title: Claudius's British triumph
events.summary: Claudius celebrated his triumph over Britain in 44 after only sixteen days on the island, climbing the Capitoline steps on his knees; he took the name Britannicus for his infant son, and arches were voted at Rome and Gesoriacum.

events.title: Claudius announces in advance the eclipse of his birthday
events.summary: Expecting a solar eclipse on his birthday, 1 August 45, Claudius issued an edict in advance explaining its time, extent and causes so that it would not be taken as an evil omen.

events.title: The prophet Theudas killed by Fadus
events.summary: Under the procurator Cuspius Fadus (44-46) the prophet Theudas led a large crowd with their possessions to the Jordan, promising to part its waters; Fadus's cavalry killed many and Theudas's head was brought to Jerusalem.

events.title: Annexation of Thrace
events.summary: After the murder of the client king Rhoemetalces III, reportedly by his wife, Claudius annexed the Thracian kingdom as a province under an equestrian procurator, completing Roman control of the Balkans south of the Danube.

events.title: Famine in Judaea and the aid of Queen Helena of Adiabene
events.summary: During a severe famine in Judaea c. 46-48, Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism, bought grain in Egypt and figs in Cyprus for the people of Jerusalem, and her son King Izates sent money; Acts records famine relief sent from the Antioch church by Barnabas and Paul.

events.title: Paul and Barnabas's mission to Cyprus and Galatia
events.summary: Sent out by the church of Antioch c. 46-48, Paul and Barnabas preached in Cyprus, where Acts says they won over the proconsul Sergius Paullus, and in the cities of southern Galatia, establishing mixed communities of Jews and Gentiles.
events.locName: Cyprus, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe

events.title: Corbulo's operations against the Chauci and Frisii
events.summary: Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, legate of lower Germany, destroyed the Chaucian pirate fleet of the Cananefate deserter Gannascus, restored discipline, and imposed a Roman settlement on the Frisii. Claudius then ordered him to withdraw west of the Rhine.

events.title: Claudius's Secular Games for the 800th year of Rome
events.summary: In 47, while censor, Claudius celebrated Secular Games for Rome's 800th year by the Varronian count, only 64 years after Augustus's, and was mocked for inviting people to games no one had seen or would see again when many present had seen those of 17 BC.

events.title: Death of Valerius Asiaticus
events.summary: In 47 Messalina, coveting the Gardens of Lucullus, had the Narbonensian ex-consul Decimus Valerius Asiaticus, twice consul and a leader in the plot against Caligula, accused of adultery and of sedition among the troops; Claudius tried him in his bedchamber and he opened his veins.

events.title: Ostorius Scapula disarms the tribes; first Iceni revolt
events.summary: Arriving in 47, Publius Ostorius Scapula ordered the disarming of suspect tribes south of the Trent and Severn; the Iceni, allies until then, rose with their neighbours and were defeated storming an earthwork, where Ostorius's son won the civic crown.

events.title: Claudius adds three letters to the Latin alphabet
events.summary: As censor in 47 Claudius introduced three new letters: the inverted digamma (for consonantal u), the antisigma (for ps or bs) and a half H (for the sound between i and u, as in optumus/optimus).

events.title: Claudius's censorship and the Lyon Tablet speech
events.summary: As censor in 47-48, Claudius persuaded the Senate to admit leading men of Gallia Comata to senatorial office, beginning with the Aedui. His speech survives in his own words on a bronze tablet found at Lyon in 1528 and in Tacitus's rewritten version.

events.title: Fall of Messalina
events.summary: While Claudius was at Ostia, his wife Valeria Messalina publicly went through a marriage ceremony with the consul-designate Gaius Silius. The freedman Narcissus alerted the emperor, took temporary command of the praetorians and had Messalina killed in the Gardens of Lucullus.

events.title: Claudius marries his niece Agrippina
events.summary: After the Senate, prompted by Lucius Vitellius, passed a decree legalising marriage between a man and his brother's daughter, Claudius married Agrippina the Younger, daughter of Germanicus and mother of Lucius Domitius (the future Nero).

events.title: Claudius expels Jews from Rome 'impulsore Chresto'
events.summary: Suetonius reports that Claudius expelled from Rome the Jews 'who were continually rioting at the instigation of Chrestus', usually understood as conflict in the synagogues over Christian preaching about Christ. Acts 18.2 says the couple Aquila and Priscilla came to Corinth because of this edict.

events.title: Foundation of the colony of Camulodunum
events.summary: Publius Ostorius Scapula moved legio XX west and founded Colonia Claudia Victricensis at Camulodunum, the first chartered Roman town in Britain, as a veteran settlement and model of urban life, with a temple to the deified Claudius.

events.title: The apostolic council at Jerusalem
events.summary: Around 48-49 Paul and Barnabas met the leaders of the Jerusalem church, James, Peter and John, who agreed that Gentile converts need not be circumcised; Paul was to go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.

events.title: War in the Bosporus and the surrender of Mithridates
events.summary: When Mithridates VIII, deposed king of the Bosporus, tried to recover his throne from his brother Cotys I, Roman cohorts under Gaius Julius Aquila and allies of the Aorsi took the Dandarid town of Uspe in 49, massacring its inhabitants; Mithridates surrendered to the Aorsian king Eunones, who interceded for his life.

events.title: Claudius adopts Nero
events.summary: Under Agrippina's influence Claudius adopted her son Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, who became Nero Claudius Caesar Drusus Germanicus, giving him precedence over Claudius's own younger son Britannicus.

events.title: Paul in Philippi, Thessalonica and Corinth; 1 Thessalonians
events.summary: Around 49-51 Paul crossed to Macedonia, founding churches at Philippi and Thessalonica, and then spent eighteen months at Corinth, from where he wrote 1 Thessalonians, the earliest surviving Christian text, c. 50.

events.title: Caratacus's last battle
events.summary: Publius Ostorius Scapula stormed the hill position, defended by a stone rampart above a river, where Caratacus had made his stand among the Ordovices. Caratacus's wife, daughter and brothers were captured; he fled to Cartimandua of the Brigantes, who handed him over in chains.
events.locName: Hill site in Ordovician territory (Cefn Carnedd? Llanymynech?)

sides.strength: Legions with auxiliaries (XIV and XX likely)

battle.significance: Ended the resistance of Caratacus, the most famous British leader before Boudica.

events.title: Radamistus seizes Armenia
events.summary: In 51 Radamistus, son of Pharasmanes of Iberia, invaded Armenia, besieged his uncle Mithridates in the fortress of Gorneae, bribed the Roman prefect of the garrison and murdered Mithridates and his family after swearing not to harm him "by sword or poison"; the legate Ummidius Quadratus did nothing.

events.title: Famine of 51 and Claudius mobbed in the Forum
events.summary: In 51 Rome was said to have only fifteen days' grain left; Claudius was pelted with crusts in the Forum and had to escape by a back door, and he responded with incentives for shipowners who would sail in winter.

events.title: Caratacus pardoned by Claudius
events.summary: Handed over in chains by Cartimandua of the Brigantes after his defeat in 51, Caratacus was paraded with his family before the people and praetorians; his dignified speech won pardon for himself and his family from Claudius, and they also paid homage to Agrippina on her own tribunal.

events.title: Aqua Claudia and Anio Novus completed
events.summary: On 1 August 52 Claudius dedicated the two greatest aqueducts of Rome, begun by Caligula in 38: the Aqua Claudia (c. 69 km, from springs near Subiaco) and the Anio Novus (c. 87 km, from the Anio), carried together on a single arcade for the last stretch into the city.

events.title: Earliest military diplomas
events.summary: The earliest surviving military diploma, issued on 11 December 52 to a sailor of the Misene fleet, attests Claudius's practice of granting Roman citizenship and legal marriage (conubium) to non-citizen auxiliaries and sailors after 25 or more years' service.

events.title: Claudius's letter naming Gallio proconsul of Achaea
events.summary: A fragmentary letter of Claudius inscribed at Delphi, dated after his 26th imperatorial acclamation (52), names Lucius Junius Gallio, Seneca's brother, as proconsul of Achaea. Since Acts 18.12-17 says Paul was brought before Gallio at Corinth, the inscription is the single fixed point in Pauline chronology.

events.title: Opening of the Fucine Lake emissary
events.summary: After eleven years' work by 30,000 men, Claudius inaugurated a 5.6 km tunnel to drain the Fucine Lake into the Liris, staging first a naumachia with 19,000 condemned combatants, whose greeting 'Hail emperor, those about to die salute you' is reported by Suetonius.

events.title: Senatus consultum Claudianum
events.summary: A decree of 52, proposed by Claudius and drafted by his freedman Pallas, provided that a free woman who cohabited with another's slave against his master's will became, after three warnings, the master's slave herself, and her children slaves.

events.title: The Silures defeat a legion; death of Ostorius Scapula
events.summary: After Caratacus's capture the Silures continued the war, killing a camp prefect and eight centurions, routing foraging parties and defeating a legion under Manlius Valens; Ostorius Scapula died worn out by the struggle in 52, and his successor Aulus Didius Gallus found the province in turmoil.

sides.strength: legio II Augusta detachments under Manlius Valens

battle.significance: Showed that Caratacus's fall had not ended Welsh resistance.

events.title: Senate honours the freedman Pallas
events.summary: In 52 the Senate voted Claudius's financial secretary (a rationibus) Pallas the praetorian insignia and 15 million sesterces and inscribed its decree on bronze; he accepted only the honours, and his reputed fortune of 300 million made him a byword for freedman power.

events.title: Claudius frees sick slaves abandoned on the Tiber island
events.summary: Claudius decreed that slaves abandoned by their masters on the Tiber island, at the temple of Aesculapius, to avoid the cost of treating them should become free (as Junian Latins) if they recovered, and that masters who killed sick slaves rather than abandoning them were liable for murder.

events.title: Paul at Ephesus and the riot of the silversmiths
events.summary: Paul spent two to three years at Ephesus c. 52-55, writing letters to Corinth and probably Philippi and Philemon; Acts says his success caused the silversmith Demetrius, maker of silver shrines of Artemis, to raise a riot in which the crowd shouted "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians" in the theatre for two hours.

events.title: Seneca's Apocolocyntosis
events.summary: Soon after Claudius's death in October 54 Seneca, who had delivered Nero's laudation of the deified emperor, wrote the Apocolocyntosis ("Pumpkinification"), a Menippean satire in prose and verse in which Claudius is refused admission to Olympus and condemned to play dice with a bottomless box and serve as a clerk in the underworld.

events.title: Death of Claudius
events.summary: Claudius died aged 63, almost certainly poisoned by Agrippina with a dish of mushrooms prepared by the poisoner Locusta and served by the taster Halotus; when he vomited, the doctor Xenophon finished him with a poisoned feather.

events.title: Accession of Nero
