events.summary: The 16-year-old Nero was presented by the prefect Burrus to the praetorians, who hailed him emperor; the Senate followed. His first speech, written by Seneca, promised to end secret trials in the palace and the power of freedmen and to restore the Senate's functions.

events.title: Murder of Britannicus
events.summary: Claudius's son Britannicus, approaching his fourteenth birthday, collapsed at a family dinner after drinking a hot drink cooled with poisoned water, the taster having tested only the hot drink. Nero said it was an epileptic fit; he was buried that night.

events.title: Seneca's De Clementia addressed to Nero
events.summary: In 55-56, after Nero's eighteenth birthday, Seneca addressed On Clemency to the young emperor, presenting mercy as the virtue that distinguishes a king from a tyrant and openly calling the princeps a king whose power over life and death is absolute.

events.title: Arrest of Paul in Jerusalem and custody at Caesarea
events.summary: Bringing his collection for the poor to Jerusalem c. 57, Paul was attacked in the Temple on the charge of bringing a Gentile inside the sacred enclosure, rescued by the tribune Claudius Lysias and held for two years at Caesarea by the procurator Felix, who hoped for a bribe.

events.title: Corbulo takes Artaxata
events.summary: Advancing in three columns after storming the fortress of Volandum, Corbulo forced Tiridates to abandon Artaxata, the Armenian capital, which opened its gates; the inhabitants were spared but the city was razed because it could not be garrisoned.

sides.strength: Legions III Gallica and VI Ferrata with auxiliaries and allies

battle.significance: Drove the Parthian-backed king out of his capital.

events.title: Nero proposes to abolish indirect taxes
events.summary: In 58, after complaints about the tax-farmers, Nero proposed abolishing all indirect taxes (vectigalia) as a gift to mankind; senators persuaded him that the empire could not survive without them, and instead he ordered the regulations of each tax to be published and limited the publicani's powers.

events.title: Murder of Agrippina the Younger
events.summary: During the Quinquatria festival at Baiae, Nero tried to drown his mother in a collapsible boat designed by Anicetus, prefect of the Misenum fleet. She swam ashore; Nero then sent Anicetus with marines to kill her at her villa, where she bade them strike her womb.

events.title: Riot in the amphitheatre at Pompeii
events.summary: At gladiatorial games given by the expelled senator Livineius Regulus, abuse between Pompeians and visitors from neighbouring Nuceria escalated into a riot in which many Nucerians were killed or wounded. The Senate banned games at Pompeii for ten years and dissolved illegal associations.

events.title: Corbulo marches through Armenia to Tigranocerta
events.summary: After burning Artaxata in 58, Corbulo led his army in summer 59 across the parched uplands of Armenia to Tigranocerta, which opened its gates; he took the fortress of Legerda and in 60 installed Tigranes VI, a Cappadocian prince educated at Rome, as king.

events.title: Suetonius Paullinus's assault on Mona
events.summary: Suetonius Paullinus crossed the Menai Strait with infantry in flat-bottomed boats and cavalry fording or swimming, to attack Mona (Anglesey), refuge of fugitives and centre of Druidism. The soldiers, frozen by the sight of women in black with torches and Druids pouring curses, were urged on and slaughtered the defenders.

sides.strength: Legio XIV, part of XX and auxiliaries

battle.significance: Struck at the Druidic centre but left the province exposed to Boudica.

events.title: Boudica sacks Camulodunum
events.summary: On the death of Prasutagus, whose will named Nero co-heir with his daughters, Roman officials seized the Icenian kingdom, flogged his widow Boudica and raped their daughters. The Iceni and Trinovantes rose and stormed the unwalled colony of Camulodunum, whose last defenders held the Temple of Claudius for two days.

sides.strength: Iceni and Trinovantes in great numbers
Veterans, 200 men sent by the procurator; relieving force of legio IX
sides.losses: colony destroyed; IX Hispana's infantry (perhaps 2,000) killed

battle.significance: The worst Roman disaster in Britain, opening the road to Londinium.

events.title: Destruction of Londinium and Verulamium
events.summary: Suetonius Paullinus reached Londinium, already a busy trading town, but judged it indefensible and abandoned it; the rebels destroyed it and the municipium of Verulamium. Tacitus says 70,000 citizens and allies died in the three towns, killed by gibbet, fire and cross.

events.title: Defeat of Boudica
events.summary: Suetonius Paullinus, with legio XIV, detachments of XX and auxiliaries, almost 10,000 men, chose a defile with a forest behind and open plain before. The British host, with families watching from wagons, charged and was broken by javelin volleys and a wedge attack; the wagons blocked their flight.

battle.significance: Saved the province of Britain for Rome.

events.title: Nero founds the Neronia
events.summary: In 60 Nero instituted the Neronia, quinquennial Greek-style games in music, gymnastics and horsemanship, opening a gymnasium with free oil for senators and knights; at the second celebration (65) he performed on the lyre himself.

events.title: The comet of 60 and the fall of Rubellius Plautus
events.summary: A comet in 60, popularly believed to portend a change of ruler, led people to speculate about Rubellius Plautus, a great-grandson of Tiberius through his mother; Nero advised him to retire to his estates in Asia, where he was killed in 62.

events.title: Earthquake destroys Laodicea on the Lycus
events.summary: An earthquake in 60 destroyed Laodicea in the Lycus valley, which Tacitus says rebuilt itself from its own resources without help from Rome.

events.title: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea
events.summary: A Greek merchant's handbook of c. 40-70, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea describes ports, goods and rulers from Egypt's Red Sea harbours of Myos Hormos and Berenice along the African coast to Rhapta and across the Arabian Sea to the Indus, Barygaza, Muziris and the Ganges.
events.locName: Red Sea and Indian Ocean (Adulis, Muziris)

events.title: Paul's voyage, shipwreck on Malta and house arrest in Rome
events.summary: Sent to Rome under guard of the centurion Julius, Paul sailed in an Alexandrian grain ship that was wrecked on Malta after a fourteen-day storm, c. 59-60; after wintering there he reached Rome, where Acts leaves him living two years under house arrest, preaching openly.

events.title: Murder of Pedanius Secundus and execution of his 400 slaves
events.summary: The city prefect Lucius Pedanius Secundus was murdered by one of his slaves. Under the senatus consultum Silanianum all slaves under the same roof were liable to execution; despite popular riots and some senatorial opposition, all 400 were put to death.

events.title: The freedman Polyclitus investigates Britain
events.summary: After Boudica's defeat the procurator Julius Classicianus, at odds with Suetonius Paullinus's harsh reprisals, reported that there would be no end to the war under him; Nero sent his freedman Polyclitus with a large retinue to investigate, and Paullinus was soon replaced by the conciliatory Petronius Turpilianus.

events.title: Parthian siege of Tigranocerta and Corbulo's truce
events.summary: In 61 Vologases I sent Monaeses with cavalry and Adiabenian troops to besiege Tigranes VI in Tigranocerta; the Roman garrison held, and Corbulo's envoy secured a Parthian withdrawal and agreement that Tiridates's claim would be referred to Rome.

sides.strength: cavalry under Monaeses and Adiabenian troops

battle.significance: Siege raised; diplomacy resumed.

events.title: Earthquake in Campania
events.summary: A severe earthquake damaged Pompeii, Herculaneum and Nuceria on 5 February. Seneca says a flock of 600 sheep died, statues split, and people went mad. Many buildings in Pompeii were still under repair when Vesuvius erupted seventeen years later.

events.title: Hero of Alexandria and the eclipse of 62
events.summary: Hero of Alexandria's Dioptra uses a lunar eclipse observed at Alexandria and Rome to compute the distance between the cities; the eclipse has been identified as that of 13 March 62, dating Hero, author of the Pneumatica with its steam-driven aeolipile and coin-operated holy water dispenser, to the mid first century.

events.title: Nero's expedition to the sources of the Nile
events.summary: Around 61-63 Nero sent a party of praetorians under two centurions south through Meroë; Seneca says they reached immense marshes so choked with vegetation that only a single-man boat could pass, probably the Sudd of South Sudan.

events.title: Plautius Silvanus resettles 100,000 Transdanubians
events.summary: Tiberius Plautius Silvanus Aelianus, legate of Moesia under Nero, brought more than 100,000 people from across the Danube, with wives, children and chiefs, into the province as tribute-payers, checked a Sarmatian movement, relieved the siege of Chersonesus in the Crimea and sent grain to Rome.

events.title: Death of Burrus, retirement of Seneca and murder of Octavia
events.summary: In 62 the praetorian prefect Burrus died (perhaps poisoned), Seneca asked leave to retire and offered back his fortune, and Nero divorced Octavia on a charge of sterility, exiled her to Pandateria on a trumped-up charge of adultery and had her killed, to marry Poppaea Sabina.

events.title: Capitulation of Paetus at Rhandeia
events.summary: Lucius Caesennius Paetus, sent to annex Armenia outright, dispersed his forces and was besieged by Vologases at Rhandeia on the Arsanias. With Corbulo's relief army three days away, he capitulated, agreeing to evacuate Armenia and to build a bridge over the river for the Parthians.
events.locName: Rhandeia on the Arsanias (Murat), near Harput

sides.strength: Legions IV Scythica and XII Fulminata (understrength) with auxiliaries

battle.significance: Forced Rome to accept an Arsacid king of Armenia.

events.title: The customs law of Asia (Monumentum Ephesenum)
events.summary: A Greek inscription from Ephesus, discovered in 1976, preserves the customs law of the province of Asia as revised by a commission of three consulars in 62, with clauses going back to 75 BC.

events.title: Stoning of James the brother of Jesus
events.summary: In the interval between the death of the procurator Festus and the arrival of Albinus in 62, the High Priest Ananus son of Ananus convened the Sanhedrin and had James "the brother of Jesus called Christ" and others stoned; Agrippa II deposed Ananus after three months.

events.title: Corbulo and Tiridates agree the settlement of Rhandeia
events.summary: In 63, after Corbulo invaded Armenia again with four legions, Tiridates met him at Rhandeia, site of Paetus's surrender, and laid his diadem before a statue of Nero, agreeing to receive it back from Nero's own hands in Rome.

events.title: Annexation of the Cottian Alps
events.summary: On the death of king Cottius II, Nero converted his Alpine kingdom, centred on Segusio and the Mont Genevre pass, into a procuratorial province in 63, as he had annexed Pontus in 64.

events.title: Seneca's Moral Letters to Lucilius
events.summary: In retirement after 62 Seneca wrote 124 Moral Letters to his friend Lucilius, procurator of Sicily, together with the Natural Questions, the most influential body of Stoic writing in Latin.

events.title: Great Fire of Rome
events.summary: Fire broke out in the shops by the Circus Maximus on the night of 18/19 July and burned for six days, then flared again from Tigellinus's estates for three more. Of Rome's fourteen regions three were destroyed, seven badly damaged and four untouched.

events.title: Annexation of Pontus Polemoniacus
events.summary: With the consent of its king Polemon II, Nero annexed the Pontic kingdom on the Black Sea coast to the province of Galatia-Cappadocia; the Cottian Alps became a procuratorial province around the same time on the death of Cottius II.

events.title: Nero's punishment of the Christians
events.summary: To deflect blame for the fire, Nero punished 'those whom the crowd called Christians, hated for their abominations'. A huge number were convicted 'not so much of arson as of hatred of the human race', torn by dogs in animal skins, crucified, or burned as torches at night in Nero's gardens.

events.title: Nero's Golden House
events.summary: On land cleared by the fire Nero built the Domus Aurea, a palace-landscape stretching from the Palatine to the Esquiline, with a colossal bronze statue of himself 120 feet high, an artificial lake, vineyards and woods. On moving in he said he could at last live like a human being.

events.title: Nero's coinage reform
events.summary: Around 64 Nero reduced the aureus from 1/40 to 1/45 of a Roman pound and the denarius from 1/84 to 1/96, while lowering the silver fineness of the denarius from about 97-98% to about 93%. Base-metal coinage was also reorganised, with brass asses briefly struck.

events.title: Lucan's civil war epic and his quarrel with Nero
events.summary: Seneca's nephew Lucan (39-65) published the first three books of his De Bello Civili ("Pharsalia") c. 62-63 with a flattering dedication to Nero, but after a falling-out the emperor forbade him to publish or recite; the poem, an anti-Caesarian epic without gods, broke off in Book 10 when Lucan was forced to suicide for his part in the Pisonian conspiracy.

events.title: Traditions of the deaths of Peter and Paul in Rome
events.summary: Early Christian tradition places the deaths of Peter, crucified, and Paul, beheaded, at Rome under Nero, probably in the persecution after the fire of 64 or a few years later; the earliest allusion is 1 Clement (c. 96).
events.locName: Vatican hill and Via Ostiensis, Rome

events.title: Pisonian conspiracy
events.summary: A broad conspiracy of senators, equites and praetorian officers planned to kill Nero at the Circus games of the Cerialia and make the aristocrat Gaius Calpurnius Piso emperor. It was betrayed the day before by Milichus, freedman of the conspirator Flavius Scaevinus.

events.title: Fire destroys Lugdunum
events.summary: A fire destroyed much of Lugdunum, capital of the Three Gauls, in a single night, probably in 64 or 65; Seneca wrote that "there was one night between a great city and none", and Nero sent four million sesterces, the sum Lugdunum had given Rome after the great fire.

events.title: Pestilence and storm of 65
events.summary: In 65 a pestilence killed some 30,000 people at Rome (the number registered at the shrine of Libitina), without any visible change in the weather, while a hurricane devastated Campania.

events.title: Columella's treatise on agriculture
events.summary: Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella of Gades wrote his twelve books On Agriculture c. 60-65, the fullest Roman manual of estate management, notable for its calculation of the profitability of vineyards and its complaint that Italian landowners neglected farming.

events.title: Outbreak of the Jewish revolt
events.summary: After the procurator Gessius Florus seized 17 talents from the Temple treasury and let his troops massacre Jerusalemites, the Temple captain Eleazar son of Ananias stopped the daily sacrifices for the emperor, effectively declaring revolt. Rebels took the Antonia fortress and Masada, and the Roman garrison was massacred after surrendering.

events.title: Defeat of Cestius Gallus at Beth Horon
events.summary: Cestius Gallus, legate of Syria, marched on Jerusalem with legio XII Fulminata, vexillations of other legions and allied troops, assaulted the Temple, then inexplicably withdrew. In the pass of Beth Horon his column was ambushed and routed, abandoning its baggage and artillery.

sides.strength: Legio XII Fulminata, 2,000 from each of three other legions, 6 cohorts, 4 alae and allied troops: c. 30,000

battle.significance: Turned a riot into a full-scale war and brought Vespasian to Judaea.

events.title: Coronation of Tiridates in Rome
events.summary: Under the Rhandeia settlement, the Arsacid Tiridates travelled overland to Rome (avoiding the sea for religious reasons as a Zoroastrian magus) with 3,000 Parthian horsemen and received the diadem from Nero in the Forum, kneeling as to Mithras; the doors of Janus were closed.

events.title: Condemnation of Thrasea Paetus and Barea Soranus
events.summary: In 66 Nero had the Stoic senator Thrasea Paetus, who had walked out of the Senate after Agrippina's murder and absented himself for three years, condemned along with Barea Soranus; Thrasea opened his veins in his garden, offering the blood as a libation "to Jupiter the Liberator".

events.title: Nero plans an expedition to the Caspian Gates
events.summary: In 66-67 Nero planned an expedition to the "Caspian Gates" against the Alans, raising a new legion, I Italica, of Italian recruits six feet tall that he called the "phalanx of Alexander the Great", and moving troops from Germany, Britain and Illyricum eastwards.

events.title: Siege of Jotapata
events.summary: Vespasian besieged the Galilean hill town of Jotapata, defended by Josephus, for 47 days, with earth ramps, rams and 160 artillery engines. The town fell at dawn after a deserter revealed the exhausted sentries slept; Josephus hid in a cave with forty others who agreed on a suicide pact by lot, and survived to surrender.

sides.strength: Legions V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XV Apollinaris with auxiliaries
sides.losses: light; Vespasian wounded in the foot

battle.significance: Broke organised resistance in Galilee and delivered Josephus, the war's historian, into Roman hands.

events.title: Siege of Gamla
events.summary: Gamla, perched on a camel-hump ridge in the Golan, repulsed Vespasian's first assault when Roman troops who broke in were trapped in collapsing houses. A month later, after a tower was undermined, Titus stormed it; Josephus says 4,000 were killed and 5,000 threw themselves into the ravine, only two women surviving.

battle.significance: Ended resistance in the Golan.

events.title: Nero's tour of Greece and the liberation of Achaea
events.summary: During a tour of Greece in 66-67, Nero competed in all the great games, which were rescheduled into a single year, and won 1,808 crowns. At the Isthmian Games on 28 November 67 he proclaimed the freedom of Achaea from Roman taxation and governors, and he cut the first sod of a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth.

events.title: Forced suicide of Corbulo
events.summary: Summoned to Greece by Nero with flattering letters, the greatest general of the age was met at Cenchreae with an order to die; he stabbed himself saying 'Axios', 'I deserved it', meaning he had been a fool to trust Nero. The Scribonii brothers, commanders in Germany, died at the same time.

events.title: Nero begins the Corinth canal
events.summary: During his tour of Greece Nero inaugurated a canal through the Isthmus of Corinth in 67, striking the first blow with a golden pickaxe; some 6,000 Jewish prisoners from Vespasian's campaign worked on it, but the project was abandoned on his death.

events.title: Revolt of Vindex
events.summary: Gaius Julius Vindex, an Aquitanian noble descended from kings and governor of Gallia Lugdunensis, rose against Nero in March 68, calling on the provincial governors to free the world from a tyrant who sang on the stage, and offered the throne to Galba in Spain.

events.title: Galba proclaimed at Carthago Nova
events.summary: Servius Sulpicius Galba, the 71-year-old governor of Hispania Tarraconensis, of ancient nobility, declared himself legate of the Senate and Roman people at Carthago Nova, raising a new legion (VII Galbiana) from provincials. Otho, governor of Lusitania, joined him.

events.title: Battle of Vesontio
events.summary: Lucius Verginius Rufus, commanding upper Germany, marched against Vindex, who was besieging Vesontio. After the two leaders apparently came to terms, their armies clashed anyway and the Rhine legions slaughtered some 20,000 Gauls; Vindex killed himself.

battle.significance: Destroyed Vindex but left Nero without the loyalty of the Rhine legions.

events.title: Death of Nero
events.summary: Deserted by the praetorians, whose prefect Nymphidius Sabinus had promised them a vast donative in Galba's name, and declared a public enemy by the Senate, Nero fled to the villa of his freedman Phaon four miles from Rome and stabbed himself with the help of his secretary Epaphroditus, saying 'What an artist dies with me!'
events.locName: Villa of Phaon, between the Via Salaria and Via Nomentana

events.title: Revolt of Clodius Macer in Africa
events.summary: In 68 Lucius Clodius Macer, legate of the African legion, rebelled against Nero, raised a second legion (I Macriana Liberatrix), cut off Rome's grain supply from Africa and struck denarii without an emperor's portrait in the name of the Senate and Roman people; Galba had him killed by the procurator Trebonius Garutianus in autumn 68.

events.title: Vitellius proclaimed by the Rhine legions
events.summary: On 1 January 69 the legions IV Macedonica and XXII Primigenia at Mogontiacum overturned Galba's images and refused the oath; the next day Fabius Valens led the lower German army at Cologne to hail its governor, Aulus Vitellius, as emperor. The upper army joined on 3 January.

events.title: Murder of Galba
events.summary: Five days after Galba adopted the aristocrat Lucius Calpurnius Piso Licinianus, Marcus Salvius Otho, passed over and in debt, was carried to the praetorian camp by 23 bodyguards and hailed emperor. Galba was cut down in the Forum near the Lacus Curtius, and Piso was dragged from the temple of Vesta and killed.

events.title: First Battle of Bedriacum
events.summary: Otho's generals, ordered to force a decision against the advice of Suetonius Paullinus and Marius Celsus, advanced from Bedriacum towards Cremona and were defeated in a confused battle along the Via Postumia by the combined Vitellian armies of Caecina and Valens.

battle.significance: Decided the war between Otho and Vitellius; Otho killed himself two days later.

events.title: Suicide of Otho
events.summary: Though his army was still largely intact and the Danube legions were coming, Otho decided to spare Rome further civil war; he burned compromising letters, distributed money, slept soundly and at dawn stabbed himself at Brixellum, aged 37. Several soldiers killed themselves at his pyre.

events.title: Vespasian proclaimed emperor at Alexandria
events.summary: On 1 July 69 Tiberius Julius Alexander, prefect of Egypt, had his legions swear allegiance to Titus Flavius Vespasianus, commander in the Jewish war; the army of Judaea followed on 3 July and Mucianus's Syrian legions soon after. Vespasian later counted his reign from 1 July.

events.title: Second Battle of Bedriacum and sack of Cremona
events.summary: Antonius Primus's Danubian army met the leaderless Vitellian legions (Caecina had tried to defect and been arrested by his own men) in a night battle before Cremona. At dawn legio III Gallica saluted the rising sun in Syrian fashion, the Vitellians thought reinforcements had come, and broke. The Flavians then sacked Cremona for four days.
events.locName: Before Cremona on the Via Postumia

sides.strength: Five Danubian legions and auxiliaries, c. 30,000-40,000

battle.significance: Decisive Flavian victory of the civil war.

events.title: Burning of the Capitol
events.summary: After Vitellius's agreement to abdicate was blocked by his soldiers and the city mob, Vespasian's brother Flavius Sabinus, prefect of the city, took refuge on the Capitol with the young Domitian. Vitellian troops stormed it; the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus burned, and Sabinus was killed.

battle.significance: Destroyed Rome's chief temple; led to the Flavian storming of the city next day.

events.title: Flavian storming of Rome and death of Vitellius
events.summary: Antonius Primus's troops fought their way into Rome against the Vitellian praetorians while crowds watched and cheered as at a show. Vitellius, found hiding in a doorkeeper's lodge, was dragged half-naked through the Forum, pelted with dung and killed at the Gemonian stairs.

events.title: Siege of Vetera
events.summary: Julius Civilis's Batavians and Germans besieged the double-legion fortress of Vetera, held by some 5,000 men of V Alaudae and XV Primigenia under Munius Lupercus, from autumn 69. After eating their horses and roots, the defenders surrendered in March 70 and were massacred five miles from the camp.

sides.strength: Eight Batavian veteran cohorts, Germanic allies
c. 5,000 of V Alaudae and XV Primigenia

battle.significance: The greatest humiliation of Roman arms on the Rhine since Varus.

events.title: The first false Nero
events.summary: Early in 69 a man resembling Nero, a slave from Pontus or a freedman from Italy who sang to the lyre, gathered deserters and sailors on the island of Cythnos until Calpurnius Asprenas, governor of Galatia and Pamphylia, captured and executed him and sent his head to Rome.

events.title: Revolt of Mariccus among the Boii
events.summary: In 69 Mariccus, a Boian of humble birth, proclaimed himself a god and liberator of Gaul and gathered 8,000 followers, raiding Aeduan villages; the Aedui and Vitellian cohorts crushed them, and Mariccus was thrown to the beasts, which refused to touch him until he was killed in front of Vitellius.

events.title: Venutius overthrows Cartimandua
events.summary: Taking advantage of the civil war, Venutius, the divorced husband of the Brigantian queen Cartimandua, who had married his armour-bearer Vellocatus, raised the Brigantes against her in 69; Roman auxiliaries under Vettius Bolanus could only rescue the queen, leaving "the kingdom to Venutius, the war to us".

events.title: Siege and destruction of Jerusalem
events.summary: Titus besieged Jerusalem from Passover 70 with four legions and allied troops. Breaching the third and second walls in May, he encircled the city with a wall to starve it, took the Antonia fortress in July, burned the Temple at the end of August and stormed the Upper City in late September.

sides.strength: Legions V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XII Fulminata, XV Apollinaris, auxiliaries and allied kings: c. 60,000-70,000
c. 23,000 fighters (Josephus) and a population swollen by Passover pilgrims
sides.losses: catastrophic; Josephus claims 1.1 million dead and 97,000 enslaved

battle.significance: Destroyed the Second Temple, ending sacrificial Judaism and reshaping both rabbinic Judaism and early Christianity.

events.title: Lex de imperio Vespasiani
events.summary: The Senate's decree of late December 69, confirmed by the people, conferring 'all the usual powers' on Vespasian survives in part on a bronze tablet in the Capitoline Museums. Its clauses grant powers 'as Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius had', omitting Caligula and Nero.

events.title: Proclamation of the Imperium Galliarum
events.summary: Julius Classicus and Julius Tutor of the Treveri and Julius Sabinus of the Lingones, all Roman officers, proclaimed an 'Empire of the Gauls'. The legions at Novaesium and Bonna, after murdering their commander Dillius Vocula, swore allegiance to it; but a council of Gallic states at Durocortorum, convened by the Remi, chose loyalty to Rome.

events.title: Battle of Rigodulum
events.summary: Quintus Petillius Cerialis, arriving with fresh legions from Italy, stormed the fortified Treveran position at Rigodulum on the Moselle, capturing its commander Julius Valentinus, and entered Augusta Treverorum the next day.

sides.strength: Legio XXI Rapax, auxiliaries and new legions from Italy

battle.significance: Broke the Imperium Galliarum.

events.title: Second battle of Vetera
events.summary: Civilis made his last stand near the ruins of Vetera, flooding the plain with a dam. After an inconclusive first day, a Batavian deserter guided Roman cavalry to the rear of the German line on the second, and Civilis was defeated.

sides.strength: Legions II Adiutrix, VI Victrix, XIV Gemina, XXI Rapax and auxiliaries

battle.significance: Effectively ended the Batavian revolt.

events.title: Vespasian's miracles at Alexandria
events.summary: Waiting at Alexandria in early 70 for the grain season and news from Rome, Vespasian was persuaded to heal a blind man by spitting in his eyes and a lame man by touching him with his foot, both on the advice of Serapis; visiting the Serapeum alone, he saw the absent Egyptian priest Basilides.

events.title: Yohanan ben Zakkai and the academy at Yavneh
events.summary: According to rabbinic tradition the sage Yohanan ben Zakkai escaped besieged Jerusalem hidden in a coffin and obtained from Vespasian permission to found a school at Yavneh (Jamnia), where the rabbinic reconstruction of Judaism without a Temple began.

events.title: The Gospel of Mark written
events.summary: The earliest gospel, attributed to Mark, was written about 66-72, probably in the shadow of the Jewish war and the destruction of the Temple, and became the narrative framework used by Matthew and Luke.

events.title: Triumph of Vespasian and Titus over Judaea
events.summary: Vespasian and Titus celebrated a joint triumph over Judaea, with Domitian riding beside them, displaying 700 picked captives, the Temple's golden table and seven-branched lampstand and a scroll of the Law. Simon bar Giora was executed at the climax.

events.title: Institution of the fiscus Judaicus
events.summary: Vespasian ordered that the half-shekel Temple tax paid by Jews everywhere be paid instead, as two drachmas or denarii a head, to the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus, and extended it to women, children and slaves.

events.title: Petillius Cerialis conquers the Brigantes
events.summary: After Venutius ousted his former wife, the pro-Roman queen Cartimandua, in 69, the Brigantes of northern England became hostile. Petillius Cerialis, as governor, waged a series of campaigns, founded the legionary fortress at Eboracum (York) for legio IX Hispana and annexed Brigantia.

events.title: Vespasian settles veterans at Emmaus and leases Judaea
events.summary: After the war Vespasian treated Judaea as his own property, ordering the land to be leased out rather than founding a city, settling only 800 veterans at Emmaus 30 stades from Jerusalem, and imposing the two-drachma fiscus Judaicus on all Jews.

events.title: Siege of Machaerus
events.summary: Lucilius Bassus, legate of Judaea, besieged Herod's fortress of Machaerus east of the Dead Sea. When a young rebel leader, Eleazar, was captured and prepared for crucifixion in view of the walls, the garrison surrendered in exchange for his life.

sides.losses: garrison released; 1,700 men of the lower town killed

battle.significance: Left Masada as the last rebel stronghold.

events.title: Annexation of Commagene and Flavian reorganisation of the East
events.summary: Accused by the Syrian governor Caesennius Paetus of plotting with Parthia, Antiochus IV of Commagene was driven out and his kingdom annexed to Syria. Lesser Armenia was also absorbed, and Vespasian combined Cappadocia and Galatia under a consular legate with legions on the upper Euphrates.

events.title: Vespasian's tax on urine and fiscal recovery
events.summary: To restore finances after the civil wars, which he said required 40 billion sesterces, Vespasian raised provincial tribute, revived lapsed taxes and imposed new ones, including a levy on the urine collected from public latrines by fullers; when Titus objected he held a coin to his nose and said "it doesn't smell" (non olet).

events.title: Censorship of Vespasian and Titus
events.summary: In 73-74 Vespasian and Titus held the censorship, revising the Senate and equestrian order after the civil wars, adlecting new members from Italy and the provinces into the Senate and the patriciate, conducting a census and extending the pomerium (75).

events.title: Siege of Masada
events.summary: Lucius Flavius Silva, with legio X Fretensis and auxiliaries, encircled Herod's desert fortress of Masada, held by about 960 Sicarii under Eleazar ben Yair, with a wall and eight camps, and built an assault ramp on the western side. When the wall was breached, Josephus says, the defenders killed their families and themselves the night before the final assault.

sides.strength: Legio X Fretensis and auxiliaries, c. 8,000

battle.significance: Ended the First Jewish Revolt; later a national myth.

events.title: Vespasian grants Latin rights to all Spain
events.summary: During his censorship with Titus (73-74), Vespasian granted the Latin right (ius Latii) to all communities of the Spanish provinces not already privileged, so that their annual magistrates acquired Roman citizenship, and Spanish towns were reorganised as Flavian municipia.
events.locName: Irni (El Saucejo, Seville): find-spot of the lex Irnitana

events.title: Frontinus conquers the Silures
events.summary: Sextus Julius Frontinus, governor of Britain c. 74-77, subdued the warlike Silures of South Wales after decades of resistance, founding the legionary fortress of Isca (Caerleon) for II Augusta and a network of auxiliary forts.

events.title: Expulsion of philosophers and execution of Helvidius Priscus
events.summary: Vespasian expelled philosophers and astrologers from Rome (71) and, after repeated public defiance, exiled and then ordered the execution of the Stoic senator Helvidius Priscus, son-in-law of Thrasea Paetus, regretting it too late to recall the executioners.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Peace
events.summary: Vespasian dedicated the Templum Pacis, a vast colonnaded garden-precinct beside the Forum of Augustus, built from Jewish war booty and housing the Temple treasures, a library and masterpieces of Greek painting and sculpture collected from Nero's palace.

events.title: Josephus publishes the Jewish War
events.summary: Living in Rome as a Flavian client, Flavius Josephus published his seven-book Greek history of the Jewish revolt, revised from an earlier Aramaic version for the Jews of Mesopotamia. Vespasian and Titus endorsed it, Titus signing copies.

events.title: Alan invasion of Media and Armenia
events.summary: Around 72-75 the Alans poured through the Caucasus passes, opened to them by the king of Hyrcania, plundering Media Atropatene, whose king Pacorus fled to the mountains, and Armenia, where Tiridates was nearly lassoed in battle; Vologases I asked Vespasian for help under Titus or Domitian, which was refused.

events.title: Pliny the Elder dedicates the Natural History
events.summary: Gaius Plinius Secundus dedicated his encyclopedic Natural History in 37 books to Titus, claiming in the preface to have assembled 20,000 facts from about 2,000 volumes by 100 principal authors.

events.title: Agricola crushes the Ordovices and takes Anglesey
events.summary: Arriving in Britain in midsummer (77 or 78), Agricola at once attacked the Ordovices, who had nearly wiped out a cavalry unit, slaughtered almost the whole tribe, and then took Mona by sending auxiliaries trained to swim with their horses across the Menai Strait.

events.title: Death of Vespasian
events.summary: Vespasian died of fever and diarrhoea at his family's spa of Aquae Cutiliae near Reate, aged 69. Feeling death approach he joked 'Oh dear, I think I am becoming a god', and struggled to his feet, saying an emperor should die standing.

events.title: Eruption of Vesuvius
events.summary: Vesuvius erupted catastrophically, burying Pompeii and Stabiae under pumice and ash and Herculaneum under pyroclastic flows. Pliny the Elder, commander of the fleet at Misenum, died at Stabiae while attempting a rescue; his nephew's two letters to Tacitus are the only eyewitness account.

events.title: Agricola's "civilising" programme
events.summary: In his second winter Agricola encouraged British communities to build temples, forums and houses, educated chiefs' sons in the liberal arts and promoted Latin and the toga, a policy Tacitus famously describes as the Britons calling "civilisation" (humanitas) what was in fact part of their enslavement.

events.title: Titus sends Berenice away
events.summary: The Jewish queen Berenice, sister of Agrippa II, came to Rome in 75 and lived with Titus on the Palatine expecting marriage, but popular hostility forced him to send her away, finally on his accession in 79: "invitus invitam" as Suetonius puts it.

events.title: Inauguration of the Colosseum
events.summary: Titus dedicated the Flavian Amphitheatre, begun by Vespasian on the site of Nero's lake, with 100 days of games in which 9,000 animals were killed and the arena was flooded for naval battles. Martial's Book of Spectacles celebrates them.

events.title: Agricola advances to the Tay
events.summary: In his third season Agricola overran new peoples as far as the estuary called Taus (the Tay), ravaging as he went, and built forts so well sited that none was stormed or abandoned.

events.title: Fire of 80 and pestilence under Titus
events.summary: A three-day fire in 80, while Titus was in Campania dealing with the aftermath of Vesuvius, destroyed the newly rebuilt Capitoline temple, the Pantheon, the Saepta, the Baths of Agrippa, the Theatre of Balbus and the stage of Pompey's theatre; a severe epidemic followed.

events.title: Death of Titus
events.summary: Titus died of fever at the same Sabine villa as his father, aged 41, after a reign of just over two years in which he was remembered as 'the delight of the human race'. He reportedly said he regretted only one act, never explained.

events.title: Agricola garrisons the Forth-Clyde isthmus
events.summary: In his fourth season Agricola consolidated the land he had overrun and fortified the narrow neck between the Clota (Clyde) and Bodotria (Forth), so that the enemy were "pushed back as if into another island".

events.title: Arch of Titus on the Sacra Via
events.summary: After Titus's death in September 81 the Senate dedicated to Divus Titus a single-bay marble arch at the top of the Sacra Via, whose reliefs show the triumph of 71 with the spoils of the Jerusalem Temple, including the seven-branched menorah, the table of shewbread and silver trumpets.

events.title: Agricola in south-west Scotland and the Irish question
events.summary: In his fifth season Agricola crossed by ship (or the Solway) and subdued previously unknown peoples in the south-west, placing troops facing Ireland; he believed Ireland could be conquered and held with one legion and a modest force of auxiliaries, and kept an exiled Irish prince in his entourage.
events.locName: Galloway and the coast facing Ireland

events.title: Battle of Mons Graupius
events.summary: Gnaeus Julius Agricola defeated a confederation of more than 30,000 Caledonians under Calgacus at Mons Graupius in north-east Scotland. He fought with 8,000 auxiliary infantry in the centre and 3,000 cavalry on the wings, keeping the legions in reserve before the camp; Tacitus reports 10,000 Caledonian and 360 Roman dead.

sides.strength: 8,000 auxiliary infantry, 3,000 cavalry in the line; legions in reserve

battle.significance: Furthest northern victory of Roman arms in Britain; conquest of Scotland nonetheless abandoned within a few years.

events.title: Domitian's campaign against the Chatti
events.summary: Domitian launched a surprise offensive from Mogontiacum against the Chatti, advancing Roman control into the Taunus and Wetterau and cutting 120 miles of military roads through the forest. He took the title Germanicus and celebrated a triumph.

events.title: Domitian raises army pay and reforms the coinage
events.summary: Domitian raised legionary pay by a third, from 225 to 300 denarii a year, by adding a fourth instalment, the first increase since Augustus. In 82 he had restored the denarius to the Augustan silver standard, but rising costs forced a reduction in 85.

events.title: The Usipi cohort mutinies and sails round Britain
events.summary: In 82 or 83 a cohort of Usipi recruited in Germany and posted to Britain murdered their centurion and drill instructors, seized three liburnian galleys and sailed round the north of Britain, reduced by hunger to cannibalism, until they were shipwrecked and enslaved by the Suebi and Frisii, some being sold back across the Rhine.

events.title: Agricola's fleet circumnavigates Britain
events.summary: After Mons Graupius Agricola's fleet sailed round the north of Britain, subdued the Orkneys and sighted Thule, proving Britain to be an island. The year before, a cohort of Usipi, recently levied in Germany, had mutinied, stolen three ships and sailed round Britain by accident.

events.title: Dacian invasion of Moesia; death of Oppius Sabinus
events.summary: In winter 85/86 Dacians under their king (Duras or Diurpaneus, soon succeeded by Decebalus) crossed the frozen Danube into Moesia and killed the governor, Gaius Oppius Sabinus, with many of his troops.

battle.significance: Opened the Dacian wars of Domitian and Trajan.

events.title: Domitian becomes censor for life
events.summary: In 85 Domitian took the title censor perpetuus, giving himself permanent control over the membership of the Senate and equestrian order and over public morals, which he exercised by reviving the adultery law, expelling a quaestorian senator for acting and dancing, and punishing Vestals.

events.title: Upper and Lower Germany become provinces; the Taunus-Wetterau limes
events.summary: After his Chattan war (83) Domitian annexed the Taunus and Wetterau, building a line of forts and watchtowers linked by a patrol road, and organised the military zones on the Rhine as the provinces of Germania Superior and Inferior, governed from Mogontiacum and Colonia Agrippinensis.

events.title: The later gospels and Acts
events.summary: Between about 80 and 100 the gospels of Matthew and Luke, both using Mark and a common sayings source (Q), and Luke's sequel Acts, were written for Greek-speaking communities; the Gospel of John, independent in structure and theology, followed c. 90-100, traditionally at Ephesus.

events.title: Defeat and death of Cornelius Fuscus
events.summary: The praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus led a Roman army across the Danube on a bridge of boats into Dacia and was killed with much of his force; a standard (or eagle) was lost, recovered by Trajan in 102.

sides.strength: Several legions or vexillations with praetorians

battle.significance: Made Decebalus Rome's most dangerous enemy on the Danube.

events.title: Revolt and destruction of the Nasamones
events.summary: In 85-86 the Nasamones of the Syrtic desert, crushed by taxation, killed the tax collectors and defeated the legate of Numidia, Gnaeus Suellius Flaccus, plundering his camp; finding wine there, they got drunk and Flaccus fell on them and wiped them out, women and children included.

events.title: Domitian founds the Capitoline Games
events.summary: In 86 Domitian instituted the Agon Capitolinus in honour of Jupiter Capitolinus, a quadrennial Greek-style festival of music, horsemanship and athletics, with oak-leaf crowns presented by the emperor wearing a Greek cloak and gold crown with images of the Capitoline triad.
events.locName: Stadium and Odeum of Domitian, Campus Martius

events.title: Moesia divided into two provinces
events.summary: After the Dacian invasion that killed Oppius Sabinus, Domitian divided Moesia in 86 into Moesia Superior (capital Viminacium) and Moesia Inferior (Novae), each with its own consular legate and legions, as the Danube became the empire's main front.

events.title: Septimius Flaccus and Julius Maternus reach Agisymba
events.summary: In the Flavian period Septimius Flaccus marched three months south of the Garamantes, and Julius Maternus travelled with the Garamantian king four months from Garama to Agisymba, "the land of the Ethiopians where the rhinoceros gathers".

events.title: Domitian styled dominus et deus
events.summary: Suetonius says Domitian dictated a circular letter in the name of "our lord and god" (dominus et deus noster) and that the formula became usual in speech and writing addressed to him; Martial uses it in his epigrams.

events.title: Martial's epigrams
events.summary: Marcus Valerius Martialis of Bilbilis published the Liber Spectaculorum for the inaugural games of the Colosseum in 80, the Xenia and Apophoreta (84-85), and then twelve books of Epigrams from 86 to 101, the definitive models of the genre.

events.title: Abandonment of the fortress at Inchtuthil
events.summary: The legionary fortress at Inchtuthil on the Tay, built for legio XX after Mons Graupius, was systematically dismantled before completion around 86-87, when legio II Adiutrix was withdrawn from Britain for the Danube wars. Ten tonnes of iron nails (about 875,000) were buried in a pit to keep them from the Caledonians.

events.title: Domitian's Secular Games
events.summary: Domitian celebrated Secular Games in 88, reckoning from Augustus's games of 17 BC rather than following Claudius's anniversary cycle of 47. Tacitus took part as praetor and member of the quindecimviri sacris faciundis.

events.title: Battle of Tapae (88)
events.summary: Lucius Tettius Julianus, governor of Upper Moesia, invaded Dacia and defeated Decebalus near Tapae, the pass leading to the Dacian heartland. Decebalus's lieutenant Vezinas survived by lying among the dead.

battle.significance: Restored Roman prestige and led to a negotiated peace.

events.title: Revolt of Antonius Saturninus
events.summary: On 1 January 89 Lucius Antonius Saturninus, governor of upper Germany, was proclaimed emperor by the two legions at Mogontiacum, using the soldiers' savings in the camp bank. A sudden thaw on the Rhine prevented his Chattan allies from crossing, and Aulus Bucius Lappius Maximus crushed him within weeks.

events.title: Peace with Decebalus
events.summary: Facing war with the Marcomanni and Quadi, Domitian made peace with Decebalus, whose brother Diegis came to receive a diadem as a client king. Rome paid Decebalus an annual subsidy and lent him engineers and craftsmen.

events.title: Execution of the Vestal Cornelia
events.summary: Domitian, as pontifex maximus, condemned the senior Vestal Cornelia for unchastity and had her buried alive in the ancient manner; her alleged lovers were beaten to death with rods in the Comitium.
events.locName: Rome (Campus Sceleratus by the Colline Gate)

events.title: Lex Irnitana: the Flavian municipal law
events.summary: Bronze tablets discovered in 1981 near El Saucejo (Seville) preserve about two-thirds of the charter of the small Baetican town of Irni, a model municipal law issued under Domitian (with a covering letter of 91) for the communities that received Latin rights from Vespasian.

events.title: Domitian's vine edict
events.summary: After an abundant vintage coincided with a grain shortage, Domitian forbade the planting of new vines in Italy and ordered half the vineyards in the provinces to be cut down. The edict was not enforced and was suspended, according to Philostratus, after an embassy from Asia led by the sophist Scopelian.

events.title: Destruction of legio XXI Rapax
events.summary: The Sarmatian Iazyges, with Suebic allies, invaded Pannonia and destroyed a legion with its legate, almost certainly XXI Rapax, which disappears from the record at this time. Domitian took the field himself for eight months.

battle.significance: Shifted Rome's military centre of gravity to the middle Danube.

events.title: Dedication of Domitian's Palatine palace
events.summary: Domitian's architect Rabirius completed the great palace on the Palatine, comprising the official Domus Flavia with its throne room (Aula Regia) and state dining hall, and the private Domus Augustana with its sunken peristyle and 'stadium' garden.

events.title: Vindolanda writing tablets
events.summary: Waterlogged deposits at the fort of Vindolanda, south of the later Hadrian's Wall, have yielded since 1973 over a thousand thin wooden leaf tablets written in ink, mostly from about 92-120: military reports, accounts and private letters of soldiers, officers and their families.

events.title: Statius publishes the Thebaid
events.summary: Publius Papinius Statius of Naples published the Thebaid, a twelve-book epic on the war of the Seven against Thebes, around 91-92, after twelve years' work; his Silvae, occasional poems on villas, statues, baths and court life, followed in 92-95.

events.title: The terror of 93: executions of senators and expulsion of philosophers
events.summary: After Agricola's death in August 93, Domitian had the senators Herennius Senecio and Arulenus Rusticus executed for writing eulogies of Helvidius Priscus and Thrasea Paetus, and the younger Helvidius for an allegedly satirical farce. Their books were burned in the Forum, and philosophers were expelled from Rome and Italy.

events.title: Epictetus founds his school at Nicopolis
events.summary: Expelled from Rome with the other philosophers in 93 (or 89), the former slave Epictetus set up a Stoic school at Nicopolis in Epirus, where young Romans and Greeks came to study; Arrian's notes of his lectures, the Discourses and the Handbook (Enchiridion), are the most vivid record of ancient philosophical teaching.

events.title: Josephus completes the Jewish Antiquities
events.summary: In the thirteenth year of Domitian (93/94) Josephus completed the twenty books of the Jewish Antiquities, a history of the Jews from the creation to the outbreak of the revolt, followed by his autobiography (Life) and Against Apion, a defence of Judaism against Greek slanders.

events.title: Execution of Flavius Clemens
events.summary: Domitian had his cousin Titus Flavius Clemens, consul with him in 95 and father of the boys he had designated as heirs, executed for 'atheism', and exiled Clemens's wife Flavia Domitilla. Dio says many others who had 'drifted into Jewish ways' were condemned.

events.title: Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria
events.summary: Marcus Fabius Quintilianus of Calagurris, the first holder of a state-salaried chair of Latin rhetoric (founded by Vespasian, 100,000 sesterces a year), published his twelve-book Education of the Orator c. 95, a complete programme from infancy to the mature speaker.

events.title: The Revelation of John
events.summary: The Apocalypse of John, written by a Christian prophet exiled on Patmos, is dated by Irenaeus to the end of Domitian's reign (c. 95), though some place it c. 68-70; its seven letters address churches in Asia, and its visions present Rome as Babylon and the beast.

events.title: Assassination of Domitian
events.summary: Domitian was stabbed to death in his bedroom by a palace conspiracy including his chamberlain Parthenius and Stephanus, steward of the exiled Domitilla, who had worn a bandage for days to hide a dagger. Both praetorian prefects and perhaps the empress Domitia knew of the plot.

events.title: Accession of Nerva
events.summary: On the day of Domitian's murder the Senate recognised Marcus Cocceius Nerva, a 65-year-old jurist-senator of no military reputation who had served Nero and the Flavians, as emperor. He swore never to execute a senator, recalled exiles and punished informers.

events.title: Letter of the Roman church to Corinth (1 Clement)
events.summary: Around 96 the church of Rome, through its leading presbyter Clement, wrote to the Corinthians urging the reinstatement of presbyters deposed by younger members, the earliest Christian text outside the New Testament.

events.title: Nerva's reforms: land law and the end of informers
events.summary: In his brief reign Nerva recalled exiles, banned prosecutions for maiestas and "Jewish living", executed informing slaves and freedmen, passed an agrarian law spending 60 million sesterces on land for poor citizens and exempted Italy from the cost of the imperial post.

events.title: Praetorian revolt and Nerva's adoption of Trajan
events.summary: In 97 the praetorians under their prefect Casperius Aelianus besieged the palace and forced Nerva to surrender Domitian's assassins for execution and even to thank the soldiers publicly. Weeks later, in the temple of Jupiter on the Capitol, Nerva announced the adoption of Marcus Ulpius Traianus, governor of upper Germany.

events.title: Nerva dedicates the Forum Transitorium
events.summary: In 97 Nerva dedicated the narrow forum built by Domitian between the Forum of Augustus and the Temple of Peace, along the line of the Argiletum, with a temple of Minerva, Domitian's patron goddess.

events.title: Frontinus becomes water commissioner and writes De Aquaeductu
events.summary: Appointed curator aquarum by Nerva in 97, the elderly Frontinus surveyed Rome's nine aqueducts, found widespread fraud by water-men and landowners tapping the conduits, and wrote On the Aqueducts of Rome, with figures for each channel's source, length and delivery.

events.title: Death of Nerva; Trajan becomes emperor
events.summary: Nerva died of a fever after a fit of anger. Trajan, at Cologne, received the news from his cousin and ward Hadrian, who raced to deliver it, and became emperor without challenge; he did not return to Rome until 99, first inspecting the Rhine and Danube armies.

events.title: Tacitus's historical works
events.summary: Publius Cornelius Tacitus published the Agricola and Germania in 98, the Dialogus on orators around 102, the Histories (from 69 to 96) around 105-110, and the Annals (from 14 to 68) in the 110s-120s, the summit of Roman historiography.

events.title: Tacitus publishes the Agricola and Germania
events.summary: In 98 Tacitus published his biography of his father-in-law Agricola and his ethnographic treatise on the peoples of Germany, his first works after the "fifteen years" of silence under Domitian.

events.title: Trajan enters Rome on foot
events.summary: After more than a year on the Rhine and Danube following his accession, Trajan entered Rome in 99 on foot, embracing senators and greeting knights by name; his wife Plotina, climbing the Palatine steps, declared that she would leave the palace the same woman she entered it.

events.title: Pliny and Tacitus prosecute Marius Priscus
events.summary: In January 100, with Trajan presiding as consul, Pliny and Tacitus prosecuted Marius Priscus, proconsul of Africa, for taking bribes to condemn and execute innocent men; the three-day trial ended in his relegation and the forfeiture of 700,000 sesterces.

events.title: Pliny's Panegyricus
events.summary: On 1 September 100 Pliny delivered his speech of thanks (gratiarum actio) for the suffect consulship before Trajan, later expanding it into the Panegyricus, the only Latin prose speech surviving from between Cicero and the fourth century.

events.title: Trajan's road and canal through the Iron Gates
events.summary: In 100 Trajan completed a road cut into the cliffs of the Danube gorge at the Iron Gates, partly carried on wooden cantilevers, and in 101 a canal at Sip (Sip) 3.2 km long to bypass the cataracts, preparing for the Dacian war.
events.locName: Iron Gates gorge of the Danube (Tabula Traiana)

events.title: Battle of Tapae (101)
events.summary: Trajan's army fought Decebalus near Tapae, the gateway to the Dacian heartland, in a hard-won Roman victory amid a violent storm. The wounded were so many that Trajan tore up his own clothing for bandages and ordered an altar and annual rites for the fallen.

battle.significance: Opened the road into Dacia but at high cost.

events.title: The Trajanic alimenta
events.summary: Building on a scheme begun by Nerva, Trajan established the alimenta in Italian towns: perpetual loans to local landowners at about 5% interest, secured on their estates, with the interest paying monthly allowances to support freeborn children.

events.title: Battle in Lower Moesia (Adamclisi)
events.summary: In winter 101/102 Dacians and Roxolani crossed the lower Danube into Moesia. Trajan hurried east by ship and defeated them in a series of fights, commemorated by the foundation of Nicopolis ad Istrum and, at Adamclisi in the Dobruja, by the colossal Tropaeum Traiani dedicated to Mars Ultor in 109.

sides.strength: Imperial army including praetorians and Moorish cavalry
sides.losses: c. 3,800 named on the Adamclisi altar (if this battle)

battle.significance: Defeated the Dacian diversion and set up the decisive 102 campaign.

events.title: Peace of 102
events.summary: As Roman columns stormed the forts of the Orăștie mountains, Decebalus submitted. He surrendered his arms, engines, engineers and deserters, agreed to demolish his forts, withdrew from conquered territory and accepted Rome's friends and enemies as his own; a Roman garrison stayed in Sarmizegetusa.

events.title: Trajan's bridge over the Danube
events.summary: Apollodorus of Damascus built a permanent bridge over the Danube between Drobeta and Pontes, about 1,135 m long, on twenty stone piers carrying timber arches, the longest arch bridge in the world for a millennium.

events.title: Bridge of Alcantara over the Tagus
events.summary: In 104-106 the architect Gaius Julius Lacer built for eleven municipia of Lusitania a granite bridge of six arches over the Tagus, 194 m long and nearly 50 m high, which he inscribed "pontem perpetui mansurum in saecula mundi".

events.title: Decebalus captures Pompeius Longinus
events.summary: At the start of the Second Dacian War in 105 Decebalus lured the Roman commander Gnaeus Pompeius Longinus to a parley and held him hostage, demanding the return of Dacian territory and war costs; Longinus took poison smuggled by a freedman so as not to be a bargaining counter.

events.title: Plutarch writes the Parallel Lives
events.summary: In the reigns of Trajan and Hadrian, Plutarch of Chaeronea, priest of Apollo at Delphi, wrote 23 surviving pairs of Greek and Roman lives, dedicated to the consular Quintus Sosius Senecio, together with the enormous corpus of essays known as the Moralia.

events.title: Annexation of Nabataea as the province of Arabia
events.summary: On the death of the Nabataean king Rabbel II, the governor of Syria, Aulus Cornelius Palma, annexed the kingdom, apparently without serious fighting; the new province of Arabia, with its capital at Bostra and legio III Cyrenaica, dated its era from 22 March 106.

events.title: Siege of Sarmizegetusa Regia
events.summary: In summer 106 Roman armies converged on Decebalus's mountain capital and religious centre, Sarmizegetusa Regia, cut its water supply and stormed it. Trajan's Column shows Dacian nobles taking poison from a cauldron rather than surrender, and the city set on fire.

sides.strength: Several armies converging, perhaps 100,000 in the theatre

battle.significance: Destroyed the Dacian state.

events.title: Death of Decebalus
events.summary: Pursued by Roman cavalry, Decebalus cut his own throat. The scout Tiberius Claudius Maximus reached him as he died, cut off his head and right hand and brought them to Trajan at Ranisstorum; the head was displayed on the Gemonian stairs in Rome.

events.title: Creation of the province of Dacia
events.summary: The conquered kingdom became the province of Dacia under a consular legate, garrisoned by legio XIII Gemina at Apulum and auxiliaries. Decimus Terentius Scaurianus founded Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa for veterans, and settlers came 'from the whole Roman world'.

events.title: The treasure of Decebalus
events.summary: After the fall of Sarmizegetusa, Decebalus's companion Bicilis revealed where the king's treasure had been hidden: under the bed of the river Sargetia, which had been diverted by prisoners who were then killed. The plunder financed Trajan's building and games.

events.title: Colonia Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa founded
events.summary: Soon after the conquest, the first governor of Dacia, Decimus Terentius Scaurianus, founded the veteran colony of Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa some 40 km west of the destroyed Dacian capital, as the provincial capital.

events.title: Trajan's Dacian triumph and the games of 107
events.summary: To celebrate the conquest Trajan gave games lasting 123 days, in which, according to Dio, some 11,000 animals were killed and 10,000 gladiators fought. In the same year he called in worn old coins and reissued 'restored' types of Republican and earlier imperial coinage.

events.title: Markets of Trajan
events.summary: Built c. 100-110 in brick-faced concrete against the cut-back slope of the Quirinal behind Trajan's Forum, the so-called Markets of Trajan comprised a hemicycle and some 150 rooms on several levels around a vaulted hall and an ancient street, the Via Biberatica.

events.title: Trajan recalls worn coinage
events.summary: In 107 Trajan, according to Dio, melted down worn-out coins; the mint struck a series of "restoration" coins reproducing Republican denarii and earlier imperial aurei with the legend REST(ituit), while the denarius was slightly debased to about 89% silver.

events.title: Dedication of the Baths of Trajan
events.summary: On 22 June 109 Trajan opened his baths on the Oppian, designed by Apollodorus over the buried wings of Nero's Golden House, the first of the great symmetrical imperial thermae with a central bathing block set in a vast walled precinct with exedrae, libraries and gardens.

events.title: Aqua Traiana opened
events.summary: On 24 June 109 Trajan opened the Aqua Traiana, bringing spring water some 57 km from around Lake Bracciano to the Janiculum and Trastevere, which had depended on the poor water of the Alsietina.

events.title: Tropaeum Traiani dedicated at Adamclisi
events.summary: In 109 Trajan dedicated to Mars Ultor a colossal circular victory monument at Adamclisi in the Dobrudja, 38 m in diameter and crowned with a trophy, near an altar listing some 3,800 Roman soldiers who died in the battle of 102.

events.title: Pliny's governorship of Bithynia and his letter on the Christians
events.summary: Sent by Trajan as special legate to reform the finances of Bithynia-Pontus, Pliny the Younger consulted the emperor on everything from aqueducts to fire brigades. His letter on Christians (Ep. 10.96) and Trajan's reply (10.97) are the earliest surviving official documents on the treatment of Christianity.

events.title: Trajan's hexagonal harbour at Portus
events.summary: Around 100-112 Trajan added an inner hexagonal basin of 32 hectares to Claudius's silting harbour at Portus, with warehouses, a canal (Fossa Traiana) to the Tiber and a palatial complex, making it the main port of Rome for the grain fleets.

events.title: Martyrdom of Ignatius of Antioch
events.summary: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was taken under guard to Rome to be thrown to the beasts under Trajan, c. 107-115, writing on the way seven letters to churches in Asia, Rome and to Polycarp of Smyrna.

events.title: Via Nova Traiana from Bostra to the Red Sea
events.summary: Between 111 and 114 the governor Gaius Claudius Severus built the Via Nova Traiana across the new province of Arabia, 430 km from Bostra to Aila on the Gulf of Aqaba, "opened and paved from the borders of Syria to the Red Sea" in the words of its milestones.

events.title: Dedication of the Forum of Trajan
events.summary: Trajan dedicated the largest and last of the imperial fora, designed by Apollodorus of Damascus and paid for 'ex manubiis' from the Dacian spoils. It comprised a vast colonnaded square with a gilded equestrian statue of the emperor, the Basilica Ulpia, Greek and Latin libraries and the Column.

events.title: Dedication of Trajan's Column
events.summary: The marble column in Trajan's Forum, 100 Roman feet high on its pedestal, carries a spiral frieze 200 metres long with some 155 scenes and 2,500 figures narrating the Dacian Wars. Trajan's ashes were later placed in its base.

events.title: Trajan annexes Armenia
events.summary: When the Parthian king Osroes replaced the Roman-approved king of Armenia with his nephew Parthamasiris, Trajan marched east. At Elegeia Parthamasiris laid his diadem at Trajan's feet expecting it back; Trajan instead declared Armenia a Roman province, and Parthamasiris was killed soon after on the road.

events.title: Arch of Trajan at Beneventum
events.summary: In 114 the Senate dedicated an arch to Trajan at Beneventum, where his new Via Traiana branched from the Appian Way towards Brundisium, its reliefs presenting the emperor's civil and military achievements, from the alimenta to the reception of eastern envoys.

events.title: Earthquake at Antioch
events.summary: A devastating earthquake struck Antioch, crowded with soldiers and visitors for Trajan's winter court. Trajan escaped through a window with minor injuries, guided, Dio says, by a figure of superhuman size; the consul Marcus Pedo Vergilianus was among the dead.

events.title: Jewish revolts in Cyrene, Egypt and Cyprus
events.summary: While Trajan fought in Parthia, Jews in Cyrenaica rose under Lukuas (Andreas), destroying temples and public buildings; the revolt spread to Egypt and Cyprus with great slaughter on both sides. Dio gives 220,000 killed in Cyrene and 240,000 in Cyprus.

events.title: Trajan conquers northern Mesopotamia
events.summary: In 115 Trajan advanced from Armenia into northern Mesopotamia, received the submission of Abgar VII of Edessa, who won favour through his handsome son, and of other dynasts, and took Nisibis and Batnae, earning the title Parthicus; Lusius Quietus cleared the Mardi east of the Tigris.

events.title: Trajan captures Ctesiphon
events.summary: Trajan descended the Euphrates with a fleet built from the forests of Nisibis, hauled it overland to the Tigris and took the Parthian winter capital Ctesiphon, capturing Osroes's daughter and golden throne. The Senate voted him the title Parthicus.

sides.losses: capital and royal family members captured

battle.significance: First capture of the Parthian capital by Rome, the high-water mark of Roman eastward expansion.

events.title: Provinces of Mesopotamia and Assyria; crowning of Parthamaspates
events.summary: Trajan organised his conquests as provinces of Mesopotamia and (according to Eutropius and Festus) Assyria. When revolts broke out across them in 116, he crowned the Parthian prince Parthamaspates king at Ctesiphon, effectively conceding that southern Mesopotamia could not be held.

events.title: Trajan reaches the Persian Gulf
events.summary: After taking Ctesiphon in 116, Trajan sailed down the Tigris to Charax Spasinou, where the king of Characene, Athambelus, submitted; seeing a ship leaving for India, he said that he would have crossed to India too if he were younger, like Alexander, and later sacrificed at Babylon in the room where Alexander died.
events.locName: Charax Spasinou, head of the Persian Gulf

events.title: Revolt of Mesopotamia against Trajan
events.summary: In 116, while Trajan was at the Gulf, the conquered territories rose: the general Maximus Santra was defeated and killed, and Seleucia and the Jewish communities of Mesopotamia revolted; Lusius Quietus retook and burned Nisibis and Edessa, Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander captured Seleucia, and Trajan crowned the Parthian prince Parthamaspates at Ctesiphon.

events.title: Death of Trajan
events.summary: On his way back to Rome Trajan suffered a stroke and dropsy and died at Selinus in Cilicia, aged 63. His widow Plotina and the prefect Attianus announced that he had adopted Hadrian on his deathbed.

events.title: Accession of Hadrian; abandonment of Trajan's eastern conquests
events.summary: Proclaimed by the Syrian army at Antioch on 11 August 117, Hadrian immediately gave up Mesopotamia and Assyria, restored Armenia to client status, and set Parthamaspates over a smaller kingdom, returning to a frontier on the Euphrates.

events.title: Siege of Hatra (117)
events.summary: Trajan attacked the desert caravan city of Hatra, but its walls, the lack of water, wood and fodder, swarms of flies and violent storms defeated him; a cavalryman beside the emperor was killed by an arrow. He withdrew, already ill.

sides.losses: considerable, including from disease and heat

battle.significance: Final failure of Trajan's eastern campaign.

events.title: Lusius Quietus governs Judaea; the "War of Qitos"
events.summary: After suppressing the Jews of Mesopotamia, the Moorish general Lusius Quietus was made governor of Judaea in 117, the province being raised to consular rank; rabbinic sources remember a "war of Qitos" (polemos shel Qitos), and Marcius Turbo crushed the revolt in Egypt and Cyrene.

events.title: Unrest in Britain at Hadrian's accession
events.summary: The Historia Augusta says that at Hadrian's accession "the Britons could not be kept under Roman control", and Fronto later compared the soldiers killed in Britain under Hadrian with the losses of the Jewish war; Quintus Pompeius Falco restored order c. 118-122 and coins of 119 show BRITANNIA.

events.title: Execution of the four consulars
events.summary: Before Hadrian reached Rome, four senior ex-consuls, Lusius Quietus, Cornelius Palma, Avidius Nigrinus and Publilius Celsus, were executed by order of the Senate for an alleged plot. Hadrian claimed he had not ordered it, blamed the prefect Attianus, and swore never to execute a senator without a senatorial trial.

events.title: Hadrian cancels 900 million sesterces of debts
events.summary: Hadrian remitted 900 million sesterces of arrears owed to the imperial treasury from the preceding sixteen years and had the records publicly burned in the Forum of Trajan.

events.title: Rebuilding of the Pantheon
events.summary: Hadrian's Pantheon, with its unreinforced concrete dome 43.3 m in diameter, the same as its height, and an oculus 8.9 m wide, remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Hadrian kept Agrippa's dedicatory inscription on the porch.

events.title: Hadrian's Villa at Tibur
events.summary: Below Tibur Hadrian built a palace-villa covering some 120 hectares, a summary of the empire with buildings named, according to the Historia Augusta, after famous places: the Lyceum, the Academy, the Prytaneum, the Canopus, the Poikile and the Vale of Tempe.

events.title: Roxolani crisis and Hadrian's reorganisation of Dacia
events.summary: In 117-119 the Iazyges and Roxolani attacked the lower Danube; Hadrian negotiated with the Roxolanian king, restoring his subsidy, while Marcius Turbo held a special command over Dacia and Pannonia Inferior. Dacia was then divided into Superior and Inferior, with Porolissensis added c. 123.

events.title: Juvenal's Satires
events.summary: Decimus Junius Juvenalis published sixteen verse satires in five books between about 110 and 130, indignant portraits of Rome's vices: the dangers of city life (3), Domitian's turbot council (4), women (6), the vanity of human wishes (10).

events.title: Hadrian's first great journey
events.summary: Hadrian left Rome in 121 on the first of his tours of the provinces, inspecting armies and cities in Gaul, the German frontier (where he had a continuous palisade of great stakes built), Britain, Spain, Mauretania, the East (averting a Parthian war by a meeting with Osroes), Asia, Greece (initiation at Eleusis) and Sicily (climbing Etna), returning in 125.
events.locName: Upper German limes and the provinces

events.title: Hadrian on the Rhine and the frontier palisade
events.summary: Setting out on his first great tour in 121, Hadrian inspected the Rhine armies, enforcing discipline, removing luxuries from the camps and living like a soldier, and ordered a continuous wooden palisade "like a wall" along the open stretches of frontier in Germany.
events.locName: Mogontiacum and the Upper German frontier

events.title: Plotina's petition for the Epicurean school at Athens
events.summary: In 121 the widowed Plotina petitioned Hadrian to allow the head of the Epicurean school at Athens to choose his successor from among non-citizens and to make his choice by will in Greek; Hadrian agreed, and her letter to the Epicureans calling him "benefactor and overseer of all culture" survives on stone.

events.title: Suetonius's Lives of the Caesars and his dismissal
events.summary: Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, Hadrian's secretary for correspondence (ab epistulis), dedicated the Lives of the Twelve Caesars to the praetorian prefect Septicius Clarus c. 121, and in 122 both were dismissed for behaving too familiarly towards the empress Sabina.

events.title: Construction of Hadrian's Wall begins
events.summary: After Hadrian's visit to Britain in 122, the governor Aulus Platorius Nepos began a wall 80 Roman miles long from the Tyne to the Solway, 'to separate the barbarians from the Romans', as the Historia Augusta puts it. It was built by the three British legions, in stone in the east and initially turf in the west.

events.title: Hadrian winters at Tarraco
events.summary: After Britain and southern Gaul, where he built a basilica at Nemausus in memory of Plotina, Hadrian wintered in 122/123 at Tarraco, restoring the temple of Augustus, convening an assembly of all Spain about army recruitment and escaping an attack by a slave with a sword, whom he handed over to doctors as insane.

events.title: Hadrian averts a Parthian war on the Euphrates
events.summary: In 123, hearing of preparations for war by Osroes, Hadrian hurried from the West to the Euphrates and settled the matter in a personal meeting, promising later to return Osroes's daughter, captured by Trajan at Ctesiphon in 116.

events.title: Hadrian in Bithynia and Asia; Antinous
events.summary: Wintering in Bithynia in 123/124, Hadrian funded the rebuilding of Nicomedia and Nicaea after a severe earthquake; it was probably here that he met Antinous of Claudiopolis (Bithynium), who became his companion.

events.title: Hadrian initiated at Eleusis
events.summary: In autumn 124 Hadrian, wintering at Athens, was initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries, as Augustus had been, and in 125 presided over the Dionysia in Greek dress as archon; he gave Athens new laws, an oil law regulating exports and lavish gifts.

events.title: Hadrian climbs Etna to see the sunrise
events.summary: On his way back to Rome in 125 Hadrian climbed Etna to watch the sunrise, which was said to appear in rainbow colours, and repeated the exploit on Mount Casius in Syria in 129, where a lightning bolt struck the victim and the attendant during his sacrifice.

events.title: Mining regulations of Vipasca
events.summary: Two bronze tablets found at Aljustrel in 1876 and 1906 preserve regulations for the imperial copper and silver mining district of Vipasca under Hadrian, setting out the rights of lessees of mine shafts and the monopolies in the mining village (baths, cobbling, barbering, auctioneering).

events.title: Hadrian's address to the army at Lambaesis
events.summary: After watching manoeuvres of legio III Augusta and its auxiliaries in Numidia, Hadrian addressed the troops, and his speeches were inscribed on a column base at Lambaesis. They are the only surviving texts of an emperor's adlocutio to soldiers.

events.title: Hadrian's second stay at Athens; pater patriae
events.summary: In 128, after accepting the title pater patriae and visiting Africa, Hadrian spent the winter of 128/129 at Athens with Sabina and Antinous, receiving the epopteia at Eleusis and planning the completion of the Olympieion.

events.title: Hadrian tours Asia, Cappadocia and Syria
events.summary: In 129 Hadrian passed through Caria, Cilicia and Cappadocia to Antioch, summoned the client kings of the East to a conference, climbed Mount Casius, and visited Palmyra, which took the name Hadriana Palmyra, and the cities of Arabia.

events.title: Death of Antinous
events.summary: Hadrian's young Bithynian favourite Antinous drowned in the Nile near Hermopolis during the imperial tour of Egypt. Hadrian wept 'like a woman', founded the city of Antinoopolis at the spot on 30 October 130, and promoted the cult of Antinous as a god throughout the Greek East.

events.title: Foundation of Antinoopolis
events.summary: On 30 October 130, near the place where Antinous drowned in the Nile, Hadrian founded the Greek city of Antinoopolis, with settlers drawn from Ptolemais and the Fayum, privileges modelled on Naucratis, and a cult of the deified youth as Osiris-Antinous.

events.title: Hadrian and Sabina hear the Colossus of Memnon
events.summary: On 19-21 November 130 Hadrian and Sabina visited the northern Colossus of Memnon at Thebes, which "sang" at dawn; the court poet Julia Balbilla carved four Greek epigrams in Aeolic dialect on its leg recording that Memnon sang for the empress only on the second day and for Hadrian on the third.

events.title: Foundation of Aelia Capitolina
events.summary: During his visit to Judaea in 130 Hadrian refounded the ruins of Jerusalem as a Roman colony, Colonia Aelia Capitolina, named after his family and Jupiter Capitolinus, with a temple to Jupiter on or near the Temple site. Dio names this as the cause of the Bar Kokhba revolt.

events.title: Codification of the praetor's edict
events.summary: On Hadrian's orders the jurist Salvius Julianus revised and fixed the text of the edict issued by the urban praetor (and the aediles' edict), which had grown by annual accretion since the Republic. Thereafter only the emperor could change it.

events.title: Hadrian at Gerasa, Petra and Jerusalem
events.summary: In winter 129/130 and spring 130 Hadrian toured Arabia and Judaea, stayed at Gerasa, where a monumental arch was built for his visit, and on seeing the ruins of Jerusalem decided to refound it as the colony Aelia Capitolina.

events.title: Hadrian in Egypt: Pompey's tomb, the Museum and the lion hunt
events.summary: Arriving in Egypt in summer 130, Hadrian restored Pompey's tomb at Pelusium, debated with the scholars of the Museum at Alexandria, and hunted a man-eating lion in the Libyan desert with Antinous, an event celebrated in verse by Pancrates and in a hunting tondo later reused on the Arch of Constantine.

events.title: Hadrian's legal and administrative reforms
events.summary: Besides the codified edict, Hadrian forbade masters to kill slaves without a magistrate's sentence, to sell slaves to gladiatorial trainers or brothel-keepers without cause, or to castrate them; abolished private prisons (ergastula); appointed four consulars as judges for Italy; and gave the agreed opinions of licensed jurists the force of law.

events.title: Dedication of the Olympieion and foundation of the Panhellenion
events.summary: Hadrian completed the colossal temple of Olympian Zeus at Athens, begun under Peisistratos six centuries earlier, and founded the Panhellenion, a league of Greek cities of proven Hellenic descent with its seat at Athens.

events.title: Arrian's Periplus of the Euxine
events.summary: Around 131-132 Arrian, governor of Cappadocia, sailed along the south-eastern Black Sea coast inspecting forts from Trapezus to Phasis and Sebastopolis (Dioscurias), and sent Hadrian a report in Greek, the Periplus Ponti Euxini, together with a Latin dispatch now lost.
events.locName: Phasis and the eastern Black Sea

events.title: Lex Hadriana de rudibus agris
events.summary: Inscriptions from the imperial estates of the Bagradas valley (Ain el-Djemala, Ain Wassel) record a "Hadrianic law on uncultivated lands" allowing tenants to occupy waste or neglected land and plant olives and vines, with rent-free periods (ten years for olives, five for fruit trees) and hereditary rights of possession.

events.title: Outbreak of the Bar Kokhba revolt
