events.summary: Soon after Hadrian left the East, the Jews of Judaea rose under Simon bar Kosiba, whom Rabbi Akiva hailed as the messianic 'son of the star'. Prepared in secret, with weapons deliberately made defective for the Romans and then kept, the rebels operated from underground hideouts and drove the Romans from much of Judaea.

events.title: Library of Hadrian at Athens
events.summary: Hadrian built at Athens a vast colonnaded enclosure of 122 by 82 m with a hundred columns of Phrygian marble, pools, a library hall and lecture rooms, dedicated c. 132 during his last visit, which Pausanias lists among his gifts to the city.
events.locName: Athens, north of the Roman Agora

events.title: Letters of Bar Kokhba and the Babatha archive
events.summary: Caves in the Judaean desert explored in 1951-1961 yielded letters in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek from Shimon bar Kosiba, "prince of Israel", to his commanders at Ein Gedi, and the legal archive of Babatha, a Jewish woman of Mahoza in Arabia, whose family fled there in 132-135.
events.locName: Nahal Hever and Wadi Murabba'at, Judaean desert

events.title: Pons Aelius built
events.summary: In 134 Hadrian built the Pons Aelius across the Tiber as a monumental approach to his mausoleum, with three main arches and ramps at either end.

events.title: Mausoleum of Hadrian
events.summary: Hadrian's dynastic tomb on the right bank of the Tiber, begun c. 130 and completed by Antoninus Pius in 139, was a cylindrical drum 64 m across on a square base, crowned with a mound and a bronze quadriga, which received the ashes of emperors down to Caracalla.

events.title: Arrian repels the Alans from Cappadocia
events.summary: When the nomadic Alans, encouraged by king Pharasmanes of Iberia, broke through the Caucasus and raided Media and Armenia, the governor of Cappadocia, the historian Flavius Arrianus, mustered legions XV Apollinaris and XII Fulminata with auxiliaries and deterred them from invading the province.

events.title: Siege of Betar
events.summary: Sextus Julius Severus, brought from Britain, ground down the revolt by attacking small groups and starving them out. The last stronghold, Betar, a hill town south-west of Jerusalem, fell after a long siege; Bar Kosiba was killed.

sides.strength: Legions X Fretensis, VI Ferrata and detachments from many others
sides.losses: unknown; Dio says many Romans died in the war

battle.significance: Ended organised Jewish resistance; final end of Jewish political independence in antiquity.

events.title: Temple of Venus and Roma
events.summary: Hadrian dedicated the largest temple in Rome, designed by himself, on the Velia between the Forum and the Colosseum, with back-to-back cellae for Venus Felix and Roma Aeterna; it was completed under Antoninus Pius.

events.title: Hadrianic decrees and the aftermath of the Bar Kokhba war
events.summary: After the revolt Jews were banned from entering Aelia Capitolina except, later, on the 9th of Av, and rabbinic tradition remembers decrees forbidding circumcision, Sabbath observance and public teaching of the Torah, with the execution of sages such as Akiva (the "Ten Martyrs").

events.title: Judaea renamed Syria Palaestina
events.summary: After the revolt the province of Judaea was renamed Syria Palaestina, erasing the name of the Jews from the map, and Jews were banned from Jerusalem. Dio records that Judaea was left almost desolate.

events.title: Hadrian's succession arrangements
events.summary: In 136 Hadrian adopted Lucius Ceionius Commodus as Lucius Aelius Caesar and forced his 90-year-old brother-in-law Servianus and Servianus's grandson Pedanius Fuscus to die. When Aelius died on 1 January 138, Hadrian adopted Titus Aurelius Antoninus on 25 February 138, on condition that Antoninus adopt both the young Marcus Annius Verus (the future Marcus Aurelius) and Aelius's son Lucius.

events.title: The Tariff of Palmyra
events.summary: In April 137 the council of Palmyra inscribed in Greek and Palmyrene a revised tax law, one of the longest inscriptions of the Roman East, listing dues on slaves, dry goods, purple wool, perfumes, olive oil, salted fish, animals and prostitutes, with earlier rulings by Roman governors such as Germanicus and Mucianus.

events.title: Death of Hadrian
events.summary: After a long, painful illness during which he repeatedly begged for poison or a sword, Hadrian died at Baiae aged 62. The Historia Augusta preserves the poem he is said to have composed on his deathbed, beginning 'animula vagula blandula' ('little soul, wandering, charming').

events.title: Accession of Antoninus Pius
events.summary: Titus Aurelius Antoninus, a wealthy 51-year-old senator from a family of Nemausus, succeeded Hadrian, secured his deification against senatorial resistance, and received the name Pius. In 23 years of rule he never left Italy.

events.title: Antoninus forces the deification of Hadrian and becomes Pius
events.summary: Hadrian died hated by the Senate, which wanted to annul his acts and refuse him divine honours; Antoninus insisted, arguing that otherwise his own adoption would be void, and secured Hadrian's consecration, earning, by most accounts, the name Pius.

events.title: Lollius Urbicus reconquers southern Scotland
events.summary: Soon after his accession Antoninus sent Quintus Lollius Urbicus to Britain; by 142 he had defeated the peoples of the Lowlands, rebuilt Corbridge as a supply base, and begun the Antonine Wall, and Antoninus took his only imperatorial acclamation (IMP II) for the victory.

events.title: Marcus Aurelius named Caesar
events.summary: In 139 the eighteen-year-old Marcus, adopted by Antoninus in 138 under Hadrian's terms, was named Caesar, made quaestor and given residence in the House of Tiberius on the Palatine; his betrothal to Lucius Commodus's sister was broken off in favour of Antoninus's daughter Faustina.

events.title: Death of Faustina the Elder; the puellae Faustinianae
events.summary: Annia Galeria Faustina, wife of Antoninus, died in late 140 and was deified. Antoninus founded an alimentary charity for girls in her name, the puellae Faustinianae, and built her a temple in the Forum, later dedicated to both of them.
events.locName: Temple of Antoninus and Faustina, Forum Romanum

events.title: Valentinus and the Gnostic schools in Rome
events.summary: The Alexandrian Christian teacher Valentinus was active in Rome c. 136-160, developing an elaborate cosmology of divine emanations (aeons) and a myth of Sophia's fall, and nearly became bishop according to Tertullian; his followers Ptolemy and Heracleon founded the most influential "Gnostic" school.

events.title: Temple of Divine Faustina in the Forum
events.summary: After the death of Faustina the Elder in late 140, Antoninus built her a temple on the Sacra Via in 141; after his own death in 161 the Senate added his name, and the inscription still reads DIVO ANTONINO ET DIVAE FAUSTINAE EX S C.

events.title: "Rex Quadis datus": client kings given to the Quadi and Armenia
events.summary: Bronze coins of c. 140-144 show Antoninus crowning a king with the legend REX QVADIS DATVS, and others REX ARMENIIS DATVS, advertising the emperor's right to appoint client rulers beyond the frontier.
events.locName: Quadi territory north of the Danube

events.title: Construction of the Antonine Wall
events.summary: Antoninus's governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus reconquered southern Scotland and built a turf rampart on a stone base, 39 Roman miles long, across the Forth-Clyde isthmus from Bo'ness to Old Kilpatrick, with about 16-19 forts. Hadrian's Wall was largely abandoned for two decades.

events.title: Earthquake in Rhodes and Lycia
events.summary: A great earthquake around 141-142 struck Rhodes, Lycia and Caria; Antoninus funded reconstruction, and the Lycian millionaire Opramoas of Rhodiapolis gave huge sums to some thirty cities, as recorded on the walls of his tomb in a dossier of letters from the emperor and governors.

events.title: Fronto's correspondence with Marcus and Lucius
events.summary: Marcus Cornelius Fronto of Cirta, consul in 143 and the leading Latin orator of his day, exchanged letters for some thirty years with his pupils Marcus and Lucius; the letters were rediscovered by Angelo Mai in palimpsests at Milan and the Vatican in 1815 and 1823.

events.title: Marcion expelled by the Roman church
events.summary: Marcion of Sinope, a wealthy shipowner, was expelled by the church at Rome, which returned his large donation. He taught that the creator god of the Jewish scriptures was distinct from the good God revealed by Jesus, and compiled the first Christian canon: an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul.

events.title: Aelius Aristides delivers the Oration to Rome
events.summary: The Greek orator Publius Aelius Aristides of Smyrna delivered in Rome his panegyric To Rome, presenting the empire as a single city embracing the whole world, governed by law, open to talent, and guarded by an army on its frontiers like a wall around a city.

events.title: Roman garrison on the Farasan islands
events.summary: Latin inscriptions found on the Farasan islands off south-west Arabia record a vexillation of legio II Traiana Fortis and the "Ferresani portus" in 144, the most remote Roman garrison known, guarding the Red Sea route to India.

events.title: Marcus marries Faustina the Younger
events.summary: In April 145 Marcus married his cousin Faustina, Antoninus's only surviving child; after the birth of their first child in late 147 Marcus received tribunician power and proconsular imperium and Faustina the title Augusta.

events.title: Antoninus's Moorish war
events.summary: Raids by Moorish tribes into Mauretania required reinforcements drawn from Spain, Pannonia, Syria and elsewhere over several years; Pausanias says Antoninus drove the Moors back to the edge of the Atlas.

events.title: Temple of Divus Hadrianus dedicated
events.summary: In 145 Antoninus dedicated the temple of the deified Hadrian in the Campus Martius, whose eleven marble columns survive embedded in the facade of the former Rome stock exchange in the Piazza di Pietra.

events.title: Celebrations of Rome's 900th year
events.summary: In 147-148 Antoninus marked the 900th anniversary of Rome's foundation with games and a coinage reviving the city's founding legends: Aeneas carrying Anchises, the wolf and twins, Mars and Rhea Silvia, the sow of Lavinium and Romulus.

events.title: Ptolemy's Almagest and Geography
events.summary: At Alexandria Claudius Ptolemy completed the Mathematike Syntaxis (later called the Almagest), the definitive geocentric model of the universe with tables for predicting planetary positions, and the Geography, listing coordinates for some 8,000 places.

events.title: Fires, floods and famine under Antoninus Pius
events.summary: The Historia Augusta lists the misfortunes of Antoninus's reign: a famine, the collapse of the Circus Maximus, an earthquake in Rhodes and Asia, a fire in Rome that destroyed 340 apartment blocks and houses, fires at Narbo, Antioch and Carthage, and a Tiber flood, all relieved from imperial funds.

events.title: The Muziris papyrus
events.summary: A papyrus in Vienna (P. Vindob. G 40822) of the mid-second century contains a maritime loan agreement for a voyage to Muziris on the Malabar coast and, on its back, the valuation of the cargo of the ship Hermapollon: some 700 to 1,100 talents' worth of nard, ivory and textiles, enough to buy a large estate in Egypt.

events.title: Antoninus Pius's rescripts on slaves
events.summary: Antoninus ruled that a master who killed his own slave without cause was as liable as if he had killed another's, and that slaves who fled to the statues of the emperor because of intolerable cruelty must be sold to new owners, as in the case of the slaves of Julius Sabinus in Baetica.

events.title: Trouble in northern Britain c. 154-158
events.summary: Pausanias says Antoninus deprived the Brigantes of much of their land because they had attacked the Genounian district, subjects of Rome; coins of 154-155 show a dejected Britannia, and the governor Gnaeus Julius Verus brought reinforcements from the German legions c. 155-158.

events.title: Polycarp and Anicetus disagree on the date of Easter
events.summary: Around 154-155 the aged bishop Polycarp of Smyrna visited Bishop Anicetus of Rome; they failed to agree whether Easter should be kept on the 14th of Nisan whatever the weekday, as Asia did, or on the following Sunday, as at Rome, but parted in peace, Anicetus letting Polycarp celebrate the Eucharist.

events.title: Justin Martyr's First Apology
events.summary: Justin, a philosopher from Flavia Neapolis in Samaria teaching in Rome, addressed an apology for the Christians to Antoninus Pius and his adopted sons, arguing that Christians should not be punished for the name alone and that Christianity was the true philosophy.

events.title: The outer limes in Upper Germany and Raetia
events.summary: Around 155-160 the Upper German frontier was moved forward up to 30 km from the Neckar-Odenwald line to a new, ruler-straight line from Miltenberg to Lorch, running some 80 km almost without deviation, with stone forts at Osterburken, Jagsthausen and elsewhere.

events.title: Martyrdom of Polycarp
events.summary: Polycarp, the aged bishop of Smyrna and reputed disciple of the apostle John, was arrested during a festival, refused to swear by the emperor's genius, declaring 'Eighty-six years I have served him and he has done me no wrong', and was burned in the stadium.

events.title: Rise of Montanism in Phrygia
events.summary: Around 156-172 (dates vary) the Phrygian convert Montanus and the prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla began to prophesy in ecstatic trances, proclaiming the outpouring of the Paraclete and a new Jerusalem at Pepuza; the "New Prophecy" spread to Rome and Carthage, where it won Tertullian.

events.title: Apuleius tried for magic at Sabratha
events.summary: Around 158-159 the philosopher and orator Apuleius of Madauros was tried before the proconsul Claudius Maximus at Sabratha on a charge of winning the rich widow Pudentilla by magic; his defence speech, the Apology, survives and he was acquitted.

events.title: Withdrawal from the Antonine Wall
events.summary: Within two decades of its construction the Antonine Wall was abandoned and Hadrian's Wall recommissioned. Pausanias mentions a war against the Brigantes, who were deprived of land, possibly the context for a temporary withdrawal c. 155-158.

events.title: Pausanias's Description of Greece
events.summary: Between about 155 and 180 Pausanias, a Greek from Lydia, wrote a ten-book guide to the sanctuaries, monuments, art and local legends of mainland Greece, the indispensable source for archaeologists at Olympia, Delphi, Athens and elsewhere.

events.title: Appian's Roman History
events.summary: Appian of Alexandria, an advocate who secured through Fronto a procuratorship from Antoninus, wrote in Greek a history of Rome's wars arranged by region and enemy, culminating in the five books of the Civil Wars, our fullest narrative from the Gracchi to Sextus Pompey.

events.title: Death of Antoninus Pius
events.summary: Antoninus died at his estate at Lorium, aged 74, after eating Alpine cheese too greedily. In a fever he gave the tribune of the guard the watchword 'aequanimitas' and had the golden statue of Fortune transferred to Marcus's bedroom.

events.title: Joint accession of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus
events.summary: Marcus Aurelius insisted that the Senate grant his adoptive brother Lucius the same powers and title of Augustus, creating for the first time two equal emperors. They promised the praetorians 20,000 sesterces each.

events.title: Gaius's Institutes
events.summary: The jurist Gaius, otherwise almost unknown, wrote an elementary textbook of Roman law in four books arranged by persons, things and actions. It is the only classical legal work to survive substantially intact.

events.title: Battle of Elegeia
events.summary: The Parthian king Vologases IV invaded Armenia and installed his own candidate. Marcus Sedatius Severianus, governor of Cappadocia, marched in with a legion, was surrounded at Elegeia on the upper Euphrates, and after three days killed himself; his army was massacred.

battle.significance: Triggered the eastern war of Lucius Verus.

events.title: Tiber flood and famine at the start of Marcus's reign
events.summary: Soon after the joint accession a great Tiber flood in 162 destroyed buildings and many animals in the city and countryside and caused a severe famine, relieved by the emperors in person.

events.title: The Chatti invade Upper Germany and Raetia
events.summary: In 162 the Chatti broke into Upper Germany and Raetia; Gaius Aufidius Victorinus, Fronto's son-in-law, was sent to repel them, while the Britons were also restless and Calpurnius Agricola was sent against them.

events.title: Galen arrives in Rome
events.summary: In 162 the 33-year-old Galen of Pergamum, former physician to the gladiators of the high priest of Asia, came to Rome, where his public anatomical demonstrations, including vivisection of pigs to show the role of the recurrent laryngeal nerve in the voice, made him famous and controversial.

events.title: Statius Priscus takes Artaxata
events.summary: Marcus Statius Priscus, transferred from Britain, invaded Armenia, took and destroyed Artaxata, and built a new capital, Kaine Polis, with a Roman garrison. Lucius Verus took the title Armeniacus.

battle.significance: Restored Roman control of Armenia.

events.title: Lucius Verus marries Lucilla at Ephesus
events.summary: In 164 Marcus escorted his daughter Lucilla, aged about fourteen, as far as Brundisium, and Lucius left the front to marry her at Ephesus, where she became Augusta.

events.title: Sohaemus installed as king of Armenia
events.summary: After Statius Priscus took Artaxata in 163, Rome built a new capital at Kainepolis (Vagharshapat) and installed Sohaemus, an Arsacid-Emesene prince and Roman senator, as king of Armenia; coins of 164 show Lucius giving him the crown with the legend REX ARMENIIS DATVS.

events.title: Avidius Cassius sacks Seleucia and Ctesiphon
events.summary: Avidius Cassius advanced down the Euphrates, then crossed to the Tigris, where the great Hellenistic city of Seleucia received the Romans as friends but was sacked and burned; the Parthian palace at Ctesiphon was destroyed.

sides.losses: light in battle; heavy later to plague

battle.significance: Destroyed the greatest Greek city of Mesopotamia; associated in tradition with the origin of the Antonine Plague.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.summary: An epidemic that broke out in the Roman army in Mesopotamia around 165 reached Rome in 166 and swept the empire for over a decade, with a severe recurrence in 189. Galen's description of fever, diarrhoea and a black pustular rash makes smallpox the most likely identification.

events.title: Raising of legions II and III Italica
events.summary: In anticipation of war on the Danube, Marcus Aurelius raised two new legions in Italy, II Italica and III Italica; they were later stationed in Noricum (Lauriacum) and Raetia (Castra Regina), provinces that had never had legions before.
events.locName: Castra Regina (Regensburg), later base of III Italica

events.title: Romans take Edessa, Nisibis and Dura-Europos
events.summary: In 165 Roman columns under Avidius Cassius advanced down the Euphrates, winning a battle at Europos (Dura) and taking the city, while Martius Verus captured Edessa and restored the pro-Roman king Mannus; Nisibis also fell.

events.title: Martyrdom of Justin and his companions
events.summary: Around 165 the Christian philosopher Justin and six companions were tried before the urban prefect Quintus Junius Rusticus, Marcus Aurelius's Stoic teacher, refused to sacrifice and were beheaded; the Acts of their martyrdom preserve the interrogation.

events.title: Parthian triumph of Marcus and Verus
events.summary: Marcus and Lucius celebrated a joint triumph for the Parthian war, taking the titles Armeniacus, Parthicus Maximus and Medicus. Marcus's sons Commodus (aged five) and Annius Verus were made Caesars.

events.title: Lucian's How to Write History
events.summary: Lucian of Samosata wrote How to Write History c. 166, satirising the flood of flattering histories of Lucius Verus's Parthian war, which invented battles, borrowed from Thucydides and made Roman generals into Achilles.

events.title: Avidius Cassius invades Media
events.summary: In 166 Avidius Cassius crossed the Tigris and invaded Media, earning Lucius and Marcus the title Medicus; but the plague, said to have broken out in Seleucia, spread through the army, which returned to Syria.

events.title: Roman "embassy" reaches the Han court
events.summary: The Book of the Later Han records that in 166 an embassy from Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus), king of Da Qin (the Roman empire), arrived from beyond Rinan (Vietnam) and presented ivory, rhinoceros horn and tortoiseshell, the first direct contact recorded between Rome and China.

events.title: The Antonine Plague reaches Rome
events.summary: Brought back by Verus's army, the plague reached Rome in 166, killing thousands; the Historia Augusta says that corpses were carried away in carts, and that Marcus buried the poor at public expense and issued laws on burial.

events.title: Alexander of Abonoteichus and the plague oracle
events.summary: The prophet Alexander of Abonoteichus, founder of the oracle of the human-headed snake god Glykon, issued during the plague a one-line verse oracle, "Phoebus the unshorn keeps off the cloud of plague", which was inscribed over doorways, ironically, Lucian says, the houses so marked suffering worst.

events.title: Langobardi and Obii cross the Danube
events.summary: Six thousand Langobardi and Obii crossed the Danube into Pannonia and were destroyed by cavalry under Vindex and infantry under Candidus. Eleven tribes then sent envoys, led by the Marcomannic king Ballomar, to the governor Iallius Bassus to make peace.

battle.significance: First of the incursions that grew into the Marcomannic Wars.

events.title: Marcus and Lucius set out for the northern front
events.summary: In spring 168 both emperors left Rome for Aquileia to meet the barbarian incursions; the Marcomanni and Victuali sought terms, the praetorian prefect Furius Victorinus died of plague, and the army was ravaged by disease in the winter of 168/169.

events.title: The three Dacias under one consular legate
events.summary: Around 168 Marcus united the three Dacian provinces (Porolissensis, Apulensis, Malvensis) under a consular legate, Marcus Claudius Fronto, who also held Moesia Superior; he was killed fighting Germans and Iazyges in 170.

events.title: Debasement of the denarius under Marcus and Commodus
events.summary: Under the fiscal strain of the plague and the northern wars the silver content of the denarius fell from about 83% under Antoninus Pius to about 75-79% by the late years of Marcus, and somewhat further under Commodus, who also lowered its weight.

events.title: Death of Lucius Verus
events.summary: Returning from Aquileia to Rome with Marcus, Lucius Verus suffered a stroke in his carriage near Altinum and died three days later, aged 38. Marcus became sole emperor.

events.title: Marcus auctions the palace treasures
events.summary: To finance the war without new taxes, Marcus held a two-month auction in the Forum of Trajan of imperial furniture, gold and crystal goblets, statues, paintings, and Faustina's silk and gold-embroidered robes and jewels.

events.title: Marcomanni and Quadi invade Italy; siege of Aquileia
events.summary: After a major Roman offensive across the Danube failed with heavy losses (Lucian gives 20,000 killed), the Marcomanni and Quadi broke through the Pannonian frontier, crossed the Julian Alps, destroyed Opitergium and besieged Aquileia, the first invasion of Italy since the Cimbri.

battle.significance: First barbarian invasion of Italy in nearly three centuries; a profound shock to the Antonine order.

events.title: Costoboci raid Greece; Moors invade Baetica
events.summary: In 170 or 171 the Costoboci from north of Dacia raided through Moesia, Thrace and Macedonia into Achaea, sacking the sanctuary of Eleusis. In 171-172 Moorish raiders crossed into Baetica and besieged Singilia Barba and threatened Italica.

events.title: Astingi and Lacringi on the Dacian frontier
events.summary: In 171 the Vandal Astingi under their kings Raus and Raptus came to Dacia seeking land in return for alliance; the governor Sextus Cornelius Clemens set them against the Costoboci, but the Lacringi, fearing their presence, attacked them, and the Astingi became Roman allies.

events.title: Marcus at Carnuntum: invaders expelled from Italy and Noricum
events.summary: In 171 Marcus established his headquarters at Carnuntum; Claudius Pompeianus and Pertinax cleared the invaders from Italy and Noricum, destroying Marcomannic war bands as they recrossed the Danube with booty, and Marcus received embassies from peoples seeking alliance or terms.

events.title: Revolt of the Bucoli in Egypt
events.summary: The 'herdsmen' (Boukoloi) of the Nile Delta marshes, led by a priest named Isidorus, rose, defeated Roman troops and nearly captured Alexandria; Avidius Cassius, sent from Syria, suppressed them by dividing their forces.

events.title: The Rain Miracle
events.summary: A Roman force surrounded by the Quadi and dying of thirst under the summer sun was saved by a sudden downpour, while hail and lightning struck the enemy, enabling a Roman victory. The Column of Marcus shows a winged rain god streaming water over the soldiers.

sides.strength: Field army, including legio XII Fulminata in the Christian version

battle.significance: Became a classic of both pagan and Christian claims to divine favour.

events.title: Marcus Aurelius writes the Meditations
events.summary: During his campaigns Marcus wrote, in Greek, private notes of Stoic self-exhortation known as 'To Himself' (Ta eis heauton), now called the Meditations. Book 1 is headed 'among the Quadi on the Granua' and Book 2 'at Carnuntum'.

events.title: Marcus defeats the Marcomanni; title Germanicus
events.summary: In 172 Marcus crossed the Danube into the Marcomannic lands, winning victories that earned him and Commodus the title Germanicus and coins proclaiming GERMANIA SVBACTA, the year also of the "rain miracle" and, according to coins and the column, a lightning miracle that destroyed an enemy siege engine.

events.title: The Chauci raid Gallia Belgica
events.summary: Around 172 the Chauci raided the coast of Gallia Belgica; the governor Didius Julianus, the future emperor, defeated them with hastily levied provincial troops.

events.title: Barbarian settlers in Italy and the revolt at Ravenna
events.summary: Marcus settled surrendered Germans within the empire, including in Italy; when those planted near Ravenna rebelled and tried to seize the city, he expelled all barbarians from Italy and settled them only in the frontier provinces.

events.title: Battle on the frozen Danube
events.summary: Iazyges cavalry, pursued onto the frozen Danube, turned to fight, hoping their horses would have the advantage on the ice. The Romans formed up, braced their feet on their shields, seized the reins and shields of the enemy and dragged riders and horses down, winning the fight.

battle.significance: Illustrates Roman adaptability against Sarmatian cavalry.

events.title: The Quadi depose Furtius; Marcus puts a price on Ariogaesus
events.summary: In 174 the Quadi expelled their Roman-approved king Furtius and chose Ariogaesus; Marcus refused to recognise him and offered 1,000 gold pieces to anyone who brought him alive and 500 for his head, and when Ariogaesus was captured, exiled him to Alexandria.

events.title: Revolt of Avidius Cassius
events.summary: On a false report of Marcus's death, Gaius Avidius Cassius, holding a special command over the whole East, was proclaimed emperor and recognised in Syria, Egypt and much of the East. After three months and six days he was murdered by a centurion and his head sent to Marcus.

events.title: Peace with the Iazyges
events.summary: To free himself to deal with Cassius, Marcus made peace with the Iazyges under their king Zanticus. They returned 100,000 Roman captives, were barred from settling within a strip along the Danube, and supplied 8,000 cavalry, of whom 5,500 were sent to Britain.

events.title: Death of Faustina the Younger at Halala
events.summary: Accompanying Marcus to the East after Avidius Cassius's revolt, Faustina, "Mother of the Camps" (mater castrorum) since 174, died in winter 175/176 at Halala in the Taurus foothills, which Marcus refounded as the colony Faustinopolis.

events.title: German and Sarmatian triumph; Column of Marcus Aurelius
events.summary: Marcus and Commodus triumphed over the Germans and Sarmatians on 23 December 176. A column with a spiral relief of the wars, modelled on Trajan's, was erected in the Campus Martius and completed by 193.

events.title: Marcus at Athens: initiation and chairs of philosophy
events.summary: Returning from the East, Marcus and Commodus were initiated into the Eleusinian mysteries, and Marcus endowed chairs of philosophy at Athens for the Platonic, Aristotelian, Stoic and Epicurean schools, with salaries of 10,000 drachmas, plus a chair of rhetoric.

events.title: Marcus's tour of the East after Cassius's revolt
events.summary: In 175-176 Marcus, with Commodus, toured Syria, Egypt and Asia; he burned Cassius's correspondence unread, pardoned most supporters, punished Antioch by suspending its games and assemblies, behaved at Alexandria as a citizen and philosopher, and at Smyrna heard Aelius Aristides declaim.

events.title: Commodus made co-Augustus
events.summary: Marcus made his 15-year-old son Commodus consul and co-Augustus with tribunician power, breaking with the century-old practice of adopting an adult successor and returning to hereditary succession.

events.title: Martyrs of Lyon and Vienne
events.summary: A pogrom against the Christians of Lugdunum and Vienne culminated in the trial and execution of some 48 believers, including the 90-year-old bishop Pothinus, who died in prison, and the slave woman Blandina, who survived days of torture and was finally gored by a bull in the amphitheatre.
events.locName: Amphitheatre of the Three Gauls, Lugdunum

events.title: Senatus consultum on the cost of gladiatorial games
events.summary: On the proposal of Marcus and Commodus, the Senate capped the prices that could be charged for gladiators by class and abolished the treasury's tax on gladiatorial sales, relieving provincial high priests burdened by the obligation to give games.

events.title: Tabula Banasitana: citizenship for a Moorish chief
events.summary: A bronze tablet found at Banasa in 1957 records grants of Roman citizenship in 168/169 and 177 by Marcus (and Commodus) to Julianus of the Zegrenses, a Moorish tribal leader, and his family, "salvo iure gentis", without prejudice to their tribal law or the taxes due to the fisc.

events.title: Marcus and Commodus leave for the second German expedition
events.summary: On 3 August 178 Marcus and Commodus left Rome for the Danube after Marcus, acting as fetial priest, hurled a bloody spear from the temple of Bellona into "enemy territory", reviving an ancient rite of declaring war.

events.title: Celsus writes the True Doctrine against the Christians
events.summary: Around 175-180 the Platonist Celsus wrote the Alethes Logos, the first known systematic pagan attack on Christianity, mocking its appeal to the uneducated, its claims about Jesus's birth and resurrection and its refusal to serve the state.

events.title: Earthquake destroys Smyrna
events.summary: A violent earthquake levelled Smyrna in 177 or 178; Aelius Aristides wrote a letter to Marcus and Commodus so moving that, according to Philostratus, Marcus wept over it and promised to rebuild the city.

events.title: Senatus consultum Orfitianum
events.summary: A decree of the Senate of 178, proposed by Marcus and Commodus in the consulship of Orfitus, gave children priority over the agnatic relatives in inheriting from their mother on intestacy.

events.title: The Laugaricio inscription
events.summary: On the castle rock at Trenčín in Slovakia, some 120 km north of the Danube, a Latin inscription records that 855 soldiers of legio II Adiutrix wintered at Laugaricio 'to the victory of the emperors' under their legate Marcus Valerius Maximianus.

events.title: Paternus's victory over the Quadi
events.summary: In 179 the praetorian prefect Tarrutenius Paternus fought a day-long battle against the barbarians, probably Quadi, and destroyed their army, earning Marcus his tenth imperatorial acclamation.

battle.significance: Final Marcan victory; opened the way to annexation that Commodus abandoned.

events.title: Valerius Maximianus kills Valao, king of the Naristi
events.summary: An inscription from Diana Veteranorum (Zana) in Numidia records that Marcus Valerius Maximianus, a cavalry prefect from Poetovio, killed with his own hand Valao, chief of the Naristi, and was rewarded by Marcus with a horse, trappings and weapons.

events.title: Plans for provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia
events.summary: The Historia Augusta says that had Marcus lived another year he would have made the lands of the Marcomanni and Sarmatians into provinces; in 179-180 some 20,000 Roman soldiers were stationed in forts in Marcomannic and Quadic territory.
events.locName: Bohemia, Moravia and the Hungarian plain

events.title: Death of Marcus Aurelius
events.summary: Marcus Aurelius died on campaign, at Vindobona according to Aurelius Victor or at Sirmium according to Tertullian, aged 58, possibly of the plague. Commodus, aged 18, became sole emperor.

events.title: Martyrs of Scilli
events.summary: On 17 July 180 twelve Christians from Scilli in Africa were tried before the proconsul Vigellius Saturninus at Carthage and beheaded; the Acts of their martyrdom are the earliest dated document of Latin Christianity.

events.title: Commodus's peace with the Marcomanni and Quadi
events.summary: Against the advice of senior generals like Pompeianus, Commodus ended the war on terms: the Marcomanni and Quadi returned prisoners and deserters, paid annual grain and supplied weapons and recruits, were forbidden to settle near the Danube or to assemble except monthly in one place under a Roman centurion. Roman garrisons in barbaricum were withdrawn.

events.title: Irenaeus of Lyon writes Against Heresies
events.summary: Around 180 Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon after the martyrdoms of 177, wrote five books of the Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called against Valentinian and other Gnostics, arguing from a four-gospel canon and the succession of bishops from the apostles.

events.title: Conspiracy of Lucilla
events.summary: Commodus's elder sister Lucilla, widow of Lucius Verus, plotted his murder with Ummidius Quadratus and Claudius Pompeianus Quintianus. Quintianus botched the attack at the entrance to the amphitheatre by brandishing his dagger and shouting 'This is what the Senate sends you!'

events.title: War in northern Britain under Commodus
events.summary: Dio calls it the greatest of Commodus's wars: northern tribes crossed 'the wall separating them from the Roman forts', killed a general and his troops, and were driven back by the harsh disciplinarian Ulpius Marcellus. Commodus took the title Britannicus in 184.

events.title: Petition of the coloni of the saltus Burunitanus
events.summary: An inscription from Souk el-Khmis in Tunisia records a petition by the tenant farmers of the imperial estate called saltus Burunitanus to Commodus (c. 180-183), complaining that the lessee Allius Maximus, with the procurator's collusion, demanded more than the six days' labour a year allowed by the Hadrianic law and had them beaten; Commodus ordered the law upheld.

events.title: Execution of the Quintilii brothers
events.summary: After the conspiracy of Lucilla, Commodus executed the brothers Sextus Quintilius Condianus and Sextus Quintilius Valerius Maximus, consuls together in 151, inseparable in life and in their joint letters, and the praetorian prefect Tarrutenius Paternus.
events.locName: Villa of the Quintilii, Via Appia

events.title: War with the free Dacians under Commodus
events.summary: Around 182-183 the free Dacians beyond the province rose and were defeated by commanders including the future rivals Clodius Albinus and Pescennius Niger; Commodus took the title Germanicus Maximus, and the governor Sabinianus settled 12,000 Dacians expelled from their land within the province.

events.title: Fall of Perennis
events.summary: The praetorian prefect Sextus Tigidius Perennis, who governed while Commodus amused himself, was overthrown when a delegation of 1,500 javelin-men from the army of Britain marched to Rome and accused him of plotting to make his son emperor. Commodus surrendered him to them, and he was killed with his family.

events.title: Pertinax suppresses a mutiny in Britain
events.summary: Sent to govern Britain after the fall of Perennis, Pertinax faced a mutiny in which a legion tried to proclaim him emperor; he refused, was left for dead in a riot, recovered and punished the mutineers severely, and asked to be recalled because of his unpopularity with the troops.

events.title: The 'War of the Deserters' of Maternus
events.summary: A deserter named Maternus led bands of fugitive soldiers and brigands who plundered Gaul and Spain, storming towns and freeing prisoners. He then plotted to infiltrate Rome disguised as a praetorian and kill Commodus at the festival of the Hilaria, but was betrayed and beheaded.

events.title: Commodus founds an African grain fleet
events.summary: Around 186 Commodus created a state fleet to carry African grain to Rome, the classis Africana Commodiana Herculea, as a reserve in case the Egyptian grain supply failed.

events.title: Return of the plague: 2,000 deaths a day in Rome
events.summary: In 189 the plague returned in the worst outbreak Dio, then a senator in Rome, ever knew, with 2,000 people often dying in a single day; Commodus withdrew to Laurentum, where the laurel groves were thought to protect against infection.

events.title: The death of Julius Alexander of Emesa
events.summary: Around 189-190 Commodus sent assassins against Julius Alexander of Emesa, a noble who had killed a lion with a javelin from horseback; Alexander killed them, fled towards Parthia with a favourite boy, and when overtaken killed the boy and himself.

events.title: Grain riot and fall of Cleander
events.summary: The freedman chamberlain Marcus Aurelius Cleander, who sold offices so freely that there were 25 consuls in a single year, was blamed for a grain shortage. A crowd at the Circus rioted, marched on Commodus at the villa of the Quintilii, and Commodus had Cleander executed and his head handed to the mob.
events.locName: Villa of the Quintilii, Via Appia

events.title: Marcia secures the release of Christians from the Sardinian mines
events.summary: Around 190 Commodus's mistress Marcia, who favoured the Christians, obtained from Bishop Victor of Rome a list of confessors condemned to the mines of Sardinia and secured their release through the presbyter Hyacinthus; among them was the future pope Callistus.

events.title: Victor of Rome and the Quartodeciman controversy
events.summary: Around 190 Bishop Victor of Rome demanded that the churches of Asia abandon their custom of celebrating Easter on 14 Nisan and threatened to excommunicate them; Polycrates of Ephesus refused, citing apostolic tradition, and Irenaeus urged Victor to keep peace as his predecessors had.

events.title: Assassination of Commodus
events.summary: On the last night of 192, as Commodus planned to enter his consulship on 1 January dressed as a gladiator, his mistress Marcia, the chamberlain Eclectus and the praetorian prefect Laetus gave him poisoned food. When he vomited it, they sent the wrestler Narcissus to strangle him in his bath.

events.title: Commodus as Hercules; Rome renamed Colonia Commodiana
events.summary: In his last years Commodus identified himself with Hercules, renamed Rome the 'Colonia Lucia Annia Commodiana', renamed the months after his twelve names, and fought as a secutor in the arena, killing animals by the hundred.

events.title: Fire of 192
events.summary: A fire, starting perhaps from an earthquake or lightning, destroyed the Temple of Peace, the warehouses along the Via Sacra, the temple of Vesta (from which the Palladium was rescued) and parts of the Palatine.
events.locName: Temple of Peace and Via Sacra, Rome

events.title: The Praetorians auction the empire to Didius Julianus
events.summary: After murdering Pertinax on 28 March 193, the Praetorian Guard sold the throne to the senator Marcus Didius Julianus, who outbid Pertinax's father-in-law Flavius Sulpicianus with a promise of 25,000 sesterces per guardsman.

events.title: Pescennius Niger proclaimed emperor at Antioch
events.summary: Gaius Pescennius Niger, governor of Syria, was acclaimed by the eastern legions and enjoyed the support of the Roman populace, but delayed in Antioch while Severus took Rome.

events.title: Septimius Severus proclaimed emperor at Carnuntum
events.summary: Lucius Septimius Severus, legate of Pannonia Superior, was hailed Augustus by the Danube legions at Carnuntum, posing as the avenger of Pertinax and adding Pertinax to his name.

events.title: Severus enters Rome and disbands the Praetorian Guard
events.summary: After the Senate condemned Julianus, who was killed in the palace on 1 June 193, Severus summoned the Praetorians unarmed, cashiered them and replaced them with a doubled guard drawn from his Danubian legionaries.

events.title: Severus stages the funeral and deification of Pertinax
events.summary: Soon after entering Rome Severus had Pertinax consecrated as divus and staged a lavish funerary consecratio with a wax effigy on a pyre in the Campus Martius, described as an eyewitness by Cassius Dio. The ceremony advertised Severus as avenger and heir of the murdered emperor, whose name he had already taken.

events.title: Clodius Albinus accepts the title of Caesar
events.summary: Decimus Clodius Albinus, governor of Britain with three legions, accepted Severus' offer of the rank of Caesar and coinage in his name, neutralising him while Severus dealt with Niger.

events.title: Battle of Cyzicus
events.summary: Severan forces defeated and killed Niger's general Asellius Aemilianus near Cyzicus, opening Asia Minor to Severus.

battle.significance: First major defeat for Niger; he withdrew behind the Taurus and the Cilician Gates.

events.title: Siege of Byzantium
events.summary: Byzantium, having sided with Niger, held out against Severan forces for some two and a half years, surviving even after Niger's death until famine forced surrender in late 195.

sides.strength: citizens and Nigerian remnants; c. 500 small boats

battle.significance: Destroyed the walls guarding the Bosporus, which Dio later blamed for opening the straits to raiders.

events.title: Clash at Perinthus
events.summary: Pescennius Niger's forces, having seized Byzantium, attempted to take Perinthus on the Propontis, but the Severan vanguard held the city; Dio records ominous prodigies and losses among Severus' troops. The check confined Niger to Byzantium and the Asian side.

battle.significance: Kept Thrace in Severan hands and opened the long siege of Byzantium.

events.title: Battle of Issus
events.summary: On the plain of Issus, where Alexander had beaten Darius, Severus' general Publius Cornelius Anullinus decisively defeated Pescennius Niger, whose army broke after a storm blew in its face.

battle.significance: Ended Niger's bid; the East passed to Severus, who punished Antioch and rewarded Laodicea.

events.title: Battle of Nicaea
events.summary: Niger in person was defeated by the Severan general Tiberius Claudius Candidus in the defiles between Cius and Nicaea, and retreated through the Cilician Gates.

battle.significance: Drove Niger out of Asia Minor.

events.title: Syria divided; Antioch humiliated
events.summary: After Niger's defeat Severus split Syria into Syria Coele and Syria Phoenice, stripped Antioch of its city status in favour of Laodicea, and punished other Nigerian cities.

events.title: Severus' first eastern campaign: Osroene and Adiabene
events.summary: In 195 Severus crossed the Euphrates against Osroene, Adiabene and Arab allies who had supported Niger and besieged Nisibis, taking the titles Arabicus and Adiabenicus.

events.title: Severus declares himself son of Marcus Aurelius
events.summary: Severus retroactively adopted himself into the Antonine house as 'divi Marci filius', renamed his son Bassianus Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (Caracalla) and made him Caesar, an open break with Albinus.

events.title: Clodius Albinus proclaimed Augustus
events.summary: Cut out of the succession, Albinus was hailed Augustus by the British legions and crossed to Gaul, setting up his base at Lugdunum, where he minted coins; the Senate declared him a public enemy in December 196.

events.title: Fall and punishment of Byzantium
events.summary: After a siege of some two and a half years, during which its engineer Priscus built machines that Dio admired, starving Byzantium surrendered. Severus executed its magistrates and soldiers, razed its famous walls, confiscated its property and made it a village subject to Perinthus; Caracalla later persuaded him to restore it.

battle.significance: Removed the last Nigrian stronghold; destruction of the walls weakened the Bosporus against later Gothic raids, as Dio notes.

events.title: Battle of Lugdunum
events.summary: Severus defeated Clodius Albinus in a vast battle north of Lyon; Dio puts some 150,000 men on each side. Albinus committed suicide or was killed and his corpse was mutilated; Lugdunum was sacked.

sides.strength: c. 150,000 (Dio); British legions and Gallic recruits

battle.significance: The largest battle between Roman armies recorded; ended the civil wars of 193-197 and left Severus sole ruler.

events.title: Severus' purge of the Senate
events.summary: Returning to Rome in June 197, Severus praised the cruelty of Marius, Sulla and Augustus before the Senate and executed 29 senators accused of supporting Albinus, while sparing 35 others.

events.title: Severan army reforms: pay, marriage and new legions
events.summary: Severus raised military pay (legionary stipendium probably from 300 to 450 or 500 denarii), allowed serving soldiers to marry legally, and raised three new legions, I, II and III Parthica, the latter two under equestrian prefects.

events.title: Parthian siege of Nisibis
events.summary: While Severus fought Albinus, Vologaeses V attacked the new Roman positions in Mesopotamia and besieged Nisibis, defended by Julius Laetus until Severus' arrival in summer 197 lifted the threat.

battle.significance: Gave Severus his casus belli for a full invasion of Parthia.

events.title: Severus sacks Ctesiphon
events.summary: Sailing down the Euphrates with a river fleet, Severus took Seleucia and Babylon, then stormed the Parthian capital Ctesiphon in late 197 or January 198, sacking it and, according to Dio, carrying off 100,000 captives.

sides.strength: perhaps 3 Parthian legions plus vexillations and a river fleet

battle.significance: Humiliated the Arsacids and made Mesopotamia a permanent Roman province.

events.title: Legio II Parthica stationed at Albanum
events.summary: Severus based the new II Parthica in a fortress at Albanum 20 km from Rome, the first legion stationed in Italy under the Principate. With the doubled Praetorian Guard and enlarged urban cohorts, it gave the emperor some 30,000 troops near the capital, a decisive military reserve.

events.title: Tertullian's Apologeticum
events.summary: Writing at Carthage in 197, the year of the Severan civil war, Tertullian addressed to the provincial governors a legal and rhetorical defence of Christians, attacking trials for "the name" alone and claiming that Christians prayed for the emperor; it contains his famous "semen est sanguis Christianorum" and marks the birth of Latin Christian literature.

events.title: Caracalla raised to Augustus, Geta to Caesar
events.summary: On the centenary of Trajan's accession and the day of the victory proclamation over Parthia, Severus made the ten-year-old Caracalla co-Augustus and his younger son Geta Caesar.

events.title: First Severan siege of Hatra
events.summary: Returning up the Tigris, Severus attacked Hatra, the walled Arab caravan city in the desert, but its engines and naphtha bombs burned his siege works and he withdrew.

battle.significance: Repeated Trajan's failure of 117 at the same city.

events.title: Creation of the province of Mesopotamia
events.summary: Severus organised northern Mesopotamia as a province under an equestrian prefect with legions I and III Parthica, centred on Nisibis, now a Roman colonia.

events.title: Numidia separated from Africa Proconsularis
events.summary: Under Severus the military zone of the legate of III Augusta became a separate province, Numidia, with its capital at Lambaesis, formalising a de facto division since Caligula. Severus also pushed the Tripolitanian and Numidian frontier south with new forts such as Gholaia (Bu Njem, 201) and Castellum Dimmidi.

events.title: Second Severan siege of Hatra
events.summary: Severus returned to Hatra in 199 with larger engines; when a breach was made, he called off the assault, hoping the city would surrender its treasure intact, but his exasperated European troops refused to renew the attack and the siege was abandoned after 20 days.

battle.significance: Ended Severus' eastern offensives.

events.title: Severus in Egypt; Alexandria receives a council
events.summary: Severus toured Egypt and Upper Egypt, visiting Memphis, Thebes and the 'singing' colossus of Memnon, and granted Alexandria and the metropoleis of the nomes town councils (boulai), a major change in Egyptian administration.

events.title: Severus visits Africa; building at Lepcis and the Tripolitanian frontier
events.summary: Severus returned to his native Lepcis Magna, which received the ius Italicum, a new forum, basilica, colonnaded street and harbour, while the frontier of Tripolitania was pushed south with forts at Gholaia (Bu Njem), Gheriat and Cidamus (Ghadames).

events.title: Persecution at Alexandria; martyrdom of Leonides
events.summary: Christians were arrested and executed in Egypt under the prefect Laetus, among them Leonides, father of the 17-year-old Origen, whose mother hid his clothes to stop him seeking martyrdom. Clement left Alexandria and Origen took over catechetical instruction. The Historia Augusta's claim that Severus banned conversion to Judaism and Christianity is doubted.

events.title: Martyrdom of Perpetua and Felicity at Carthage
events.summary: The young noblewoman Vibia Perpetua and her slave Felicitas, catechumens, were killed in the amphitheatre of Carthage at games for Geta's birthday; the Passio preserves Perpetua's own prison diary, the earliest surviving text by a Christian woman.

events.title: Arch of Septimius Severus dedicated in the Forum
events.summary: The Senate dedicated a triple arch at the foot of the Capitol celebrating the Parthian victories, with panels showing the sieges of Nisibis, Edessa, Seleucia and Ctesiphon; Geta's name was later erased from the inscription.

events.title: Septizodium built on the Palatine
events.summary: Severus erected a three-storeyed columnar façade, the Septizodium, at the south-east corner of the Palatine facing the Via Appia, so that travellers from Africa would see his monument first (HA). Its remains were demolished by Sixtus V in 1588-89 for building material.
events.locName: Via Appia front of the Palatine, Rome

events.title: Secular Games of Septimius Severus
events.summary: Severus celebrated the seventh Ludi Saeculares in June 204, following the Augustan schedule of 110-year cycles; the acta, partly preserved on inscriptions, list Julia Domna leading 109 matrons in prayers.

events.title: Fall of the praetorian prefect Plautianus
events.summary: Gaius Fulvius Plautianus, Severus' fellow Lepcitane and all-powerful praetorian prefect, whose daughter Plautilla had married Caracalla in 202, was accused of conspiracy and cut down in the palace in Caracalla's presence.

events.title: Severan Marble Plan of Rome
events.summary: Between about 203 and 211 a marble plan of the entire city at roughly 1:240, some 18 x 13 m on 150 slabs, was fixed to a wall of the Templum Pacis (now part of Santi Cosma e Damiano). About 10-15% survives in over 1,100 fragments, the most important document of ancient Rome's topography.

events.title: Bulla Felix's bandit band in Italy
events.summary: For two years the brigand Bulla Felix and 600 followers plundered Italy, freeing imperial slaves and robbing travellers under the noses of the emperors, until he was betrayed by a mistress and thrown to the beasts.

events.title: Severus' expedition to Britain and Caledonia
events.summary: Severus, his sons and the court moved to Britain in 208, made Eboracum the imperial capital and campaigned deep into Caledonia in 209 and 210 against the Caledonii and Maeatae, building a legionary base at Carpow on the Tay.

events.title: Death of Septimius Severus at Eboracum
events.summary: Severus died of illness, probably gout-related, at York aged 65, leaving his sons as joint emperors with the advice, per Dio, to 'agree with each other, enrich the soldiers and scorn all others'.

events.title: Caracalla murders Geta
events.summary: After ten months of joint rule, during which the brothers divided the palace and reportedly considered splitting the empire, Caracalla had centurions kill Geta in the arms of their mother Julia Domna.

events.title: Caracalla's purge and the execution of Papinian
events.summary: After Geta's murder Caracalla killed his brother's friends and supporters, about 20,000 people according to Dio, including Pertinax's son, Marcus Aurelius' last daughter Cornificia and the great jurist Papinian, praetorian prefect, beheaded with an axe after allegedly refusing to justify the fratricide ('it is not as easy to defend a murder as to commit it'). Geta's name and images were erased across the empire.

events.title: Constitutio Antoniniana: citizenship for all free inhabitants
events.summary: Caracalla granted Roman citizenship to virtually all free inhabitants of the empire, excepting only the dediticii; Dio says the real motive was to extend the 5% inheritance tax (raised to 10%) and the manumission tax.

events.title: Caracalla's campaign against the Alamanni
events.summary: Caracalla crossed the Raetian limes in August 213 and defeated a Germanic coalition near the Main, taking the title Germanicus Maximus; Dio's account contains the first apparent mention of the Alamanni.
events.locName: Beyond the Raetian limes, Main region

events.title: Britain divided into Superior and Inferior
events.summary: To prevent any future governor from commanding three legions, as Clodius Albinus had, Britain was split into Britannia Superior (Londinium, legions II Augusta and XX Valeria Victrix) and Britannia Inferior (Eboracum, VI Victrix). Herodian attributes it to Severus in 197; inscriptions show it in force under Caracalla by about 213-216.

events.title: Caracalla honours Achilles at Ilium
events.summary: Marching east in imitation of Alexander, Caracalla visited Troy, sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles and staged a funeral for his freedman Festus, said by Herodian to have been poisoned for the purpose, so that he could play Achilles mourning Patroclus. He also formed a phalanx of 16,000 Macedonians armed in the ancient manner.

events.title: Introduction of the antoninianus
events.summary: Caracalla introduced a new silver coin, the radiate 'antoninianus', apparently tariffed at two denarii but weighing only about 1.5 denarii, a concealed debasement to fund army pay.

events.title: Caracalla's massacre at Alexandria
events.summary: Offended by Alexandrian lampoons mocking him as a fratricide and his pretensions to be Alexander, Caracalla had the city's youths assembled for supposed recruitment into a phalanx and massacred, then expelled non-resident Egyptians.

events.title: Baths of Caracalla dedicated
events.summary: The Thermae Antoninianae on the Via Appia, begun by Severus around 211, were dedicated in 216; the central block covered c. 2.5 hectares and could serve perhaps 1,600 bathers at once.

events.title: Caracalla's invasion of Parthia
events.summary: After Artabanus IV refused Caracalla's request to marry his daughter (a project to unite the two empires, according to Herodian), Caracalla invaded Media and Adiabene in 216, sacking towns and desecrating the royal tombs at Arbela.

events.title: Assassination of Caracalla near Carrhae
events.summary: Travelling from Edessa to the temple of the Moon god at Carrhae, Caracalla dismounted to relieve himself and was stabbed by the guardsman Julius Martialis, acting for the praetorian prefect Macrinus, who feared exposure by an astrologer's prophecy.

events.title: Battle of Nisibis
events.summary: Artabanus IV invaded Mesopotamia to avenge Caracalla's attacks and fought Macrinus near Nisibis for three days; the outcome was bloody and inconclusive, and Macrinus bought peace with 200 million sesterces.

battle.significance: Last great Roman-Arsacid battle; Macrinus' payment damaged his standing with the troops.

events.title: Revolt of Elagabalus at Raphanea
events.summary: Julia Maesa, sister of Julia Domna, had her fourteen-year-old grandson Varius Avitus Bassianus, priest of the sun god Elagabal at Emesa, presented to Legio III Gallica at Raphanea as Caracalla's bastard son; the troops proclaimed him emperor as 'Marcus Aurelius Antoninus'.

events.title: Execution of Macrinus and Diadumenian
events.summary: Beaten at Immae near Antioch on 8 June 218, Macrinus fled disguised towards Rome but was caught at Chalcedon and killed in Cappadocia; his son Diadumenian, made Augustus weeks before, was taken at Zeugma and executed. Macrinus, the first equestrian emperor, had never visited Rome as emperor.

events.title: Battle of Antioch (Immae)
events.summary: Macrinus' Praetorians were winning against the army of Elagabalus at a village about 180 stades from Antioch when Macrinus fled the field; his son Diadumenianus was caught and killed and Macrinus himself was captured in Cappadocia and executed.

battle.significance: Restored the Severan house through its Syrian female line.

events.title: Macrinus buys peace from Artabanus IV
events.summary: After the bloody drawn battle at Nisibis, Macrinus ended the Parthian war by returning prisoners and paying Artabanus IV about 200 million sesterces in gifts, while keeping the province of Mesopotamia. The payment undermined Macrinus with the army and the Senate.

events.title: Elagabalus imposes the cult of Elagabal on Rome
events.summary: The boy emperor brought the black conical baetyl of the Emesene sun god to Rome, built the Elagabalium on the Palatine, placed Elagabal above Jupiter and married the Vestal Virgin Aquilia Severa as a sacred union.

events.title: Elagabalus marries the Vestal Aquilia Severa
events.summary: Elagabalus divorced Julia Cornelia Paula and married the Vestal Virgin Julia Aquilia Severa, claiming the union of priest and priestess would produce godlike children; he also "married" his sun-stone god to the Palladium and then to the Carthaginian Caelestis. Roman opinion saw it as sacrilege punishable by burial alive.

events.title: Assassination of Elagabalus
events.summary: After Elagabalus tried to remove his popular cousin and adopted Caesar Alexianus, the Praetorians killed him and his mother Julia Soaemias, dragged the bodies through the streets and threw them into the Tiber, and hailed the thirteen-year-old Severus Alexander.

events.title: Murder of the jurist Ulpian by the Praetorians
events.summary: Domitius Ulpianus, praetorian prefect and the most prolific Roman jurist, was killed by his own guardsmen in the palace before the emperor and his mother, after three days of street fighting between the Praetorians and the people of Rome.

events.title: Battle of Hormozgan: end of the Arsacids
events.summary: Ardashir, Sasanian king of Persis, defeated and killed the last Parthian great king Artabanus IV on the plain of Hormozgan, ending 470 years of Arsacid rule and founding the Sasanian Empire.
events.locName: Plain of Hormozgan (exact site unknown, probably in Khuzestan or near Golpayegan)

battle.significance: Replaced the Arsacids with the Sasanians, Rome's principal rival until 628.

events.title: Ardashir crowned King of Kings at Ctesiphon
events.summary: Having taken Ctesiphon, Ardashir I was crowned 'King of Kings of Iran' (shahanshah eran), inaugurating a Sasanian era and an ideology tied to Zoroastrian kingship and the land of Eran.

events.title: Fall of Seius Sallustius, Severus Alexander's father-in-law
events.summary: Lucius Seius Herennius Sallustius, made Caesar when his daughter Orbiana married Severus Alexander (225), was executed for an alleged plot, and Orbiana was exiled to Libya; Herodian blames the jealousy of Julia Mamaea.

events.title: Cassius Dio's second consulship and the end of his History
events.summary: Lucius Cassius Dio, senator from Nicaea, held his second consulship with Severus Alexander as colleague and retired to Bithynia, where he completed his 80-book Roman History to 229.

events.title: Ardashir invades Roman Mesopotamia
events.summary: Ardashir attacked Roman Mesopotamia, besieged Nisibis and raided toward Cappadocia and Syria, the first Sasanian war against Rome.

events.title: Julius Africanus organises a library in the Pantheon
events.summary: The Christian chronographer Sextus Julius Africanus, who had served at Edessa and led an embassy for Emmaus-Nicopolis, designed a library in the Pantheon for Severus Alexander, as recorded in a papyrus fragment of his miscellany Kestoi (P.Oxy. 412). His Chronographiai, dating creation to 5500 BC, became the foundation of Christian world chronology.

events.title: Severus Alexander's three-pronged Persian campaign
events.summary: Alexander launched three columns, through Armenia into Media, through Mesopotamia, and under his own command in the centre; the southern column was destroyed, the northern suffered in the winter mountains, and Alexander's own force never pushed hard. Both sides were exhausted and Ardashir did not attack again for several years.

events.title: Church house at Dura-Europos
events.summary: A private house at Dura was converted around 232/3-241 into a Christian meeting place with an assembly room and a painted baptistery showing the Good Shepherd, Adam and Eve, the healing of the paralytic, Christ walking on water and women at the tomb. Buried under the rampart in 256, it is the oldest securely identified church building.

events.title: Alamanni break through the Raetian and Upper German limes
events.summary: While Severus Alexander was in the east, Germanic raiders crossed the Rhine and Danube frontier; burnt forts and coin hoards ending c. 233 cluster in the Taunus, Wetterau and Raetia (Pfünz, Saalburg). Alarming reports brought Alexander west in 234.

events.title: Murder of Severus Alexander and Julia Mamaea near Mogontiacum
events.summary: Preparing to buy peace from the Germans rather than fight, Alexander and his mother were killed by mutinous soldiers at Vicus Britannicus near Mogontiacum, and the army proclaimed the Thracian officer Maximinus.

events.title: Pontian and Hippolytus deported to Sardinia
events.summary: Under Maximinus the bishop of Rome Pontian and the rival presbyter Hippolytus were exiled to the mines of Sardinia; Pontian resigned on 28 September 235, the first exactly dated papal abdication, and both died there. Their remains were brought back by Fabian and the schism ended.

events.title: Battle at the Harzhorn
events.summary: A Roman army returning from a deep penetration into northern Germany fought its way through a Germanic blockade at the Harzhorn ridge in Lower Saxony, some 200 km beyond the limes; the battlefield, found by metal detectorists in 2008, revolutionised views of third-century Roman offensive capacity.

sides.strength: legionary vexillations, auxiliaries, Moorish and Osroene archers, artillery

battle.significance: Archaeological proof that Roman armies still campaigned far beyond the Rhine in the 230s.

events.title: The 'Crisis of the Third Century'
events.summary: Conventional label for the half-century from the murder of Severus Alexander (235) to the accession of Diocletian (284), marked by some 26 legitimate emperors and dozens of usurpers, simultaneous wars on the Rhine, Danube and Euphrates, plague, the temporary secession of Gaul and the East, and the collapse of the silver coinage.

events.title: Maximinus campaigns against Dacians and Sarmatians
events.summary: After his victory in Germany Maximinus wintered at Sirmium and campaigned beyond the middle Danube in 236-237, taking the titles Dacicus Maximus and Sarmaticus Maximus. His exactions to pay the army provoked the revolts of 238.

events.title: Revolt of the Gordians in Africa
events.summary: Young landowners at Thysdrus killed Maximinus' procurator in a tax revolt and proclaimed the aged proconsul of Africa, Marcus Antonius Gordianus, emperor with his son Gordian II; the Senate recognised them and declared Maximinus a public enemy.

events.title: Battle of Carthage
events.summary: Capelianus, the loyal governor of Numidia, marched Legio III Augusta on Carthage and crushed the Gordians' untrained militia; Gordian II was killed and his father hanged himself.

sides.strength: Legio III Augusta and Numidian auxiliaries

battle.significance: Ended the African revolt but not the senatorial rebellion it had started.

events.title: Senate elects Pupienus and Balbinus
events.summary: On news of the Gordians' death the Senate chose two of the vigintiviri, the soldier Pupienus Maximus and the aristocrat Balbinus, as joint Augusti with equal powers, including the pontificate; the Roman crowd forced them to add the thirteen-year-old Gordian III as Caesar.

events.title: Siege of Aquileia and death of Maximinus
events.summary: Maximinus crossed the Julian Alps but was stopped at Aquileia, defended by the senators Crispinus and Menophilus; his starving army, short of supplies in a stripped countryside, murdered him and his son in their tents.

sides.losses: emperor murdered by his own troops

battle.significance: Death of the first soldier-emperor; vindicated the senatorial coup.

events.title: Murder of Pupienus and Balbinus; Gordian III sole emperor
events.summary: After 99 days of quarrelling joint rule, the two senatorial emperors were seized by the Praetorians, stripped, dragged through the city and killed; Gordian III, aged 13, was proclaimed sole Augustus.

events.title: Goths and Carpi sack Histria
events.summary: Gothic and Carpic raiders sacked Histria near the Danube mouth, the first securely recorded Gothic attack on the empire; Tullius Menophilus, governor of Moesia Inferior, bought them off with subsidies.

events.title: Ardashir takes Nisibis and Carrhae
events.summary: Exploiting the chaos of 235-238, Ardashir and his son Shapur seized the Roman strongholds of Nisibis and Carrhae in Mesopotamia (Syncellus, Zonaras), and by 240 had taken Hatra. Dura-Europos records a Persian approach in 239.

events.title: Legio III Augusta disbanded
events.summary: Because its legate Capelianus had crushed the Gordians at Carthage, Gordian III's regime dissolved legio III Augusta and erased its name from inscriptions; its men were sent to Raetia. The legion was reconstituted at Lambaesis by Valerian in 253.

events.title: Shapur I crowned co-ruler; sole King of Kings from 242
events.summary: Ardashir crowned his son Shapur co-ruler, probably on 12 April 240, and Shapur ruled alone from around 242 to 270, the most dangerous enemy Rome faced in the third century.

events.title: Sasanian capture of Hatra
events.summary: Hatra, which had become a Roman ally with a Roman garrison, fell to Ardashir and his son Shapur after a long siege; the city was destroyed and never reoccupied, which preserved its spectacular temples until ISIS damaged them in 2015.

sides.strength: city garrison with a Roman cohort

battle.significance: Removed the last buffer between Rome and Persia in the Jazira.

events.title: Timesitheus becomes praetorian prefect; Gordian marries Tranquillina
events.summary: Gaius Furius Sabinius Aquila Timesitheus, an equestrian with a long career of procuratorships, became praetorian prefect and married his daughter Furia Sabinia Tranquillina to the 16-year-old Gordian III, effectively directing the government until his death of illness in 243.

events.title: Gordian III opens the gates of Janus and marches east
events.summary: Gordian III ceremonially opened the gates of the Temple of Janus and led an army east through the Balkans, defeating Goths, Carpi and Sarmatians in Moesia and Thrace on the way (HA mentions a battle near Philippopolis with the Alans). The expedition reached Antioch late in 242.

events.title: Battle of Rhesaina
events.summary: Gordian III's army, directed by his father-in-law and praetorian prefect Timesitheus, defeated Shapur near Rhesaina and recovered Carrhae and Nisibis.

sides.strength: large expeditionary army including Germanic and Gothic contingents

battle.significance: Restored Roman Mesopotamia.

events.title: Battle of Misiche and death of Gordian III
events.summary: Advancing down the Euphrates toward Ctesiphon, Gordian's army was defeated by Shapur at Misiche near modern Fallujah; Gordian died soon after, either of wounds (Persian version) or murdered by his troops at the instigation of Philip the Arab (Roman version).
events.locName: Misiche (Peroz-Shapur, later al-Anbar), on the Euphrates

sides.strength: Roman field army including Gothic and Germanic contingents (ŠKZ)

battle.significance: First of Shapur's three triumphs over Roman emperors; led to Philip's costly peace.

events.title: Philip the Arab's peace with Shapur
events.summary: The new emperor Philip made peace with Shapur, paying 500,000 denarii (aurei, according to the ŠKZ) and apparently recognising Persian influence in Armenia, while Roman coins proclaimed PAX FUNDATA CUM PERSIS.

events.title: Painting of the Dura-Europos synagogue
events.summary: The enlarged synagogue at Dura, dated by Aramaic inscriptions to 244/5, was decorated with some 58 narrative panels of biblical scenes (Exodus, Ezekiel's dry bones, Esther, the Ark among the Philistines), overturning assumptions that Jewish art avoided figuration. It survived because it was buried in the defensive embankment of 256.

events.title: Plotinus founds his school in Rome
events.summary: After eleven years with Ammonius Saccas at Alexandria and joining Gordian III's Persian expedition to learn Persian and Indian philosophy, Plotinus settled in Rome in 244 and taught in the house of the widow Gemina; his circle included senators such as Rogatianus, who gave up his property, the physician Eustochius, Amelius and, from 263, Porphyry. He began writing only in 253-254.

events.title: Philip's war against the Carpi
events.summary: Philip campaigned personally on the lower Danube against the Carpi in 245-247, taking the title Carpicus Maximus; a letter of his commander in Moesia complains of Carpic demands for subsidies already paid to the Goths. Philip celebrated the victory in Rome in 247 and raised his son to Augustus.

events.title: Philip celebrates Rome's millennium
events.summary: On 21 April 248 Philip staged the Ludi Saeculares for the thousandth anniversary of Rome's foundation, with games in which, according to later tradition, a thousand pairs of gladiators and exotic animals collected by Gordian III appeared.

events.title: Revolts of Pacatianus and Jotapianus
events.summary: In 248 Tiberius Claudius Marinus Pacatianus was proclaimed by the Danube legions and Jotapianus, claiming kinship with Severus Alexander, rose in Syria or Cappadocia; both were soon killed by their own troops.

events.title: Gothic siege of Marcianopolis
events.summary: A Gothic force, led according to Jordanes by Argaith and Guntheric, crossed the Danube after Philip stopped subsidies, ravaged Moesia and besieged Marcianopolis, which bought them off; Dexippus describes the defence. It foreshadowed the great invasion of 250.

battle.significance: City ransomed; showed the weakness of the lower Danube defences after the Carpic wars.

events.title: Battle of Verona
events.summary: Decius, proclaimed by the Danubian army, marched into Italy and defeated and killed Philip near Verona; Philip's son Philip II was murdered by the Praetorians in Rome.

battle.significance: Brought the Danubian Decius to power.

events.title: Plague of Cyprian
events.summary: A pandemic, probably originating in Ethiopia and reaching Alexandria by 249, swept the empire for over a decade; Bishop Cyprian of Carthage describes bloody diarrhoea, vomiting, eye haemorrhage, gangrene of the limbs and loss of hearing and sight.

events.title: Anti-Christian riot at Alexandria
events.summary: A year before Decius' edict, a mob stirred up by a pagan poet attacked Christians in Alexandria, killing the old man Metras, the woman Quinta and the virgin Apollonia, whose teeth were broken before she leapt into the fire; Bishop Dionysius described it in a letter to Fabius of Antioch.

events.title: Martyrdom of Pope Fabian
events.summary: Fabian, bishop of Rome since 236, who had organised the city into seven ecclesiastical regions under deacons, was among the first victims of Decius, dying on 20 January 250; his epitaph survives in the papal crypt of the catacomb of Callixtus. The see remained vacant for 14 months.
events.locName: Rome; buried in the Catacomb of Callixtus

events.title: Decius' edict of universal sacrifice
events.summary: Decius ordered every inhabitant of the empire to sacrifice to the gods, taste the sacrificial meat and obtain a certificate (libellus) from local commissioners; Christians who refused were imprisoned or executed, including Pope Fabian (20 January 250).

events.title: Siege and sack of Philippopolis
events.summary: The Gothic king Cniva besieged Philippopolis in Thrace, whose governor Lucius Priscus, despairing of help from Decius, proclaimed himself emperor and allied with the Goths; the city fell and Ammianus says 100,000 people were killed or captured.

battle.significance: First sack of a major Balkan city by the Goths.

events.title: Battle of Beroe (Augusta Traiana)
events.summary: Cniva surprised Decius' army in camp near Beroe-Augusta Traiana, routing it and forcing the emperor to retreat to Moesia to regroup, leaving Philippopolis to its fate.

battle.significance: Left Thrace open to the Goths.

events.title: Certificates of sacrifice (libelli) issued in Egypt
events.summary: Some 46 papyrus libelli survive, dated June-July 250, in which individuals, including a priestess of Petesouchos, declare that they have always sacrificed and have now poured libations and tasted the offerings before the commissioners, who countersign. They show that the edict targeted the whole population, not only Christians.

events.title: Julius Valens Licinianus proclaimed at Rome
events.summary: While Decius fought the Goths, Julius Valens Licinianus was proclaimed emperor in Rome, apparently with some popular support, but was killed within days.

events.title: Council of Carthage on the lapsed
events.summary: Returning from hiding after Easter 251, Cyprian held a council that set graded penances for those who had sacrificed (sacrificati) or bought certificates (libellatici), rejecting both the rigorism of Novatian and the confessors' indulgences; he wrote De Lapsis and De Ecclesiae Catholicae Unitate for the occasion.

events.title: Battle of Abritus
events.summary: Decius and his son Herennius Etruscus were killed when Cniva's Goths lured the Roman army into a marsh near Abritus in Moesia Inferior; Decius was the first emperor to die fighting a foreign enemy, and his body was never found.

sides.losses: very heavy; emperor and heir killed

battle.significance: First Roman emperor killed by a foreign enemy; symbol of the third-century nadir.

events.title: Novatianist schism at Rome
events.summary: When Cornelius was elected bishop of Rome in March 251 and favoured readmitting the lapsed after penance, the learned presbyter Novatian had himself consecrated rival bishop, founding a rigorist church that survived for centuries.

events.title: Trebonianus Gallus pays off the Goths
events.summary: After Abritus Gallus allowed Cniva's Goths to go home with their booty and prisoners, including captured nobles from Philippopolis, and promised an annual payment; Gallus' son Hostilian, the surviving son of Decius, died of the plague in Rome soon after.

events.title: Battle of Barbalissos
events.summary: Opening his second war, Shapur I destroyed a Roman army of 60,000 (his figure) at Barbalissos on the Euphrates, then overran Syria and Cappadocia; the ŠKZ lists 37 captured cities.

battle.significance: Left the Roman East defenceless.

events.title: Pope Cornelius exiled to Centumcellae
events.summary: In a renewed wave of arrests under Gallus, perhaps triggered by the plague, Cornelius of Rome was banished to Centumcellae, where he died in June 253; his successor Lucius was also exiled briefly. Cyprian wrote a letter of congratulation to the exiled confessor.

events.title: Shapur I sacks Antioch
events.summary: Shapur took and sacked Antioch, the third city of the empire, guided (according to Ammianus and the Thirteenth Sibylline Oracle) by a renegade Antiochene councillor named Mariades; thousands were deported to Persia.

battle.significance: The greatest humiliation inflicted on Rome in the East to that date.

events.title: Uranius Antoninus defends Emesa
events.summary: Lucius Julius Aurelius Sulpicius Severus Uranius Antoninus, priest of Elagabal at Emesa, led local resistance to Shapur and struck gold and silver coins as emperor in 253-254.

events.title: Aemilianus overthrows Gallus; Valerian seizes power
events.summary: Aemilius Aemilianus, governor of Moesia, won a victory over the Goths, was proclaimed emperor and invaded Italy; Trebonianus Gallus and his son Volusian were killed by their own men near Interamna. Three months later Aemilianus met the same fate near Spoletium as Valerian approached with the Rhine army.

events.title: Death of Origen at Tyre
events.summary: Origen, imprisoned and tortured in the Decian persecution (chained, his legs stretched in the stocks), survived but died at Tyre around 253-254 aged about 69. His Hexapla, commentaries and De Principiis made him the most prolific and influential theologian before Augustine; his tomb was shown at Tyre in the Middle Ages.

events.title: Gothic siege of Thessalonica; Greece refortifies
events.summary: Goths overran Macedonia and besieged Thessalonica without taking it; panic spread to southern Greece, where the Isthmus wall was repaired and Athens rebuilt its city wall (the so-called Valerianic wall), for the first time since Sulla.

battle.significance: City held; start of a refortification of Greece.
