events.title: Councils of Carthage and the rebaptism controversy
events.summary: Cyprian's African councils of 255-256, culminating on 1 September 256 with 87 bishops whose individual votes survive (Sententiae episcoporum), insisted that heretics be rebaptised, against Stephen of Rome, who threatened excommunication and claimed the authority of Peter's see. Stephen's death (257) and Cyprian's martyrdom ended the clash; Africa's position later underpinned Donatism.

events.title: Sasanian siege of Dura-Europos
events.summary: Shapur's army besieged and destroyed the Roman frontier fortress of Dura-Europos on the Euphrates; excavations revealed siege mines and countermines in which some twenty Roman soldiers and one Persian died, perhaps the earliest archaeological evidence of chemical warfare.

battle.significance: Its ramp-buried buildings are among the most important finds of Roman archaeology.

events.title: Gothic and Boranoi sea raids: Pityus and Trapezus
events.summary: Using ships commandeered from the Bosporan Kingdom, Boranoi and Goths raided the eastern Black Sea, taking Pityus at the second attempt and storming Trapezus, whose large garrison fled by night.

events.title: Valerian's persecution of the clergy
events.summary: Valerian's first edict (257) ordered clergy to sacrifice and banned Christian meetings and cemeteries; a second (258) ordered execution of bishops, priests and deacons and confiscated property of Christian senators and equestrians.

events.title: Goths sack Chalcedon, Nicomedia and the Bithynian cities
events.summary: Sailing along the western Black Sea coast with boats built by captives, Goths crossed to Asia; the garrison of Chalcedon fled, and Nicomedia, Nicaea, Cius, Apamea and Prusa were sacked and burned (Zosimus), while Valerian, delayed at Antioch and Cappadocia, failed to intervene.

events.title: Martyrdom of Pope Sixtus II and the deacon Lawrence
events.summary: Under Valerian's second rescript, Sixtus II was seized while preaching in a cemetery on 6 August 258 and beheaded with four deacons; his archdeacon Lawrence followed on 10 August. Ambrose and Prudentius tell how Lawrence presented the poor as the church's treasure and was roasted on a gridiron, a legend probably arising from a misreading of 'passus est' for 'assus est'.

events.title: Martyrdom of Cyprian of Carthage
events.summary: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage, was beheaded at the villa Sexti outside Carthage before a large crowd after a trial before the proconsul Galerius Maximus, the first African bishop to be martyred.

events.title: Martyrdom of Fructuosus of Tarraco
events.summary: Bishop Fructuosus of Tarraco and his deacons Augurius and Eulogius were burned alive in the amphitheatre on 21 January 259; their authentic Acta are among the best of the period, and a Visigothic basilica was later built in the arena over the spot.

events.title: Battle of Mediolanum
events.summary: Gallienus defeated a vast Alamannic army (Zonaras says 300,000) near Milan with a force of 10,000, after the invaders had crossed the Alps and reached the outskirts of Rome, where the Senate armed the plebs.

battle.significance: Saved Italy from the first major barbarian invasion since the Cimbri.

events.title: Battle at Augusta Vindelicum
events.summary: On 24-25 April 260 the Raetian governor Marcus Simplicinius Genialis, with soldiers and local levies, defeated Semnones or Juthungi returning from Italy laden with booty and freed 'many thousands of Italian captives', as recorded on a victory altar found in Augsburg in 1992.

battle.significance: Epigraphic snapshot of invasion, captives and the Gallic secession.

events.title: Revolts of Ingenuus and Regalianus on the Danube
events.summary: Ingenuus, governor of Pannonia, was proclaimed emperor and defeated by Gallienus' cavalry commander Aureolus at Mursa; his successor as usurper, Regalianus, struck coins at Carnuntum before being killed after Sarmatian (Roxolani) attacks.

events.title: Battle of Mursa (260)
events.summary: Gallienus and his cavalry commander Aureolus crushed the usurper Ingenuus near Mursa; Ingenuus was killed or drowned himself.

battle.significance: Early display of Gallienus' mobile cavalry.

events.title: Battle of Edessa and capture of Valerian
events.summary: Shapur I defeated Valerian between Carrhae and Edessa and captured him, the only Roman emperor ever taken prisoner by a foreign enemy, along with his praetorian prefect, senators and, by Shapur's count, an army of 70,000.

battle.significance: Nadir of Roman prestige; precipitated the Gallic and Palmyrene secessions.

events.title: Usurpation of the Macriani
events.summary: After Valerian's capture, his finance official Fulvius Macrianus and the prefect Ballista had Macrianus' sons Macrianus Minor and Quietus proclaimed emperors in the East; the Macriani invaded the Balkans in 261 and were destroyed by Aureolus, while Odaenathus of Palmyra killed Quietus and Ballista at Emesa.

events.title: Postumus founds the Gallic Empire
events.summary: Marcus Cassianius Latinius Postumus, commander on the Rhine, quarrelled with Gallienus' son Saloninus and his guardian Silvanus over booty, besieged them in Colonia Agrippinensis and had them killed; he then ruled Gaul, Germany, Britain, Spain and briefly Raetia for nine years.

events.title: Gallienus' rescript restoring Christian property
events.summary: Gallienus ended his father's persecution and restored churches and cemeteries to the bishops, effectively recognising the Church as a property-holding body; peace for Christians lasted until 303.

events.title: Frankish raiders sack Tarraco and cross to Africa
events.summary: In the earliest major Frankish invasion, raiders swept through Gaul into Spain, sacked Tarraco and, seizing ships, reached Mauretania (Aurelius Victor, Orosius). Destruction layers at Tarraco and Emporiae and the walling of Spanish towns may relate to it.

events.title: Abandonment of the Upper German-Raetian limes
events.summary: In the turmoil of 259-260 the forts of the Upper German and Raetian limes between the Rhine and Danube were given up; coin series at sites such as Saalburg and Osterburken end, and the frontier fell back to the Rhine, Lake Constance, Iller and Danube. A Verona list (Laterculus Veronensis) later notes the lands beyond the Rhine lost "under Gallienus".

events.title: Shapur takes Caesarea in Cappadocia
events.summary: On the third campaign after capturing Valerian, Shapur besieged Caesarea, defended by the physician Demosthenes, and took it through treachery; Zonaras puts the population at 400,000 and claims many were slaughtered. Persian columns also ravaged Cilicia and Lycaonia.

battle.significance: The deepest Persian penetration into Anatolia in the Roman period.

events.title: Ballista defeats the Persians in Cilicia
events.summary: Valerian's officer Ballista (Callistus), acting for Macrianus, surprised the scattered Persian columns near Pompeiopolis and Corycus, capturing part of Shapur's harem and treasure; Odaenathus harried the retreating army at the Euphrates. Shapur withdrew across the river, paying the Edessenes for passage.

battle.significance: Turned the Persian victory into a costly withdrawal and gave the Macriani the prestige to usurp.

events.title: Defeat of the Macriani in the Balkans
events.summary: Macrianus the Elder and his son Macrianus the Younger marched west with some 30,000 men and were met by Gallienus' general Aureolus (and Domitianus) in Illyricum or Thrace; their army went over, and both Macriani were killed. Their brother Quietus, left in the east with Ballista, was then besieged at Emesa by Odaenathus and killed.

battle.significance: Restored the east nominally to Gallienus, in practice to Odaenathus.

events.title: Odaenathus kills Quietus and Ballista at Emesa
events.summary: Acting for Gallienus, Odaenathus besieged the last Macrianic claimant Quietus in Emesa; the citizens killed Quietus and Ballista, and Odaenathus was rewarded with the titles dux Romanorum and corrector totius Orientis.

events.title: Revolt of the prefect Mussius Aemilianus in Egypt
events.summary: Lucius Mussius Aemilianus, prefect of Egypt who had backed the Macriani, assumed imperial power in Alexandria after their fall; Gallienus' general Aurelius Theodotus crushed him in 262. Dionysius of Alexandria describes the civil war in the city, the plague and the street fighting that left the Bruchion quarter half-deserted.

events.title: Odaenathus' counter-offensives against Persia
events.summary: Septimius Odaenathus of Palmyra, acting as Gallienus' commander in the East, recovered Mesopotamia including Carrhae and Nisibis and twice advanced to Ctesiphon (262 and c. 266), taking the title King of Kings while Gallienus called him 'corrector totius Orientis'.

events.title: Gallienus excludes senators from military command
events.summary: Aurelius Victor reports that Gallienus forbade senators to serve in the army, after which legionary commands and most frontier governorships passed to equestrian professionals (praefecti legionis, praesides), many of them risen from the ranks.

events.title: Goths burn the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus
events.summary: Gothic raiders, led according to Jordanes by Respa, Veduc and Thuruar, crossed to Asia and burned the Artemision, one of the Seven Wonders; it was patched up afterwards but never regained its former splendour, and its stones were later quarried for Christian churches.

events.title: Earthquakes and plague in the reign of Gallienus
events.summary: The Historia Augusta reports an earthquake felt in Rome, Libya and Asia, with chasms opening and a long darkness, followed by a plague that killed 5,000 a day at Rome; Gallienus consulted the Sibylline books and sacrificed to Jupiter Salutaris.

events.title: Gallienus at Athens and Eleusis
events.summary: Gallienus visited Athens, became archon and Areopagite and was initiated into the Eleusinian Mysteries; coins of the period honour Demeter and style him GALLIENAE AUGUSTAE, perhaps alluding to the goddess. His philhellenism matched his patronage of Plotinus, who asked him to found a Platonic city, Platonopolis, in Campania.

events.title: Gallienus' failed campaign against Postumus
events.summary: Gallienus invaded Gaul with Aureolus and defeated Postumus in battle but failed to finish him; besieging Postumus in an unnamed Gallic town, he was wounded by an arrow and withdrew. The Gallic Empire was left alone thereafter.

events.title: Herulian sack of Athens
events.summary: A great seaborne invasion of Heruli and Goths, reported as 500 ships, broke into the Aegean, sacking Byzantium's suburbs, Cyzicus, the islands, Corinth, Argos, Sparta and Athens; the Athenian historian Dexippus then led 2,000 men in guerrilla resistance from the olive groves.

sides.strength: part of a fleet of 500 ships (Syncellus)

battle.significance: Ended classical Athens' urban continuity; the Agora was abandoned behind a reduced circuit.

events.title: Murder of Odaenathus
events.summary: Septimius Odaenathus, King of Kings and corrector of the East, was assassinated with his eldest son Herodes (Hairan) by a kinsman, Maeonius, at Emesa or, according to Syncellus, at Heraclea Pontica after repelling the Goths. His widow Zenobia took power for their young son Vaballathus.

events.title: The Herul chief Naulobatus enters Roman service
events.summary: After his defeat at the Nestus, the Herul leader Naulobatus surrendered to Gallienus and was given the consular ornaments, the first barbarian king known to receive them.

events.title: Siege of Mediolanum and murder of Gallienus
events.summary: While besieging his rebellious cavalry commander Aureolus in Milan, Gallienus was lured from his tent at night by a false alarm and killed by a conspiracy of his officers, including Heraclianus, Marcianus and probably Claudius and Aurelian.

battle.significance: Brought the 'Illyrian emperors' to power.

events.title: Battle of Lake Benacus
events.summary: Claudius II defeated the Alamanni, who had crossed into Italy during the siege of Milan, near Lake Garda; the Epitome claims half the enemy were killed.

battle.significance: Secured northern Italy for the new emperor.

events.title: Battle of the Nestus
events.summary: Gallienus defeated the Herulian raiders on the river Nestus in Thrace and accepted the surrender of their leader Naulobatus, who received consular insignia, an early example of enrolling a barbarian chief in Roman service.

battle.significance: Partially checked the great raid before Gallienus turned to deal with Aureolus.

events.title: Goths besiege Thessalonica and Cassandreia
events.summary: The great Gothic and Herul fleet of 268 landed in Macedonia and besieged Cassandreia and Thessalonica; on news of Claudius' approach they abandoned the siege and moved north up the Axius, to be destroyed at Naissus.

events.title: Battle of Naissus
events.summary: Claudius II crushed a huge Gothic army near Naissus in Moesia Superior, earning the title Gothicus Maximus; survivors were pursued through the Balkans, starved and dissolved by plague, and many captives were settled as farmers or enrolled in the army.

sides.strength: imperial field army with Dalmatian cavalry

battle.significance: Broke the great Gothic invasions; the Goths made no major attack for half a century.

events.title: Revolt of Laelianus and murder of Postumus
events.summary: Ulpius Cornelius Laelianus revolted at Mogontiacum; Postumus took the city but, forbidding his troops to sack it, was murdered by them. The soldier Marius ruled briefly before Victorinus took power.

events.title: Siege of Augustodunum
events.summary: Autun, capital of the Aedui, appealed to Claudius II and declared for the central empire; Victorinus besieged it for seven months and sacked it, a destruction still lamented by the orator Eumenius in a panegyric of 298.

battle.significance: Showed that Claudius would not intervene in Gaul.

events.title: Gothic raids on Crete, Rhodes and Cyprus
events.summary: Remnants of the Gothic fleet raided Crete, Rhodes and Cyprus, but plague and Roman naval forces under the future emperor Probus (or Tenagino Probus) dispersed them. Surviving Goths were settled as farmers or enrolled in the army.

events.title: Spain returns to the central emperor
events.summary: After Postumus' death the Spanish provinces recognised Claudius II, and Claudius' general Julius Placidianus occupied Gallia Narbonensis; an inscription at Cularo (Grenoble) records his vexillations. Victorinus responded by besieging Augustodunum, which had declared for Claudius.

events.title: Zenobia's forces take Egypt and Asia Minor
events.summary: Ruling for her son Vaballathus after Odaenathus' murder, Zenobia sent her general Zabdas with 70,000 men into Egypt, defeating the prefect Tenagino Probus, and pushed Palmyrene control through Asia Minor as far as Ancyra and the borders of Bithynia.

events.title: Death of Claudius II; Quintillus and Aurelian
events.summary: Claudius II died of plague at Sirmium early in 270; his brother Quintillus was recognised by the Senate but abandoned by his troops within weeks, and the cavalry commander Aurelian took power.

events.title: Aurelian defeats the Juthungi; the embassy in Dexippus
events.summary: Early in his reign Aurelian defeated Juthungi returning from a raid into Italy. Dexippus preserves a set-piece account of their envoys before the emperor, who received them seated high on a tribunal amid the gilded standards, rejecting their demand for continued subsidies.

events.title: Aurelian's treaty with the Vandals
events.summary: After defeating Asding Vandals raiding Pannonia, Aurelian made a treaty under which their two kings gave their children as hostages and 2,000 Vandal horsemen joined the Roman army; Dexippus reports both sides voting on the terms.

events.title: Porphyry writes Against the Christians
events.summary: Porphyry composed fifteen books against the Christians, using historical criticism to date Daniel to the Maccabean era and exposing contradictions in the Gospels; it was answered by Methodius, Eusebius and Apollinaris and burned by order of Constantine and again of Theodosius II and Valentinian III in 448. Only fragments survive.

events.title: Battle of Placentia
events.summary: Juthungi (or Alamanni and Marcomanni) invading Italy ambushed Aurelian's army in woods near Placentia and inflicted a severe defeat, causing panic in Rome.

battle.significance: Triggered the building of the Aurelian Walls.

events.title: Battle of Fanum Fortunae
events.summary: Aurelian defeated the invaders on the Metaurus near Fanum Fortunae, the river where Hasdrubal had died in 207 BC, as they marched along the Via Flaminia toward Rome.

battle.significance: Turned the invaders back from Rome.

events.title: Battle of Ticinum
events.summary: Aurelian annihilated the retreating invaders on the plain of Ticinum (Pavia), ending the threat to Italy.

battle.significance: Ended the last great barbarian invasion of Italy for over a century.

events.title: Revolt of the moneyers in Rome
events.summary: The workers of the Rome mint, led by the rationalis Felicissimus and facing exposure for embezzling silver, rose in revolt; Aurelian suppressed them in fighting on the Caelian hill in which, according to the sources, 7,000 soldiers died.

events.title: Construction of the Aurelian Walls
events.summary: Aurelian began a new circuit of brick-faced concrete walls around Rome, 19 km long, about 6-8 m high, with 381 towers and 18 main gates, finished under Probus; it was the first city wall built since the Republic and enclosed the whole fourteen-region city.

events.title: Aurelian defeats the Goths beyond the Danube
events.summary: Marching east against Zenobia, Aurelian crossed the Danube and defeated a Gothic force, killing their leader Cannabaudes with 5,000 men, and took the title Gothicus Maximus.

battle.significance: Secured the lower Danube before the eastern campaign.

events.title: Abandonment of Trajanic Dacia
events.summary: Aurelian withdrew the army and administration from Trajan's province north of the Danube and created a new Dacia (later Dacia Ripensis and Dacia Mediterranea) south of the river, carved out of Moesia, with its capital at Serdica.
events.locName: Dacia north of the Danube; new Dacia with capital Serdica

events.title: Domitianus, usurper in Gaul
events.summary: A Gallic claimant Domitianus, mentioned in passing by Zosimus and the HA, was proved real when a coin reading IMP C DOMITIANVS P F AVG was found in a hoard at Chalgrove, Oxfordshire, in 2003, joining a single French specimen once dismissed as a forgery. He probably revolted against Victorinus or Tetricus c. 271.

events.title: Aurelian takes Tyana
events.summary: Tyana in Cappadocia, held for Palmyra, was betrayed by a citizen named Heraclammon; Aurelian forbade a sack, saying he would leave 'not a dog alive' and then ordering the dogs killed instead, and the clemency induced other cities to surrender.

battle.significance: Opened the Cilician Gates; clemency won over Asia Minor.

events.title: Battle of Immae
events.summary: Near Antioch, Aurelian's cavalry feigned flight before Zabdas' heavy-armoured Palmyrene cataphracts, wore them out in the heat and then turned and destroyed them.

sides.strength: Dalmatian and Moorish light cavalry and infantry

battle.significance: Broke Palmyrene power in Syria's north.

events.title: Battle of Emesa
events.summary: Zenobia and Zabdas made a stand with 70,000 men on the plain before Emesa; the Roman cavalry was routed by the cataphracts, but Aurelian's legionary infantry, including clubmen from Palestine, broke the Palmyrene line, and Zenobia fled to Palmyra.

sides.strength: field army incl. Palestinian clubmen, Moesian and Pannonian legions

battle.significance: Decisive defeat of the Palmyrene army.

events.title: Siege of Palmyra and capture of Zenobia
events.summary: Aurelian besieged Palmyra, harassed by desert Arabs; Zenobia tried to escape on a female camel to seek Persian help but was captured on the Euphrates, and the city surrendered.

battle.significance: Ended the Palmyrene Empire.

events.title: Aurelian decides the Paul of Samosata case
events.summary: Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, deposed by a synod in 268 for heresy (adoptionism) but kept in his church house under Palmyrene protection, was evicted when the Christians appealed to Aurelian, who ruled the building should go to those in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome.

events.title: Aurelian defeats the Carpi
events.summary: Between the Palmyrene campaigns Aurelian defeated the Carpi, settling captives within the empire and taking the title Carpicus Maximus; the HA tells that the Senate offered the title and he joked about "Carpisculus", a kind of shoe.

events.title: Aurelian destroys the Bruchion at Alexandria
events.summary: During fighting between the Palmyrene party and Roman troops in Alexandria, the palace quarter of the Bruchion, home of the Museum, was destroyed and its walls razed (Ammianus). Some modern scholars see this, rather than Caesar's fire, as the end of the Museum and much of the Library.

events.title: Second Palmyrene revolt and the sack of Palmyra
events.summary: Palmyra rose again under Septimius Antiochus, massacring its Roman garrison of 600 archers; Aurelian returned at speed, sacked the city and reduced it to a garrison town, ending its role in the caravan trade. A related rising in Egypt under Firmus was crushed.

events.title: Aurelian dedicates the temple of Sol Invictus
events.summary: Aurelian dedicated a great temple of the Sun on the Campus Agrippae in Rome, staffed it with a new college of pontifices Solis and instituted games (agon Solis) every four years; 25 December is attested in the Chronograph of 354 as the Natalis Invicti.

events.title: Battle of Châlons (Catalaunian Fields)
events.summary: Aurelian defeated the army of the Gallic Empire at the Catalaunian Fields near Châlons-en-Champagne; the Gallic emperor Tetricus I, according to a widely repeated story, had secretly arranged to desert his own army, which fought on with heavy losses.

battle.significance: Reunified the empire.

events.title: Aurelian's triumph as Restitutor Orbis
events.summary: Aurelian celebrated a spectacular triumph over Palmyra and Gaul, with Zenobia and Tetricus displayed among captives, and was hailed Restitutor Orbis ('restorer of the world').

events.title: Aurelian's coin reform
events.summary: Aurelian reopened and reorganised the mints and issued a heavier radiate with a fixed silver content of about 5%, marked XXI or KA (in Greek), probably signifying 20 units of bronze to 1 of silver, together with a new aureus at 50 to the pound.

events.title: Aurelian's reform of the Roman dole
events.summary: Aurelian replaced the monthly grain ration with a daily distribution of baked bread of two pounds, added pork (from levies on southern Italy), olive oil and salt, and planned free wine. The arca vinaria and the forum suarium mark the institutional shift from grain to processed food, and from the Annona to the corporations of bakers.

events.title: Assassination of Aurelian at Caenophrurium
events.summary: Marching against Persia, Aurelian was murdered at Caenophrurium in Thrace by officers duped by his secretary Eros, who forged a list of men marked for execution.

events.title: Death of Mani in prison at Gundeshapur
events.summary: The prophet Mani, who had enjoyed Shapur I's patronage, was imprisoned by Bahram I under pressure from the Zoroastrian priest Kartir and died in chains at Bet Lapat (Gundeshapur) after 26 days.

events.title: Deaths of Tacitus and Florianus; Probus emperor
events.summary: Tacitus, after a campaign against Goths or Heruli in Asia Minor, died or was killed at Tyana in mid-276; his half-brother Florianus seized power but was killed by his own troops at Tarsus after a standoff with Probus, proclaimed by the eastern army.

events.title: Gothic invasion of Pontus and Cappadocia
events.summary: In 275-276 Goths, apparently from the Maeotis, crossed into Pontus and raided as far as Cappadocia, Galatia and Cilicia. The emperor Tacitus and his brother, the praetorian prefect Florianus, defeated them, earning Tacitus the title Gothicus Maximus, but Tacitus died soon after at Tyana or Zela.

events.title: Probus restores Gaul and the Rhine
events.summary: Probus drove Franks, Alamanni, Burgundians and Vandals out of Gaul, recovered (by his own count) 60 or 70 cities, crossed the Rhine, and settled tens of thousands of captives in the provinces.

events.title: Siege of Cremna: the Isaurian bandit Lydius
events.summary: The Isaurian brigand Lydius held the Pisidian hill city of Cremna against Probus' general Terentius Marcianus, expelling useless mouths and growing grain inside; he was killed by a disaffected artillerist, and excavation has revealed the Roman siege mound and the defenders' counter-wall.

battle.significance: Archaeologically documented Roman siege; shows endemic Isaurian banditry.

events.title: Probus defeats Burgundians and Vandals
events.summary: Probus fought a coalition of Burgundians and Vandals across a river in Raetia, lured them over by provoking them with archers and destroyed them; he sent surviving captives to Britain, where they later helped suppress a revolt.

events.title: Blemmyes occupy Coptos and Ptolemais
events.summary: The Blemmyes, nomads of the Eastern Desert, seized Coptos and Ptolemais Hermiou in Upper Egypt; Probus' generals recovered them and Probus celebrated a triumph that included Blemmye captives.

events.title: Revolts of Saturninus, Proculus and Bonosus
events.summary: Probus faced the usurpation of Julius Saturninus in Syria or Egypt, and of Proculus at Lugdunum and Bonosus at Colonia Agrippinensis in the West; all were suppressed.

events.title: Probus permits vine-growing in the western provinces
events.summary: Probus allowed the inhabitants of Gaul, Spain, Britain and Pannonia to plant vines and make wine, revoking (in tradition) the restrictions attributed to Domitian; he used soldiers to plant vineyards on Mons Almus (Fruška Gora) near Sirmium and on Mount Aureus near Moesia. The army's resentment at such labour is said to have caused his murder in 282.
events.locName: Gaul, Spain, Britain; Mons Almus near Sirmium

events.title: Probus settles 100,000 Bastarnae in Thrace
events.summary: Probus transplanted a large body of Bastarnae, reportedly 100,000, into Thrace, where they remained loyal; similar settlements of Gepids, Greuthungi and Vandals rebelled and plundered when Probus was occupied elsewhere.

events.title: The odyssey of the Pontic Franks
events.summary: Franks whom Probus had settled on the Black Sea coast seized ships, sailed through the Bosporus raiding Greece and Asia, sacked Syracuse, attacked Carthage and, passing the Straits of Gibraltar, returned home to the Rhine mouth; the panegyrist of 297 cites it as proof that nothing was beyond barbarian daring.
events.locName: Black Sea to Syracuse and the Rhine

events.title: Kartir's inscriptions and the Zoroastrian state church
events.summary: Under Bahram II the high priest Kartir carved inscriptions boasting that he had established fire temples across the empire and in conquered Roman lands and struck down Jews, Buddhists, Brahmins, Nazarenes, Christians and Manichaeans; they document the formation of a Zoroastrian orthodoxy that later shaped Persian treatment of Christians.

events.title: Murder of Probus at Sirmium
events.summary: Probus was killed by soldiers at Sirmium, allegedly resentful at being made to drain marshes and plant vines, after the praetorian prefect Marcus Aurelius Carus had been proclaimed emperor in Raetia.

events.title: Carus' Persian campaign and death
events.summary: Exploiting Sasanian dynastic strife under Bahram II, Carus invaded Mesopotamia with his son Numerian, took Seleucia and Ctesiphon, and died in his camp beyond the Tigris in July or August 283, reportedly struck by lightning.

events.title: Diocletian proclaimed emperor at Nicomedia
events.summary: After Numerian was found dead in his closed litter on the march back from Persia, the army near Nicomedia chose Diocles, commander of the protectores domestici, who personally ran through the praetorian prefect Arrius Aper before the assembled troops.

events.title: Battle of the Margus
events.summary: Diocletian met Carinus, the legitimate western emperor, on the Margus (Morava) near its confluence with the Danube; Carinus' army was winning when he was murdered by one of his own officers, allegedly a tribune whose wife he had seduced, leaving Diocletian sole emperor.
events.locName: River Margus near Margum, Moesia Superior

battle.significance: Last battle of the 'military anarchy'; Diocletian became sole ruler.

events.title: Carinus defeats Sabinus Julianus near Verona
events.summary: Marcus Aurelius Sabinus Julianus, corrector of Venetia or governor in Pannonia, proclaimed himself emperor after the death of Numerian; Carinus crushed him near Verona early in 285 before turning to fight Diocletian on the Margus.

battle.significance: Briefly secured the west for Carinus.

events.title: Antony withdraws to the desert fort of Pispir
events.summary: About 285 the Coptic-speaking farmer Antony, who had given away his inheritance c. 270 after hearing Matthew 19:21 read in church, shut himself in an abandoned fort at Pispir for some twenty years, emerging c. 305 to organise disciples; c. 313 he moved to the "Inner Mountain" near the Red Sea, where the Monastery of St Antony still stands. Athanasius' Life made him the model of the solitary monk.
events.locName: Pispir (Outer Mountain), east bank of the Nile

events.title: Maximian raised to Caesar and Augustus
events.summary: Diocletian appointed his fellow Pannonian officer Maximian as Caesar in 285 and as Augustus in 286, creating a dyarchy in which Diocletian took the name Jovius and Maximian Herculius, divine patronage expressing seniority.

events.title: Maximian suppresses the Bagaudae
events.summary: Maximian crushed the Bagaudae, bands of rural rebels in Gaul led by Aelianus and Amandus, who had taken advantage of the collapse of order.

events.title: Carausius seizes Britain
events.summary: Mausaeus Carausius, a Menapian commander of the Channel fleet based at Gesoriacum, accused of letting Frankish and Saxon pirates raid in order to seize their loot, was condemned by Maximian and proclaimed himself emperor in Britain and northern Gaul.

events.title: Maximian campaigns beyond the Rhine
events.summary: In 287 Maximian crossed the Rhine and ravaged Alamannic and Burgundian territory, while Diocletian advanced from Raetia; the panegyric of 289 hails it as the first Roman offensive beyond the river in a generation, and Maximian repelled raiders who attacked Gaul on 1 January 287 as he took up his consulship at Trier.

events.title: Diocletian's settlement with Bahram II
events.summary: Weakened by the revolt of his brother Hormizd in the east, Bahram II sent gifts to Diocletian, who claimed a diplomatic victory (Persicus Maximus) and restored the Arsacid Tiridates III to part of Armenia with Roman backing.

events.title: The Frankish king Gennobaudes receives his kingdom from Maximian
events.summary: Maximian forced Frankish groups on the lower Rhine to submit; their king Gennobaudes "received his kingdom" as a gift from the emperor, and Franks were settled in Roman territory as laeti, the beginning of an enduring Frankish presence in Toxandria and the lower Rhine.

events.title: Maximian's failed naval expedition against Carausius
events.summary: A fleet built by Maximian to invade Britain in 289 failed, the panegyrist of 291 hinting at bad weather; for a few years Carausius was tolerated de facto.

events.title: Diocletian and Maximian meet at Milan
events.summary: In midwinter 290-291 the two Augusti crossed the Alps from Sirmium and Gaul to meet at Milan, appearing together in a staged adventus that the panegyric of 291 describes as a near-epiphany of Jupiter and Hercules. The meeting probably planned the Tetrarchy and the campaign against Carausius.

events.title: Codex Gregorianus and Codex Hermogenianus
events.summary: The jurists Gregorius and Hermogenianus, working in Diocletian's chancery, compiled the first collections of imperial constitutions (mostly rescripts), the Gregorianus (c. 291-292, from Hadrian onward) and the Hermogenianus (c. 295, Diocletian's own rescripts of 293-294).

events.title: First mention of the Tervingi and Gepids
events.summary: The panegyric delivered to Maximian in 291 mentions the Tervingi, "another division of the Goths", fighting Vandals and Gepids, the first appearance of the Tervingi name. The orator presents barbarian infighting as a gift of the emperors' good fortune.

events.title: Creation of the Tetrarchy
events.summary: On 1 March 293 Maximian appointed Constantius (Chlorus) as his Caesar at Milan and Diocletian appointed Galerius at Sirmium (or Nicomedia), creating a college of two Augusti and two Caesars bound by adoption and marriage.

events.title: Siege of Gesoriacum
events.summary: Constantius, newly made Caesar, blockaded Carausius' continental base at Boulogne with a mole across the harbour mouth and forced its surrender, cutting the usurper off from Gaul.

battle.significance: Isolated Britain and precipitated Carausius' murder.

events.title: Carausius murdered by Allectus
events.summary: After the loss of Boulogne, Carausius was killed by his finance minister (rationalis) Allectus, who ruled Britain for three more years and built a large palace in London, perhaps the structure found under Cannon Street.

events.title: Diocletian's provincial reorganisation and the dioceses
events.summary: Diocletian roughly doubled the number of provinces from about 50 to about 100, separated civil governors from military commanders (duces), included Italy in the provincial system, and grouped provinces into twelve dioceses under vicarii responsible to the praetorian prefects.

events.title: Strata Diocletiana and the fortified eastern frontier
events.summary: Diocletian built or rebuilt a chain of forts along a military road from north-east Arabia through Damascus and Palmyra to Sura on the Euphrates, marked by milestones naming the Strata Diocletiana.
events.locName: Syrian desert from Bostra to Sura via Palmyra

events.title: Galerius suppresses revolt at Coptos and Busiris
events.summary: Before the Persian war Galerius put down unrest in Egypt; Eusebius' Chronicle (via Jerome) records that Busiris and Coptos, which had revolted, were destroyed. Papyri place Galerius in Egypt in 293-294, and the Thebaid was soon reorganised with new military commands.

events.title: Diocletian's currency reform
events.summary: Around 294 Diocletian created a unified empire-wide coinage: a gold aureus at 60 to the pound, a near-pure silver argenteus at 96 to the pound (reviving Neronian standards), and a large silver-washed bronze 'nummus' (modern 'follis') with the GENIO POPVLI ROMANI reverse, struck at mints marked in a uniform system.
events.locName: Imperial mints (about 15, from London to Alexandria)

events.title: Constantius clears the Rhine delta of Franks
events.summary: After taking Gesoriacum, Constantius swept the Rhine mouths of Franks allied to Carausius and resettled captives as farmers in the depopulated territories of the Nervii and Treveri, a scene the panegyric of 297 describes with captive families waiting in the porticoes of Gallic cities for distribution.

events.title: Galerius defeats the Carpi; mass resettlement
events.summary: After victories by Galerius, the Carpi of the eastern Carpathians were transplanted wholesale into the empire and settled in Pannonia, a large-scale deportation of the type the Tetrarchs used to repopulate land and supply recruits.

events.title: Diocletian's palace at Spalatum
events.summary: Diocletian built a fortified retirement palace near Salona on the Dalmatian coast, a 215 x 180 m enclosure combining fortress plan, residence, mausoleum (now Split cathedral) and temple (now baptistery), which became the nucleus of the city of Split.

events.title: Constantius recovers Britain
events.summary: Constantius' praetorian prefect Asclepiodotus landed in fog, slipping past Allectus' fleet off the Isle of Wight, burned his boats and defeated and killed Allectus somewhere in southern Britain; Constantius' squadron reached London and saved it from Frankish mercenaries.

battle.significance: Ended the ten-year Britannic secession.

events.title: Battle of Callinicum (Galerius' defeat)
events.summary: Narseh, who had seized the Persian throne in 293, invaded Roman Armenia and Mesopotamia; Galerius, attacking with too small a force, was defeated between Callinicum and Carrhae.

battle.significance: Prompted the reinforcement of Galerius with Danubian troops for the decisive campaign of 298.

events.title: Diocletian's new tax system (capitatio-iugatio and the indiction)
events.summary: An edict of the prefect of Egypt Aristius Optatus dated 16 March 297 announces a new empire-wide assessment of land (iuga) and people (capita) to calculate annual requisitions in kind, set in a regular budget, the indiction.

events.title: Revolt of Domitius Domitianus and siege of Alexandria
events.summary: Lucius Domitius Domitianus, with his corrector Aurelius Achilleus, revolted in Egypt in 297, perhaps provoked by the new tax census; Diocletian came in person, besieged Alexandria for eight months, cut the aqueducts, and after its fall vowed to kill until the blood reached his horse's knees.

battle.significance: Ended the last major revolt of Roman Egypt; followed by Diocletian's reorganisation of Egypt into separate provinces.

events.title: Maximian's war against the Quinquegentiani
events.summary: Maximian crossed from Spain in 296-297 and campaigned against the Quinquegentiani, mountain tribes of Mauretania who had raided Roman towns, pursuing them into the Atlas; he entered Carthage in triumph on 10 March 298. Rebuilding at Carthage followed, and the campaign secured the African grain supply on which Rome depended.

events.title: Execution of the centurion Marcellus at Tingis
events.summary: At a birthday feast for the emperors on 21 July 298 the centurion Marcellus of the legio Traiana threw down his belt and vine staff, declaring he would serve only Christ; he was tried and beheaded on 30 October. His Acta are an important source for Christian attitudes to military service.

events.title: Diocletian withdraws from the Dodecaschoenus
events.summary: Visiting Upper Egypt, Diocletian withdrew the frontier from the Dodecaschoenus to Philae and the First Cataract, settling Nobatae in the evacuated zone as a buffer against the Blemmyes and paying both peoples annual subsidies.

events.title: Galerius' victory in Armenia
events.summary: With a new army of Danubian veterans, Galerius advanced through Armenia, personally reconnoitred the Persian camp and fell on Narseh by surprise, routing his army and capturing his treasury, harem, wife Arsane and children.
events.locName: Armenia, probably between Satala and Erzurum

battle.significance: Greatest Roman victory over the Sasanians before Heraclius.

events.title: Battles of Lingones and Vindonissa
events.summary: Constantius, nearly captured and hauled over the walls of Lingones (Langres) by a rope, defeated the Alamanni outside the city the same day, killing 60,000 according to Eutropius, and won a second victory near Vindonissa.

battle.significance: Secured the upper Rhine for a generation.

events.title: Baths of Diocletian in Rome
events.summary: Maximian began, in Diocletian's name, the largest baths ever built in Rome, covering 13 hectares on the Viminal, dedicated 305-306; Michelangelo converted the frigidarium into the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli.

events.title: "Pompey's Pillar" raised for Diocletian at Alexandria
events.summary: After the siege of 297-298, the prefect Publius set up a red Aswan granite column 26.85 m high on the Serapeum hill with a statue of Diocletian, honouring him as "the protector of Alexandria" (IGRR I 1068), probably for remitting part of the grain levy to the city. Crusaders later misnamed it Pompey's Pillar.

events.title: Peace of Nisibis
events.summary: Diocletian's envoy Sicorius Probus imposed terms on Narseh: Persia ceded five regions beyond the Tigris (Arzanene, Moxoene, Zabdicene, Rehimene and Corduene), recognised Roman control of Armenia (border at Zintha) and Iberia, and accepted Nisibis as the sole point of trade exchange.

events.title: Galerius' palace and arch at Thessalonica
events.summary: Galerius turned Thessalonica into a residence with a palace, hippodrome, octagon and a monumental four-way arch whose reliefs depict his Persian victory of 298, including Galerius on horseback duelling Narseh and the capture of the Persian harem; to the north rose the domed Rotunda, possibly intended as his mausoleum and later a church.

events.title: Christians purged from the army and palace
events.summary: When the haruspices at a sacrifice in Antioch claimed that Christian officials making the sign of the cross were spoiling the omens, Diocletian ordered all palace staff and soldiers to sacrifice or be flogged and dismissed; the magister Veturius carried out the purge in the army. Christian veterans such as Marcellus of Tingis (298) had already been executed for refusing service.

events.title: Luxor temple converted into a legionary camp
events.summary: Around 300 the Temple of Amun at Luxor was enclosed in a fortress for the legion stationed at Thebes, and a chapel in front of the sanctuary was turned into an imperial cult room painted with life-size frescoes of the four Tetrarchs, among the finest late Roman paintings.

events.title: Arnobius writes Against the Pagans
events.summary: Arnobius, a rhetor at Sicca Veneria and teacher of Lactantius, wrote seven books Adversus Nationes around 300 to prove the sincerity of his conversion to his bishop; they are a mine of information on the pagan cults they ridicule.

events.title: Currency edict of 301 (Aphrodisias)
events.summary: An edict, known from an inscription at Aphrodisias and effective 1 September 301, retariffed the coinage, apparently doubling the face value of the nummus and the argenteus, a revaluation that preceded the Price Edict by three months.

events.title: Edict on Maximum Prices
events.summary: Issued between 20 November and 9 December 301 in the names of all four Tetrarchs, the Edictum de pretiis rerum venalium fixed maximum prices and wages for over 1,200 goods and services, from wheat and wine to lion skins, freight charges and a lawyer's fee, on pain of death.
events.locName: Issued probably from Nicomedia; copies across the eastern provinces

events.title: Conversion of Armenia under Tiridates III
events.summary: King Tiridates III of Armenia, restored by Rome, accepted Christianity through the preaching of Gregory the Illuminator, who was consecrated bishop at Caesarea in Cappadocia; Armenia claims to be the first Christian kingdom.

events.title: Porphyry publishes the Enneads
events.summary: About 301, some thirty years after Plotinus' death, Porphyry arranged his master's 54 treatises into six groups of nine (Enneads), prefacing them with the Life of Plotinus; his Isagoge, an introduction to Aristotle's Categories, became the most-read logic textbook of the Middle Ages.

events.title: Diocletian's edict against the Manichaeans
events.summary: Diocletian ordered the leaders of the Manichaeans burned with their books and their followers executed or sent to the mines, condemning the sect as a Persian import that corrupted the 'modest and tranquil Roman people'.
events.locName: Rescript to the proconsul of Africa

events.title: The Great Persecution begins
events.summary: On the feast of the Terminalia, 23 February 303, soldiers demolished the church of Nicomedia, visible from the palace; the next day an edict ordered churches destroyed, scriptures surrendered and burned, Christian meetings banned and Christians of rank stripped of privileges.

events.title: Martyrdom of Felix of Thibiuca
events.summary: Bishop Felix of Thibiuca refused to surrender the scriptures under the first edict and was sent to Carthage and executed on 15 July 303, probably the first African martyr of the Great Persecution; his Acta are early and largely authentic.

events.title: Diocletian's vicennalia in Rome
events.summary: Diocletian visited Rome, probably for the only time, to celebrate his twentieth anniversary and a joint triumph with Maximian; the Decennalia base of the Tetrarchs in the Forum survives. Irritated by Roman freedom of speech, he left in December before taking up his consulship.

events.title: Mutiny of Eugenius at Seleucia Pieria
events.summary: Some 500 soldiers digging out the harbour of Seleucia, overworked and unable to sleep at night because of the labour, proclaimed their commander Eugenius emperor and marched on Antioch, where the citizens killed them; Diocletian later punished the city's leading men, as Libanius and Eusebius recount.

events.title: Martyrdom of Agnes at Rome
events.summary: The girl Agnes, aged about 12 or 13, was executed in Rome, probably in 304, and buried on the Via Nomentana; Damasus wrote her epitaph and Ambrose and Prudentius her legend. Constantina built the funerary basilica of Sant'Agnese and her own mausoleum (Santa Costanza) beside the tomb.

events.title: Martyrs of Abitinae
events.summary: Forty-nine Christians, including the priest Saturninus, were arrested celebrating the eucharist in a house at Abitinae and taken to Carthage on 12 February 304; asked why they had disobeyed, they replied "sine dominico non possumus" (we cannot live without the Lord's day). Their Acta were later embellished by Donatists.

events.title: The fourth edict: universal sacrifice
events.summary: Early in 304, with Diocletian ill, a fourth edict ordered all inhabitants of the empire to sacrifice and pour libations, renewing the Decian model; it was enforced vigorously in Galerius' and later Maximinus' territories but hardly at all in Constantius' Gaul and Britain.

events.title: Abdication of Diocletian and Maximian
events.summary: On 1 May 305 Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan simultaneously abdicated; Constantius and Galerius became Augusti, and the new Caesars were Galerius' protégés Severus and Maximinus Daia, passing over Constantine and Maxentius, the sons of emperors.
events.locName: Hill three miles from Nicomedia; Mediolanum

events.title: Synod of Elvira
events.summary: Nineteen Spanish bishops, including Ossius of Corduba, met at Iliberris (Granada) and issued 81 canons, the earliest surviving disciplinary code of a church council, including clerical celibacy, bans on images painted on church walls and on marriage of Christian girls to Jews or pagans.

events.title: Constantine escapes from Galerius' court
events.summary: Passed over in the succession of 1 May 305, Constantine obtained permission from Galerius to join his father and rode off at night, killing or maiming the post-horses behind him to prevent pursuit (Lactantius, Origo); he found Constantius at Gesoriacum about to sail for Britain.

events.title: Constantius' campaign against the Picts
events.summary: Constantius and Constantine campaigned beyond Hadrian's Wall against the Picts, here named for the first time in a panegyric of 297/310, perhaps reaching the far north ("the woods and marshes of the Caledonians"); Constantius died at York on 25 July 306 after the campaign.

events.title: Iamblichus' school at Apamea
events.summary: Iamblichus of Chalcis, Porphyry's pupil and critic, taught at Apamea from about 305 a Neoplatonism centred on theurgy, ritual that united the soul with the gods; his pupils Aedesius, Sopater and the Maximus who taught Julian made his system the philosophy of the late pagan revival.

events.title: Lactantius writes the Divine Institutes
events.summary: Lactantius, an African rhetor appointed to teach Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia by Diocletian and dismissed in the persecution, wrote seven books of Divine Institutes (c. 303-310), the first systematic Latin exposition of Christianity, aimed at educated pagans; later he tutored Crispus in Trier and wrote De Mortibus Persecutorum (c. 314-315).

events.title: Galerius builds Felix Romuliana
events.summary: Galerius built a fortified palace at his birthplace, naming it after his mother Romula, with temples, baths and on the nearby hill of Magura the mausolea and consecration mounds of Romula and Galerius himself, who was buried there in 311. An archivolt inscribed FELIX ROMULIANA confirmed the identification in 1984.

events.title: Constantine proclaimed at Eboracum
events.summary: Constantius I died at York after a campaign against the Picts, and his army, prompted by the Alamannic king Crocus, proclaimed his son Constantine Augustus; Galerius grudgingly recognised him as Caesar.

events.title: Maxentius seizes Rome
events.summary: Angered by Galerius' plan to extend the census and taxation to the city of Rome and to abolish the Praetorian Guard, the Praetorians and people proclaimed Maximian's son Maxentius princeps, and Maximian came out of retirement to support him.

events.title: Ascaric and Merogaisus given to the beasts at Trier
events.summary: After defeating Frankish raiders, Constantine had their captured kings Ascaric and Merogaisus thrown to wild animals in the amphitheatre at Trier, and the captives were exposed in the arena, a spectacle celebrated as the Ludi Francici and praised by the panegyrists.

events.title: The Melitian schism in Egypt
events.summary: While Peter of Alexandria was in hiding, Melitius bishop of Lycopolis ordained clergy in other dioceses and adopted a harsher line on the lapsed, founding a "Church of the Martyrs" that survived into the eighth century; Nicaea tried to reabsorb it, and Melitians allied with Arius' supporters against Athanasius.

events.title: Severus' invasion of Italy and death
events.summary: Severus, sent by Galerius against Maxentius, advanced on Rome but his troops, many of them former soldiers of Maximian, deserted; he fled to Ravenna, surrendered on promise of his life, and was later killed or forced to suicide at Tres Tabernae.

events.title: Galerius' failed invasion of Italy
events.summary: Galerius marched on Rome in summer 307 but, finding the city too large and well defended to besiege and his troops wavering, retreated, allowing his army to plunder Italy on the way.

events.title: Constantine marries Fausta and is made Augustus by Maximian
events.summary: At Trier, Maximian gave his daughter Fausta to Constantine in marriage and named him Augustus, an alliance celebrated in a panegyric (Pan. Lat. 7(6)) that describes a painting of the betrothal at Aquileia.

events.title: Successive reductions of the nummus (follis)
events.summary: Diocletian's silver-washed nummus of c. 10 g (1/32 pound) was cut to about 1/40 pound in 307, 1/48 in 310, 1/72 by 313 and about 3 g (1/96) by 318, while its silver wash shrank; prices in papyri rise accordingly. These cuts were made at different moments by rival emperors, creating regional differences.

events.title: Maximian tries to depose his son Maxentius
events.summary: In April 308 Maximian, emboldened by his son's victory over Galerius, called an assembly of soldiers and people in Rome and tore the purple from Maxentius' shoulders; the troops sided with the son, and the old emperor fled to Constantine in Gaul.

events.title: Conference of Carnuntum
events.summary: Galerius summoned Diocletian from retirement to Carnuntum; Maximian was forced to abdicate again, Licinius was made Augustus of the West directly, Constantine was demoted to Caesar, and Maxentius was declared a public enemy.

events.title: Revolt of Domitius Alexander in Africa
events.summary: Lucius Domitius Alexander, vicarius of Africa, rebelled against Maxentius, cutting Rome's grain supply; Maxentius' praetorian prefect Rufius Volusianus crushed him around 310 and sacked Carthage and Cirta.

events.title: Basilica Nova of Maxentius
events.summary: Maxentius built the vast Basilica Nova on the Velia with three cross-vaulted bays over a 25 m-wide nave, the last great vaulted civic building of pagan Rome, completed by Constantine, who placed his colossal seated statue (whose head and hand survive in the Capitoline Museums) in a new apse.

events.title: Hilarion introduces monasticism to Palestine
events.summary: According to Jerome's Life, Hilarion of Thabatha, who had studied at Alexandria and visited Antony, settled as a hermit near Gaza around 306-308 and attracted disciples, the first monastic movement in Palestine; Sozomen, from the region, confirms his fame.

events.title: Constantine introduces the solidus
events.summary: Around 309-310, at the Trier mint, Constantine began striking a lighter gold coin at 72 to the Roman pound (c. 4.5 g), the solidus, which became the stable standard of the late Roman and Byzantine world for some 700 years.

events.title: Volusianus crushes Domitius Alexander; Carthage sacked
events.summary: Maxentius sent his praetorian prefect Gaius Ceionius Rufius Volusianus with a small force to Africa, which had cut Rome's grain supply; Alexander was defeated and strangled, and Carthage and Cirta were sacked. Constantine later refounded Cirta as Constantina.

events.title: Maxentius' villa, circus and mausoleum on the Via Appia
events.summary: Maxentius built a palace complex at the third mile of the Via Appia with a circus 513 m long, its spina adorned with the obelisk now in Piazza Navona, and a rotunda mausoleum where his son Valerius Romulus (d. 309) was buried; he also restored the Temple of Venus and Roma after a fire and began the Basilica Nova.

events.title: Revolt and death of Maximian at Massilia
events.summary: Living at Constantine's court, Maximian proclaimed himself emperor again at Arles while Constantine was on the Rhine; Constantine marched south, besieged him in Massilia and Maximian was forced to hang himself.

events.title: Constantine's 'pagan vision' at Grand
events.summary: The panegyrist of 310 describes Constantine visiting a temple of Apollo (probably at Grand in the Vosges), where he saw Apollo with Victory offering him laurel wreaths each bearing the sign XXX, foretelling a thirty-year reign.

events.title: The Aula Palatina at Trier
events.summary: Constantine built a vast brick audience hall at Trier, 67 m long, 27.5 m wide and about 30 m high, with heated floors and a raised apse for the throne, as part of a palace quarter that also included the Kaiserthermen and the double cathedral. Restored after 1945, it is the largest surviving single-room Roman structure.

events.title: Rhine bridge at Cologne and the fort of Divitia
events.summary: Constantine bridged the Rhine at Cologne with a permanent bridge on piers and built the fortified bridgehead of Divitia (Deutz) on the right bank, about 140 m square with 14 towers, garrisoned by the Divitenses; the panegyrist presents it as a yoke on the Franks.

events.title: Galerius' edict of toleration and death
events.summary: Dying of a horrible disease (Lactantius describes his body consumed by worms), Galerius issued an edict, posted at Nicomedia on 30 April 311, ending the persecution and permitting Christians to 'exist again and hold their meetings' on condition they pray to their god for the emperors' safety; he died days later.

events.title: Martyrdom of Peter of Alexandria
events.summary: Peter, bishop of Alexandria, who had hidden during the persecution and quarrelled with Melitius over the lapsed, was beheaded on 25 November 311 on Maximinus' orders, the "seal of the martyrs" in Coptic tradition. His canons on penance remain part of Orthodox canon law.

events.title: Outbreak of the Donatist schism
events.summary: The consecration of Caecilian as bishop of Carthage by Felix of Abthugni, accused of being a traditor in the persecution, was rejected by Numidian bishops, who elected Majorinus and then Donatus; the African church split into two hierarchies for over a century.

events.title: Maximinus Daia organises a pagan priesthood
events.summary: Ignoring Galerius' toleration, Maximinus appointed high priests for each city and province, dressed in white, with authority to prevent Christians from assembling; he encouraged cities to petition for the expulsion of Christians and had forged "Acts of Pilate" taught in schools. Julian later imitated the scheme.

events.title: Death of Diocletian at Spalatum
events.summary: Diocletian died in retirement in his palace at Split, embittered by the destruction of his statues and the murder of his wife Prisca and daughter Valeria by Licinius and Maximinus; Lactantius claims he starved himself. He was buried in the octagonal mausoleum, now the cathedral of St Domnius.

events.title: Martyrdom of Lucian of Antioch
events.summary: The scholar-presbyter Lucian of Antioch, reviser of the Greek Septuagint and New Testament text and teacher of Arius, Eusebius of Nicomedia and other "Collucianists", was executed at Nicomedia on 7 January 312 after defending his faith before Maximinus. Helenopolis was built near his shrine at Drepanum.

events.title: Constantine's vision and the Christian sign
events.summary: Before the battle against Maxentius, Constantine was, according to Lactantius, told in a dream to mark 'the heavenly sign of God' on his soldiers' shields; Eusebius, writing after Constantine's death and claiming the emperor's own sworn account, describes a cross of light in the sky with the words 'by this conquer' (touto nika) followed by a dream and the making of the labarum.

events.title: Battle of the Milvian Bridge
events.summary: On the sixth anniversary of his accession, Maxentius left the Aurelian Walls, crossed the Tiber on a pontoon bridge beside the cut Milvian Bridge and drew up with the river at his back near Saxa Rubra; Constantine's cavalry routed his wings, the army collapsed toward the river, the pontoon gave way and Maxentius drowned.
events.locName: Milvian Bridge and Saxa Rubra, north of Rome

sides.strength: c. 40,000 (modern estimate); Zosimus claims 90,000 foot, 8,000 horse
Zosimus claims 170,000 foot, 18,000 horse (impossible); Praetorians, Italian and African troops

battle.significance: Gave Constantine the West and Rome; traditionally the turning point toward a Christian empire.

events.title: Battle of Turin
events.summary: After storming Segusio at the foot of the Alps, Constantine met Maxentius' heavily armoured cavalry (clibanarii) on the plain west of Turin; his men opened ranks and clubbed the armoured riders down with iron-bound maces, and Turin shut its gates on the fleeing Maxentians.

sides.strength: perhaps 40,000 (panegyric of 313 says under a quarter of his army, c. 25,000-40,000)

battle.significance: Opened the Po valley; Milan welcomed Constantine.

events.title: Siege and battle of Verona
events.summary: Constantine besieged Verona, held by Maxentius' praetorian prefect Ruricius Pompeianus, who broke out to bring a relief army; Constantine defeated and killed him in a night battle, after which Verona and Aquileia surrendered.

battle.significance: Destroyed Maxentius' northern army, leaving Rome exposed.

events.title: Abolition of the Praetorian Guard
events.summary: Constantine dissolved the Praetorian cohorts and the equites singulares Augusti, who had fought for Maxentius, demolished the internal walls of the Castra Praetoria, and replaced them with the new scholae palatinae, cavalry guard regiments attached to the emperor's person.

events.title: Foundation of the Lateran Basilica
events.summary: Constantine gave the bishop of Rome the Lateran property and built the Basilica Constantiniana (later St John Lateran) over the barracks of the disbanded horse guard, a five-aisled basilica about 100 m long, the first great church of Rome and cathedral of its bishop.

events.title: Constantine's military reorganisation
events.summary: Constantine developed a permanent mobile field army (comitatenses) separate from the frontier forces (ripenses, later limitanei), created the commands of magister peditum and magister equitum, and stripped the praetorian prefects of military authority, turning them into the highest civil officials.

events.title: The Arycanda petition against the Christians
events.summary: An inscription from Arycanda in Lycia preserves a Greek petition from the people of Lycia and Pamphylia asking Maximinus, Constantine and Licinius to suppress the "atheist" Christians, together with part of Maximinus' Latin reply; a similar rescript to Tyre is paraphrased by Eusebius.

events.title: Maximinus Daia's Armenian war, famine and plague
events.summary: In 312 Maximinus fought an unsuccessful war against the Christian Armenians, Rome's allies; at the same time drought, famine and an epidemic with an "eye disease" (perhaps smallpox) struck his provinces, events Eusebius interprets as divine punishment.

events.title: The 'Edict of Milan'
events.summary: Meeting at Milan in February 313, where Licinius married Constantine's half-sister Constantia, the two Augusti agreed on a policy of religious freedom for all and restoration of confiscated church property; the text survives as a letter issued by Licinius at Nicomedia on 13 June 313.

events.title: Battle of Tzirallum (Campus Ergenus)
events.summary: Maximinus Daia crossed into Europe and took Byzantium and Heraclea, but Licinius, with about 30,000 men against 70,000, defeated him on the Campus Ergenus near Tzirallum; Lactantius says an angel dictated a prayer to Licinius that his soldiers recited before battle.

battle.significance: Left the empire divided between two Augusti, Constantine and Licinius.

events.title: Council of Rome on the Donatists
events.summary: At Constantine's request, Pope Miltiades with three Gallic and fifteen Italian bishops heard the Donatist complaint against Caecilian in the house of Fausta on the Lateran (2-4 October 313), acquitting Caecilian and condemning Donatus; the Donatists appealed, leading to Arles in 314.

events.title: Death of Maximinus Daia at Tarsus
events.summary: Fleeing to Asia Minor, Maximinus issued his own toleration edict and died at Tarsus in summer 313, of poison or disease; Licinius then killed his family and the families of Galerius, Severus and Diocletian, including Diocletian's widow Prisca and daughter Valeria.

events.title: Eusebius publishes the Ecclesiastical History
events.summary: Eusebius of Caesarea, pupil of Pamphilus and heir to Origen's library, published the first church history in successive editions (books 1-7 perhaps before 303; books 8-10 added 313-325), quoting hundreds of documents; with his Chronicle, which tabulated sacred and secular chronology in parallel columns, it created the framework of Christian historiography.

events.title: Council of Arles
events.summary: Constantine summoned bishops from across the West, including three from Britain (York, London and probably Lincoln), to Arles to judge the Donatist appeal; they upheld Caecilian and issued canons, including one threatening excommunication for soldiers who threw down their arms in peacetime.

events.title: Arch of Constantine dedicated
events.summary: For his decennalia in 315 the Senate dedicated a triple arch beside the Colosseum, celebrating victory over the 'tyrant' Maxentius; it reused reliefs from monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius with heads recut as Constantine, together with a contemporary frieze of the campaign of 312.

events.title: Battle of Cibalae
events.summary: In the first war between Constantine and Licinius, Constantine with 20,000 men defeated Licinius' 35,000 in a day-long battle in the narrow ground between a hill and a marsh near Cibalae in Pannonia; Licinius retreated to Sirmium and then Thrace.

battle.significance: Constantine gained the initiative in the Balkans.

events.title: Constantine rules for Caecilian at Milan
events.summary: After Arles and the inquiry of 315 that cleared Felix of Abthugni of traditio, Constantine himself heard the case at Milan and on 10 November 316 found for Caecilian, ordering Donatist basilicas confiscated.

events.title: Battle of Mardia
events.summary: Constantine and Licinius fought an indecisive battle at Campus Mardiensis in Thrace in late 316 or early 317; the peace concluded at Serdica gave Constantine all the Balkans except Thrace (the dioceses of Pannonia and Moesia).

battle.significance: Led to a negotiated peace and redistribution of the Balkans.

events.title: Crispus, Constantine II and Licinius II made Caesars
events.summary: At Serdica on 1 March 317 Constantine's sons Crispus (about 12-17) and the infant Constantine II and Licinius' infant son Licinius II were proclaimed Caesars, sealing the peace and establishing hereditary succession for both houses.

events.title: Coercion of the Donatists and the Carthage massacre
events.summary: Imperial troops under the comes Leontius and dux Ursatius seized Donatist churches; at Carthage on 12 March 317 soldiers killed worshippers including the bishop of Advocata, events commemorated in the Donatist Passio Donati. In 321 Constantine abandoned coercion and left the Donatists "to God".

events.title: Arius and the beginning of the Arian controversy
events.summary: Arius, presbyter of the Baucalis church in Alexandria, taught that the Son was created by the Father and that 'there was when he was not'; Bishop Alexander condemned him at a synod of about 100 Egyptian bishops, but Arius found support from Eusebius of Nicomedia and other Lucianist bishops in the East.

events.title: Constantine authorises episcopal courts
events.summary: A law of 318 (CTh 1.27.1) allowed parties in a civil suit to transfer it to a bishop's tribunal, whose decision was final; a later constitution (Sirmondian 1, 333) extended it even to cases moved by one party. Bishops thereby became judges, a role Augustine complained consumed his mornings.

events.title: Old St Peter's Basilica begun
events.summary: Constantine built a vast five-aisled basilica over the reputed tomb of the apostle Peter on the Vatican hill, levelling part of the hillside and burying a pagan necropolis to centre the building on the second-century aedicula.

events.title: The Forty Martyrs of Sebaste
events.summary: Forty soldiers of legio XII Fulminata, refusing to sacrifice under Licinius, were left naked on a frozen lake at Sebaste to die of exposure, according to Basil and Gregory of Nyssa; one defected and a guard took his place. Their cult became one of the most popular in the Greek world.

events.title: Licinius restricts the church
events.summary: From about 320 Licinius expelled Christians from his palace, required officials to sacrifice, banned synods, forbade men and women to worship together and ordered services held outside city walls; some churches in Pontus were destroyed. Constantine used this as a pretext for war in 324.

events.title: Villa del Casale at Piazza Armerina
events.summary: A vast late Roman villa built c. 310-340 with some 3,500 m² of mosaics, including a 60 m corridor of the Great Hunt showing animals captured in Africa and India for the games, and the "bikini girls" exercising; its owner was an imperial-level senator, perhaps a Ceionius or Maximian himself.

events.title: Constantine's law on the 'venerable day of the Sun'
events.summary: Constantine ordered that magistrates, city people and craftsmen rest on the 'venerable day of the Sun' (dies Solis), while allowing farmers to work; a July 321 law permitted manumissions and emancipations on that day.

events.title: Constantine defeats the Sarmatian king Rausimodus
events.summary: Constantine repelled a Sarmatian invasion under Rausimodus, besieging them at Campona and pursuing them across the Danube where the king was killed; coins with SARMATIA DEVICTA followed. In 323 he chased Goths into Licinius' Thracian territory, provoking a protest that contributed to the war of 324.

events.title: Pachomius founds the monastery of Tabennesi
events.summary: The former conscript Pachomius, converted by Christian charity to recruits at Thebes, founded a community at the deserted village of Tabennesi c. 323, then Pbow; by his death in 346 his koinonia had nine monasteries and two nunneries with a written rule, shared work and a hierarchy, the beginning of cenobitic monasticism. Jerome translated the Rule into Latin.

events.title: Battle of the Hellespont
events.summary: Crispus with Constantine's fleet of 200 smaller warships defeated Licinius' admiral Abantus (Amandus) with 350 triremes in the Hellespont over two days, a storm on the second day wrecking much of the enemy fleet.

battle.significance: Opened the straits; prerequisite for Chrysopolis.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople (324)
events.summary: Constantine, now openly fighting under the labarum, crossed the Hebrus with a small detachment upstream and fell on Licinius' fortified camp near Adrianople, winning a major victory; Licinius retreated to Byzantium.

battle.significance: Drove Licinius out of Thrace.

events.title: Battle of Chrysopolis
events.summary: Constantine crossed the Bosporus and crushed Licinius' army, reinforced by Gothic auxiliaries under Alica, at Chrysopolis opposite Byzantium; Licinius fled to Nicomedia and surrendered on the plea of his wife Constantia.

sides.losses: very heavy; Zosimus says scarcely 30,000 of 130,000 escaped (exaggerated)

battle.significance: Made Constantine sole emperor; led to the foundation of Constantinople.

events.title: Foundation of Constantinople
events.summary: On 8 November 324 Constantine traced the boundary of a greatly enlarged city on the site of Byzantium, about four times its former size, as his eponymous residence and 'New Rome'.

events.title: Optatianus Porfyrius' figured poems for Constantine
events.summary: Publilius Optatianus Porfyrius, exiled under unclear circumstances, won his recall and later the urban prefecture by sending Constantine a book of carmina cancellata: grids of letters in which coloured verses form chi-rhos, palm branches, a ship and other images inside the poem.

events.title: First Council of Nicaea
events.summary: Constantine convened some 250-300 bishops (later tradition: 318) at Nicaea in Bithynia, opening the council in person in the imperial palace; it condemned Arius, adopted a creed declaring the Son 'homoousios' (of the same substance) with the Father, set rules for the date of Easter and issued twenty canons.

events.title: Execution of Licinius at Thessalonica
events.summary: Spared at first and sent to Thessalonica, Licinius was executed in spring 325, accused of plotting with barbarians; his son Licinius II was killed in 326.

events.title: Council of Antioch (early 325)
events.summary: A synod of some 56 bishops under Ossius of Cordoba, meeting at Antioch early in 325 to elect a bishop, issued an anti-Arian creed and provisionally excommunicated Eusebius of Caesarea and two others pending the great council; its synodal letter survives in Syriac.

events.title: Introduction of the siliqua and miliarense
events.summary: Constantine introduced new silver denominations in the 320s, the miliarense (1/72 and 1/60 pound) and later the siliqua (1/96 pound), named for the carob seed (1/24 solidus); they served largely as donatives to the army and court rather than everyday money.

events.title: Constantine's vicennalia in Rome
events.summary: Constantine celebrated the close of his twentieth year in Rome in July 326, his last visit; Zosimus claims he refused to join the traditional procession to the Capitol, offending the Senate and people. The executions of Crispus and Fausta took place the same year.

events.title: Execution of Crispus and death of Fausta
events.summary: In 326 Constantine had his eldest son Crispus, Caesar and victor of the Hellespont, executed at Pola in Istria; shortly afterwards the empress Fausta died, reportedly suffocated in an overheated bath.

events.title: Helena's pilgrimage and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
events.summary: Constantine ordered Bishop Macarius to demolish the Hadrianic temple over the supposed tomb of Christ in Jerusalem and build a basilica; his mother Helena toured the Holy Land in 326-328 founding churches at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. The Holy Sepulchre was dedicated in September 335.

events.title: Confiscation of temple treasures and the chrysargyron
events.summary: After 324 Constantine's agents stripped temples of gold and silver, bronze doors and cult statues, funding the new gold coinage and Constantinople, and he introduced the collatio lustralis (chrysargyron), a tax on merchants and craftsmen paid every five years, and the collatio glebalis on senators.

events.title: Arius readmitted by Constantine
events.summary: After submitting an ambiguous creed, Arius was recalled from exile and readmitted at a second session of Nicaea or a synod at Nicomedia (327-328), and Eusebius of Nicomedia and Theognis returned to their sees; Athanasius' refusal to receive Arius began his long conflict with the court.

events.title: Athanasius becomes bishop of Alexandria
events.summary: On 8 June 328, after the death of Alexander, the deacon Athanasius, about thirty and below canonical age, was consecrated by a minority of bishops amid Melitian protests; he would hold the see for 45 years, 17 of them in five exiles.

events.title: Constantine's Danube bridge at Oescus
events.summary: Constantine opened a bridge of about 2.4 km across the Danube between Oescus and Sucidava, the longest bridge of the ancient world, reasserting Roman power north of the river in the old Dacian lands.

events.title: Juvencus versifies the Gospels
events.summary: The Spanish priest Gaius Vettius Aquilinus Juvencus composed the Evangeliorum libri IV, a Virgilian hexameter harmony of the Gospels of some 3,200 lines, around 329; it is the first Christian Latin epic and was a school text through the Middle Ages.

events.title: Dedication of Constantinople
events.summary: On 11 May 330 the new city was formally dedicated with forty days of celebrations; the anniversary was marked annually in the Hippodrome by a procession of a gilded statue of Constantine holding a figure of the city's Tyche.

events.title: Constantine destroys the temples of Aphaca, Aegeae and Heliopolis
events.summary: Eusebius reports that Constantine had the shrine of Aphrodite at Aphaca on Mount Lebanon demolished for its ritual prostitution, the healing sanctuary of Asclepius at Aegeae in Cilicia torn down, and the temple of Aphrodite at Heliopolis replaced by a church, while statues from across the east were carried to adorn Constantinople.

events.title: Amoun founds Nitria; Macarius settles in Scetis
events.summary: About 330 Amoun settled on the mountain of Nitria south of Alexandria and Macarius the Egyptian in the desert of Scetis; by the 390s Palladius found some 5,000 monks at Nitria, with bakeries, doctors and a church, and the outlying Kellia, where Evagrius wrote. Scetis produced the Apophthegmata Patrum.

events.title: Constantine orders a church at Mamre
events.summary: Informed by his mother-in-law Eutropia that pagans, Jews and Christians were sacrificing together at the oak of Mamre where Abraham received the three angels, Constantine wrote to the bishops of Palestine ordering the altars destroyed and a basilica built within Herod's enclosure.

events.title: GLORIA EXERCITVS and the small Constantinian nummus
events.summary: From 330 all mints struck a light nummus (c. 2.5 g, later c. 1.7 g from 335) with two soldiers and two standards (later one) and the legend GLORIA EXERCITVS, alongside URBS ROMA and CONSTANTINOPOLIS commemorative types; these are among the commonest ancient coins found today.

events.title: Constantine restricts unilateral divorce
events.summary: A law of 331 (CTh 3.16.1) allowed a wife to repudiate her husband only if he was a murderer, poisoner or tomb violator, and a husband his wife only for adultery, poisoning or procuring, with severe property penalties otherwise, a sharp break with the classical freedom of divorce often attributed to Christian influence.

events.title: Constantine's Gothic war and treaty
events.summary: Intervening for the Sarmatians against the Tervingi, Constantine's son Constantine II won a great victory on 20 April 332, said to have killed 100,000 Goths through hunger and cold; the ensuing treaty made the Tervingi allies who supplied troops in return for subsidies and trading rights.

events.title: Constantine's law on fugitive coloni
events.summary: A law of 30 October 332 ordered that a colonus found on another's land be returned to the estate of his origin, and permitted fugitive coloni to be chained like slaves, a key text in the history of the 'tied colonate'.

events.title: Church of the Nativity at Bethlehem
events.summary: A basilica built at Constantine's and Helena's initiative over the cave venerated as Christ's birthplace, with an octagon above the grotto, was complete by 333 when the Bordeaux pilgrim saw it; its mosaic floors lie beneath the Justinianic church.

events.title: The Bordeaux pilgrim travels to Jerusalem
events.summary: An anonymous Christian from Burdigala travelled overland via Arles, Milan, Sirmium, Constantinople and Antioch to Jerusalem in 333, listing every mansio and mutatio with distances and noting holy sites, including the newly built Holy Sepulchre; it is the earliest surviving Christian pilgrim itinerary.

events.title: Settlement of 300,000 Sarmatians
events.summary: When the Sarmatian 'Argaragantes' were overthrown by their armed slaves (the Limigantes), Constantine received more than 300,000 Sarmatian refugees and distributed them across Thrace, Scythia, Macedonia and Italy.

events.title: Revolt of Calocaerus in Cyprus
events.summary: Calocaerus, magister of the imperial camel herd on Cyprus, proclaimed himself emperor; Constantine's nephew Dalmatius crushed him and had him burned alive at Tarsus.

events.title: Dedication of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
events.summary: Bishops from the Council of Tyre moved to Jerusalem to dedicate Constantine's basilica on Golgotha (the Martyrium) on 13 September 335, with the rotunda of the Anastasis still unfinished; the feast of the Encaenia became one of Jerusalem's great annual festivals, described by Egeria. The synod also readmitted Arius.

events.title: Constantine divides the empire among his heirs
events.summary: On 18 September 335 Constantine made his nephew Dalmatius Caesar, giving him Thrace, Macedonia and Achaea, while Constantine II held Gaul, Spain and Britain, Constans Italy, Africa and Pannonia, and Constantius II the east; another nephew, Hannibalianus, became "King of Kings" over Armenia and the Pontic peoples, a calculated affront to Persia.

events.title: Council of Tyre and the first exile of Athanasius
events.summary: A council at Tyre, dominated by Eusebius of Nicomedia's allies, tried Athanasius of Alexandria on charges including violence against Melitian clergy, the breaking of a chalice and the murder of Bishop Arsenius (who was produced alive); Athanasius fled to Constantinople and Constantine exiled him to Trier after he was accused of threatening the Alexandrian grain fleet.

events.title: Constantine's tricennalia
