events.summary: On 25 July 336 Constantine became the first emperor since Augustus to reign thirty years; Eusebius delivered his Tricennial Oration in the palace, setting out the theory of the emperor as image of the divine Logos ruling a world empire mirroring heaven. Constantius II married a daughter of Julius Constantius the same year.

events.title: Death of Arius at Constantinople
events.summary: On the eve of his planned readmission to communion at Constantinople, Arius died suddenly in a public latrine; his opponents (Athanasius, Socrates) saw divine judgement, comparing his end to Judas' bursting asunder.

events.title: Baptism and death of Constantine
events.summary: Preparing a war against Shapur II, Constantine fell ill, was baptised by Eusebius of Nicomedia at the villa of Achyron near Nicomedia, and died at Pentecost, 22 May 337, aged about 65; he was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople amid cenotaphs of the twelve apostles.

events.title: The three sons of Constantine become Augusti
events.summary: After the massacre of their cousins, Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans took the title Augustus on 9 September 337 and met in Pannonia in 338 to share the empire: Constantine II kept the west beyond the Alps, Constans took Italy, Africa and Illyricum including Dalmatius' share, and Constantius the east and Thrace.

events.title: Athanasius returns from his first exile
events.summary: Released by Constantine II from exile at Trier after Constantine's death, Athanasius re-entered Alexandria on 23 November 337, but the Eusebian bishops at once accused him of violence and of selling grain meant for widows.

events.title: Massacre of the Constantinian princes
events.summary: In the summer of 337 the army at Constantinople murdered Constantine's half-brothers Julius Constantius and Flavius Dalmatius, his nephews the Caesar Dalmatius and Hannibalianus ('King of Kings and of the Pontic peoples'), the patrician Optatus and the prefect Ablabius, leaving only Constantine's three sons and two small boys, Gallus and Julian.

events.title: First siege of Nisibis by Shapur II
events.summary: Shapur II besieged Nisibis for some 63 or 70 days; the city held, its defence later credited by Syriac tradition to the prayers of Bishop Jacob of Nisibis, who reportedly sent a plague of gnats against the Persian elephants.

battle.significance: Opened 25 years of Persian attempts on Roman Mesopotamia.

events.title: Second exile of Athanasius; Gregory of Cappadocia installed
events.summary: A synod at Antioch deposed Athanasius again and Constantius had the Cappadocian Gregory installed as bishop by the prefect Philagrius in March 339, amid violence in the churches; Athanasius fled on 16 April to Rome, where he spent seven years under the protection of Pope Julius and Constans.

events.title: Constantine II killed invading Italy
events.summary: Constantine II, claiming seniority and resentful of his share, invaded Constans' territory and was ambushed and killed near Aquileia (at the river Alsa) in spring 340; Constans took over the whole West.

events.title: Funerary basilica of Sant'Agnese and the mausoleum of Constantina
events.summary: Constantine's daughter Constantina built a huge U-shaped funerary basilica beside Agnes' tomb, one of a series of circus-shaped cemetery basilicas (San Lorenzo, Santi Marcellino e Pietro with Helena's mausoleum, San Sebastiano); her domed mausoleum, now Santa Costanza, keeps vault mosaics of vintage scenes with putti treading grapes.

events.title: Ulfilas consecrated bishop of the Goths
events.summary: Ulfilas (Wulfila), a Goth descended from Cappadocian captives of the 250s raids, was consecrated 'bishop of the Christians in the Getic land' by Eusebius of Nicomedia, probably at the Dedication Council of Antioch; he devised a Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible, omitting, it was said, the Books of Kings as too warlike.

events.title: Pope Julius' council of Rome acquits Athanasius and Marcellus
events.summary: A synod of some fifty western bishops under Julius I acquitted Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra; Julius' letter to the eastern bishops, rebuking them for acting without consulting Rome, is an early statement of Roman appellate authority.

events.title: The Dedication Council of Antioch
events.summary: Some 90-97 eastern bishops gathered with Constantius II to dedicate the Great Church (Golden Octagon) of Antioch, begun by Constantine in 327; they issued four creeds avoiding homoousios, of which the "second creed", said to be Lucian's, became a rallying point, and 25 canons later received into church law.

events.title: Constans' law: "let superstition cease"
events.summary: A law of Constans to the vicar of Italy (CTh 16.10.2) ordered "cesset superstitio, sacrificiorum aboleatur insania", the first imperial prohibition of sacrifice, invoking a (lost) law of Constantine; a law of 342 nevertheless protected temples outside Rome connected with games.

events.title: Constans' Frankish war
events.summary: Constans fought the Franks on the lower Rhine in 341-342 and imposed a treaty; Libanius later praised the campaign as having made the Franks quiet.

events.title: Riot at Constantinople; the magister Hermogenes lynched
events.summary: When the magister equitum Hermogenes tried to expel the Nicene bishop Paul in favour of Macedonius, the people burned his house and dragged him through the streets to his death; Constantius rode from Antioch in midwinter, halved the city's free grain allowance and exiled Paul.

events.title: Constans' winter crossing to Britain
events.summary: Constans crossed the Channel from Boulogne in midwinter 343, an unusual feat celebrated by Firmicus Maternus, apparently to deal with trouble on the northern frontier involving the areani (frontier scouts) or with Picts and Scots.

events.title: Council of Serdica
events.summary: Called by Constans and Constantius to settle the Athanasian dispute, the council split on arrival: about 90 western bishops under Ossius met in Serdica, restored Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra and gave the bishop of Rome a right to hear appeals, while some 80 eastern bishops withdrew to Philippopolis and excommunicated Julius of Rome and Ossius.

events.title: Shapur II's persecution of Christians
events.summary: Shapur II imposed a double tax on Christians and, when Catholicos Simeon bar Sabba'e of Seleucia-Ctesiphon refused to collect it, had him executed with many clergy at Karka d-Ledan, beginning a 'Great Persecution' in Persia that lasted intermittently until Shapur's death in 379.

events.title: Night battle of Singara
events.summary: Constantius II's army stormed Shapur's camp near Singara and appeared victorious, but in the disordered night fighting the Persians counterattacked and inflicted heavy losses; Shapur's heir Narseh was captured and killed.

battle.significance: Bloodiest battle of Constantius' Persian war; neither side gained ground.

events.title: The Macrostich ("long-lined") creed
events.summary: An eastern synod at Antioch sent western bishops in Milan a long, conciliatory creed condemning both Arius' extreme formulas and Marcellus and Photinus, the high-water mark of eastern attempts at compromise before the 350s polarisation.

events.title: Athanasius' triumphal return to Alexandria
events.summary: Pressed by Constans, who threatened war, Constantius allowed Athanasius to return after Gregory's death; he met the emperor at Antioch and entered Alexandria on 21 October 346 to a reception Gregory of Nazianzus compares to an imperial adventus. The following decade was his "golden decade".

events.title: Second Persian siege of Nisibis
events.summary: Shapur II besieged Nisibis again for some 78 days without success; the Chronicle of Edessa and Jerome record the siege, and Ephrem's hymns celebrate the city's survival.

battle.significance: Second failure of Shapur before the fortress.

events.title: Firmicus Maternus urges the destruction of paganism
events.summary: Julius Firmicus Maternus, a Sicilian senator who had written the Mathesis, the most complete Latin astrological handbook (c. 335), converted and addressed to Constantius and Constans On the Error of Profane Religions (c. 346), urging them to stamp out pagan cults by force and providing unique detail on mystery rituals.

events.title: The mission of Paul and Macarius and the Bagai massacre
events.summary: Constans sent the commissioners Paul and Macarius to Africa with donations for the poor and pressure for unity; Donatus rejected them ("what has the emperor to do with the church?"), and at Bagai, where Bishop Donatus of Bagai had gathered circumcellions, troops massacred the defenders. Donatist leaders were exiled and the "Macarian times" remembered as persecution.

events.title: FEL TEMP REPARATIO coin reform
events.summary: For Rome's 1100th anniversary in 348 Constans and Constantius issued a new bronze coinage in two or three sizes with a small silver content, carrying the legend FEL(icium) TEMP(orum) REPARATIO ("restoration of happy times") and types such as a soldier spearing a fallen horseman, the phoenix and the emperor on a galley. The large coin was soon reduced and the series debased.

events.title: Usurpation of Magnentius and death of Constans
events.summary: At a birthday banquet at Augustodunum, the comes Flavius Magnentius, of part-Frankish or British origin, appeared in purple and was acclaimed emperor by officers alienated from the unpopular Constans, who fled and was killed by Gaiso near Helena (Elne) in the Pyrenees.

events.title: Third siege of Nisibis
events.summary: Shapur II besieged Nisibis for about four months (his second attempt had failed in 346), damming the Mygdonius river and releasing the floodwater against the walls, which partly collapsed; the defenders under Lucillianus built a new wall behind the breach overnight and repelled the attack with Persian elephants bogged in mud.

sides.strength: royal army with elephants and Indian contingents

battle.significance: Nisibis' successful defence preserved Roman Mesopotamia until 363.

events.title: Vetranio and Nepotianus
events.summary: On 1 March 350 the old general Vetranio was proclaimed in Illyricum, apparently at the instigation of Constantina, sister of Constantius, to block Magnentius; in June Constantine's nephew Nepotianus seized Rome with gladiators for 28 days before Magnentius' officer Marcellinus killed him and massacred his supporters. Vetranio abdicated before Constantius' army at Naissus on 25 December 350 and retired to Prusa.

events.title: Ulfilas translates the Bible into Gothic
events.summary: After leading his persecuted Gothic Christians into Moesia (c. 348), Ulfilas invented a Gothic alphabet from Greek, Latin and runic letters and translated the Bible, leaving out the Books of Kings to avoid encouraging the warlike Goths (Philostorgius). The Codex Argenteus in Uppsala preserves much of the Gospels.

events.title: Gallus made Caesar at Sirmium
events.summary: On 15 March 351 Constantius made his cousin Constantius Gallus, survivor of the 337 massacre, Caesar with residence at Antioch and married him to his sister Constantina, so as to free himself for the war with Magnentius.

events.title: The cross of light over Jerusalem
events.summary: On 7 May 351 a luminous cross was seen over Golgotha stretching to the Mount of Olives; Bishop Cyril reported it to Constantius in a surviving letter as a sign of divine favour in the war against Magnentius. It was probably a solar halo phenomenon.

events.title: Battle of Mursa
events.summary: Constantius II defeated Magnentius on the Drava near Mursa in one of the bloodiest battles in Roman history: Zonaras reports 30,000 of Constantius' 80,000 and 24,000 of Magnentius' 36,000 killed. Constantius' heavily armoured cavalry (cataphracts and clibanarii) turned Magnentius' left.

battle.significance: Decided the civil war; remembered as a catastrophic bleeding of Roman military manpower.

events.title: First Council of Sirmium condemns Photinus
events.summary: Eastern bishops meeting at Sirmium with Constantius deposed the local bishop Photinus, a pupil of Marcellus who taught that Christ was a mere man adopted by God, and issued the First Sirmian Creed with 26 anathemas.

events.title: Jewish revolt in Galilee
events.summary: Jews of Diocaesarea rose under a certain Patricius (Isaac in some sources), killing soldiers; Gallus' general Ursicinus crushed the revolt, destroying Diocaesarea, Tiberias and Diospolis according to Jerome and Socrates. Archaeology shows destruction at Sepphoris, though much may be due to the earthquake of 363.

events.title: Battle of Mons Seleucus and death of Magnentius
events.summary: After Constantius forced the Alpine passes, Magnentius was defeated at Mons Seleucus in the Cottian Alps; abandoned by his troops, he killed his family and committed suicide at Lugdunum on 10 August 353, and his brother Decentius hanged himself at Senones.

battle.significance: Left Constantius sole emperor.

events.title: Council of Arles condemns Athanasius
events.summary: Wintering at Arles after his victory, Constantius had Gallic bishops condemn Athanasius; Paulinus of Trier refused and was exiled to Phrygia, and even the papal legate Vincent of Capua signed, to Liberius' dismay.

events.title: The Chronograph of 354
events.summary: The calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus produced an illustrated almanac for a wealthy Christian Roman, Valentinus, combining the pagan festival calendar, consular fasti, a list of popes, the earliest list of Christian feasts (Depositio Martyrum, including 25 December as Christ's birth), a city chronicle and the regionary catalogue of Rome.

events.title: Execution of the Caesar Gallus
events.summary: Constantius Gallus, Caesar at Antioch since 351, ruled by terror (Ammianus' extant narrative opens with his excesses, including a lynching of the governor of Syria during a famine); summoned west, he was arrested and beheaded near Pola.

events.title: Constantius against Gundomad and Vadomar
events.summary: Constantius marched to the Rhine near Augst against the Alamannic brother-kings Gundomad and Vadomar, but finding the crossing blocked made peace; in 355 his magister Arbitio was ambushed by the Lentienses near Lake Constance before winning a victory.

events.title: Laws against melting and trading coin
events.summary: Laws of the 350s (CTh 9.23.1, 356) forbade merchants to carry more than 1,000 folles for trade and banned melting down or separating silver from the large bronze (maiorina), which was demonetised; the hoarding of the larger pieces shows public distrust of the coinage.

events.title: Usurpation of Silvanus at Cologne
events.summary: Silvanus, Frankish magister militum in Gaul, framed by a forged letter at court, proclaimed himself emperor at Cologne; after 28 days he was murdered in a chapel by soldiers suborned by Ursicinus, whose staff included Ammianus Marcellinus.

events.title: Julian made Caesar and sent to Gaul
events.summary: Constantius summoned his last male relative, the philosophy student Julian, from Athens, married him to his sister Helena and proclaimed him Caesar at Milan, sending him to Gaul with a small force and close supervision.

events.title: Council of Milan; exile of Liberius
events.summary: At Milan in 355 Constantius, reportedly drawing his sword and saying "what I will must be regarded as a canon", forced some 300 bishops to condemn Athanasius; Eusebius of Vercelli, Lucifer of Cagliari and Dionysius of Milan refused and were exiled, and Pope Liberius, who also refused, was taken from Rome to Beroea in Thrace.

events.title: Franks capture Cologne
events.summary: In late 355, after a long siege, a large Frankish force took and sacked Cologne; with the murder of Silvanus the Rhine defences collapsed, and some 40-45 towns were reported in barbarian hands when Julian arrived in Gaul. Julian retook the city in 356.

battle.significance: Symbol of the collapse of Rhine defences that made Julian's Caesarship necessary.

events.title: Third exile of Athanasius: the night attack on the church of Theonas
events.summary: On the night of 8-9 February 356 the dux Syrianus with 5,000 soldiers surrounded the church of Theonas during a vigil; Athanasius escaped in the crowd and spent six years hidden among the monks of Egypt, writing his Apologies and the History of the Arians, while George of Cappadocia was installed as bishop (February 357).

events.title: Julian's victory at Brocomagus
events.summary: Julian's first battle: marching from Autun via Auxerre and Troyes to Reims and then into Alsace, he repelled an Alamannic attack at Brocomagus by enveloping them with his two wings, after an earlier ambush of his rearguard near Decem Pagi. He then recovered Cologne and made peace with the Frankish kings.

battle.significance: Julian's first field success, restoring confidence in the Gallic army.

events.title: Julian besieged at Senones
events.summary: Wintering at Sens with few troops, Julian was besieged for thirty days by Alamanni while the magister equitum Marcellus, nearby, failed to help; Julian had Marcellus dismissed, beginning his fight for control of the Gallic command.

events.title: Constantius orders temples closed and sacrifice punished with death
events.summary: Laws of 356 (CTh 16.10.4 and 16.10.6) ordered temples closed in all places and cities and threatened capital punishment and confiscation for sacrifice or the worship of images. Enforcement was sporadic: Constantius himself admired the temples of Rome in 357.

events.title: Hilary of Poitiers exiled to Phrygia
events.summary: Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, condemned at the synod of Béziers in 356 for opposing Saturninus of Arles, was exiled to Phrygia, where he learned eastern theology and wrote De Trinitate and De Synodis, explaining the eastern homoiousians to the west; he returned in 360-361 and became the leading anti-Arian in Gaul.

events.title: Constantius II visits Rome
events.summary: Constantius entered Rome on 28 April 357 for his vicennalia in a triumphal adventus, motionless in his carriage 'as if a statue'; he admired the Forum of Trajan, erected the obelisk of Thutmose III (now the Lateran obelisk) in the Circus Maximus and removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house.

events.title: Battle of Argentoratum (Strasbourg)
events.summary: Julian, with 13,000 men, defeated an Alamannic coalition of seven kings under Chnodomar, perhaps 35,000 strong, near Strasbourg; 243 Romans and 4 tribunes fell against some 6,000 Alamanni killed on the field and many more drowned in the Rhine. Chnodomar was captured.

sides.losses: 6,000 killed on the field, many more drowned

battle.significance: The most complete late Roman battle narrative; restored the Rhine frontier.

events.title: Constantius removes the Altar of Victory from the Curia
events.summary: During his visit to Rome in 357 Constantius had the statue and altar of Victory, set up by Augustus after Actium, removed from the Senate house, because senators burned incense on it at meetings; it was restored, probably under Julian, and became the symbol of the pagan senators' resistance in 382-394.

events.title: Constantius raises an obelisk in the Circus Maximus
events.summary: The obelisk of Thutmose III and IV from Karnak, which Constantine had planned to bring to Constantinople, was shipped to Rome on a specially built vessel and erected on the spina of the Circus Maximus in 357; at 32 m (without base) it is the tallest standing ancient obelisk, re-erected at the Lateran in 1588.

events.title: Defeat of Barbatio near Augst
events.summary: In the pincer plan of 357 the magister peditum Barbatio advanced with 25,000 men from Italy to Rauracum, but refused to cooperate with Julian, was surprised by the Alamanni and driven back with the loss of his baggage, leaving Julian to face Chnodomar alone at Strasbourg.

sides.losses: baggage, pack animals and camp followers

battle.significance: Encouraged Chnodomar to attack Julian.

events.title: Julian besieges Franks in the Meuse forts
events.summary: After Strasbourg, 600 Frankish raiders shut themselves in two abandoned forts on the Meuse; Julian besieged them for 54 days in midwinter, breaking the river ice each night, until they surrendered and were sent to Constantius as recruits.

events.title: The Second Creed of Sirmium (the "Blasphemy")
events.summary: A small group of western bishops (Ursacius, Valens, Germinius, Potamius) at Sirmium forbade the use of ousia, homoousios and homoiousios and declared the Father greater than the Son; the aged Ossius of Cordoba signed under pressure. Hilary called it the "Blasphemy", and it drove moderate easterners into the homoiousian camp under Basil of Ancyra.

events.title: Earthquake destroys Nicomedia
events.summary: At dawn on 24 August 358 an earthquake followed by fire destroyed Nicomedia, Diocletian's capital; Ammianus describes the catastrophe and Libanius wrote a monody for the city, where the vicar Aristaenetus died in the ruins. A synod planned there was moved, eventually becoming the twin councils of 359.

events.title: Julian subdues the Salian Franks and Chamavi
events.summary: Julian accepted the surrender of the Salian Franks settled in Toxandria, allowing them to stay as subjects, and drove back the Chamavi, opening the Rhine to grain ships from Britain (600 ships, says Julian) and rebuilding forts at Castra Herculis, Quadriburgium and Novaesium.

events.title: Constantius against the Limigantes
events.summary: Constantius campaigned from Sirmium against the Sarmatians and Quadi in 358, restored the "free" Sarmatians under a client king Zizais, and attacked the Limigantes, their former serfs; in 359 a parley with the Limigantes near Acimincum turned into a massacre when they attacked the emperor's tribunal.

events.title: Basil of Ancyra's homoiousian synod
events.summary: Alarmed by the Anomoean teaching of Aetius and Eunomius, Basil of Ancyra assembled bishops before Easter 358 who declared the Son "like in essence" (homoiousios) to the Father; Constantius briefly backed them and exiled Aetius.

events.title: Basil and Gregory compile the Philocalia of Origen at Annesi
events.summary: Basil, after visiting the monks of Egypt and Syria, retired with his family's ascetic household at Annesi (led by his sister Macrina) and was joined by Gregory of Nazianzus; they compiled the Philocalia, an anthology of Origen's writings, and the Moralia, laying the foundations of Byzantine monasticism.

events.title: The sarcophagus of Junius Bassus
events.summary: Junius Bassus, prefect of Rome, died in office on 25 August 359 aged 42, "newly baptised", and was buried near St Peter's in a marble sarcophagus whose two registers of biblical scenes, with Christ enthroned above Caelus, are a masterpiece of early Christian sculpture.

events.title: Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia and the Homoian creed
events.summary: Constantius convened twin councils, some 400 western bishops at Ariminum and about 160 eastern at Seleucia in Isauria; under pressure, both accepted a creed saying the Son was 'like (homoios) the Father according to the Scriptures', banning the term ousia. A council at Constantinople ratified it in January 360.

events.title: Siege of Amida
events.summary: Shapur II, invading with allied Chionites under King Grumbates and guided by the Roman defector Antoninus, besieged Amida for 73 days; Ammianus Marcellinus, inside the city, describes the death of Grumbates' son before the walls, siege towers, sallies by Gallic legionaries, plague and the final storming via a collapsed siege mound.

sides.strength: royal army with Chionite, Albanian and Segestani allies and elephants
seven legions and citizens, c. 20,000 in the city (Ammianus)
sides.losses: city stormed; garrison killed or captured

battle.significance: Persian victory, but costly delay that saved the rest of Mesopotamia that year.

events.title: Homoian council of Constantinople
events.summary: In January 360 a council at Constantinople ratified the Homoian creed of Rimini and Seleucia ("the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures"), deposed Basil of Ancyra and other homoiousians, and made Eudoxius bishop of the capital; Ulfilas attended. This creed was the faith the Goths received.

events.title: Julian proclaimed Augustus at Paris
events.summary: Ordered to send his best auxiliary units east for the Persian war, Julian's troops at Lutetia, many recruited on the promise of never serving beyond the Alps, mutinied and raised him on a shield as Augustus, crowning him with a soldier's torque in place of a diadem.

events.title: Dedication of the first Hagia Sophia
events.summary: The Great Church (Megale Ekklesia) of Constantinople, begun under Constantine, was dedicated on 15 February 360 by the newly installed Homoian bishop Eudoxius; a timber-roofed basilica, it burned in the riots over John Chrysostom's exile in 404.

events.title: Siege of Singara
events.summary: Shapur took Singara with a ram that broke a newly repaired stretch of wall, deporting its garrison, legions I Flavia and I Parthica, and the inhabitants to Persia.

sides.strength: legions I Flavia and I Parthica, cavalry and citizens

battle.significance: Loss of a key Roman base in Mesopotamia.

events.title: Sieges of Bezabde
events.summary: Shapur stormed Bezabde on the Tigris, defended by three legions (II Flavia, II Armeniaca and II Parthica), and garrisoned it; Constantius' autumn counter-siege failed in the rains.

battle.significance: Persia gained a bridgehead in the Transtigritane regions ceded in 299.

events.title: Death of Constantius II at Mopsucrenae
events.summary: Marching against Julian, Constantius died of fever at Mopsucrenae in Cilicia aged 44, reportedly naming Julian his successor on his deathbed after being baptised by the Homoian bishop Euzoius; civil war was averted.

events.title: Lynching of George of Cappadocia
events.summary: When news of Constantius' death arrived, the Alexandrian mob dragged the hated Arian bishop George, who had sneered at the temple of the Genius of the city, from prison, killed him with two officials on 24 December 361, paraded his body on a camel and burned it. Julian rebuked the city but claimed George's library.

events.title: Julian's march down the Danube
events.summary: Breaking with Constantius, Julian sent columns through Italy and Raetia while he himself boarded river boats with 3,000 men and sailed down the Danube, reaching Sirmium in October 361 to a surprised welcome, then held the Succi pass and waited at Naissus, where news of Constantius' death arrived.

events.title: The tribunal of Chalcedon
events.summary: In December 361 Julian set up a commission at Chalcedon under Salutius Secundus, with army officers including Arbitio, Nevitta and Jovinus, to try Constantius' ministers; the grand chamberlain Eusebius and the notary Paul "the Chain" were burned alive, but the execution of the finance minister Ursulus shocked even Ammianus.

events.title: Aurelius Victor writes De Caesaribus
events.summary: Sextus Aurelius Victor, a self-made African of humble birth, finished his short imperial history from Augustus to 360 in 361; Julian, meeting him at Sirmium, made him consular of Pannonia Secunda and honoured him with a bronze statue, and he later served as prefect of Rome (389).

events.title: Julian's edict on teachers
events.summary: A law of 17 June 362 (CTh 13.3.5) required civic approval for teachers, and an accompanying letter argued that Christians who did not believe in the gods could not honestly teach Homer and Hesiod and should "go to the churches of the Galilaeans and expound Matthew and Luke". Marius Victorinus and Prohaeresius resigned; Ammianus called it harsh and best buried in silence.

events.title: Fourth exile of Athanasius under Julian
events.summary: Angered that Athanasius was baptising pagan women of rank, Julian ordered him expelled on 23 October 362 as a "disturber of the peace"; Athanasius told his followers it was "a little cloud that will pass" and hid on the Nile until Julian's death.

events.title: Julian's restoration of paganism
events.summary: Sole emperor from December 361, Julian reopened temples and restored sacrifices, recalled exiled bishops of all factions (to let Christians quarrel, Ammianus says), purged the palace staff, and tried to create a pagan priestly hierarchy imitating Christian charity.

events.title: Julian at Antioch: the Daphne fire and the Misopogon
events.summary: Wintering at Antioch, Julian alienated the Christian and pleasure-loving city with his sacrifices, his beard and price controls during a grain shortage; when the temple of Apollo at Daphne burned on 22 October 362, he blamed Christians and closed the cathedral. Lampooned by the Antiochenes, he replied with the satirical Misopogon ('Beard-Hater').

events.title: Athanasius' "Council of the Confessors" at Alexandria
events.summary: Returned under Julian's amnesty, Athanasius held a small synod which accepted repentant Arians, affirmed the divinity of the Holy Spirit and recognised that "one hypostasis" and "three hypostases" could be orthodox if properly understood, laying the groundwork for the Cappadocian settlement; Lucifer of Cagliari rejected it.

events.title: Julian's bull coinage
events.summary: Julian issued a large bronze coin with a bull and two stars and the legend SECURITAS REIPUB; Christians mocked it as an emblem of his sacrifices, though it may represent Apis or his zodiac sign. His bearded philosopher portrait broke with the clean-shaven Constantinian image and was mocked by the Antiochenes.

events.title: Proba composes her Virgilian cento
events.summary: Faltonia Betitia Proba, a Christian aristocrat of the Anician circle, retold the Creation and the life of Christ in 694 lines stitched together entirely from Virgil (Cento Vergilianus de laudibus Christi), the first substantial surviving work by a Christian Latin woman poet; Jerome disliked it, but it was widely copied.

events.title: Siege of Maiozamalcha
events.summary: Marching down the Euphrates, Julian took the fortress-town of Pirisabora and then stormed Maiozamalcha near Ctesiphon by mining under the walls, Roman soldiers emerging inside a house while the defenders watched the assault on the walls.

battle.significance: Cleared the approach to Ctesiphon.

events.title: Battle of Ctesiphon (363)
events.summary: Julian's army made a night crossing of the Tigris under fire and defeated the Persian army under the Surena before the walls of Ctesiphon, killing 2,500 for about 70 Roman losses (Ammianus); but Julian judged the city too strong to besiege.

battle.significance: Tactical victory that brought no strategic result.

events.title: Battle of Maranga
events.summary: On 22 June 363 the retreating Roman army fought a pitched battle at Maranga with a Persian army under Merena with cataphracts and elephants; Julian closed quickly to avoid the archers and won, but could not stop the harassment that killed him four days later.

sides.strength: army under Merena with cataphracts and elephants

battle.significance: Tactical success that did not change the strategic trap.

events.title: Battle near Samarra and death of Julian
events.summary: Retreating north up the Tigris under constant Persian harassment, Julian rushed into a skirmish without his breastplate and was struck by a cavalry spear that pierced his liver; he died that night in his tent, discussing the soul with the philosophers Maximus and Priscus.
events.locName: Near Samarra (Toummara/Maranga region), on the Tigris

sides.losses: significant, incl. generals Merena and Nohodares (Ammianus)

battle.significance: Death of the last pagan emperor; ended the Constantinian dynasty and forced the peace of 363.

events.title: Jovian's peace with Shapur II
events.summary: Trapped without supplies near Dura on the Tigris, Jovian accepted a thirty-year peace ceding five Transtigritane regions, Nisibis, Singara and Castra Maurorum, and abandoning Rome's alliance with Armenia; the citizens of Nisibis were evacuated, weeping, to Amida.

events.title: Julian's attempt to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem
events.summary: Julian ordered the Jewish Temple rebuilt under the supervision of Alypius of Antioch, to falsify Christian prophecy; Ammianus reports that 'fearful balls of fire' burst from the foundations, burning workmen, and the project was abandoned, probably also because of the earthquake of 19 May 363 and Julian's death.

events.title: Julian storms Pirisabora
events.summary: Marching down the Euphrates with 65,000 men and a fleet of 1,100 ships, Julian took the strong city of Pirisabora after two days of assault, Julian himself trying to batter a gate under a hail of missiles; the garrison of 2,500 surrendered and the city was burned.

battle.significance: Opened the road down the Euphrates towards Ctesiphon.

events.title: Julian burns his fleet
events.summary: Unable to take Ctesiphon and misled, Ammianus hints, by Persian deserters, Julian ordered his river fleet burned except for a few boats so that 20,000 men would not be needed to tow it upstream, and turned inland; the decision is judged among his worst.

events.title: Julian writes Against the Galilaeans
events.summary: In the winter of 362-363 at Antioch Julian composed three books attacking Christianity as an apostasy from both Hellenism and Judaism; the work survives only in fragments quoted in Cyril of Alexandria's refutation of the 430s. The same winter he wrote the Misopogon against the Antiochenes.

events.title: Austuriani raids on Lepcis Magna and the Romanus affair
events.summary: Austuriani nomads ravaged the territory of Lepcis in 363-365; the comes Romanus demanded 4,000 camels before acting, and when the Tripolitanians complained to Valentinian, Romanus' relative, the master of offices Remigius, ensured the envoys were punished and some executed, a scandal Ammianus narrates in detail.

events.title: Themistius' oration on religious toleration
events.summary: On 1 January 364, at Jovian's consular inauguration in Ancyra, the pagan philosopher-senator Themistius delivered Oration 5, praising Jovian's law granting freedom of worship and arguing that God delights in diversity of worship, as the constitution of the universe delights in variety.

events.title: Death of Jovian at Dadastana
events.summary: Jovian died on his way to Constantinople at Dadastana on the Bithynian-Galatian border, apparently from charcoal fumes from a brazier in a freshly plastered bedroom, after a reign of eight months in which he restored Christian privileges.

events.title: Valentinian I and Valens become emperors
events.summary: The army at Nicaea chose Valentinian, a Pannonian guards officer, as emperor on 26 February 364; on 28 March at the Hebdomon outside Constantinople he made his younger brother Valens co-Augustus, and at Mediana near Naissus they divided the court, army and empire, Valentinian taking the West and Valens the East.

events.title: Valentinian bans nocturnal sacrifices; Praetextatus' plea
events.summary: A law of September 364 (CTh 9.16.7) banned nocturnal sacrifices and magical rites; Vettius Agorius Praetextatus, proconsul of Achaea, persuaded Valentinian to exempt the Eleusinian Mysteries, telling him that life would be unlivable for the Greeks without them.

events.title: The Cretan earthquake and tsunami
events.summary: A massive earthquake off western Crete, estimated at magnitude 8 or more, uplifted the western end of the island by up to 9 m and sent a tsunami across the eastern Mediterranean; Ammianus describes the sea withdrawing at Alexandria and ships being hurled onto rooftops.
events.locName: Off western Crete; tsunami at Alexandria and across the eastern Mediterranean

events.title: Revolt of Procopius
events.summary: Procopius, a maternal relative of Julian rumoured to have been designated his successor, emerged from hiding and was proclaimed emperor in Constantinople while Valens was away; he won over units passing through Thrace by displaying Constantius II's widow Faustina and her infant daughter, last of the Constantinian line.

events.title: Fifth exile of Athanasius
events.summary: Valens' order of May 365 that bishops exiled by Constantius and restored by Julian should leave again led to riots; Athanasius withdrew on 5 October 365 to a family tomb outside the city for four months, until the emperor, alarmed by Procopius, allowed him back on 1 February 366.

events.title: Alamanni cross the frozen Rhine
events.summary: Insulted by meagre gifts from Valentinian's master of offices Ursatius, the Alamanni broke across the Rhine in January 365 and defeated the comites Charietto and Severianus; Valentinian, on his way to the Rhine, heard of Procopius' revolt the same autumn but chose to stay in Gaul.

events.title: Damasus and Ursinus: the papal election riots
events.summary: After the death of Pope Liberius, rival factions elected Ursinus and Damasus as bishop of Rome; in the fighting, Damasus' supporters stormed the basilica of Sicininus and, Ammianus reports, 137 corpses were found there in a single day.

events.title: Battles of Thyatira and Nacolia
events.summary: Valens defeated Procopius' general Gomoarius at Thyatira in Lydia, and in May 366 at Nacolia in Phrygia Procopius' remaining troops deserted after his commander Agilo defected; Procopius was betrayed and beheaded on 27 May 366.

sides.strength: Thracian and palatine units, Gothic auxiliaries

battle.significance: Ended the last Constantinian bid for power.

events.title: Jovinus defeats the Alamanni at Scarponna and Catalauni
events.summary: The magister equitum Jovinus surprised one Alamannic band bathing and drinking at Scarponna on the Moselle, another at a river crossing, and then defeated the main force near Catalauni (Châlons), where Ammianus reports 6,000 Alamanni killed and 4,000 wounded against 1,200 Roman dead.

battle.significance: Cleared Gaul of the 365 invaders.

events.title: Gratian proclaimed Augustus at Ambiani
events.summary: After a serious illness, Valentinian raised his eight-year-old son Gratian directly to Augustus (not Caesar) before the army at Ambiani (Amiens), securing the dynasty; the poet Ausonius became his tutor.

events.title: The 'Barbarian Conspiracy' in Britain
events.summary: In 367 Picts, Attacotti and Scotti attacked Britain while Franks and Saxons raided Gaul; the count of the Saxon Shore Nectaridus was killed and the dux Fullofaudes ambushed. Valentinian sent Count Theodosius (the Elder), who recovered London and restored order in 368-369.

events.title: Gold refining and the OB mark
events.summary: Between 366 and 368 Valentinian and Valens ordered all gold received in taxes to be melted into bullion and that solidi be struck only at the court (comitatus), adding OB (obryzum, refined gold; also the Greek numeral 72) to the mintmark; the purity of the solidus rose to about 99%. Laws of the same years tie this to the comes sacrarum largitionum.

events.title: Battle of Solicinium
events.summary: Valentinian and Gratian led a punitive expedition across the Rhine after the Alamanni sacked Mogontiacum during a Christian festival; the Alamanni held a steep hill at Solicinium but were driven off with heavy losses after Valentinian nearly fell in an ambush.
events.locName: Solicinium (unidentified; perhaps near Rottenburg am Neckar or Heidelberg)

battle.significance: Punitive victory followed by major fortification programme.

events.title: Treason and magic trials at Rome and Antioch
events.summary: At Rome the prefect of the annona Maximinus (later praetorian prefect) prosecuted senators and their wives for adultery and magic with torture; at Antioch in 371-372 a séance using a magic tripod that spelled out THEOD as the next emperor's name led to the execution of the notary Theodorus and many others, and burnings of books.

events.title: Alamanni sack Mogontiacum at Easter
events.summary: The Alamannic prince Rando slipped into undefended Mainz during a Christian festival, probably Easter 368, and carried off men and women of every rank with their possessions; Valentinian responded with the campaign that ended at Solicinium.

events.title: Siege of Artogerassa; Queen Pharantzem's defence
events.summary: After Shapur II seized King Arsaces (Arshak) II by treachery, the queen Pharantzem held out in the fortress of Artogerassa with Arsaces' treasure for over a year, while their son Pap escaped to the Romans; the fortress eventually fell and the queen was taken to Persia and killed.

battle.significance: Demonstrated the collapse of Roman influence in Armenia after 363.

events.title: De Rebus Bellicis
events.summary: An anonymous treatise addressed to emperors (probably Valentinian and Valens, c. 368-369) proposes reforms of coinage, taxation and the army along with illustrated war machines, including an ox-powered paddle-wheel warship and a mobile bridge on inflated skins; it diagnoses gold hoarding by the rich as the root of the empire's troubles.

events.title: Creation of the defensor civitatis
events.summary: Valentinian I instructed the prefect Probus to appoint in each city of Illyricum a "defender of the plebs" to protect the humble against the powerful (CTh 1.29.1, 368 or 364), giving them summary jurisdiction in small cases; the office spread to the whole empire and later passed largely to bishops.

events.title: Athanaric's persecution of Gothic Christians; Saba the Goth
events.summary: After the war with Valens, Athanaric persecuted Christians among the Tervingi, seeing them as a Roman fifth column; the Passion of Saba the Goth describes a village protecting its Christians and Saba's drowning in the river Musaeus (Buzău) on 12 April 372, his relics being sent by Junius Soranus, dux of Scythia, to Basil of Caesarea.

events.title: Valens' Gothic war and the treaty on the Danube
events.summary: After three years of campaigns north of the Danube (367-369) against the Tervingi, hampered by floods in 368, Valens met the Tervingian 'judge' Athanaric on a boat in midstream, since Athanaric had sworn never to set foot on Roman soil; trade was restricted to two Danube towns and subsidies ended.

events.title: Valentinian's Rhine and Danube fortification programme
events.summary: From 369 Valentinian fortified the Rhine from Raetia to the North Sea with new forts, watchtowers (burgi) and landing places on the far bank (e.g. Altrip, Mannheim-Neckarau, Engers), and diverted the Neckar to protect a fort; Ammianus also describes a fort at Mons Piri destroyed by Alamanni while under construction. Many Danube burgi date from the same years.

events.title: Conspiracy of Valentinus in Britain
events.summary: Valentinus, a Pannonian exiled to Britain for a serious crime and the brother-in-law of the notorious prefect Maximinus, plotted with exiles and soldiers to seize power during Count Theodosius' restoration of the province; Theodosius had him and his closest associates executed but forbade further inquiries.

events.title: Eutropius dedicates his Breviarium to Valens
events.summary: Eutropius, magister memoriae, wrote a ten-book summary of Roman history from Romulus to Jovian for Valens in about 369, as Festus did shortly after, to prepare the emperor for war with Persia; it was translated into Greek within a generation and became a school book for over a millennium.

events.title: Saxon raiders massacred after a truce
events.summary: A Saxon war band that had raided along the coast to the Rhine was defeated by Severus, magister peditum, and granted safe passage in return for recruits; Roman troops then ambushed and annihilated them. Ammianus admits the treachery but calls it just; Jerome locates a Saxon defeat at Deuso.

events.title: Basil becomes bishop of Caesarea; the Basileias
events.summary: Basil, who had founded ascetic communities in Pontus and written the "Longer Rules", became bishop of Caesarea in 370 and built outside the city a complex of hospital, poorhouse, hostel and workshops, the Basileias, admired by Gregory of Nazianzus as a "new city". He stood up to Valens' prefect Modestus, who said no one had ever spoken to him so boldly.

events.title: Damasus restores the martyrs' tombs
events.summary: Pope Damasus I monumentalised the tombs of Roman martyrs with verse epitaphs carved by the calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus in a distinctive lettering (the Filocalian script), turning the catacombs into pilgrimage shrines and promoting Rome's apostolic and martyr prestige; his inscription for the Crypt of the Popes survives in Callixtus.

events.title: Martin becomes bishop of Tours
events.summary: Martin, a Pannonian ex-soldier who had founded the first Gallic monastery at Ligugé c. 361, was acclaimed bishop of Tours on 4 July 371 (or 372) despite opposition from bishops who disliked his shabby appearance; he founded Marmoutier across the Loire and campaigned against rural shrines, as told in Sulpicius Severus' Life.

events.title: Battle of Bagavan
events.summary: Roman troops under Traianus and Vadomarius, sent to support King Pap, together with the Armenian sparapet Mushegh, defeated a Persian army at Bagavan; a truce followed, with Shapur refusing to recognise Roman influence in Armenia and Iberia divided between rival kings.

battle.significance: Temporarily restored a Roman-aligned Armenia.

events.title: Ausonius writes the Mosella
events.summary: Ausonius, rhetor of Bordeaux and tutor of Gratian at the court of Trier, composed the Mosella, 483 hexameters on a journey down the Moselle from Bingen, celebrating its villas, vineyard-clad slopes and fishes (some 15 species named); it is the finest poem of fourth-century Gaul and an early witness to Moselle viticulture.

events.title: Revolt of Firmus in Mauretania
events.summary: Firmus, son of the Moorish prince Nubel, rebelled after a dispute with the rapacious comes Africae Romanus; Count Theodosius waged a hard campaign through Mauretania until Firmus hanged himself to avoid capture.

events.title: Death of Athanasius
events.summary: Athanasius died in Alexandria on 2 May 373, having designated his brother Peter as successor; Valens' prefect Palladius immediately installed the Arian Lucius with violence, and Peter fled to Rome.

events.title: Ambrose elected bishop of Milan
events.summary: Ambrose, governor of Aemilia-Liguria, intervened to calm the crowds at the disputed election to succeed the Homoian bishop Auxentius, and was himself acclaimed bishop by the people, according to legend after a child cried 'Ambrose bishop'; he was baptised and consecrated within a week.

events.title: Valentinian's treaty with Macrianus on the Rhine
events.summary: After failing to kidnap him in 372, Valentinian met the Bucinobantian king Macrianus in boats on the Rhine near Mainz and made a treaty; Macrianus remained loyal until killed fighting the Franks.

events.title: Quadi and Sarmatians invade Pannonia
events.summary: The murder of the Quadic king Gabinius at a banquet by the dux Marcellianus provoked a Quadic and Sarmatian invasion that caught the princess Constantia (Gratian's bride) at a villa near Sirmium, nearly captured her, and destroyed two legions; the young Theodosius, dux of Moesia, defeated the Sarmatians.

events.title: Romans murder King Pap of Armenia
events.summary: Suspecting Pap of dealing with Persia, Valens had the dux Traianus invite him to a banquet where he was murdered (374 or 375); Ammianus condemns the treachery, recalling the precedent of Fabricius who refused to murder Pyrrhus.

events.title: Libanius writes his autobiography
events.summary: Libanius, official sophist of Antioch, composed the first part of his Autobiography (Oration 1) in 374, extending it until 393; with 64 orations and about 1,500 letters it gives the most intimate surviving view of a late antique city, its council, schools and quarrels.

events.title: Valentinian makes infanticide a capital crime
events.summary: A law of Valentinian, Valens and Gratian of 374 (CTh 9.14.1) declared the killing of an infant a capital crime, and another of the same year (CJ 8.51.2) ordered every parent to rear their offspring and threatened penalties for exposure; the sale and exposure of newborns nevertheless continued, as later legislation shows.

events.title: Death of Valentinian I at Brigetio
events.summary: After campaigning against the Quadi, who had invaded Pannonia in 374 after the murder of their king Gabinius by a Roman officer, Valentinian received a Quadic embassy at Brigetio, flew into a rage at their insolence and died of a stroke.

events.title: Valentinian II proclaimed at Aquincum
events.summary: Six days after Valentinian I's death, the generals Merobaudes and Equitius had his four-year-old son by Justina proclaimed Augustus at Aquincum on 22 November 375 without consulting Gratian or Valens, who accepted the fait accompli.

events.title: Revolt of Queen Mavia's Saracens
events.summary: After her husband's death the Saracen queen Mavia led her people (probably Tanukh) against Roman Arabia, Palestine and Phoenicia, defeating Roman forces; she made peace on condition that the hermit Moses be consecrated bishop for her people, and gave her daughter in marriage to the magister Victor. Her cavalry served Valens in 378.

events.title: The Goths cross the Danube
events.summary: Driven by the Huns, who had destroyed the Greuthungian kingdom of Ermanaric and defeated Athanaric's Tervingi on the Dniester, a large body of Tervingi under Alavivus and Fritigern petitioned Valens for land and were admitted across the Danube, probably near Durostorum, in exchange for military service; the Greuthungi under Alatheus and Saphrax crossed without permission.

events.title: Lupicinus' banquet and the battle of Marcianople
events.summary: At a banquet at Marcianople the comes Lupicinus tried to seize or murder Fritigern and Alavivus; Fritigern escaped, rallied the Goths and destroyed Lupicinus' army nine miles from the city, beginning the Gothic war.

battle.significance: Turned the Gothic settlement into open war.

events.title: Execution of Count Theodosius at Carthage
events.summary: Early in 376, after suppressing Firmus, the magister equitum Theodosius was beheaded at Carthage in obscure circumstances, probably a victim of court factions after Valentinian's death; he was baptised beforehand. His son retired to Spain until recalled in 378.

events.title: Battle of Ad Salices
events.summary: Roman forces under Richomeres, Profuturus and Trajanus fought the Goths behind their wagon-laager at Ad Salices ('By the Willows') in the Dobruja; the battle was bloody and indecisive, and Ammianus says the bones of the dead still whitened the field years later.

sides.strength: Gothic warriors behind the wagon circle

battle.significance: Showed the Goths could not be easily contained.

events.title: Battle of Argentaria
events.summary: Gratian's generals Nannienus and Mallobaudes, king of the Franks and comes domesticorum, destroyed the Lentienses, an Alamannic people who had crossed the frozen Rhine, near Argentaria (Horbourg near Colmar); Ammianus says only 5,000 of 40,000 escaped.

battle.significance: Delayed Gratian's eastern march.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.summary: Valens, refusing to wait for Gratian, marched out from Adrianople in the August heat and attacked Fritigern's wagon camp; while negotiations dragged on, Roman units engaged prematurely, the returning Greuthungian cavalry of Alatheus and Saphrax struck the Roman left, and the infantry, crushed together so they could not draw swords, were annihilated. Valens died and two-thirds of the army perished.
events.locName: About 13 km north of Hadrianopolis (Edirne), Thrace

sides.losses: two-thirds of the army (Ammianus); emperor killed

sides.strength: Tervingi, Greuthungi and Alans; perhaps 15,000-20,000 warriors

battle.significance: Death of an emperor and destruction of the eastern field army; led to the settlement of Goths inside the empire.

events.title: Massacre of Gothic youths in the east
events.summary: After Adrianople the magister Julius, fearing a rising, had Gothic youths and hostages who had been distributed among eastern cities gathered on a fixed day on pretext of pay and massacred.

events.title: The Gothic attack on Constantinople and the Saracen sortie
events.summary: After Adrianople the Goths advanced on Constantinople but were repulsed by a sortie of Mavia's Saracen cavalry; Ammianus describes a long-haired Saracen, naked but for a loincloth, cutting a Goth's throat and drinking his blood, which terrified the Goths into withdrawing. The widow Domnica paid volunteers.

battle.significance: Saved the capital; the Goths turned back to the Balkans.

events.title: Theodosius made Augustus at Sirmium
events.summary: Gratian recalled Theodosius, son of the executed Count Theodosius, from his Spanish estates, gave him a command against the Goths and Sarmatians and proclaimed him Augustus of the East at Sirmium, together with the dioceses of Dacia and Macedonia.

events.title: Gregory of Nazianzus leads the Nicenes of Constantinople
events.summary: Invited by the small Nicene congregation, Gregory preached in a private house chapel, the Anastasia, from 379, delivering the five Theological Orations (27-31) in 380; on 27 November 380 Theodosius expelled the Homoian bishop Demophilus and led Gregory into the Holy Apostles under military guard.

events.title: Edict of Thessalonica (Cunctos populos)
events.summary: Theodosius, Gratian and Valentinian II decreed that all peoples should follow the faith 'which the divine apostle Peter delivered to the Romans' as taught by Damasus of Rome and Peter of Alexandria, belief in the one deity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit; others were 'demented and insane' heretics.

events.title: Theodosius defeated by the Goths in Macedonia
events.summary: In 380 Theodosius, campaigning with an army padded out with Gothic recruits, was routed in Macedonia when barbarians in his own ranks went over to Fritigern; he fell ill at Thessalonica, was baptised by Acholius, and left the war to Gratian's generals Bauto and Arbogast.

battle.significance: Confirmed that the Goths could not be destroyed militarily, leading to the 382 treaty.

events.title: Melania the Elder and Rufinus found monasteries on the Mount of Olives
events.summary: The Roman aristocrat Melania the Elder, widowed at 22, after visiting the Egyptian monks founded a convent on the Mount of Olives (c. 378-380), while Rufinus of Aquileia founded a men's monastery nearby; their hospitality made Jerusalem a centre of Latin asceticism, and Rufinus later translated Origen and Eusebius.

events.title: Athanaric received at Constantinople
events.summary: Expelled by his own people, the Tervingian judge Athanaric, who had sworn never to set foot on Roman soil, arrived in Constantinople on 11 January 381; Theodosius met him outside the city, and when he died two weeks later (25 January) gave him a magnificent funeral. His followers entered Roman service.

events.title: First Council of Constantinople
events.summary: About 150 eastern bishops, summoned by Theodosius, reaffirmed the Nicene faith, condemned Macedonians (who denied the divinity of the Spirit) and others, and in canon 3 gave the bishop of Constantinople 'precedence of honour after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome'.

events.title: Council of Aquileia
events.summary: Ambrose presided over a western council at Aquileia on 3 September 381 that condemned the Homoian bishops Palladius of Ratiaria and Secundianus of Singidunum; the stenographic minutes survive, with Palladius' Arian rebuttal in the margins of a Paris manuscript.

events.title: Egeria's pilgrimage
events.summary: Between about 381 and 384 Egeria, a well-born woman probably from Gallaecia, travelled to Sinai, Egypt, Jerusalem, Mount Nebo, Edessa and Carrhae, writing letters to her "sisters" at home. Her surviving account describes the liturgy of Jerusalem in detail, including Holy Week, Palm Sunday and the veneration of the cross.

events.title: Gratian moves the western court from Trier to Milan
events.summary: After 378 Gratian spent more time in the Danube and Italian theatres and by 381 had settled at Milan, close to Ambrose, whose influence on him grew; Trier ceased to be the main western residence, and the Gallic army, feeling neglected, backed Magnus Maximus in 383.

events.title: Theodosius' treaty with the Goths
events.summary: On 3 October 382, after Theodosius' generals had contained but not defeated the Goths, the magister Saturninus made peace: the Goths were settled in northern Thrace and along the Danube as a people under their own leaders, providing troops under their own commanders while remaining legally autonomous.
events.locName: Constantinople; settlement in Thrace and Moesia

events.title: Gratian removes the Altar of Victory and disendows the cults
events.summary: Gratian ordered the Altar of Victory removed from the Senate house again, confiscated the endowments of the Vestals and priestly colleges, and abolished their immunities; a senatorial embassy under Symmachus was refused an audience at Pope Damasus' instigation.

events.title: Gratian gives up the title pontifex maximus
events.summary: Zosimus tells how Gratian refused the robe of pontifex maximus offered by the pontiffs, one of whom remarked that "if the emperor will not be pontifex, Maximus will soon be pontifex", foreshadowing Magnus Maximus. Inscriptions show Gratian with the title until about 379-382.

events.title: Jerome in Rome begins revising the Latin Bible
events.summary: As secretary to Damasus from 382, Jerome revised the Old Latin Gospels against the Greek, completed by 384, and gathered a circle of ascetic aristocratic women on the Aventine (Marcella, Paula, Eustochium). Forced out of Rome in 385, he settled at Bethlehem (386) and translated the Old Testament from Hebrew (390-405), producing the core of the Vulgate.

events.title: Arcadius proclaimed Augustus
events.summary: On 19 January 383, at the Hebdomon parade ground, Theodosius raised his six-year-old elder son Arcadius to Augustus, establishing a dynasty that would rule the east until 450.

events.title: Usurpation of Magnus Maximus and death of Gratian
events.summary: Magnus Maximus, a Spanish officer serving in Britain and a relative of Theodosius, was proclaimed emperor by the British army and crossed to Gaul; Gratian's troops deserted near Paris, and Gratian was caught and killed at Lugdunum on 25 August 383.

events.title: Evagrius Ponticus withdraws to Nitria and the Kellia
events.summary: Evagrius, a deacon ordained by Gregory of Nazianzus who fled Constantinople after an affair, settled in Nitria and then the Kellia in 383, where he wrote the Praktikos and the theory of eight evil thoughts (logismoi) that became, via Cassian and Gregory the Great, the seven deadly sins.

events.title: The Altar of Victory controversy
events.summary: In 382 Gratian removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house and cut state funding of the pagan cults and the Vestals; in 384 the urban prefect Symmachus petitioned Valentinian II for its restoration in his Third Relatio, and Ambrose answered with two letters ensuring the request failed.

events.title: Execution of Priscillian at Trier
events.summary: Priscillian, an ascetic bishop of Avila accused by Spanish bishops of Manichaeism and sorcery, was tried before Magnus Maximus at Trier and beheaded with several followers, including the noblewoman Euchrotia, the first Christians executed by Christian authorities for heresy.

events.title: Conversion of Augustine at Milan
events.summary: In August 386 Augustine, imperial professor of rhetoric at Milan, after reading Neoplatonist books (Plotinus and Porphyry in Victorinus' Latin), hearing Ambrose preach and the story of Antony, heard a child chanting "tolle lege" and opened Paul's letter to the Romans; he resigned, retired to Cassiciacum, and was baptised by Ambrose at Easter (24-25 April) 387.

events.title: Ambrose and the Milan basilica conflict
events.summary: The empress mother Justina and the court of Valentinian II demanded a basilica in Milan for Homoian worship; Ambrose and his congregation occupied the church through Holy Week of 386, singing antiphonal hymns, while troops surrounded it, and the court backed down. Weeks later Ambrose discovered the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and installed them under the altar of his new basilica.

events.title: Maternus Cynegius and the destruction of eastern temples
events.summary: The praetorian prefect Maternus Cynegius, a pious Spaniard, toured Egypt and the east from 384 to 388 closing temples; at Apamea Bishop Marcellus demolished the great temple of Zeus with soldiers and a fire under its columns, and was later killed by pagans while destroying a shrine near Aulon. Libanius' Oration 30, "For the Temples", protests against black-robed monks wrecking rural shrines.

events.title: Promotus destroys the Greuthungi of Odotheus on the Danube
events.summary: When the Greuthungian chieftain Odotheus tried to cross the Danube with a large following in dugout canoes, the magister Promotus, having lured them with false deserters, met them midstream with warships and slaughtered them; survivors were settled in Phrygia. Claudian later celebrated the victory.

battle.significance: Prevented a second mass crossing of the Danube.

events.title: Rebuilding of St Paul's Outside the Walls
events.summary: Valentinian II, Theodosius and Arcadius wrote to the prefect of Rome Sallustius in 384-386 ordering a great new basilica over Paul's tomb on the Via Ostiensis, replacing the small Constantinian church; the five-aisled building, finished under Honorius, rivalled St Peter's until it burned in 1823.

events.title: The Riot of the Statues at Antioch
events.summary: A new tax levy, perhaps for Theodosius' decennalia, provoked Antioch's crowd to smash the statues and portraits of the emperor and his family; facing imperial vengeance, the city was saved by the embassy of Bishop Flavian and the intercession of monks, while the young priest John Chrysostom preached his 21 Homilies on the Statues.

events.title: Partition of Armenia between Rome and Persia
events.summary: Theodosius and Shapur III agreed to divide Armenia: the Persian zone (Persarmenia), about four-fifths of the kingdom, under Khosrov IV, and a smaller Roman zone in the west under Arsaces III, ending decades of struggle since Shapur II had captured King Arsaces II and Rome's protégé Pap had been murdered by a Roman officer (374/375).

events.title: Magnus Maximus invades Italy
events.summary: Exploiting a mission by Domninus to obtain troops, Maximus crossed the Alps behind the envoys in late summer 387; Valentinian II and Justina fled by sea from Aquileia to Thessalonica, where Theodosius married Valentinian's sister Galla and agreed to war.

events.title: Battle of Siscia
events.summary: After Magnus Maximus invaded Italy in 387, driving Valentinian II and Justina to Thessalonica, Theodosius marched west; at Siscia on the Save his Hunnic, Alan and Gothic horse archers swam the river and routed Maximus' army.

sides.strength: eastern army with Gothic, Hunnic and Alan auxiliaries

battle.significance: Opened the road to Italy.

events.title: Battle of Poetovio and death of Magnus Maximus
events.summary: Theodosius defeated Maximus' brother Marcellinus at Poetovio; Maximus was surrounded at Aquileia, handed over by his own troops, and executed on 28 August 388. His son Victor was killed in Gaul by the Frankish general Arbogast.

battle.significance: Ended Maximus' regime; Theodosius effectively ruled the whole empire.

events.title: The Callinicum synagogue affair
events.summary: Christians at Callinicum on the Euphrates, incited by their bishop, burned a synagogue and a Valentinian gnostic chapel; Theodosius ordered the bishop to rebuild the synagogue, but Ambrose refused to celebrate the Eucharist in the emperor's presence until he withdrew the order.

events.title: Frankish invasion and the disaster in the Silva Carbonaria
events.summary: While Maximus fought in Italy, Franks under Genobaudes, Marcomer and Sunno raided Germania Secunda; the Roman commander Quintinus pursued them across the Rhine and was ambushed among swamps and forest, losing most of his army. The account survives from Sulpicius Alexander via Gregory of Tours.
events.locName: Germania Secunda and the Silva Carbonaria

battle.significance: Exposed the Lower Rhine and led to Arbogast's punitive campaigns.

events.title: Theodosius in Rome
events.summary: Theodosius entered Rome on 13 June 389 with his son Honorius and Valentinian II, celebrating a triumph over Maximus; he showed courtesy to the Senate and Pacatus Drepanius delivered his panegyric. Symmachus, who had praised Maximus, had to seek pardon in a speech of apology.

events.title: Massacre of Thessalonica and Theodosius' penance
events.summary: After the people of Thessalonica lynched the Gothic magister militum Butheric, who had jailed a popular charioteer for homosexual assault, troops were turned on the crowd in the hippodrome and some 7,000 were killed (Theodoret); Ambrose, in a private letter, required Theodosius to do public penance before readmitting him to communion.

events.title: Obelisk of Theodosius raised in the Hippodrome
events.summary: The prefect Proclus re-erected an obelisk of Thutmose III, brought from Karnak, on the spina of the Hippodrome of Constantinople in 32 days, as its Latin and Greek inscriptions boast; the marble base shows Theodosius and his family in the kathisma receiving tribute.

events.title: Ammianus Marcellinus completes his Res Gestae
events.summary: Ammianus Marcellinus, a Greek-speaking former protector from Antioch living in Rome, completed his Latin history in 31 books from Nerva to the death of Valens (378); books 14-31, covering 353-378, survive and are the finest narrative history of late antiquity.

events.title: Destruction of the Serapeum and the Theodosian decrees
events.summary: Theodosius' laws of 24 February and 16 June 391 banned sacrifice and visits to temples; in Alexandria, rioting between pagans and Christians led by Bishop Theophilus ended with the destruction of the great Serapeum and its cult statue by Bryaxis, with imperial permission. A law of 8 November 392 banned all forms of pagan cult, even private household worship.

events.title: Death of Valentinian II; Eugenius proclaimed
events.summary: Valentinian II, aged 21 and humiliated by his magister militum Arbogast, who had torn up his letter of dismissal, was found hanged at Vienne; on 22 August Arbogast, unable as a Frank to take the throne himself, proclaimed the rhetor and court official Eugenius emperor.

events.title: Theodosius bans all pagan cult
events.summary: A law of 8 November 392 to the prefect Rufinus (CTh 16.10.12) banned sacrifice and divination under penalty of treason and forbade even private worship of the lares with fire, the genius with wine or the penates with incense, garlands or lamps, with fines for decurions who failed to enforce it; it is often treated as the formal end of legal paganism.

events.title: Honorius proclaimed Augustus
events.summary: On 23 January 393, in answer to Eugenius' proclamation, Theodosius made his eight-year-old younger son Honorius Augustus at the Hebdomon, signalling that he would not accept Arbogast's emperor.

events.title: Synod of Hippo and the African canon of Scripture
events.summary: A plenary African council at Hippo on 8 October 393, at which the priest Augustine preached De fide et symbolo, listed the canonical books of the Bible, including the deuterocanonical books; the list was reaffirmed at Carthage in 397.

events.title: End of the ancient Olympic Games (traditional)
events.summary: The ancient Olympic Games are traditionally said to have ended after the 293rd Olympiad in 393, under Theodosius' anti-pagan legislation, though no law specifically abolishing them is known.

events.title: The pagan revival under Eugenius and Flavianus
events.summary: Under Eugenius, a Christian rhetor dependent on Arbogast, the praetorian prefect Virius Nicomachus Flavianus celebrated festivals, purified the city, restored the temple of Venus at Rome and set up statues of Jupiter and a Hercules banner for the army at the Frigidus. The anonymous Carmen contra paganos may attack him; after the Frigidus Flavianus committed suicide.

events.title: The last dated hieroglyphic inscription
events.summary: On 24 August 394, the birthday of Osiris, a priest named Esmet-Akhom carved a figure of the god Mandulis with a hieroglyphic text in the Gate of Hadrian at Philae, the last known hieroglyphic inscription; the last demotic graffito there dates to 452. The temple served the Blemmyes and Nobades until closed under Justinian.

events.title: Battle of the Frigidus
events.summary: Theodosius forced the Julian Alps and attacked Eugenius and Arbogast on the river Frigidus (Vipava) on 5-6 September 394; on the first day his 20,000 Gothic federates under Gainas and Alaric were thrown back with heavy losses, but on the second a violent bora wind blew dust into the western army's faces and turned its missiles back, and part of Arbogast's force defected. Eugenius was captured and beheaded; Arbogast killed himself two days later.

sides.strength: eastern army with c. 20,000 Gothic federates
western army with Frankish and Alamannic contingents

battle.significance: Last time the whole empire was united under one emperor; traditionally the victory of Christianity over paganism.

events.title: Death of Theodosius I and division of the empire
events.summary: Theodosius I died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the East to Arcadius (about 17) and the West to Honorius (10). It was meant as a collegiate division within one empire, but the two courts never again had a single ruler with real power over both.

events.title: Murder of the prefect Rufinus at the Hebdomon
events.summary: Gainas's returning eastern troops, saluting Arcadius at the Hebdomon parade ground outside Constantinople, surrounded and hacked to death the praetorian prefect Rufinus; his head and right hand were paraded through the city.

events.title: Composition of the Historia Augusta
events.summary: The Historia Augusta, a collection of imperial biographies from Hadrian to Carinus (117-284) purporting to be by six authors writing under Diocletian and Constantine, was in fact written by a single author around the 390s, as Hermann Dessau showed in 1889.

events.title: Alaric's Goths revolt and ravage the Balkans and Greece
events.summary: The Gothic federates who had bled at the Frigidus (394) rose under Alaric, marched to the walls of Constantinople, then turned into Thessaly and Greece, sacking Corinth, Argos and Sparta in 395-396. Athens was spared, probably by payment.

events.title: Huns raid Armenia, Cappadocia and Syria through the Caucasus
events.summary: In 395, while the eastern army was still in Italy after the Frigidus, Hunnic horsemen crossed the Caucasus by the Caspian Gates and ravaged Armenia, Cappadocia, Cilicia and Syria, threatening Antioch and Edessa. Jerome, at Bethlehem, describes the panic and the hasty repair of Jerusalem's walls. The raiders withdrew with captives; the eunuch Eutropius claimed a victory over them in 398.

events.title: Stilicho traps Alaric at Pholoe
events.summary: Stilicho landed at Corinth and hemmed Alaric's Goths in on the Pholoe plateau in Elis, but Alaric slipped away to Epirus. Eutropius had the eastern senate declare Stilicho a public enemy, and soon gave Alaric an eastern command in Illyricum.

battle.significance: Showed the cost of the two courts' rivalry: Stilicho was ordered off eastern soil and Alaric was rewarded with the magisterium per Illyricum, the official post he would seek ever after.

events.title: Augustine writes the Confessions
events.summary: Newly bishop of Hippo, Augustine wrote the thirteen books of the Confessions between about 397 and 401: a prayer addressed to God recounting his youth at Thagaste and Carthage, his Manichaean years, his career as rhetor in Rome and Milan and his conversion in a Milanese garden in 386. It created the genre of introspective autobiography.

events.title: Battle of the Ardalio: fall of Gildo
events.summary: Gildo, the Moorish comes Africae who had transferred Africa's allegiance to Constantinople and stopped the grain to Rome, was routed between Theveste and Ammaedara by his own brother Mascezel, sent by Stilicho with about 5,000 veterans. Gildo fled and killed himself at Thabraca.
events.locName: River Ardalio, between Theveste and Ammaedara

battle.significance: Restored the African grain supply to Rome and the West's control of its richest provinces for another generation.

events.title: Consulship and fall of the eunuch Eutropius
events.summary: Eutropius, Arcadius's grand chamberlain and a former slave, became the first eunuch consul in 399, to western outrage; Claudian's In Eutropium is pure venom. By August the revolt of Tribigild in Phrygia and Gainas's pressure forced his dismissal; he took sanctuary in Hagia Sophia, was exiled to Cyprus and executed at Chalcedon.

events.title: Revolt of Tribigild in Phrygia
events.summary: Tribigild, commander of Gothic federates settled in Phrygia, revolted in spring 399 after being snubbed by Eutropius and plundered Phrygia, Pisidia and Pamphylia. The general Leo was defeated and Gainas, sent against him, colluded with the rebels and demanded the fall of Eutropius, triggering the Gothic crisis of 399-400 in Constantinople.

events.title: Massacre of Gainas's Goths in Constantinople
events.summary: After months in which the Gothic general Gainas dominated the capital, the citizens rose on 12 July 400 while he was outside the walls and slaughtered his Gothic troops, reportedly about 7,000, many burned alive in a church near the palace where they had fled.

battle.significance: Ended the threat of a barbarian generalissimo controlling the eastern court.

events.title: Fravitta destroys Gainas's rafts on the Hellespont
events.summary: Trying to cross from the Thracian Chersonese to Asia on improvised rafts, Gainas's army was shattered by the Liburnian galleys of Fravitta, a pagan Goth loyal to Rome. Gainas fled north of the Danube, where the Hun Uldin killed him and sent his head to Constantinople (arrived 3 January 401).

sides.strength: fleet of Liburnian galleys under Fravitta

battle.significance: First appearance of a Hunnic ruler, Uldin, acting as a diplomatic partner of Constantinople.

events.title: Alaric invades Italy
events.summary: Displaced from his Illyrian command after the fall of Eutropius, Alaric crossed the Julian Alps in November 401 while Stilicho was fighting Vandals and Alans in Raetia. He besieged Aquileia and threatened Milan, where Honorius was cut off until Stilicho returned with troops stripped from the Rhine and Britain.

events.title: Battle of Pollentia
events.summary: On Easter Sunday 402 Stilicho attacked Alaric's camp at Pollentia in Liguria, gambling that the Christian Goths would not expect battle on the feast. The fight was bloody and inconclusive, but Alaric's camp, treasure, wife and children were captured, forcing him to negotiate.

sides.strength: western field army with Alan federates; perhaps 15,000-20,000

battle.significance: A tactical draw but strategic success: Alaric lost his baggage and hostages, and his army began to fray.

events.title: Battle of Verona
events.summary: When Alaric broke the Pollentia truce and moved on Raetia or Gaul, Stilicho caught him near Verona and defeated him; desertions followed and Alaric withdrew to the Balkans with a much reduced following. Stilicho let him go, apparently wanting him as an ally against the East.

battle.significance: Ended Alaric's first invasion of Italy; Honorius celebrated a triumph in Rome in 404, the last imperial triumph held in the old capital.

events.title: The western court moves to Ravenna
events.summary: Shaken by the siege of Milan, Honorius moved the court to Ravenna around the end of 402. Protected by marshes and with the fleet base at Classis giving access to the Adriatic and Constantinople, Ravenna remained the western capital until 476 and the seat of Odoacer, Theodoric and the exarchs.

events.title: Destruction of the Marneion at Gaza
events.summary: With an imperial order said to have been obtained from Empress Eudoxia at the birth of Theodosius II, Bishop Porphyry of Gaza had the city's great temple of Marnas burned in 402 and a cruciform church, the Eudoxiana, built on its site, using its marble paving for a pathway so that pagans would tread on it.

events.title: Synod of the Oak
events.summary: In summer 403 Theophilus of Alexandria and 36 mostly Egyptian bishops met at the imperial estate called 'the Oak' near Chalcedon and deposed John Chrysostom on 29 charges, with the backing of Empress Eudoxia. John was exiled, recalled within days after riots and a portent in the palace, and finally exiled for good in 404.

events.title: Second exile of John Chrysostom
events.summary: Deposed by the Synod of the Oak (403) under Theophilus of Alexandria, recalled after an earthquake frightened the empress Eudoxia, then exiled again in June 404 after sermons read as attacks on her silver statue, John Chrysostom left Constantinople. That night Hagia Sophia and the senate house burned. He died on a forced march at Comana in 407.

events.title: Radagaisus invades Italy
events.summary: A large Gothic-led force under the pagan king Radagaisus crossed the Alps from the middle Danube in late 405 and spread through northern Italy, one of several shock waves set off by Hunnic expansion west of the Carpathians.

events.title: Mesrop Mashtots creates the Armenian alphabet
events.summary: Around 405, with the support of Catholicos Sahak and King Vramshapuh, the cleric Mesrop Mashtots devised a 36-letter alphabet for Armenian, followed by alphabets for Georgian and Caucasian Albanian according to his biographer Koriwn. The first texts were translations of Proverbs and the Bible, inaugurating Armenian literature.

events.title: Jerome completes his translation of the Old Testament from Hebrew
events.summary: Working at Bethlehem from about 390, Jerome translated the Hebrew Bible directly into Latin rather than from the Greek Septuagint, completing it around 405. Augustine objected that it would separate the Latin church from the Greek; the translation became the core of the Vulgate, the Bible of the Latin West until modern times.

events.title: Battle of Faesulae: destruction of Radagaisus
events.summary: Radagaisus besieged Florence; Stilicho, with 30 numeri plus Uldin's Huns and Sarus's Goths, relieved the city and blockaded the invaders on the heights of Faesulae until hunger broke them. Radagaisus was executed on 23 August 406; 12,000 of his best men were enrolled in the Roman army and so many captives were sold that slaves went for a solidus a head.

sides.strength: 30 numeri (Zosimus), plus Hunnic and Gothic auxiliaries

sides.losses: army surrendered; 12,000 drafted, the rest enslaved

battle.significance: Stilicho's last great victory. The 12,000 recruits later joined Alaric after Stilicho's fall, swelling the force that sacked Rome.

events.title: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine
