events.summary: On the last day of 406 (per Prosper) Hasding and Siling Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine near Mainz after defeating Frankish federates who killed the Hasding king Godigisel. For three years they plundered Gaul, then in 409 crossed into Spain; the Hasdings under Gaiseric would end in Carthage.

events.title: Constantine III proclaimed in Britain
events.summary: After the brief usurpers Marcus and Gratian were murdered, the British garrison proclaimed a common soldier named Constantine, chosen for his name. He crossed to Gaul in 407, took over the Rhine army and the Gallic prefecture, made Arles his capital and extended his rule into Spain.

events.title: Death of Arcadius; accession of Theodosius II
events.summary: Arcadius died on 1 May 408 aged about 31, leaving his seven-year-old son Theodosius II, already Augustus since 402. Real power lay with the praetorian prefect Anthemius, who negotiated peace with Persia and began the great land walls.

events.title: Execution of Stilicho
events.summary: After a mutiny at Ticinum on 13 August 408, engineered by the court official Olympius, slaughtered Stilicho's senior officials, Stilicho surrendered from sanctuary at Ravenna and was beheaded on 22 August. Roman troops then massacred the families of barbarian federates across Italy, driving perhaps 30,000 soldiers to join Alaric.

events.title: Alaric's first siege of Rome
events.summary: In autumn 408 Alaric blockaded Rome and cut the Tiber supply from Portus. Famine and plague followed. The Senate bought him off with 5,000 lbs of gold, 30,000 lbs of silver, 4,000 silk tunics, 3,000 scarlet hides and 3,000 lbs of pepper, partly by melting down statues of the gods.

sides.losses: many dead of famine and disease

sides.strength: Alaric's Goths swollen by Stilicho's former federates and fugitive slaves

battle.significance: Showed that Ravenna would not defend Rome; Alaric used the city as a hostage to extract a settlement from Honorius.

events.title: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Pyrenees
events.summary: In late September or October 409 the Rhine invaders crossed into Spain, apparently admitted by Gerontius, Constantine III's general, who had rebelled and set up his own emperor Maximus. In 411 they divided the provinces by lot: Hasdings and Suebi in Gallaecia, Alans in Lusitania and Carthaginiensis, Silings in Baetica.

events.title: Second siege of Rome and the elevation of Priscus Attalus
events.summary: After Honorius rejected Alaric's demands at Ariminum (first gold, grain and the Venetian and Noric provinces, then only Noricum), Alaric again blockaded Rome in late 409. The Senate proclaimed the urban prefect Priscus Attalus emperor, who named Alaric magister utriusque militiae and his brother-in-law Athaulf comes domesticorum.

battle.significance: Produced the only Senate-made emperor of the period, a puppet whose failure showed that Rome without Africa could not stand.

events.title: Gerontius proclaims Maximus in Spain
events.summary: Constantine III's general Gerontius rebelled in Spain in 409 and proclaimed his own dependant Maximus emperor, probably at Tarraco, apparently letting the Vandals, Alans and Suebi into the peninsula. He killed Constantine's son Constans at Vienne and besieged Arles in 411, but his troops deserted when Honorius's general Constantius arrived; Gerontius killed his wife and himself in his burning house.

events.title: Sack of Rome by Alaric
events.summary: On 24 August 410 Alaric's Goths entered Rome by the Salarian Gate and sacked the city for three days, the first fall of Rome to a foreign enemy since the Gauls c. 390 BC. The basilicas of Peter and Paul were respected as sanctuaries; Galla Placidia, Honorius's sister, was carried off.

sides.strength: no field army; city walls held by civilians
sides.losses: unknown; probably low by the standards of sacks

battle.significance: No strategic consequence in itself, but a symbolic catastrophe that reshaped Christian historiography and political theology.

events.title: End of Roman rule in Britain
events.summary: Zosimus records that around 409 the Britons, abandoned by Constantine III and harried by Saxons, expelled Roman officials and defended themselves; and that in 410 Honorius wrote to the cities telling them to look to their own defence. No Roman administration returned.

events.title: Death and river burial of Alaric
events.summary: Alaric marched to Rhegium intending to cross to Sicily and Africa, but a storm wrecked his ships. He died near Consentia late in 410; Jordanes says his men diverted the river Busentus, buried him and his treasure in the bed, let the waters return and killed the labourers. His brother-in-law Athaulf succeeded.

events.title: Synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon
events.summary: Under the tolerant Yazdegerd I, the Roman envoy Marutha of Maypherqat and the catholicos Isaac convened a synod of the Persian church in 410 that adopted the Nicene creed and canons and organised the church under the bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon. The King of Kings allowed it to meet; it laid the foundation of the Church of the East.

events.title: Honoratus founds the monastery of Lérins
events.summary: Around 410 the aristocrat Honoratus settled on the island of Lerina off Cannes and founded a monastery that became the training ground of the Gallic episcopate: Hilary of Arles, Eucherius of Lyon, Lupus of Troyes, Faustus of Riez and later Caesarius of Arles all passed through it. It linked monasticism to the Gallo-Roman aristocracy.

events.title: Conference of Carthage
events.summary: From 1 to 8 June 411 the imperial tribune Marcellus presided over a debate between 286 Catholic and 279 Donatist bishops in the Baths of Gargilius at Carthage. Augustine led the Catholic case. Marcellus ruled for the Catholics; the edict of 412 outlawed Donatism, confiscating its churches and fining its adherents. The stenographic minutes partly survive.

events.title: Siege of Arles and fall of Constantine III
events.summary: Honorius's new general Constantius (the future Constantius III) and Ulfilas besieged Constantine III in Arles, after Gerontius's own siege collapsed. They defeated a relief army under Edobich by an ambush across the Rhône, and Constantine surrendered after being ordained a priest; he was beheaded on the road to Ravenna in September 411.

sides.strength: garrison of Arles; relief army of Franks and Alamanni under Edobich

battle.significance: Restored Ravenna's authority in southern Gaul and launched Constantius's career as the West's strongman.

events.title: Usurpation of Jovinus at Mainz
events.summary: A Gallo-Roman noble, Jovinus, was proclaimed emperor at Mainz in 411 with the support of the Burgundian king Gundahar and the Alan king Goar. Athaulf's Goths at first joined him but changed sides; Athaulf killed Jovinus's brother Sebastianus, and Jovinus, besieged at Valence in 413, was handed over and executed at Narbonne by the prefect Dardanus.

events.title: Construction of the Theodosian Land Walls
events.summary: Under the regent Anthemius, praetorian prefect of the East, a new land wall was completed by 413 about 1.5 km west of Constantine's, enclosing a much larger city. Running c. 5.7 km from the Propontis to the Golden Horn with 96 towers, it was the core of the defences that held Constantinople until 1453.

events.title: Revolt of Heraclianus
events.summary: Heraclianus, comes Africae, who had personally killed Stilicho in 408 and kept Africa loyal against Attalus, rebelled in 413, held back the grain fleet and sailed for Italy with an armada Orosius absurdly numbers at 3,700 ships. Defeated after landing near Rome, he fled back to Carthage, where he was executed. His property went to Constantius.

events.title: Burgundians settled on the left bank of the Rhine
events.summary: Prosper records that in 413 the Burgundians obtained the part of Gaul adjoining the Rhine, apparently as federates of Jovinus confirmed by Honorius's government. Later legend placed their capital at Worms under King Gundahar (Gunther of the Nibelungenlied). Aetius and his Huns destroyed this kingdom in 436.

events.title: Athaulf marries Galla Placidia at Narbonne
events.summary: In January 414, in the house of the Narbonne notable Ingenuus, the Gothic king Athaulf married his captive Galla Placidia in Roman dress, with Priscus Attalus singing the epithalamium. Their son, named Theodosius, died in infancy at Barcelona.

events.title: Pulcheria proclaimed Augusta
events.summary: On 4 July 414 Pulcheria, aged fifteen, was proclaimed Augusta and took over guardianship of her brother Theodosius II, displacing the prefect Anthemius. She and her sisters took public vows of virginity, turning the palace into something like a convent, and she shaped the court's piety and Marian devotion for a generation.

events.title: Murder of Hypatia
events.summary: In March 415 a Christian mob led by a lector named Peter dragged the Neoplatonist philosopher and mathematician Hypatia from her carriage in Alexandria, killed her in the Caesareum church, flayed her with potsherds and burned her remains. She had been an adviser to the prefect Orestes in his feud with Bishop Cyril.

events.title: Synod of Diospolis acquits Pelagius
events.summary: In December 415 fourteen Palestinian bishops at Diospolis (Lydda) heard charges brought by two exiled Gallic bishops and acquitted Pelagius after he disowned some of his disciple Caelestius's propositions. Augustine responded with De gestis Pelagii, and the African councils of 416-418 secured papal and imperial condemnation.

events.title: Murder of Athaulf at Barcelona
events.summary: Athaulf, who had married Galla Placidia and lost their infant son Theodosius, was stabbed in a stable at Barcelona in August or September 415 by a retainer avenging his former master Sarus. His successor Sigeric killed Athaulf's children by an earlier marriage and made Placidia walk before his horse with other captives, but was murdered after seven days; Wallia succeeded.

events.title: Wallia's treaty: Placidia returned for grain
events.summary: Starved by Constantius's naval blockade of the Mediterranean coast, the Goths in Spain under their new king Wallia made peace in 416: they returned Galla Placidia, received 600,000 modii of grain, and agreed to fight the Vandals and Alans in Spain on Rome's behalf.

events.title: Visigoths destroy the Siling Vandals and Alans
events.summary: Fighting as Roman federates, Wallia's Goths annihilated the Siling Vandals in Baetica (their king Fredbal was sent to Honorius) and so mauled the Alans that their king Addac fell; the survivors placed themselves under the Hasding king Gunderic, whence the later royal title 'king of the Vandals and Alans'.

events.title: Orosius writes the Seven Books of History against the Pagans
events.summary: Commissioned by Augustine, the Spanish priest Orosius wrote in 416-417 a universal history from Adam to 417 designed to show that disasters had been worse before Christ. It became the most widely read history book of the Middle Ages and is an important source for the years 395-417, written with a providential optimism that Augustine himself did not share.

events.title: Rutilius Namatianus's De reditu suo
events.summary: In autumn 417 the Gallic pagan aristocrat Rutilius Namatianus, former urban prefect, sailed from Rome to his ravaged estates in Gaul and described the voyage in elegiacs. His hymn to Rome contains the line 'you made one fatherland of diverse peoples', while he attacks Jews, monks and Stilicho, whom he accuses of burning the Sibylline Books.

events.title: Honorius establishes the Council of the Seven Provinces
events.summary: An edict of 17 April 418 to the prefect Agricola ordered an annual assembly of the provincial notables and officials of the Seven Provinces of southern Gaul at Arles between 13 August and 13 September, an attempt to bind the Gallic aristocracy to Ravenna at the moment the Goths were settled among them.

events.title: Imperial condemnation of Pelagianism
events.summary: Lobbied by the African bishops led by Augustine, Honorius issued a rescript on 30 April 418 expelling Pelagius and Caelestius from Rome; the Council of Carthage on 1 May condemned the doctrine that humans can avoid sin without grace. Pope Zosimus, who had exonerated Pelagius, reversed himself in his Epistula tractoria.

events.title: Visigoths settled in Aquitaine
events.summary: Recalled from Spain by Constantius in 418, Wallia's Goths were settled in Aquitania Secunda and adjoining parts of Novempopulana and Narbonensis, with Toulouse as their centre. Wallia died soon after and was succeeded by Theodoric I. This is conventionally the birth of the Visigothic kingdom.

events.title: The Notitia Dignitatum
events.summary: The Notitia Dignitatum, a register of all civil and military offices of both halves of the empire with the units under each commander and their shield emblems, survives in Renaissance copies of a Carolingian manuscript. The eastern part reflects the situation around 395-400; the western part was updated haphazardly into the 420s.

events.title: John Cassian at Marseille: the Institutes and Conferences
events.summary: John Cassian, who had lived among the monks of Egypt, founded two monasteries at Marseille around 415 and wrote the Institutes (c. 420) and Conferences (c. 426-429), transmitting Egyptian desert spirituality to the Latin West. His semi-Pelagian views on grace drew attacks from Prosper of Aquitaine, but Benedict prescribed his works for monastic reading.

events.title: Constantius III made co-emperor
events.summary: Constantius, married to Galla Placidia since 1 January 417 and father of Valentinian (born 2 July 419), was raised to Augustus on 8 February 421; Constantinople refused to recognise him. He died on 2 September 421, complaining that the purple had cost him his freedom.

events.title: Theodosius II marries Athenais-Eudocia
events.summary: On 7 June 421 Theodosius II married Athenais, daughter of the Athenian pagan sophist Leontius, baptised Eudocia, reportedly chosen by his sister Pulcheria. A poet and later patron of Jerusalem, she became Augusta in 423.

events.title: Roman-Persian war and the Peace of 422
events.summary: A persecution of Christians under Bahram V and Roman refusal to return fugitives led to war in 421: Ardabur ravaged Arzanene and besieged Nisibis, the Persians besieged Theodosiopolis. The 422 peace bound each side to tolerate the other's religious minority and to build no new forts near the frontier.

events.title: Defeat of Castinus in Baetica
events.summary: The magister militum Castinus, having quarrelled with Bonifatius (who left for Africa), led a Roman army with Gothic federates against the Vandals in Baetica. Betrayed by his Gothic allies, he was routed and lost 20,000 men according to Hydatius, leaving southern Spain to the Vandals.

sides.strength: field army with Gothic federates; commander Castinus
Hasding Vandals and Alans under Gunderic

battle.significance: The last major western offensive in Spain for a generation; it opened the road to Cartagena and Seville and to the sea.

events.title: Death of Honorius; usurpation of Joannes
events.summary: Honorius died of oedema at Ravenna on 15 August 423, after 28 years of nominal rule. Galla Placidia and her children were in exile at Constantinople after a quarrel with him, so the western court proclaimed the senior bureaucrat Joannes, primicerius notariorum, on 20 November.

events.title: Theodosius II founds the Capitolium school
events.summary: A law of 27 February 425 established 31 salaried chairs at the Capitolium in Constantinople: 3 Latin and 5 Greek rhetors, 10 Latin and 10 Greek grammarians, 1 philosopher and 2 jurists, with a ban on private teachers lecturing in public. Greek outnumbering Latin in the rhetoric chairs signals where the eastern court's culture was heading.

events.title: Valentinian III proclaimed Augustus at Rome
events.summary: Valentinian III, aged six, was proclaimed Augustus in Rome on 23 October 425 by the eastern master of offices Helion. His mother Galla Placidia governed as regent until about 437, balancing the generals Felix, Bonifatius and Aetius against one another.

events.title: Eastern army overthrows Joannes
events.summary: Theodosius II sent Ardabur and his son Aspar to install Valentinian. Ardabur was captured at sea, but Aspar seized Ravenna, guided, Socrates says, by an angel in the form of a shepherd across the marshes. Joannes was taken to Aquileia, mutilated, paraded on an ass in the hippodrome and beheaded. Aetius arrived three days later with a reported 60,000 Huns and had to be bought off.

events.title: The Law of Citations
events.summary: A constitution issued at Ravenna on 7 November 426 in the name of the child Valentinian III restricted courts to the writings of five jurists, Papinian, Paul, Ulpian, Modestinus and Gaius. Where they disagreed the majority prevailed, and on a tie Papinian's view decided. It sought certainty in a legal system swamped by conflicting authorities.

events.title: Augustine completes the City of God
events.summary: Begun in 413 as a reply to pagans who blamed the sack of 410 on Christianity, Augustine's De Civitate Dei was completed around 426 in 22 books. Books 1-10 refute pagan religion and its claims to have preserved Rome; books 11-22 trace the two cities, earthly and heavenly, from creation to the Last Judgement, detaching Christian hope from the fortunes of the Roman state.

events.title: End of the Arsacid kingdom of Armenia
events.summary: At the request of Armenian nobles hostile to King Artashir IV, Bahram V deposed him in 428, ending the Arsacid dynasty that had ruled Armenia since the first century AD. Persarmenia became a province under a Persian marzban, while the Roman sector had already been absorbed into the empire.

events.title: Theodosius II orders a codification of imperial laws
events.summary: On 26 March 429 Theodosius II ordered a commission to collect all general constitutions issued since Constantine and to prepare a second, more ambitious code combining laws with juristic writings. The second plan was abandoned; a new commission of sixteen under Antiochus, appointed in 435, completed the Codex Theodosianus in 437.

events.title: Vandals and Alans cross to Africa
events.summary: In May 429 Gaiseric led the Vandals and Alans across the Straits of Gibraltar from around Iulia Traducta. Victor of Vita says he counted 80,000 people, including old men, children and slaves, to give an impression of numbers. Within ten years they held Carthage.

events.title: End of the Jewish patriarchate
events.summary: The Jewish patriarch Gamaliel VI was stripped of his honorary prefecture in 415 for building synagogues and owning Christian slaves. By 429 a law refers to the time 'after the passing of the patriarchs' and diverts to the imperial treasury the annual dues Jews had paid to the patriarchate. The office of the Nasi, recognised by Rome since the third century, lapsed.

events.title: Siege of Hippo Regius and death of Augustine
events.summary: From about June 430 Gaiseric besieged Bonifatius in Hippo Regius for fourteen months. In the third month, on 28 August 430, the city's bishop Augustine died aged 75, reading the penitential psalms fixed to his wall. The Vandals lifted the siege in summer 431 and the inhabitants then abandoned the city; Augustine's library survived.

sides.strength: Bonifatius's Gothic federates and local levies

sides.losses: heavy from hunger, according to Procopius

battle.significance: The Vandals lacked siege skills; an eastern army under Aspar arrived in 431 but was defeated with Bonifatius in 432, leaving Africa open.

events.title: The so-called Mausoleum of Galla Placidia
events.summary: A small cruciform chapel attached to Galla Placidia's church of Santa Croce in Ravenna, built c. 425-450, with the most complete early Christian mosaic interior to survive: a starry vault, the Good Shepherd, and St Lawrence with his gridiron. Placidia died in Rome in 450 and was probably buried there, not in this building.

events.title: First Council of Ephesus
events.summary: Summoned by Theodosius II, the council opened on 22 June 431 under Cyril of Alexandria before John of Antioch and the eastern bishops arrived, and deposed Nestorius of Constantinople for refusing Mary the title Theotokos (God-bearer). John's rival council deposed Cyril. The emperor at first confirmed both depositions, then sided with Cyril.

events.title: Palladius sent to the Irish; the mission of Patrick
events.summary: Prosper records that in 431 Pope Celestine ordained Palladius 'first bishop to the Irish believing in Christ'. The more famous mission of Patrick, a Romano-British decurion's son once enslaved in Ireland, is traditionally dated to 432; his own Confessio and Letter to Coroticus are the only texts surviving from fifth-century Britain or Ireland written by a named individual.

events.title: Battle of Rimini: Aetius against Bonifatius
events.summary: Placidia recalled Bonifatius from Africa, made him patricius and magister militum and dismissed Aetius. Aetius marched on Italy; near Ariminum Bonifatius won but was mortally wounded and died months later. Aetius fled to the Huns and returned in 433 with Hunnic backing, forcing Placidia to accept him as patricius in 435.

battle.significance: A pyrrhic victory for the court: it removed Aetius's main rival and opened two decades of Aetius's ascendancy, built on Hunnic support.

events.title: Santa Maria Maggiore built by Sixtus III
events.summary: Soon after the Council of Ephesus proclaimed Mary Theotokos, Pope Sixtus III (432-440) built the great basilica on the Esquiline dedicated to the Virgin, whose triumphal arch inscription reads 'Xystus episcopus plebi Dei'. Its nave mosaics of Old Testament scenes are the largest surviving cycle of fifth-century Roman mosaic.

events.title: Treaty of Hippo with the Vandals
events.summary: On 11 February 435 Ravenna recognised the Vandals as federates in Mauretania Sitifensis and parts of Numidia, in return for tribute and Gaiseric's son Huneric as hostage, keeping Carthage and the rich Proconsular province for Rome.

events.title: Treaty of Margus with the Huns
events.summary: After the death of Rua, his nephews Bleda and Attila met eastern envoys on horseback outside Margus on the Danube. Constantinople agreed to double the annual payment to 700 lbs of gold, return Hunnic fugitives, pay 8 solidi for each escaped Roman prisoner and open markets on equal terms.

events.title: The Bacaudae of Tibatto
events.summary: The Gallic Chronicle of 452 says that in 435 'farther Gaul followed Tibatto, the leader of the rebellion, and seceded from Roman society; from this beginning almost all the servile population of Gaul conspired in Bacaudae'. Aetius's general Litorius crushed the revolt by 437. The nature of the Bacaudae, peasant rebels or local self-defence, remains debated.

events.title: Huns destroy the Burgundian kingdom on the Rhine
events.summary: After the Burgundians under King Gundahar pushed into Belgica, Aetius defeated them in 435 and then set Hunnic auxiliaries on them in 436/437: Gundahar was killed with, according to Hydatius, 20,000 of his people. The survivors were resettled in Sapaudia (Savoy) in 443. The catastrophe became the core of the Nibelungenlied.

battle.significance: Demonstrated Aetius's method of using Huns to discipline federates, and fixed the Burgundians in the Rhône valley, where they founded their second kingdom.

events.title: Publication of the Theodosian Code
events.summary: Promulgated by Theodosius II on 15 February 438 and in force from 1 January 439 in both halves of the empire, the Codex Theodosianus collected about 2,500 general constitutions issued since Constantine in 312, arranged in 16 books by subject and date. On 25 December 438 the Roman Senate received it with recorded acclamations, chanted 28 times or more.

events.title: Gaiseric seizes Carthage
events.summary: Breaking the 435 treaty, Gaiseric took Carthage by surprise on 19 October 439. The second city of the West, its fleet, and the Proconsular province, the West's richest tax base and Rome's granary, passed to the Vandals. The Vandal kingdom dated its years from this day.

sides.strength: city garrison; no field army in Africa

battle.significance: The most damaging single loss the western empire suffered: revenue, grain and a naval base turned against Italy.

events.title: Battle of Toulouse: capture of Litorius
events.summary: Litorius, Aetius's deputy, who had relieved the Gothic siege of Narbonne in 437, attacked Theodoric I's capital Toulouse with Hunnic auxiliaries. Salvian and Prosper say he consulted pagan auspices. He was defeated, captured and executed; Avitus then negotiated peace with the Goths.

sides.strength: Roman troops and Hunnic auxiliaries under Litorius

battle.significance: Ended Roman attempts to reduce the Visigoths by force; thereafter they were managed by treaty.

events.title: The Suebi take Mérida
events.summary: King Rechila of the Suebi took Emerita Augusta, capital of the diocese of the Spains, in 439 and Hispalis in 441, making the Suebi masters of Lusitania, Baetica and Carthaginiensis. Hydatius, bishop in Gallaecia, records the conquest from the Roman provincials' point of view.

events.title: Brief Roman-Persian war of 440
events.summary: Yazdegerd II attacked Roman territory around 440, perhaps over Roman fortifications and Christian refugees, while Roman forces were committed against the Vandals. The magister militum per Orientem Anatolius made a quick peace in which both sides agreed not to build new forts near the border, a clause later invoked against Anastasius's Dara.

events.title: Salvian's On the Government of God
events.summary: The Marseille priest Salvian argued in De gubernatione Dei (c. 440) that the barbarian conquests were God's just punishment of Roman vice, contrasting chaste Goths and Vandals with corrupt Romans, and that oppressed provincials fled to the Bacaudae or the barbarians to escape tax collectors. It is a central text for the social history of the western collapse.

events.title: Aborted East-West expedition against the Vandals
events.summary: Theodosius II assembled a fleet of about 1,100 transports under five generals in Sicily in 441 to retake Carthage, but recalled it when the Persians attacked in Armenia and the Huns crossed the Danube. The 442 treaty left the Vandals the Proconsularis, Byzacena and Tripolitania and engaged Huneric to Valentinian's daughter Eudocia.

events.title: 'Britain passes into the power of the Saxons'
events.summary: The Gallic Chronicle of 452 states under 441 that the British provinces, after various defeats, passed into the power of the Saxons. Gildas tells of a 'proud tyrant' (later named Vortigern) who hired Saxon mercenaries, who then rebelled; Bede dated the adventus Saxonum to 449, with Hengest and Horsa.

events.title: Huns sack Viminacium, Margus, Singidunum and Sirmium
events.summary: Accusing the bishop of Margus of robbing Hunnic royal tombs, Attila and Bleda crossed the Danube in 441 while Roman forces were in Sicily for the Vandal expedition. The bishop betrayed Margus to save himself; Viminacium, Singidunum and Sirmium fell. Excavated Viminacium shows abandonment after this date.

events.title: Huns sack Naissus
events.summary: In 441-442 the Huns of Bleda and Attila took Viminacium, Margus (betrayed by its bishop), Singidunum and Sirmium, then besieged Naissus, Constantine's birthplace, with rams and siege towers (Priscus describes their wheeled beams). The city fell; years later Priscus found the riverbank still strewn with bones.

battle.significance: Showed that the Huns, unlike earlier steppe raiders, could take fortified cities with captured Roman engineering skills.

events.title: Treaty of 442 with Gaiseric
events.summary: After the aborted eastern expedition, Valentinian III recognised Gaiseric's possession of Proconsularis, Byzacena and eastern Numidia, the richest provinces of the West, in exchange for the return of the Mauretanias and western Numidia. Gaiseric's son Huneric, a hostage in Italy, was betrothed to Valentinian's daughter Eudocia, and Huneric's Visigothic wife was sent home mutilated.

events.title: Aetius settles Alans at Valence and Orléans
events.summary: The Gallic Chronicle records that Aetius gave deserted lands around Valence to Alans under Sambida (440) and settled the Alans of King Goar in farther Gaul (442), where they expelled the landowners by force. These Alans, based on Orléans, fought for Aetius at the Catalaunian Plains in 451.

events.title: Peace of Anatolius with the Huns
events.summary: After defeats in Thrace, Constantinople agreed to pay 6,000 lbs of gold in arrears and to triple the annual tribute to 2,100 lbs, and to ransom Roman prisoners at 12 solidi each. Priscus describes senators selling their wives' jewellery and furniture to raise the sums.

events.title: Burgundians settled in Sapaudia
events.summary: The surviving Burgundians, broken by the Huns in 436, were settled by Aetius in 443 in Sapaudia, the region around Lake Geneva, 'to be divided with the natives', according to the Gallic Chronicle. From this base they expanded down the Rhône to create the kingdom of Gundioc, Chilperic and Gundobad centred on Lyon and Geneva.

events.title: Valentinian III's law on papal authority
events.summary: On 8 July 445, at Pope Leo I's request, Valentinian III issued a constitution (Novel 17) declaring that the primacy of the apostolic see was confirmed by Peter's merit, Rome's dignity and a holy synod, and ordering provincial governors to compel bishops to attend the pope's tribunal. It was aimed at Hilary of Arles and gave imperial sanction to papal jurisdiction over the western church.

events.title: Attila murders Bleda
events.summary: Around 445 Attila killed his elder brother and co-ruler Bleda and became sole king of the Huns. Bleda's widow continued to hold a village, where Priscus's embassy was entertained in 449, and Bleda's Moorish jester Zercon was passed to Aetius.

events.title: The 'Groans of the Britons' to Aetius
events.summary: Gildas quotes a letter sent by the Britons to 'Agitius, thrice consul', usually identified as Aetius (consul for the third time in 446): 'The barbarians drive us to the sea; the sea drives us back to the barbarians; between these two kinds of death we are either drowned or slaughtered.' No help came.

events.title: Earthquake and rebuilding of the Theodosian Walls
events.summary: An earthquake on 26 January 447 threw down much of the land wall, including 57 towers, as Attila advanced. The praetorian prefect Constantinus mobilised the Blue and Green circus factions and rebuilt it in about two months, adding the outer wall and moat. Inscriptions at the Mevlevihane Gate boast that 'not even Pallas could have built so quickly'.

events.title: Battle of the Utus
events.summary: In 447 Attila's army met the eastern field army under the magister Arnegisclus on the river Utus (Vit) in Dacia Ripensis. Arnegisclus was killed fighting after his horse fell; the Huns won but at heavy cost, then sacked Marcianople and raided as far as Thermopylae and the Gallipoli peninsula.

battle.significance: The last pitched battle of the eastern army against Attila; afterwards Theodosius accepted humiliating terms, including a demilitarised strip south of the Danube five days' journey wide.

events.title: The Tome of Leo
events.summary: On 13 June 449 Pope Leo I sent Patriarch Flavian of Constantinople a dogmatic letter condemning Eutyches and defining Christ as one person in two natures, each performing what is proper to it. Suppressed at Ephesus II, it was acclaimed at Chalcedon with the cry 'Peter has spoken through Leo' and became the touchstone of Chalcedonian orthodoxy and the main target of its opponents.

events.title: Second Council of Ephesus (the 'Robber Synod')
events.summary: Presided over by Dioscorus of Alexandria with imperial backing, the August 449 council rehabilitated the monk Eutyches, refused to read Pope Leo's Tome, and deposed Flavian of Constantinople, who died after rough handling. Leo called it a latrocinium, a gang of robbers.

events.title: Embassy of Maximinus and Priscus to Attila
events.summary: Priscus of Panium accompanied the envoy Maximinus to Attila's wooden capital north of the Danube, unaware that the eunuch Chrysaphius had bribed Attila's officer Edeco to murder the king. Edeco betrayed the plot. Priscus's account is the only eyewitness description of the Hunnic court: Attila's simple wooden cup amid gold plate, the stone bath built by a captured Roman engineer, and a Greek merchant turned Hun who praised life outside Roman taxes and lawyers.

events.title: Death of Theodosius II; Marcian chosen
events.summary: Theodosius II died on 28 July 450 after a fall from his horse while hunting. His sister Pulcheria, a consecrated virgin, married the retired officer Marcian (with a vow of chastity respected) and he was crowned on 25 August. Chrysaphius was executed and the tribute to Attila stopped.

events.title: Honoria's appeal to Attila
events.summary: Justa Grata Honoria, Valentinian III's sister, disgraced after an affair with her steward Eugenius and betrothed against her will to the senator Herculanus, sent her eunuch Hyacinthus with a ring to Attila asking for help. Attila claimed her as his bride with half the western empire as dowry, a pretext for invading Gaul.

events.title: Marcian stops the tribute to Attila
events.summary: Marcian, on his accession in August 450, executed the eunuch Chrysaphius and announced that he would no longer pay Attila the 2,100 lb of gold a year agreed in 447, offering gifts only for peace and war for aggression. Attila, drawn to the West by the Honoria affair, never turned on the East, where Marcian's refusal and the Hunnic collapse left a full treasury.

events.title: Huns sack Metz
events.summary: Crossing the Rhine in spring 451, Attila's army stormed Divodurum (Metz) on the eve of Easter, 7 April, burning the city and killing the priest at the altar; only the oratory of St Stephen survived, according to Gregory of Tours.

battle.significance: Opened Attila's march into the heart of Gaul.

events.title: Battle of Avarayr
events.summary: Armenian nobles under Vardan Mamikonian, rebelling against Yazdegerd II's attempt to impose Zoroastrianism, were crushed on the plain of Avarayr. Vardan and eight other commanders were killed; Marcian refused to help. The resistance continued as guerrilla war and won religious freedom in the Treaty of Nvarsak (484).

battle.significance: A defeat remembered as a national-religious victory; it also demonstrated Constantinople's refusal to break the peace with Persia while Attila threatened.

events.title: Siege of Orléans
events.summary: Attila besieged Aurelianum, where an Alan group was settled; Bishop Anianus organised the defence. The Huns had breached the walls when Aetius and Theodoric I arrived around mid-June and forced them to withdraw eastward toward the Catalaunian Plains.

sides.strength: citizens and Alan settlers, relieved by Aetius's coalition

battle.significance: The turning point of the 451 campaign: the relief of Orléans denied Attila the Loire and the Visigothic south.

events.title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.summary: Aetius, with Visigoths under Theodoric I, Alans under Sangiban, Franks, Burgundians and others, fought Attila's Huns, Ostrogoths and Gepids on the Campus Mauriacus or Catalaunian Plains in Champagne. Theodoric was killed, but Attila was driven into his wagon laager, reportedly ready to burn himself on a pyre of saddles. Aetius let him withdraw.

sides.strength: unknown; perhaps 30,000-50,000 including Visigoths, Alans, Franks, Burgundians, Saxons, Armoricans
unknown; Huns with Ostrogoths under Valamir, Gepids under Ardaric and others

battle.significance: Halted Attila in Gaul and preserved Aetius's coalition, but did not destroy Hunnic power. It was the last great campaign of a western Roman field army in Gaul.

events.title: Council of Chalcedon
events.summary: Convened by Marcian and Pulcheria at Chalcedon, across the Bosporus from Constantinople, from 8 October to 1 November 451, with some 520 bishops (tradition says 630). It deposed Dioscorus, accepted Leo's Tome and defined Christ as one person 'in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation'.

events.title: Attila destroys Aquileia
events.summary: In spring 452 Attila crossed the Julian Alps and besieged Aquileia for some three months; Procopius and Jordanes tell that he was about to give up when he saw storks carrying their young out of the city and took it as an omen. The city was stormed and destroyed so thoroughly that it never fully recovered.

battle.significance: Aquileia's fall opened the Po valley; refugees fleeing to the lagoons figure in the foundation legends of Venice and Grado.

events.title: Pope Leo meets Attila on the Mincio
events.summary: After sacking Patavium, Vicetia, Verona, Brixia, Bergamum, Mediolanum and Ticinum, Attila received an embassy of Pope Leo I, the ex-consul Gennadius Avienus and the ex-prefect Trygetius at the ager Ambuleius on the Mincio near Mantua. He withdrew from Italy soon after.
events.locName: Ager Ambuleius on the Mincio, near Mantua

events.title: Death of Attila
events.summary: Attila died in early 453 on the night of his wedding to a girl named Ildico, choking on a haemorrhage from the nose while drunk, according to Priscus via Jordanes. His men cut their faces so that the greatest of warriors would be mourned with blood, not tears, and buried him secretly in coffins of gold, silver and iron.

events.title: Assassination of Thorismund
events.summary: Thorismund, who had succeeded his father Theodoric I on the Catalaunian battlefield, was murdered in 453 at Toulouse by his brothers Theodoric II and Frederic, reputedly for his anti-Roman policy. Theodoric II became a close ally of Aetius's successors and of the emperor Avitus.

events.title: Valentinian III murders Aetius
events.summary: During a financial report at the palace in Rome on 21 (or 22) September 454, Valentinian III, aged 35 and at last asserting himself, attacked Aetius with his own sword, and the chamberlain Heraclius finished him. A courtier is supposed to have told the emperor he had cut off his right hand with his left.

events.title: Battle of the Nedao
events.summary: Attila's sons quarrelled over the subject peoples 'as if they were household slaves' (Jordanes). Ardaric of the Gepids led a revolt and defeated the Huns on the unidentified river Nedao in Pannonia; Attila's eldest son Ellac was killed with 30,000 of his followers. The Hunnic empire disintegrated.

sides.strength: Gepids under Ardaric with Rugii, Suebi, Heruli and others

battle.significance: Freed the Danubian peoples (Gepids, Ostrogoths, Rugii, Heruli, Sciri) who would dominate the next generation of Balkan and Italian politics.

events.title: Assassination of Valentinian III
events.summary: On 16 March 455, while Valentinian watched athletic exercises on the Campus Martius, two of Aetius's former bucellarii, Optila and Thraustila, cut him down along with Heraclius. The Theodosian dynasty in the West ended. The senator Petronius Maximus, probably the instigator, took the throne the next day and forced Valentinian's widow Licinia Eudoxia to marry him.

events.title: Vandal sack of Rome
events.summary: Claiming that the 442 betrothal of Huneric to Eudocia had been broken, Gaiseric landed at Portus. Petronius Maximus, fleeing, was stoned or torn apart by the crowd on 31 May 455. The Vandals entered on 2 June and, after Pope Leo secured a promise to avoid burning and massacre, systematically plundered the city for fourteen days.

sides.losses: emperor killed by mob; city plundered

sides.strength: Vandal and Moorish fleet and army

battle.significance: A far more thorough plundering than 410. It removed the last members of the Theodosian house from Italy and began twenty years of Vandal naval terror in the western Mediterranean.

events.title: Avitus proclaimed emperor with Visigothic support
events.summary: Eparchius Avitus, a Gallic aristocrat sent as envoy to the Visigothic king Theodoric II at Toulouse, was proclaimed emperor at Ugernum near Arles on 9 July 455 with Gothic backing and acclaimed by Gallic notables. His son-in-law Sidonius Apollinaris delivered his panegyric in Rome on 1 January 456.

events.title: Battle of the Órbigo: Visigoths crush the Suebi
events.summary: Acting nominally for Avitus, Theodoric II invaded Gallaecia and destroyed the army of the Suebic king Rechiar on the river Órbigo, twelve miles from Asturica (Astorga). Rechiar was captured and executed in December; the Suebic kingdom split into factions for a generation.
events.locName: Campus Paramus on the Órbigo, near Astorga

sides.strength: Visigothic army with Burgundian contingents under Theodoric II

sides.losses: heavy; king captured and later executed

battle.significance: Started the Visigothic shift into Spain that would eventually make it the heart of their kingdom.

events.title: Battle of Placentia: fall of Avitus
events.summary: Ricimer and Majorian turned on Avitus, whose Visigothic allies were away in Spain. He was defeated at Placentia on 17 October 456, his general Messianus killed. Avitus was spared and consecrated bishop of Placentia, but died within months.

battle.significance: Ended the Gallo-Gothic experiment of an emperor from Gaul and established that Italy's army, under Ricimer, made emperors.

events.title: Ricimer defeats the Vandals at Agrigentum and Corsica
events.summary: Ricimer, a general of Suevic and Visigothic royal descent, defeated a Vandal force near Agrigentum in Sicily and then a Vandal fleet of 60 ships off Corsica in 456. The prestige made him the decisive figure in Italy.

battle.significance: Launched Ricimer's sixteen-year dominance as king-maker of the West.

events.title: Accession of Leo I
events.summary: After Marcian's death on 27 January 457, Aspar, who as an Arian Alan could not take the throne himself, chose Leo, a tribune from Dacia. Leo was crowned on 7 February 457, possibly by the patriarch Anatolius, and later began building an Isaurian counterweight to Aspar's Goths.

events.title: Murder of Patriarch Proterius of Alexandria
events.summary: When news of Marcian's death reached Alexandria in early 457, anti-Chalcedonians consecrated Timothy Aelurus ('the Cat') patriarch, and on Holy Thursday, 28 March 457, a mob killed the Chalcedonian patriarch Proterius in the baptistery, dragged his body through the city and burned it. It marked Egypt's lasting rejection of Chalcedon.

events.title: Majorian becomes emperor
events.summary: After months without an emperor in the West, Majorian, Aetius's former officer and Ricimer's comrade, was acclaimed by the army on 1 April 457 at Ad Columellas near Ravenna and became Augustus on 28 December 457. He was the last western emperor to campaign in person with real energy.

events.title: The Codex Encyclius
events.summary: Leo I, unsure whether to uphold Chalcedon, wrote in 457-458 to the metropolitans and leading holy men of the empire asking their opinion on the council and on Timothy Aelurus. The replies, collected as the Codex Encyclius, overwhelmingly supported Chalcedon, and Timothy was exiled to Gangra and then Cherson in 460.

events.title: Earthquake at Antioch
events.summary: On 13-14 September 458 an earthquake destroyed much of the New City on the Orontes island at Antioch, including part of the palace and colonnades. Evagrius, citing earlier chroniclers, lists the buildings lost. It was the first of a series of catastrophes, culminating in 526 and 528, that ended Antioch's classical prosperity.

events.title: Majorian's legislation
events.summary: Majorian's Novels attacked tax arrears and abuses by collectors, restored the office of defensor civitatis, protected curiales, and in Novel 4 (11 July 458) forbade the stripping of ancient public buildings in Rome for building stone, with fines of 50 lbs of gold for officials who allowed it.

events.title: Majorian defeats Vandal raiders in Campania
events.summary: A Vandal and Moorish raiding force led by Gaiseric's brother-in-law landed at the mouth of the Liris (Garigliano) near Sinuessa and plundered Campania. Majorian's troops caught them laden with booty and drove them back to their ships with heavy losses; the Vandal leader was killed.

battle.significance: A morale boost that encouraged Majorian's plan to strike Carthage directly.

events.title: The Orthodox (Neonian) Baptistery of Ravenna
events.summary: The octagonal baptistery beside Ravenna's cathedral, begun under Bishop Ursus around 400, was given its mosaic dome under Bishop Neon c. 450-460: the baptism of Christ, with a personified river Jordan, surrounded by the twelve apostles. It is the best-preserved baptistery of the fifth century.

events.title: Death of Simeon the Stylite
events.summary: Simeon, who had lived on top of a column near Telanissos in northern Syria since about 423, raising it in stages to some 18 m, died on 2 September 459. His body was taken to Antioch under military guard. Pilgrims from as far as Gaul and Britain had visited him; the vast cruciform pilgrimage church of Qal'at Sim'an was built round his column c. 476-490.

events.title: Vandals burn Majorian's fleet in Spain
events.summary: Majorian, having forced the Visigoths and Burgundians back into alliance, assembled a fleet of about 300 ships in the Spanish harbour of Portus Illicitanus (near Elche) and around Carthago Nova to invade Africa. Traitors guided Vandal raiders who burned or seized much of it in 460. Majorian made peace and returned to Italy.

sides.losses: most of the fleet destroyed or captured

battle.significance: The failure destroyed Majorian's prestige and led directly to his deposition.

events.title: Ricimer deposes and executes Majorian
events.summary: Returning to Italy after dismissing his army, Majorian was arrested by Ricimer at Dertona on 2 August 461, stripped of his purple, beaten and beheaded on 7 August near the river Iria. Procopius praises him as a ruler surpassing all who had gone before.

events.title: Aegidius defeats the Visigoths at Orléans
events.summary: Aegidius, magister militum per Gallias, refused to recognise Ricimer's puppet Libius Severus and fought the Visigoths, to whom Ricimer had ceded Narbonne. With Frankish help (Childeric?) he defeated a Gothic army near Orléans, killing Frederic, brother of Theodoric II. He died in 464 or 465, perhaps poisoned, leaving a Roman enclave around Soissons to his son Syagrius.

sides.strength: Gallic field army remnant with Frankish allies

battle.significance: Kept northern Gaul out of Visigothic hands, leaving it to be fought over by Romans and Franks.

events.title: Great fire of Constantinople
events.summary: A fire that started in the dockside quarter on the Golden Horn on 2 September 465 burned for days and destroyed, according to Evagrius, eight of the city's fourteen regions, including the area from the Neorion to the Forum of Constantine. Leo I moved to the palace of St Mamas for six months.

events.title: Death of Aegidius
events.summary: Aegidius, Majorian's magister militum in Gaul who refused to recognise Ricimer's emperors and ruled an independent command in the north, died in 465, by poison or ambush according to Hydatius. He had sent envoys to the Vandals proposing an alliance. His son Syagrius inherited his power at Soissons.

events.title: Tarasis the Isaurian becomes Zeno and marries Ariadne
events.summary: The Isaurian chieftain Tarasis son of Kodisa, from Rousoumblada, won Leo I's favour in 466 by producing letters proving that Aspar's son Ardabur was intriguing with Persia. He took the Greek name Zeno, married Leo's daughter Ariadne and became magister militum, creating an Isaurian counterweight to Aspar's Gothic following.

events.title: Anthemius sent from Constantinople as western emperor
events.summary: After the death of Libius Severus in 465 and nearly two years without an emperor, Leo I sent the eastern aristocrat Anthemius, son-in-law of Marcian, with an army and Marcellinus of Dalmatia. He was proclaimed near Rome on 12 April 467; his daughter Alypia married Ricimer to seal the arrangement.

events.title: Battle of Cape Bon: the great Vandal expedition fails
events.summary: The largest naval expedition of late antiquity, sent by Leo I under his brother-in-law Basiliscus, anchored off Cape Bon (Promunturium Mercurii) some 60 km from Carthage. Gaiseric bought a five-day truce, then sent fireships among the crowded fleet with a favourable wind. Half the fleet was lost; Basiliscus fled.

battle.significance: The decisive failure of the late Roman effort to recover Africa; it sealed the western empire's fiscal fate and crippled eastern finances until Anastasius.

events.title: Battle of Déols: Riothamus defeated
events.summary: Anthemius's ally Riothamus, 'king of the Britons', crossed with an army Jordanes puts at 12,000 to Berry to fight Euric, but was defeated near Bourg-de-Déols before Roman forces could join him and fled to the Burgundians. Euric then took much of central Gaul.

battle.significance: Removed the last field army able to contest Euric's expansion north of the Loire.

events.title: Death of Dengizich
events.summary: Attila's son Dengizich, who had crossed the frozen Danube against the empire, was defeated and killed in 469 by the magister militum per Thracias Anagast. His head was brought to Constantinople, paraded through the streets and fixed on a pole at the Xylokirkos for days. It marks the end of Hunnic power in the Balkans.

battle.significance: End of the Attilid Huns.

events.title: Leo I murders Aspar
events.summary: After fifty years as Constantinople's kingmaker, the Alan general Aspar and his son Ardabur were cut down by palace eunuchs in 471 on Leo's orders; Leo earned the nickname Makelles, 'the Butcher'. The Isaurian Zeno, married to Leo's daughter Ariadne since 466/467, inherited Aspar's role. Aspar's Gothic followers rose under Theodoric Strabo.

events.title: Sieges of Clermont
events.summary: For four summers the Arverni, led by Bishop Sidonius Apollinaris and his brother-in-law Ecdicius (who once broke through the Gothic lines with eighteen horsemen), resisted Euric's Goths. In 475 Julius Nepos ceded Auvergne in exchange for Provence; Sidonius, who felt betrayed, was briefly imprisoned.

sides.strength: citizens and private retainers of Ecdicius

battle.significance: The Auvergne's sacrifice in the 475 treaty marked Ravenna's abandonment of Roman Gaul north of the Durance.

events.title: Euric defeats Anthemius's son near Arles
events.summary: Anthemius sent his son Anthemiolus with the generals Thorisarius, Everdingus and Hermianus to stop Euric's expansion; they were defeated and killed by the Visigoths east of the Rhône near Arles in 471. It was the last campaign of an imperial army in Gaul and left the Auvergne isolated.

battle.significance: Last imperial army in Gaul destroyed.

events.title: Ricimer besieges Rome; death of Anthemius
events.summary: Ricimer quarrelled with his father-in-law Anthemius and besieged him in Rome in spring 472, proclaiming Olybrius emperor in April. After famine and street fighting the city fell; Anthemius, hiding disguised as a beggar in St Peter's or Santa Maria in Trastevere, was beheaded by Ricimer's nephew Gundobad on 11 July 472.

sides.strength: Anthemius's guards, citizens and Gothic troops under Bilimer from Gaul

battle.significance: The first time Rome was stormed by a Roman army since 312, and the end of the last East-backed attempt to stabilise the West.

events.title: Death of Ricimer
events.summary: Ricimer died on 18 August 472, vomiting blood, five weeks after killing Anthemius. Olybrius died on 2 November. Gundobad inherited the post of patricius and in March 473 made the comes domesticorum Glycerius emperor before leaving to claim the Burgundian throne.

events.title: Euric conquers Tarraconensis
events.summary: In 472-473 Euric's count Gauterit took Pamplona, Zaragoza and the neighbouring cities, while Heldefred with Vincentius besieged Tarragona and took the coastal cities of Tarraconensis, the last Roman province in Spain. Visigothic rule now covered most of the peninsula outside Suebic Gallaecia.

events.title: Leo I's treaty with Theodoric Strabo
events.summary: After Strabo's Thracian Goths rebelled following Aspar's murder, Leo I agreed in 473 to pay them 2,000 lb of gold a year, to make Strabo magister militum praesentalis and to recognise him as sole king of the Goths, provided he served the emperor against all enemies except the Vandals.

events.title: Zeno becomes emperor
events.summary: Leo I died on 18 January 474, leaving his seven-year-old grandson Leo II, son of Zeno and Ariadne. Leo II crowned his father Zeno co-emperor on 9 February and died in November 474, leaving the Isaurian, born Tarasis son of Kodisa, sole Augustus.

events.title: Julius Nepos deposes Glycerius
events.summary: Leo I refused to recognise Glycerius and sent Julius Nepos, magister militum of Dalmatia and nephew of Marcellinus, who landed at Portus in June 474. Glycerius surrendered without a fight and was consecrated bishop of Salona.

events.title: Zeno's 'endless peace' with Gaiseric
events.summary: Zeno's envoy, the senator Severus, negotiated a perpetual peace: Constantinople recognised Vandal rule in Africa, Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and the Balearics, and Gaiseric released captives and allowed Nicene worship in Carthage. It held until 533.

events.title: Usurpation of Basiliscus
events.summary: In January 475 Leo's widow Verina and her brother Basiliscus drove Zeno back to Isauria. Basiliscus issued an Encyclical condemning Chalcedon, sparking riots led by Daniel the Stylite, then withdrew it. Illus and Verina's associates switched sides, and Zeno re-entered Constantinople in August 476. Basiliscus and his family were starved to death in a cistern at Limnae in Cappadocia.

events.title: Orestes drives out Nepos; Romulus Augustulus proclaimed
events.summary: Orestes, a Pannonian Roman who had been Attila's secretary and was now Nepos's magister militum, turned the army on his master. Nepos fled from Ravenna to Dalmatia on 28 August 475, and on 31 October Orestes proclaimed his own adolescent son Romulus emperor, mocked as Augustulus.

events.title: Julius Nepos cedes the Auvergne to Euric
events.summary: After four years of resistance led by Sidonius Apollinaris and Ecdicius, Nepos's envoys, among them Epiphanius of Pavia, ceded the Auvergne to Euric in 475 in exchange for Provence. Sidonius wrote bitterly that 'our servitude has been made the price of others' security'. He was imprisoned by the Goths before being restored to his see.

events.title: The Encyclical of Basiliscus
events.summary: Basiliscus issued an encyclical in 475 anathematising the Tome of Leo and Chalcedon and recalled Timothy Aelurus. Constantinople rose against it; the stylite Daniel came down from his column for the only time to lead the protest. Basiliscus retracted with an Antencyclical in 476, too late to save his throne from Zeno.

events.title: Odoacer kills Orestes at Placentia
events.summary: The barbarian federates of the Italian army, Heruli, Sciri, Rugii and Turcilingi, demanded a third of the land of Italy. Orestes refused. They proclaimed the Scirian officer Odoacer king on 23 August 476, besieged Orestes in Ticinum, and captured and executed him at Placentia on 28 August; his brother Paulus was killed in the pine forest outside Ravenna on 4 September.

sides.strength: federate troops of the Italian army

battle.significance: Destroyed the last Roman regime in Italy and transferred power to the federate army that had long been its real base.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.summary: Odoacer entered Ravenna, deposed the boy emperor Romulus but spared him 'because of his beauty', gave him a pension of 6,000 solidi and sent him to live with his relatives at the Castellum Lucullanum near Naples. Odoacer ruled Italy as king, nominally under Constantinople, and did not appoint another western emperor.

events.title: Death of Gaiseric
events.summary: Gaiseric died on 25 January 477 after nearly fifty years as king, having led the Vandals from Spain to Carthage, sacked Rome and defeated two imperial armadas. His law of succession gave the throne to the eldest male of the royal house (agnatic seniority), which would bring Gelimer's coup in 530.

events.title: Theodoric the Amal seizes Dyrrachium
events.summary: Frustrated by Zeno's broken promises, Theodoric marched his Goths west in 479 and seized Dyrrachium on the Adriatic by a ruse. The envoy Adamantius offered lands in Dardania; while talks went on, the general Sabinianus ambushed the Gothic rearguard under Theodimund and captured 2,000 wagons and 5,000 prisoners. Malchus's account of the negotiations is unusually detailed.

events.title: Revolt of Marcian in Constantinople
events.summary: Marcian, son of the western emperor Anthemius and husband of Ariadne's sister Leontia, claimed the throne in late 479, arguing that Leontia, born after Leo I's accession, had a better right than Ariadne. His men nearly took the palace, but Illus brought Isaurian troops across from Chalcedon overnight; Marcian was ordained a priest and exiled to Cappadocia.

events.title: Murder of Julius Nepos
events.summary: Julius Nepos, still recognised in Constantinople and on Odoacer's coinage as western emperor, was murdered by his retainers at his villa near Salona on 9 May 480, possibly at the instigation of Glycerius, now bishop of Salona. Odoacer invaded Dalmatia in 481 on the pretext of avenging him.

events.title: Death of Theodoric Strabo
events.summary: After a failed attack on Constantinople in 481, Theodoric Strabo marched into Greece and was killed when his rearing horse threw him onto a spear hanging by his tent. His son Recitach was murdered by Theodoric the Amal in 484, who absorbed Strabo's Goths and became the sole leader of the Balkan Goths.

events.title: Zeno's Henotikon
events.summary: Drafted by the patriarch Acacius and accepted by Peter Mongus of Alexandria, Zeno's 'Act of Union' affirmed Nicaea, Constantinople and Ephesus and Cyril's Twelve Anathemas while passing over Chalcedon in silence, condemning anyone who held otherwise 'whether at Chalcedon or any other synod'. It pleased neither side fully and Rome rejected it.

events.title: Sabas founds the Great Lavra
events.summary: The Cappadocian monk Sabas founded the Great Lavra in the gorge of the Kidron between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea in 483. It became the leading monastery of Palestine and a stronghold of Chalcedonian orthodoxy; Sabas twice travelled to Constantinople as spokesman of the Palestinian monks. The monastery is still inhabited.

events.title: Huneric's persecution of Nicene Christians
events.summary: After a staged conference at Carthage in February 484 between Nicene and Arian bishops, Huneric issued an edict on 25 February turning against the Nicenes the very penalties of Honorius's anti-Donatist laws. Some 46 bishops were exiled to Corsica to cut timber and over 300 to the south; Victor of Vita's History is the passionate testimony.

events.title: Acacian Schism begins
events.summary: Pope Felix III excommunicated Acacius of Constantinople on 28 July 484 for supporting the Henotikon and communing with Peter Mongus; Acacius struck Felix's name from the diptychs. The first great schism between Rome and Constantinople lasted 35 years, until 519.

events.title: Revolt of Illus and Leontius
events.summary: The Isaurian general Illus, after years as Zeno's indispensable minister and an assassination attempt instigated by Ariadne, rebelled in 484 and with the dowager Verina crowned the patrician Leontius emperor at Tarsus on 19 July. Defeated near Antioch by Zeno's army with Theodoric's Goths, Illus and Leontius held out in the Isaurian fortress of Papyrius for four years until betrayed and beheaded in 488.
events.locName: Tarsus and the fortress of Papyrius, Isauria

events.title: Death of Peroz against the Hephthalites
events.summary: Peroz I, who had already been captured once by the Hephthalites and ransomed, invaded their territory again in 484 and was killed with most of his army and several sons when his cavalry charged into a concealed trench. Procopius tells that he threw away his famous pearl earring as he fell. Persia paid tribute to the Hephthalites for years, a weakness that drove Kavad's demands for Roman gold.

battle.significance: Worst Sasanian defeat before the Arab conquest.

events.title: Battle of Soissons: Clovis defeats Syagrius
events.summary: Clovis, the young king of the Salian Franks of Tournai, defeated Syagrius, son of Aegidius and ruler of the last Roman enclave in northern Gaul, in 486 (or 487). Syagrius fled to Alaric II at Toulouse, who handed him over to be executed. Clovis made Soissons his base and absorbed the Roman administration of Belgica Secunda.

sides.strength: Salian Frankish warband with kinsman Ragnachar

battle.significance: Ended the last Roman political unit in northern Gaul and laid the foundation of the Frankish kingdom.

events.title: Odoacer destroys the Rugian kingdom
events.summary: In 487 Odoacer crossed the Danube against the Rugians of King Feletheus (Feva), whose son Fredericus had murdered his uncle. He captured Feletheus and Queen Giso, brought them to Italy and executed them. Fredericus fled to Theodoric, and in 488 Odoacer ordered the Roman population of Noricum evacuated to Italy.

events.title: Odoacer evacuates the Romans of Noricum
events.summary: After destroying the Rugian kingdom north of the Danube in 487 and capturing King Feletheus, Odoacer ordered the Roman provincials of Noricum Ripense to withdraw to Italy in 488. They carried with them the body of St Severinus, the holy man who had organised their defence, eventually enshrined at Castellum Lucullanum, where Romulus Augustulus lived.

events.title: Battle of the Isonzo
events.summary: After a winter march from Novae and a fight with the Gepids near Sirmium, Theodoric's Goths, perhaps 100,000 people with 20,000 or so warriors, entered Italy and on 28 August 489 forced the crossing of the Isonzo at the Pons Sontii against Odoacer's fortified camp.

sides.strength: perhaps 20,000 warriors with families and Rugian allies

battle.significance: Opened Italy to the Goths.

events.title: Battle of Verona (489)
events.summary: Theodoric defeated Odoacer again outside Verona on 30 September 489; Ennodius describes Theodoric's mother and sister watching. Odoacer fled to Ravenna, and Milan and Pavia submitted. Odoacer's general Tufa then defected to Theodoric, only to betray a Gothic force at Faventia.

sides.losses: heavy; many drowned in the Adige

battle.significance: Gave Theodoric the Po valley; Verona became one of his favourite residences, remembered as Dietrich von Bern in Germanic legend.

events.title: Zeno closes the School of the Persians at Edessa
events.summary: Zeno ordered the closure in 489 of the 'School of the Persians' at Edessa, a centre of Antiochene, Theodoran theology. Its teachers, led by Narsai who had already moved to Nisibis, re-established it across the frontier. The School of Nisibis became the intellectual centre of the Church of the East and transmitted Greek learning in Syriac.

events.title: Battle of the Adda
events.summary: Reinforced by Visigoths sent by Alaric II, Theodoric routed Odoacer on the river Adda on 11 August 490; Odoacer's magister militum Pierius was killed. Odoacer shut himself in Ravenna for a siege that lasted two and a half years.

battle.significance: Decided the war in the field.

events.title: Siege of Ravenna and murder of Odoacer
events.summary: Theodoric blockaded Ravenna from August 490; Odoacer's sortie at the Pineta on 10 July 491 failed. With a fleet closing the port at Classis from 492, famine forced a treaty on 25 February 493, mediated by Bishop John, for joint rule. Theodoric entered on 5 March and on 15 March killed Odoacer with his own hands at a banquet, reportedly remarking that the wretch had no bones in him. Odoacer's men were massacred.

battle.significance: Founded the Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy, which lasted until 553.

events.title: Accession of Anastasius I
events.summary: Zeno died on 9 April 491. The Senate and court left the choice to the empress Ariadne, who chose Anastasius, an elderly silentiarius (palace usher) from Dyrrachium known for piety and financial competence. Crowned on 11 April after swearing to uphold orthodoxy, he married Ariadne on 20 May. Zeno's brother Longinus and the Isaurian faction were expelled.

events.title: Battle of Cotyaeum: start of the Isaurian War
events.summary: The Isaurians expelled from the capital raised a huge army under Lingis and Longinus of Cardala and marched into Phrygia, where they were routed at Cotyaeum by John the Scythian and John the Hunchback. The war continued in the Taurus until 497-498, when the last strongholds fell and many Isaurians were deported to Thrace.

sides.strength: field army with Gothic, Hunnic and Bessian troops under John the Scythian and John the Hunchback

battle.significance: Broke Isaurian power, removing the faction that had dominated Constantinople under Zeno.

events.title: Baptism of Clovis
events.summary: Clovis was baptised at Reims by Bishop Remigius on a Christmas Day, with 3,000 warriors, choosing Nicene Catholicism rather than the Arian Christianity of the Goths, Burgundians and Vandals. 'Bow your head, proud Sicambrian; adore what you have burned and burn what you have adored.'

events.title: Battle of Tolbiac (Zülpich)
events.summary: According to Gregory of Tours, Clovis, facing defeat against the Alamanni, vowed to become a Christian if the God of his wife Clotilde gave him victory; the Alamannic king fell and his people submitted. Gregory sets the battle in Clovis's fifteenth year (496).

sides.strength: Frankish army, perhaps with Ripuarian Franks

battle.significance: Began the Frankish subjection of the Alamanni; in Gregory's narrative it is Clovis's 'Milvian Bridge'.

events.title: Deposition and restoration of Kavad I
events.summary: Kavad I, who backed the egalitarian preaching of Mazdak, was deposed by the nobles and priests in 496 and imprisoned in the 'Castle of Oblivion'. Escaping with his wife's help, he fled to the Hephthalites, married a Hephthalite princess and returned with an army in 498 or 499 to oust his brother Zamasp. Needing money to pay his allies, he demanded Roman subsidies and invaded in 502.

events.title: Anastasius recognises Theodoric
events.summary: After years of negotiation by the senator Festus, Anastasius in 497 or 498 returned to Theodoric the palace regalia (ornamenta palatii) that Odoacer had sent to Zeno in 476, acknowledging his rule in Italy. Theodoric ruled the Romans as a Roman official in form, and the Goths as their king; the consulship and Senate continued under him.

events.title: Anastasius abolishes the chrysargyron
events.summary: Anastasius abolished the collatio lustralis or chrysargyron, the five-yearly tax in gold and silver on merchants and craftsmen introduced by Constantine, and publicly burned its registers. Joshua the Stylite describes rejoicing across Edessa. He replaced the revenue from imperial estates managed by a new comes patrimonii.

events.title: Anastasius's copper coinage reform
events.summary: In 498, under the comes sacrarum largitionum John the Paphlagonian, Anastasius introduced large copper coins marked with their value in Greek numerals: the follis of 40 nummi (M), and half (K), quarter (I) and later pentanummium (E). It replaced the chaos of tiny nummi and gave the eastern economy a stable small change for over a century.

events.title: End of the Isaurian War
events.summary: The last Isaurian strongholds fell in 497-498; Longinus of Selinus and Indes were captured and paraded in chains in Constantinople and Longinus was tortured to death at Nicaea. Many Isaurians were resettled in Thrace. Anastasius commemorated the victory with a hymn sung in the Hippodrome.

events.title: Bulgars defeat the Illyrian army on the Tzurta
events.summary: In 499 Bulgars raiding Thrace annihilated an army of 15,000 under Aristus, magister militum per Illyricum, at the river Tzurta; Marcellinus Comes says more than 4,000 Romans died, including four named comites. It is one of the first recorded Bulgar victories over the empire and spurred Anastasius to build the Long Walls.

battle.significance: Prompted the Anastasian Wall.

events.title: Battle of Mount Badon
events.summary: Gildas, writing in the sixth century, refers to the siege of Mount Badon (obsessio Badonici montis) as the last great British victory over the Saxons, which brought a generation of peace, in the year of his own birth. The ninth-century Historia Brittonum makes it the twelfth battle of Arthur.
events.locName: Mons Badonicus (unidentified; Bath is one candidate)

battle.significance: Gildas presents it as halting Saxon expansion for some decades, consistent with a pause in archaeological expansion in the early sixth century.

events.title: Battle of Dijon
events.summary: Allied with Godegisel, who betrayed his brother, Clovis defeated the Burgundian king Gundobad near Dijon on the Ouche in 500. Gundobad fled to Avignon and survived a siege by agreeing to pay tribute, then in 501 recovered and killed Godegisel at Vienne. The Burgundian kingdom survived another three decades.

battle.significance: Burgundy made tributary for a time.

events.title: The Edictum Theoderici
events.summary: A collection of 154 short articles applying Roman law, much of it drawn from the Theodosian Code and Pauli Sententiae, to Goths and Romans alike. It survives only in Pierre Pithou's edition of 1579, the manuscripts having been lost, and is traditionally attributed to Theodoric the Great around 500-512.

events.title: Siege of Amida
events.summary: Kavad I, needing money to pay the Hephthalites and refused subsidies by Anastasius, invaded and besieged Amida from 5 October 502. After three months the Persians entered on the night of 10/11 January 503 through a tower guarded by monks who had drunk too much. The massacre and enslavement were vast; Pseudo-Joshua says 80,000 bodies were carried out. The Romans bought the city back in 505.

sides.losses: tens of thousands killed or enslaved

sides.strength: Persian royal army with Arab and Hephthalite contingents

battle.significance: Opened the first major Roman-Persian war in over sixty years and led to the building of Dara.

events.title: The Long Walls of Thrace
events.summary: Anastasius built or rebuilt a wall some 56 km long from the Black Sea to Selymbria on the Propontis, about 65 km west of Constantinople, to protect the capital's hinterland against Bulgars, Slavs and later Avars. It proved hard to man and was often breached.

events.title: Foundation of Dara (Anastasiopolis)
events.summary: After the war of 502-506 exposed the lack of a Roman base near Nisibis, Anastasius built the fortress-city of Dara, renamed Anastasiopolis, only 18 km from Nisibis, in about 505-507, in defiance of the treaty of 422. It became the seat of the dux of Mesopotamia and the hinge of every later war on that front.

events.title: Theodoric's palace church: Sant'Apollinare Nuovo
events.summary: Theodoric built an Arian palace church dedicated to Christ the Redeemer in Ravenna around 505, with mosaics of the life of Christ and a depiction of his palace and Classe. After the reconquest Archbishop Agnellus rededicated it to St Martin (c. 561) and replaced the Gothic court figures with processions of martyrs and virgins; hands of the erased figures still show on the palace columns.

events.title: Breviary of Alaric (Lex Romana Visigothorum)
events.summary: Promulgated by Alaric II at Aire-sur-l'Adour on 2 February 506 after review by a council of bishops and provincials, this abridgement of the Theodosian Code, post-Theodosian Novels, the Sentences of Paul, Gaius's Institutes and other texts, with explanatory interpretationes, became the main vehicle of Roman law in the early medieval West.

events.title: Council of Agde
events.summary: In September 506 the Arian king Alaric II allowed 35 Catholic bishops of his kingdom to meet at Agde under Caesarius of Arles, months after promulgating the Breviary. Its 48 canons on clerical discipline, property and marriage became standard in Gallic church law. Vouillé followed a year later.

events.title: Battle of Vouillé
events.summary: In spring 507 Clovis, with Burgundian allies and the blessing of the Gallo-Roman bishops, attacked the Arian Visigoths and defeated them at the Campus Vogladensis near Poitiers; Clovis is said to have killed Alaric II with his own hand. The Visigoths lost almost all of Gaul except Septimania, which Theodoric's Ostrogoths secured, and their kingdom's centre shifted to Spain.

sides.strength: Visigothic army with Gallo-Roman levies (including Arvernians under Sidonius's son Apollinaris)

battle.significance: Made the Franks the dominant power in Gaul and pushed the Visigoths into Spain; one of the formative battles of medieval Europe.

events.title: Clovis receives the consulship from Anastasius
events.summary: At Tours in 508 Clovis received letters from Anastasius granting him the consulship (probably honorary). Gregory says he put on a purple tunic and chlamys and a diadem in the church of St Martin and rode to the cathedral scattering coins, and was hailed as consul and Augustus. He then made Paris his seat.

events.title: Ostrogoths relieve Arles
events.summary: After Vouillé, Franks and Burgundians besieged Arles in 507-508; Bishop Caesarius was suspected of treason. Theodoric sent an army under Ibba and Tuluin that lifted the siege; Jordanes claims 30,000 Franks died. Provence became an Ostrogothic province governed by a praetorian prefect of the Gauls, and Theodoric saved Septimania for the Visigoths.

battle.significance: Created Ostrogothic Provence and checked Clovis.

events.title: Pactus Legis Salicae
events.summary: Issued under Clovis around 507-511, the Salic Law set out in 65 titles the compensations (wergild) for crimes among the Franks: 200 solidi for killing a free Frank, 100 for a Roman landowner, 600 for a royal follower. Its Malberg glosses preserve Frankish legal words. A clause on inheritance of land was later invoked to bar women from the French throne.

events.title: Anastasius deposes Patriarch Macedonius II
events.summary: Patriarch Macedonius II of Constantinople, who refused to anathematise Chalcedon, was deposed and exiled in August 511 after being accused of heresy and immorality; Anastasius installed Timothy I. The crowds of the capital, largely Chalcedonian, never forgave the emperor and rioted over the Trisagion in 512.

events.title: Death of Clovis; Council of Orléans
events.summary: Clovis died in Paris on 27 November 511, months after presiding over the Council of Orléans, where 32 bishops regulated church asylum, ordination and church property in the new Frankish kingdom. His kingdom was divided among his four sons, setting the pattern of Merovingian partitions. The Pactus Legis Salicae was probably issued in his last years.

events.title: Theodoric becomes regent of the Visigoths
events.summary: After Ibba's army drove out the Visigothic king Gesalec in 511, Theodoric ruled the Visigothic kingdom as guardian of his grandson Amalaric, Alaric II's son, until 526, governing through the Ostrogoth Theudis and sending Visigothic treasure to Ravenna. For fifteen years one king ruled from the Danube to the Atlantic.

events.title: Trisagion riots in Constantinople
events.summary: Anastasius's addition to the liturgy of the anti-Chalcedonian phrase 'who was crucified for us' to the Trisagion triggered riots in November 512; crowds burned houses and acclaimed the general Areobindus emperor. Anastasius appeared in the Hippodrome without his diadem and offered to abdicate; the crowd relented and he later punished the leaders.

events.title: Severus becomes patriarch of Antioch
events.summary: In November 512, after a synod at Sidon and the deposition of Flavian II, Anastasius made the brilliant anti-Chalcedonian monk and former Beirut law student Severus patriarch of Antioch. His theology defined the miaphysite position; deposed by Justin I in 518, he fled to Egypt and remained the movement's leading thinker.

events.title: Vitalian routs Hypatius and captures him
events.summary: In the first year of his rebellion, Vitalian defeated the army of Anastasius's nephew Hypatius near Odessus on the Black Sea coast and captured him; Hypatius was later ransomed. The defeat forced Anastasius to negotiate and promise a church council, which he never honoured.

battle.significance: Strengthened Vitalian's position.

events.title: Defeat of Vitalian's fleet before Constantinople
events.summary: The Thracian federate commander Vitalian, demanding the restoration of Chalcedonian bishops and federate pay, marched on Constantinople three times between 513 and 515. In 515 his fleet was destroyed in the Bosporus near Sosthenion by Marinus the Syrian, using a sulphur-based incendiary supplied, Malalas says, by the Athenian philosopher Proclus. Vitalian fled.

sides.strength: rebel fleet of perhaps 200 ships with federate army

battle.significance: Ended Vitalian's rebellion militarily, though he returned to power under Justin I.

events.title: The Burgundian Liber Constitutionum
events.summary: Promulgated by King Sigismund at Lyon on 29 March 517, the Liber Constitutionum (Lex Gundobada) compiled laws of his father Gundobad regulating relations between Burgundians and Romans, including the division of estates with 'guests' (hospites). A separate Lex Romana Burgundionum applied Roman law to the Roman population.

events.title: Accession of Justin I
events.summary: Anastasius died on 9 July 518 aged about 88 with no designated heir. Justin, the elderly Thracian commander of the excubitors, reportedly given money by the eunuch Amantius to bribe the guards for another candidate, used it for himself and was crowned on 10 July. A Chalcedonian, he reconciled with Rome. His nephew and adopted son Justinian was the power behind him.

events.title: End of the Acacian Schism
events.summary: On 28 March 519 Patriarch John II signed the Libellus of Pope Hormisdas, accepting Chalcedon and striking Acacius, Zeno and Anastasius from the diptychs. Anti-Chalcedonian bishops, including Severus of Antioch, were expelled, driving the miaphysite movement toward a separate hierarchy.

events.title: Murder of Vitalian
events.summary: Vitalian, rehabilitated by Justin I as magister militum praesentalis and consul for 520, was stabbed to death in the palace in July 520 with two attendants. Procopius and others blame Justinian, removing a rival for the succession.

events.title: Mausoleum of Theodoric
events.summary: Built c. 520 outside Ravenna's walls, Theodoric's two-storey decagonal tomb of Istrian limestone is roofed by a single monolith about 10 m across and weighing some 230 tonnes, with twelve pierced handles used to set it in place. The Anonymus Valesianus says Theodoric had a great stone found to cover it. His porphyry bathtub-sarcophagus now stands inside, empty.

events.title: Execution of Boethius
