events.summary: Boethius, magister officiorum and the West's most learned man, defended the senator Albinus against a charge of treasonable correspondence with Constantinople and was himself convicted. Imprisoned near Pavia, he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, then was tortured and clubbed to death in 524 (or 525). His father-in-law Symmachus was executed soon after, and Pope John I died in Theodoric's prison in 526.

events.title: Anicia Juliana builds St Polyeuktos
events.summary: Anicia Juliana, great-granddaughter of Valentinian III and daughter of the emperor Olybrius, built the church of St Polyeuktos in Constantinople in 524-527, then the largest church in the city, with an epigram claiming it surpassed Solomon's Temple and with dimensions apparently modelled on it. Excavated in the 1960s, it is often read as an aristocratic challenge that Justinian answered with Hagia Sophia.

events.title: Revolt and flight of Gourgenes of Iberia
events.summary: When Kavad tried to impose Zoroastrian rites, including exposure of the dead, on Christian Iberia, King Gourgenes appealed to Justin I, who sent only a small force. Gourgenes and his nobles fled to Lazica and then Constantinople. The episode opened the Iberian war of 526-532.

events.title: Boethius writes the Consolation of Philosophy
events.summary: Condemned without trial for treason, Boethius wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison near Pavia in 524, a dialogue in alternating prose and verse in which Lady Philosophy leads him from self-pity to the knowledge of providence and the true good. Translated by Alfred the Great, Chaucer and Elizabeth I, it was among the most read books of the Middle Ages.

events.title: Aksumite invasion of Himyar
events.summary: After the Jewish Himyarite king Yusuf As'ar Yath'ar (Dhu Nuwas) massacred the Christians of Najran in 523, Kaleb Ella Asbeha of Aksum, encouraged by Justin I and supplied with Roman ships from Egyptian and Red Sea ports, invaded South Arabia around 525 and destroyed him, installing a Christian client regime.

events.title: Dionysius Exiguus introduces the Anno Domini era
events.summary: Asked by Pope John I to calculate Easter dates, the Scythian monk Dionysius Exiguus in Rome produced in 525 a table for 532-626 in which he replaced Diocletian's era, named after a persecutor, with years counted from the Incarnation. Bede's use of the system in the eighth century spread the Anno Domini count across the Latin West.

events.title: Execution of Symmachus
events.summary: Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, head of the Senate, historian and Boethius's father-in-law and guardian, was taken to Ravenna and executed in 525 or 526, fearing, says the Anonymus Valesianus, that grief for Boethius would drive him to plot. Procopius links Theodoric's remorse for these deaths to his own end.

events.title: Kavad's request that Justin adopt Khosrow
events.summary: Seeking to secure his favourite son's succession, Kavad asked Justin I around 525 to adopt Khosrow. The quaestor Proclus warned that adoption could give Khosrow a claim to the Roman empire, and Justin offered only adoption 'by arms', as among barbarians. The insult wrecked talks at the frontier, the Persian negotiator Seoses was executed, and war followed.

events.title: Priscian's Institutes of Grammar
events.summary: Priscian of Caesarea in Mauretania, teaching Latin in Constantinople, wrote the Institutiones Grammaticae in 18 books around 500-526, the largest Latin grammar from antiquity, quoting hundreds of passages from classical authors. A copy was made by the palace scribe Flavius Theodorus in 526-527; it became the standard medieval grammar.

events.title: Pope John I sent to Constantinople
events.summary: Theodoric forced Pope John I to lead an embassy to Justin I in 525-526 to obtain the restoration of churches confiscated from Arians in the East. John was received with unprecedented honours and celebrated Easter in Hagia Sophia, but secured only part of his brief. On his return Theodoric imprisoned him at Ravenna, where he died on 18 May 526.

events.title: Earthquake and fire of Antioch
events.summary: An earthquake struck Antioch around midday on 29 May 526, during the festival of the Ascension when the city was full of visitors; fire followed and burned for days. Malalas, a native, gives 250,000 dead, including Patriarch Euphrasius. Another quake in 528 completed the ruin; the city was renamed Theoupolis, 'City of God'.

events.title: Death of Theodoric the Great
events.summary: Theodoric died at Ravenna on 30 August 526, probably of dysentery; Procopius says he was haunted by a fish head on his table resembling the face of Symmachus. His ten-year-old grandson Athalaric succeeded under the regency of his daughter Amalasuntha. He was buried in the mausoleum he had built, capped by a single block of Istrian limestone some 230 tonnes in weight.

events.title: Accession of Justinian I
events.summary: Crowned co-emperor with Theodora on 1 April 527, Justinian became sole ruler when Justin died on 1 August 527. He reigned for 38 years, undertaking the reconquest of Africa, Italy and part of Spain, the codification of Roman law, the rebuilding of Hagia Sophia and a sustained programme of religious unification, while surviving the Nika revolt and the first pandemic of plague.

events.title: Church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus
events.summary: Built by Justinian and Theodora c. 527-536 beside the palace of Hormisdas, the octagon-in-a-square church of Sergius and Bacchus, with its carved inscription praising 'God-crowned Theodora', anticipated Hagia Sophia's domed central plan. It survives as the Küçük Ayasofya mosque.

events.title: Battle of Mindouos
events.summary: Belisarius, newly dux of Mesopotamia, tried to build a fort at Mindouos (Thannuris?) near Nisibis; a Persian army attacked the work and routed the Roman force. Several commanders were captured. The defeat preceded his appointment as magister militum per Orientem.

battle.significance: Belisarius's first recorded command ended in defeat.

events.title: Massacre of the Mazdakites
events.summary: Late in Kavad's reign, around 528, Prince Khosrow, the designated heir, invited Mazdak and his followers to a debate or banquet and had them massacred; tradition says they were buried alive head down. The suppression of the Mazdakite movement, which had preached communal property and women, was followed by Khosrow's reconstruction of noble estates and taxation.

events.title: First Codex Justinianus
events.summary: Promulgated on 7 April 529 by the constitution Summa rei publicae, the first Codex Justinianus combined the Gregorian, Hermogenian and Theodosian codes and later constitutions into a single code in 12 books, prepared in just 14 months by a commission including John the Cappadocian and Tribonian. It does not survive; we have only the revised edition of 534.

events.title: Justinian's ban on pagan teaching and the end of the Athenian Academy
events.summary: Malalas records that in 529 Justinian sent an order to Athens forbidding anyone to teach philosophy or interpret law there; laws in the Codex barred pagans from teaching. In 531/532 seven Neoplatonists including Damascius and Simplicius went to the court of Khosrow I, returning after the peace of 532 guaranteed their safety.

events.title: Benedict founds Monte Cassino
events.summary: Benedict of Nursia, leaving his monasteries at Subiaco, founded a community on the summit of Monte Cassino above Casinum, on the site of a temple of Apollo, traditionally in 529. His Rule, written there, became the foundation of western monasticism.

events.title: Samaritan revolt of Julian ben Sabar
events.summary: Provoked by anti-heretical laws, Samaritans in Palestine proclaimed Julian ben Sabar king, sacked Neapolis and killed its bishop, and held chariot races there. The revolt was crushed with the help of Ghassanid Arab allies; Malalas says 20,000 Samaritans were killed and 20,000 sold to Persia and India. Justinian closed synagogues and the Mount Gerizim cult.

events.title: Justinian makes al-Harith supreme phylarch
events.summary: After the Lakhmid al-Mundhir III raided as far as Antioch, Justinian conferred on al-Harith ibn Jabala of the Ghassanid (Jafnid) family 'the dignity of king' over the Arab federates of the eastern provinces around 529. The Ghassanids became Rome's principal desert shield and, as Miaphysites, patrons of the anti-Chalcedonian church.

events.title: Battle of Dara
events.summary: Before the walls of Dara, Belisarius and Hermogenes, with 25,000 men, met a Persian army of 40,000 to 50,000 under Firuz (Perozes). Belisarius dug a system of ditches with gaps and angles, placed his infantry behind them and his Hunnic and Herul cavalry at the corners. On the second day a flank attack by Herul cavalry hidden behind a hill and a counter-charge by Sunicas and Aigan's Huns broke the Persian wings; 5,000 Persians died.

sides.strength: 25,000 (Procopius), incl. Huns under Sunicas and Aigan and Heruli under Pharas
40,000 then reinforced to 50,000 (Procopius); commander Firuz the mirranes, with Immortals

battle.significance: Restored Roman confidence after a century of caution on the eastern front and made Belisarius the empire's leading general.

events.title: Gelimer deposes Hilderic
events.summary: Hilderic, grandson of Valentinian III through Eudocia, had ended persecution of Catholics and favoured Justinian. In June 530 his cousin Gelimer, leader of the Vandal war party after a defeat by the Moors, deposed and imprisoned him. Justinian's demand for Hilderic's restoration was rejected, giving the pretext for the Vandal war.

events.title: Battle of Satala
events.summary: In Armenia in summer 530, Sittas and Dorotheus with some 15,000 men defeated a Persian army of 30,000 under Mihr-Mihroe near Satala. Sittas's surprise attack with 1,000 horsemen from behind a hill threw the Persians into confusion; the Romans then took the Persarmenian forts of Bolum and Pharangium and its gold mines.

battle.significance: Secured the Armenian front in the same season as Dara.

events.title: Battle of Callinicum
events.summary: A Persian and Lakhmid army under Azarethes and al-Mundhir III raided along the Euphrates into Commagene. Belisarius shadowed them until, under pressure from his troops, he gave battle on Easter Saturday, 19 April 531, by the Euphrates opposite Callinicum. The Roman right, held by Ghassanid allies under al-Harith, collapsed; Belisarius dismounted and fought on foot with the infantry, their backs to the river, and held until nightfall. Both sides lost heavily.

sides.strength: 15,000 Persian cavalry and Lakhmid Arabs under Azarethes and al-Mundhir
sides.losses: heavy; Azarethes disgraced by Kavad for losing so many men

battle.significance: Tactically a Persian win but strategically barren; Belisarius was recalled and an inquiry held.

events.title: Death of Kavad; accession of Khosrow I
events.summary: Kavad I died on 13 September 531. His favoured younger son Khosrow I Anushirvan ('of the immortal soul') succeeded over his elder brothers, crushed the Mazdakite movement and launched fiscal and military reforms: a fixed land tax by survey, a poll tax, four regional commanders (spahbeds) and a salaried cavalry of lesser nobility (dehqans).

events.title: The Fifty Decisions
events.summary: In 530-531, in preparation for the Digest, Justinian issued a series of constitutions, the Quinquaginta decisiones, settling long-standing controversies among the classical jurists, for instance on legacies and freeing slaves. They were later absorbed into the second edition of the Code in 534.

events.title: Nika riots
events.summary: After a botched execution left a Blue and a Green condemned man alive under the protection of monks, the two circus factions united on 13 January 532 under the cry 'Nika!' ('Conquer!'), burned the city centre including Hagia Sophia and the Chalke gate, and forced Justinian to dismiss John the Cappadocian, Tribonian and the urban prefect Eudaemon. On 18 January they crowned Hypatius, nephew of Anastasius, in the Hippodrome.

sides.strength: Belisarius's bucellarii and Gothic and Herul troops under Mundus
crowd of Blue and Green partisans with senatorial backers

battle.significance: Secured Justinian's throne and freed his hand for the codification, the rebuilding of the capital and the Vandal war.

events.title: Building of Hagia Sophia
events.summary: Begun on 23 February 532, forty days after the Nika riots destroyed the Theodosian basilica, Justinian's Great Church was designed by the mathematician Anthemius of Tralles and the engineer Isidore of Miletus and dedicated on 27 December 537. Its dome, about 31 m across, appeared, Procopius said, to hang from heaven by a golden chain.

events.title: The 'Eternal Peace' with Persia
events.summary: Khosrow I and Justinian agreed a peace without time limit: Rome paid 110 centenaria (11,000 lbs of gold) as a lump sum toward the defence of the Caucasus passes, moved the dux of Mesopotamia from Dara to Constantina, and the two sides returned captured forts in Lazica and Persarmenia. It freed Justinian's armies for the West and lasted eight years.

events.title: The Basilica Cistern
events.summary: After the Nika riots Justinian rebuilt the Stoa Basilica and beneath it constructed a vast underground cistern, 138 by 65 m, its roof carried by 336 columns, many reused, two resting on Medusa heads. It held some 80,000 cubic metres of water fed by the Valens aqueduct for the Great Palace and the Hagia Sophia quarter.

events.title: Romanos the Melode and the kontakion
events.summary: Romanos, a Syrian deacon from Emesa serving at the church of the Theotokos in Kyros in Constantinople, composed some 80 surviving kontakia, long metrical sermons sung with refrains. His hymn On Earthquakes and Fires reflects the Nika riot and the rebuilding of Hagia Sophia and praises Justinian; tradition credits him with a thousand hymns.

events.title: Justinian's Theopaschite edict
events.summary: On 15 March 533 Justinian issued an edict affirming that 'one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh', a formula championed by Scythian monks that he hoped would reconcile Chalcedonians and Miaphysites. Pope John II accepted it in 534; it was a first step in the policy that led to the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

events.title: Belisarius's expedition sails for Africa
events.summary: Using Gelimer's deposition of the pro-Roman Hilderic (530) as pretext, and against the advice of John the Cappadocian, Justinian sent Belisarius in June 533 with 10,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry (including 1,500 bucellarii, 600 Huns and 400 Heruli), 500 transports with 30,000 sailors and 92 dromons. Procopius sailed with him. A revolt in Sardinia and another in Tripolitania, encouraged by Constantinople, drew off Vandal forces.

events.title: Battle of Ad Decimum
events.summary: Landing at Caput Vada and marching up the coast, Belisarius approached Carthage. Gelimer planned a three-way trap at the tenth milestone (Ad Decimum): his brother Ammatas from Carthage, his nephew Gibamund from the west, and himself from the rear. The parts arrived out of time. Ammatas was killed, Gibamund's 2,000 were destroyed by 600 Huns at Pedion Halon, and Gelimer, after scattering the Roman vanguard, stopped to mourn his brother. Belisarius rallied and routed him.
events.locName: Ad Decimum, 10 miles south-west of Carthage

sides.strength: c. 15,000 with allied Huns and Heruli

battle.significance: Opened Carthage to Belisarius, who entered on 15 September and dined on Gelimer's prepared meal in the palace.

events.title: Battle of Tricamarum
events.summary: Reinforced by his brother Tzazon's army returning from Sardinia, Gelimer advanced on Carthage. At Tricamarum, about 30 km west, in mid-December 533, Roman cavalry under John the Armenian charged three times across a stream and killed Tzazon; the Vandal line collapsed. Procopius counts fewer than 50 Roman and about 800 Vandal dead. Gelimer fled, and the Roman troops lost all discipline plundering the Vandal camp.

battle.significance: Destroyed the Vandal kingdom after a century; Africa was reorganised as a praetorian prefecture in April 534.

events.title: Publication of the Digest and Institutes
events.summary: The Digest (Pandects), commissioned on 15 December 530 by the constitution Deo auctore and published on 16 December 533 (constitution Tanta), distilled the writings of classical jurists, chiefly Ulpian, Paul and Papinian, into 50 books. Tribonian's commission reduced some 2,000 books and 3 million lines to about 150,000. The Institutes, a textbook for students, were published on 21 November 533; both took force on 30 December 533.

events.title: Surrender of Gelimer on Mount Papua
events.summary: Besieged through the winter by the Herul Pharas in a Moorish hill town on Mount Papua, Gelimer asked for a lyre to sing a lament he had composed on his misfortunes, a sponge for his eyes and a loaf of bread. He surrendered in March 534, laughing hysterically when brought before Belisarius.

events.title: Codex Justinianus, second edition
events.summary: The Codex repetitae praelectionis, promulgated on 16 November 534 (constitution Cordi), replaced the 529 edition with an updated code in 12 books incorporating the Fifty Decisions and later laws. Justinian's subsequent legislation, mostly in Greek, survives as the Novels; together the four parts were later called the Corpus Iuris Civilis, a name first used by Dionysius Gothofredus in 1583.

events.title: Triumph of Belisarius
events.summary: Belisarius celebrated a triumph in Constantinople in 534, walking rather than riding, the first triumph by a private citizen since Cornelius Balbus in 19 BC. Gelimer and Vandal nobles were paraded with the treasure of Carthage, including the Temple vessels of Jerusalem, which Justinian sent to churches in Jerusalem. Before the emperor, Gelimer kept repeating 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity'. Belisarius was consul for 535.

events.title: Frankish conquest of the Burgundian kingdom
events.summary: After the Burgundian king Godomar beat the Franks at Vézeronce in 524, killing Clovis's son Chlodomer, the Franks returned under Childebert and Chlothar, defeated Godomar near Autun in 532 and partitioned his kingdom in 534. The Franks now ruled almost all of Gaul; Provence followed in 537, ceded by Witiges.

sides.strength: armies of Childebert I and Chlothar I

battle.significance: Ended the last independent Burgundian kingdom and made the Franks neighbours of Ostrogothic Italy at a critical moment.

events.title: Battle of Mammes
events.summary: Solomon, left in command of Africa after Belisarius's departure, attacked a Moorish army in Byzacena at Mammes in 534. The Moors formed a circle of camels twelve deep to protect their women and children; Solomon's dismounted men broke into the ring and Procopius claims 10,000 Moors were killed.

battle.significance: First test of Roman Africa against the Moors.

events.title: Murder of Amalasuntha
events.summary: After her son Athalaric drank himself to death in 534, Amalasuntha made her cousin Theodahad co-ruler. He confined her on the island of Martana in Lake Bolsena, where relatives of Gothic nobles she had executed strangled her in her bath, probably on 30 April 535. Justinian, with whom she had been negotiating a flight to Constantinople, used her murder as the casus belli for the Gothic War.

events.title: Belisarius conquers Sicily
events.summary: Sent with only 7,500 men, Belisarius took Sicily in 535 with little resistance except at Panormus, where he hoisted archers in boats to the mastheads of his ships to shoot over the walls. He entered Syracuse on 31 December 535, the last day of his consulship, scattering gold coins to the crowd.

events.title: Battle of Mount Bourgaon
events.summary: In 535 the Moors of Byzacena regrouped on Mount Bourgaon. Solomon sent a force under Theodorus to climb the far side by night; attacked from above, the Moors fled down the slopes into the main Roman army. Procopius claims 50,000 Moors died without a Roman loss, an obvious exaggeration.

battle.significance: Pacified Byzacena until the mutiny of 536.

events.title: Siege and sack of Naples
events.summary: Belisarius crossed to Italy in spring 536 and besieged Naples, held by a Gothic garrison and its pro-Gothic citizens, including the Jewish community, for some twenty days. An Isaurian soldier found a dry aqueduct channel; 400 men crept through it, and the city was taken and sacked in November 536.

battle.significance: The Goths deposed Theodahad for inaction and elected Witiges; Rome opened its gates to Belisarius on 9 December 536.

events.title: Witiges elected king; Theodahad killed
events.summary: Disgusted with Theodahad's inaction as Belisarius took Naples, the Gothic army raised the veteran officer Witiges on a shield at Regata near Terracina in November 536. Theodahad fled toward Ravenna and was killed on the road by a personal enemy. Witiges married Amalasuntha's daughter Matasuntha to gain Amal legitimacy.

events.title: The 'year without summer' of 536
events.summary: Procopius records that throughout 536 'the sun gave forth its light without brightness, like the moon'; Cassiodorus in Italy describes a bluish sun, summer frosts and failed harvests; John Lydus and Syriac chroniclers concur. Ice cores and tree rings now show major volcanic eruptions in 536 and 539/540, triggering the coldest decade in two millennia.

events.title: Military mutiny in Africa under Stotzas
events.summary: At Easter 536 Roman troops in Africa, many married to Vandal widows who claimed their estates and Arian soldiers denied baptism for their children, mutinied against Solomon and chose the guardsman Stotzas as leader. Belisarius hurried from Sicily and scattered them at Membresa; Justinian's cousin Germanus won back most of the mutineers with pay and defeated Stotzas at Scalae Veteres in 537.

events.title: Pope Agapetus deposes Anthimus; Synod of 536
events.summary: Sent by Theodahad to avert war, Pope Agapetus arrived in Constantinople in February 536 and persuaded Justinian, over Theodora's objections, to depose the patriarch Anthimus as a crypto-Miaphysite. Agapetus consecrated Menas and died in the capital on 22 April. A synod in May-June 536 condemned Anthimus and Severus of Antioch, whose books Justinian ordered burned.

events.title: Witiges besieges Rome
events.summary: From March 537 to March 538 Witiges besieged Belisarius's 5,000 men in Rome with an army Procopius puts at 150,000. The Goths cut all fourteen aqueducts, ending Rome's baths and forcing the use of floating mills on the Tiber. Belisarius beat off a general assault on the Salarian and Praenestine gates, defenders on Hadrian's mausoleum hurled its statues on the attackers, and Roman horse-archers bled the Goths in repeated sorties. Witiges withdrew after a year and nine days.

sides.strength: c. 5,000, later reinforced by 1,600 Huns, Slavs and Antae and further troops

sides.losses: heavy from sorties, disease and famine

battle.significance: The decisive phase of the first Gothic war; it proved the superiority of Roman horse-archers over Gothic cavalry but devastated the city.

events.title: Belisarius deposes Pope Silverius
events.summary: During the siege of Rome, Pope Silverius was accused of offering to open the Asinarian Gate to the Goths. In March 537 Belisarius and Antonina had him stripped of his pallium and replaced by the deacon Vigilius, Theodora's candidate. Silverius died in exile on the island of Palmaria later that year.

events.title: Battle of Scalae Veteres
events.summary: Justinian's cousin Germanus, sent to deal with the mutiny of Stotzas in Africa, won back much of the army by paying arrears and in spring 537 defeated the mutineers and their Moorish allies at Scalae Veteres in Numidia. Stotzas fled to Mauretania.

battle.significance: Ended the great African mutiny.

events.title: Siege and destruction of Milan
events.summary: Milan's archbishop Datius invited the Romans in 538, and Belisarius sent 1,000 men under Mundilas. Goths under Uraias, reinforced by 10,000 Burgundians sent by the Frankish king Theudebert, besieged the city. The rivalry between Belisarius and Narses delayed relief; the garrison surrendered in early 539 and Procopius says 300,000 men of the city were massacred and the women given to the Burgundians.

battle.significance: The worst atrocity of the war; it led Justinian to recall Narses and restore Belisarius's sole command.

events.title: Cassiodorus publishes the Variae
events.summary: Around 537-538, as the Gothic War raged, the praetorian prefect Cassiodorus published the Variae, 468 official letters and formulae he had drafted for Theodoric and his successors, in 12 books. They are the richest picture of late Roman administration in the post-imperial West, from aqueduct maintenance to the appointment of officials. He later founded the monastery of Vivarium in Calabria, a centre of manuscript copying.

events.title: Siege of Ariminum
events.summary: John, nephew of Vitalian, seized Ariminum against Belisarius's orders in 538, drawing Witiges away from Rome. Besieged, he refused to withdraw; the newly arrived Narses persuaded Belisarius to relieve him and the Goths fled at the sight of the converging armies. The episode began the quarrel between Narses and Belisarius.

battle.significance: Divided the Roman command.

events.title: Belisarius takes Ravenna
events.summary: After taking Fiesole and Auximum, Belisarius blockaded Witiges in Ravenna in late 539; a fire destroyed the Gothic grain stores. The Goths offered to make Belisarius emperor of the West. He feigned acceptance, entered Ravenna in May 540 and took Witiges, his wife Matasuntha and the royal treasure to Constantinople, where Witiges became a patrician.

battle.significance: Apparently ended the war; but Justinian, alarmed by Persia and suspicious of Belisarius, recalled him before the north was secured, and the Goths rallied under Ildibad and Totila.

events.title: Siege of Auximum
events.summary: Belisarius besieged the strongly sited Gothic garrison of Auximum (Osimo) in the Marche for some seven months in 539, fouling its only water cistern with corpses and quicklime. The garrison surrendered late in the year and many enrolled in the Roman army, opening the road to Ravenna.

battle.significance: Cleared the approach to Ravenna.

events.title: Theudebert invades Italy
events.summary: In 539 the Frankish king Theudebert I, courted by both sides, crossed the Alps with an army Procopius numbers at 100,000, slaughtered the Goths at the bridge of Ticinum and then the Romans, and plundered Liguria until dysentery killed a third of his men. He later struck gold coins in his own name, an affront Procopius noted.

events.title: Khosrow I sacks Antioch
events.summary: Encouraged by Witiges's envoys and alarmed by Roman success, Khosrow I broke the Eternal Peace in spring 540, burned Sura, ransomed Hierapolis and Beroea, and took Antioch in June after its 6,000 troops fled. The city was looted and burned, its population deported to a new city near Ctesiphon, Weh Antiok Khosrow ('Better than Antioch, Khosrow built this'), with its own hippodrome.

sides.strength: 6,000 soldiers sent under Theoctistus and Molatzes, plus circus faction youths
sides.losses: city taken; many civilians killed or deported

battle.significance: The worst humiliation of Justinian's reign; it began twenty years of war and showed Persia could strike the heart of Roman Syria.

events.title: The Rule of Saint Benedict
events.summary: Around 540 Benedict of Nursia composed at Monte Cassino a Rule in 73 chapters, drawing heavily on the anonymous Rule of the Master, that organised monks' lives under an abbot around the divine office, manual labour and reading, with moderation in food and sleep. Promoted by the Carolingians, it became the standard rule of western monasticism.

events.title: Gildas's On the Ruin of Britain
events.summary: Written in Britain probably in the 530s or 540s, Gildas's De Excidio Britanniae denounces five British kings and the clergy as sinners whose vices invited the Saxon conquest. Its historical prologue, with the 'groans of the Britons', the 'proud tyrant' who invited the Saxons and the victory at Mount Badon, is the only British narrative of the fifth century.

events.title: Outbreak of the Justinianic Plague
events.summary: Bubonic plague appeared at Pelusium in Egypt in July 541, spread along shipping routes and reached Constantinople in spring 542, where Procopius says it killed 5,000 and then 10,000 or more a day for four months. Justinian himself caught it and recovered. Recurring waves struck the Mediterranean every 10-20 years until about 750.

events.title: Last ordinary consul: Basilius
events.summary: Anicius Faustus Albinus Basilius, consul in 541, was the last private citizen to hold the ordinary consulship, an office dating from 509 BC. Justinian let it lapse, partly because of its ruinous cost in games and largesse; thereafter the title was absorbed into the emperor's regalia. The West's last consul had been Paulinus in 534.

events.title: Totila becomes king of the Goths
events.summary: After the murders of Ildibad and Eraric, the Goths in the north chose Baduila, known in Greek sources as Totila, nephew of Ildibad, in autumn 541. He won over peasants and slaves by targeting senatorial landlords and treating captured Roman soldiers well, and in five years undid most of Belisarius's conquest.

events.title: Khosrow takes Petra: start of the Lazic War
events.summary: The Lazi, resenting the Roman trade monopoly imposed by the general John Tzibus from the new fortress of Petra, invited Khosrow I, who marched into Lazica in 541 and took Petra, giving Persia a foothold on the Black Sea. Twenty years of war in the mountains of western Georgia followed.

sides.strength: garrison under John Tzibus, who was killed
Persian royal army with Lazic support

battle.significance: Opened the Lazic War and raised Roman fears of a Persian fleet on the Black Sea.

events.title: Battle of Faventia
events.summary: Eleven Roman generals with 12,000 men, lacking a commander-in-chief after Belisarius's recall, failed to take Verona and were defeated by Totila's 5,000 near Faventia (Faenza) in spring 542, when a flank attack by 300 Gothic horsemen panicked them. Totila then defeated another army at Mucellium and marched south.

battle.significance: Showed the cost of divided command and let Totila retake central and southern Italy.

events.title: Jacob Baradaeus builds the miaphysite hierarchy
events.summary: Consecrated bishop of Edessa around 542 at the request of the Ghassanid king al-Harith and with Theodora's protection, Jacob Baradaeus ('the ragged') travelled in disguise across Syria, Asia Minor and Egypt, ordaining, according to John of Ephesus, two patriarchs, 27 bishops and up to 100,000 clergy. He made the anti-Chalcedonians a separate church, later called 'Jacobite' (the Syriac Orthodox Church).

events.title: The Nea church in Jerusalem
events.summary: Justinian's church of Mary Mother of God, the Nea, was dedicated on 20 November 543 on the slope of Mount Zion, its platform carried on vast vaults. Procopius describes columns quarried locally because none could be brought; an inscription found in its cistern in 1977 names Justinian and the abbot Constantine. The Madaba map shows it at the end of the cardo.

events.title: Battle of Anglon
events.summary: Taking advantage of plague in Persia, a Roman army of some 30,000 under multiple commanders invaded Persarmenia without unified command. At Anglon, near Dvin, Nabedes with only 4,000 men laid an ambush in a village and ravine; the disordered Roman columns were routed with heavy losses. Procopius calls it the greatest Roman disaster yet.

sides.strength: c. 30,000 under Martin, Valerian, Peter, Isaac and others
sides.losses: very heavy; Narses the Persarmenian killed

battle.significance: Ended the Roman counter-offensive of 543 and confirmed the danger of divided command.

events.title: Theodora's Miaphysite mission to Nobatia
events.summary: John of Ephesus relates that around 543 Theodora sent the priest Julian to convert the Nubian kingdom of Nobatia to Miaphysite Christianity, ordering the governor of the Thebaid to delay a rival Chalcedonian mission sent by Justinian. Julian arrived first; the Nobadian king and nobles were baptised and Nubia's church remained Miaphysite.

events.title: Siege of Edessa
events.summary: Khosrow besieged Edessa in 544, building a huge timber-and-earth mound against the walls. The defenders tunnelled under it and set fire to the timbers inside, using sulphur, bitumen and cedar oil; the mound burned for days. A final assault failed and Khosrow accepted 500 lbs of gold. Evagrius later credited a miracle-working image of Christ (the Mandylion), unmentioned by Procopius.

sides.strength: garrison under Martin and Peter with citizens

battle.significance: Persia's failure here led to the five-year truce of 545 (Rome paid 2,000 lbs of gold) covering Mesopotamia, though not Lazica.

events.title: Battle of Cillium: death of Solomon
events.summary: After Solomon's nephew Sergius murdered 80 Leuathae (Laguatan) envoys at Leptis Magna, the Moors of Tripolitania and Byzacena under Antalas rose. Solomon, prefect and magister of Africa, attacked them near Cillium in 544 with mutinous troops and was killed when his horse fell in a ravine.

sides.strength: Moors of Byzacena under Antalas and Laguatan

battle.significance: Plunged Roman Africa into four years of war and mutiny.

events.title: Edict against the Three Chapters
events.summary: To win over the Miaphysites, Justinian condemned in 543-544 the 'Three Chapters': the person and works of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret's writings against Cyril, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa to Mari, all associated with Chalcedon. Western bishops saw an attack on the council; the African and Italian churches refused, and Pope Vigilius was summoned to Constantinople.

events.title: Totila captures Rome
events.summary: After a long blockade in which Belisarius's relief attempt at Portus failed, Isaurian sentries opened the Asinarian Gate to Totila on the night of 17 December 546. Totila wrote to Justinian threatening to destroy Rome; Belisarius urged him not to destroy the world's greatest city. Totila tore down a third of the walls and left the city almost empty; Belisarius reoccupied it in spring 547.

battle.significance: Rome changed hands for the second time in the war; Procopius claims only 500 inhabitants remained.

events.title: Consecration of San Vitale, Ravenna
events.summary: Begun under Ostrogothic rule with money from the banker Julianus Argentarius, the octagonal church of San Vitale in Ravenna was consecrated by Archbishop Maximian in 547 or 548. Its apse mosaics show Justinian and Theodora with their courts bearing offerings, the most famous images of the two rulers, neither of whom ever visited Ravenna.

events.title: The Iudicatum of Vigilius
events.summary: Brought to Constantinople in 547, Pope Vigilius issued on 11 April 548 a judgement (Iudicatum) condemning the Three Chapters while affirming Chalcedon. The western backlash was so fierce, with African bishops excommunicating him, that Justinian let him withdraw it in 550; Vigilius was later dragged from a church altar and twice fled to sanctuary.

events.title: Death of Theodora
events.summary: The empress Theodora died on 28 June 548, probably of cancer, aged about 48. Former actress, daughter of a bear-keeper of the Greens, she had been Justinian's partner in government, protector of the anti-Chalcedonians and the moving force, according to Procopius, behind the fall of John the Cappadocian in 541.

events.title: Battle of the Campi Catonis
events.summary: John Troglita, sent to Africa in 546, was defeated by the Laguatan under Carcasan at Marta in 547, but in summer 548 crushed the Moorish coalition at the Fields of Cato; Carcasan and 17 chieftains were killed. The victory brought Roman Africa fifteen years of peace and is the climax of Corippus's Latin epic, the Iohannis.

sides.strength: Roman army with loyal Moorish allies under Cusina
Laguatan and Byzacene Moors under Carcasan and Antalas

battle.significance: Ended the Moorish wars; Africa remained relatively prosperous under Roman rule until the 640s.

events.title: Fortified monastery of Mount Sinai
events.summary: Between about 548 and 565 Justinian built a fortified monastery of the Theotokos at the foot of Mount Sinai around the site of the Burning Bush, with a garrison to protect the monks from Saracen raids. Its basilica's apse mosaic of the Transfiguration, dated by inscription, and its icons, including the sixth-century encaustic Christ Pantokrator, survive in situ.

events.title: Abraha repairs the Marib dam and receives four embassies
events.summary: A long Sabaic inscription (CIH 541) records that the Aksumite ruler of Himyar, Abraha, put down a revolt and repaired the great dam of Marib in 548, and received envoys from the Negus of Aksum, the Roman emperor, the King of Kings, al-Harith the Ghassanid and al-Mundhir the Lakhmid. It shows Yemen as a node of great-power diplomacy.

events.title: Corippus's Iohannis
events.summary: Flavius Cresconius Corippus, an African grammarian, recited at Carthage around 549-550 a Latin epic in eight books on John Troglita's campaigns against the Moors of 546-548. Its ethnographic catalogues of Moorish tribes and descriptions of their camel laagers and rites are unique.

events.title: Totila retakes Rome
events.summary: After Belisarius's recall in 549, Totila besieged Rome again; Isaurian soldiers unpaid for years opened the Gate of St Paul on 16 January 550. This time Totila repopulated the city, restored buildings, and held chariot races in the Circus Maximus, the last recorded there.

battle.significance: The Gothic recovery's high-water mark; Totila sent envoys seeking peace, which Justinian refused.

events.title: Church of the Holy Apostles rebuilt
events.summary: Justinian replaced Constantine's church of the Holy Apostles with a cruciform church of five domes, dedicated on 28 June 550, adjoining the mausoleum of Constantine where emperors were buried until 1028. Its design inspired San Marco in Venice; the church was demolished after 1461 for the Fatih Mosque.

events.title: Procopius writes the Secret History
events.summary: Around 550 Procopius wrote, but did not publish, the Anekdota, a savage attack on Justinian and Theodora as demons who destroyed the empire, with pornographic slander of Theodora's youth, and on Belisarius and Antonina. Its text surfaced in the Vatican Library and was first printed by Niccolò Alemanni in 1623.

events.title: Cosmas Indicopleustes's Christian Topography
events.summary: An Alexandrian merchant who had sailed to Aksum and the Red Sea, known as Cosmas Indicopleustes ('sailor to India'), wrote c. 550 a treatise arguing that the universe has the shape of the Tabernacle with a flat earth. His digressions preserve invaluable observations on Aksum, the inscription of Adulis, the trade of Taprobane (Sri Lanka) and Indian Ocean commerce.

events.title: Slav invasion of 550
events.summary: In 550 a large Sclavene army crossed the Danube, approached Naissus intending to attack Thessalonica, then turned east, defeated an imperial army near Adrianople and raided to the Long Walls. Germanus's army gathering at Serdica for Italy deterred them for a time. Procopius describes their savagery in detail.

battle.significance: Showed that Slav raiders could beat field armies.

events.title: Earthquake and tsunami at Berytus
events.summary: On 9 July 551 a great earthquake struck the Levantine coast, destroying Berytus, where Agathias says thousands died including many foreign law students, and causing a tsunami. The famous law school moved to Sidon and never recovered its former standing.

events.title: Jordanes writes the Getica
events.summary: At Constantinople in 551, Jordanes, a Latin-speaking official of Gothic descent, wrote De origine actibusque Getarum, a short summary of Cassiodorus's lost twelve-book Gothic History, which he claims to have had for only three days. It is our main narrative source for Gothic origins, the Catalaunian Plains and Attila's death, and ends by celebrating the union of Amal blood with the Anicii in Germanus's son.

events.title: Battle of Sena Gallica
events.summary: Off Sena Gallica in autumn 551, a Roman fleet of 50 ships under John, nephew of Vitalian, and the Lombard-friendly Valerian met 47 Gothic ships besieging Ancona. Roman crews kept formation while the Goths crowded and fouled one another; 36 Gothic ships were lost, ending Totila's naval power in the Adriatic.

battle.significance: Restored Roman control of the Adriatic, protecting the supply route for Narses's offensive.

events.title: Bessas storms Petra in Lazica
events.summary: The Persian-held coastal fortress of Petra in Lazica, besieged without success by Dagisthaeus in 549, was stormed in spring 551 by the aged general Bessas, who led the assault personally. Procopius describes the Roman engineers' light rams carried by men inside, Persian incendiaries of sulphur and bitumen, and the final escalade. The Romans razed the walls.

sides.strength: c. 6,000 under Bessas with Lazic allies

sides.losses: almost all killed or captured; 500 burned in the citadel

battle.significance: Turned the Lazic War in Rome's favour on the Black Sea coast.

events.title: Procopius publishes the Wars
events.summary: Procopius of Caesarea, Belisarius's assessor, published Books 1-7 of his History of the Wars, on the Persian, Vandal and Gothic campaigns, around 550-551, adding Book 8 in 553-554. Modelled on Thucydides and Herodotus, it is the last great classical history and the main source for Justinian's wars.

events.title: Siege of Archaeopolis
events.summary: The Persian general Mermeroes attacked Archaeopolis, the strongest fortress of Lazica, in 551 with elephants and Sabir Huns. The Roman garrison sallied, a wounded elephant panicked the Persian ranks and Mermeroes withdrew with about 4,000 dead.

battle.significance: Saved inner Lazica.

events.title: Battle of Busta Gallorum (Taginae)
events.summary: Narses, marching from Ravenna along the Via Flaminia with some 20,000-30,000 men, met Totila at Busta Gallorum near Taginae in the Apennines in late June or July 552. He placed dismounted Lombard and Herul heavy infantry in the centre and 8,000 foot archers on the wings angled forward. Totila delayed, performing a war dance on horseback in gilded armour while waiting for 2,000 reinforcements, then launched a cavalry charge into the crescent of archers. The Gothic horse were shot down, the infantry fled, and Totila was mortally wounded in the rout.
events.locName: Busta Gallorum, near Taginae (Gualdo Tadino), Umbria

sides.strength: perhaps 20,000-30,000 incl. 5,500 Lombards, 3,000 Heruli, Gepids and Huns

battle.significance: Broke the Ostrogothic kingdom; the remaining Goths could no longer field a royal army capable of winning a pitched battle.

events.title: Battle of Mons Lactarius
events.summary: Teia, Totila's successor, marched south to relieve his brother Aligern guarding the Gothic treasure at Cumae and held the Sarno river for two months until Roman ships cut his supplies. Withdrawing to Mons Lactarius, the Goths attacked on foot in a desperate two-day battle in October 552 (or early 553). Teia fought in the front rank until killed while changing a shield heavy with twelve spears. The survivors were allowed to leave Italy.

battle.significance: End of the Ostrogothic monarchy, where Procopius ends his Wars.

events.title: Silkworm eggs smuggled to Constantinople
events.summary: Procopius records that monks from 'Serinda', perhaps Sogdiana or Khotan, offered to bring silkworms to Justinian to free the empire from buying silk through Persia, and returned with eggs hidden, according to Theophanes of Byzantium, in a hollow cane. A Byzantine sericulture industry grew, though imports from the East continued.

events.title: Roman expedition to Spain: Spania
events.summary: Invited by the Visigothic rebel Athanagild against King Agila, Justinian sent the octogenarian patrician Liberius with a small force in 552. When Athanagild won the throne in 555, the Romans kept a coastal strip from about Cartagena to Malaga and the lower Guadalquivir, the province of Spania, under a magister militum, held until about 624.

events.title: Second Council of Constantinople (Fifth Ecumenical)
events.summary: Hoping to reconcile the anti-Chalcedonians, Justinian had condemned the 'Three Chapters' (the person and works of Theodore of Mopsuestia and some writings of Theodoret and Ibas) in 543/544. The council of 5 May-2 June 553, of some 160 bishops, confirmed the condemnation and struck Pope Vigilius, held in Constantinople since 547 and refusing to attend, from the diptychs. Vigilius gave in later that year.

events.title: Schism of the Three Chapters in northern Italy
events.summary: When Vigilius and his successor Pelagius I accepted the condemnation of the Three Chapters by the council of 553, the metropolitans of Aquileia and Milan broke communion with Rome. The Aquileian schism, sheltered after 568 by the Lombards, lasted until the Synod of Pavia in 698 and split the patriarchate into Grado and Aquileia.

events.title: Pragmatic Sanction for Italy
events.summary: Issued on 13 August 554 at Pope Vigilius's request, the Pragmatic Sanction extended Justinian's legislation to Italy, confirmed the acts of the Gothic kings before Totila but annulled Totila's, restored lands and slaves to their former owners, and gave bishops and notables a role in choosing provincial governors.

events.title: Battle of the Volturnus (Casilinum)
events.summary: Two Alamannic brothers serving the Franks, Butilinus and Leutharis, invaded Italy in 553 with a large army and raided to the Straits. Leutharis's column, laden with plunder, perished of disease on the way home. Narses met Butilinus on the Volturnus at Casilinum near Capua in autumn 554, enveloping the Frankish wedge of infantry between his cavalry wings while Herul foot held the centre. Agathias says only five of the enemy escaped.
events.locName: Casilinum on the Volturnus, near Capua

battle.significance: Ended Frankish attempts to take over Italy after the Goths and made Narses master of the peninsula until 568.

events.title: Cassiodorus founds Vivarium
events.summary: Returning from Constantinople after the Gothic war, Cassiodorus founded the monastery of Vivarium, named after its fishponds, on his family estates at Squillace in Bruttium. For its monks he wrote the Institutiones (c. 562), a guide to sacred and secular reading, and organised a scriptorium to copy and correct texts, making manuscript copying a monastic duty.

events.title: Siege of Phasis
events.summary: After the Roman generals murdered the Lazic king Gubazes in 555 and nearly lost Lazica's loyalty, the Persian commander Nachoragan besieged Phasis at the mouth of the Rioni. Martin and the young officer Justin, son of Germanus, defended it; a sortie routed the Persians. Agathias's account includes a ruse in which Martin faked the arrival of reinforcements.

sides.strength: Roman garrison and fleet under Martin

battle.significance: Persia's last major offensive in Lazica; a truce followed in 557. Nachoragan was flayed alive by Khosrow.

events.title: Roman generals murder King Gubazes of Lazica
events.summary: Gubazes II of Lazica, who had returned to the Roman alliance, accused the generals Martin and Rusticus of incompetence. In 555 Rusticus's brother John stabbed him during a meeting by the river Chobus. Justinian sent the senator Athanasius to try the killers publicly in Lazica, an exceptional judicial spectacle described by Agathias.

events.title: Samaritan and Jewish revolt at Caesarea
events.summary: In July 556 Samaritans and Jews at Caesarea Maritima, joining forces against the Christians, killed the proconsul Stephen in his praetorium. Justinian sent Amantius, who executed and mutilated the ringleaders. It followed the great Samaritan revolt of 529 and preceded another in 572.

events.title: Collapse of Hagia Sophia's first dome
events.summary: Weakened by earthquakes in December 557, the eastern part of Hagia Sophia's shallow dome collapsed on 7 May 558, crushing the altar, ambo and ciborium. Isidore the Younger, nephew of Isidore of Miletus, rebuilt it about 6 m higher with a steeper profile and 40 ribs, the dome that still stands; the church was rededicated in December 562.

events.title: First Avar embassy to Constantinople
events.summary: Fleeing the Turks, the Avars reached the Caucasus and, through the Alan king Sarosius, sent an envoy named Kandikh to Justinian in 557/558. Their wild appearance, with hair in long braids, caused a sensation. Justinian granted gifts and subsidies and used them against the Kutrigurs, Utigurs and Sabirs, a policy that soon brought them to the Danube.

events.title: Second plague wave in Constantinople
events.summary: In spring 558, shortly after the earthquake that cracked Hagia Sophia's dome, the bubonic plague returned to Constantinople. Agathias describes young men dying suddenly as if struck by apoplexy, noting that it had never fully left the empire since 542. Evagrius counted recurrences in roughly fifteen-year cycles.

events.title: Belisarius's last victory: Melantias
events.summary: In winter 558/559 the Kutrigur Huns under Zabergan crossed the frozen Danube and split into three columns, one reaching Melantias 30 km from Constantinople. The retired Belisarius, with 300 veterans and a mass of peasants and townsmen, laid an ambush in a wooded valley near the village of Chettus, making noise and dust to simulate a large army; the Kutrigurs fled.

battle.significance: Saved the capital's suburbs; Justinian then paid the Kutrigurs to leave and set the Utigurs against them.

events.title: The Madaba mosaic map
events.summary: A floor mosaic in a church at Madaba in Jordan, laid c. 560-565, depicts the Holy Land from Lebanon to the Nile Delta with over 150 labelled sites. Its vignette of Jerusalem shows the colonnaded cardo, the Holy Sepulchre and the Nea church, and it is the oldest surviving map of the region.

events.title: Persians and Turks destroy the Hephthalites
events.summary: Around 557-560 Khosrow I allied with the Turkic ruler Istämi to destroy the Hephthalite empire, the Turks winning the decisive battle near Bukhara. The two victors divided the Hephthalite lands along the Oxus. Persia was freed from tribute, but now bordered the more dangerous Turks.

battle.significance: Created the Turkic-Persian frontier on the Oxus.

events.title: Death of Chlothar I and the partition of 561
events.summary: Chlothar I, last surviving son of Clovis and sole king of the Franks since 558, died at Compiègne in late 561. His kingdom was partitioned by lot among his four sons: Charibert at Paris, Guntram at Orléans, Sigibert at Reims and Chilperic at Soissons, the arrangement whose rivalries Gregory of Tours chronicles.

events.title: Rededication of Hagia Sophia
events.summary: After the dome collapsed on 7 May 558, Isidore the Younger rebuilt it with a higher profile and steeper curvature; the church was rededicated on 24 December 562. Paul the Silentiary recited his Ekphrasis, a verse description of the building, at the ceremonies in early 563.

events.title: The Fifty Years' Peace with Persia
events.summary: Concluded by Peter the Patrician and the Persian Yazdgushnasp at Dara in late 561 and ratified in 562, the treaty gave Lazica to Rome, set a Roman payment of 30,000 nomismata (about 420 lbs of gold) a year, with the first seven years paid up front, restricted trade to designated customs posts, forbade enticing Arab allies, limited Dara's garrison, and allowed Christians in Persia to worship and bury their dead.

events.title: Justinian's last heresy: aphthartodocetism
events.summary: In his final months Justinian issued an edict declaring that Christ's earthly body was incorruptible, a doctrine of Julian of Halicarnassus. Patriarch Eutychius refused and was deposed on 22 January 565; Evagrius says the emperor died before the decree could be enforced across the empire.

events.title: Death of Justinian
events.summary: Justinian died on the night of 14/15 November 565 aged about 83, having outlived Theodora, Belisarius (d. March 565) and most of his generation, and spent his last years absorbed in theology (he had just proclaimed the doctrine of the incorruptibility of Christ's body, Aphthartodocetism). His nephew Justin II, curopalates, was crowned at once.

events.title: Accession of Justin II; Avar subsidies refused
events.summary: Justin II, son of Justinian's sister Vigilantia, was crowned on 14/15 November 565 by Patriarch John Scholasticus, with his wife Sophia, Theodora's niece. Days later he received the Avar envoy Targitius and refused the subsidies Justinian had paid, a policy of firmness celebrated by Corippus that soon cost dearly in the Balkans and the East.

events.title: Murder of Justin son of Germanus at Alexandria
events.summary: Justin, son of Justinian's cousin Germanus and the most experienced general of the dynasty, had been a rival candidate in 565. Justin II sent him to Alexandria as a quasi-exile and had him killed there in 566; Evagrius says his head was brought to the emperor and empress, who kicked it.

events.title: Execution of the senators Aetherius and Addaeus
events.summary: Two senior senators, the curator Aetherius and the former prefect Addaeus, were accused of plotting to poison Justin II and executed in 566. Evagrius treats the charge as a pretext to remove survivors of Justinian's inner circle.

events.title: Lombards and Avars destroy the Gepid kingdom
events.summary: Alboin's Lombards, allied with the Avars of Bayan on condition of giving them the Gepid lands and a tenth of their livestock, crushed the Gepids in 567. King Cunimund was killed; Alboin made his skull a drinking cup and married his daughter Rosamund. Sirmium was occupied by the Romans, and the Avars took the Carpathian basin.

battle.significance: Gave the Avars the Carpathian basin, from which they dominated the middle Danube for 250 years, and set the Lombards moving toward Italy.

events.title: Lombard invasion of Italy
events.summary: On 2 April 568, Easter Monday, Alboin led the Lombards with Saxons, Gepids, Bulgars and others out of Pannonia, leaving it to the Avars, and entered Italy through the Julian Alps. Forum Iulii (Cividale) became the first duchy, under Alboin's nephew Gisulf; Milan fell on 3 September 569. Fourteen years after the Pragmatic Sanction, Roman Italy began to break into a patchwork of Lombard and Roman territories that lasted until the nineteenth century.

events.title: Siege of Pavia
events.summary: Ticinum held out against Alboin for three years. When it finally surrendered, Paul the Deacon says Alboin swore to massacre the inhabitants but relented after his horse stumbled at the gate. Pavia became the Lombard royal capital.

battle.significance: Gave the Lombards their royal seat for two centuries.

events.title: Zemarchus's embassy to the Turks
events.summary: After a Sogdian-led Turkic embassy under Maniakh came to Constantinople in 568 seeking a silk trade route bypassing Persia, Justin II sent Zemarchus, magister militum of the East, to the court of the Turkic yabghu Istämi (Sizabul) in the Altai or Tian Shan. Menander's account describes exorcisms with incense and bells and a golden throne on wheels. The anti-Persian alliance helped trigger the war of 572.
events.locName: Court of Istämi, Tian Shan / Ektag

events.title: Justin II sends a relic of the True Cross to Radegund at Poitiers
events.summary: At the request of the Frankish ex-queen Radegund, Justin II and Sophia sent a fragment of the True Cross in a jewelled reliquary to her convent at Poitiers, which took the name Sainte-Croix. For its reception Venantius Fortunatus composed the hymns Vexilla regis prodeunt and Pange lingua, still sung in the Latin liturgy of Holy Week.
events.note: Fortunatus's poem In laudem Iustini et Sophiae thanks the imperial couple; the reliquary's identification with the surviving Poitiers staurotheke is plausible but not certain.

events.title: Tiberius defeated by the Avars
events.summary: As comes excubitorum, the future Tiberius II led an army against the Avars on the lower Danube and was beaten around 570-571. The defeat forced Justin II, who had haughtily refused Avar subsidies in 565, to accept a truce, while the khagan Bayan turned to the Gepid inheritance and Sirmium.

battle.significance: Showed the limits of Justin II's refusal to pay the Avars.

events.title: Abraha's expedition against Mecca: the 'Year of the Elephant'
events.summary: Muslim tradition holds that Abraha, the Aksumite viceroy of Yemen, marched on Mecca with an elephant to destroy the Kaaba, and that his army was destroyed by birds pelting stones (Qur'an 105) in the year of Muhammad's birth, conventionally 570. Abraha's own Murayghan inscription (Ry 506) records a campaign deep into central Arabia in 552.

events.title: Sasanian conquest of Yemen
events.summary: Khosrow I sent a small force under the general Wahriz, reputedly drawn from prisoners, to help the Himyarite prince Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan expel the Aksumites. The Ethiopian dynasty of Abraha's sons fell and Yemen became a Persian dependency ruled by a marzban until the 620s, giving Persia control of the southern Red Sea and the incense route.

events.title: Plague in Italy and Gaul
events.summary: A further wave of the bubonic plague swept northern Italy and Gaul around 570-571. Marius of Avenches records a great mortality of men and cattle; Gregory of Tours describes the inguinal plague at Clermont, where on one Sunday 300 bodies were counted in the basilica of St Peter. Paul the Deacon's picture of empty villas and unharvested fields in Liguria belongs to these years.

events.title: Justin II turns on the miaphysites
events.summary: After his compromise edict, sometimes called the second Henotikon, failed to win over the anti-Chalcedonians, Justin II and Patriarch John Scholasticus enforced communion from 571: miaphysite clergy were reordained or imprisoned and monasteries in the capital emptied. John of Ephesus, himself jailed, wrote much of his Ecclesiastical History in prison as a record of the persecution.

events.title: Lombard duchies of Spoleto and Benevento founded
events.summary: Lombard war bands moving south of Roman-held Ravenna and Rome set up autonomous duchies around Spoleto, under Faroald, and Benevento, under Zotto, in the 570s. They cut the Via Flaminia between Rome and Ravenna and would remain largely independent of the kings at Pavia for two centuries.

events.title: Leovigild takes Asidona from the Romans
events.summary: John of Biclaro says Leovigild seized the strongly fortified city of Asidona (Medina Sidonia) by night through the treachery of a certain Framidaneus, killed its Roman garrison and restored it to Gothic rule. It was the first major Visigothic gain against Justinian's province of Spania.

battle.significance: Opened Leovigild's reconquest of southern Spain.

events.title: Assassination of Alboin
events.summary: Alboin was murdered at Verona on 28 June 572 by his armour-bearer Helmichis and the warrior Peredeo, instigated by Queen Rosamund, whom he had forced to drink from her father's skull. The conspirators fled to Ravenna with the Lombard treasure; Rosamund tried to poison Helmichis, who forced her to drink the rest of the cup.

events.title: Outbreak of the Persian war of 572
events.summary: Justin II refused the annual payment due under the 562 treaty, supported a revolt in Persarmenia, where Vardan Mamikonian killed the Persian governor at Dvin in February 572, and received the Armenian rebels into Roman protection. Twenty years of war followed, ending only with Khosrow II's restoration in 591.

events.title: Leovigild takes Córdoba
events.summary: Córdoba, which had defied the Gothic kings since the 550s and had defeated Agila, fell to a night attack by Leovigild in 572. John of Biclaro calls it 'long rebellious against the Goths'; Leovigild then took many towns and forts in the region, killing many peasants (rustici).

events.title: Fall of Dara
events.summary: After the Roman siege of Nisibis collapsed in panic and the general Marcian was recalled, Khosrow I besieged Dara for six months and took it in November 573, while his general Adarmahan ravaged Syria and burned Apamea. The news drove Justin II insane; he had to be soothed with organ music and a toy cart, says John of Ephesus. Sophia bought a one-year truce for 45,000 nomismata.

battle.significance: The loss of Rome's key Mesopotamian fortress caused a constitutional crisis and the elevation of Tiberius as Caesar.

events.title: Failed Roman siege of Nisibis
events.summary: Justin II's cousin Marcian besieged Nisibis in spring 573. Suspecting slackness, Justin replaced him with Acacius Archelaus, who removed him in front of the troops; when Khosrow I approached in person, the leaderless besiegers burned their siege engines and fled. The disaster opened the way to the Persian siege of Dara.

battle.significance: Rout that preceded the loss of Dara.

events.title: Adarmahan sacks Apamea
events.summary: While Khosrow besieged Dara, his general Adarmahan with a raiding army crossed the Euphrates at Circesium, plundered northern Syria, burned the suburbs of Antioch and took Apamea, whose bishop and citizens had trusted to its relic of the True Cross. Evagrius, an Antiochene, saw the devastation; the captives were marched to Persia.

battle.significance: Deepest Persian raid into Syria since 540.

events.title: Tiberius proclaimed Caesar
events.summary: In a lucid interval on 7 December 574, Justin II proclaimed Tiberius, commander of the excubitors, Caesar, with a speech recorded by Theophylact and John of Ephesus warning him not to imitate Justin's own mistakes: 'Do not delight in bloodshed... Let not the glory of these garments mislead you as it did me'. Tiberius and Sophia governed jointly until Justin's death.

events.title: Madness of Justin II
events.summary: The loss of Dara broke Justin II. John of Ephesus describes the emperor hiding under beds, biting his attendants, and being pacified by organ music and by being pulled around in a little wagon. Sophia took control and in December 574 Justin, in a lucid moment, proclaimed Tiberius Caesar with a speech the sources quote as a confession of failure.

events.title: Sophia buys a truce with Persia
events.summary: Empress Sophia sent the physician Zacharias to Khosrow and bought a one-year truce for 45,000 solidi; it was later extended for three years at 30,000 a year but covered only Mesopotamia, leaving Armenia as an open war zone. The arrangement freed Roman forces to rebuild but confirmed the loss of Dara.

events.title: Murder of Cleph and the rule of the dukes
events.summary: Alboin's successor Cleph was murdered after eighteen months in 574. For ten years the Lombards elected no king; Paul the Deacon says some 35 dukes ruled their cities independently, killing or dispossessing Roman landowners and making the rest tributary for a third of their produce.

events.title: Lombard and Saxon raids into Gaul defeated by Mummolus
events.summary: In the years after 569 Lombard war bands, and Saxons who had come to Italy with Alboin, crossed the Alps into Burgundian Gaul. The Gallo-Roman patrician Mummolus destroyed one army near Embrun and another at Mustiae Calmes, and the Saxons were forced back across the Rhône. The raids ended Lombard ambitions beyond the Alps.

battle.significance: Closed the Alpine passes to Lombard raiding.

events.title: Assassination of Sigibert I at Vitry
events.summary: In the civil war between Sigibert I of Austrasia and his brother Chilperic I, Sigibert had overrun Neustria and was raised on a shield at Vitry as king of Chilperic's people when two servants sent by Chilperic's queen Fredegund stabbed him with poisoned scramasaxes. The murder, revenge for Chilperic's killing of Brunhild's sister Galswintha, made the feud of Brunhild and Fredegund the axis of Frankish politics for forty years.

events.title: Battle of Melitene
events.summary: Khosrow I, aged about 75, invaded Armenia and Cappadocia in 576, failed before Theodosiopolis and Caesarea, and burned Sebasteia and Melitene. Near Melitene the Romans under Justinian, son of Germanus, caught his army; the Persian camp and royal baggage including the sacred fire were taken, and Khosrow escaped across the Euphrates on an elephant, then decreed that no Persian king should campaign in person again.

sides.strength: eastern field army under Justinian son of Germanus

battle.significance: Khosrow's last campaign; the Roman counter-raid reached the Caspian.

events.title: Baduarius defeated by the Lombards
events.summary: Justin II sent his son-in-law Baduarius, husband of Arabia, with an army to Italy. John of Biclaro records laconically that he was defeated by the Lombards and soon afterwards died. It was the last attempt by Constantinople to reconquer Lombard Italy with a field army; Tiberius II turned to bribing dukes and inviting the Franks.

battle.significance: Ended direct Roman offensives in Italy for a generation.

events.title: The Turks take Bosporus in the Crimea
events.summary: The envoy Valentinus reached the Western Turks in 576 to find the old ruler Istämi dead and his successor Turxanthus enraged that Tiberius had received the fleeing Avars, whom the Turks counted as runaway slaves. Turxanthus, putting ten fingers in his mouth to mock Roman duplicity, sent an army that captured the Roman city of Bosporus (Kerch).

battle.significance: Rupture of the Turkish alliance; the Turks reached the Black Sea coast.

events.title: Justinian son of Germanus defeated in Armenia
events.summary: After the Roman victory at Melitene (576), the magister militum per Orientem Justinian, son of Germanus, wintered in Persarmenia but was defeated in 577 by the Persian general Tamkhosrow. He was recalled and replaced by Maurice, then comes excubitorum.

battle.significance: Brought Maurice to the eastern command.

events.title: Eutychius restored; his debate with Gregory on the resurrection body
events.summary: Deposed by Justinian in 565 for resisting aphthartodocetism, Patriarch Eutychius returned from exile in 577. He taught that resurrected bodies would be impalpable, 'finer than air', and was opposed by the papal apocrisiarius Gregory, the future pope, in a debate before Tiberius II, who ordered Eutychius's treatise burned. Gregory retold the dispute in his Moralia on Job.

events.title: Lombards destroy Monte Cassino
events.summary: Lombards of the duchy of Benevento under Zotto attacked Benedict's monastery at night and destroyed it. The monks escaped to Rome, according to Paul the Deacon carrying Benedict's autograph Rule, a measure of bread and a measure of wine. Gregory's Dialogues present the destruction as foretold by Benedict. The site lay abandoned until c. 717.

events.title: Tiberius II Constantine becomes Augustus
events.summary: Crowned Augustus on 26 September 578, nine days before Justin II's death, Tiberius took the name Constantine. His generosity (he cut taxes by a quarter and lavished donatives) won popularity but emptied the treasury Justin had refilled. He recruited a new corps of 15,000 foederati and appointed Maurice to the East.

events.title: Maurice invades Arzanene
events.summary: As new magister militum per Orientem, Maurice answered a Persian raid on Roman Mesopotamia by invading Arzanene east of the Tigris in 578, taking the fortress of Aphumon and others and deporting some 10,000 captives, who were resettled on Cyprus. He then raided as far as Corduene, demonstrating that Roman armies could carry the war into Persian territory.

events.title: Leovigild founds Reccopolis
events.summary: Having pacified his kingdom, Leovigild founded a city in Celtiberia named after his son Reccared, the first new city founded in western Europe since Roman times. Excavations at Zorita de los Canes have revealed a palace complex, a church and a street of shops behind an imposing wall, and a mint struck coins there.

events.title: Romans ferry the Avars across the Danube against the Slavs
events.summary: Unable to defend Thrace against Slav raiders while fighting Persia, Tiberius invited the khagan Bayan to attack the Sclaveni in their own lands. John, prefect of Illyricum, transported 60,000 Avar horsemen down the Danube on Roman ships and across it; Bayan ravaged the territory of the Slav leader Daurentius, who had reputedly killed an Avar envoy.

events.title: Gennadius defeats the Moorish king Garmul
events.summary: John of Biclaro records that the magister militum Gennadius ravaged the Moors in Africa and killed in battle the very powerful king Garmul, who had already killed three Roman commanders. Gennadius later appears as the first attested exarch of Africa.

battle.significance: Stabilised Roman Africa for a generation.

events.title: Death of Khosrow I; accession of Hormizd IV
events.summary: Khosrow I Anushirvan died in early 579 after 48 years on the throne, while peace talks were under way. His son Hormizd IV, a ruler later remembered for favouring the peasants and clashing with the great nobles and priests, broke off negotiations and refused to restore Dara.

events.title: Revolt of Hermenegild
events.summary: Leovigild's elder son Hermenegild, governing Baetica from Seville and married to the Catholic Frankish princess Ingund, converted to Catholicism under Leander of Seville and rebelled in 579, seeking help from the Romans of Spania and the Suebi. Leovigild took Seville in 584 after diverting the Guadalquivir, captured his son at Córdoba, and he was killed at Tarragona in 585. Gregory the Great later honoured him as a martyr.

events.title: Slav settlement in the Balkans and Greece
events.summary: John of Ephesus wrote in 584 that Slavs had overrun Thrace, Thessaly and Greece, lived there 'as in their own land', grew rich in gold, silver and herds, and learned to fight better than the Romans. Over the following decades Slavic settlement spread through much of the Balkans and the Peloponnese, the Monemvasia Chronicle claiming that Roman rule there lapsed for 218 years.

events.title: Maurice and al-Mundhir's expedition toward Ctesiphon
events.summary: In 581 Maurice and the Ghassanid king al-Mundhir marched down the Euphrates with a river fleet intending to strike at Ctesiphon, but found the bridge at the frontier destroyed and Adarmahan raiding Osrhoene behind them. The fiasco led to bitter recriminations, with Maurice accusing al-Mundhir of betraying the plan to the Persians.

events.title: Battle of Constantina
events.summary: In June 582 Maurice met a Persian invasion of Mesopotamia under Tamkhosrow and Adarmahan before Constantina (Tella) and won a clear victory in which Tamkhosrow was killed. Weeks later Tiberius II, dying, made Maurice Caesar and married him to his daughter Constantina.

battle.significance: Secured Maurice's succession.

events.title: Accession of Maurice
events.summary: Dying, Tiberius II named Maurice, a Cappadocian notary turned general who had won victories in the East, as Caesar on 5 August and Augustus on 13 August 582, and married him to his daughter Constantina. Tiberius died on 14 August.

events.title: Avars take Sirmium
events.summary: Bayan built bridges across the Sava with the help of Roman craftsmen and blockaded Sirmium from 579. With Roman armies tied down in the East, Tiberius gave up the city in 582 in exchange for the garrison's freedom, paying the arrears of subsidy (240,000 nomismata). The old imperial capital became the Avar khagan's bridgehead.

battle.significance: Broke the middle Danube line; Avar and Slav raids into the Balkans followed for fifty years.

events.title: Arrest of the Ghassanid king al-Mundhir
events.summary: Suspected of treachery, al-Mundhir ibn al-Harith, the Miaphysite supreme phylarch who had defeated the Lakhmids repeatedly, was arrested in 582 by the curator Magnus at the consecration of a church at Huwwarin and exiled to Sicily. His son al-Nu'man rebelled, was in turn arrested (584), and the Ghassanid federation broke into some fifteen rival groups, weakening Rome's desert shield half a century before the Arab conquests.

events.title: Creation of the Exarchate of Ravenna
events.summary: By 584 an exarch (first attested Decius, then Smaragdus) combined supreme civil and military authority over Roman Italy, a response to the Lombard threat that broke the late Roman separation of civil and military command. A parallel Exarchate of Carthage is attested from 591 (Gennadius).

events.title: Avars take Singidunum, Viminacium and Anchialus
events.summary: When Maurice refused Bayan's demand for an extra 20,000 solidi on top of the 80,000 paid annually, the Avars surprised Singidunum while its people were harvesting, then took Viminacium and Augustae and swept to Anchialus on the Black Sea, where Bayan spared the empress's warm baths. Peace was restored for an annual payment of 100,000 solidi, but Slavs then raided to the Long Walls.

events.title: Lombards restore the kingship: Authari
events.summary: Under pressure from Frankish and Roman attacks, the Lombard dukes elected Cleph's son Authari king in 584 and each gave half his substance to endow the royal fisc. Authari took the Roman name Flavius, used by later Lombard kings, and Paul the Deacon describes his reign as an idyll of peace without violence or plotting.

events.title: Murder of Chilperic I
events.summary: Chilperic I of Neustria was stabbed to death returning from a hunt at his villa of Chelles near Paris in autumn 584. Gregory of Tours, whom he had once tried for slander, calls him 'the Nero and Herod of our time', mocking his Latin verse and his attempt to add letters to the alphabet. His four-month-old son Chlothar II survived under Fredegund's protection.

events.title: Arrest of al-Nu'man and the break-up of the Ghassanid federation
events.summary: Al-Mundhir's son al-Nu'man, who had raided Roman territory in revenge for his father's exile, was lured to Constantinople and arrested in 584. John of Ephesus says the Arab federation split into fifteen factions, many joining the Persians; Rome never recreated a single supreme phylarchate.

events.title: The Gundovald affair
events.summary: Gundovald, who claimed to be a son of Chlothar I and had lived in Constantinople, landed at Marseille in 582 with imperial money, was raised on a shield at Brive in late 584 and won over much of Aquitaine. Besieged by Guntram's army in the hilltop town of Convenae (Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges) in 585, he was betrayed by his ally Mummolus and killed; the town was sacked. Gregory of Tours suspected Byzantine sponsorship.

battle.significance: Last Byzantine-backed pretender in Gaul.

events.title: Leovigild annexes the Suebic kingdom
events.summary: After Audeca usurped the Suebic throne from the young Eboric, Leovigild invaded Gallaecia in 585, captured Audeca, made him a cleric and annexed the kingdom of the Suebi, which had existed since 409. A brief rising under Malaric was crushed. The Visigoths now held all Iberia except the Basque lands and the Roman coast.

events.title: Avaro-Slav siege of Thessalonica
events.summary: A huge Slav army sent by the Avar khagan besieged Thessalonica for a week in September 586 (or 597), with siege engines including stone throwers and testudos. The city's defence was credited to its patron St Demetrius, who appeared on the walls; the episode is the core of Book I of the Miracles of St Demetrius.

battle.significance: Thessalonica's survival made it the Roman bulwark in the Slavicised Balkans.

events.title: Battle of Solachon
events.summary: In spring 586 Maurice's brother-in-law Philippicus met the Persian general Kardarigan on the plain of Solachon south of Mardin. Before battle he paraded the Camuliana image of Christ 'not made by human hands'. The Roman centre under Heraclius the Elder broke the Persians, who were cut off from water; Kardarigan fled to a hilltop.

sides.strength: eastern field army; centre under Heraclius the Elder

battle.significance: The first major Roman field victory of the war; an early example of an icon used as a military palladium.

events.title: Siege of Chlomaron
events.summary: Following his victory at Solachon, Philippicus invaded Arzanene and besieged the fortress of Chlomaron. When a Persian relief army appeared he lost his nerve and retreated in disorder by night, abandoning much of the campaign's gains. Theophylact's account is one of the frankest descriptions of a Roman command collapse.

battle.significance: Squandered the advantage won at Solachon.

events.title: Treaty of Andelot
events.summary: On 28 November 587 Guntram of Burgundy, his nephew Childebert II of Austrasia and Childebert's mother Brunhild agreed at Andelot to divide disputed cities, guarantee Brunhild's lands, and make Childebert Guntram's heir. Gregory of Tours, who helped negotiate it, copied the full text into his Histories, a rare surviving Merovingian treaty.

events.title: Comentiolus's Haemus campaign: 'torna, torna, fratre'
events.summary: During a night march against the Avars in the Haemus mountains in 587, a pack animal shed its load and a soldier called to its driver in the local Latin vernacular 'torna, torna, fratre' (turn back, brother). The cry was taken as an order to retreat and both the Roman army of Comentiolus and the Avars it was stalking fled in panic. The phrase is prized as one of the earliest records of Balkan Romance.

battle.significance: Famous for its linguistic evidence.

events.title: Reccared converts to Catholicism
events.summary: Ten months after succeeding Leovigild (586), Reccared privately accepted Nicene Christianity in early 587 and persuaded many Arian bishops and nobles to follow. Arian conspiracies at Mérida, in Septimania and at court, including one involving Leovigild's widow Goiswintha, were suppressed before the public abjuration at the Third Council of Toledo (589).

events.title: Mutiny of the eastern army
events.summary: Maurice's order to cut military pay by a quarter provoked a mutiny of the eastern army at Easter 588 at Monocarton; the new commander Priscus fled after being stoned, and the troops chose Germanus, dux of Phoenicia. The mutineers still beat the Persians at Martyropolis; Gregory of Antioch restored order in 589.

events.title: The mutinous eastern army defeats the Persians near Martyropolis
events.summary: Even while in mutiny against Maurice's pay cut and his general Priscus, the eastern army under its elected leader Germanus beat a Persian invasion near Martyropolis in 588, killing the commander Maruzas and sending his head and captured standards to the emperor as proof of loyalty to the empire, if not to its officers.

battle.significance: Paved the way for reconciliation of the army in 589.

events.title: Bahram Chobin defeats the Turks
events.summary: A Turkic invasion of Khurasan was crushed by the Persian general Bahram Chobin, probably near Herat, in 588; the Turkic ruler, called Shaba or Sabeh in Persian tradition, was killed.
