Persian sources inflate the enemy to 300,000. The victory made Bahram a hero and gave him the prestige to rebel after Hormizd IV humiliated him for a later defeat by the Romans.

battle.significance: Created the war hero who would usurp the throne in 590.

events.title: Third Council of Toledo: Visigoths become Catholic
events.summary: King Reccared, who had converted privately in 587, presided at the Third Council of Toledo opened on 8 May 589, where the Visigothic nobility and Arian bishops abjured Arianism and accepted Nicene Christianity. The council also adopted the Filioque in its creed, a seed of the later East-West dispute.

events.title: Martyropolis betrayed to the Persians
events.summary: A Roman officer named Sittas betrayed Martyropolis to the Persians in 589 by bringing in Persian soldiers disguised as deserters. Roman sieges under Philippicus and then Comentiolus failed against a reinforced garrison; the city was handed back only through Khosrow II's restoration treaty in 591.

battle.significance: Strategic city lost by treachery and regained by diplomacy.

events.title: Battle of Sisarbanon
events.summary: In autumn 589 Comentiolus defeated a Persian army near Nisibis at Sisarbanon (Sisauranon). Theophylact says Comentiolus fled at the crisis but Heraclius the Elder, father of the future emperor, rallied the troops; the Persian general was killed and the Romans then took the fort of Akbas.

battle.significance: Contributed to the crisis that toppled Hormizd IV.

events.title: Battle of Carcassonne
events.summary: Guntram's Franks invaded Visigothic Septimania in 589 and were routed near Carcassonne by Claudius, dux of Lusitania. Isidore boasts that 300 Goths beat 60,000 Franks; John of Biclaro calls it the greatest Gothic victory in Spain. It secured Septimania for the Visigoths until the Arab conquest.

battle.significance: Confirmed Gothic Septimania.

events.title: Deposition and murder of Hormizd IV
events.summary: With Bahram Chobin marching on Ctesiphon, the brothers Vistahm and Vinduyih (Bindoe), Hormizd's brothers-in-law, staged a palace coup in February 590, blinded the king and proclaimed his son Khosrow II; Hormizd was killed soon after. Khosrow's complicity was later debated, but Bahram used it as justification for his own claim.

events.title: Gregory the Great becomes pope
events.summary: Gregory, former urban prefect, monk and papal envoy to Constantinople, was consecrated on 3 September 590 after Pelagius II died of plague, which Gregory fought with penitential processions (legend later put the archangel Michael atop Hadrian's mausoleum, hence Castel Sant'Angelo). He ran Rome's food supply, defence and diplomacy from the papal estates.

events.title: Death of Authari; Agilulf marries Theodelinda
events.summary: Authari died at Pavia on 5 September 590, perhaps poisoned. The Lombards allowed his Bavarian Catholic widow Theodelinda to choose the next king; she married Agilulf, duke of Turin, who was proclaimed in November 590 and recognised at Milan in May 591.

events.title: Bahram Chobin's revolt; Khosrow II flees to the Romans
events.summary: The general Bahram Chobin, victor over the Turks but then defeated by the Romans in the Caucasus and insulted by Hormizd IV with a woman's dress, rebelled. Hormizd was overthrown and killed in a palace coup (590) and his son Khosrow II crowned, but Bahram took Ctesiphon and proclaimed himself king, the first non-Sasanian to do so. Khosrow fled to Roman Circesium and appealed to Maurice.

events.title: Plague in Rome and the sevenfold litany
events.summary: After the Tiber flooded in late 589, plague struck Rome; Pope Pelagius II died on 7 February 590. The deacon Gregory, elected to succeed him, organised a sevenfold procession of clergy, monks, nuns, children, laymen, widows and married women converging on Santa Maria Maggiore; Gregory of Tours heard that eighty people dropped dead during it. The legend of Michael sheathing his sword over Hadrian's mausoleum, hence Castel Sant'Angelo, is medieval.

events.title: Frankish-Roman offensive against the Lombards
events.summary: Financed by Maurice, Childebert II sent twenty dukes into Italy in 590 while the exarch Romanus advanced from Ravenna, recovering Modena, Altinum and Mantua. The Franks, ravaged by dysentery and suspicious of Roman delays, made a separate truce and withdrew; letters of Romanus to Childebert in the Epistolae Austrasicae preserve the coalition's frustrations.

events.title: Columbanus founds Luxeuil
events.summary: The Irish monk Columbanus from Bangor arrived in Gaul with twelve companions around 590 and, with the support of the Burgundian king, founded monasteries at Annegray and then Luxeuil in the ruins of a Roman spa in the Vosges. His harsh Rule and Irish penitential practice inspired dozens of foundations across Francia in the seventh century.

events.title: John of Biclaro writes his Chronicle
events.summary: John, a Goth from Scallabis (Santarém) who had studied seventeen years in Constantinople, was exiled to Barcelona by the Arian Leovigild, founded a monastery at Biclaro and became bishop of Gerona. His chronicle, continuing Victor of Tunnuna from 567 to 590, is the main source for Leovigild and Reccared and is dated by both imperial and Gothic regnal years.

events.title: Battle of the Blarathon
events.summary: Against the advice of his senate, Maurice backed Khosrow II. A Roman army under Narses and John Mystacon with Armenian contingents and Khosrow's loyalists defeated Bahram Chobin on the river Blarathon near Ganzak in Atropatene in late summer 591. Bahram fled to the Turks and was murdered; Khosrow was restored.

sides.strength: Roman and Armenian troops under the magister militum per Orientem Narses and John Mystacon with Khosrow II's loyalists, perhaps 40,000-60,000

battle.significance: Restored a grateful Sasanian king and brought the most favourable peace Rome ever made with Persia.

events.title: Peace of 591 with Khosrow II
events.summary: In return for his restoration, Khosrow II returned Dara and Martyropolis and ceded most of Persarmenia, including Dvin, and part of Iberia, without any Roman payment. Rome's eastern frontier reached its farthest extent, and Maurice could switch his armies to the Balkans.

events.title: The exarchate of Africa
events.summary: By 591 the governor of Roman Africa combined civil and military power with the title exarch, first attested for Gennadius in Gregory the Great's letters. Like Ravenna, Carthage became a semi-autonomous military command; in 608 the exarch Heraclius the Elder launched from it the revolt that put his son on the throne.

events.title: Death of Guntram
events.summary: Guntram, king of Burgundy since 561 and the most pious of Chlothar I's sons, died on 28 March 592; under the Treaty of Andelot his kingdom passed to Childebert II. Popular devotion soon venerated him as a saint, despite Gregory of Tours's record of his executions.

events.title: Khosrow II's dedications to St Sergius at Resafa
events.summary: Restored by Roman arms, Khosrow II sent votive gifts to the shrine of St Sergius at Sergiopolis: a gold cross for the victory over Bahram, and later offerings in thanks for the pregnancy of his Christian wife Shirin. Evagrius quotes the Greek texts of the dedicatory inscriptions, in which the Zoroastrian King of Kings addresses the saint directly.

events.title: Exarch Romanus reopens the Rome-Ravenna corridor
events.summary: The exarch Romanus retook Sutri, Bomarzo, Orte, Todi, Amelia, Perugia and Luceoli from the Lombards around 592, securing the route along the Via Amerina that became the spine of the Byzantine duchy of Perugia linking Rome to Ravenna. Agilulf retook Perugia in 593 and marched on Rome.

events.title: Agilulf threatens Rome; Gregory buys peace
events.summary: After the exarch Romanus recovered the Rome-Ravenna corridor, the Lombard king Agilulf retaliated by marching on Rome in 593. Gregory, interrupting his homilies on Ezekiel, saw Romans led off roped like dogs to be sold in Gaul, and paid 500 lbs of gold to buy Agilulf off, then negotiated a separate peace, angering Maurice, who called him a fool.

events.title: Maurice's offensives beyond the Danube
events.summary: From 593 Maurice took the war to the enemy. Priscus crossed the lower Danube and smashed the Slav chief Ardagastus in his home territory; Maurice's brother Peter campaigned in 594-597. Theophylact preserves the tension between commanders and troops, who hated campaigning in winter beyond the river and resisted orders to live off the land.

events.title: Gregory the Great's Dialogues
events.summary: In 593-594 Gregory wrote four books of Dialogues on the miracles of the Italian fathers in conversation with his deacon Peter. Book 2, devoted entirely to Benedict of Nursia, is the only life of Benedict and made his Rule famous. Book 4 on the afterlife became a foundation of the medieval doctrine of purgatory.

events.title: Peter's campaign beyond the Danube
events.summary: Maurice replaced Priscus with his own brother Peter, who in 594 pushed against the Sclaveni north of the Danube and killed the Slav chief Peiragastus at the crossing of the river Helibacias, though his army then suffered from lack of water and a costly ambush. Theophylact presents Peter as incompetent, a view shaped by his sources' loyalty to Priscus.

battle.significance: Kept the Slavs on the defensive north of the river.

events.title: Gregory of Tours completes the Ten Books of Histories
events.summary: Gregory, bishop of Tours from 573, completed his Decem libri historiarum around 594, the year of his death, carrying the story from Creation to 591. Books 5-10 are an eyewitness record of the civil wars of Chilperic, Guntram, Sigibert and Brunhild. His self-consciously rustic Latin and taste for violent anecdote created the lasting image of Merovingian barbarism.

events.title: Evagrius completes his Ecclesiastical History
events.summary: Evagrius Scholasticus, lawyer to the patriarch Gregory of Antioch, finished his six-book Ecclesiastical History, covering 431 to 594, in Maurice's twelfth year. A Chalcedonian who had survived the plague four times and lost children and grandchildren to it, he preserves documents such as Zeno's Henotikon and the dedications of Khosrow II.

events.title: Avar attack on Singidunum and raid into Dalmatia
events.summary: Angered by Roman campaigns against the Slavs, Bayan attacked Singidunum in 595 and began to dismantle its walls, but withdrew after Priscus's fleet appeared on the Danube. The Avars then invaded Dalmatia, taking Bonkeis and some forty forts, while a Roman force under Guduin could only shadow them.

battle.significance: Avars turned to Dalmatia.

events.title: Gregory's mission to the English
events.summary: Gregory sent the monk Augustine with about 40 companions from his monastery of St Andrew in Rome; they landed in Kent in 597 and were received by King Æthelberht, whose Frankish wife Bertha was already Christian. Æthelberht's baptism followed, and Canterbury became the metropolitan see.

events.title: Avar siege of Tomis and the Easter truce
events.summary: In winter 597-598 the Avars besieged Priscus's army at Tomis. When the Romans ran out of food at Easter, Bayan granted a five-day truce and sent wagons of provisions, an episode Theophylact relates with wonder. Comentiolus then failed to relieve Tomis; the Avars marched to Drizipera near the capital, where plague killed seven of the khagan's sons.

battle.significance: Led to the peace of 598.

events.title: Maurice's testament
events.summary: During an illness in 597 Maurice drafted a will, discovered after his death, dividing the empire between his sons: Theodosius was to rule from Constantinople and Tiberius from Rome over Italy and the islands, with other provinces for the younger sons. It shows that the idea of a resident western emperor was still alive at the end of the sixth century.

events.title: Peace of 598 with the Avars
events.summary: After the plague at Drizipera, Bayan agreed to a treaty raising the annual subsidy by 20,000 solidi, fixing the Danube as the frontier, and allowing the Romans to cross it to campaign against the Sclaveni. Maurice broke it the next year by sending Priscus across at Viminacium.

events.title: Gregory brokers peace between Agilulf and the exarch
events.summary: Pope Gregory, who had already paid Agilulf 500 lb of gold to spare Rome in 593 and had been rebuked by Maurice as a simpleton, finally brought the exarch Callinicus and Agilulf to a truce in 598, renewed in following years. The episode shows the papacy acting as an independent power in Italian diplomacy.

events.title: Bayan massacres 12,000 Roman prisoners
events.summary: After Comentiolus's disastrous retreat at Iatrus in 598, the Avars took some 12,000 Roman prisoners. Maurice refused to pay the khagan's ransom, reportedly a nomisma each, then half, then a quarter, and Bayan had them all killed. The atrocity was one of the grievances against Maurice in 602.

events.title: Battles of Viminacium and the Tisza
events.summary: In 599 Priscus crossed the Danube at Viminacium and won a series of battles against the Avars on Pannonian soil, killing, says Theophylact, four sons of the khagan. He then struck into the Avar heartland on the Tisza, destroying villages of Gepids under Avar rule and taking 3,000 Avars, 6,200 other barbarians and 8,000 Slavs captive.

sides.losses: heavy; four sons of the khagan killed (Theophylact)

battle.significance: The high point of Roman power on the Danube in the late sixth century; it seemed to vindicate Maurice's policy just before the 602 collapse.

events.title: Plague of 599-600
events.summary: A renewed outbreak of bubonic plague struck Constantinople, Asia Minor, Syria and Italy in 599-600; Theophanes reports great mortality in the capital, and Gregory the Great's letters describe sickness in Italy and Africa. The epidemic had already hit the Avar army at Drizipera in 598.

events.title: The Strategikon of Maurice
events.summary: Composed around 592-610 and traditionally attributed to Maurice, the Strategikon is a 12-book field manual: cavalry organisation into banda, drill with Latin words of command, march and camp procedure, ambushes, and ethnographic chapters on how to fight Persians, Scythians (Avars and Turks), 'light-haired peoples' (Franks and Lombards) and Slavs and Antes.

events.title: Maurice stoned at the Hypapante
events.summary: During a food shortage in February 602, a crowd attacked Maurice with stones during the procession of the Hypapante (Purification); he escaped to the palace with his son Theodosius. The mob then paraded a man resembling the emperor on a donkey, crowned with garlic, chanting insults about his avarice. The Greens' hostility would help Phocas in November.

events.title: Mutiny of the Danube army and revolt of Phocas
events.summary: Ordered in autumn 602 to winter north of the Danube to live off Slav lands, the army mutinied, raised the centurion Phocas on a shield and marched on Constantinople. The Greens rose in the capital, Maurice fled across the Bosporus, and Phocas was crowned at the Hebdomon on 23 November 602, the first successful violent usurpation in Constantinople since its founding.

events.title: Execution of Maurice and his sons
events.summary: On 27 November 602 Phocas's men executed Maurice at the harbour of Eutropius at Chalcedon after making him watch the beheading of five of his sons. Theophylact says Maurice repeated 'You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is righteous', and that when a nurse tried to substitute her own child for one of his sons, he revealed the deception. His eldest son Theodosius was later killed, though rumours of his survival persisted.

events.title: Khosrow II ends the Lakhmid kingdom
events.summary: Khosrow II deposed and imprisoned (later killed) al-Nu'man III, the Christian Lakhmid king of al-Hira, around 602 and replaced him with Iyas ibn Qabisa of Tayy and a Persian resident. The end of the Lakhmid buffer, following the Roman break-up of the Ghassanids, removed both empires' Arab shields; the Persian defeat at Dhi Qar soon followed.

events.title: Avar attack on the Antes
events.summary: In 602 the khagan sent his general Apsich to destroy the Antes, a Slavic people east of the Carpathians allied with the Romans. Theophylact notes that many Avars deserted to the emperor during the campaign. It is the last mention of the Antes in the sources.

events.title: Agilulf takes Cremona and Mantua
events.summary: After the truce with the exarch lapsed and the Romans seized Agilulf's daughter at Parma, the Lombard king took Padua (601), then Cremona on 21 August 603, which he razed, and Mantua on 13 September 603 after breaching its walls with rams. Roman territory in the Po valley was reduced to the coastal strip around Ravenna and the Venetian lagoons.

battle.significance: Last major Lombard gains of the period.

events.title: Khosrow II declares war to avenge Maurice
events.summary: Khosrow II, who owed his throne to Maurice, imprisoned Phocas's envoy and declared war in 603, sponsoring a pretender claiming to be Maurice's son Theodosius. Narses, magister militum of the East, rebelled against Phocas at Edessa and called in the Persians; he was later lured to Constantinople and burned alive. The last and greatest war of antiquity had begun.

events.title: Revolt of Narses at Edessa
events.summary: Narses, Maurice's veteran magister militum per Orientem and the victor of the Blarathon, refused to recognise Phocas, seized Edessa in 603 and appealed to Khosrow II. Khosrow relieved the city and defeated the besieging general Germanus, who died of his wounds. Narses was later persuaded by Domentziolus to surrender under a safe-conduct and was burned alive in Constantinople.

events.title: Catholic baptism of the Lombard heir Adaloald
events.summary: Agilulf and Theodelinda's son Adaloald was baptised a Catholic at Monza at Easter 603, Gregory the Great sending gifts preserved in the Monza treasury. It marked a step in the gradual conversion of the Arian Lombard elite, though the next kings Arioald and Rothari were Arians.

events.title: Death of Gregory the Great
events.summary: Gregory died on 12 March 604 after fourteen years as pope, crippled by gout. He left some 850 letters in his Register, the Pastoral Rule, Moralia, Dialogues and homilies, the English mission and a papacy that managed estates from Sicily to Gaul and functioned as Rome's government. His epitaph called him God's consul.

events.title: Persians take Dara
events.summary: Khosrow II besieged Dara in person from 603; after about nine months his engineers undermined the walls and the city fell in 604 (or 605). The fall of the frontier citadel opened Roman Mesopotamia: Mardin, Amida, Resaina, Edessa and Theodosiopolis fell over the next six years.

battle.significance: Broke the Mesopotamian frontier for the rest of the war.

events.title: Phocas buys peace from the Avars
events.summary: To free the Balkan army for the Persian war, Phocas increased the annual payment to the Avars in 604 and transferred troops from Thrace to Asia. The decision effectively ended the Roman counter-offensive of Maurice's reign on the Danube and left the provinces south of it open to Slav settlement.

events.title: Battle of Arxamoun
events.summary: Khosrow II, campaigning in person in Mesopotamia, defeated a Roman army under the eunuch Leontius at Arxamoun near Dara, taking many prisoners, and then besieged and took Dara itself after nine months. Phocas had Leontius arrested.

battle.significance: Opened the way to Dara.

events.title: Execution of Maurice's widow and daughters
events.summary: Maurice's widow Constantina and her three daughters, confined in a monastery, were implicated in a conspiracy with the patrician Germanus, whose daughter had married Maurice's son Theodosius. Tortured by Phocas's agents, Constantina named accomplices; she and her daughters were beheaded at the harbour of Eutropius at Chalcedon, where Maurice had died.

events.title: Column of Phocas in the Roman Forum
events.summary: On 1 August 608 the exarch Smaragdus re-dedicated an older honorific column in the Forum Romanum, topping it with a gilded statue of Phocas and an inscription praising his benefactions to Italy. It was the last monument added to the Forum. In 609 Phocas also allowed Pope Boniface IV to consecrate the Pantheon as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres (13 May 609).

events.title: Heraclian revolt in Africa
events.summary: Heraclius the Elder, exarch of Africa, and his brother Gregory rebelled against Phocas in 608, cutting the grain from Africa and striking coins showing father and son as consuls. Gregory's son Nicetas marched overland to Egypt, defeating Phocas's general Bonosus at Alexandria in 609-610, while the younger Heraclius sailed with a fleet via Sicily and Thessalonica.

events.title: The Pantheon becomes Santa Maria ad Martyres
events.summary: With the permission of Phocas, Pope Boniface IV converted Hadrian's Pantheon into a church dedicated to the Virgin and all martyrs, consecrated on 13 May 609. It was the first pagan temple in Rome to be Christianised, which is why it survives with its dome and bronze doors intact; the feast of All Saints derives from its dedication.

events.title: Riots in Antioch and the murder of Patriarch Anastasius
events.summary: In September 609 Antioch erupted; the Chalcedonian patriarch Anastasius II was murdered, his body dragged through the streets. Theophanes blames the Jews; the comes Orientis Bonosus and Kottanas restored order with exemplary brutality. Similar factional violence between Blues and Greens shook Palestine, Syria and Egypt in Phocas's last years.

events.title: Persian conquest of Roman Mesopotamia
events.summary: After Dara (604), Persian armies took Mardin, Amida, Theodosiopolis in Armenia (with the aid of the pretender 'Theodosius', supposedly Maurice's son), Rhesaina and finally Edessa in 609. In 610 they crossed the Euphrates. The whole frontier system built since Diocletian had collapsed before Heraclius took power.

events.title: Nicetas wins Egypt for the Heraclians
events.summary: While Heraclius prepared the fleet, his cousin Nicetas marched from Cyrenaica into Egypt in 608-609 with Moorish and Roman troops, won over the Alexandrians and the Greens, and defeated Phocas's commander Bonosus outside Alexandria. Control of the Egyptian grain fleet doomed Phocas.

battle.significance: Cut Constantinople's grain supply.

events.title: Battle of Dhi Qar
events.summary: After Khosrow II killed the Lakhmid king al-Nu'man III, the tribe of Bakr ibn Wa'il refused to surrender his property and defeated a Persian army with Arab allies at Dhi Qar near Kufa. Arabic tradition remembered it as the first time Arabs beat the Persians; it showed the frontier was now unguarded.

battle.significance: Symbolic Arab victory over Persia.

events.title: Fall of Phocas; Heraclius crowned
events.summary: Heraclius's fleet reached Constantinople on 3 October 610; the Greens and the excubitors under Phocas's son-in-law Priscus deserted Phocas, who was dragged before Heraclius. 'Is this how you have governed the empire?' 'Will you govern it better?' Phocas was beheaded and mutilated. Heraclius was crowned by Patriarch Sergius on 5 October and married Fabia-Eudocia the same day.

events.title: Revolt of Phocas's brother Comentiolus
events.summary: Phocas's brother Comentiolus, commanding in Asia Minor, refused to recognise Heraclius and held Ancyra with eastern troops through the winter of 610-611 before being murdered by the patrician Justin. The diversion of forces helped the Persians cross the Euphrates and enter Anatolia.

events.title: Shahin takes Caesarea in Cappadocia
events.summary: Shahin's army took Caesarea, the capital of Cappadocia, in 611. Priscus, Phocas's former son-in-law now serving Heraclius, besieged the Persians in the city for a year but could not prevent them breaking out in 612 and burning it. Heraclius came in person and quarrelled with Priscus, whom he soon removed.

battle.significance: First deep Persian penetration of Anatolia in the war.

events.title: Heraclius removes Priscus
events.summary: In December 612 Heraclius summoned Priscus to Constantinople, accused him before the senate of insulting the emperor, and had him tonsured and confined in the monastery of Chora, where he died in 613. His bucellarii were absorbed into the imperial army. It removed the last great general of Maurice's generation.

events.title: Sisebut orders the conversion of the Jews
events.summary: Early in his reign Sisebut ordered the Jews of his kingdom to accept baptism or leave. Isidore commented that he acted 'with zeal, but not according to knowledge'; the Fourth Council of Toledo (633) condemned forced conversion yet insisted that those baptised must remain Christians, setting the pattern of Visigothic anti-Jewish legislation.

events.title: Coronation of Constantine III
events.summary: Heraclius's first wife Fabia-Eudokia died in August 612, three months after bearing a son, Heraclius Constantine. The infant was crowned co-emperor on 22 January 613, securing the dynasty during the darkest years of the Persian war.

events.title: Battle of Antioch
events.summary: Heraclius, his brother Theodore and cousin Nicetas tried to stop the Persian advance near Antioch in 613. After initial success they were beaten by Shahrbaraz and Shahin. Antioch, Damascus and Tarsus fell; Roman territory was cut in two, Syria and Palestine severed from Anatolia.

battle.significance: The decisive Roman defeat of the war's first phase; it opened Palestine and Egypt to the Persians.

events.title: Heraclius marries his niece Martina
events.summary: Heraclius married Martina, daughter of his sister Maria, against the protests of Patriarch Sergius and popular opinion, which saw the deformities and early deaths of several of their children as divine punishment. Martina accompanied him on his campaigns and her ambitions for her son Heraclonas shaped the succession crisis of 641.

events.title: Persians take Damascus
events.summary: After defeating Heraclius near Antioch in 613, Shahrbaraz split Roman Syria in two, occupied Damascus and pushed into Cilicia, taking Tarsus. Damascus surrendered with little fighting, a pattern repeated by many Syrian cities that preferred terms to sack.

events.title: Execution of Brunhild; Chlothar II reunites Francia
events.summary: Betrayed by the Austrasian nobles led by Pippin and Arnulf, the queen Brunhild, nearly seventy, was handed to Chlothar II, son of her enemy Fredegund. Charged with the deaths of ten kings, she was tortured for three days, paraded on a camel and torn apart tied to a wild horse. Chlothar became sole king of all the Franks.

events.title: Persian capture of Jerusalem
events.summary: After the city first submitted and then revolted, killing the Persian garrison, Shahrbaraz besieged Jerusalem for about three weeks and stormed it in May 614. Churches including the Holy Sepulchre were burned, thousands killed, and Patriarch Zacharias and the relic of the True Cross were carried off to Ctesiphon. The monk Antiochus Strategos's account lists bodies counted in the city.

sides.strength: Persian army with local Jewish auxiliaries

battle.significance: A religious catastrophe for the Christian empire; the True Cross became the symbol of Heraclius's war of revenge.

events.title: Edict of Paris
events.summary: Issued by Chlothar II on 18 October 614 after a council of 79 bishops, the edict confirmed canonical election of bishops, forbade appointment of royal judges from outside the region they governed, and abolished unjust new tolls. Historians long read it as a Merovingian Magna Carta for the aristocracy; recent work stresses continuity with royal practice.

events.title: Jewish administration of Jerusalem under the Persians
events.summary: After the capture of Jerusalem the Persians entrusted the city to its Jewish population, apparently led by a figure known from apocalyptic texts as Nehemiah ben Hushiel, and expelled Christians. Around 617 the Persians reversed course, restored Christian control under the abbot Modestus, who rebuilt the Holy Sepulchre, and expelled the Jews, a reversal that fuelled messianic literature such as the Sefer Zerubbabel.

events.title: Columbanus founds Bobbio
events.summary: Expelled from Burgundy by Brunhild and Theuderic II, Columbanus crossed to Lombard Italy and in 614 received from Agilulf the site of Bobbio in the Apennines, where he died on 23 November 615. Bobbio's library became one of the great repositories of late antique texts, preserving palimpsests of Cicero's De re publica and Fronto.

events.title: Sisebut's campaigns against Roman Spania
events.summary: The scholarly Visigothic king Sisebut (612-621) waged two campaigns against the Byzantine province around 614-615, taking Malaga and other cities. Isidore praises his clemency in ransoming captives. His Latin correspondence with the Roman patrician Caesarius over a peace settlement survives in the Epistolae Wisigoticae.

events.title: Persian army at Chalcedon; embassy to Khosrow
events.summary: Shahin's army marched across Anatolia to Chalcedon, opposite Constantinople, in 615. Heraclius parleyed with him and the Senate sent a letter (preserved in the Chronicon Paschale) asking Khosrow to accept Heraclius as his 'son'. Khosrow imprisoned the envoys. Heraclius's desperate measures followed: a silver coin made from church plate and cuts in official pay.

events.title: Heraclius introduces the silver hexagram
events.summary: To pay troops amid the collapse of revenue, Heraclius struck a heavy silver coin, the hexagram (6 grammata, about 6.5 g), from 615, bearing the legend Deus adiuta Romanis ('God help the Romans'). Official salaries were halved in 616, and in 622 church plate was melted down with Patriarch Sergius's consent.

events.title: Slav siege of Thessalonica under Chatzon
events.summary: A coalition of Slav tribes settled in Macedonia, the Drogubites, Sagudates, Belegezites, Baiunetes and Berzetes, attacked Thessalonica by land and sea with dugout boats lashed together around 615. Their leader Chatzon was captured and, according to the Miracles of St Demetrius, stoned to death by the city's women. The city held, credited to its patron saint.

sides.strength: coalition of five tribes with monoxyla

battle.significance: Shows Slav settlement as far as the Aegean coast.

events.title: Persian raids across Anatolia
events.summary: Between 615 and the early 620s Persian armies repeatedly crossed Asia Minor: Shahin reached Chalcedon in 615, and destruction layers at Sardis (with coins ending in 615-616), Pergamon, Ephesus and Ancyra (said to fall in 622) have been linked to these raids. They mark the beginning of the end of classical urban life in much of Anatolia.

events.title: End of the free bread distribution in Constantinople
events.summary: With Egypt about to fall, the free bread ration of Constantinople, instituted by Constantine in 332 on the model of Rome's annona, was first made chargeable at 3 nomismata per ration and then abolished altogether in 618. The capital's population, perhaps 400,000-500,000 under Justinian, shrank drastically in the following decades.

events.title: Avar siege of Thessalonica
events.summary: Encouraged by the Slavs after Chatzon's failure, the Avar khagan besieged Thessalonica with a large army and siege engines for 33 days around 617-618 before accepting gifts and withdrawing. The Miracles of St Demetrius describe refugees from Naissus, Serdica and other inland cities already sheltering inside.

sides.strength: Avar army with Slav allies and siege engines

battle.significance: The Danubian cities were already lost.

events.title: Heraclius plans to move the capital to Carthage
events.summary: With Egypt falling, the grain dole abolished and plague and famine in the capital, Heraclius loaded treasure onto ships bound for Carthage in 618-619. Nikephoros says the people and Patriarch Sergius persuaded him to swear in Hagia Sophia never to abandon the city; a storm sank the treasure ships.

events.title: Persian conquest of Egypt and fall of Alexandria
events.summary: Shahrbaraz invaded Egypt in 618 and took Alexandria in 619 after a siege; the city reportedly fell when a defector showed the Persians a way in through a canal or gate during the night, or with the help of a student from Afghanistan in the Enaton monasteries, as later sources say. Egypt, the empire's granary and richest province, remained under Persian rule for a decade.

sides.strength: garrison under Nicetas, who escaped to Cyprus

battle.significance: Deprived Constantinople of Egyptian grain and tax; the Sasanian empire briefly reached its greatest extent, recreating the Achaemenid western border.

events.title: Revolt of the exarch Eleutherius
events.summary: After the exarch John was murdered in Ravenna in 615, the eunuch Eleutherius punished the killers and crushed the revolt of John of Conza at Naples. In 619 he proclaimed himself emperor and set out to be crowned in Rome, but his own soldiers killed him at Castrum Luceoli and sent his head to Heraclius.

events.title: Heraclius takes the field against Persia
events.summary: After Easter, on 5 April 622, Heraclius left Constantinople carrying an icon of Christ 'not made by human hands', trained his army through the summer in Bithynia and Pontus, and in the autumn outmanoeuvred and defeated Shahrbaraz in the highlands of Cappadocia or Armenia. It was the first emperor-led campaign since Theodosius I.

events.title: The Hijra: Muhammad moves to Medina
events.summary: In September 622, persecuted at Mecca, Muhammad and his followers migrated to Yathrib, later Medina, where he became arbiter of its tribes; the so-called Constitution of Medina defined a community (umma) including Jewish clans. The year was later fixed as the start of the Islamic calendar under Umar.

events.title: Heraclius borrows the church treasures
events.summary: To finance the counter-offensive, Patriarch Sergius lent Heraclius the treasures of the churches; candelabra and plate were melted into gold nomismata and silver hexagrams, and pay was halved. The loan, a precedent for church-state crisis finance, was repaid after victory by the restoration of revenues.

events.title: The 'Avar surprise' at Heraclea
events.summary: Heraclius rode to Heraclea (Perinthus) on 5 June 623 to meet the Avar khagan for a peace ceremony with chariot races; the khagan had hidden troops to seize him. Heraclius escaped to Constantinople, reportedly carrying his crown under his arm, while the Avars plundered the suburbs, carrying off the regalia, the court's silver and, Nikephoros says, 270,000 captives. Peace was bought for 200,000 nomismata a year.
events.locName: Heraclea Perinthus and the suburbs of Constantinople

battle.significance: Showed the khagan's willingness to strike at Constantinople, a prelude to the joint siege of 626.

events.title: Samo and the revolt of the Wends
events.summary: Fredegar relates that the Frankish merchant Samo joined the Wends (western Slavs), who were rebelling against Avar exploitation, led them to victory and was made their king around 623, reigning 35 years with twelve Slav wives. His kingdom, probably centred in Moravia or Bohemia, is the first recorded Slavic polity.

events.title: Battle of Badr
events.summary: In March 624 (Ramadan 2 AH) about 313 Muslims from Medina, intending to intercept a Meccan caravan, defeated a relief force of around 950 Quraysh at the wells of Badr. Abu Jahl and other Meccan leaders were killed. The Qur'an (8) presents the victory as divine vindication, and it made Muhammad the leading power of the Hijaz.

battle.significance: Established the military credibility of the Medinan community.

events.title: Heraclius destroys the fire temple of Adur Gushnasp
events.summary: Leaving on 25 March 624, Heraclius marched through Armenia via Dvin and Nakhchivan to Atropatene. Khosrow II fled from Ganzak; Heraclius sacked the city and destroyed the great fire temple of Adur Gushnasp at Thebarmais (Takht-i Suleiman), one of the three holiest fires of Zoroastrianism, in revenge for Jerusalem. He wintered in Caucasian Albania.

events.title: Visigoths complete the conquest of Spania
events.summary: Sisebut took Malaga and other Roman towns in 614-621, and around 624-625 King Suinthila captured the last Roman positions on the south-east coast. Isidore of Seville praised him as the first king to rule all of Spain. Cartagena was destroyed. The empire, at war with Persia, sent no help.

events.title: Heraclius winters in Caucasian Albania
events.summary: After sacking Ganzak and Takht-i Suleiman, Heraclius withdrew north into Caucasian Albania for the winter of 624-625 rather than retreating home. Theophanes says he released 50,000 captives there; Movses Daskhurantsi describes his army's presence. From Albania he summoned allies from Lazica, Abasgia and Iberia.

events.title: Isidore's History of the Goths
events.summary: Isidore wrote his History of the Goths, Vandals and Suebi in a longer version ending with Suintila's expulsion of the Romans in 624-625. Its prefatory Laus Spaniae, praising Spain as the fairest of lands now wedded to the Goths, is a founding text of Spanish identity.

events.title: Battle of Uhud
events.summary: A Meccan army of some 3,000 under Abu Sufyan attacked Medina in March 625. The Muslims held the slope of Mount Uhud until archers left their post to plunder and the Meccan cavalry under Khalid ibn al-Walid broke their rear. Muhammad was wounded and his uncle Hamza killed, but the Meccans did not exploit their victory.

battle.significance: Khalid's first appearance as a cavalry commander.

events.title: Battle of the Sarus
events.summary: Returning west through Armenia after a season of manoeuvre against three Persian armies, Heraclius met Shahrbaraz across the Sarus river in Cilicia in late 625. When Roman troops crossing the bridge were cut up, Heraclius himself fought on the bridge and killed a giant Persian, throwing him into the river; Shahrbaraz is said to have admired him openly. The Persians withdrew.

battle.significance: Shahrbaraz then marched to Chalcedon to join the Avars for the siege of 626.

events.title: Heraclius defeats three Persian armies
events.summary: In spring 625 Khosrow sent Shahrbaraz, Shahin and Shahraplakan to trap Heraclius in the Caucasus. Heraclius beat Shahraplakan, who was killed, then Shahrbaraz, and evaded Shahin, before marching through Syunik and Arzanene and crossing the Taurus to the decisive encounter on the Sarus.

battle.significance: Heraclius kept his army intact deep in enemy territory.

events.title: Isidore's Etymologies
events.summary: Isidore of Seville's Etymologiae, an encyclopaedia in 20 books (as divided by his editor Braulio of Zaragoza) covering grammar, medicine, law, theology, animals, geography, warfare and agriculture through the supposed origins of words, was left unfinished at his death in 636. It became after the Bible the most copied book of the early Middle Ages, transmitting fragments of lost Roman learning.

events.title: Avar-Persian siege of Constantinople
events.summary: From 29 July to 7 August 626 the Avar khagan, with perhaps 80,000 Avars, Slavs, Bulgars and Gepids and siege towers, attacked the Theodosian Walls while Shahrbaraz's army watched from Chalcedon, unable to cross. Heraclius stayed in the East, having sent troops home; the defence was led by the magister Bonus and Patriarch Sergius, who carried icons of the Virgin around the walls. On 7 August the Roman fleet destroyed the Slav monoxyla attempting to ferry Persians and attack the sea walls in the Golden Horn; the khagan burned his engines and withdrew.

sides.strength: 12,000 cavalry sent by Heraclius plus citizens and fleet; commander the magister Bonus
80,000 (Chronicon Paschale) Avars, Slavs, Bulgars and Gepids; Persian army of Shahrbaraz at Chalcedon
sides.losses: heavy, especially among Slavs in the Golden Horn

battle.significance: The turning point of the war: the capital survived, the Avar-Persian coalition collapsed, and Heraclius was free to strike Persia's heart.

events.title: Theodore defeats Shahin
events.summary: While Shahrbaraz waited at Chalcedon for the Avar assault, Heraclius sent his brother Theodore against Shahin's army, which was defeated in 626, Theophanes says with help from a hailstorm. Shahin died soon afterwards, and Khosrow, enraged, had his body preserved in salt to abuse it. Constantinople was thus spared a second Persian army on the Asian shore.

battle.significance: Removed one of the two Persian armies converging on Constantinople.

events.title: Battle of Nineveh
events.summary: Heraclius invaded Assyria in autumn 627 and on 12 December 627 fought the Persian army of Rhahzadh near the ruins of Nineveh. In an eleven-hour battle in fog, Heraclius, on his horse Dorkon, is said to have killed Rhahzadh in single combat and two other champions; the Persian army was destroyed, losing 6,000 men and 28 standards (Theophanes). Heraclius then marched on Khosrow's palace at Dastagird.

battle.significance: The decisive battle of the last Roman-Persian war; within weeks Khosrow II was overthrown and Persia sued for peace.

events.title: Siege of Tbilisi with the Western Turks
events.summary: Heraclius allied with the Western Turkic Khaganate, whose forces under Böri Shad (a relative of the yabghu Tong) broke through the Caspian Gates at Derbent in 626 and joined Heraclius before Tbilisi in 627. Heraclius met the Turkic leader (Ziebel in Theophanes), placed his own crown on his head and promised his daughter Eudocia in marriage. The defenders mocked the Turks; the siege failed and the Turks withdrew for the winter, but left 40,000 men with Heraclius.

battle.significance: The siege failed, but the Turkic alliance gave Heraclius the manpower for his winter invasion of Mesopotamia.

events.title: Siege of Medina: the Battle of the Trench
events.summary: In 627 a confederacy of Quraysh and Bedouin allies, perhaps 10,000 strong, besieged Medina, which Muhammad had protected with a trench, a stratagem tradition credits to the Persian convert Salman. After two weeks of stalemate and bad weather the coalition dispersed; the Jewish tribe of Qurayza, accused of treason, was then destroyed.

battle.significance: Last Meccan offensive.

events.title: Heraclius sacks Dastagird
events.summary: After Nineveh, Heraclius marched on Khosrow's favourite residence at Dastagird, which Khosrow abandoned. The Romans plundered its treasures, menageries and paradises, freed captives including Edessenes, and recovered 300 Roman standards taken over the previous decades before burning the palace in January 628. Khosrow's flight destroyed his prestige and precipitated his fall.

events.title: Overthrow of Khosrow II and peace with Persia
events.summary: Khosrow II was deposed in a palace coup around 23-25 February 628 and killed by order of his son Kavad II, who made peace with Heraclius in April: return of all Roman territory, prisoners and the True Cross. Heraclius's dispatch announcing the death of the 'God-hating' Khosrow was read from the ambo of Hagia Sophia on 15 May 628.

events.title: Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya
events.summary: In March 628 Muhammad led about 1,400 followers toward Mecca for pilgrimage and, halted at al-Hudaybiyya, concluded a ten-year truce with the Quraysh allowing pilgrimage the following year. Although the terms disappointed his followers, the truce freed him to conquer the Jewish oasis of Khaybar and attract tribes to his cause.

events.title: Death of Kavad II and the Persian plague
events.summary: Kavad II (Sheroe), who had killed his father and some seventeen brothers to secure his throne, died in September 628 after a reign of about seven months, apparently during a plague that ravaged Mesopotamia. His seven-year-old son Ardashir III succeeded under the regent Mah-Adhur Gushnasp, inaugurating four years of chaos in which at least eight rulers claimed the throne.

events.title: Heraclius's triumphant return to Constantinople
events.summary: In September 628 Heraclius returned from six years of campaigning and was met at Hieria on the Asian shore by his son Constantine and the people of the capital with olive branches and candles. Theophanes says four elephants, perhaps from the Persian royal stables, were paraded in the Hippodrome.

events.title: Heraclius adopts the title basileus
events.summary: In a law of March 629 Heraclius styled himself pistos en Christo basileus ('faithful in Christ, emperor') instead of the traditional Latin imperator Caesar Augustus rendered in Greek. Basileus, the old Greek word for king, which Romans had long avoided for themselves, became the official imperial title; Greek fully displaced Latin in government in these decades.

events.title: Heraclius and Shahrbaraz meet at Arabissus
events.summary: In July 629 Heraclius met Shahrbaraz, the Persian general still occupying Egypt and Syria, at Arabissus in Cappadocia. They agreed on the evacuation of Roman territory, and Heraclius apparently backed Shahrbaraz's bid for the Persian throne; Shahrbaraz's son, baptised Niketas, became a Roman patrician and Shahrbaraz's daughter may have married Heraclius's son Theodosius.

events.title: Battle of Mu'ta
events.summary: A Muslim force of some 3,000 sent north by Muhammad met Roman troops and their Arab allies (Ghassanid, Lakhm, Judham, Bali) at Mu'ta, east of the Dead Sea, in September 629. The three successive Muslim commanders, Zayd ibn Haritha, Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and Abd Allah ibn Rawaha, were killed; Khalid ibn al-Walid extracted the survivors.

sides.losses: leaders killed; small number of others

sides.strength: 100,000-200,000 (Muslim tradition, impossible); local garrison and Arab federates under the vicarius Theodore

battle.significance: The first clash between Rome and the new Islamic state; Theophanes records it as a Roman victory, Muslim sources as an honourable withdrawal.

events.title: Dagobert I sole king of the Franks
events.summary: On the death of Chlothar II in 629, his son Dagobert, already king of Austrasia since 623, took Neustria and Burgundy and moved to Paris. The last Merovingian to rule effectively, he patronised Saint-Denis, issued coinage at many mints, and appears in Fredegar receiving Heraclius's warning about a circumcised people.

events.title: George of Pisidia's Heraclias
events.summary: The deacon George of Pisidia, a court poet in Patriarch Sergius's circle, composed the Heraclias in 628-629 celebrating the victory over Khosrow as Heraclius's labours of Hercules. With his earlier Expeditio Persica and Bellum Avaricum, these classicising iambic poems are contemporary witnesses to the war.

events.title: Muslim conquest of Mecca
events.summary: Claiming the Quraysh had broken the Hudaybiyya truce, Muhammad marched on Mecca with about 10,000 men in January 630 (Ramadan 8 AH). Abu Sufyan submitted and the city fell almost without fighting; the idols of the Kaaba were destroyed and a general amnesty granted. Within weeks Muhammad defeated the Hawazin at Hunayn.

events.title: Heraclius restores the True Cross to Jerusalem
events.summary: On 21 March 630 (some argue 629) Heraclius entered Jerusalem in procession with the True Cross, recovered from Shahrbaraz's custody, and restored it to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. Later legend has him unable to pass the gate on horseback in imperial regalia until he dismounted and walked barefoot. The feast of the Exaltation of the Cross acquired this story.
events.locName: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem

events.title: Shahrbaraz seizes the Persian throne
events.summary: With Roman support Shahrbaraz marched on Ctesiphon, killed the boy king Ardashir III on 27 April 630 and took the throne, the only Sasanian king not of the house of Sasan. After about forty days he was murdered by nobles at a parade on 9 June 630, his body dragged through the streets.

events.title: Expedition to Tabuk
events.summary: In autumn 630 Muhammad led a large army, tradition says 30,000, north to Tabuk on rumours of a Roman offensive. No battle followed, but the Christian ruler of Ayla (Aila) and the communities of Adhruh, Jarba and Maqna submitted and agreed to pay tribute, the first Muslim agreements with communities on the Roman frontier.

events.title: Queen Boran
events.summary: Khosrow II's daughter Boran became the first woman to rule Persia in her own right in June 630. She remitted taxes, sent the catholicos Ishoyahb II on an embassy to Heraclius at Aleppo or Beroea to confirm peace, and struck silver drachms with her own portrait. She died or was deposed in 631.

events.title: The Chronicon Paschale
events.summary: An anonymous cleric in Constantinople, probably close to Patriarch Sergius, compiled an Easter chronicle from Adam to 628, ending with the full text of Heraclius's dispatch announcing the fall of Khosrow. Its entries for 600-628 are an independent contemporary record of Phocas's reign and the Avar siege of 626.

events.title: Theophylact Simocatta writes his History
events.summary: Encouraged by Patriarch Sergius, the Egyptian-born official Theophylact Simocatta wrote eight books on the reign of Maurice (582-602) in the late 620s or 630s, in elaborately classicising Greek. It is the last secular history in the Procopian tradition; after it no Byzantine historiography survives until the ninth century.

events.title: Azarmidokht and the murder of Farrukh Hormizd
events.summary: Boran's sister Azarmidokht ruled briefly in 631. When the powerful spahbed Farrukh Hormizd proposed marriage, she had him killed; his son Rustam Farrokhzad marched from Khurasan, took Ctesiphon and blinded and killed her. The episode exposed the feud between the Pahlav nobility of the north-east and the Parsig faction.

events.title: Battle of Wogastisburg
events.summary: After Wends killed Frankish merchants, Dagobert I sent three armies against Samo in 631-632. The Austrasian army was defeated after a three-day battle at the fortress of Wogastisburg, whose location is unknown; Fredegar blames the Austrasians' unwillingness to fight for a Neustrian-dominated king.

battle.significance: Secured Samo's realm.

events.title: Sisenand deposes Suintila
events.summary: Suintila, who had expelled the last Romans from Spain, was overthrown in 631 by Sisenand with Frankish help; Fredegar says Sisenand promised Dagobert a gold dish weighing 500 pounds from the Gothic treasury, which the Goths later refused to hand over. The Fourth Council of Toledo condemned Suintila and his family.

events.title: Cyrus sent to Alexandria; persecution of the Copts
events.summary: Heraclius appointed Cyrus, bishop of Phasis, as Chalcedonian patriarch of Alexandria in 631 with civil authority over Egypt. Coptic tradition remembers ten years of persecution under 'al-Muqawqis', the name Arab sources give him: the Coptic patriarch Benjamin I fled to Upper Egypt and his brother Menas was drowned. The alienation of Egypt's majority eased the Arab conquest.

events.title: Accession of Yazdegerd III
events.summary: A grandson of Khosrow II, found in hiding at Istakhr, was crowned there as Yazdegerd III in June 632, aged about eight, the choice of a compromise between noble factions. The Zoroastrian Yazdegerdi calendar era still counts from his accession (16 June 632). He would preside over the Arab conquest and die a fugitive at Merv in 651.

events.title: Death of Muhammad
events.summary: Muhammad died at Medina on 8 June 632 (traditional date). Abu Bakr was chosen as his successor (khalifa) and spent 632-633 suppressing the Ridda, the defection of Arabian tribes, uniting the peninsula under Medina for the first time and creating the forces that would be turned on Syria and Iraq.

events.title: The Ridda wars
events.summary: After Muhammad's death many Arabian tribes stopped paying the alms tax or followed rival prophets: Tulayha among the Asad, Musaylima among the Hanifa of Yamama, Sajah of the Tamim and al-Aswad in Yemen. Abu Bakr sent eleven columns, Khalid ibn al-Walid's being the most effective, and by 633 all Arabia was under Medinan control, creating the united military force that then turned north.

events.title: Battle of Yamama (Aqraba)
events.summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid defeated the Banu Hanifa of the 'false prophet' Musaylima at Aqraba in Yamama around December 632, after the Muslim army nearly broke. The last of the Hanifa were cut down in a walled orchard, the 'Garden of Death', where Musaylima was killed. Heavy losses among Qur'an reciters are traditionally said to have prompted the first collection of the Qur'an.

battle.significance: Decisive battle of the Ridda.

events.title: Heraclius orders the baptism of Jews
events.summary: Around 632 Heraclius decreed the compulsory baptism of Jews throughout the empire. The Doctrina Jacobi nuper baptizati, set in Carthage in 634, describes forcibly baptised Jews and contains one of the earliest references to an Arab prophet. Fredegar's story that Heraclius foresaw ruin from a circumcised people and urged Dagobert to baptise the Jews reflects the same policy.

events.title: Battle of Walaja
events.summary: In May 633 Khalid met a Persian army reinforced by Christian Arabs of the Bakr ibn Wa'il at Walaja on the lower Euphrates. Tradition says he hid cavalry behind ridges and enveloped the Persians from both flanks after the frontal fight, a double envelopment often compared with Cannae.

battle.significance: Classic of Khalid's generalship in the Arabic tradition.

events.title: Battle of Ullais
events.summary: Weeks after Walaja Khalid defeated Persians and Christian Arabs again at Ullais on the Euphrates. Tradition says he vowed to make the river run with enemy blood, had prisoners beheaded over the water for a day and diverted a canal to complete the oath, hence its name 'River of Blood'.

battle.significance: Cleared the road to al-Hira.

events.title: Monoenergism: the Pact of Union at Alexandria
events.summary: Cyrus, Heraclius's appointee as patriarch of Alexandria, united the Chalcedonians and the Theodosian miaphysites on 3 June 633 on the formula that Christ acted through 'one theandric energy', a compromise devised by Patriarch Sergius and the emperor. The monk Sophronius protested, and in 634 Sergius forbade further talk of energies.

events.title: Fourth Council of Toledo
events.summary: Presided over by Isidore of Seville and opening on 5 December 633 with 62 bishops, the council unified the liturgy of Spain and Septimania, ordered cathedral schools, condemned forced conversion while binding converts, and in canon 75 defined the kingship as elective by nobles and bishops, anathematising rebels against an anointed king.

events.title: Battle of the Chains (Kazima)
events.summary: Khalid's first battle against Persia, fought at Kazima near the head of the Gulf in spring 633. Tradition says the Persian commander Hormozd chained his men together to prevent flight and was killed by Khalid in single combat. Modern historians treat the chain story as etymology for the battle's name.

battle.significance: Opened the conquest of Iraq.

events.title: Surrender of al-Hira
events.summary: The old Lakhmid capital of al-Hira, a wealthy Christian Arab city, surrendered to Khalid in 633 on terms, paying a fixed annual tribute. Its notables' treaty served as a model for later capitulations in Iraq.

battle.significance: First major Iraqi city taken.

events.title: The Psephos of Sergius
events.summary: After the monk Sophronius protested at Alexandria against the Pact of Union's 'one energy' formula, Patriarch Sergius issued a ruling (psephos) in 633 forbidding anyone to speak of either one or two energies in Christ. It shifted the controversy to the question of wills and led to the Ekthesis.

events.title: Armenian church accepts union at Theodosiopolis
events.summary: At a council at Theodosiopolis (Karin) around 631-633 the Armenian catholicos Ezr accepted communion with the imperial church on Heraclius's Chalcedonian-monoenergist terms, receiving estates in return. Armenian tradition later condemned Ezr; the union collapsed under the Arab conquest.

events.title: Battle of Firaz
events.summary: In January 634, at Firaz on the Euphrates where Roman and Persian territory met, Khalid is said to have defeated a joint force of Romans, Persians and Christian Arabs. Tradition's claim of 100,000 enemy dead is impossible, and some historians doubt a Roman-Persian alliance at all; it marks the end of Khalid's Iraqi campaign before his march to Syria.

battle.significance: Literary climax of Khalid's Iraq campaign.

events.title: Battle of Dathin
events.summary: Near Gaza on 4 February 634, an Arab army under Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan defeated a Roman force under the candidatus Sergius, perhaps dux of Palestine; Sergius was killed. The Syriac Chronicle of 640 by Thomas the Presbyter notes 'a battle between the Romans and the Arabs of Muhammad' with 4,000 Palestinian villagers killed, the first securely dated event of the conquest in a non-Muslim source.

sides.strength: Arab army under Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan
local Roman forces under the candidatus Sergius
sides.losses: commander killed; 4,000 villagers killed (Thomas the Presbyter)

battle.significance: Opened southern Palestine to the conquerors.

events.title: Khalid ibn al-Walid's desert crossing
events.summary: Ordered by Abu Bakr to reinforce the armies in Syria, Khalid led perhaps 500-800 picked men from Iraq across the waterless desert between Qurraqir and Suwa in about five days, watering camels in advance and slaughtering some to drink the water stored in their stomachs, according to tradition. He appeared near Damascus at Marj Rahit around Easter 634, took Bosra and joined the other commanders.

events.title: Battle of Ajnadayn
events.summary: The united Arab armies, including Khalid, defeated a Roman army in southern Palestine at Ajnadayn, between Ramla and Beit Guvrin, traditionally on 30 July 634. Arab tradition names its commander as 'Artabun'; Theodore, Heraclius's brother, may have been in command in the region. Palestine's open country fell to the invaders; cities held out behind their walls.

sides.strength: Roman field army of Palestine, size unknown (Arab sources: 100,000)

battle.significance: The first major pitched-battle victory of the conquests in Syria.

events.title: Death of Abu Bakr; Umar becomes caliph
events.summary: Abu Bakr died at Medina on 23 August 634, having nominated Umar ibn al-Khattab, who took the title amir al-mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful). One of Umar's first acts, according to tradition, was to remove Khalid from supreme command in Syria in favour of Abu Ubayda.

events.title: Battle of the Bridge
events.summary: In autumn 634 Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi crossed the Euphrates by a bridge of boats near al-Hira to attack a Persian army under Bahman Jadhuyih with war elephants. Abu Ubayd was trampled by a white elephant; panic on the bridge drowned many, and only al-Muthanna's rearguard saved a remnant. Tradition gives 4,000 Muslim losses, the worst Arab defeat in Iraq.

battle.significance: Last major Persian victory over the Arabs.

events.title: Surrender of Bostra
events.summary: Bostra, capital of Provincia Arabia and the first great Roman city to fall in Syria, surrendered in 634 after a brief siege by Shurahbil ibn Hasana, joined by Khalid after his desert march, on terms of tribute per head and per measure of land.

battle.significance: First provincial capital lost.

events.title: Pope Honorius's letter on 'one will'
events.summary: Replying to Sergius, Pope Honorius I wrote in 634 approving silence on energies and confessing 'one will' (unam voluntatem) in Christ. The Sixth Ecumenical Council (680-681) anathematised him as a heretic, a condemnation that later became a key argument against papal infallibility in the debates of 1870.

events.title: Sophronius patriarch of Jerusalem
events.summary: Elected patriarch of Jerusalem in 634, the Damascene monk Sophronius sent a long synodical letter defending two natural energies in Christ. His Christmas sermon of 634 laments that the Saracens prevented the faithful from going to Bethlehem, one of the earliest Christian references to the Arab invasion.

events.title: Battle of Fahl (Pella)
events.summary: Roman troops who had flooded the Jordan valley around Baysan to block the Arabs were defeated near Pella (Fahl) in January 635, a battle the tradition calls 'the Day of the Mud'. Jordan and the Galilee fell, and the road to Damascus was open.

battle.significance: Secured the Jordan valley and isolated Damascus.

events.title: Battle of Marj al-Saffar
events.summary: A Roman force advancing to relieve Damascus was defeated by Khalid and the Arab commanders at Marj al-Saffar south of the city, probably in January 635, opening the blockade of Damascus. Later tradition embroidered it with the story of Umm Hakim, a bride who killed seven Romans with a tent pole on her wedding day.

battle.significance: Isolated Damascus.

events.title: Surrender of Damascus
events.summary: After a six-month blockade, Damascus surrendered in September 635 on terms negotiated, according to tradition, by Mansur ibn Sarjun, the city's fiscal official and grandfather of John of Damascus: security of life, property and churches in return for tribute. Khalid is said to have entered by force at the east gate at the same time Abu Ubayda entered by treaty at the west.

battle.significance: Gave the conquerors the main city of interior Syria; abandoned briefly before Yarmuk, it was reoccupied in 636 and became the Umayyad capital in 661.

events.title: Battle of al-Buwayb
events.summary: Months after the Bridge, al-Muthanna ibn Haritha with reinforcements including Christian Arabs of the Namir defeated a Persian army under Mihran at al-Buwayb near the later site of Kufa, restoring the Arab position in Iraq before Qadisiyya.

battle.significance: Recovered from the Bridge.

events.title: Kubrat rebels against the Avars
events.summary: Kubrat, lord of the Onogundur Bulgars, who had been raised at the court of Constantinople, threw off Avar rule around 635 and allied with Heraclius, who made him a patrician. His 'Old Great Bulgaria' north of the Black Sea broke the Avars' hold on the Pontic steppe. The treasure of Malaya Pereshchepina, with rings naming a patrikios Kubrat, may come from his burial.

events.title: Death of Isidore of Seville
events.summary: Isidore died at Seville on 4 April 636 after 36 years as bishop. His deathbed public penance is described by his disciple Redemptus. Braulio of Zaragoza drew up the catalogue of his works, and the Eighth Council of Toledo (653) called him 'the outstanding teacher of our age'.

events.title: Battle of the Yarmuk
events.summary: Heraclius gathered a great army in 636 under the Armenian Vahan, the sakellarios Theodore Trithyrios, and the Ghassanid king Jabala ibn al-Ayham, which forced the Arabs to abandon Damascus and Emesa. The Arabs concentrated on the plateau near the Yarmuk river, and after weeks of skirmishing and some six days of battle, traditionally ending on 20 August 636, the Roman army was routed, many trapped against the ravine of the Wadi al-Ruqqad.
events.locName: Yarmuk river and Wadi al-Ruqqad, Golan / Hauran

sides.strength: perhaps 15,000-40,000 (Arab sources: 100,000-240,000), incl. Armenians and Ghassanids

battle.significance: One of the most consequential battles in history: it ended Roman rule in Syria and Palestine after seven centuries and opened the way to Egypt and Mesopotamia.

events.title: Heraclius abandons Syria
events.summary: After the Yarmuk, Heraclius left Antioch for Constantinople. Arab tradition has him say from a height on his way north: 'Peace be upon you, Syria, and what a fine country this is for the enemy.' He withdrew garrisons behind the Taurus and created a depopulated buffer, a zone of raids that would define the Arab-Byzantine frontier for three centuries.

events.title: Surrender of Emesa
events.summary: Emesa (Hims) surrendered to Abu Ubayda in 636 on payment of tribute. When Heraclius's great army advanced before the Yarmuk, the Arabs evacuated it, and al-Baladhuri says they returned the tribute because they could no longer protect the city; Emesa reopened its gates after the battle.

events.title: Battle of al-Qadisiyya
events.summary: The decisive battle for Iraq. Yazdegerd III's general Rustam Farrokhzad, with an army including war elephants, faced the Arab army of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas near al-Hira over three or four days of fighting, known in the tradition as the Day of Armath, the Day of Aghwath, the Day of Imas and the Night of Clamour. Rustam was killed and the Persian army destroyed. The road to Ctesiphon lay open.

battle.significance: Ended Sasanian rule in Mesopotamia.

events.title: Rothari becomes king of the Lombards
events.summary: Rothari, the Arian duke of Brescia, became king in 636 after Arioald, marrying Theodelinda's daughter Gundeperga. He would conquer Liguria from the Romans and issue the Edict of Rothari (643), the first written Lombard law code.

events.title: Fall of Ctesiphon (al-Mada'in)
events.summary: After Qadisiyya Sa'd besieged the western twin city of Veh-Ardashir until the Persians abandoned it; Yazdegerd III fled east and in March 637 the Arabs crossed the Tigris and took Ctesiphon itself. The great hall of the Taq-i Kisra was used as a mosque and the booty, including the jewelled 'Spring of Khosrow' carpet cut up for distribution, became proverbial.

battle.significance: Loss of the Sasanian capital.

events.title: Surrender of Jerusalem to Umar
events.summary: Blockaded since 636, Jerusalem under Patriarch Sophronius surrendered in 637 or early 638 on condition that the caliph Umar come in person to accept it. Tradition tells of Umar arriving in a simple patched cloak, touring the Holy Sepulchre but praying outside so that Muslims would not claim it, and clearing the Temple Mount. Sophronius, who had lamented the 'Saracens' in his Christmas sermon of 634, died soon after.

battle.significance: The holy city of Christianity passed to Muslim rule, which lasted, apart from 1099-1187 and 1229-1244, until 1917.

events.title: Battle of Jalula
events.summary: Late in 637 the Persian army that had retreated from Ctesiphon entrenched behind a ditch and caltrops at Jalula on the road to the Zagros. After a long siege Hashim ibn Utba's army broke the position. Tradition calls it 'the victory of victories' for its booty; Yazdegerd fled from Hulwan to the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia was lost to Persia.

battle.significance: Drove the Sasanians from Mesopotamia.

events.title: Battle of Hazir and the fall of Chalcis
events.summary: Khalid ibn al-Walid destroyed a Roman force under Menas at Hazir near Chalcis (Qinnasrin) in 637; Chalcis then surrendered. Umar is said to have exclaimed that Khalid had made himself commander, and soon afterwards dismissed him for good.

battle.significance: Opened northern Syria.

events.title: Fall of Aleppo and Antioch
events.summary: Abu Ubayda's armies took Beroea (Aleppo) and then Antioch in 637, the great city of the East surrendering on terms that allowed those who wished to leave to go. Heraclius had already left for Constantinople with the words, as the Arabic tradition has it, 'Farewell Syria, a long farewell'. The Taurus became the new frontier.

events.title: John Kateas buys off the Arabs in Osrhoene
events.summary: John Kateas, governor of Osrhoene, agreed in 637-638 to pay the Arab commander Iyad ibn Ghanm 100,000 nomismata a year to spare Mesopotamia. Heraclius, judging this treason, dismissed and exiled him and sent the general Ptolemaios; the tribute stopped and Iyad conquered the region in 639.

events.title: Plague of Amwas
events.summary: A wave of the Justinianic plague struck the Arab armies in Syria and Palestine in 638-639, named for their camp at Emmaus (Amwas). Arab tradition says 25,000 died, including the commanders Abu Ubayda and Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, whose brother Mu'awiya succeeded him in Syria.

events.title: The Ecthesis: Monotheletism decreed
events.summary: Drafted by Patriarch Sergius and posted in the narthex of Hagia Sophia in 638, Heraclius's Ecthesis forbade discussion of 'one or two energies' and declared that Christ had a single will. Councils in Constantinople accepted it; Rome rejected it, and its condemnation at the Sixth Ecumenical Council in 680-681 made Heraclius a posthumous heretic in Chalcedonian eyes.

events.title: Foundation of Kufa and Basra
events.summary: The Arab armies in Iraq were settled in purpose-built garrison cities (amsar): Basra near the Gulf, founded by Utba ibn Ghazwan around 635-638, and Kufa on the Euphrates near al-Hira, laid out by Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas in 638 with a central mosque and tribal quarters. Living apart from the conquered population, they became the political and intellectual centres of early Islam.

events.title: Amr ibn al-As invades Egypt
events.summary: With perhaps 4,000 men and only the reluctant approval of Umar, Amr ibn al-As crossed from Palestine into Egypt in December 639, reaching al-Arish at the Feast of Sacrifice. He took Pelusium after a siege of about a month, then Bilbays, and marched on the fortress of Babylon at the apex of the Delta.

events.title: Arab conquest of Roman Mesopotamia
events.summary: After Antioch and northern Syria fell in 637-638, Iyad ibn Ghanm crossed the Euphrates and in 639-640 took the cities of the Jazira, Raqqa, Edessa, Harran, Amida, Dara and Resaina, mostly by treaty. Edessa surrendered on terms that the Arabs would keep its walls and churches, and pay tribute.

events.title: Fall of Pelusium
events.summary: After crossing Sinai, Amr ibn al-As besieged Pelusium (al-Farama), the gateway to the Delta, for about a month and took it around January 640. Coptic villagers were said to have aided the Arabs; John of Nikiu blames Roman governors' quarrels and the hatred aroused by Cyrus's persecution.

battle.significance: Opened the Delta to invasion.

events.title: Battle of Heliopolis
events.summary: Reinforced by 4,000 or more men under al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Amr drew the Roman army of Egypt under Theodore into battle near Heliopolis in July 640, using a concealed detachment that attacked from the rear. The Roman force broke; part fled to the fortress of Babylon, part to Alexandria.

sides.strength: Roman field army of Egypt under Theodore, perhaps 15,000-20,000

battle.significance: Decided the fate of Egypt in the field; the rest was sieges and negotiation.

events.title: Arab sack of Dvin
events.summary: An Arab army from Mesopotamia crossed into Armenia and sacked Dvin, the capital of Persarmenia, on 6 October 640 according to Sebeos, killing and enslaving thousands. It was the first Arab incursion into Armenia, where Heraclius's ally the Armenian commander Theodore Rshtuni would lead resistance.

battle.significance: Opened the Arab-Byzantine contest for Armenia.

events.title: Fall of Caesarea Maritima
events.summary: The capital of Palaestina Prima, supplied by sea, held out for years against blockade until Mu'awiya took it by storm in 640 or 641, reportedly guided by a Jewish informer through an aqueduct. The last Roman city in Palestine fell; the tradition says 7,000 defenders were killed.

battle.significance: Completed the conquest of Palestine.

events.title: Umar's diwan: the register of stipends
events.summary: Umar organised the distribution of conquest revenues through a diwan, a register of fighters and their families paid annual stipends graded by precedence in Islam, from 12,000 dirhams for Muhammad's widow Aisha down to a few hundred for late converts. The system, adapted from Roman and Persian bureaucratic practice, bound the Arab armies to the state.

events.title: Arab raid on the Fayyum
events.summary: In spring 640 Amr sent a column into the Fayyum, where Roman commanders failed to coordinate; John of Nikiu describes the slaughter of the garrison of Bahnasa and the flight of the general John of the Maros, killed and fished out of the Nile. The Arabs then returned to face the main Roman army at Heliopolis.

events.title: Pope John IV condemns the Ekthesis
events.summary: A Roman synod under Pope John IV in January 641 condemned Monotheletism and the Ekthesis. Heraclius, dying, wrote to the pope disowning the Ekthesis as Sergius's work. The dispute would escalate under Constans II into the Lateran Synod of 649 and the trial of Pope Martin and Maximus the Confessor.

events.title: Death of Heraclius
events.summary: Heraclius died on 11 February 641 aged about 66, of a disease Nikephoros describes as dropsy, which some contemporaries saw as punishment for his uncanonical marriage to his niece Martina. He left the empire jointly to Constantine III, his son by Fabia-Eudocia, and Heraclonas, his son by Martina, with Martina to be honoured as 'mother and empress'. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles.

events.title: Surrender of the fortress of Babylon
events.summary: Besieged since September 640, the Roman fortress of Babylon (Old Cairo), guarding the Nile crossing at the head of the Delta, surrendered on 9 April 641, Easter Monday, after news of Heraclius's death and the recall of the patriarch Cyrus had undermined resistance. Amr founded the camp-city of Fustat beside it.

battle.significance: Gave the Arabs control of the Nile and Upper Egypt; Fustat became the capital of Islamic Egypt.

events.title: Treaty of Alexandria
events.summary: Restored to Alexandria by the new regime, Patriarch Cyrus agreed with Amr on 8 November 641 to surrender Egypt: an armistice of eleven months, a poll tax of two dinars per adult man, protection of churches, and evacuation of the Roman army by sea. The last Roman troops left Alexandria in September 642, ending nearly 700 years of Roman rule in Egypt.

events.title: Constantine III, Heraclonas and the fall of Martina
events.summary: Constantine III, consumptive, died after a reign of about three months (May 641), amid rumours that Martina had poisoned him. Martina and Heraclonas governed briefly, but the army under Valentinus and the people of Constantinople forced the coronation of Constantine III's son Constans II in September, and in late 641 Martina's tongue and Heraclonas's nose were slit and they were exiled to Rhodes, the first use of such mutilation to disqualify a ruler.

people.name: Romulus
people.summary: Legendary founder and first king of Rome, son of Mars and the Vestal Rhea Silvia, suckled with his twin Remus by a she-wolf; tradition gives him a reign of 753-716 and a disappearance in a storm on the Campus Martius, after which he was worshipped as Quirinus.
people.death: vanished in a storm during a review on the Campus Martius (legend); alternatively murdered by senators

people.name: Numa Pompilius
people.summary: Second king in the Roman tradition, a Sabine from Cures credited with founding Rome's religious institutions under the guidance of the nymph Egeria.

people.name: Servius Tullius
people.summary: Sixth king, of slave or captive birth in Roman tradition and identified in an Etruscan tradition (Claudius' Lyons speech) with the adventurer Mastarna; credited with the census, centuriate assembly, tribes, the temple of Diana on the Aventine and a city wall.
people.death: murdered at the instigation of Tarquinius Superbus and Tullia

people.name: Tarquinius Superbus
people.summary: Seventh and last king of Rome in tradition, a tyrant who extended Roman power over Latium, began the Capitoline temple and was expelled c. 509, after which he sought restoration through Veii, Tarquinii, Porsenna and the Latins before dying in exile at Cumae.
people.death: died in exile at Cumae, at the court of Aristodemus

people.name: Lucretia
people.fullName: Lucretia, wife of L. Tarquinius Collatinus
people.summary: Roman matron whose rape by Sextus Tarquinius and subsequent suicide, after summoning her father and husband to swear vengeance, triggered the expulsion of the kings.

people.name: Lucius Junius Brutus
people.summary: Legendary liberator of Rome and first consul, Tarquin's nephew who feigned dullness (brutus) to survive, led the revolt after Lucretia's death, executed his own sons for plotting a Tarquin restoration, and died in single combat with Arruns Tarquinius at the Silva Arsia.
people.death: killed in a cavalry duel with Arruns Tarquinius at the Silva Arsia

people.name: Tarquinius Collatinus
people.summary: Husband of Lucretia and colleague of Brutus as first consul; forced to resign and go into exile at Lavinium because he bore the hated name of Tarquin.

people.name: Publius Valerius Publicola
people.summary: Co-founder of the Republic, four times consul, who demolished his own grand house on the Velia when suspected of aiming at kingship, lowered the fasces before the people and is credited with the first law of appeal (provocatio).
people.death: died poor and was buried at public expense within the city

people.name: Lars Porsenna
people.summary: Etruscan king of Clusium who attacked Rome c. 508, nominally to restore Tarquin; Roman legend has him withdraw out of admiration for Roman heroism, but Tacitus and Pliny indicate he captured the city and imposed terms.

people.name: Horatius Cocles
people.summary: One-eyed (cocles) hero who held the Pons Sublicius against Porsenna's army while it was demolished behind him, then swam the Tiber in armour.

people.name: Mucius Scaevola
people.summary: Young Roman who infiltrated Porsenna's camp to kill him, stabbed the wrong man, and when captured thrust his right hand into a brazier to show Roman contempt for pain, earning the name Scaevola ('left-handed').

people.name: Cloelia
people.summary: Roman girl given as hostage to Porsenna who led other girls in escaping across the Tiber; returned by Rome under the treaty, she was released by Porsenna in admiration with a group of hostages of her choosing.

people.name: Aristodemus of Cumae
people.summary: Cumaean general who defeated the Etruscans in 524 and, leading the Cumaean contingent, destroyed Arruns Porsenna's army at Aricia c. 504; he then seized power as tyrant of Cumae and sheltered the exiled Tarquinius Superbus.
people.death: killed in an uprising of returned exiles

people.name: Aulus Postumius Albus
people.summary: Dictator who won the battle of Lake Regillus against the Latins (499 or 496), taking the cognomen Regillensis; he vowed the temples of Castor and of Ceres, Liber and Libera.

people.name: Octavius Mamilius

roles.t: Leader (dictator?) of Tusculum and of the Latin League army

people.summary: Leading man of Tusculum and son-in-law of Tarquinius Superbus, who raised the Latin League against Rome and was killed at Lake Regillus.
people.death: killed at the battle of Lake Regillus

people.name: Spurius Cassius
people.summary: Three times consul, author of the Foedus Cassianum with the Latins (493) and the treaty with the Hernici (486), dedicator of the temple of Ceres; condemned and executed for aiming at kingship after proposing the first agrarian law.
people.death: executed for adfectatio regni (by the quaestors or by his father)

people.name: Coriolanus
people.summary: Patrician hero of the capture of Corioli (493) who opposed the plebs during the famine of 492-491, was exiled, and led the Volsci against Rome (c. 488) until his mother Veturia and wife Volumnia persuaded him to turn back.
