people.death: drowned in the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge, 28 October 312

people.name: Licinius
people.summary: Galerius' comrade from Dacia, made Augustus at Carnuntum (308); defeated Maximinus Daia (313), co-authored the 'Edict of Milan', and ruled the East until his defeats by Constantine in 316 and 324.

people.name: Constantia
people.summary: Half-sister of Constantine married to Licinius at Milan in 313; she obtained her husband's life after Chrysopolis and later sympathised with Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia.

people.name: Constantine the Great
people.summary: Son of Constantius I and Helena, born at Naissus on 27 February; proclaimed at York (306), he won the West at the Milvian Bridge (312), the whole empire at Chrysopolis (324), convened Nicaea (325), founded Constantinople (324-330), introduced the solidus and made Christianity the favoured religion of the emperor.
people.death: illness near Nicomedia after baptism, 22 May 337

people.name: Fausta
people.summary: Daughter of Maximian, married to Constantine in 307, mother of Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans; she died in 326, reportedly in an overheated bath, soon after the execution of her stepson Crispus.
people.death: suffocated or scalded in a bath, 326

people.name: Crispus
people.summary: Constantine's eldest son by Minervina, pupil of Lactantius, Caesar in Gaul and victor over Licinius' fleet in the Hellespont (324); executed by his father at Pola in 326 for unknown reasons.

people.name: Constantine II
people.summary: Eldest son of Constantine and Fausta, victor over the Goths in 332; as Augustus he claimed seniority over his brothers and was killed invading Constans' territory.
people.death: killed in an ambush near Aquileia, 340

people.name: Constans
people.summary: Youngest son of Constantine, ruler of the West after 340, a Nicene supporter of Athanasius who campaigned against Franks and crossed to Britain in winter 343; overthrown by Magnentius.
people.death: killed at Helena (Elne) in the Pyrenees, 350

people.name: Constantius II
people.summary: Son of Constantine who ruled the East for 24 years against Shapur II, won the civil war against Magnentius at Mursa (351), promoted Homoian Christianity and the Senate of Constantinople, and died marching against his cousin Julian.

people.name: Constantius Gallus
people.summary: Julian's half-brother, survivor of the 337 massacre, Caesar at Antioch who governed violently with his wife Constantina; recalled and executed by Constantius.

people.name: Magnentius
people.summary: Officer of barbarian descent born at Samarobriva (Amiens), proclaimed at Autun in 350; defeated at Mursa (351) and Mons Seleucus (353).

people.name: Vetranio
people.summary: Aged, reputedly illiterate general proclaimed in Illyricum in March 350 to forestall Magnentius; he abdicated before Constantius at Naissus in December and lived out his life at Prusa.

people.name: Silvanus
people.summary: Frankish officer who deserted Magnentius before Mursa, commanded in Gaul, and was driven to usurpation by court intrigue in 355; killed after 28 days.

people.name: Julian
people.summary: Nephew of Constantine and survivor of the massacre of 337, raised a Christian but secretly a Neoplatonist; as Caesar he won at Strasbourg (357) and restored the Rhine, was proclaimed Augustus at Paris (360), attempted to restore traditional cults and died on campaign in Persia.
people.death: mortally wounded by a spear near Samarra, 26 June 363

people.name: Jovian
people.summary: Christian guards officer chosen after Julian's death; he extricated the army by ceding Nisibis and the Transtigritane regions to Shapur II and died eight months later.
people.death: asphyxiated by fumes at Dadastana, 17 February 364

people.name: Valentinian I
people.summary: Pannonian officer from Cibalae, emperor of the West, who fought the Alamanni (Solicinium 368), fortified the Rhine and Danube, sent Count Theodosius to Britain and Africa and died of rage at a Quadic embassy.

people.name: Valens
people.summary: Younger brother of Valentinian and emperor of the East; defeated Procopius (366) and the Tervingi (367-369), supported Homoian Christianity, admitted the Goths in 376 and died at Adrianople.
people.death: killed at Adrianople, 9 August 378; body never found

people.name: Procopius
people.summary: Cilician relative of Julian, commander of the northern army in 363, who seized Constantinople in 365 claiming Constantinian legitimacy; betrayed and executed.

people.name: Gratian
people.summary: Son of Valentinian I, Augustus at eight; won at Argentaria (378), appointed Theodosius, removed the Altar of Victory and ended state funding of pagan cults, and was overthrown by Magnus Maximus.

people.name: Valentinian II
people.summary: Son of Valentinian I and Justina, proclaimed at four; expelled from Italy by Maximus (387), restored by Theodosius under Arbogast's control, and found hanged at Vienne.

people.name: Justina
people.summary: Widow of Magnentius and then wife of Valentinian I, mother of Valentinian II and Galla; a Homoian Christian who clashed with Ambrose over the basilicas of Milan in 385-386.

people.name: Count Theodosius
people.summary: Spanish general, father of Theodosius I, who restored Britain after 367, fought the Alamanni and suppressed Firmus in Mauretania; executed at Carthage early in 376 after Valentinian's death.

people.name: Theodosius I
people.summary: Spaniard from Cauca, made Augustus in 379 to retrieve the Gothic disaster; settled the Goths by treaty (382), made Nicene Christianity the state religion (380-381), defeated Magnus Maximus (388) and Eugenius at the Frigidus (394), and was the last emperor to rule both halves of the empire.

people.name: Magnus Maximus
people.summary: Spanish officer in Britain proclaimed in 383; overthrew Gratian, ruled from Trier, executed Priscillian, invaded Italy in 387 and was defeated by Theodosius.

people.name: Arbogast
people.summary: Frankish general who dominated Valentinian II, set up Eugenius as emperor in 392 and lost at the Frigidus.
people.death: suicide two days after the Frigidus, September 394

people.name: Eugenius
people.summary: Teacher of rhetoric and magister scrinii raised to the throne by Arbogast in 392; his toleration of pagan senators made the Frigidus campaign appear a religious war.

people.name: Firmus
people.summary: Moorish prince who revolted against the comes Africae Romanus and was hunted down by Count Theodosius.

people.name: Carausius
people.summary: Menapian sailor and fleet commander who seized Britain and northern Gaul, issuing high-quality coinage with Virgilian legends; murdered by Allectus.

people.name: Allectus
people.summary: Carausius' finance officer and murderer, who ruled Britain until defeated by Asclepiodotus.
people.death: killed in battle in southern Britain, 296

people.name: Domitius Domitianus
people.summary: Usurper in Egypt in 297, known from coins and papyri; his revolt, continued by Aurelius Achilleus, was crushed by Diocletian after the eight-month siege of Alexandria.

people.name: Narseh
people.summary: Son of Shapur I who overthrew Bahram III in 293 (commemorated in the Paikuli inscription), defeated Galerius in 296/297, but lost his harem and treasury in 298 and accepted the Peace of Nisibis (299).

people.name: Shapur II
people.summary: Crowned, according to legend, in his mother's womb, Shapur II reigned seventy years; he campaigned against the Arabs, besieged Nisibis three times, persecuted Christians, took Amida (359), Singara and Bezabde (360), repelled Julian (363) and recovered Nisibis and Armenia by Jovian's treaty.

people.name: Tiridates III
people.summary: Arsacid king of Armenia restored by Roman arms (287 and again after 298), who adopted Christianity through Gregory the Illuminator, traditionally in 301, probably c. 314.

people.name: Gregory the Illuminator
people.summary: Parthian-born apostle of Armenia, consecrated at Caesarea in Cappadocia, who converted Tiridates III and founded the Armenian church; his descendants held the patriarchate for generations.

people.name: Athanaric
people.summary: Leader of the Tervingi who fought Valens (367-369), made peace on a boat in the Danube, persecuted Gothic Christians, was defeated by the Huns on the Dniester (376), and finally came to Constantinople, where he died and received a state funeral from Theodosius.

people.name: Fritigern

roles.t: Leader of the Tervingi in the empire

people.summary: Tervingian leader, rival of Athanaric and patron of Christianity, who led the Goths across the Danube in 376, escaped Lupicinus' trap at Marcianople and commanded at Adrianople; he disappears from the sources before 382.

people.name: Chnodomar
people.summary: The most powerful Alamannic king of the 350s, who defeated Constantius' Caesar Decentius and ravaged Gaul; captured at Strasbourg in 357 and sent to Rome, where he died of illness in the camp of the foreigners on the Caelian.

people.name: Ursicinus
people.summary: Senior general of Constantius II and patron of Ammianus Marcellinus, who suppressed Silvanus (355) and was scapegoated for the loss of Amida in 359.

people.name: Ambrose
people.summary: Son of a praetorian prefect, governor turned bishop of Milan, who fought Homoians and pagans, defeated Symmachus over the Altar of Victory, resisted Justina, forced Theodosius to back down over Callinicum and do penance after Thessalonica, and baptised Augustine.

people.name: Athanasius
people.summary: Deacon at Nicaea and bishop of Alexandria from 328, the champion of the homoousios, exiled five times by Constantine, Constantius II, Julian and Valens; author of Against the Arians, the Life of Antony and the Festal Letter of 367 listing the 27 books of the New Testament canon.

people.name: Arius

roles.t: Presbyter of the Baucalis church, Alexandria

people.summary: Libyan-born presbyter of Alexandria whose teaching that the Son was a created being, subordinate to the Father, sparked the Trinitarian controversy; condemned at Nicaea, rehabilitated by Constantine, he died suddenly in 336.

people.name: Eusebius of Caesarea
people.summary: Scholar of the Origenist library at Caesarea, author of the Ecclesiastical History, Chronicle, Martyrs of Palestine, Preparation for the Gospel and the Life of Constantine; the founder of church history and the architect of the image of Constantine as God's chosen emperor.

people.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia
people.summary: Fellow pupil of Lucian of Antioch with Arius and leader of the anti-Nicene bishops, exiled after Nicaea but restored; he baptised Constantine in 337 and consecrated Ulfilas.

people.name: Lactantius

roles.t: Professor of Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia

people.summary: African rhetorician appointed by Diocletian at Nicomedia, who converted and lost his post in the persecution; author of the Divine Institutes and On the Deaths of the Persecutors (c. 315), a vivid but fiercely partisan account of 303-313 arguing that God punished every persecuting emperor.

people.name: Ossius of Corduba
people.summary: Spanish bishop and Constantine's chief ecclesiastical adviser, present at Elvira, probably president at Nicaea and leader of the westerners at Serdica; nearly a centenarian, he was forced at Sirmium in 357 to sign a non-Nicene creed.

people.name: Donatus
people.summary: Leader of the rigorist African church that took his name, rival bishop of Carthage from 313; exiled after the Macarian repression of 347, he died in Gaul or Spain. He is credited with asking 'What has the emperor to do with the church?'

people.name: Damasus I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome after the bloody contest with Ursinus, who promoted the cult of the Roman martyrs with verse epitaphs carved by Filocalus, commissioned Jerome's Latin revision of the Gospels and asserted Rome's Petrine primacy.

people.name: Ulfilas
people.summary: Gothic bishop of Cappadocian descent who created the Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible, spreading Homoian Christianity among the Goths; died at Constantinople during a council.

people.name: Priscillian
people.summary: Ascetic Spanish lay teacher and bishop accused of Manichaeism, magic and sexual immorality, the first Christian executed for heresy, by Magnus Maximus at Trier.

people.name: Ammianus Marcellinus

roles.t: Protector domesticus on the staff of Ursicinus

people.summary: Greek-born soldier from Antioch who wrote the last great Latin history of Rome, the Res Gestae, of which books 14-31 (353-378) survive; an eyewitness of Silvanus' fall, the siege of Amida and Julian's Persian campaign.

people.name: Libanius

roles.t: Official sophist (teacher of rhetoric) of Antioch

people.summary: Pagan rhetorician of Antioch whose 64 orations and over 1,500 letters illuminate fourth-century urban society; friend and eulogist of Julian, teacher of Christians such as John Chrysostom, and author of the plea For the Temples (Or. 30).

people.name: Symmachus
people.summary: Pagan senator and orator whose Third Relatio (384) pleaded for the restoration of the Altar of Victory; his ten books of letters document senatorial life.

people.name: Tiberius Claudius Candidus
people.summary: Severan general who won at Nicaea (194) and probably Cyzicus; his career inscription from Tarraco records commands against Niger, Albinus and the Parthians.

people.name: Publius Cornelius Anullinus
people.summary: Spanish senator and friend of Severus who commanded at Issus (194) and later held a second consulship and the urban prefecture.

people.name: Asellius Aemilianus
people.summary: Proconsul of Asia and Niger's commander, defeated and killed at Cyzicus in 193.

people.name: Marius Maximus

roles.t: Commander of Moesian troops at Byzantium

people.summary: Severan general and senator who wrote lost biographies of emperors from Nerva to Elagabalus in the manner of Suetonius, a major (and gossipy) source of the Historia Augusta.

people.name: Julius Laetus
people.summary: Severan commander whose late cavalry charge decided Lugdunum and who defended Nisibis in 197; executed by Severus, jealous of his popularity with the troops.

people.name: Abdsamiya of Hatra
people.summary: King of Hatra attested in Aramaic inscriptions, who supported Niger and resisted Severus' sieges of 198 and 199.

people.name: Sanatruq II
people.summary: Last securely attested king of Hatra, son of Abdsamiya, under whom the city allied with Rome before falling to the Sasanians in 240/241.

people.name: Bulla Felix
people.summary: Italian bandit chief with 600 men who eluded capture for two years under Severus; betrayed and thrown to the beasts.

people.name: Gannys
people.summary: Eunuch tutor in Julia Maesa's household who organised the coup of 218 and commanded at the battle near Antioch; killed by Elagabalus himself soon after.

people.name: Capelianus
people.summary: Governor of Numidia loyal to Maximinus who crushed the Gordians at Carthage in 238 with Legio III Augusta.

people.name: Rutilius Pudens Crispinus

roles.t: One of the vigintiviri; defender of Aquileia

people.summary: Consular senator who, with Tullius Menophilus, organised the defence of Aquileia against Maximinus in 238.

people.name: Tullius Menophilus
people.summary: Senator who held Aquileia against Maximinus and then governed Moesia Inferior, dealing with the Goths and Carpi after the sack of Histria; executed around 241.

people.name: Lucius Priscus
people.summary: Governor of Thrace besieged in Philippopolis by Cniva, who proclaimed himself emperor in alliance with the Goths; declared a public enemy, he vanished after the city fell.

people.name: Mariades
people.summary: Antiochene councillor expelled for embezzlement who defected to Shapur I and guided the Persians to the sack of Antioch; later executed by Shapur. The HA's usurper 'Cyriades' is a distortion.

people.name: Successianus
people.summary: Former defender of Pityus against the Boranoi, praetorian prefect of Valerian, captured with him at Edessa in 260.

people.name: Simplicinius Genialis
people.summary: Equestrian acting governor of Raetia who defeated the Semnones/Juthungi near Augsburg on 24-25 April 260 and recorded it on a victory altar dated by Postumus' consulship.

people.name: Naulobatus
people.summary: Herulian chief who surrendered to Gallienus at the Nestus and received consular insignia.

people.name: Felicissimus

roles.t: Rationalis (finance officer) of the Rome mint

people.summary: Mint official who led the moneyers' revolt in Rome in 271 after being implicated in debasement fraud.

people.name: Cannabaudes
people.summary: Gothic leader killed with 5,000 men by Aurelian north of the Danube, known only from the Historia Augusta.

people.name: Terentius Marcianus
people.summary: Governor who besieged Lydius' Isaurian bandits in Cremna under Probus, attested on an inscription from the site.

people.name: Lydius
people.summary: Isaurian brigand who seized Cremna in Pisidia and held it against a Roman siege until killed by a deserting artillerist.
people.death: killed by a catapult bolt during the siege, 278

people.name: Arrius Aper
people.summary: Numerian's father-in-law and praetorian prefect, accused of his murder and killed by Diocletian before the army.

people.name: Asclepiodotus
people.summary: Praetorian prefect of Constantius I who landed in Britain under cover of fog and defeated Allectus in 296.

people.name: Aurelius Achilleus

roles.t: Corrector in Egypt during the revolt

people.summary: Leading figure in the Egyptian revolt of 297-298, named in papyri as corrector under Domitius Domitianus and treated by Latin sources as the usurper; executed after the fall of Alexandria.

people.name: Sicorius Probus
people.summary: Diocletian's envoy who negotiated the Peace of Nisibis with Narseh at the river Asprudis in Media.

people.name: Crocus
people.summary: Alamannic king commanding a contingent in Constantius' army at York who, according to the Epitome, led the acclamation of Constantine in 306.

people.name: Ruricius Pompeianus
people.summary: Maxentius' commander in northern Italy, killed in battle near Verona in 312.

people.name: Abantus
people.summary: Commander of Licinius' fleet defeated by Crispus in the Hellespont in 324.

people.name: Jacob of Nisibis
people.summary: Bishop of Nisibis, reputed participant at Nicaea and teacher of Ephrem, credited by hagiography with saving the city in Shapur's siege of 338.

people.name: Lucillianus
people.summary: Officer who held Nisibis against Shapur's flood siege of 350; later father-in-law of Jovian, killed by mutinous troops at Rheims in 364.

people.name: Severus
people.summary: Julian's cavalry commander at Strasbourg, who led the Roman left wing and detected the Alamannic ambush.

people.name: Serapio
people.summary: Nephew of Chnodomar who commanded the Alamannic right at Strasbourg; his father, a hostage in Gaul, had renamed him after Serapis.

people.name: Grumbates
people.summary: Chionite king allied to Shapur II at Amida (359), whose son was killed before the walls, leading to a ritual mourning and the furious assault on the city.

people.name: Aelianus
people.summary: Officer who as a protector had led a famous sally at Singara (348) and commanded at Amida; crucified by the Persians after its fall.

people.name: The Surena (363)
people.summary: Head of the great Suren family, second in rank to the king, who commanded Persian forces against Julian's army before Ctesiphon and negotiated with Jovian.

people.name: Sebastianus
people.summary: Veteran general who fought at Solicinium and under Julian, won a skirmish against Gothic raiders in 378 and urged Valens to fight at once; killed at Adrianople.

people.name: Trajanus
people.summary: Officer who assassinated King Pap of Armenia at a banquet (374/375) on Valens' orders and was killed at Adrianople.

people.name: Victor
people.summary: Sarmatian-born Nicene general who served from Julian's campaign to Adrianople, from which he escaped; consul 369.

people.name: Richomeres
people.summary: Frankish officer who led Gratian's reinforcements at Ad Salices, volunteered as a hostage during negotiations at Adrianople, and became a magister militum under Theodosius; uncle of Arbogast.

people.name: Lupicinus
people.summary: Commander in Thrace whose extortion of the Goths and attempted seizure of their leaders at Marcianople triggered the war of 376-382.

people.name: Alatheus
people.summary: Co-leader with Saphrax of the Greuthungi, guardians of the boy king Videric, whose cavalry decided Adrianople.

people.name: Saphrax
people.summary: Co-leader of the Greuthungi with Alatheus, perhaps of Alan origin, whose cavalry struck the Roman flank at Adrianople.

people.name: Mallobaudes

roles.t: Comes domesticorum; king of the Franks

people.summary: Frankish king serving as Gratian's comes domesticorum, co-commander in the victory over the Lentienses at Argentaria (378).

people.name: Priarius
people.summary: King of the Lentienses, killed in their defeat at Argentaria.

people.name: Marcellinus
people.summary: Brother of Magnus Maximus who commanded his army at Poetovio in 388.

people.name: Timasius
people.summary: Senior general of Theodosius who commanded the Roman (non-Gothic) troops at the Frigidus; later exiled by Eutropius in 396.

people.name: Bacurius
people.summary: Iberian (Georgian) prince in Roman service who fought at Adrianople and commanded at the Frigidus, where he was killed; Rufinus knew him personally.

people.name: Honorius
people.summary: Younger son of Theodosius I, western emperor from age ten. His reign saw Stilicho's regency and execution, the Rhine crossing, the loss of Britain and the sack of Rome, which he watched from Ravenna.

people.name: Arcadius
people.summary: Elder son of Theodosius I, eastern emperor 395-408, dominated in turn by Rufinus, the eunuch Eutropius, Gainas and his wife Aelia Eudoxia. His reign saw the Gothic crisis of 400 and the exile of John Chrysostom.

people.name: Theodosius II
people.summary: Eastern emperor for 48 years, the longest reign of any Roman emperor. Under him came the Theodosian Walls, the Theodosian Code, the councils of Ephesus (431 and 449), and the humiliating payments to Attila.
people.death: spinal injury after falling from his horse, 28 July 450

people.name: Constantius III
people.summary: Illyrian general who restored Ravenna's authority after 410: he crushed Constantine III, starved the Goths into returning Galla Placidia, married her, settled the Visigoths in Aquitaine and was briefly co-emperor. Father of Valentinian III.

people.name: Constantine III (usurper)

roles.t: Usurper in Britain, Gaul and Spain

people.summary: A common soldier proclaimed by the British army in 407, chosen, Orosius says, for his name. He held Gaul and Spain from Arles, was briefly recognised by Honorius in 409, and surrendered to Constantius in 411.
people.death: executed on the road to Ravenna, September 411

people.name: Priscus Attalus
people.summary: Ionian-born senator twice made emperor by the Goths, in 409-410 by Alaric and in 414-415 by Athaulf. Captured in 416, he was paraded in Honorius's triumph in Rome, had two fingers cut off, and was exiled to Lipari.

people.name: Joannes
people.summary: Senior civil servant proclaimed at Ravenna after Honorius's death in 423 and backed by Aetius. Defeated by Aspar's eastern army, he was mutilated, paraded on a donkey in the hippodrome at Aquileia and beheaded.

people.name: Valentinian III
people.summary: Son of Constantius III and Galla Placidia, emperor at six. His 30-year reign saw the loss of Africa, Attila's invasions and the dominance of Aetius, whom he murdered in 454; Aetius's men killed him six months later, ending the Theodosian dynasty in the West.
people.death: assassinated on the Campus Martius, 16 March 455

people.name: Petronius Maximus
people.summary: Immensely rich senator, twice consul, who probably arranged Valentinian III's murder and seized the throne on 17 March 455. His 75-day reign ended as the Vandals approached Rome: fleeing, he was killed by the crowd or by soldiers.
people.death: killed in Rome while fleeing, 31 May 455

people.name: Avitus
people.summary: Arvernian aristocrat and friend of the Visigothic court who was made emperor in 455 with Theodoric II's support. Deposed by Ricimer and Majorian after the battle of Placentia, he was made bishop of Placentia and died soon after. Father-in-law of Sidonius Apollinaris.

people.name: Majorian
people.summary: Officer of Aetius, emperor 457-461 and the last western emperor to pursue a coherent programme of recovery: reforms against tax abuses, protection of Rome's monuments, campaigns restoring Gaul and an attempted invasion of Africa. When his fleet was destroyed in Spain, Ricimer had him beheaded.
people.death: executed by Ricimer's order near Dertona, 7 August 461

people.name: Libius Severus
people.summary: Lucanian senator installed by Ricimer after Majorian's execution, never recognised by Leo I, Aegidius in Gaul or Marcellinus in Dalmatia.
people.death: died at Rome, 14 November 465, perhaps poisoned (Cassiodorus)

people.name: Anthemius
people.summary: Eastern aristocrat, son-in-law of Marcian and grandson of the prefect Anthemius, sent by Leo I to rule the West in 467. He backed the great Vandal expedition and fought Euric, then fell out with his son-in-law Ricimer, who besieged and killed him in Rome.
people.death: beheaded by Gundobad in Rome, 11 July 472

people.name: Olybrius
people.summary: Anician senator married to Placidia, daughter of Valentinian III, and so Gaiseric's preferred candidate. Ricimer proclaimed him in April 472 during the siege of Rome. His daughter Anicia Juliana became Constantinople's greatest aristocratic patron.

people.name: Glycerius
people.summary: Gundobad's candidate, proclaimed at Ravenna on 3 March 473. Deposed without a fight by Julius Nepos in June 474, he was made bishop of Salona, where Nepos was murdered in 480, possibly at his instigation.

people.name: Julius Nepos
people.summary: Nephew of Marcellinus and ruler of Dalmatia, installed as western emperor by Leo I in 474. Driven out by Orestes in 475, he continued to claim the throne from Dalmatia and was recognised by Zeno and on Odoacer's coins until his murder.
people.death: murdered by his retainers near Salona, 9 May 480

people.name: Romulus Augustulus
people.summary: Teenage son of Orestes, proclaimed emperor on 31 October 475 and deposed by Odoacer on 4 September 476; conventionally the last western Roman emperor. He was pensioned off with 6,000 solidi a year to the Castellum Lucullanum near Naples.

people.name: Marcian
people.summary: Thracian officer and protégé of Aspar, chosen by Pulcheria as husband and emperor in 450. He stopped tribute to Attila, convened the Council of Chalcedon, and left a full treasury, but refused to help the West or the Armenians.

people.name: Leo I
people.summary: Thracian or Dacian officer raised to the throne by Aspar in 457. He sent Anthemius and Julius Nepos to the West and launched the ruinous 468 expedition against Carthage, then murdered Aspar in 471 and built up Isaurian power through his son-in-law Zeno.

people.name: Zeno
people.fullName: Flavius Zeno (born Tarasis son of Kodisa)
people.summary: Isaurian chieftain who married Leo I's daughter Ariadne and became emperor in 474. Overthrown by Basiliscus in 475-476, he survived the revolt of Illus, issued the Henotikon, accepted the end of the western emperorship, and sent Theodoric to Italy.

people.name: Basiliscus
people.summary: Brother of the empress Verina, commander of the disastrous 468 expedition against the Vandals, and usurper in 475-476. His anti-Chalcedonian Encyclical alienated the capital; he surrendered to Zeno on a promise that his blood would not be shed and was starved to death instead.
people.death: starved to death with his family at Limnae, Cappadocia, 476/477

people.name: Anastasius I
people.summary: Palace usher from Dyrrachium chosen by the empress Ariadne in 491, whose financial reforms (abolition of the chrysargyron, the copper follis, tax collection by vindices, commutation of levies into gold) left a surplus of 320,000 lbs of gold. He won the Isaurian War, fought Persia (502-506), founded Dara and faced Vitalian's rebellion over his miaphysite sympathies.

people.name: Justin I
people.summary: Peasant from Bederiana near Naissus who walked to Constantinople as a youth, rose through the guards to command the excubitors, and was elected emperor in 518. A Chalcedonian, he ended the Acacian Schism. His nephew Justinian, whom he adopted, effectively ran his government.

people.name: Justinian I
people.summary: The great restorer of the sixth century: codified Roman law in the Corpus Iuris Civilis, rebuilt Hagia Sophia, reconquered Vandal Africa, Ostrogothic Italy and part of Spain, and fought Persia and the Balkan peoples, while surviving the Nika revolt and the plague.

people.name: Justin II
people.summary: Justinian's nephew, who refused subsidies to the Avars and Persians, lost much of Italy to the Lombards (568) and provoked the Persian war of 572. The fall of Dara in 573 drove him insane; his wife Sophia and Tiberius governed for him.

people.name: Tiberius II Constantine
people.summary: Thracian officer, Caesar from 574 and emperor 578-582. Generous to the point of extravagance, he cut taxes and paid donatives, fought Persia with mixed success and lost Sirmium to the Avars. He chose Maurice as heir.

people.name: Maurice
people.summary: Cappadocian notary turned general and emperor. He restored Khosrow II and gained the favourable peace of 591, created the exarchates of Ravenna and Carthage, and fought a long and finally successful war against Avars and Slavs, but his economies with army pay provoked the mutiny of 602 that killed him.
people.death: executed with five sons at Chalcedon by Phocas, 27 November 602

people.name: Phocas
people.summary: Junior officer raised on a shield by the mutinous Danube army in 602. His reign of purges, conspiracies and military collapse before the Persians made him the archetype of the tyrant in Byzantine historiography; Heraclius overthrew him in 610.
people.death: beheaded and dismembered at Constantinople, 5 October 610

people.name: Heraclius
people.summary: Son of the exarch of Africa, who overthrew Phocas in 610, lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt to Persia, and then in the campaigns of 622-628 carried the war into Persia and destroyed Khosrow II. Within a decade of his triumph the Arabs took Syria, Palestine, Mesopotamia and most of Egypt.

people.name: Constantine III
people.summary: Heraclius's son by Fabia-Eudocia, co-emperor from infancy. He reigned with his half-brother Heraclonas for about three months after their father's death and died of tuberculosis, amid rumours that Martina had poisoned him.

people.name: Heraclonas
people.summary: Heraclius's son by Martina, co-emperor with Constantine III in 641 and briefly senior emperor under his mother's regency. Popular and military hostility forced the coronation of Constans II; late in 641 his nose was slit and he was exiled to Rhodes.

people.name: Galla Placidia
people.summary: Daughter of Theodosius I, captured at the sack of Rome in 410, wife of the Gothic king Athaulf, then of Constantius III, and regent of the West for her son Valentinian III. She played Bonifatius, Felix and Aetius against one another until Aetius prevailed.

people.name: Aelia Eudoxia
people.summary: Daughter of the Frankish general Bauto, married to Arcadius in 395 through Eutropius's scheming. Proclaimed Augusta in 400, she was a dominant figure at court and the enemy of John Chrysostom; mother of Theodosius II and Pulcheria.

people.name: Pulcheria
people.summary: Elder sister and guardian of Theodosius II, Augusta at fifteen, consecrated virgin and champion of the Theotokos. She probably helped bring down Nestorius, and in 450 married Marcian to legitimise his reign, presiding with him over Chalcedon.

people.name: Eudocia
people.summary: Daughter of an Athenian sophist, married to Theodosius II in 421. A poet (Homeric centos, a verse life of St Cyprian), she fell from favour around 441-443, reportedly over a suspected affair with the master of offices Paulinus, and spent her last years in Jerusalem as a patron of churches.

people.name: Licinia Eudoxia
people.summary: Daughter of Theodosius II, married to Valentinian III in 437. Forced to marry his murderer Petronius Maximus, she was carried off to Carthage by Gaiseric in 455 with her daughters and released in 462.

people.name: Honoria
people.summary: Sister of Valentinian III, whose letter and ring to Attila, after her affair with her steward and forced betrothal, gave Attila a pretext to claim half the West. Her fate after 450 is unknown.

people.name: Verina
people.summary: Wife of Leo I and sister of Basiliscus, an inveterate conspirator: she helped overthrow her son-in-law Zeno in 475, turned against Basiliscus, and in 484 crowned Leontius for Illus's rebellion.
people.death: natural causes during the siege of Papyrius, 484

people.name: Ariadne
people.summary: Daughter of Leo I, wife of Zeno and then of Anastasius I, whom she chose as emperor in 491. Her role as the bearer of dynastic legitimacy across three reigns made her the pivot of eastern politics for forty years.

people.name: Theodora
people.summary: Daughter of a bear-keeper of the Green faction and a former actress, married Justinian around 525 and was crowned with him in 527. Procopius credits her with saving the throne in the Nika riots; she protected the anti-Chalcedonians and was a powerful political partner.

people.name: Sophia
people.summary: Theodora's niece and wife of Justin II, who governed during his madness, bought a truce from Persia in 574, and engineered Tiberius's elevation as Caesar. Later tradition blames her insult to Narses for the Lombard invasion.

people.name: Martina
people.summary: Heraclius's niece and second wife (married c. 613), who accompanied him on campaign and bore him at least nine children. Her attempt to rule for her son Heraclonas in 641 failed; her tongue was slit and she was exiled to Rhodes.

people.name: Amalasuntha
people.summary: Daughter of Theodoric, highly educated in Greek and Latin, regent for her son Athalaric. Opposed by Gothic nobles for giving him a Roman education, she negotiated secretly with Justinian, and her murder by her co-ruler Theodahad gave Justinian his casus belli.
people.death: strangled in her bath on Martana island, Lake Bolsena, 535

people.name: Serena
people.summary: Niece and adopted daughter of Theodosius I, wife of Stilicho and mother-in-law of Honorius. During Alaric's siege of Rome in 408 the Senate, suspecting her of collusion, had her strangled with Galla Placidia's assent. Zosimus says she had once taken a necklace from the statue of Rhea.
people.death: strangled at Rome by Senate decree, 408

people.name: Hypatia
people.summary: Mathematician, astronomer and Neoplatonist philosopher of Alexandria, daughter of the mathematician Theon, who edited commentaries on Ptolemy and Diophantus and taught pupils such as Synesius of Cyrene. She was murdered by a Christian mob in 415 during the feud between Bishop Cyril and the prefect Orestes.
people.death: murdered by a Christian mob in Alexandria, March 415

people.name: Antonina
people.summary: Wife of Belisarius, daughter of a charioteer, and close ally of Theodora. She accompanied Belisarius on campaign, organised the deposition of Pope Silverius in 537, and helped Theodora bring down John the Cappadocian in 541. The Secret History portrays her adultery with her godson Theodosius in lurid detail.

people.name: Stilicho
people.summary: Son of a Vandal officer and a Roman mother, husband of Theodosius I's niece Serena, and effective ruler of the West from 395 to 408. He fought Alaric at Pholoe, Pollentia and Verona, crushed Gildo and Radagaisus, and was destroyed by a court coup.

people.name: Rufinus
people.summary: Gallic-born minister who dominated Arcadius's early reign and resisted Stilicho's claims over the East. Claudian's In Rufinum makes him a demon of greed. He was hacked to death at a military parade by Gainas's soldiers.

people.name: Eutropius
people.summary: Former slave and eunuch chamberlain who arranged Arcadius's marriage to Eudoxia, ruled the East from 395 to 399, campaigned against the Huns in Armenia and became the first eunuch consul. Brought down by Tribigild's revolt and Gainas, he was executed.

people.name: Gainas
people.summary: Gothic general in eastern service who murdered Rufinus (395), forced Eutropius's fall (399) and dominated Constantinople in 400 until the massacre of his troops. Defeated on the Hellespont, he fled north and was killed by the Hun Uldin.
people.death: killed by the Huns of Uldin, December 400

people.name: Aetius
people.summary: The dominant figure of the West from 433 to 454: hostage as a youth among Alaric's Goths and the Huns, then master of Valentinian III's government. He used Hunnic auxiliaries to crush Burgundians and Goths, and in 451 united Romans and Goths against Attila at the Catalaunian Plains.
people.death: killed by Valentinian III in the palace at Rome, 21/22 September 454

people.name: Bonifatius
people.summary: Heroic defender of Marseille against Athaulf (413) and correspondent of Augustine, later comes Africae. He rebelled against Placidia in 427, failed to stop the Vandals, held Hippo in 430-431, and defeated Aetius at Rimini in 432 but died of his wounds.

people.name: Aspar
people.summary: Alan Arian general, son of Ardabur, who installed Valentinian III in 425, fought the Vandals in Africa, and as kingmaker chose Marcian (450) and Leo I (457). Leo had him murdered in 471.

people.name: Ricimer
people.summary: Grandson of the Visigothic king Wallia through his mother and of Suevic royal blood through his father, Ricimer dominated Italy for sixteen years, making and unmaking the emperors Avitus, Majorian, Libius Severus, Anthemius and Olybrius. As an Arian barbarian he could not take the throne himself.

people.name: Orestes
people.summary: Roman from Pannonia who served Attila as secretary and envoy (he appears in Priscus), later Julius Nepos's commander. He drove Nepos out in 475 and made his son Romulus emperor, then refused the federates' demand for land and was killed by Odoacer.

people.name: Marcellinus
people.summary: Friend of Aetius who after 454 made Dalmatia an autonomous command, refused to recognise Libius Severus, fought the Vandals in Sicily and Sardinia, and joined Anthemius's 468 expedition. A pagan admired for his learning, he was murdered in Sicily, probably at Ricimer's instigation. Uncle of Julius Nepos.

people.name: Aegidius
people.summary: Gallo-Roman general and loyal officer of Majorian, who after Majorian's murder refused to recognise Ricimer's emperors and governed northern Gaul independently, defeating the Visigoths at Orléans in 463. Gregory of Tours says the Franks made him their king for eight years while Childeric was in exile.

people.name: Syagrius
people.summary: Son of Aegidius, ruler of the Roman enclave around Soissons, called 'king of the Romans' by Gregory of Tours. Defeated by Clovis in 486, he fled to the Visigoths, who surrendered him to be executed.

people.name: Illus
people.summary: Isaurian general whose defection restored Zeno in 476 and who dominated his government until 484, when he rebelled and crowned Leontius. A patron of intellectuals, he held out in the fortress of Papyrius until 488.
people.death: beheaded after the fall of Papyrius, 488

people.name: Vitalian
people.summary: Thracian commander who led three rebellions (513-515) against Anastasius in the name of Chalcedonian orthodoxy and federate pay. Rehabilitated by Justin I, he was consul in 520 and murdered that year, probably at Justinian's instigation.

people.name: Belisarius
people.summary: Justinian's greatest general, born in Germania on the Thracian-Illyrian border. He won at Dara (530), lost at Callinicum (531), suppressed the Nika riots (532), destroyed the Vandal kingdom (533-534), took Sicily, Naples, Rome and Ravenna (535-540), fought Persia (541-542) and returned to Italy (544-549) with inadequate resources. In 559 he saved Constantinople from the Kutrigurs.

people.name: Narses
people.summary: Persarmenian eunuch and chamberlain who bribed the Blues during the Nika riots, served in Italy alongside Belisarius in 538-539, and in 551-554, in his seventies, finished the Gothic War with victories at Busta Gallorum and Mons Lactarius and destroyed the Frankish-Alamannic invasion at the Volturnus. He governed Italy until 568.

people.name: John the Cappadocian
people.summary: Justinian's ruthless finance minister, who abolished much of the public post, centralised tax collection and squeezed provincials and the wealthy. Dismissed at the crowd's demand during Nika and reinstated, he was brought down in 541 by a sting organised by Theodora and Antonina, ordained a priest by force and exiled.

people.name: Tribonian
people.summary: Pamphylian lawyer who directed the compilation of the Digest, edited the Institutes and the second Codex, and drafted many Novels. Procopius accuses him of selling justice and of paganism; he was dismissed during Nika and restored.

people.name: Germanus
people.summary: Justinian's cousin, who defeated the Antae in Thrace, won back the mutinous army of Africa and defeated Stotzas (537), and in 550 married Matasuntha, Theodoric's granddaughter, as he prepared to lead the final Italian campaign. He died before setting out; Jordanes celebrates his son as a union of Amal and Anician blood.

people.name: John Troglita
people.summary: Veteran of Belisarius's African and eastern campaigns, sent to Africa in 546. After a defeat at Marta in 547, he crushed the Moorish confederation at the Campi Catonis in 548. He is the hero of Corippus's eight-book Latin epic, the Iohannis.

people.name: Solomon

roles.t: Praetorian prefect and magister militum of Africa
Praetorian prefect and magister militum of Africa

people.summary: Eunuch officer from Dara who governed Roman Africa twice, fought the Moors of the Aurès mountains and built the network of fortifications whose ruins survive across Tunisia and Algeria. Killed fighting the Moors at Cillium.

people.name: Priscus
people.summary: Maurice's most successful Balkan commander, who campaigned beyond the Danube against the Slavs (593) and won the victories of 599 deep in Avar territory. Under Phocas he married Phocas's daughter and commanded the excubitors, then helped Heraclius take power, but was forced into a monastery in 612.
people.death: died as a monk at Constantinople, 613

people.name: Philippicus
people.summary: Maurice's brother-in-law, victor at Solachon (586) where he paraded the Camuliana icon; sometimes proposed as the author of the Strategikon. He became a monk under Phocas and served Heraclius as a general in 611-613.
people.death: died as a monk at Chrysopolis, c. 614

people.name: Comentiolus
people.summary: Maurice's loyal but much criticised general, active in the Balkans, the East and Spain (an inscription at Cartagena records his fortification of the city). Theophylact blames him for the disastrous retreat of 598-599 that led to the massacre of 12,000 captives. Phocas executed him.

people.name: Shahrbaraz
people.summary: Khosrow II's greatest general ('Boar of the Empire'), conqueror of Jerusalem (614) and Egypt (619), who camped at Chalcedon during the siege of 626. Alienated from Khosrow, he negotiated with Heraclius, returned the True Cross and evacuated Roman lands, then seized the Sasanian throne in 630.
people.death: murdered after a reign of about 40 days, June 630

people.name: Shahin
people.summary: Persian general who campaigned in Armenia and Anatolia, reached Chalcedon in 615, and fought alongside Shahrbaraz at Antioch (613). Defeated by Heraclius's brother Theodore in 626, he is said to have died of grief, after which Khosrow abused his corpse.

people.name: Theodore (brother of Heraclius)
people.summary: Heraclius's brother and chief lieutenant, who fought at Antioch (613), defeated Shahin (626), and commanded against the Arabs in Syria in 634-636, probably losing at Ajnadayn. Disgraced after quarrelling with Martina, he was sent to Constantinople in chains.

people.name: Vahan
people.summary: Armenian commander of the Roman army at the Yarmuk (636). Theophanes says his troops proclaimed him emperor before the battle. His fate after the defeat is unknown; Arab tradition says he died or became a monk at Sinai.

people.name: Alaric I
people.summary: Gothic leader who forged the people later called Visigoths out of Theodosius's federates, ravaged Greece (395-397), invaded Italy twice, and in 410 sacked Rome. His aims were consistent and Roman: a regular command, pay, grain and land for his people.

people.name: Athaulf
people.summary: Brother-in-law and successor of Alaric, who led the Goths from Italy to Gaul (412), married Galla Placidia at Narbonne (414), and moved to Barcelona, where he was murdered by a retainer. Orosius credits him with wishing to restore the Roman name with Gothic strength.

people.name: Wallia
people.summary: Gothic king who made peace with Constantius in 416, returned Galla Placidia for grain, destroyed the Siling Vandals and Alans in Spain as Roman federates, and received the settlement in Aquitaine in 418. Grandfather of Ricimer.

people.name: Theodoric I
people.summary: King of the Visigoths at Toulouse for 33 years, who tried repeatedly to expand toward Arles and Narbonne, defeated Litorius in 439, and died leading his people against Attila at the Catalaunian Plains.

people.name: Euric
people.summary: Murdered his brother Theodoric II in 466 and broke with Rome, conquering Gaul south of the Loire and west of the Rhône (with Provence by 476) and most of Spain. His Code (Codex Euricianus, c. 475) is the earliest surviving Germanic law code, written in Latin by Roman jurists.

people.name: Alaric II
people.summary: Son of Euric, who issued the Breviary of Alaric (506) and convened the Council of Agde (506) to win his Catholic Roman subjects. Married to Theodoric the Great's daughter Thiudigotho, he was killed by Clovis at Vouillé.

people.name: Radagaisus
people.summary: Pagan Gothic king who invaded Italy from the middle Danube in 405 with a large following, probably displaced by the Huns. Trapped by Stilicho at Faesulae, he was executed; 12,000 of his men were drafted into the Roman army.

people.name: Gaiseric

roles.t: King of the Vandals and Alans

people.summary: The most formidable barbarian king of the fifth century: he led the Vandals and Alans to Africa (429), took Carthage (439), built the only barbarian navy, sacked Rome (455) and destroyed Majorian's (460) and Leo's (468) expeditions, before making perpetual peace with Zeno (474).

people.name: Huneric

roles.t: King of the Vandals and Alans

people.summary: Son of Gaiseric, hostage in Italy after 435 and husband of Eudocia, daughter of Valentinian III. His reign culminated in the persecution of Nicene Christians in 484 described by Victor of Vita.

people.name: Gelimer

roles.t: King of the Vandals and Alans

people.summary: Last Vandal king, who deposed his pro-Roman cousin Hilderic in 530, providing Justinian's pretext for war. Defeated at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum, he surrendered on Mount Papua and walked in Belisarius's triumph, then retired to estates in Galatia.

people.name: Attila
people.summary: Ruler of a Hunnic empire stretching from the Alps to the Black Sea steppe, who extracted vast tribute from Constantinople, devastated the Balkans (441-447), invaded Gaul (451) and Italy (452), and died on his wedding night in 453. His empire collapsed within a year.
people.death: haemorrhage on his wedding night, early 453

people.name: Bleda
people.summary: Attila's elder brother and co-ruler, who negotiated the Treaty of Margus and shared the Balkan campaigns of 441-442. Priscus tells of his fondness for the Moorish dwarf Zercon, whom he dressed in a comic suit of armour. Attila had him killed.

people.name: Rua
people.summary: Uncle of Attila and Bleda, the first Hunnic king to receive a regular annual tribute (350 lbs of gold) from Constantinople; he supported Aetius in 425 and 433. He died, struck by lightning according to Socrates, while threatening Thrace.

people.name: Theodoric the Great
people.summary: Amal Gothic king, raised as a hostage in Constantinople from age eight, who after years of Balkan warfare invaded Italy for Zeno in 488, killed Odoacer (493), and ruled Italy for 33 years, also regent of the Visigothic kingdom from 511. His reign preserved Roman administration, Senate and culture under Gothic military rule.

people.name: Theodoric Strabo
people.summary: 'The Squinter', leader of the Gothic federates in Thrace and kinsman of Aspar's wife, rival of Theodoric the Amal for Roman favour throughout the 470s. He died when his horse threw him onto a spear rack; his followers joined the Amal.

people.name: Witiges
people.summary: Gothic soldier elected king in 536 after Theodahad's failure, who married Theodoric's granddaughter Matasuntha, besieged Rome for a year (537-538), sought Persian help against Justinian, and surrendered Ravenna to Belisarius in 540. He died a patrician in Constantinople.

people.name: Totila
people.summary: Gothic king who revived the war after 541, retook most of Italy, captured Rome twice (546 and 550), and won over Italian peasants and slaves against senatorial landowners. He was killed at Busta Gallorum. His coins bear the name Baduila.

people.name: Teia
people.summary: Last Ostrogothic king, elected at Pavia after Totila's death. He killed Roman hostages, then marched south to relieve Cumae and died fighting at Mons Lactarius; Procopius praises his courage as equal to any hero's.

people.name: Clovis I
people.summary: Merovingian king who united the Franks, defeated Syagrius (486), the Alamanni, and the Visigoths at Vouillé (507), and converted to Catholic Christianity, aligning his kingdom with the Gallo-Roman church. Recognised by Anastasius in 508, he made Paris his capital.

people.name: Alboin
people.summary: Lombard king who destroyed the Gepids with Avar help (567) and in 568 led his people into Italy, taking the Po valley. He was murdered at Verona at the instigation of his wife Rosamund, daughter of the Gepid king whose skull he used as a cup.

people.name: Bayan I
people.summary: Avar khagan who led his people into the Carpathian basin (567-568), took Sirmium (582) and for thirty years raided and extorted the Balkans with Slav auxiliaries. Menander and Theophylact portray him as a cunning negotiator. His death date is uncertain; his sons led the Avars in the 599 campaign and the siege of 626.

people.name: Kavad I
people.summary: Sasanian king who supported the egalitarian Mazdakite movement, was deposed and escaped to the Hephthalites, and returned to power in 499. His demand for Roman subsidies led to the wars of 502-506 and 526-532 (the sieges of Amida, Dara and Callinicum).

people.name: Khosrow I
people.summary: The greatest Sasanian king in Persian memory, 'of the immortal soul'. He reformed taxation and the army, made the Eternal Peace (532), sacked Antioch (540), fought the Lazic War, made the Fifty Years' Peace (562), destroyed the Hephthalites with Turkic help, and took Dara (573).

people.name: Khosrow II
people.summary: 'The Victorious', restored by Maurice in 591, who after Maurice's murder waged the great war of 603-628, conquering Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine (with the True Cross), Egypt and much of Anatolia, before Heraclius's counteroffensive led to his overthrow and execution by his own son.
people.death: executed on the orders of Kavad II, February 628

people.name: Bahram Chobin
people.summary: Parthian noble of the Mihran house who defeated the Turks, rebelled against Hormizd IV, and became the first non-Sasanian to take the Persian throne. Defeated by Khosrow II with Roman help at the Blarathon, he fled to the Turks and was assassinated. He became a hero of Persian romance.

people.name: Odoacer
people.summary: Officer of Scirian origin, son of Edeco (Attila's envoy in 449), who as leader of the federate army deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476 and ruled Italy as king for 17 years, keeping the Senate and Roman administration. He took Dalmatia (481) and destroyed the Rugii (487). Zeno sent Theodoric against him; Theodoric killed him at a banquet.
people.death: killed by Theodoric at Ravenna, 15 March 493

people.name: Gundobad
people.summary: Ricimer's nephew, who beheaded Anthemius in 472, made Glycerius emperor, then returned to rule the Burgundians for over forty years. He issued the Liber Constitutionum (Lex Gundobada) and a Roman law for his Roman subjects, and allied with Clovis at Vouillé.

people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.summary: North African rhetorician turned bishop, the most influential Latin theologian: the Confessions (c. 397-400), On the Trinity, and the City of God (413-426), written in answer to the sack of Rome. He fought Donatists, Manichaeans and Pelagians and died during the Vandal siege of Hippo.
people.death: fever during the Vandal siege of Hippo, 28 August 430

people.name: Jerome
people.summary: Dalmatian-born scholar and ascetic, translator of most of the Latin Vulgate Bible, who lived at Bethlehem from 386. His letters on the Rhine crossing (Ep. 123) and the sack of Rome (Ep. 127, 128) are among the most quoted responses to the western catastrophe.

people.name: John Chrysostom
people.summary: Antiochene preacher of genius, archbishop of Constantinople from 398, whose reforming zeal and sermons against the rich and the court earned the enmity of the empress Eudoxia and Theophilus of Alexandria. Deposed at the Synod of the Oak and exiled in 404, he died on a forced march.
people.death: exhaustion during forced march at Comana Pontica, 14 September 407

people.name: Cyril of Alexandria
people.summary: Combative patriarch who expelled Alexandria's Jews and Novatians, was implicated by association in the murder of Hypatia, and engineered the condemnation of Nestorius at Ephesus in 431. His Christology, emphasising the one nature of the incarnate Word, was claimed by both Chalcedonians and their opponents.

people.name: Nestorius
people.summary: Antiochene monk made archbishop of Constantinople in 428, who objected to calling Mary Theotokos ('God-bearer'), preferring Christotokos. Condemned at Ephesus in 431 and exiled to Egypt, he wrote a defence, the Book of Heracleides, surviving in Syriac. The Church of the East venerates him.

people.name: Pope Leo I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome whose Tome (449) defined the two natures of Christ and was acclaimed at Chalcedon ('Peter has spoken through Leo'). He led the embassy that met Attila in 452 and negotiated with Gaiseric in 455. He articulated the theory of papal primacy as the heir of Peter.

people.name: Dioscorus of Alexandria
people.summary: Cyril's successor, who presided over the 'Robber Synod' of Ephesus in 449, rehabilitating Eutyches and deposing Flavian. Deposed at Chalcedon in 451 (formally for contumacy) and exiled to Gangra. Venerated as a saint by the Coptic Church.

people.name: Eutyches
people.summary: Elderly archimandrite and godfather of the eunuch Chrysaphius, who taught that after the union Christ had only one nature, his humanity absorbed in his divinity. Condemned by Flavian in 448, rehabilitated in 449, condemned again at Chalcedon. Both Chalcedonians and miaphysites rejected his views.

people.name: Severus of Antioch
people.summary: Leading anti-Chalcedonian theologian, patriarch of Antioch under Anastasius, deposed by Justin I in 518. From exile in Egypt he shaped miaphysite doctrine; his huge corpus survives mainly in Syriac. Justinian condemned him in 536.

people.name: Pope Vigilius
people.summary: Roman deacon installed as pope by Belisarius and Antonina in 537 after the deposition of Silverius, allegedly with a secret promise to Theodora to reject Chalcedon. Detained in Constantinople from 547, he vacillated over the Three Chapters, fled to sanctuary, and finally accepted the council of 553.
people.death: at Syracuse on his way back to Rome, 7 June 555

people.name: Gregory the Great
people.summary: Aristocratic urban prefect turned monk and pope, who governed Rome amid Lombard war and plague, negotiated with Agilulf, sent Augustine to the English (597), and wrote the Pastoral Rule, the Moralia on Job and the Dialogues. His Register of 854 letters is a unique window on late sixth-century Italy and the papal estates.

people.name: Sergius I of Constantinople
people.summary: Syrian-born patriarch, Heraclius's closest collaborator: he crowned him, lent church treasure for the Persian war, led the defence of Constantinople in 626 with icon processions, and devised Monoenergism and the Ecthesis. Condemned posthumously as a heretic in 681.

people.name: Sophronius of Jerusalem
people.summary: Damascene monk and travelling companion of John Moschus, leading opponent of Monoenergism, elected patriarch of Jerusalem in 634. His Christmas sermon of 634 laments that Christians could not reach Bethlehem because of the 'Saracens'. He surrendered the city to Umar.

people.name: Cyrus of Alexandria
people.summary: Heraclius's patriarch and governor of Egypt, who imposed the Monoenergist union of 633 and persecuted the Coptic church. Probably the al-Muqawqis of Arab tradition, he negotiated the surrender of Babylon and the Treaty of Alexandria with Amr ibn al-As in 641.

people.name: Procopius of Caesarea
people.summary: The great historian of Justinian's age. Present at Dara, in Africa and in Italy with Belisarius, he wrote the Wars (8 books), the Buildings (a panegyric of Justinian's construction), and the Secret History (Anekdota), a savage, unpublished attack on Justinian, Theodora, Belisarius and Antonina.

people.name: Zosimus
people.summary: Pagan historian writing in Constantinople around 500, whose New History in six books blames Rome's decline on the abandonment of the traditional gods. For 395-410 he follows Eunapius and then Olympiodorus closely, making him the main narrative source for Stilicho and Alaric. His text breaks off in summer 410, just before the sack.

people.name: Olympiodorus of Thebes
people.summary: Egyptian poet and diplomat who travelled with a pet parrot, went on an embassy to the Huns, and wrote a history of the West from 407 to 425 in 22 books, surviving only in Photius's summary and through Zosimus, Sozomen and Philostorgius. It is the best-informed source for the fall of Stilicho, the sack of Rome and Galla Placidia.

people.name: Priscus of Panium

roles.t: Member of the embassy to Attila

people.summary: Thracian rhetor and diplomat, eyewitness of Attila's court in 449, whose classicising history (covering c. 434-474) survives only in fragments in the tenth-century Excerpta de legationibus and in Jordanes and Evagrius. His Hunnic material is unique and vivid but literary, including the famous debate with a Greek who had become a Hun.

people.name: Agathias
people.summary: Poet and lawyer from Myrina who continued Procopius with a history of 552-559 in five books: Narses's Italian campaigns, the Lazic war, the Kutrigur invasion and Belisarius's last victory, with a digression on Persian customs drawn from royal annals via the interpreter Sergius. He also compiled the Cycle, an anthology of epigrams.

people.name: Theophylact Simocatta
people.summary: Egyptian-born official under Heraclius, last of the classicising historians, whose History in eight books covers Maurice's reign (582-602) in a famously florid style. Indispensable for the Persian war of 572-591, the restoration of Khosrow II and the Balkan campaigns, it ends with Phocas's coup.

people.name: Jordanes

roles.t: Notarius of the magister militum Gunthigis

people.summary: Latin-speaking official of Gothic descent in Constantinople who in 551 wrote the Romana and the Getica, a summary of Cassiodorus's lost Gothic History. The Getica's account of Gothic origins in 'Scandza', the Catalaunian Plains and Attila's death is central to Gothic history but heavily debated.

people.name: Orosius
people.summary: Spanish priest from Bracara who joined Augustine in Africa and wrote the Seven Books of History against the Pagans (416-417), a providential universal history and a contemporary source for the Gothic wars and the sack of 410.

people.name: Sidonius Apollinaris
people.summary: Gallo-Roman aristocrat, poet and letter-writer, son-in-law of Avitus, who delivered panegyrics on three emperors (Avitus, Majorian, Anthemius), became urban prefect, and as bishop of Clermont led its resistance to Euric. His letters are the best portrait of Gallic aristocratic society as Roman rule ended.

people.name: Boethius
people.summary: Roman senator and philosopher who translated and commented on Aristotle's logic, wrote on music, arithmetic and theology, and served Theodoric as magister officiorum. Convicted of treason, he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison before his execution; it became one of the most read books of the Middle Ages.

people.name: Cassiodorus
people.summary: Calabrian senator who served the Ostrogothic kings for thirty years, writing their official letters (Variae), a Chronicle and a lost Gothic History used by Jordanes. After years in Constantinople he founded the monastery of Vivarium, where his Institutiones laid out a programme for preserving sacred and secular learning.
people.death: natural causes at Vivarium, c. 585, aged about 100

people.name: Claudian

roles.t: Court poet of Honorius and Stilicho

people.summary: Alexandrian Greek who became the last great classical Latin poet, writing panegyrics for Stilicho and Honorius and invectives against Rufinus and Eutropius. His poems are propaganda but our main contemporary source for western politics 395-404.

people.name: John Malalas
people.summary: Antiochene official whose Chronographia in 18 books, from Adam to 563, written in a Greek closer to the spoken language, is the first surviving Byzantine world chronicle. Uncritical for earlier periods but valuable for sixth-century Antioch and Constantinople, including Nika, the Antioch earthquake and the Academy edict.

people.name: Gregory of Tours
people.summary: Gallo-Roman aristocrat and bishop of Tours whose Ten Books of Histories are the principal source for Clovis and the Merovingian Franks, as well as hagiographies of Martin and other saints. His account of Clovis's conversion and wars is shaped by his theological purposes.

people.name: Menander Protector
people.summary: Constantinopolitan who, after a dissolute youth, joined the palace guard and wrote a continuation of Agathias covering 558-582 under Maurice's patronage. Fragments preserved in the Excerpta de legationibus contain the full terms of the 562 treaty with Persia and accounts of embassies to the Avars and Turks.

people.name: Anthemius of Tralles
people.summary: Mathematician and engineer from Tralles, co-designer of Hagia Sophia with Isidore of Miletus. He wrote on burning mirrors and conic sections, and Agathias tells that he frightened a neighbour with a simulated earthquake made with steam-driven leather tubes.

people.name: Isidore of Miletus
people.summary: Geometer and engineer who completed Hagia Sophia with Anthemius of Tralles and edited Archimedes' works, an edition that helped them survive. His nephew Isidore the Younger rebuilt the dome after 558.

people.name: George of Pisidia

roles.t: Deacon and skeuophylax of Hagia Sophia

people.summary: Court poet of Heraclius and Patriarch Sergius, whose iambic poems (Expeditio Persica on the 622 campaign, Bellum Avaricum on the 626 siege, Heraclias on the victory) are the main contemporary literary sources for the Persian war, used by Theophanes.

people.name: Evagrius Scholasticus

roles.t: Lawyer, adviser to the patriarch of Antioch

people.summary: Lawyer from Epiphania in Syria whose Ecclesiastical History (431-594) is a key Chalcedonian source for the period. He survived the plague as a child and lost wife, children and grandchildren to its later waves, which he describes vividly.

people.name: Hydatius
people.summary: Bishop in Gallaecia whose chronicle (379-468) is the main source for fifth-century Spain under Sueves, Vandals and Goths, written in an apocalyptic mood from a province abandoned by imperial power. He went on an embassy to Aetius in 431.

people.name: Victor of Vita
people.summary: African cleric who around 484-489 wrote the History of the Vandal Persecution, a passionate account of Arian persecution of the Nicene church under Gaiseric and Huneric, and the source of the figure of 80,000 Vandals crossing in 429.

people.name: Muhammad

roles.t: Prophet and leader of the community at Medina

people.summary: Meccan merchant and prophet of Islam, who migrated to Medina in 622, unified much of Arabia by 630, and sent the first expeditions against Roman Syria (Mu'ta, 629; Tabuk, 630). The armies of his successors overran Syria, Egypt and Persia within a decade of his death.

people.name: Abu Bakr
people.summary: Muhammad's companion and father-in-law, first caliph, who crushed the Ridda revolts and launched the invasions of Iraq and Syria, sending Khalid ibn al-Walid across the desert to Syria in 634.

people.name: Umar ibn al-Khattab
people.summary: Second caliph, under whom the Arabs conquered Syria (Yarmuk 636), Iraq (Qadisiyya c. 636), Jerusalem, Mesopotamia and Egypt. He received Jerusalem's surrender in person, created the diwan register of pensions, and fixed the Hijra calendar. Murdered in 644 by a Persian slave.
people.death: stabbed in the mosque at Medina, November 644

people.name: Khalid ibn al-Walid

roles.t: Commander in the Ridda wars and Iraq

people.summary: 'The Sword of God': Meccan cavalry commander who fought against Muhammad at Uhud, converted in 629, saved the army at Mu'ta, crushed the Ridda, campaigned in Iraq, crossed the desert to Syria in 634 and was a leading commander at Ajnadayn, Damascus and the Yarmuk. Umar removed him from supreme command.

people.name: Amr ibn al-As
people.summary: Meccan Qurashi commander who had traded in Egypt before Islam, led the army of Palestine (634-639), invaded Egypt in December 639, won at Heliopolis, took Babylon and negotiated the Treaty of Alexandria. He founded Fustat and later supported Mu'awiya.

people.name: Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah
people.fullName: Amir ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah
people.summary: Early companion of Muhammad, appointed by Umar to replace Khalid as supreme commander in Syria; overall commander at the Yarmuk and in the conquest of Damascus, Emesa, Antioch and Jerusalem. He died in the plague of Amwas.

people.name: Titus Larcius
people.summary: Consul 501 and 498 and, according to Livy, the first Roman dictator (501), appointed against a Latin threat and the Sabines, with Sp. Cassius as master of horse.

people.name: Manius Valerius Maximus
people.summary: Popular dictator of 494 who won the plebs' trust by protecting debtors during the levy, triumphed over the Sabines, and resigned rather than break his promises when the Senate refused debt relief.

people.name: Attius Tullius
people.summary: Chief of the Volsci at Antium who received the exiled Coriolanus and led the Volscian war against Rome of 488; Plutarch calls him Tullus Aufidius, the name Shakespeare used.

people.name: Anaxilas
people.fullName: Anaxilas son of Cretines, tyrant of Rhegium
people.summary: Tyrant of Rhegium c. 494-476 of Messenian descent, who seized Zancle across the Strait and renamed it Messana, controlling both shores; ally of Terillus of Himera and father-in-law of Hiero of Syracuse.

people.name: Theron
people.fullName: Theron son of Aenesidamus, tyrant of Acragas
people.summary: Tyrant of Acragas c. 488-472, Gelon's father-in-law and partner at Himera (480), whose expulsion of Terillus from Himera provoked the Carthaginian invasion; he used Carthaginian prisoners to build the Olympieion.

people.name: Caeso Fabius
people.summary: Consul 484, 481 and 479, the most prominent of the three Fabian brothers; after first opposing agrarian reform he proposed distributing conquered land, then led his gens to private war against Veii and died with the 306 Fabii at the Cremera (477).
people.death: killed with the Fabii at the Cremera

people.name: Marcus Fabius
people.summary: Consul 483 and 480, who won the bloody battle before Veii in 480 but refused the triumph because his brother Quintus and his colleague Cn. Manlius had fallen; he joined the Cremera expedition.

people.name: Veturia
people.summary: Mother of Cn. Marcius Coriolanus who, at the head of the Roman matrons, went to his camp at the Fossae Cluiliae and shamed him into withdrawing the Volscian army; Plutarch calls her Volumnia.

people.name: Volumnia
people.summary: Wife of Coriolanus (Vergilia in Plutarch) who went with Veturia and her children to his camp in 488; she appears in Livy holding their two small sons.

people.name: Valeria
people.fullName: Valeria, sister of P. Valerius Publicola
people.summary: Sister of Publicola who, according to Dionysius and Plutarch, proposed that the matrons go to Coriolanus' camp and became the first priestess of Fortuna Muliebris.

people.name: Gnaeus Genucius
people.summary: Tribune of the plebs in 473 who indicted the consuls of 474 for failing to implement the agrarian law and was found dead in his house on the day of the trial.
people.death: found dead in his home, presumed murdered

people.name: Gaius Terentilius Harsa
people.summary: Tribune of the plebs in 462 whose bill for a commission to define and limit consular imperium began the decade-long campaign for written law that produced the Twelve Tables.

people.name: Caeso Quinctius
people.summary: Son of Cincinnatus, a giant and orator who led young patricians in driving tribunes from the Forum; accused of causing a plebeian's death, he jumped bail and fled to Etruria in 461, ruining his father.

people.name: Ducetius
people.summary: Hellenised Sicel leader who in the 450s united the native towns of eastern Sicily, founded Menaenum and Palike, fought Syracuse and Acragas, and after defeat and exile at Corinth returned to found Kale Akte; he died in 440.

people.name: Lucius Siccius Dentatus
people.summary: Legendary plebeian soldier, the 'Roman Achilles', credited with 120 battles, 45 frontal wounds, eight single combats, 14 civic crowns and many other decorations; murdered on the decemvirs' orders in 449.
people.death: killed by soldiers sent with him by the decemvirs

people.name: Lucius Valerius Potitus
people.summary: Leader with M. Horatius of the senatorial opposition to the decemvirs, consul 449, who carried the leges Valeriae Horatiae and defeated the Aequi and Volsci, triumphing by vote of the people.

people.name: Marcus Horatius Barbatus
people.summary: Consul 449 with L. Valerius, co-author of the leges Valeriae Horatiae restoring provocatio and tribunician sacrosanctity, and victor over the Sabines.

people.name: Lucius Icilius
people.summary: Tribune of the plebs 456, who carried the law distributing the Aventine to the plebs, betrothed of Verginia in 449, and again tribune in 449, when he carried the popular vote granting triumphs to Valerius and Horatius.

people.name: Lucius Verginius
people.summary: Plebeian centurion who killed his daughter Verginia in the Forum with a butcher's knife rather than let Appius Claudius claim her as a slave, roused the army to secession, and as tribune of the plebs (449) prosecuted Appius.

people.name: Lucius Papirius Mugillanus
people.summary: Suffect consul 444 with L. Sempronius Atratinus after the first consular tribunes abdicated, and with him the first censors (443); his name in the treaty with Ardea and the linen books was cited by Licinius Macer.

people.name: Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus
people.summary: Three times dictator (437, 434, 426) and consular tribune, victor over Veii and Fidenae, author of the law limiting the censorship to eighteen months, for which the censors degraded him to the status of aerarius.

people.name: Aulus Postumius Tubertus
people.summary: Dictator 431 who defeated the Aequi and Volsci at Mount Algidus; a story, rejected by Livy, said he executed his son for leaving his post, the 'imperia Postumiana'.

people.name: Hermocrates
people.summary: Syracusan aristocrat who at the Congress of Gela (424) urged 'Sicily for the Sicilians', organised resistance to the Athenian expedition (415-413), led a Syracusan squadron in the Aegean, and was killed in 407 trying to force his way back into Syracuse.

people.name: Postumia
people.summary: Vestal tried for unchastity in 420 on the grounds of her elegant dress and free speech, acquitted, and told by the pontifex maximus to dress more soberly.

people.name: Velthur Spurinna
people.summary: Tarquinian magistrate honoured in the Elogia Tarquiniensia as the first Etruscan to lead an army across the sea to Sicily, probably in support of Athens against Syracuse (414-413).

people.name: Hannibal son of Gisco (409)
people.fullName: Hannibal son of Gisco, grandson of Hamilcar the Magonid
people.summary: Carthaginian general who led the great invasion of Sicily in 409, destroying Selinus and Himera, and died of plague while besieging Acragas in 406.

people.name: Himilco
people.summary: Carthaginian general who completed the sack of Acragas (406), took Gela, made the treaty of 405 with Dionysius, destroyed Messana and besieged Syracuse (396), where plague ruined his army; he bribed his way out and killed himself at Carthage.
people.death: suicide by starvation after the disaster at Syracuse

people.name: Dionysius II
people.summary: Tyrant of Syracuse 367-357 and 346-344, son of Dionysius I by the Locrian Doris; Plato tried to make him a philosopher-king; expelled by Dion, he ruled Locri, returned to Syracuse, and surrendered Ortygia to Timoleon, ending his days in Corinth.

people.name: Dion

roles.t: General with full powers of Syracuse

people.summary: Brother-in-law of Dionysius I and disciple of Plato, who brought Plato to Syracuse, was exiled by Dionysius II, returned with a small mercenary force in 357 to liberate the city, and was murdered by Callippus in 354.

people.name: Hicetas
people.summary: Syracusan exile and tyrant of Leontini who invited Corinthian help against Dionysius II and then allied with Carthage against Timoleon; defeated at Adranum and later captured and executed with his family.

people.name: Archidamus III
people.summary: Eurypontid king of Sparta (360-338), son of Agesilaus, who led mercenaries to Italy at Tarentum's request and was killed by the Messapians and Lucanians at Manduria in 338.

people.name: Lucius Manlius Imperiosus
people.summary: Dictator 363 to drive the ceremonial nail against plague, who tried to raise an army and was forced to resign; prosecuted in 362 for harshness, he was saved when his son Titus (later Torquatus) forced the prosecutor to drop the case.

people.name: Marcus Popillius Laenas
people.summary: Plebeian consul four times (359, 356, 350, 348), who defeated the Tiburtines and in 350 the Gauls, fighting wounded in the front line; ancestor of the Popillii Laenates.

people.name: Lucius Furius Camillus
people.summary: Grandson (or son) of the great Camillus; dictator 350 and 345, consul 349, when his military tribune Valerius Corvus fought the Gallic champion; he vowed the temple of Juno Moneta during the Auruncan war of 345.

people.name: Brutulus Papius
people.summary: Powerful Samnite noble blamed by his people for breaking the truce with Rome; he killed himself in 322 before he could be surrendered, and the Samnites sent his body to Rome.

people.name: Gaius Junius Bubulcus
people.summary: Plebeian consul 317, 313 and 311, censor 307 and dictator 302, who campaigned in Samnium and Apulia, vowed the temple of Salus in 311 and dedicated it as dictator in 302.

people.name: Hamilcar son of Gisco
people.summary: Carthaginian general who defeated Agathocles at the Himeras (311) and besieged Syracuse, but was captured in a failed night assault in 309 and executed; his head was sent to Agathocles in Africa.
people.death: captured and killed by the Syracusans

people.name: Ophellas
people.summary: Macedonian officer of Alexander, governor of Cyrene for Ptolemy and then independent, who marched an army and colonists across the Syrtis to join Agathocles against Carthage and was murdered by him in 308.

people.name: Bomilcar
people.summary: Carthaginian general who, during Agathocles' invasion, attempted to make himself tyrant of Carthage in 308; defeated in street fighting, he was crucified in the agora.

people.name: Archagathus
people.summary: Elder son of Agathocles, left in command in Africa; defeated in the interior and abandoned by his father in 307, he was killed by the mutinous army.

people.name: Gaius Fabius Pictor
people.summary: Patrician who painted the walls of the temple of Salus (dedicated 302) and was the first Roman noble known as a painter, giving his branch of the Fabii the cognomen Pictor; grandfather of the historian Q. Fabius Pictor.

people.name: Lucius Volumnius Flamma
people.summary: Plebeian consul 307 and 296, colleague of Appius Claudius Caecus both times; in 296 he defeated Samnite raiders on the Volturnus, and his patrician wife Verginia founded the cult of Plebeian Chastity.

people.name: Marcus Atilius Regulus (cos. 294)
people.summary: Plebeian consul 294 who, his camp attacked near Luceria, vowed a temple to Jupiter Stator and defeated the Samnites; probably father of the Regulus of the First Punic War.

people.name: Spurius Carvilius Maximus
people.summary: Plebeian consul 293 and 272, who took Cominium while Papirius won at Aquilonia, cast a colossal Jupiter for the Capitol from Samnite armour and built the temple of Fors Fortuna; in 272 he completed the Samnite war.

people.name: Publius Cornelius Rufinus
people.summary: Consul 290 and 277 and dictator, who was beaten in the Cranita hills but took Croton by a ruse; in 275 the censor Fabricius expelled him from the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate. Ancestor of Sulla.

people.name: Decius Vibellius

roles.t: Commander of the garrison of Rhegium

people.summary: Commander of the Campanian legion of 4,000 placed in Rhegium by Rome in 282, who in 280 massacred or expelled the citizens and held the city until Rome retook it in 270; he went blind and killed himself.

people.name: Lucius Aemilius Barbula
people.summary: Consul 281 who led the first Roman campaign against Tarentum, ravaging its territory and withdrawing before Pyrrhus' vanguard, and triumphed in 280 over the Tarentines, Samnites and Sallentini.

people.name: Milo

roles.t: Commander of the garrison of Tarentum

people.summary: Pyrrhus' trusted general who led the advance guard to Tarentum in 281, commanded the city's garrison, and in 272 surrendered the citadel to the Romans in exchange for safe passage.

people.name: Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus Maximus
people.fullName: Gnaeus Domitius Cn. f. Calvinus Maximus
people.summary: Plebeian consul 283, dictator 280 for holding elections, and the first plebeian censor to complete the lustrum (280); founder of the Domitii who later produced the Ahenobarbi and the emperor Nero.

people.name: Marcus Fulvius Flaccus (cos. 264)
people.summary: Plebeian consul 264 who completed the destruction of Volsinii, brought its god Vortumnus to Rome, and triumphed; his colleague Appius Claudius Caudex led the first army to Sicily.

people.name: Fabia
