people.fullName: Fabia, younger daughter of M. Fabius Ambustus
people.summary: Patrician wife of the plebeian C. Licinius Stolo whose envy of her sister, married to a consular tribune, Livy makes the spark of the Licinio-Sextian agitation.

people.name: Spurius Lucretius
people.summary: Father of Lucretia, prefect of the city under Tarquin, who joined the conspiracy of Brutus, was elected suffect consul in 509 after Collatinus' resignation and died in office within days.

people.name: Marcus Horatius Pulvillus
people.summary: Suffect consul 509 and consul 507, who dedicated the Capitoline temple; told during the ceremony that his son had died, he finished the dedication with his hand on the doorpost. Polybius' treaty with Carthage names him with Brutus.

people.name: Titus Herminius
people.summary: One of the two companions of Horatius Cocles at the bridge (508), consul 506, killed fighting at Lake Regillus (496); the Herminii, of Etruscan name, vanish after the mid-5th century.

people.name: Sextus Tarquinius
people.summary: Son of Tarquinius Superbus who took Gabii by treachery and whose rape of Lucretia provoked the expulsion of the kings; he fled to Gabii and was killed there in revenge.

people.name: Arruns Tarquinius
people.summary: Son of Tarquinius Superbus who, at the Silva Arsia in 509, charged the consul Brutus; the two killed each other.
people.death: killed in single combat with Brutus

people.name: Arruns Porsenna
people.summary: Son of Porsenna who led a Clusine army against Aricia and was defeated and killed by the Latins and Aristodemus of Cumae (504); survivors found refuge at Rome, origin of the Vicus Tuscus.

people.name: Thefarie Velianas
people.summary: Ruler of Caere (zilath or 'king' in the Phoenician text) who around 500 dedicated a sanctuary at Pyrgi to Uni-Astarte, recorded on the bilingual gold tablets found in 1964.

people.name: Lucius Sicinius Vellutus
people.summary: Leader of the First Secession who urged the plebs to the Mons Sacer and was among the first tribunes elected (493); Dionysius makes him prosecutor of Coriolanus.

people.name: Publius Licinius Calvus
people.summary: First plebeian elected military tribune with consular power (400); elected again in 396, he yielded his place to his son.

people.name: Lucius Genucius Aventinensis
people.summary: Second plebeian consul (365) and consul again in 362, the first plebeian consul to make war under his own auspices; he was ambushed and killed by the Hernici.
people.death: killed in battle with the Hernici

people.name: Gaius Poetelius Libo Visolus
people.summary: Tribune of the plebs 358 who carried the first law against canvassing, plebeian consul 360, 346 and 326, triumphing over the Gauls and Tiburtines (360); the abolition of nexum (lex Poetelia Papiria, 326) bears his name.

people.name: Gaius Maenius
people.summary: Plebeian consul 338 who defeated the Latins and Antiates at the Astura and fixed the beaks of Antium's ships to the speakers' platform; honoured with the Maenian column; censor 318 (balconies called maeniana) and dictator 320 and 314, when he investigated the Capuan conspiracy.

people.name: Titus Veturius Calvinus
people.summary: Consul 334 and 321, colleague of Sp. Postumius in the Caudine Forks disaster, and one of the guarantors handed over to the Samnites in 320.

people.name: Gaius Plautius Venox
people.summary: Censor 312 with Appius Claudius, credited with finding the springs of the Aqua Appia (hence 'Venox', the vein-finder); he resigned when Appius refused to lay down office after eighteen months.

people.name: Quintus Marcius Tremulus
people.summary: Plebeian consul 306 and 288, who crushed the Hernican revolt and was honoured with an equestrian statue before the temple of Castor.

people.name: Herennius Pontius
people.summary: Aged father of Gavius Pontius who, asked how to treat the Roman army trapped at Caudium, advised either releasing it unharmed or killing every man, and warned that a middle course would make enemies without weakening them.

people.name: Ovius Paccius
people.summary: Aged Samnite priest who in 293 at Aquilonia administered the terrible oath of the 'linen legion', reading from an ancient linen book, by which Samnite nobles swore to fight to the death.

people.name: Verginia (wife of Volumnius)
people.summary: Patrician woman who in 296, excluded from the shrine of Pudicitia Patricia for marrying the plebeian consul L. Volumnius, founded a shrine of Pudicitia Plebeia in her house on the Vicus Longus.

people.name: Minucia
people.summary: Vestal suspected because of her dress and convicted on a slave's evidence of unchastity, she was buried alive at the Colline Gate in 337.

people.name: Lucius Albinius
people.summary: Plebeian who, fleeing Rome before the Gauls in 390, made his wife and children get down from his cart so that the Vestals and the sacred objects could ride to Caere.

people.name: Sthenius Statilius
people.summary: Lucanian leader who twice attacked Thurii in the 280s, provoking the Thurians' appeal to Rome and the tribune C. Aelius' measure against him.

people.name: Britomaris
people.summary: Senonian chief who, according to Appian, killed Roman envoys in 284 to avenge his father, killed in the fighting at Arretium; his act provoked Dolabella's destruction of the Senones.

people.name: Phintias
people.summary: Tyrant of Acragas in the 280s who styled himself king, destroyed Gela and moved its people to his new city of Phintias (Licata), and fought Hicetas of Syracuse; his coins bear his name and the portrait of Artemis.

people.name: Gaius Atilius Regulus Serranus
people.summary: Consul 257, when he rushed ahead of his fleet off Tyndaris and was nearly caught before winning the battle, and again 250, when with Manlius Vulso he opened the siege of Lilybaeum. The cognomen Serranus was later explained by the tale that he was found sowing (serere) when called to office.

people.name: Lucius Manlius Vulso Longus
people.summary: Regulus' colleague in 256, commanding the third and fourth squadrons at Ecnomus. After the landing at Aspis he was recalled with most of the fleet, 27,000 prisoners and the booty, leaving Regulus 15,500 men; he triumphed for the naval victory. Consul again 250 at the siege of Lilybaeum.

people.name: Servius Fulvius Paetinus Nobilior
people.summary: Consul 255 who with Marcus Aemilius Paullus took 350 ships to rescue the survivors of Regulus' army, won off Cape Hermaeum, and then lost most of the fleet in the storm off Camarina. Both consuls nonetheless triumphed for the naval victory in 254.

people.name: Marcus Aemilius Paullus
people.summary: Consul 255, victor with Fulvius Nobilior off Cape Hermaeum and survivor of the Camarina disaster. He triumphed in January 254 and a column with ships' beaks was set up on the Capitol in his honour; it was struck by lightning and destroyed in 172 (Livy 42.20).

people.name: Lucius Junius Pullus
people.summary: Consul 249 whose huge supply convoy was destroyed by Carthalo and a storm off Pachynus. Undaunted, he seized the summit of Mount Eryx and the town below. Tradition paired him with Claudius Pulcher as consuls who ignored the sacred chickens; Cicero says he killed himself rather than face trial.

people.name: Quintus Valerius Falto
people.summary: Praetor 241 who commanded the fleet at the Aegates while the consul Lutatius Catulus lay wounded. He claimed the triumph; the dispute went to a formal sponsio before the judge Atilius Calatinus, who ruled for the consul, but Falto was allowed his own naval triumph. Consul 239.

people.name: Aulus Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 242 and flamen Martialis. When he wished to go to Sicily, the pontifex maximus Lucius Caecilius Metellus forbade him to leave Rome and neglect his priesthood, an early documented clash between religious and military duty. Censor 234.

people.name: Titus Manlius Torquatus
people.summary: Consul 235, when he subdued Sardinia and closed the doors of Janus for the first time since Numa, and 224, when he invaded the Boii. In 216 he argued against ransoming the Cannae prisoners; in 215 he crushed Hampsicora's Sardinian revolt. Famous for old-fashioned severity.

people.name: Gaius Atilius Regulus
people.summary: Consul 225 who brought his army back from Sardinia, landed at Pisae, and blundered into the Gallic host at Telamon from the north, trapping it against Papus' army. He was killed leading the cavalry for the hill and his head was carried to the Gallic kings.

people.name: Lucius Aemilius Papus
people.summary: Consul 225 who shadowed the Gallic army down Etruria and, with Regulus arriving from the north, destroyed it at Telamon; he then ravaged the Boian country and triumphed, hanging Gallic standards and torques on the Capitol. Censor 220 with Gaius Flaminius.

people.name: Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus
people.summary: Consul 229 who took 200 ships across the Adriatic in the First Illyrian War, received Corcyra from Demetrius of Pharos, relieved Epidamnus and Issa and celebrated a naval triumph over the Illyrians in 228.

people.name: Lucius Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 234 and 229 (when he led the land army into Illyria) and praetor 216, sent to hold the Gauls. In the Litana forest the Boii cut the trees to topple on his column; he was killed and his skull, gilded, became a sacred drinking cup in a Boian temple. He had already been elected consul for 215.
people.death: killed in the Litana forest ambush

people.name: Publius Furius Philus
people.summary: Consul 223 with Flaminius, defeating the Insubres; praetor 216, wounded at sea off Africa. As censor in 214 he and Marcus Atilius Regulus degraded those who had talked of leaving Italy after Cannae; he died before the lustrum.

people.name: Gnaeus Servilius Geminus
people.summary: Flaminius' colleague in 217, whose advance cavalry under Centenius was destroyed after Trasimene. He took a fleet to raid the African coast and Cercina, then held the line in Apulia under Fabius' system, and was killed at Cannae commanding the Roman centre as proconsul.

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus
people.summary: Son of the Cunctator. When his father rode up to him as consul at Suessula, he ordered the old man to dismount, to the father's pride. He recaptured Arpi in 213 by a night attack in a rainstorm. He died before his father, who gave the funeral speech.

people.name: Appius Claudius Pulcher
people.summary: A survivor of Cannae, praetor in Sicily 215 and Marcellus' second in command against Syracuse, where his assault on the sea walls broke on Archimedes' engines. As consul 212 he began the siege of Capua; he was mortally wounded repelling a sortie in 211.

people.name: Gnaeus Fulvius Flaccus
people.summary: Brother of the conqueror of Capua. As praetor in Apulia in 212 he let his army fall into indiscipline and was destroyed by Hannibal near Herdonia, fleeing early. Prosecuted by a tribune on a capital charge in 211, he went into exile at Tarquinii.

people.name: Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus Maximus
people.summary: Consul 211, who helped defend Rome during Hannibal's march to the Colline Gate. As proconsul in 210 he was trying to recover Herdonia when Hannibal caught and destroyed his army; he died with eleven military tribunes.
people.death: killed at the second battle of Herdonia

people.name: Titus Quinctius Crispinus
people.summary: Consul 208 with Marcellus; earlier famed for a duel with his Campanian guest-friend Badius at Capua (212). Wounded in the ambush near Venusia in which Marcellus died, he escaped, warned the towns that Hannibal had Marcellus' signet ring, and died of his wounds later that year.

people.name: Marcus Cornelius Cethegus
people.summary: Censor 209 though not yet consul, consul 204 and, as proconsul with Quinctilius Varus, victor over Mago in the land of the Insubres in 203. Ennius called him 'the marrow of Persuasion' (Suadai medulla), and Cicero names him the first Roman remembered as an orator.

people.name: Publius Licinius Crassus Dives
people.summary: Elected pontifex maximus in 212 though he had held no curule office, over two senior consulars; censor 210, consul 205 with Scipio, keeping Hannibal penned in Bruttium while a plague hit his army. Livy calls him handsome, rich, eloquent and learned in pontifical law. His funeral games in 183 included 120 gladiators.

people.name: Quintus Pleminius
people.summary: Scipio's legate who recaptured Locri in 205 and then plundered the city and the treasury of Persephone; he had two military tribunes flogged to death. Sent to Rome in chains, he died in prison, reportedly after a plot to burn the city to escape (Livy 34.44).

people.name: Gaius Cornelius Cethegus
people.summary: Consul 197 who split the Cenomani from the Insubres and won at the Mincius, triumphing with Hamilcar the Carthaginian among his captives; he vowed the temple of Juno Sospita. As censor 194 he gave senators separate seats at the games.

people.name: Lucius Furius Purpurio
people.summary: As praetor in 200 he defeated the Gauls who had sacked Placentia outside Cremona, killing the Carthaginian Hamilcar (in one version) and triumphing without his army. Consul 196, a commissioner at Apamea in 188, and a critic of Manlius Vulso.

people.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus
people.summary: Son of the great Marcellus, who escaped the ambush that killed his father in 208. He dedicated the temple of Honos and Virtus in 205, triumphed as consul over the Insubres and Comum in 196, and was censor in 189 with Titus Flamininus.

people.name: Lucius Quinctius Flamininus
people.summary: Brother of Titus; commanded the fleet in the Second Macedonian War and took Eretria. Consul 192. In 184 Cato expelled him from the Senate for killing a Gallic deserter (in another version a condemned man) at dinner in Gaul to amuse a favourite who had never seen a man killed.

people.name: Quintus Minucius Thermus
people.summary: Won a victory at Turda in Spain (196) and fought the Ligurians from Pisae for four years after his consulship (193-190). Cato attacked him in two speeches, one charging that he had flogged ten Ligurian magistrates for poor supplies. He was killed in Thrace in 188 when Thracians ambushed Manlius Vulso's returning army.

people.name: Lucius Aemilius Regillus
people.summary: Praetor 190 who with the Rhodians destroyed Polyxenidas' fleet at Myonessus, opening the sea route for the Scipios. He triumphed at sea in 189 and vowed a temple to the Lares Permarini, dedicated in 179 with a tablet recording the victory.

people.name: Gaius Livius Salinator
people.summary: Commander of the Roman fleet in 191 who, with Eumenes II, defeated Polyxenidas off Corycus and crossed into the Hellespont. Consul 188. A kinsman of the victor of the Metaurus.

people.name: Spurius Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 186 who, warned by Hispala Faecenia and Aebutius, laid the Bacchic conspiracy before the Senate and ran the inquiry that followed throughout Italy. In 185-184 he also uncovered slave conspiracies among Apulian herdsmen. He died in the epidemic of 180.

people.name: Quintus Marcius Philippus
people.summary: Consul 186, when he lost 4,000 men in the Ligurian 'Saltus Marcius'. As envoy in 172 he lulled Perseus with a truce while Rome prepared, a trick older senators condemned as 'new wisdom' (nova sapientia). As consul again in 169, aged about 60, he forced the passes into Pieria. Censor 164.

people.name: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus
people.summary: Victor over the Celtiberians at Aebura and in the Manlian pass (181-180), when he vowed the temple of Fortuna Equestris. As censor in 174 he stripped half the marble roof tiles from Juno Lacinia at Croton for his temple; the Senate ordered them returned. Hearing that one son had died and another was dying in Illyria, he hanged himself in 172.

people.name: Gaius Claudius Pulcher
people.summary: Consul 177 who finished the Istrian war at Nesactium and recaptured Mutina from the Ligurians. As censor in 169 with Tiberius Gracchus he was prosecuted by the tribune Publius Rutilius; eight of the twelve centuries of the first class voted to convict before Gracchus' oath to share his fate turned the vote.

people.name: Quintus Petillius Spurinus
people.summary: As urban praetor in 181 he examined the 'Books of Numa' found on the Janiculum and had them burned in the Comitium. As consul 176 he was killed attacking the Ligurians on Mons Letum, having (Livy says) remarked before the battle that he would 'take Letum', an omen on the word letum, death.
people.death: killed in battle with the Ligurians

people.name: Lucius Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 173 who, angry at a past slight from Praeneste, ordered the town to receive him with lodging, transport and a public welcome when he went to sacrifice at the shrine of Fortuna. Livy marks it as the first time a Roman magistrate imposed such burdens on allies, and a precedent that grew.

people.name: Marcus Popillius Laenas
people.summary: Consul 173 who attacked the Ligurian Statellates, who had not fought Rome, and sold 10,000 of them after their surrender. He defied the Senate's order to free them and was shielded by his brother, consul in 172, and by delays in the inquiry voted by plebiscite. Censor 159.

people.name: Publius Licinius Crassus
people.summary: Consul 171, first commander against Perseus. His cavalry and light infantry were beaten near the hill of Callinicus outside Larissa; he spent the rest of the year plundering Boeotian and Thessalian allies and was later accused of extortion.

people.name: Gaius Lucretius Gallus
people.summary: Praetor 171 in command of the fleet, who sacked Haliartus and plundered Chalcis and other allied towns. In 170 two tribunes prosecuted him on the complaint of the Chalcidians, and all 35 tribes condemned him to a fine of a million asses.

people.name: Aulus Hostilius Mancinus
people.summary: Consul 170 whose year against Perseus produced no result. On his way to the army through Epirus he narrowly escaped a plot by the Molossian leaders Theodotus and Philostratus to hand him over to the Macedonians.

people.name: Gnaeus Octavius
people.summary: Praetor 168 who blockaded Perseus on Samothrace and took his surrender, triumphing at sea and building the Porticus Octavia with its bronze capitals. Consul 165, the first of his family. Sent to Syria to enforce the Apamea limits, he burned ships and hamstrung the Seleucid elephants and was murdered at Laodicea in 162; the Senate set up his statue on the Rostra.

people.name: Gaius Sulpicius Galus
people.summary: Aemilius Paullus' military tribune who, on the eve of Pydna (21 June 168), told the troops that a lunar eclipse was coming and why, so that they were not alarmed. Consul 166, triumphing over the Ligurians; Cicero presents him as Rome's first serious astronomer.

people.name: Quintus Fulvius Nobilior
people.summary: Consul 153, the first to take office on 1 January for the Spanish emergency. He was ambushed on the feast of the Vulcanalia by the Segedans under Carus, losing 6,000 citizens, and his elephants stampeded before Numantia. Patron of Ennius, to whom his father gave citizenship.

people.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus
people.summary: Grandson of the hero of Syracuse; consul three times (166, 155, 152), the third time against the custom that led to the ban on iteration. In Spain he founded Corduba and negotiated a moderate peace with the Celtiberians in 152-151. He drowned in a storm on an embassy to Masinissa in 148.

people.name: Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus
people.summary: Consul 148 who took over the stalled siege of Carthage, failed against Clupea and Hippo Diarrhytus and achieved nothing, which fed the popular demand for Scipio Aemilianus. Earlier, as praetor in Ulterior in 154, he had been beaten by the Lusitanians.

people.name: Gaius Vetilius
people.summary: Praetor in Hispania Ulterior who had surrounded a Lusitanian force and was negotiating its settlement when Viriathus took command. Lured into the defile of Tribola in 147, his army was cut to pieces; an old and fat man, he was captured and killed by a soldier who did not recognise him.
people.death: killed after the defeat at Tribola

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Aemilianus
people.summary: Eldest son of Aemilius Paullus, adopted into the Fabii Maximi, and brother of Scipio Aemilianus. He fought at Pydna and as consul in 145 took raw levies to Spain, trained them for a season, and in 144 drove Viriathus back and took two of his towns.

people.name: Quintus Pompeius
people.summary: A new man who won the consulship of 141 against Laelius, having promised Scipio Aemilianus not to stand. At Numantia he lost men in repeated failures, then in 140/139 made a secret treaty with the Numantines for a payment of 30 talents, which he denied before the Senate when his successor arrived. Censor 131, the first plebeian censor pair.

people.name: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus Porcina
people.summary: Consul 137, sent to replace Mancinus. Wanting glory, he attacked the Vaccaei and besieged Pallantia in 136 despite the Senate's envoys forbidding it; he retreated in disorder, losing 6,000 men, and was stripped of command and fined. Cicero rated him the first Roman orator to use smooth periodic style.

people.name: Lucius Furius Philus
people.summary: Consul 136 who handed the naked, bound Mancinus over to the Numantines, who refused him. A friend of Scipio Aemilianus and Laelius and a learned Hellenist, he speaks in Cicero's De re publica, where he argues Carneades' case against justice.

people.name: Appius Claudius Pulcher
people.summary: Consul 143 who attacked the Alpine Salassi, triumphed without senatorial approval, and was protected from a tribune's veto by his Vestal daughter riding in his chariot. Censor 136 and princeps senatus, rival of Scipio Aemilianus, father-in-law of Tiberius Gracchus and member of the agrarian commission of 133.

people.name: Quintus Marcius Rex
people.summary: Praetor 144 entrusted by the Senate with 180 million sesterces to repair the Aqua Appia and Anio Vetus and to build a new aqueduct; his command was prorogued to finish the Aqua Marcia, which he carried to the Capitol despite objections from the decemviri sacris faciundis.

people.name: Lucius Hostilius Tubulus
people.summary: Praetor 142 who presided over a murder court and took bribes so openly that in 141 a special quaestio was voted against him on the tribune Publius Mucius Scaevola's bill. He went into exile and, recalled to stand trial, took poison. Cicero uses him as a byword for judicial corruption.

people.name: Aulus Postumius Albinus
people.summary: Consul 151 (when he and Lucullus were imprisoned by tribunes over the levy) and author of a Roman history in Greek. In its preface he begged pardon for errors in a foreign tongue; Cato asked who had compelled him to write in Greek. Polybius thought him a vain Hellenomaniac.

people.name: Lucius Cincius Alimentus
people.summary: Praetor 210, then commander in Sicily, who was captured by Hannibal and, as he wrote, heard from Hannibal himself that 36,000 men had been lost crossing from the Rhône to Italy. He wrote a history of Rome in Greek from the foundation, which he dated to 729/8 BC.

people.name: Gaius Acilius
people.summary: Senator who interpreted for the Athenian philosophers before the Senate in 155 and wrote a history of Rome in Greek, later translated into Latin by one Claudius. Livy cites him for the conference between Hannibal and Scipio at Ephesus.

people.name: Naevius

roles.t: Soldier in the First Punic War

people.summary: Campanian-born poet, veteran of the First Punic War, author of comedies, tragedies, the first Roman historical plays (fabulae praetextae such as Clastidium) and the Bellum Punicum in Saturnian verse. His jibes at the Metelli ('fato Metelli Romae fiunt consules') reportedly brought prison and exile; he died at Utica.

people.name: Caecilius Statius
people.summary: An Insubrian Gaul enslaved as a boy, perhaps in the wars of the 190s, freed and active as a writer of comedies after Plautus, adapting Menander. Volcacius Sedigitus ranked him first of Roman comic poets. He died the year after Ennius and was buried near him on the Janiculum.

people.name: Pacuvius
people.summary: Nephew of Ennius from Brundisium, painter (a work of his hung in the temple of Hercules in the Forum Boarium) and the leading Roman tragedian between Ennius and Accius. He wrote a praetexta, Paullus, and tragedies such as Dulorestes and Iliona. In 140 he and the young Accius staged plays at the same games; he retired to Tarentum.

people.name: Lucius Cassius Hemina
people.summary: The first known annalist to write Roman history in Latin prose on a large scale after Cato, writing around 146 (he mentions the fourth Secular Games, which he dated to 146). Fragments survive chiefly through Pliny and the grammarians, including the arrival of the first Greek doctor, Archagathus, in 219.

people.name: Sextus Aelius Paetus Catus
people.summary: Consul 198 and censor 194, the jurist Ennius called 'egregie cordatus homo'. His Tripertita set out the Twelve Tables, their interpretation and the legis actiones, and was called the 'cradle of the law' (cunabula iuris) by Pomponius.

people.name: Gaius Licinius Crassus
people.summary: Tribune 145 who proposed that vacancies in the priestly colleges be filled by popular election instead of co-option. Laelius' speech on the antiquity of the pontifical rites defeated the bill. Cicero says Crassus was the first to address the people facing the Forum rather than the Comitium and Curia.

people.name: Hieronymus
people.summary: Grandson and successor of Hiero II, aged fifteen. Led by his uncles Andranodorus and Zoippus and the Carthaginian agents Hippocrates and Epicydes, he broke with Rome and negotiated with Carthage for all Sicily. After thirteen months he was assassinated at Leontini in 214; his family was then massacred.

people.name: Hippocrates
people.summary: Born at Carthage to a Syracusan exile and a Carthaginian mother, he served with Hannibal in Italy and was sent with his brother Epicydes to Hieronymus. Elected general after the king's murder, he broke the Roman alliance, provoked Marcellus at Leontini, held the field against him in the siege and died of plague in the Carthaginian camp in 212.

people.name: Epicydes
people.summary: Brother of Hippocrates, also raised at Carthage and an officer of Hannibal. He commanded inside Syracuse during the siege, escaped to Agrigentum before the fall of Achradina in 212 and fled to Carthage when Agrigentum was betrayed in 210.

people.name: Antigonus III Doson
people.summary: Guardian of the young Philip V who took the royal title, rebuilt Macedonian power, and at Aratus' invitation intervened in the Peloponnese against Cleomenes III, forming the Hellenic Symmachy (224) and winning at Sellasia (222). He died after defeating an Illyrian invasion in 221.

people.name: Aratus of Sicyon

roles.t: Strategos of the Achaean League (17 times)

people.summary: Liberator of Sicyon (251), who brought it into the Achaean League and made the League the main power of the Peloponnese, seizing Acrocorinth from Macedon in 243. Threatened by Cleomenes III, he reversed his life's policy and called in Antigonus Doson. Adviser to Philip V, he was alienated by Philip's turn west and, according to Polybius and Plutarch, slowly poisoned by him. His memoirs were a source for Polybius.
people.death: believed poisoned on Philip V's orders

people.name: Cleomenes III
people.summary: Spartan king who in 227 killed the ephors, cancelled debts and redistributed land, enlarged the citizen body and nearly broke the Achaean League. Defeated at Sellasia in 222 by Antigonus Doson, he fled to Ptolemy III and, held at Alexandria under Ptolemy IV, died in a failed rising in 219.
people.death: suicide during a failed coup in Alexandria

people.name: Seleucus IV Philopator
people.summary: Son of Antiochus III, who commanded at Magnesia and inherited a kingdom burdened by the Apamea indemnity. He sent his chancellor Heliodorus to seize the Jerusalem temple treasure and exchanged his son Demetrius as hostage for his brother Antiochus. Heliodorus murdered him in 175.

people.name: Ptolemy V Epiphanes
people.summary: Child king whose regents lost Coele-Syria to Antiochus III at Panium (200). Crowned at Memphis in 196, an event commemorated by the decree on the Rosetta Stone, he married Antiochus' daughter Cleopatra I in 194/3 and crushed the Theban revolt in 186. He died, perhaps poisoned, in 180.

people.name: Ptolemy VI Philometor
people.summary: Son of Ptolemy V and Cleopatra I. Defeated and captured by Antiochus IV in 170-169, he was saved by Popillius at Eleusis. Expelled by his brother Ptolemy VIII, he came to Rome in 164 dressed as a commoner. Restored, he ruled a strong Egypt until he died of wounds after defeating Alexander Balas near Antioch in 145.
people.death: died of wounds after the battle of the Oenoparas

people.name: Cleopatra I Syra
people.summary: Daughter of Antiochus III, married to Ptolemy V at Raphia in winter 194/3 with a dowry that, Ptolemaic courtiers later claimed, included Coele-Syria's revenues. As regent for Ptolemy VI she kept peace with her brother Seleucus IV; the first Ptolemaic queen to issue coins in her own name.

people.name: Sosibius
people.summary: The minister who dominated Ptolemy IV's court, organised the murders of the king's mother, brother and uncle, and trained the native Egyptian phalanx that won Raphia (217). With Agathocles he concealed the king's death in 204 and had Queen Arsinoe III killed.

people.name: Scopas
people.summary: Aetolian leader who began the Social War of 220 and later, as a mercenary captain in Ptolemaic service, recruited 6,000 Aetolians and reconquered Judaea, only to be routed by Antiochus III at Panium (200) and forced to surrender in Sidon. Plotting a coup in Alexandria, he was executed in 196.

people.name: Achaeus
people.summary: Cousin of Antiochus III who restored Seleucid rule in Asia Minor against Attalus I, then took the diadem at Laodicea in 220. Besieged in the acropolis of Sardis from 215/4, he was betrayed by the Cretan Bolis, captured, mutilated and executed in 213.

people.name: Molon
people.summary: Satrap of Media who revolted against the young Antiochus III in 222, took Seleucia-on-the-Tigris and defeated royal armies. In 220 Antiochus met him in Apolloniatis; Molon's left wing went over to the king, and he killed himself; his body was impaled on the Zagros pass.

people.name: Demetrius
people.summary: Younger son of Philip V, a hostage in Rome after Cynoscephalae. Sent back in 184/3 to answer complaints, he was so well received by the Senate, which said it pardoned Philip for Demetrius' sake, that his brother Perseus could paint him as Rome's candidate for the throne. Philip had him poisoned in 180, reportedly on forged evidence.

people.name: Prusias I
people.summary: Bithynian king who fought Byzantium (220) and Pergamon, allied with Philip V and was rewarded with Cius and Myrlea. He sheltered Hannibal, who commanded his fleet against Eumenes II and, Nepos says, threw jars full of snakes onto the enemy decks. Under Roman pressure Prusias agreed to surrender Hannibal in 183.

people.name: Prusias II
people.summary: Married Perseus' sister but stayed neutral in the Third Macedonian War; in 167 he appeared before the Senate with shaven head and a freedman's cap, greeting it as 'saviour gods'. He invaded Pergamon in 156, sacking temples, until Rome forced peace and reparations (154). His son Nicomedes, aided by Attalus II, overthrew and killed him in 149.
people.death: killed at Nicomedia on his son's orders

people.name: Attalus II Philadelphus
people.summary: Brother and loyal general of Eumenes II, at Magnesia and in the Galatian wars. In Rome in 167 senators tempted him to ask for part of his brother's kingdom; he declined. As king he survived Prusias II's invasion, helped Rome against Andriscus and at Corinth, founded Attaleia and gave Athens the Stoa of Attalus.

people.name: Pharnaces I
people.summary: Pontic king who seized Sinope in 183, making it his capital, and fought Eumenes II, Ariarathes IV and Prusias II until compelled by Roman envoys and military pressure to accept peace in 179, giving up his gains in Galatia and Paphlagonia. Grandfather of Mithridates VI.

people.name: Callicrates
people.summary: Achaean politician who in 180 urged the Senate to back its friends in Greek states and so created, in Polybius' view, the class of informers who served Rome. After Pydna he denounced about 1,000 Achaeans, Polybius among them, who were deported to Italy. Hated at home, he died in 149 on an embassy to Rome.

people.name: Aristaenus
people.summary: Achaean strategos in 199/8 who persuaded the League at Sicyon to leave Philip V for Rome, and the leading advocate of compliance with Roman wishes in rivalry with Philopoemen, whose policy of defending Achaean rights within the alliance he opposed.

people.name: Lycortas
people.summary: Philopoemen's political heir and the father of Polybius. As strategos in 183/2 he avenged Philopoemen by capturing Messene and punishing his killers. In the Third Macedonian War he advocated strict neutrality, which put his circle, including his son, on Callicrates' list.

people.name: Polyxenidas
people.summary: Rhodian exile who commanded Antiochus III's Aegean fleet. Beaten off Corycus (191), he destroyed the Rhodian squadron of Pausistratus at Panormus on Samos by a feigned negotiation (190), but lost the decisive battle of Myonessus to Regillus and the Rhodians later that year.

people.name: Hannibal the Rhodian
people.summary: Carthaginian noble whose fast ship repeatedly ran the Roman blockade of Lilybaeum in broad daylight, taunting the Romans. He was finally caught by a captured four-banked ship of fine build; the Romans then used his vessel as the model for the fleet that won the Aegates.

people.name: Spendius
people.summary: A Campanian slave who had deserted from Rome to Carthaginian service and, fearing extradition, became with the Libyan Mathos the leader of the mercenary revolt. He ordered the torture and murder of Gesco and 700 prisoners, was trapped at the Saw and crucified before Tunis.

people.name: Gesco
people.summary: Carthaginian commander at Lilybaeum who after the peace shipped the army home in detachments, a prudent arrangement the authorities wrecked by concentrating the men at Sicca unpaid. Sent to negotiate with the mutineers at Tunis, he was seized, and in 239 he and some 700 others were mutilated and buried alive.
people.death: tortured to death by the mercenaries

people.name: Himilco
people.summary: Commander of the Carthaginian army of some 25,000 foot, 3,000 horse and 12 elephants that landed at Heraclea Minoa in 213, took Agrigentum and won over many Sicilian towns. He died with much of his army in the plague that swept the marshy camp outside Syracuse in 212.

people.name: Muttines
people.summary: A Libyphoenician of Hippo Acra trained under Hannibal, whose Numidian horse ravaged Roman Sicily from Agrigentum. Slighted by the jealous Carthaginian general Hanno, he betrayed Agrigentum to Laevinus in 210, received Roman citizenship as Marcus Valerius Muttines, and is honoured with his sons in a Delphic inscription of 190.

people.name: Gulussa
people.summary: Son of Masinissa, envoy to Rome in 172 and 168, and commander of the Numidian cavalry for Scipio Aemilianus in the Third Punic War. On Masinissa's death Aemilianus divided the royal functions, giving Gulussa command of the army; with Laelius he destroyed the Carthaginian field force at Nepheris.

people.name: Scerdilaidas
people.summary: Illyrian chieftain, brother or kinsman of Agron, who led the land army in 230 and later ruled the Ardiaean kingdom. He switched between Philip V and Rome, joining the Roman-Aetolian coalition in 211; with his son Pleuratus he was named among Rome's adherents in the Peace of Phoenice.

people.name: Alexander Balas
people.summary: A youth from Smyrna presented as a son of Antiochus IV, promoted by Attalus II and the Seleucid exile Heraclides and recognised by the Roman Senate in 153/2. With Ptolemy VI and Jonathan Maccabaeus he defeated and killed Demetrius I in 150, married Cleopatra Thea, lost Ptolemy's support and was killed fleeing after the battle of the Oenoparas in 145.

people.name: Panaetius
people.summary: Rhodian Stoic who joined Scipio Aemilianus' household around 144, accompanied him on his eastern embassy of 140-139, and adapted Stoic ethics to Roman aristocratic life; his On Duties was the model for Cicero's De officiis. He succeeded Antipater as head of the Stoa at Athens.

people.name: Crates of Mallos

roles.t: Envoy of Attalus II to Rome

people.summary: Stoic scholar and head of the library at Pergamon, rival of Aristarchus, who built a terrestrial globe. Sent to Rome as envoy (Suetonius dates it to the time of Ennius' death, c. 168), he broke his leg in an opening of the Cloaca Maxima on the Palatine and, while convalescing, gave lectures that Suetonius calls the beginning of grammatical studies at Rome.

people.name: Hampsicora
people.summary: Sardo-Punic magnate, the most powerful man in Sardinia, who raised the island against Rome after Cannae and called in Carthaginian help. His son Hostus lost a battle to Manlius Torquatus near Cornus; Hampsicora killed himself when the joint Sardinian-Carthaginian army under Hasdrubal the Bald was destroyed.

people.name: Hispala Faecenia
people.summary: A freedwoman and courtesan who, having been initiated as a slave, revealed the Bacchic rites to the consul Postumius to save her lover Aebutius. The Senate rewarded her with 100,000 asses and extraordinary legal rights, including the right to marry a freeborn man without disgrace.

people.name: Claudia Quinta

roles.t: Matron at the reception of the Magna Mater

people.summary: Noblewoman who, in Livy, was one of the matrons who received the sacred stone of the Magna Mater at Ostia in 204. Later tradition (Ovid, Suetonius) has her, accused of unchastity, single-handedly drawing the grounded ship upriver to prove her purity; her statue stood in the goddess' temple vestibule.

people.name: Aemilia Tertia
people.summary: Daughter of Lucius Aemilius Paullus (killed at Cannae), wife of Scipio Africanus and mother of Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi. Polybius describes the splendour of her processions; she knowingly tolerated her husband's affair with a slave girl, whom she freed after his death. Her estate passed to Scipio Aemilianus.

people.name: Chiomara

roles.t: Wife of the Tolistobogian chief Orgiagon

people.summary: Wife of a Galatian chieftain captured in Manlius Vulso's campaign of 189. Raped by a centurion who then sold her ransom back, she had her countrymen behead him at the exchange and threw the head at her husband's feet. Polybius met her later at Sardis and admired her intelligence.

people.name: Gaius Memmius (tribune 111)
people.summary: Tribune of 111 who denounced the Senate's dealings with Jugurtha and had him summoned to Rome under safe conduct; Sallust gives him a fierce speech against the nobility. Clubbed to death in 100 while standing for the consulship against Glaucia.
people.death: killed by supporters of Saturninus and Glaucia at the consular elections

people.name: Quintus Varius Hybrida
people.summary: Tribune of 90 from Sucro in Spain (hence 'Hybrida', the half-breed), whose lex Varia set up a court to try those who had encouraged the Italian revolt, striking at Drusus' friends. Condemned under his own law in 89 and, Cicero says, died in agony.

people.name: Ariobarzanes I of Cappadocia
people.summary: Cappadocian noble chosen king about 95 under Roman supervision and installed by Sulla; expelled by Mithridates or Tigranes at least three times and restored by Rome each time. His epithet Philoromaios ('friend of the Romans') summed up the role of the Anatolian client kings. Abdicated in favour of his son about 63.

people.name: Publius Vettius Scato
people.summary: Marsic or Paelignian commander in the Social War who defeated Perperna and the consul Lucius Caesar in 90. Captured in 89, he was killed by his own slave, who stabbed him to save him from humiliation and then killed himself. Cicero recalls his courteous meeting with Pompeius Strabo between the lines.

people.name: Lucius Julius Caesar (consul 90)
people.summary: Consul of 90 who commanded on the southern front of the Social War and carried the lex Julia granting citizenship to loyal Latin and Italian communities, the decisive political concession of the war. Censor in 89; murdered in the Marian massacres of 87 with his brother Gaius Julius Caesar Strabo.
people.death: killed in the Marian massacres, his head displayed on the Rostra

people.name: Marius Egnatius
people.summary: Samnite commander in the Social War who took Venafrum by treachery in 90 and defeated Lucius Caesar near Teanum. Killed in battle in 89. Velleius lists him among the leading commanders of the Italian confederation.

people.name: Gaius Vidacilius
people.summary: Picene commander from Asculum who defeated Pompeius Strabo near Firmum in 90 and fought his way into besieged Asculum. When the town's fall was imminent he executed his political opponents, built his own pyre in a temple, took poison at a banquet and had himself burned.

people.name: Lucius Porcius Cato (consul 89)
people.summary: Great-grandson of Cato the Censor. As praetor in 90 he subdued Etruria, and as consul in 89 fought the Marsi with some success before being killed attacking their camp by the Fucine Lake, according to one tradition by the younger Marius.
people.death: killed in battle against the Marsi near the Fucine Lake

people.name: Quintus Pompeius Rufus
people.summary: Sulla's colleague as consul in 88, whose son married Sulla's daughter and was killed in the Sulpician riots. He joined Sulla's march on Rome, then was sent to take over Pompeius Strabo's army in Picenum and murdered by the soldiers.
people.death: murdered by Pompeius Strabo's soldiers while sacrificing

people.name: Nicomedes IV Philopator
people.summary: King of Bithynia from about 94, twice expelled by Mithridates and restored by Rome. His raid on Pontus at Roman instigation in 89 started the First Mithridatic War. The young Caesar's stay at his court in 80 gave rise to lasting gibes about Caesar as 'the queen of Bithynia'. He bequeathed his kingdom to Rome.

people.name: Aristion
people.summary: Philosopher, said to have been a Peripatetic or Epicurean, who led Athens into alliance with Mithridates in 88 and ruled as tyrant during Sulla's siege, mocking the Romans from the walls. Captured on the Acropolis after the sack and executed.
people.death: executed on Sulla's orders after the fall of the Acropolis

people.name: Lucius Cornelius Merula
people.summary: Flamen Dialis, made suffect consul in 87 when Cinna was deposed. When Marius and Cinna took the city he opened his veins on the Capitol, leaving a note that he had removed his priestly cap first so as not to pollute it.

people.name: Gaius Norbanus
people.summary: Tribune of 103 who prosecuted Caepio for Arausio, defended in 95 by Marcus Antonius. As consul in 83 he was beaten by Sulla at Mount Tifata and again at Faventia in 82. Fled to Rhodes and killed himself when Sulla demanded his surrender.

people.name: Quintus Lutatius Catulus Capitolinus
people.summary: Son of the victor of Vercellae, consul in 78 with Lepidus, whose revolt he defeated outside Rome in 77. He rebuilt and dedicated the Capitoline temple (69) and the Tabularium, opposed the lex Gabinia and Manilia, and as princeps senatus led the optimates until his death; he lost the election for pontifex maximus to Caesar in 63.

people.name: Gaius Herennius
people.summary: Sertorius' legate in eastern Spain, tribune in 80 who had blocked a bill restoring Pompey's father's allies. Defeated and killed by Pompey before Valentia in 75.

people.name: Lucius Afranius
people.summary: Picene follower of Pompey who served him in Spain against Sertorius, in the East, and as consul in 60, elected by open bribery. Commanded Pompey's Spanish legions with Petreius in 49, surrendered at Ilerda, rejoined Pompey, and after Thapsus was captured and killed by Sittius' troops.

people.name: Gaius Cornelius (tribune 67)
people.summary: Former quaestor of Pompey; as tribune in 67 proposed laws against lending to foreign envoys and against Senate dispensations, and carried the lex Cornelia binding praetors to their edicts. Prosecuted for maiestas in 65 and successfully defended by Cicero in a speech known through Asconius' commentary.

people.name: Gaius Manilius
people.summary: Tribune 67/66 who carried the lex Manilia transferring the war against Mithridates and Tigranes to Pompey, supported by Cicero's speech De imperio Cn. Pompei and by Caesar. His bill on freedmen's votes was annulled. Convicted after his tribunate amid riots.

people.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Creticus
people.summary: Consul in 69 who conquered Crete in a brutal three-year war (69-67), clashing with Pompey's legate over the islanders' wish to surrender to Pompey. Kept from his triumph by Pompey's partisans until 62. Grandfather of Caecilia Metella of the famous tomb on the Via Appia.

people.name: Aristobulus II
people.fullName: Aristobulus II, Hasmonean king and high priest

roles.t: King and high priest of Judaea

people.summary: Younger son of Alexander Jannaeus and Salome Alexandra; seized the throne and high priesthood from his brother Hyrcanus in 67. Defied Pompey, was besieged in the Temple in 63, and walked in Pompey's triumph. Escaped twice to raise revolts in Judaea; poisoned by Pompeians in 49 after Caesar freed him.

people.name: Hyrcanus II
people.summary: Elder son of Alexander Jannaeus, high priest under his mother Salome Alexandra (76-67), displaced by his brother in 67 and restored by Pompey in 63 as high priest without the royal title, guided by Antipater. Confirmed as ethnarch by Caesar. Mutilated by Antigonus in 40, he lived in Babylon, returned to Herod's court and was executed by Herod in 30 as a potential rival.

people.name: Antipater the Idumaean
people.summary: Idumaean noble who made himself indispensable to Hyrcanus II and to every Roman commander in the East: Pompey, Scaurus, Gabinius, Caesar. He led 3,000 Jewish troops to relieve Caesar at Alexandria and was rewarded with citizenship and the procuratorship of Judaea. Poisoned at a banquet by a rival, Malichus. Father of Herod.

people.name: Salome Alexandra
people.summary: Widow of Alexander Jannaeus and the only Jewish queen regnant of the Second Temple period (76-67). She reversed her husband's hostility to the Pharisees, gave them control of internal affairs, made her elder son Hyrcanus high priest, and kept peace with Tigranes by diplomacy. Rabbinic memory recalled her reign as a golden age.

people.name: Phraates III
people.summary: Arsacid king of Parthia (c. 70-57) who negotiated with both Lucullus and Pompey, backed his son-in-law Tigranes the Younger against Tigranes II, and was offended when Pompey refused him the title King of Kings. Murdered by his sons Orodes and Mithridates.

people.name: Machares
people.summary: Son of Mithridates VI, made ruler of the Cimmerian Bosporus. He sent Lucullus a golden crown in 70 and made peace with Rome; when his father arrived in 65 he fled to the Tauric Chersonese and killed himself, or was killed.

people.name: Gaius Antonius Hybrida
people.summary: Son of the orator Marcus Antonius and uncle of the triumvir. Expelled from the Senate in 70 for plundering Greece under Sulla, he was nevertheless elected consul with Cicero for 63, after Cicero bought his loyalty with the province of Macedonia. Defeated by the Dardani and Bastarnae, condemned in 59, recalled by Caesar, censor in 42.

people.name: Posidonius
people.summary: Stoic philosopher, polymath and historian from Apamea in Syria who settled at Rhodes, served as its envoy to Rome in 87/86, and taught Cicero; Pompey visited him twice. His History continued Polybius from 146 to the 80s and preserved an ethnography of the Gauls and the Sicilian slave wars that survives through Diodorus, Strabo and Athenaeus. He measured the earth and studied tides at Gades.

people.name: Lucius Licinius Murena
people.summary: Son of the Murena of the Second Mithridatic War, legate of Lucullus in the East, praetor 65, governor of Narbonensis. Elected consul for 62 and prosecuted for bribery by Sulpicius Rufus and Cato; Cicero's Pro Murena won his acquittal.

people.name: Servius Sulpicius Rufus
people.summary: The leading jurist of the late Republic, author of some 180 books, who turned Roman law from practical responses into a systematic science by applying dialectic; his pupils founded the later schools. Consul in 51, he sought compromise in 50-49, accepted Caesar, and governed Achaea. His consolation to Cicero on Tullia's death is famous. Died on an embassy to Antony at Mutina; the Senate voted him a statue on the Rostra.
people.death: died of illness on the embassy to Antony

people.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Nepos
people.summary: Pompey's legate in the East. As tribune in 62 he vetoed Cicero's farewell speech as consul, sought to recall Pompey with his army, was suspended and fled to Pompey. Reconciled with Cicero as consul in 57, when he allowed his recall; governed Nearer Spain.

people.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer
people.summary: Praetor in 63 who blocked Catiline's escape route in Picenum. As consul in 60 he opposed the land bill for Pompey's veterans, though Pompey had divorced his half-sister Mucia, and was imprisoned by the tribune Flavius. Husband of Clodia; his sudden death in 59 was rumoured to be her doing.

people.name: Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus
people.summary: Caesar's father-in-law, consul in 58 when he acquiesced in Cicero's exile, then governor of Macedonia (57-55), attacked in Cicero's In Pisonem as a debauched Epicurean. Censor in 50, he tried to mediate in 49 and 44-43 and resisted Antony. Patron of Philodemus and probably owner of the Villa of the Papyri.

people.name: Orgetorix
people.summary: The richest and noblest of the Helvetii, who planned the migration of his people and conspired with Casticus of the Sequani and Dumnorix of the Aedui to seize kingship in their three states. Tried in chains by his people, he came with 10,000 dependants and debtors to overawe the court, then died, Caesar says, probably by suicide.

people.name: Divico
people.summary: Helvetian leader who as a young man led the Tigurini in the defeat of Lucius Cassius at Burdigala in 107 and, aged, headed the Helvetian embassy to Caesar after the battle of the Arar in 58, reminding him of that disaster and declaring that the Helvetii were accustomed to take hostages, not give them.

people.name: Berenice IV
people.summary: Eldest daughter of Ptolemy XII, made queen by the Alexandrians when her father was expelled in 58. She married Archelaus, son of Mithridates' general, who fell fighting Gabinius' army; when Ptolemy XII was restored in 55 he had her executed.

people.name: Marcus Caelius Rufus
people.summary: Brilliant, dissolute protégé of Crassus and Cicero, lover of Clodia, acquitted in 56 with Cicero's Pro Caelio. His letters to Cicero in Cilicia in 51-50 (Ad familiares 8) are the liveliest political reportage from Rome. He joined Caesar in 49, but as praetor in 48 agitated for debt relief and was killed raising revolt near Thurii.
people.death: killed by Caesarian cavalry near Thurii

people.name: Publius Cornelius Lentulus Spinther
people.summary: Consul in 57 who worked for Cicero's recall, then governor of Cilicia hoping to restore Ptolemy XII, a commission blocked by the Sibylline oracle. A friend of Caesar who joined Pompey; pardoned at Corfinium, he fought at Pharsalus and was killed afterward. Nicknamed after an actor he resembled.

people.name: Galba of the Suessiones
people.summary: King of the Suessiones and commander of the Belgic coalition against Caesar in 57, chosen for his justice and wisdom; his predecessor Diviciacus had ruled much of Gaul and Britain. Surrendered his sons as hostages at Noviodunum.

people.name: Clodia Metelli
people.fullName: Clodia, wife of Quintus Metellus Celer
people.summary: Sister of Publius Clodius and wife of Metellus Celer, a wealthy and politically active widow after 59, savaged by Cicero in Pro Caelio as 'the Medea of the Palatine'. Apuleius identifies her with Catullus' Lesbia, and the identification is generally accepted. Still alive in 45, when Cicero considered buying her gardens.

people.name: Quintus Titurius Sabinus
people.summary: Caesar's legate from 58, who defeated the Venelli in 56 by a ruse. In winter 54 he and Cotta commanded a legion and five cohorts at Atuatuca; Sabinus, against Cotta's advice, trusted Ambiorix's offer of safe passage and was killed with nearly all his men.
people.death: killed at a parley with Ambiorix

people.name: Indutiomarus
people.summary: Leader of the anti-Roman faction among the Treveri and rival of his son-in-law Cingetorix. After Atuatuca he incited the Gauls and attacked Labienus' camp, and was killed at a river crossing by Labienus' cavalry, who had orders to hunt him alone.

people.name: Lucterius
people.summary: Cadurcan noble sent by Vercingetorix to raise the Ruteni and threaten the Narbonese province in 52. After Alesia he and the Senonian Drappes held Uxellodunum; Lucterius was later handed over to Caesar by the Arvernian Epasnactus.

people.name: Litaviccus
people.summary: Young Aeduan noble who in 52 led the Aeduan contingent marching to Caesar into revolt with a false story of Caesar's massacre of Aeduan leaders, then fled to Vercingetorix at Gergovia. His agitation brought the Aedui into the general revolt.

people.name: Drappes
people.summary: Senonian adventurer who with Lucterius led the remnant of the western rebels into Uxellodunum in 51. Captured during the siege, he starved himself to death.

people.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus (consul 51)
people.summary: Consul in 51 and leader of the hardline attempts to recall Caesar from Gaul; flogged a magistrate of Novum Comum to deny Caesar's grants of citizenship. After Pharsalus he lived in exile at Mytilene; pardoned by Caesar in 46 at the Senate's request, prompting Cicero's Pro Marcello, he was murdered at Piraeus on his way home by a friend.
people.death: murdered at Piraeus by his companion Magius Cilo

people.name: Pothinus
people.summary: Eunuch regent of the young Ptolemy XIII who drove out Cleopatra and, with Achillas and the rhetor Theodotus, decided on the murder of Pompey. Caesar had him executed when he was found plotting during the Alexandrian War.

people.name: Achillas
people.summary: Commander of Ptolemy XIII's army who personally carried out the murder of Pompey at Pelusium with the Roman officers Septimius and Salvius, then besieged Caesar in Alexandria with 20,000 men, many of them Gabinius' former Roman soldiers. Murdered by Arsinoe IV's eunuch Ganymedes.
people.death: killed by Ganymedes on Arsinoe's orders

people.name: Publius Cornelius Dolabella (consul 44)
people.summary: Patrician rake who married Cicero's daughter Tullia in 50 (divorced 46), joined Caesar, lost a fleet in Illyricum in 49, and as tribune in 47 agitated for debt cancellation. Caesar named him suffect consul for 44 over Antony's objections; after the Ides he courted the Liberators, then seized Syria, murdering Trebonius on the way. Besieged by Cassius at Laodicea, he had a soldier kill him.

people.name: Publius Sittius
people.summary: Campanian financier, suspected of involvement with Catiline, who fled his debts in 64 to Mauretania and became a mercenary captain there. In 46 he and Bocchus II attacked Juba's kingdom, took Cirta and destroyed Metellus Scipio's fleet. Caesar gave him and his men the territory of Cirta; he was murdered by a Numidian noble in 44.
people.death: assassinated by Arabio, son of Masinissa II

people.name: Marcus Petreius
people.summary: A professional soldier of thirty years' service who commanded the army that destroyed Catiline at Pistoria in 62 when the consul Antonius pleaded gout. Pompey's legate in Spain with Afranius in 49, he fought on in Africa and killed himself with Juba after Thapsus.

people.name: Mithridates of Pergamon
people.summary: Son of a Galatian tetrarch's daughter, claimed as a natural son of Mithridates VI. He raised the relief army that saved Caesar in Alexandria in 47, storming Pelusium, and was rewarded with the Bosporan kingdom and part of Galatia, but was killed trying to take the Bosporus from Asander.

people.name: Ptolemy XIV
people.summary: Younger brother of Cleopatra, made co-ruler and nominal husband by Caesar in 47 after Ptolemy XIII drowned. He accompanied Cleopatra to Rome and died in summer 44, probably poisoned on her orders to clear the way for Caesarion.

people.name: Tullia
people.summary: Cicero's beloved daughter, married to Gaius Calpurnius Piso Frugi, Furius Crassipes and Publius Dolabella. She died at Tusculum in February 45, a month after giving birth to Dolabella's son. Cicero's grief led him to plan a shrine (fanum) to her and to write a Consolatio, and drove his philosophical writing.

people.name: Titus Pomponius Atticus
people.fullName: Titus Pomponius Atticus (Quintus Caecilius Pomponianus Atticus)
people.summary: Equestrian banker, publisher and antiquarian, Cicero's closest friend and the recipient of 16 books of his letters. Living in Athens from 85 to 65 (hence his cognomen), he refused all office and stayed on good terms with every faction from Sulla to Antony and Octavian; his daughter married Agrippa. He starved himself to death when terminally ill.

people.name: Aulus Hirtius
people.summary: Caesar's officer and literary aide, who wrote the eighth book of the Gallic War to bridge Caesar's commentaries and probably edited the Alexandrian War. Praetor 46, he struck Caesar's great gold issue. As consul in 43 he fell in the victory outside Mutina; he and his colleague Pansa were given a public funeral.
people.death: killed storming Antony's camp at Mutina

people.name: Gaius Vibius Pansa Caetronianus
people.summary: Son of a proscribed Marian, a loyal Caesarian, governor of Bithynia and Cisalpine Gaul, and consul with Hirtius in 43. Wounded at Forum Gallorum leading recruits against Antony, he died at Bononia days later; rumour accused Octavian of having his wounds poisoned.
people.death: died of wounds after Forum Gallorum

people.name: Lucius Munatius Plancus
people.summary: Caesar's legate in Gaul and the civil war, governor of Gallia Comata in 44-43, founder of Lugdunum and Raurica, who wavered elegantly before joining Antony in 43. Consul 42, he followed Antony to the East, then defected to Octavian in 32 and revealed Antony's will. In 27 he proposed the name Augustus; censor in 22. His tomb survives at Gaeta.

people.name: Gaius Asinius Pollio
people.summary: Marrucinian new man, Caesar's officer at the Rubicon and Pharsalus, governor of Further Spain in 44-43, who joined Antony and as consul in 40 helped negotiate the Treaty of Brundisium. After triumphing over the Parthini he withdrew from politics, founded Rome's first public library, introduced public readings (recitationes), and wrote a history of the civil wars from 60 used by Appian and Plutarch. Patron of Virgil.

people.name: Quintus Salvidienus Rufus
people.summary: Of humble origins, a companion of the young Octavian at Apollonia, his first general against Sextus Pompey and at Perusia, governor of Gaul with eleven legions and consul designate for 39. Denounced by Antony at Brundisium for proposing to defect, he was condemned by the Senate and killed himself or was executed.
people.death: condemned as a public enemy; suicide or execution

people.name: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus (consul 32)
people.summary: Son of Caesar's enemy Lucius Domitius, captured at Corfinium and pardoned. Condemned under the lex Pedia though probably not a conspirator, he commanded the Liberators' fleet, destroyed the triumviral convoy on the day of Philippi, then made peace with Antony. Consul in 32, he fled to Antony, opposed Cleopatra's presence, and deserted to Octavian just before Actium, dying soon after. Great-grandfather of Nero.
people.death: died of illness shortly after deserting to Octavian

people.name: Gaius Sosius
people.summary: Antony's governor of Syria who with Herod took Jerusalem in 37 and triumphed in 34. As consul in 32 he denounced Octavian in the Senate and fled to Antony; commanded the left wing of Antony's fleet at Actium. Pardoned by Octavian at Arruntius' request, he rebuilt the Temple of Apollo Medicus (Apollo Sosianus), whose restored columns stand near the Theatre of Marcellus.

people.name: Gaius Trebonius
people.summary: Tribune of 55 whose lex Trebonia gave Pompey and Crassus their five-year commands, then Caesar's legate in Gaul who commanded the siege of Massilia. Suffect consul 45, he joined the conspiracy and detained Antony outside the Senate on the Ides. Murdered by Dolabella at Smyrna as proconsul of Asia, the first of the assassins to die.

people.name: Antigonus II Mattathias

roles.t: King and high priest of Judaea

people.summary: Son of Aristobulus II, twice a fugitive from Roman custody, who with Parthian backing took Jerusalem in 40 and reigned as king and high priest, mutilating his uncle Hyrcanus. Besieged by Herod and Sosius in 37, he surrendered and was beheaded by Antony at Antioch, the last Hasmonean ruler.
people.death: beheaded at Antioch on Antony's orders

people.name: Arsinoe IV
people.summary: Younger sister of Cleopatra who escaped Caesar's palace during the Alexandrian War, was proclaimed queen by the Alexandrian army, and had Achillas killed. Captured, she walked in Caesar's triumph of 46, where her dignity moved the crowd, and was allowed into sanctuary at Ephesus until Antony had her killed in 41.
people.death: killed at Ephesus on Antony's orders

people.name: Gaius Licinius Macer Calvus
people.summary: Son of the tribune-historian Licinius Macer, a tiny man and fierce Atticist orator who prosecuted Vatinius, and a neoteric poet, Catullus' closest friend, author of an epyllion Io and an elegy for his wife Quintilia. Only fragments survive.

people.name: Gaius Helvius Cinna
people.summary: Neoteric poet from Brixia or nearby, friend of Catullus, whose learned epyllion Zmyrna took nine years to write. As tribune in 44 he was mistaken for the anti-Caesarian praetor Lucius Cinna and lynched by the crowd at Caesar's funeral.
people.death: lynched by mistake at Caesar's funeral

people.name: Cornelius Nepos
people.summary: Biographer from Cisalpine Gaul, friend of Atticus and Cicero and dedicatee of Catullus' book. His Chronica summarised world history in three books; his De viris illustribus, partly extant, is the oldest surviving Latin biography. He refused a political career.

people.name: Diodorus Siculus
people.summary: Sicilian Greek who spent thirty years on a forty-book universal history, the Bibliotheca, ending with Caesar's Gallic War; he visited Egypt in the 180th Olympiad (60-56) and lived in Rome. A compiler rather than a critic, he is precious for preserving lost sources: Hecataeus of Abdera, Agatharchides, Timaeus, Posidonius.

people.name: Philodemus of Gadara
people.summary: Epicurean philosopher and epigrammatist from Gadara in the Decapolis, pupil of Zeno of Sidon, who lived in Italy under the patronage of Piso Caesoninus and taught Virgil, Varius and others in the circle at Naples and Herculaneum. Many of his treatises survive charred among the papyri of the Villa of the Papyri; some thirty of his erotic epigrams are in the Greek Anthology.

people.name: Servilia
people.summary: Half-sister of Cato the Younger, mother of Marcus Brutus by her first husband and of three daughters by Decimus Silanus, consul 62. Caesar's most famous mistress, to whom he gave a pearl worth six million sesterces. After the Ides she chaired a family council at Antium in June 44 that discussed the Liberators' future, with Cicero present.

people.name: Terentia
people.summary: Cicero's wealthy and forceful wife, half-sister of a Vestal, who managed his property during his exile and, Plutarch says, urged him to act against the Catilinarians and to testify against Clodius. They divorced in 47/46 amid quarrels over money; she reputedly lived to 103.

people.name: Marcus Tullius Tiro
people.summary: Cicero's slave, freed in 53, his secretary and literary executor, who edited and published Cicero's letters and speeches, collected his jokes, wrote his biography, and developed or perfected the Latin shorthand system ('Tironian notes') used into the Middle Ages.

people.name: Atia
people.summary: Daughter of Julia, Caesar's sister, and Marcus Atius Balbus; mother of Octavia and of Octavian by Gaius Octavius, and later wife of Lucius Marcius Philippus. Tacitus praises her strict upbringing of her son; she urged caution when he accepted Caesar's inheritance. Died during his first consulship.

people.name: Scribonia
people.summary: Sister of Lucius Scribonius Libo, Sextus Pompey's father-in-law; married Octavian in 40 to win Sextus' goodwill, bore Julia, and was divorced on the day of Julia's birth in 39 so that Octavian could marry Livia. She later chose to accompany Julia into exile on Pandateria.

people.name: Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus
people.summary: Patrician who fought for the Liberators at Philippi, then joined Antony and finally Octavian, commanding at Naulochus and Actium. Consul in 31, he triumphed over Aquitania in 27, was briefly first prefect of the city (26), and proposed the title Pater Patriae (2 BC). Orator, patron of Tibullus and Ovid.

people.name: Publius Canidius Crassus
people.summary: Antony's general who conquered the Iberians and Albanians of the Caucasus in 36 and commanded his land army at Actium. He advised Antony to send Cleopatra home and fight on land, and after the naval defeat abandoned the army, which surrendered. Executed by Octavian after Alexandria.

people.name: Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta
people.summary: Caesar's legate who shared command at Atuatuca with Sabinus in winter 54 and argued against leaving camp on Ambiorix's word. When the column was ambushed he fought on, wounded in the face by a sling bullet, and died with most of his men.
people.death: killed in the ambush at Atuatuca

people.name: Catuvolcus
people.summary: Elderly co-king of the Eburones with Ambiorix, who joined the attack on Sabinus and Cotta in 54. When Caesar ravaged his country in 53 he cursed Ambiorix and poisoned himself with yew.

people.name: Vercassivellaunus
people.summary: Cousin of Vercingetorix and one of the four commanders of the Gallic relief army at Alesia. He led 60,000 picked men in the decisive attack on the weak point of Caesar's northern lines on Mont Réa and was captured when the attack failed.

people.name: Boduognatus
people.summary: Commander of the Nervii who led the surprise attack on Caesar's army at the Sabis in 57, which nearly destroyed it; Caesar says that the Nervii were all but annihilated in the battle.

people.name: Antiochus XIII Asiaticus
people.summary: Son of Antiochus X and Cleopatra Selene, who lobbied the Senate in Rome in the 70s for recognition of his claim to Egypt; Verres robbed him in Sicily on his way home. Installed in Antioch by Lucullus after 69, he was deposed by Pompey in 64, ending Seleucid rule, and murdered by the Emesene dynast Sampsiceramus.

people.name: Taxiles
people.summary: Mithridates' general who brought an army of some 100,000 to join Archelaus in Greece in 86 and shared the command at Chaeronea, and later led the cavalry against Lucullus at Cabira and fought at Tigranocerta.

people.name: Publius Nigidius Figulus
people.summary: Praetor in 58, a Pompeian, and, after Varro, the most learned Roman of his age: a Neo-Pythagorean scholar of grammar, astrology, natural science and divination, consulted by Cicero in 63. Legend said he cast Octavian's horoscope on the day of his birth and announced a ruler of the world. Died in exile.
people.death: died in exile, unpardoned by Caesar

people.name: Sosigenes of Alexandria
people.summary: Peripatetic astronomer whom Pliny names as Caesar's adviser for the calendar reform of 46, which adopted a solar year of 365 days with a leap day every fourth year, based on Egyptian practice. He also wrote on the planets.

people.name: Lucius Hirtuleius
people.summary: Sertorius' quaestor and best lieutenant, who defeated the governor of Narbonensis, Manlius, at Ilerda in 78 and held Metellus Pius in check, but was destroyed by Metellus at Italica in 76 and killed near Segovia in 75.
people.death: killed in battle against Metellus Pius

people.name: Lucius Cornelius Lentulus Crus
people.summary: Consul in 49, heavily in debt, who refused to read Caesar's last proposals to the Senate, carried the senatus consultum ultimum of 7 January and fled Rome leaving the treasury unopened. After Pharsalus he followed Pompey to Egypt and was killed in prison there.
people.death: put to death in Egypt after Pompey's murder

people.name: Gaius Scribonius Curio (consul 76)
people.summary: Sulla's legate in Greece, consul 76 and the first Roman general to reach the Danube, campaigning against the Dardani in 75-73. An orator of Cicero's acquaintance and enemy of Caesar, he wrote a dialogue attacking Caesar's consulship and called him 'every woman's husband and every man's wife'. Father of the tribune of 50.

people.name: Gaius Memmius (praetor 58)
people.summary: Praetor in 58 who attacked Caesar's consular acts, governor of Bithynia in 57 with Catullus and Helvius Cinna on his staff, and dedicatee of Lucretius' De rerum natura. As consular candidate in 54 he exposed in the Senate the corrupt pact he had made with the consuls, ending his career; convicted of ambitus, he retired to Athens, where he planned to demolish Epicurus' house, to Cicero's dismay.

people.name: Juba II
people.fullName: Gaius Julius Juba, King of Mauretania
people.summary: Son of the Numidian king Juba I, paraded as a child in Caesar's triumph of 46 BC and raised in Rome, Juba was made king of Mauretania in 25 BC and married Cleopatra Selene; a learned Greek author, he ruled from Iol Caesarea for nearly fifty years.

people.name: Cleopatra Selene
people.fullName: Cleopatra Selene II, Queen of Mauretania
people.summary: Daughter of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII, twin of Alexander Helios, Cleopatra Selene walked in Octavian's triumph of 29 BC, was raised by Octavia and married to Juba II, ruling Mauretania with him and promoting Ptolemaic and Egyptian imagery at Caesarea.

people.name: Livy
people.summary: Historian from Patavium whose 142-book history of Rome from the foundation to 9 BC, written over some forty years under Augustus, became the canonical narrative of the Republic; 35 books survive.

people.name: Vitruvius
people.summary: Architect and military engineer who served Caesar and Octavian on artillery and dedicated to Augustus the ten books On Architecture, the only complete architectural treatise from antiquity.

people.name: Strabo
people.summary: Greek geographer and historian from Amaseia in Pontus whose seventeen-book Geography, completed under Tiberius, is the fullest description of the Augustan world.

people.name: Nicolaus of Damascus
people.summary: Peripatetic philosopher and historian, adviser and envoy of Herod the Great, author of a 144-book Universal History and a Life of Augustus, both partly preserved, which are major sources for Josephus.

people.name: Antonius Musa
people.summary: Greek freedman physician of Augustus who cured the princeps of his near-fatal illness in 23 BC with cold baths and cold drinks, and was rewarded with a statue and equestrian rank; the same treatment failed to save Marcellus.

people.name: Vipsania Agrippina
people.summary: Daughter of Agrippa by his first wife, Caecilia Attica, granddaughter of Cicero's friend Atticus; first wife of Tiberius and mother of Drusus the Younger, she was divorced in 11 BC on Augustus's orders so that Tiberius could marry Julia.

people.name: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus
people.summary: Consul in 16 BC, husband of Antonia the Elder (Antony and Octavia's daughter) and grandfather of Nero, Ahenobarbus crossed the Elbe as legate in Germany, set up an altar to Augustus beyond it and built the causeways called pontes longi.

people.name: Cossus Cornelius Lentulus
people.summary: Consul in 1 BC who as proconsul of Africa (c. AD 6) defeated the Gaetuli and Musulamii, winning triumphal ornaments and the cognomen Gaetulicus for his son; late in life he was Tiberius's trusted urban prefect, reputedly a heavy drinker who never betrayed a secret.

people.name: Lucius Calpurnius Piso the Pontifex
people.summary: Son of Caesar's father-in-law, consul in 15 BC, Piso crushed the Bessian revolt in Thrace (13-11 BC) and served as urban prefect for some twenty years under Augustus and Tiberius; Horace addressed the Ars Poetica to him and his sons.

people.name: Labeo
people.summary: Leading jurist of the Augustan age and founder of the school later called Proculian, Labeo, a republican by conviction, refused the consulship Augustus offered and wrote some 400 books, of which fragments survive in the Digest.

people.name: Ateius Capito
people.summary: Jurist and consul suffect in AD 5, a loyal servant of Augustus and Tiberius, Capito founded the school later called Sabinian and served as water commissioner from 13 to his death.

people.name: Masurius Sabinus
people.summary: Jurist of modest means who under Tiberius became the first equestrian granted the right to give opinions by the emperor's authority; his three books on civil law (Libri tres iuris civilis) became the standard framework for later commentaries "ad Sabinum".

people.name: Judas the Galilean
people.summary: Leader of the resistance to the census of Quirinius in AD 6 who taught that paying tribute to Rome was slavery and that God alone was master; Josephus calls his movement the "fourth philosophy" and traces the later revolt to it.

people.name: Herod Antipas
people.fullName: Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea
people.summary: Son of Herod the Great and Malthace, tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea from 4 BC to AD 39, builder of Sepphoris and Tiberias, who executed John the Baptist and, in Luke's account, examined Jesus; Caligula exiled him to Gaul in 39.

people.name: Herodias
people.summary: Granddaughter of Herod the Great and Mariamme, sister of Agrippa I, Herodias left her husband (another Herod) to marry his half-brother Herod Antipas; the gospels blame her for the execution of John the Baptist.

people.name: John the Baptist
people.summary: Jewish ascetic prophet who preached repentance and baptism in the Jordan in the late 20s, baptised Jesus, and was executed by Herod Antipas at Machaerus; Josephus and the gospels both record him.

people.name: Caiaphas
people.summary: High Priest of the Jerusalem Temple from c. 18 to 36, the longest tenure of the Roman period, son-in-law of the former High Priest Annas, who according to the gospels presided over the hearing that handed Jesus to Pilate.

people.name: James the Just
people.summary: Brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church from the 40s, known for strict Torah observance; Paul met him in Jerusalem and he presided at the apostolic council. The High Priest Ananus had him stoned in 62.

people.name: Stephen
people.summary: Leader of the Greek-speaking followers of Jesus in Jerusalem, one of the seven deacons of Acts, stoned c. 34 after a speech against the Temple; venerated as the first Christian martyr.

people.name: Barnabas
people.summary: A Cypriot Levite in the Jerusalem community who introduced Paul to the apostles, led the church at Antioch and accompanied Paul on the mission to Cyprus and Galatia, before they parted over John Mark.
people.death: unknown; later tradition says martyred at Salamis

people.name: Aretas IV
people.fullName: Aretas IV Philopatris, King of the Nabataeans
people.summary: King of the Nabataeans from 9 BC to AD 40, under whom Petra reached its height (the Khazneh is often attributed to his reign); he defeated Herod Antipas c. 36 and controlled Damascus when Paul escaped it.

people.name: Artabanus II
people.summary: Arsacid king of Parthia c. 12-38, of partly Dahae descent, who displaced the Roman-raised Vonones, sought to put his sons on the Armenian throne and clashed with Tiberius's diplomacy, before reaching terms with Lucius Vitellius on the Euphrates.

people.name: Pharasmanes I
people.summary: King of Caucasian Iberia who, as Tiberius's ally, installed his brother Mithridates in Armenia in 35, defeating the Parthians with Alan help; later he encouraged his son Radamistus to murder Mithridates and seize Armenia (51).

people.name: Mithridates of Armenia
people.summary: Iberian prince installed as king of Armenia by Tiberius in 35, recalled and imprisoned by Caligula, restored by Claudius in 42, and murdered by his nephew Radamistus at Gorneae in 51.

people.name: Radamistus
people.summary: Son of Pharasmanes I of Iberia who seized Armenia in 51 by murdering his uncle Mithridates after a false oath, was expelled by the Parthian Tiridates, and was executed by his own father c. 58.

people.name: Lucius Vitellius
people.summary: Father of the emperor Vitellius, a skilful governor of Syria (35-39) who outmanoeuvred Parthia, removed Pilate and Caiaphas, and later became Claudius's indispensable colleague, three times consul and censor in 47-48.

people.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
people.summary: Consul in AD 8 who as proconsul of Africa won the first Roman victory over Tacfarinas in 17, gaining triumphal ornaments; Tacitus notes that the glory returned to the house of the great Camillus after four centuries.

people.name: Vannius
people.summary: Quadian noble whom Drusus the Younger made king over the followers of Maroboduus and Catualda settled beyond the Danube in 19; he grew rich on raiding and trade for thirty years until his nephews Vangio and Sido, backed by the Hermunduri and Lugii, overthrew him c. 50.

people.name: Rhescuporis II
people.summary: Brother of Rhoemetalces I who received the wilder western part of Thrace on his death (AD 12), murdered his nephew Cotys at a banquet in 19, and was tried at Rome, exiled to Alexandria and killed there.

people.name: Artaxias III
people.summary: Son of Polemon I of Pontus and Pythodoris, crowned king of Armenia by Germanicus at Artaxata in 18 under the name Artaxias; his long peaceful reign ended with his death c. 34.

people.name: Polemon II
people.fullName: Marcus Antonius Polemon, King of Pontus
people.summary: Son of Antonia Tryphaena, raised with Caligula, who gave him Pontus in 38; Claudius added part of Cilicia. Nero annexed Pontus in 64. He married Agrippa II's sister Berenice, who soon left him.

people.name: Asinius Gallus
people.summary: Son of the historian Asinius Pollio, consul in 8 BC, who married Tiberius's divorced wife Vipsania and spoke with provocative freedom in the Senate; arrested in 30, he died of starvation in custody in 33.

people.name: Valerius Maximus
people.summary: Author of the nine books of Memorable Deeds and Sayings, a collection of moral exempla dedicated to Tiberius c. 31, who had accompanied his patron Sextus Pompeius (cos. AD 14) to Asia.

people.name: Apion

roles.t: Grammarian; envoy of the Alexandrian Greeks
