people.summary: Alexandrian Homeric scholar and showman lecturer who led the Greek embassy against the Jews before Caligula in 39-40; his anti-Jewish writings provoked Josephus's Against Apion.

people.name: Julia Livilla
people.summary: Youngest child of Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, exiled by her brother Caligula in 39 for her part in the Lepidus plot, recalled by Claudius in 41, then exiled again on Messalina's charge of adultery with Seneca and starved to death.

people.name: Pallas
people.summary: Greek freedman of Antonia Minor who as Claudius's financial secretary amassed a fortune of 300 million sesterces, promoted Agrippina's marriage and Nero's adoption, and was dismissed by Nero in 55 and killed in 62.

people.name: Aulus Didius Gallus
people.summary: Senator who installed Cotys I in the Bosporan kingdom c. 45 and as governor of Britain (52-57) held the line against the Silures and intervened in the Brigantian civil war, though Tacitus calls him elderly and content to let others act.

people.name: Mithridates of the Bosporus
people.fullName: Tiberius Claudius Mithridates, King of the Bosporus
people.summary: King of the Cimmerian Bosporus installed by Caligula, deposed by Claudius in favour of his brother Cotys I, he tried to regain the throne with Sarmatian allies, surrendered in 49 and lived in Rome until Galba executed him.

people.name: Helena of Adiabene
people.summary: Queen of the Parthian vassal kingdom of Adiabene who converted to Judaism with her son Izates, moved to Jerusalem, relieved the famine of c. 46-48 and was buried in the monumental "Tomb of the Kings".
people.death: natural causes in Adiabene, c. 56; buried in Jerusalem

people.name: Antonius Felix
people.summary: Freedman brother of Pallas who governed Judaea c. 52-59, married three queens (including Drusilla, sister of Agrippa II), crushed bandits and the "Egyptian" prophet, and held Paul prisoner hoping for a bribe.

people.name: Porcius Festus
people.summary: Procurator of Judaea c. 59-62 who heard Paul's appeal to Caesar and sent him to Rome after consulting Agrippa II; he died in office, and the interregnum allowed the stoning of James.

people.name: Venutius
people.summary: Brigantian noble, former husband of Queen Cartimandua and once loyal to Rome, who led the anti-Roman faction against her in the 50s and overthrew her in 69; the war against him was taken up by Petillius Cerialis from 71.

people.name: Clodius Macer

roles.t: Legate of the legion in Africa

people.summary: Legate of III Augusta who rebelled against Nero in 68, raised a new legion and cut Rome's African grain supply, striking coins in the name of the Senate without claiming the title of emperor; Galba had him killed.

people.name: Yohanan ben Zakkai

roles.t: Head of the court at Yavneh

people.summary: Pharisaic sage whom rabbinic tradition credits with escaping besieged Jerusalem and founding the academy at Yavneh, laying the foundations of rabbinic Judaism after the Temple's destruction.

people.name: Columella
people.summary: Agronomist from Gades who wrote twelve books On Agriculture and a shorter On Trees, the most complete Roman account of estate farming, including a famous calculation of vineyard profits.

people.name: Hero of Alexandria
people.summary: Mathematician and engineer of the mid first century AD whose works on pneumatics, automata, mechanics, surveying and artillery describe the aeolipile steam turbine, programmable automata and the formula for the area of a triangle from its sides.

people.name: Quintilian
people.summary: Rhetorician from Calagurris in Spain, first holder of the state chair of Latin rhetoric founded by Vespasian, and author of the twelve-book Institutio Oratoria, the most complete ancient treatise on education and oratory.

people.name: Statius
people.summary: Neapolitan poet of Domitian's court, author of the epic Thebaid, the unfinished Achilleid and the Silvae, occasional poems on court life, villas and friends.

people.name: Juvenal
people.summary: Satirist whose sixteen verse Satires, published c. 110-130, are the fiercest Roman portraits of urban life, social injustice and vice.

people.name: Suetonius
people.summary: Biographer and imperial secretary, protege of Pliny the Younger, author of the Lives of the Twelve Caesars and of lives of grammarians, rhetoricians and poets; dismissed by Hadrian in 122 for overfamiliarity with Sabina.

people.name: Plutarch
people.summary: Platonist philosopher and biographer from Chaeronea in Boeotia, priest at Delphi for some thirty years, author of the Parallel Lives and the Moralia.

people.name: Clement of Rome
people.summary: Leading presbyter of the Roman church in the 90s, traditionally its third or fourth bishop, to whom the letter of the Roman church to the Corinthians (1 Clement, c. 96) is attributed.
people.death: unknown (later legend: martyred in the Chersonese)

people.name: Ignatius of Antioch
people.summary: Bishop of Antioch condemned under Trajan and taken to Rome for the beasts, writing on the journey seven letters that are the earliest witness to the single bishop as head of each church and the first use of "catholic church".
people.death: thrown to the beasts in Rome, c. 107-115

people.name: Polycarp
people.summary: Bishop of Smyrna for some fifty years, linked by Irenaeus to John and the apostles, recipient of a letter from Ignatius and author of a letter to the Philippians; burned at Smyrna aged 86, probably in 155-156.

people.name: Marcion
people.summary: Wealthy shipowner from Sinope who taught at Rome that the God of the Jewish scriptures was a lesser, just creator distinct from the good Father revealed by Jesus, and compiled the first Christian canon (a version of Luke and ten Pauline letters); expelled by the Roman church c. 144.

people.name: Valentinus
people.summary: Egyptian-born Christian teacher active at Rome c. 136-160 whose mythological theology of aeons and the fallen Sophia founded the most important Gnostic school, the Valentinians.

people.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
people.summary: Bishop of Lyon after the persecution of 177, a native of Asia who had heard Polycarp, author of Against Heresies (c. 180), the foundational statement of apostolic succession and the four-gospel canon.

people.name: Montanus
people.summary: Phrygian convert who with the prophetesses Prisca and Maximilla launched the ecstatic "New Prophecy" c. 156-172, announcing the age of the Paraclete and the descent of the new Jerusalem at Pepuza.

people.name: Victor I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome c. 189-199, an African and the first Latin-speaking holder of the see, who tried to impose Sunday Easter on the churches of Asia and gave Marcia the list of confessors in the Sardinian mines.

people.name: Callistus

roles.t: Deacon in charge of the cemetery

people.summary: Former slave of an imperial freedman, condemned to the Sardinian mines and freed through Marcia c. 190, who became deacon in charge of the Christian cemetery on the Via Appia (the Catacomb of Callistus) and bishop of Rome 217-222.

people.name: Fronto

roles.t: Tutor of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus

people.summary: Orator from Cirta in Numidia, the leading Latin rhetorician of the Antonine age, tutor and lifelong correspondent of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, consul in 143.

people.name: Apuleius

roles.t: Priest of the provincial cult of Africa

people.summary: Platonist philosopher, orator and novelist from Madauros in Numidia, author of the Metamorphoses (The Golden Ass), the only complete surviving Latin novel, and of the Apology, his defence against charges of magic at Sabratha.

people.name: Lucian of Samosata
people.summary: Syrian-born Greek satirist and sophist whose some 80 works mock philosophers, frauds, historians, the gods and the credulous, among them How to Write History, True Histories and Alexander the False Prophet.

people.name: Pausanias
people.summary: Greek traveller from Lydia whose ten-book Description of Greece (c. 155-180), concentrating on sanctuaries, monuments, art and local myth, is the basic guide for the archaeology of mainland Greece.

people.name: Appian

roles.t: Advocate of the fisc and procurator

people.summary: Alexandrian Greek who practised law at Rome, received a procuratorship through Fronto under Antoninus Pius and wrote a Roman History arranged by peoples and wars, including five books on the Civil Wars.

people.name: Celsus
people.summary: Platonist author of the True Doctrine (Alethes Logos, c. 175-180), the first known systematic philosophical attack on Christianity, preserved through Origen's reply Contra Celsum.

people.name: Alexander of Abonoteichus
people.summary: Paphlagonian founder of the oracle of the snake god Glykon at Abonoteichus, which attracted Roman senators and an oracle request from Marcus Aurelius; Lucian's hostile Alexander the False Prophet exposes his tricks.
people.death: gangrene of the leg (Lucian), aged nearly 70

people.name: Julia Balbilla
people.summary: Greek poet and companion of the empress Sabina, granddaughter of Antiochus IV of Commagene, who carved four epigrams in Aeolic Greek on the Colossus of Memnon during the imperial visit of November 130.

people.name: Tarrutenius Paternus
people.summary: Equestrian officer and military jurist (author of De re militari) who served Marcus as secretary and praetorian prefect, won the last great battle against the Quadi in 179, and was executed by Commodus in 182 after the Lucilla conspiracy, having been elevated to the Senate to remove him from the prefecture.

people.name: Junius Rusticus
people.summary: Stoic philosopher, grandson of the Arulenus Rusticus executed by Domitian, Marcus Aurelius's most valued teacher, who introduced him to Epictetus; as urban prefect he condemned Justin Martyr c. 165.

people.name: Sohaemus
people.fullName: Gaius Julius Sohaemus, King of Armenia
people.summary: Prince of the Emesene and Arsacid lines, a Roman senator and consul, who was installed as king of Armenia by Lucius Verus in 164 at the new capital Kainepolis, expelled c. 172 and restored by Martius Verus.

people.name: Ariogaesus
people.summary: Elected king by the Quadi in 174 after they expelled the Roman nominee Furtius; Marcus put a price on his head and, when he was captured, exiled him to Alexandria.

people.name: Aufidius Victorinus
people.summary: Fronto's son-in-law and Marcus's fellow student, who repelled the Chatti from Upper Germany in 162, governed Dacia and the Spanish provinces, and as urban prefect under Commodus was the most respected senator of his day; he was consul again with Commodus in 183.

people.name: Pompeius Falco
people.summary: Trajanic and Hadrianic general who governed Judaea, Lower Moesia and Britain, where he restored order after the unrest at Hadrian's accession, before Platorius Nepos took over and built the Wall; correspondent of Pliny the Younger.

people.name: Gnaeus Julius Verus
people.summary: Son of Sextus Julius Severus, governor of Britain c. 155-158, who brought reinforcements from Germany after trouble in the north and began the recommissioning of Hadrian's Wall; later legate of Syria in the Parthian war.

people.name: Terentius Scaurianus
people.summary: First consular governor of the province of Dacia (c. 106-110), founder of the colony Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa according to its foundation inscription.

people.name: Abgar VII
people.fullName: Abgar VII bar Ezad, King of Osroene
people.summary: King of Edessa who submitted to Trajan in 114-115, winning favour through his son Arbandes, but joined the Mesopotamian revolt of 116 and was killed when Lusius Quietus sacked Edessa.

people.name: Valerius Asiaticus
people.summary: Senator from Vienna in Narbonensis, the first Gaul to hold two consulships, a ringleader in the murder of Caligula, who owned the Gardens of Lucullus and was destroyed by Messalina's intrigue in 47.

people.name: Opramoas of Rhodiapolis
people.summary: Lycian millionaire whose tomb at Rhodiapolis carries some seventy letters from Antoninus Pius, governors and the Lycian League honouring his donations of over 500,000 denarii to cities rebuilding after the earthquake of c. 141.

people.name: Ummidius Quadratus
people.summary: Long-serving governor of Syria (c. 51-60) who failed to prevent Radamistus's seizure of Armenia, adjudicated the Samaritan-Jewish conflict under Cumanus, and quarrelled with Corbulo over the eastern command.

people.name: Septicius Clarus
people.summary: Friend of Pliny the Younger, to whom Pliny dedicated his letters, and of Suetonius, who dedicated the Lives of the Caesars to him; praetorian prefect from 119, dismissed with Suetonius in 122.

people.name: Crispina
people.summary: Daughter of the consular Bruttius Praesens, married to Commodus in 178 before the second German expedition; accused of adultery, she was exiled to Capri c. 182 or later and put to death.

people.name: Milonia Caesonia
people.summary: Fourth wife of Caligula, older than he and already mother of three daughters, whom he married in 39 when she bore him a daughter, Julia Drusilla; she and the child were killed immediately after his assassination.
people.death: killed by a centurion with her daughter, January 41

people.name: Statilia Messalina
people.summary: Third wife of Nero, married in 66 after Nero forced her husband Atticus Vestinus to suicide; a highly educated woman who survived Nero and was courted by Otho in 69.

people.name: Matidia the Elder
people.summary: Daughter of Trajan's sister Marciana, mother of Hadrian's wife Sabina, named Augusta in 112; Hadrian deified her on her death in 119, delivered her funeral oration and built a temple to her in the Campus Martius, the first temple to a deified mother-in-law.

people.name: Marciana
people.summary: Elder sister of Trajan, made Augusta c. 105, mother of Matidia and grandmother of Sabina; she lived in harmony with Plotina in the palace and was deified on her death in 112, when Matidia succeeded to her title.

people.name: Domitia Lucilla
people.summary: Mother of Marcus Aurelius, heiress of an immense fortune including brickworks near Rome, a cultivated woman whose house was a centre of Greek culture; Marcus thanks her in the Meditations for her piety, generosity and simple living.

people.name: Julia Titi
people.summary: Daughter of Titus, given the title Augusta, who after her husband Flavius Sabinus was executed lived openly with her uncle Domitian; her death in 91, rumoured to have followed an abortion he forced on her, was followed by her deification.

people.name: Furius Victorinus
people.summary: Equestrian prefect of Egypt and praetorian prefect from 159, who accompanied Lucius Verus to the East and died of plague with part of his army on the northern front in 168.

people.name: Claudius Severus
people.summary: First governor of the province of Arabia (c. 107-115), builder of the Via Nova Traiana from Bostra to Aila, whose name appears on its milestones; a letter of a soldier named Julius Apollinaris on papyrus mentions him.

people.name: Anicetus
people.summary: Bishop of Rome c. 155-166, from Emesa according to the Liber Pontificalis, who received Polycarp of Smyrna and agreed to differ with him on the date of Easter.

people.name: Fabian
people.summary: Bishop of Rome 236-250, chosen, Eusebius says, when a dove settled on his head although he was a layman. He organised Rome into seven ecclesiastical regions under deacons, brought back the bodies of Pontian and Hippolytus from Sardinia, and was martyred on 20 January 250 at the start of the Decian persecution; his Greek epitaph is in the Crypt of the Popes.
people.death: executed in the Decian persecution, 20 January 250

people.name: Cornelius
people.summary: Elected bishop of Rome in March 251 after a 14-month vacancy, Cornelius favoured readmitting the lapsed after penance and was opposed by Novatian, whose rigorist party elected him antipope. His letter to Fabius of Antioch gives the size of the Roman clergy (46 presbyters, 7 deacons, 7 subdeacons, 42 acolytes, 52 exorcists, readers and doorkeepers) and over 1,500 widows and poor on its rolls. Exiled by Gallus to Centumcellae, he died there in June 253.

people.name: Stephen I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome 254-257, Stephen accepted baptisms performed by heretics and threatened to break communion with Cyprian and the Asian churches who rebaptised, appealing to his succession from Peter; Firmilian of Caesarea attacked his arrogance in a letter preserved in Cyprian's correspondence. He died on 2 August 257, later venerated, without good evidence, as a martyr.

people.name: Sixtus II
people.summary: A Greek elected bishop of Rome in 257, Sixtus restored communion with Carthage after the rebaptism quarrel; on 6 August 258, under Valerian's second rescript, he was arrested while preaching in the cemetery of Callixtus and beheaded with four deacons, followed by Lawrence on 10 August. Damasus' epigram commemorates the scene.
people.death: beheaded in the catacomb of Callixtus, 6 August 258

people.name: Miltiades
people.summary: African-born bishop of Rome from July 311 to January 314, Miltiades recovered church property confiscated in the persecution, received the Lateran palace from Constantine and presided over the council of October 313 that heard the Donatist case in Fausta's house; he died on 10 or 11 January 314 before Arles met.

people.name: Julius I
people.summary: Bishop of Rome 337-352, Julius sheltered Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra, acquitted them at a Roman synod (340/341) and rebuked the eastern bishops for acting without Rome; Serdica's canons (343) gave the Roman bishop an appellate role. The Liber Pontificalis credits him with several churches, including the titulus Iulii in Trastevere traditionally identified with Santa Maria in Trastevere.

people.name: Liberius
people.summary: Bishop of Rome from 352, Liberius refused to condemn Athanasius at Milan in 355 and was carried off to Beroea in Thrace; after two years, broken by exile, he signed a compromise formula at Sirmium and returned in 358 to a Rome where the deacon Felix had been installed as rival, provoking riots. His reputation for lapsing made him the only early pope not venerated in the west. He died on 24 September 366, precipitating the Damasus-Ursinus clash.

people.name: Hippolytus
people.summary: Greek-writing presbyter and theologian at Rome, Hippolytus attacked Bishop Callistus for laxity and modalism and was set up as rival bishop by his followers, the first antipope; his works include the Refutation of All Heresies, a Commentary on Daniel and a Chronicle, and the Apostolic Tradition is attributed to him. A seated statue found in 1551 lists his works and an Easter table. Exiled with Pontian to Sardinia in 235, he died there and was reconciled as a martyr.

people.name: Dionysius of Alexandria
people.fullName: Dionysius the Great, bishop of Alexandria
people.summary: Pupil of Origen, head of the catechetical school and bishop of Alexandria from 247/8, Dionysius survived the Decian and Valerian persecutions in hiding and exile at Kephro in Libya, and his letters preserved by Eusebius are the main eyewitness source for the Alexandrian pogrom, the plague, the civil war of 261-262 and the rebaptism dispute. His stylistic argument that Revelation was not by the author of John's Gospel is a landmark of ancient literary criticism.

people.name: Julius Africanus
people.summary: Christian scholar from Aelia Capitolina who served under Severus at Edessa and built a library in the Pantheon for Severus Alexander. His Chronographiai in five books synchronised biblical and pagan history from creation to 221, setting the birth of Christ in the year 5500 of the world, and his Kestoi was a miscellany of magic, medicine and military lore. His letter to Origen doubting the authenticity of Susanna survives.

people.name: Caecilian
people.summary: Archdeacon and then bishop of Carthage (c. 311/312), Caecilian had opposed the cult of unauthorised martyrs and was consecrated by bishops accused of handing over scriptures; the Numidian episcopate rejected him, beginning the Donatist schism. Constantine, the Council of Rome (313), Arles (314) and the emperor in person (316) upheld him, and he attended Nicaea in 325.

people.name: Peter of Alexandria
people.summary: Bishop of Alexandria from 300, Peter fled during the Great Persecution, issued moderate canons on the readmission of the lapsed (306) and clashed with Melitius of Lycopolis, whom he excommunicated. Returning in 311, he was beheaded on Maximinus Daia's orders on 25 November 311, venerated by the Copts as the "seal of the martyrs".

people.name: Lucian of Antioch
people.summary: Presbyter and biblical scholar at Antioch, possibly a pupil of Paul of Samosata, whose revision of the Septuagint ("Lucianic recension") and New Testament text became standard in Syria and Constantinople. His pupils, the "Collucianists", included Arius, Eusebius of Nicomedia, Maris of Chalcedon and Theognis of Nicaea, so that later writers saw him as the root of Arianism. He was martyred at Nicomedia on 7 January 312.

people.name: Melitius of Lycopolis
people.summary: Bishop of Lycopolis in the Thebaid who during the Great Persecution ordained clergy in sees whose bishops were in prison or hiding and took a rigorist line on the lapsed, founding the schismatic "Church of the Martyrs". Nicaea allowed his clergy to keep their rank subordinate to Alexander's; his followers later joined the anti-Athanasian coalition, providing the charges at Tyre in 335.

people.name: Alexander of Alexandria
people.summary: Bishop of Alexandria from 312/313, Alexander condemned his presbyter Arius at a synod of about 100 bishops (c. 318-321) and circulated encyclicals against him; he led the anti-Arian side at Nicaea with his deacon and secretary Athanasius, whom he designated as successor before his death on 17 April 328.

people.name: Antony the Great
people.summary: Egyptian Christian from Coma in Middle Egypt who, after hearing the Gospel read c. 270, gave away his land and withdrew first to the edge of his village, then to tombs, then to a deserted fort at Pispir (c. 285) and finally to the Inner Mountain near the Red Sea (c. 313). Visited by crowds, he twice came to Alexandria (311 to encourage martyrs; 338 against the Arians) and corresponded with Constantine. He died in 356 aged about 105; Athanasius' Life of Antony made him the archetype of the monk across east and west.
people.death: natural causes on the Inner Mountain, 17 January 356 (trad.)

people.name: Pachomius
people.summary: Born to pagan parents in the Thebaid, Pachomius was conscripted c. 312 and converted after Christians fed the recruits; after baptism and training with the hermit Palamon he founded the koinonia at Tabennesi (c. 323), creating cenobitic monasticism: walled communities under a written Rule, with houses grouped by craft, daily work, fixed prayer and obedience to superiors. At his death in the plague of 9 May 346 the federation numbered nine male monasteries and two convents.

people.name: Hilarion
people.summary: Founder of Palestinian monasticism according to Jerome's Life, Hilarion was born at Thabatha near Gaza, studied at Alexandria, visited Antony, and lived as a hermit near Gaza from about 306; fleeing fame and persecution under Julian, he travelled to Egypt, Sicily, Dalmatia and finally Cyprus, where he died.

people.name: Evagrius Ponticus
people.summary: Born at Ibora in Pontus, ordained lector by Basil and deacon by Gregory of Nazianzus, Evagrius left Constantinople after a dangerous attachment to a married woman, stayed with Melania and Rufinus in Jerusalem and from 383 lived as a monk in Nitria and the Kellia. His Praktikos, Gnostic Chapters and On Prayer systematised desert spirituality, including the eight logismoi; condemned as an Origenist in 553, his works survived partly under others' names and in Syriac.

people.name: Melania the Elder
people.summary: Daughter of a consular Spanish-Roman family, widowed at 22, Melania left her son in Rome and went to Egypt (372), supporting the Nitrian monks exiled by Valens, then founded a convent on the Mount of Olives (c. 378-380) with Rufinus of Aquileia. Returning to Italy in 399, she inspired her granddaughter Melania the Younger; she died in Jerusalem c. 410.

people.name: Rufinus of Aquileia
people.summary: Monk, translator and historian from Concordia, Rufinus studied in Rome with Jerome, spent years among the Egyptian monks and founded a monastery on the Mount of Olives (c. 380). His Latin translations of Origen's De Principiis and Eusebius' Ecclesiastical History, which he continued to 395 with two new books, shaped western knowledge of Greek theology; the Origenist controversy turned Jerome into his bitter enemy.

people.name: Macrina the Younger
people.summary: Eldest child of a wealthy Christian family of Pontus, Macrina turned the family estate at Annesi into an ascetic community of women and men including her mother, and is credited by her brother Gregory of Nyssa with converting Basil to the ascetic life; Gregory's Life of Macrina and Dialogue on the Soul and Resurrection portray her as a philosopher.

people.name: Basil of Caesarea
people.summary: Cappadocian aristocrat educated at Caesarea, Constantinople and Athens (with Gregory of Nazianzus and the future emperor Julian), Basil turned to asceticism, writing the monastic Rules, and became bishop of Caesarea in 370. He built the Basileias charitable complex, resisted Valens' Homoian policy, and in On the Holy Spirit and Against Eunomius developed the formula of one ousia in three hypostases that triumphed at Constantinople in 381. His Address to Young Men defended reading pagan literature.

people.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
people.summary: Son of the bishop of Nazianzus, friend of Basil from student days in Athens, Gregory was a reluctant bishop of Sasima, then led the small Nicene community of Constantinople from 379, preaching the Theological Orations in the Anastasia. Installed in the Holy Apostles by Theodosius (380) and confirmed as bishop at the council of 381, he resigned amid quarrels over his translation from Sasima and retired to write poetry, including a long autobiographical poem.

people.name: Hilary of Poitiers
people.summary: Convert from a pagan family and bishop of Poitiers from c. 350, Hilary was exiled to Phrygia in 356 after the synod of Béziers; there he wrote De Trinitate and De Synodis, interpreting eastern theology for Latins, and addressed bitter invectives to Constantius. Returning c. 360, he led the restoration of Nicene orthodoxy in Gaul, sponsored Martin of Tours, and wrote some of the earliest Latin hymns.

people.name: Martin of Tours
people.summary: Son of a tribune from Savaria in Pannonia, Martin served in the guard cavalry (famously cutting his cloak for a beggar at Amiens) and left the army before a battle in 356 saying he was a soldier of Christ. A disciple of Hilary, he founded the monastery of Ligugé (c. 361), became bishop of Tours (371/2) and founded Marmoutier, destroying rural temples and sacred trees. He opposed the execution of Priscillian. Sulpicius Severus' Life made him the patron saint of Gaul and the Franks.

people.name: Cyril of Jerusalem
people.summary: Bishop of Jerusalem from c. 350, Cyril delivered the Catecheses (Catechetical Lectures), the fullest record of fourth-century baptismal instruction, preached in the Holy Sepulchre. He reported the cross of light of 351 to Constantius and was exiled three times by his metropolitan Acacius of Caesarea and by Valens, before attending the council of 381 as an accepted Nicene.

people.name: George of Cappadocia
people.summary: A former army contractor (Ammianus calls him born in a fuller's shop at Epiphania in Cilicia), George was installed as bishop of Alexandria in place of Athanasius in 357; he denounced citizens to Constantius, imposed taxes and attacked temples, and was lynched by the mob on 24 December 361. Julian demanded his large library, rich in philosophy, for himself.

people.name: Gregory of Cappadocia
people.summary: Imposed as bishop of Alexandria by a synod at Antioch and installed by the prefect Philagrius in March 339 during Athanasius' second exile, Gregory held the see amid violence until his death in June 345, which opened the way for Athanasius' return in 346.

people.name: Marcellus of Ancyra
people.summary: A champion of Nicaea, Marcellus taught that the Son and Spirit were extensions of the single divine monad that would return into God at the end, provoking the clause "of whose kingdom there shall be no end" in later creeds. Deposed in 336, defended by Julius of Rome and Serdica, he was a liability to Athanasius; his pupil Photinus went further.

people.name: Photinus
people.summary: Pupil of Marcellus and bishop of Sirmium, Photinus taught that Christ was a man born of Mary who became Son of God by adoption, a doctrine condemned by east and west alike; deposed at Sirmium in 351, he was briefly recalled by Julian, who praised him in a letter, and died in exile in Galatia in 376.

people.name: Basil of Ancyra
people.summary: A physician turned bishop of Ancyra (336), Basil led the homoiousian ("like in essence") party in the 350s, influential with Constantius until the Homoians Valens and Ursacius outmanoeuvred him at Rimini and Seleucia; he was deposed and exiled to Illyricum at the council of Constantinople in 360.

people.name: Aetius
people.summary: A former goldsmith and doctor turned dialectician, Aetius taught that the Son is "unlike" (anomoios) the Father in essence, since the unbegotten and begotten cannot share an essence; his Syntagmation survives in Epiphanius. Exiled by Constantius at Basil of Ancyra's urging, he was patronised by Gallus and Julian, and his disciple Eunomius gave the Anomoeans their name.

people.name: Eudoxius
people.summary: Leading Homoian prelate, successively bishop of Germanicia, Antioch (358) and Constantinople (360-370), Eudoxius dedicated the first Hagia Sophia and baptised Valens; famous for a flippant sermon beginning "the Father is impious, the Son pious", he was the chief architect of the Homoian church of the 360s.

people.name: Eusebius of Vercelli
people.summary: A Sardinian lector of Rome who became bishop of Vercelli (c. 345), Eusebius was the first western bishop to live communally with his clergy. Refusing to condemn Athanasius at Milan in 355, he was exiled to Scythopolis, Cappadocia and the Thebaid, joined the Council of Alexandria of 362 and, back in Italy, combated Homoianism with Hilary. The Codex Vercellensis of the Old Latin Gospels is traditionally his.

people.name: Lucifer of Cagliari
people.summary: Bishop of Caralis in Sardinia, exiled after Milan (355), Lucifer addressed to Constantius pamphlets of unprecedented violence (De non parcendo in Deum delinquentibus, Moriundum esse pro Dei Filio). Refusing the reconciliation of Alexandria (362), he consecrated Paulinus as bishop at Antioch, deepening its schism, and his followers, the Luciferians, formed a rigorist sect.

people.name: Macrianus the Elder
people.summary: A rich and lame officer in charge of Valerian's finances and supplies in the east (procurator arcae et praepositus annonae), Macrianus took control of the remnants of the army after Valerian's capture in 260 and, judging himself too old and crippled, had his sons Macrianus and Quietus proclaimed emperors. Dionysius of Alexandria blames him for Valerian's persecution. He marched west with the younger Macrianus and was killed in 261.
people.death: killed with his army's defection in the Balkans, 261

people.name: Macrianus the Younger
people.summary: Proclaimed Augustus with his brother Quietus in 260 and recognised in Egypt and much of the east (coins at Antioch and Alexandria), he marched with his father against Gallienus and was killed when Aureolus' army defeated them in Illyricum or Thrace in 261.

people.name: Quietus
people.summary: Younger son of Macrianus, proclaimed Augustus in 260 and left in Syria with the prefect Ballista; after his family's defeat he was besieged at Emesa by Odaenathus and killed by the townspeople in late 261.

people.name: Ballista
people.summary: Praetorian prefect under Valerian and the Macriani, Ballista (called Callistus by Zonaras and Syncellus) defeated the Persians in Cilicia in 260, capturing part of Shapur's harem, and engineered the proclamation of Macrianus' sons. He was killed with Quietus at Emesa in 261; the Historia Augusta invents a later usurpation.

people.name: Sabinus Julianus
people.summary: Governor (corrector) in northern Italy or Pannonia who claimed the purple on hearing of Numerian's death in 284 and struck coins at Siscia; Carinus defeated and killed him near Verona early in 285.

people.name: Rufius Volusianus
people.summary: Senator with an exceptional career straddling five regimes: corrector of Italy (c. 281-289), proconsul of Africa (305-306), Maxentius' praetorian prefect who crushed Domitius Alexander (309/310), consul in 311 and, under Constantine, prefect of Rome (313-315) and consul again in 314. Ancestor of the great Ceionii Rufii of fourth-century Rome.

people.name: Dalmatius
people.summary: Son of Constantine's half-brother Flavius Dalmatius, educated at Narbo, he suppressed Calocaerus' revolt in Cyprus (334) and was made Caesar on 18 September 335 with Thrace, Macedonia and Achaea. He was murdered by the soldiers in the purge of summer 337, which removed the collateral line from the succession.

people.name: Hannibalianus

roles.t: King of Kings and of the Pontic peoples

people.summary: Brother of the Caesar Dalmatius and husband of Constantine's daughter Constantina, Hannibalianus was appointed in 335 "King of Kings and of the Pontic peoples" (rex regum et Ponticarum gentium), apparently intended to rule Armenia after a Persian war; his unique coins show the Euphrates reclining. He was murdered in 337.

people.name: Constantina
people.summary: Elder daughter of Constantine and Fausta, styled Augusta by her father, she married her cousin Hannibalianus (335) and, after his murder, Constantius Gallus (351). In 350 she persuaded the old general Vetranio to take the purple against Magnentius. Ammianus portrays her as a "Megaera" goading Gallus to cruelty; she died of fever in Bithynia in 354 on her way to plead with Constantius, and was buried in her mausoleum on the Via Nomentana.
people.death: fever at Caeni Gallicani in Bithynia, 354

people.name: Gennobaudes
people.summary: Frankish king on the lower Rhine who submitted to Maximian about 288 and, according to the panegyrist, received his kingdom back as a gift from the emperor, the first named Frankish ruler to become a Roman client.

people.name: Bahram II
people.summary: Sasanian King of Kings 274-293, grandson of Shapur I, who ruled under the influence of the Zoroastrian high priest Kirdir (Kartir), persecuting Manichaeans, Christians and Jews. Faced with Carus' invasion (283) and his brother Hormizd's revolt in Sakastan, he made peace with Diocletian in 287. His rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam and Sar Mashhad show him with his family and killing lions.

people.name: Arsaces II
people.summary: Arsacid king of Armenia c. 350-368, married first to the Roman Olympias (fiancée of Constans) and then to Pharantzem; caught between Rome and Persia, he was abandoned by the treaty of 363, lured to Persia by Shapur II, blinded and imprisoned in the Castle of Oblivion, where Armenian tradition says he killed himself.

people.name: Pap
people.summary: Son of Arsaces II and Pharantzem, Pap escaped from besieged Artogerassa and was restored to the Armenian throne by Valens (c. 370); the battle of Bagavan secured him, but his independence and contacts with Persia led Valens to have him murdered at a banquet given by the dux Traianus in 374 or 375.

people.name: Arbitio
people.summary: A soldier who rose from the ranks to magister equitum (351-361) and consul (355), Arbitio was a feared intriguer at Constantius' court who helped ruin Ursicinus and Silvanus. He sat on Julian's commission at Chalcedon, and in 366, called out of retirement, persuaded Procopius' troops to desert by appealing to them as their old commander.

people.name: Barbatio
people.summary: Commander of Gallus' guard who arrested his master in 354, then magister peditum (355-359); he failed to cooperate with Julian in 357 and was defeated by the Alamanni near Augst. In 359 he and his wife Assyria were executed after she wrote him a letter hoping he would become emperor, an episode Ammianus links to an omen of bees swarming in his house.

people.name: Nevitta
people.summary: A German (perhaps Frankish) officer, Nevitta led one of Julian's columns through Raetia in 361, was made magister equitum and consul for 362, sat on the Chalcedon tribunal, and commanded in the Persian campaign; Ammianus calls him uncouth and cruel, and criticises Julian for giving barbarians the consulship.

people.name: Salutius
people.summary: Gallic pagan and friend of Julian, praetorian prefect of the East 361-367, Salutius presided over the Chalcedon trials and was twice offered the throne, after Julian's death in 363 and after Jovian's in 364, refusing both on grounds of age; he negotiated the treaty of 363. He is perhaps the Sallustius who wrote the Neoplatonic catechism On the Gods and the Cosmos.

people.name: Jovinus
people.summary: Magister equitum in Gaul from 361 under Julian, Jovian and Valentinian I, consul in 367, Jovinus defeated the Alamannic invaders of 366 at Scarponna and Catalauni; a Christian, he built the church of St Agricola at Reims, where his sarcophagus with a lion hunt is preserved.

people.name: Julius
people.summary: Magister militum per Orientem 371-378, Julius ordered the massacre of Gothic youths and hostages in the eastern provinces after Adrianople, a deed Ammianus calls salutary and Zosimus describes in detail.

people.name: Merobaudes
people.summary: Frankish general, magister peditum in the west from 375 to 388 and consul in 377 and 383, Merobaudes engineered the proclamation of Valentinian II in 375 and dominated Gratian's government; he joined Magnus Maximus after Gratian's fall and died, by suicide or murder, during or after the war of 388.

people.name: Promotus
people.summary: Magister peditum in Thrace who destroyed Odotheus' Greuthungi on the Danube in 386, commanded cavalry against Maximus in 388 and was consul in 389; quarrelling with the prefect Rufinus, he was sent to Thrace and killed in a barbarian ambush in 391, which Zosimus attributes to Rufinus' intrigue. Stilicho buried him and avenged him on the Bastarnae.
people.death: killed in an ambush in Thrace, 391

people.name: Vadomarius
people.summary: Alamannic king opposite Augst and brother of Gundomad, Vadomarius made a treaty with Constantius in 354 and, secretly encouraged by him, raided Raetia in 361; Julian had him seized at a dinner and sent to Spain. He later served Rome as dux of Phoenicia, besieged Nicaea for Valens against Procopius (365), and fought the Persians in Armenia (371).

people.name: Macrianus
people.summary: King of the Bucinobantes opposite Mainz, the most formidable Alamannic leader of the 370s; Valentinian tried to kidnap him in 372 but made a treaty with him in boats on the Rhine in 374. He remained a loyal ally until killed fighting the Frankish king Mallobaudes.

people.name: Mavia
people.summary: Arab queen, probably of the Tanukh federation, who after her husband's death c. 375 led raids into Phoenicia, Palestine and Egypt, defeating Roman forces, then made peace on condition that the monk Moses be made bishop of her people. Her daughter married the magister Victor, and her cavalry helped defend Constantinople in 378. An inscription at Anasartha may commemorate her.

people.name: Cynegius
people.summary: Spanish Christian and close associate of Theodosius, praetorian prefect of the East 384-388 and consul 388, Cynegius toured Egypt and Syria closing temples and encouraging their destruction, earning Libanius' hostility (Oration 30). He died in office at Constantinople in March 388; his widow Acanthia carried his body back to Spain.

people.name: Praetextatus
people.summary: Leading pagan senator, priest of many cults (pontifex, augur, initiate of Eleusis, Mithraic pater patrum, hierophant of Hecate), proconsul of Achaea (362-364), prefect of Rome (367-368) and praetorian prefect (384). Jerome reports him joking to Pope Damasus: "Make me bishop of Rome and I will become a Christian at once." His funerary monument with his wife Paulina (CIL VI 1779) is a manifesto of late paganism; Macrobius made him host of the Saturnalia.
people.death: died before taking up the consulship of 385

people.name: Nicomachus Flavianus
people.summary: Senator, historian (his lost Annales were dedicated to Theodosius) and friend of Symmachus, praetorian prefect of Italy under Theodosius (390-392) and again under Eugenius, whose pagan revival he led; consul 394. After the Frigidus he committed suicide; his memory was rehabilitated in 431. Many scholars think his Annales underlie the Latin historical tradition of Ammianus and the Historia Augusta.
people.death: suicide after the battle of the Frigidus, September 394

people.name: Junius Bassus
people.summary: Son of the consul of 331, Junius Bassus was prefect of Rome when he died on 25 August 359 aged 42, having been baptised shortly before; his sarcophagus from St Peter's, with its double register of Old and New Testament scenes, is the finest example of fourth-century Christian sculpture.

people.name: Optatian
people.summary: Poet, probably African, exiled for an unknown offence, who won Constantine's pardon with a book of figured poems in which highlighted letters form images and secondary verses; Constantine replied in a surviving letter. He became prefect of Rome in 329 and 333.

people.name: Porphyry
people.summary: Born Malchus at Tyre, student of Longinus at Athens and from 263 of Plotinus in Rome, Porphyry edited Plotinus' Enneads with a Life of the master, wrote the Isagoge (the standard logic primer for a millennium), On Abstinence from animal food, Letter to Marcella, the Philosophy from Oracles and the fifteen books Against the Christians, the most learned ancient attack on Christianity, burned by imperial order in 448.

people.name: Iamblichus
people.summary: Syrian philosopher, possibly of the Emesene royal line, pupil of Porphyry, who taught at Apamea and turned Neoplatonism towards theurgy, defending ritual in On the Mysteries against Porphyry and writing a Pythagorean encyclopedia (On the Pythagorean Life). Through Aedesius, Maximus of Ephesus and Sallustius his system became the intellectual basis of Julian's pagan restoration.

people.name: Themistius
people.summary: Paphlagonian philosopher and paraphrast of Aristotle who taught at Constantinople, was adlected to the Senate by Constantius (355) and served six emperors as official orator, arguing for religious toleration (Or. 5 to Jovian) and, after Adrianople, for peace with the Goths (Or. 16). Theodosius made him prefect of Constantinople in 384 and tutor of Arcadius. His Aristotle paraphrases were read in Arabic and Hebrew.

people.name: Prohaeresius
people.summary: Armenian-born Christian sophist who held the leading chair of rhetoric at Athens, teaching Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus; Rome set up his statue inscribed "Queen of Cities to the King of Eloquence". He resigned in 362 rather than accept Julian's exemption from the school law.

people.name: Marius Victorinus
people.summary: African rhetor at Rome honoured with a statue in Trajan's Forum, translator of Porphyry's Isagoge and Neoplatonic texts into Latin, whose late conversion (c. 355), professed publicly in church, Augustine describes as a model for his own. As a Christian he wrote dense Neoplatonic treatises against the Arians and the first Latin commentaries on Paul; he resigned his chair under Julian's school law.

people.name: Ausonius
people.summary: Rhetor of Bordeaux for thirty years, summoned c. 364 to tutor Gratian at Trier, Ausonius rose with his pupil to the praetorian prefecture of Gaul (377-379) and the consulship of 379, filling offices with his family. His varied poems include the Mosella, the Parentalia on his relatives, the Professores of Bordeaux and the Ordo urbium nobilium; he corresponded with his pupil Paulinus of Nola, who renounced poetry for asceticism.

people.name: Aurelius Victor
people.summary: African of humble rural origin who rose through the imperial bureaucracy, Aurelius Victor wrote the Liber de Caesaribus (361), a moralising history of emperors from Augustus to Constantius; Julian made him consular of Pannonia Secunda and Theodosius prefect of Rome (389).

people.name: Eutropius
people.summary: Bureaucrat who served under Julian in Persia (363) and as magister memoriae under Valens, for whom he wrote the Breviarium ab urbe condita (c. 369), a lucid ten-book survey of Roman history; often identified with the Eutropius who was proconsul of Asia (371-372) and praetorian prefect of Illyricum (380-381), and perhaps consul in 387.

people.name: Arnobius
people.summary: Rhetor at Sicca Veneria in Africa Proconsularis and teacher of Lactantius, who wrote the seven books Adversus Nationes around 300 to convince his bishop of his conversion; vivid and sarcastic, they preserve much about pagan myth and ritual and show an idiosyncratic theology little shaped by Scripture.

people.name: Firmicus Maternus
people.summary: Sicilian of senatorial rank, author of the Mathesis (c. 335), the most complete Latin astrological manual, which includes a horoscope probably of Ceionius Rufius Albinus; after conversion he wrote On the Error of Profane Religions (c. 346), urging Constantius and Constans to destroy paganism by force.

people.name: Proba
people.summary: Roman aristocrat, wife of Clodius Celsinus Adelphius (prefect of Rome 351) and ancestor of the Anicii, who wrote a lost epic on the war of Constantius and Magnentius and the surviving Cento Vergilianus de laudibus Christi, retelling Genesis and the Gospels in Virgil's own lines.

people.name: Novatian
people.summary: Leading Roman presbyter and the first Roman theologian to write in Latin (De Trinitate), Novatian ran the Roman church's correspondence during the vacancy of 250-251. Defeated by Cornelius in the episcopal election, he was consecrated rival bishop by rigorists who refused readmission to the lapsed, founding the Novatianist church, which survived in Constantinople and Phrygia into the fifth century. Tradition makes him a martyr under Valerian.

people.name: Kartir
people.summary: Zoroastrian priest who rose under Shapur I to become, under Bahram I and Bahram II, the most powerful religious figure of the Sasanian state; his four inscriptions (Naqsh-e Rostam, Naqsh-e Rajab, Sar Mashhad and the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht) boast of founding fire temples and persecuting Jews, Buddhists, Brahmins, Nazarenes, Christians, Baptists and Manichaeans, and he engineered the death of Mani (276/7).

people.name: Tertullian
people.summary: Carthaginian rhetorician and the first major Christian writer in Latin, Tertullian addressed the Apologeticum (197) to provincial governors, coined the Latin theological terms trinitas and persona, wrote against Marcion and Praxeas, on the spectacles, idolatry and the soldier's crown, and later joined the rigorist New Prophecy (Montanism). His "the blood of Christians is seed" and "what has Athens to do with Jerusalem?" became proverbial.

people.name: Gregory Thaumaturgus
people.summary: Born Theodore to a pagan family of Neocaesarea in Pontus, he studied law and then philosophy under Origen at Caesarea, whose method he describes in a farewell Panegyric. As bishop of Neocaesarea (c. 240-270) he converted much of Pontus, reputedly finding 17 Christians and leaving 17 pagans; his Canonical Letter deals with Christians who collaborated with Gothic raiders c. 254.

people.name: Methodius of Olympus
people.summary: Bishop in Lycia (Olympus) and author of the Symposium of the Ten Virgins, a Christian imitation of Plato praising virginity, and of treatises against Origen's views on the resurrection and against Porphyry; tradition, doubted by some, makes him a martyr in 311.

people.name: Eunomius
people.summary: Cappadocian secretary and disciple of Aetius, briefly bishop of Cyzicus (360), Eunomius systematised the Anomoean doctrine that God's essence is "unbegottenness" and can be known, so that the begotten Son cannot share it; refuted at length by Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, he was exiled repeatedly and his followers, the Eunomians, survived as a sect.

people.name: Petronius Probus
people.summary: Head of the Anician clan and the richest man of the west, Probus held four praetorian prefectures (Illyricum 364, Gaul, Italy-Illyricum-Africa 368-375 and 383) and the consulship of 371. Ammianus portrays him as greedy and fearful, "like a fish out of water" out of office; he patronised the young Ambrose, sending him to govern Aemilia-Liguria with the words "act not as a judge but as a bishop". His Christian epitaph and sarcophagus stood behind St Peter's.

people.name: Yazdegerd I
people.fullName: Yazdegerd I, King of Kings of Iran and non-Iran
people.summary: Sasanian king remembered by Christians as tolerant and by Zoroastrian priests as 'the sinner'. He allowed the synod of 410 that organised the Persian church, and Procopius claims Arcadius named him guardian of the infant Theodosius II.
people.death: died in Hyrcania; tradition says kicked to death by a mysterious horse

people.name: Bahram V
people.summary: Son of Yazdegerd I, raised at the Lakhmid court of al-Hira, who won the throne with Arab help in 420. His persecution of Christians caused the Roman war of 421-422; he ended the Arsacid kingdom of Armenia in 428. Persian legend made him the great hunter 'Bahram Gur'.
people.death: disappeared hunting, legend says swallowed by a swamp

people.name: Yazdegerd II
people.summary: Sasanian king who briefly attacked Rome in 440 and spent most of his reign fighting the Kidarites in the east. His attempt to impose Zoroastrianism on Armenia provoked the revolt crushed at Avarayr in 451.

people.name: Peroz I
people.summary: Sasanian king who seized the throne from his brother Hormizd III with Hephthalite help, then fought the Hephthalites three times, was captured and ransomed, and was killed with his army in 484. His defeats left Persia tributary to the Hephthalites.
people.death: killed in a trench ambush by the Hephthalites, 484

people.name: Mazdak
people.summary: Zoroastrian heterodox preacher whose movement, as reported by hostile sources, demanded the sharing of property and women. Kavad I supported him early in his reign, for which he was deposed in 496; Mazdak and his followers were massacred around 528 at the instigation of Prince Khosrow.

people.name: Hormizd IV
people.summary: Son of Khosrow I and a Turkic princess. He refused Roman peace terms, fought Rome, the Turks and the Khazars simultaneously, executed many nobles and clashed with the priesthood. He humiliated his victorious general Bahram Chobin, provoking the revolt that led to his blinding and death.
people.death: blinded and killed in a palace coup by his brothers-in-law Vistahm and Vinduyih, 590

people.name: Tamkhosrow
people.summary: Persian general who fought the Romans in Armenia and Mesopotamia in 576-582, defeating Justinian son of Germanus in 577. He was killed in the battle of Constantina against Maurice in June 582.
people.death: killed at the battle of Constantina, 582

people.name: Adarmahan
people.summary: Persian general and raider who sacked Apamea and burned the suburbs of Antioch in 573, raided Osrhoene in 581 and was defeated with Tamkhosrow at Constantina in 582.

people.name: Kavad II
people.summary: Son of Khosrow II and his Christian wife Maria (according to tradition), who overthrew and killed his father in February 628, executed his brothers and made peace with Heraclius, returning all Roman territory. He died of plague after about seven months.

people.name: Ardashir III
people.summary: Seven-year-old son of Kavad II, enthroned in 628 under the regent Mah-Adhur Gushnasp. He was killed in April 630 when Shahrbaraz seized Ctesiphon with Roman support.

people.name: Boran
people.summary: Khosrow II's daughter and the first woman to rule the Sasanian empire, from June 630 to 631. She sought to restore order, remit taxes and confirm peace with Heraclius through an embassy of the catholicos Ishoyahb II, and struck coins bearing her portrait.

people.name: Azarmidokht
people.summary: Sister of Boran who ruled briefly in 630-631. She had the spahbed Farrukh Hormizd killed when he sought to marry her and was herself killed by his son Rustam Farrokhzad.
people.death: blinded and killed by Rustam Farrokhzad, 631

people.name: Yazdegerd III
people.summary: Last Sasanian King of Kings, crowned as a child at Istakhr in 632. He lost Mesopotamia at Qadisiyya and Jalula (636-637), the Iranian plateau at Nahavand (642), and fled east through Iran; he was killed near Merv in 651. His son Peroz took refuge at the Tang court.

people.name: Rustam Farrokhzad
people.summary: Persian noble from the Ispahbudhan house of Khurasan who avenged his father's murder by killing Azarmidokht, became the power behind Yazdegerd III and commanded the Persian army at Qadisiyya, where he was killed. Firdawsi's Shahnameh gives him a prophetic lament for Iran.

people.name: Abraha
people.summary: Aksumite general who seized power in Himyar (Yemen) after the Aksumite conquest of 525, defied the Negus and ruled as king, repairing the Marib dam (548) and receiving embassies from Rome and Persia. His inscription records a campaign into central Arabia in 552; Islamic tradition makes him the leader of the elephant expedition against Mecca.

people.name: al-Mundhir III
people.summary: Lakhmid king of al-Hira and Persia's chief Arab ally for half a century. He raided Roman Syria repeatedly, reaching Antioch's territory in 529, fought at Callinicum (531), sacrificed a son of al-Harith to al-Uzza according to Procopius, and was killed by the Ghassanids at the battle of Halima in 554.
people.death: killed in battle against al-Harith ibn Jabala, 554

people.name: al-Harith ibn Jabala

roles.t: Supreme phylarch and king of the Arab federates

people.summary: Ghassanid (Jafnid) ruler made 'king' of Rome's Arab federates by Justinian around 529. He fought at Callinicum (531), killed al-Mundhir III in 554, visited Constantinople in 563, and as a Miaphysite obtained the consecration of Jacob Baradaeus and Theodore as bishops in 542.

people.name: al-Mundhir ibn al-Harith
people.summary: Son of al-Harith, victorious over the Lakhmids in 570 and 578, who sacked al-Hira. A committed Miaphysite and patron of churches, he quarrelled with Justin II, joined Maurice's failed Euphrates expedition of 581 and was arrested in 582 and exiled to Sicily.

people.name: al-Nu'man III
people.summary: Last Lakhmid king of al-Hira, a Christian convert and patron of poets. Khosrow II, offended by his refusal of a marriage alliance and suspecting disloyalty, deposed and killed him around 602, ending the Lakhmid buffer state.
people.death: killed in Persian custody, c. 602 (tradition: trampled by elephants)

people.name: al-Muthanna ibn Haritha
people.summary: Chief of the Shayban of the Bakr ibn Wa'il whose raids on the Persian frontier drew Medina into Iraq. He served under Khalid, saved the remnant of the army at the Battle of the Bridge (634) and won at al-Buwayb, dying of his wounds before Qadisiyya.

people.name: Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas
people.fullName: Sa'd ibn Malik ibn Abi Waqqas
people.summary: Early Companion of Muhammad from the Quraysh who commanded the Arab army at Qadisiyya (636), took Ctesiphon (637) and founded Kufa (638). One of the six electors of Umar's successor, he withdrew from politics during the first civil war and died at his estate near Medina.
people.death: died at al-Aqiq near Medina, c. 674

people.name: Shurahbil ibn Hasana
people.summary: One of the four commanders sent by Abu Bakr to Syria in 633-634; he took Bostra, fought at Ajnadayn, Fahl and the Yarmuk, and conquered much of Jordan and Galilee. He died in the plague of Amwas.

people.name: Marcian
people.summary: Patrician and cousin of Justin II who opened the Persian war of 572 by raiding Arzanene and besieged Nisibis in 573, until Justin humiliatingly dismissed him in front of his troops, provoking the panic that preceded the loss of Dara.

people.name: Justinian son of Germanus
people.summary: Son of Justinian I's cousin Germanus and brother of the murdered Justin. He fought in Italy and commanded in the East, sharing in the victory at Melitene (576) before his defeat in Armenia (577). He was suspected of plotting against Tiberius II, who forgave him.

people.name: Peter
people.summary: Maurice's brother, made curopalates, who replaced Priscus in Thrace (594) and commanded again in 601-602. Theophylact, following sources favourable to Priscus, portrays him as incompetent. He was killed by Phocas's men after Maurice's fall.
people.death: killed after the fall of Maurice, 602

people.name: Constantina
people.fullName: Constantina Augusta, daughter of Tiberius II
people.summary: Daughter of Tiberius II and Ino-Anastasia, married to Maurice in 582, mother of nine children including Theodosius. After Maurice's murder she was confined with her daughters, implicated in a plot and executed with them at Chalcedon.
people.death: executed with her three daughters at the harbour of Eutropius, c. 605-607

people.name: Theodosius
people.summary: Maurice's eldest son, crowned co-emperor in 590 and married to the daughter of the patrician Germanus. Sent to seek Persian help in 602, he was overtaken and killed; rumours of his survival let Khosrow II sponsor a pretender in his name.
people.death: killed near Nicaea on Phocas's orders, 602

people.name: Narses
people.summary: Persarmenian-born Roman general, distinct from Justinian's eunuch, who led the army that restored Khosrow II at the Blarathon (591). He rebelled against Phocas at Edessa (603) and, surrendering on a safe-conduct, was burned alive.

people.name: Heraclius the Elder
people.summary: Armenian-born general who distinguished himself at Solachon (586) and Sisarbanon (589), then as exarch of Africa raised the revolt against Phocas in 608 with his brother Gregory, sending his son Heraclius by sea and nephew Nicetas by land. He died soon after his son's coronation.

people.name: Nicetas
people.summary: Cousin of Heraclius who won Egypt from Phocas's forces in 608-610, governed it as patrician and fought beside Heraclius at Antioch (613). He held Alexandria until the Persian conquest of 619. His daughter married Heraclius's son Constantine III.

people.name: Bonosus
people.summary: Phocas's ruthless comes Orientis who crushed the riots of Antioch (609) and was sent to Egypt against Nicetas, by whom he was defeated. He was killed when Heraclius took Constantinople.

people.name: Fabia-Eudokia
people.summary: African noblewoman betrothed to Heraclius, held hostage by Phocas, and crowned and married to him on 5 October 610. She bore Epiphania and Constantine III and died of epilepsy in August 612.

people.name: Romanus
people.summary: Exarch of Ravenna who coordinated with the Frankish invasion of 590, recovered towns in the Po valley and the Via Amerina corridor (592), and opposed Gregory the Great's separate negotiations with the Lombards.

people.name: Gennadius
people.fullName: Gennadius, magister militum and exarch of Africa
people.summary: Roman commander in Africa who killed the Moorish king Garmul (578) and is the first attested exarch of Africa (591), corresponding with Gregory the Great about the Donatists and church estates.

people.name: Eleutherius
people.summary: Eunuch exarch of Ravenna who suppressed the killers of his predecessor and the rebel John of Conza, then proclaimed himself emperor in 619 and was killed by his soldiers on the way to Rome.
people.death: killed by his troops at Castrum Luceoli, 619

people.name: Hypatius
people.summary: Nephew of Anastasius I, an unlucky general captured by Vitalian (513) and beaten by the Persians at Amida (503). In the Nika riot the crowd crowned him emperor in the Hippodrome against his will; he was executed the next day.
people.death: executed after the Nika riot, January 532

people.name: John nephew of Vitalian
people.summary: Bold and insubordinate commander in the Gothic war, nicknamed 'the Sanguinary', who seized Ariminum (538), sided with Narses against Belisarius, married Germanus's daughter Justina and fought at Taginae (552).

people.name: Stotzas
people.summary: Bodyguard soldier who led the great mutiny of the African army in 536, besieged Carthage, was beaten by Belisarius and Germanus (Scalae Veteres, 537) and fought on with the Moors until killed in single combat with John at Thacia in 545.

people.name: Chrysaphius
people.summary: Eunuch who dominated Theodosius II's court in the 440s, ousted Pulcheria's and Eudocia's influence, supported Eutyches and Ephesus II, and plotted the assassination of Attila in 449. Marcian executed him in 450.

people.name: Eutychius
people.summary: Patriarch who presided over the council of 553, was deposed by Justinian in 565 for rejecting aphthartodocetism, and returned in 577, when he debated with Gregory (the future pope) on the nature of the resurrected body.

people.name: John of Ephesus
people.fullName: John of Amida, Miaphysite bishop of Ephesus
people.summary: Syriac Miaphysite historian from Amida, who under Justinian led missions that he claimed converted 80,000 pagans in Asia Minor, then was imprisoned under Justin II. His Lives of the Eastern Saints and Ecclesiastical History, Part III of which survives complete, are key sources for the plague, Justin II's madness and the Slavs.

people.name: Timothy Aelurus
people.summary: Anti-Chalcedonian patriarch of Alexandria consecrated in 457, implicated in the murder of Proterius, exiled to Gangra and Cherson (460-475), and restored by Basiliscus. His nickname means 'the Cat' or 'the Weasel'.

people.name: Simeon the Stylite

roles.t: Ascetic on a column near Telanissos

people.summary: Syrian shepherd turned ascetic who lived on a column for some 36 years, preaching to crowds and advising emperors; Theodoret, who knew him, wrote his life. His cult produced the pilgrimage complex of Qal'at Sim'an.

people.name: John Cassian
people.summary: Monk from Scythia Minor who lived in Bethlehem and among the Egyptian desert fathers, was ordained deacon by John Chrysostom, and founded monasteries at Marseille. His Institutes and Conferences shaped western monasticism.

people.name: Patrick
people.summary: Romano-British son of a decurion, kidnapped by Irish raiders at sixteen, who escaped and later returned to Ireland as a bishop. His Confessio and Letter to the soldiers of Coroticus are unique first-person sources for fifth-century Britain and Ireland.

people.name: Honoratus
people.summary: Gallo-Roman aristocrat who founded the island monastery of Lérins around 410 and became bishop of Arles; his kinsman Hilary wrote his Life.

people.name: Caesarius of Arles
people.summary: Monk of Lérins and bishop of Arles under Visigothic, Ostrogothic and Frankish rulers. He presided at the councils of Agde (506) and Orange (529), which settled the grace controversy, wrote some 250 popular sermons and the first Rule for nuns.

people.name: Benedict of Nursia
people.summary: Umbrian who abandoned studies in Rome for a hermit's cave at Subiaco, founded monasteries there and around 529 at Monte Cassino, where he wrote his Rule. Almost everything known of him comes from Book 2 of Gregory the Great's Dialogues, including his meeting with Totila in 542.
people.death: died at Monte Cassino, traditionally 21 March 547

people.name: Dionysius Exiguus
people.summary: Scythian monk ('the Small', from his humility) in Rome who translated Greek canons and decretals into Latin, creating the Collectio Dionysiana, and in 525 devised the Easter tables counting years from the Incarnation.

people.name: Romanos the Melode
people.summary: Syrian-born deacon from Emesa who served in Constantinople under Anastasius and Justinian and composed the greatest Byzantine kontakia; legend says the Theotokos gave him the gift of song in a dream.

people.name: Cosmas Indicopleustes
people.summary: Alexandrian merchant who travelled to Aksum and the Red Sea, later a monk, author of the Christian Topography (c. 550) with its Tabernacle-shaped cosmos and valuable notes on Indian Ocean trade.

people.name: Priscian
people.summary: Grammarian from Caesarea in Mauretania who taught Latin in Constantinople and wrote the Institutiones Grammaticae, the most comprehensive Latin grammar from antiquity and the standard textbook of the Middle Ages.

people.name: Corippus
people.summary: African Latin poet, author of the Iohannis on John Troglita's Moorish wars and of the panegyric In laudem Iustini minoris (566), which describes Justinian's funeral and Justin II's coronation ceremonies in detail.

people.name: Gildas
people.summary: British monk and author of De Excidio Britanniae, the only substantial narrative of the end of Roman Britain by an insular writer; later Breton tradition linked him to Rhuys.

people.name: Venantius Fortunatus
people.summary: Italian poet from near Treviso, educated at Ravenna, who crossed into Gaul in 566, wrote an epithalamium for Sigibert and Brunhild, and settled at Poitiers as friend of Radegund. His hymns Vexilla regis and Pange lingua were written for the True Cross relic of 569.

people.name: Radegund
people.summary: Thuringian princess captured as a child by Chlothar I and married to him; after he killed her brother she left him and founded the convent of the Holy Cross at Poitiers, obtaining a relic of the True Cross from Justin II.

people.name: Isidore of Seville
people.summary: Younger brother of Leander, bishop of Seville for 36 years and the most influential scholar of Visigothic Spain. He wrote the Etymologies, the History of the Goths, On the Nature of Things, Chronicles and On Famous Men, and presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo (633).

people.name: Leander of Seville
people.summary: Hispano-Roman bishop from a Cartagena family who converted Hermenegild, met Gregory the Great in Constantinople (where Gregory dedicated the Moralia to him), and guided Reccared's conversion and the Third Council of Toledo.

people.name: Columbanus
people.summary: Irish monk who founded Annegray, Luxeuil and Fontaine in Burgundy, defied Brunhild and Theuderic II and was expelled in 610, then founded Bobbio in Lombard Italy. His letters to popes defend Irish Easter reckoning in remarkably blunt Latin.

people.name: Maximus the Confessor
people.summary: Former imperial secretary under Heraclius who became a monk and the leading theologian of dyotheletism, opposing the Ekthesis from Africa. He was condemned under Constans II, had his tongue and right hand cut off, and died in exile in Lazica.
people.death: died in exile in Lazica, 13 August 662

people.name: Honorius I
people.summary: Campanian pope who restored Roman churches, including Sant'Agnese fuori le mura and the bronze roof tiles of St Peter's from the temple of Venus and Rome, and supported the English mission. His letter accepting 'one will' in Christ led to his posthumous anathema in 681.

people.name: Benjamin I
people.fullName: Benjamin I, Coptic patriarch of Alexandria
people.summary: Miaphysite patriarch of Alexandria who fled to Upper Egypt when Cyrus arrived in 631 and spent ten years in hiding. After the Arab conquest Amr ibn al-As restored him to Alexandria; he rebuilt the Coptic church under Muslim rule.

people.name: Leovigild
people.summary: The most successful Visigothic king. He took Asidona and Córdoba (571-572), subdued Cantabria and Orospeda, founded Reccopolis (578), crushed his son Hermenegild's revolt (579-584) and annexed the Suebic kingdom (585). He adopted throne, crown and imperial-style coinage and tried to reconcile Catholics with a modified Arianism.

people.name: Hermenegild
people.summary: Elder son of Leovigild, married to the Frankish princess Ingund, who converted to Catholicism and rebelled at Seville in 579, striking coins with the legend 'Regi a Deo vita'. Captured in 584, he was killed at Tarragona in 585 and honoured by Gregory the Great as a martyr.

people.name: Reccared I
people.summary: Younger son of Leovigild who converted to Catholicism in 587 and led the Goths into the Catholic church at the Third Council of Toledo (589), suppressing Arian plots. His general Claudius defeated the Franks at Carcassonne (589). He took the imperial name Flavius.

people.name: Sisebut
people.summary: Learned Visigothic king who wrote a Life of Desiderius of Vienne and an astronomical poem, campaigned against Roman Spania and the Asturians, built a fleet, and ordered the forced baptism of the Jews. Isidore dedicated On the Nature of Things to him.

people.name: Suintila
people.summary: Visigothic king who completed the conquest of Roman Spania around 624-625, earning Isidore's praise as the first king of all Spain; he was deposed by Sisenand with Frankish help in 631 and condemned by the Fourth Council of Toledo.

people.name: Theudis
people.summary: Ostrogothic officer who governed Visigothic Spain for Theodoric, married a rich Hispano-Roman heiress, and became king after Amalaric's murder in 531. He failed to take Septem (Ceuta) from the Romans in 547 and was assassinated in his palace.

people.name: Theudebert I
people.summary: Grandson of Clovis, king at Reims, who extended Frankish power over Alamannia, Provence and parts of northern Italy, invaded Italy in 539, and was the first barbarian king to strike gold solidi in his own name. A letter to Justinian boasts of his dominion from the Danube to the Ocean.

people.name: Sigibert I
people.summary: Son of Chlothar I and king at Reims and Metz from 561, husband of the Visigothic princess Brunhild, who fought the Avars in 562 and 566 and his brother Chilperic for most of his reign, until he was assassinated at Vitry in 575.
people.death: stabbed by Fredegund's agents at Vitry, 575

people.name: Chilperic I
people.summary: Son of Chlothar I, king at Soissons, who murdered his Visigothic wife Galswintha to marry Fredegund, waged war on Sigibert, wrote Latin hymns and a treatise on the Trinity, and proposed new letters for the alphabet. Gregory of Tours called him the Nero and Herod of the age.

people.name: Guntram
people.summary: Son of Chlothar I, king of Burgundy at Chalon, mediator between his warring brothers and protector of his nephews. He crushed the pretender Gundovald (585), concluded the Treaty of Andelot (587) and was venerated as a saint for his piety.

people.name: Brunhild

roles.t: Regent for her son and grandsons

people.summary: Visigothic princess, daughter of Athanagild, married to Sigibert I in 567. After his murder she governed Austrasia and Burgundy for her son Childebert II and grandsons, corresponded with Gregory the Great and Maurice, and fought a long feud with Fredegund. Chlothar II had her torn apart by horses in 613.

people.name: Fredegund
people.summary: Servant who became Chilperic I's wife after the murder of Galswintha; Gregory of Tours accuses her of the assassinations of Sigibert I and Bishop Praetextatus among others. She preserved the throne of her infant son Chlothar II.

people.name: Chlothar II
people.summary: Son of Chilperic and Fredegund, king from infancy, who destroyed Brunhild and her great-grandsons in 613 and reunited Francia, issuing the Edict of Paris (614) and making his son Dagobert king of Austrasia (623).

people.name: Dagobert I
people.summary: Last powerful Merovingian, who ruled from Paris, made treaties with Heraclius, intervened in Visigothic Spain (631), fought Samo's Wends (631) and endowed the abbey of Saint-Denis, where he was buried.

people.name: Gundovald
people.summary: Claimant to be a son of Chlothar I, mocked as 'Ballomer', who lived in Constantinople and returned with imperial money in 582. Raised on a shield at Brive in 584, he was besieged at Convenae and killed in 585.

people.name: Mummolus
people.summary: Gallo-Roman general of Guntram who defeated Lombard and Saxon invaders (570s) and later defected to Gundovald; he was killed after betraying the pretender at Convenae in 585.

people.name: Authari
people.summary: Son of Cleph elected king in 584 to restore Lombard unity against Franks and Romans. He married the Bavarian Catholic princess Theodelinda in 589 and reportedly rode to Reggio and touched a column in the sea, claiming Italy to that point.

people.name: Agilulf
people.summary: Thuringian-born duke of Turin chosen by Theodelinda as husband and king in 590. He threatened Rome (593), made truces brokered by Gregory the Great, took Padua, Cremona and Mantua (601-603), granted Bobbio to Columbanus and allowed his son's Catholic baptism. A gilded plaque from his helmet shows him enthroned.

people.name: Theodelinda
people.summary: Bavarian Catholic princess, wife of Authari and then Agilulf, friend and correspondent of Gregory the Great, who built the basilica of St John at Monza and promoted the conversion of the Lombards. The Monza treasury preserves gifts associated with her.

people.name: Rothari
people.summary: Arian duke of Brescia, king from 636, who conquered Liguria and Oderzo from the Romans and in 643 issued the Edict of Rothari, the first written code of Lombard law, in 388 chapters.

people.name: Zotto
people.summary: First Lombard duke of Benevento, who carved out an autonomous duchy in southern Italy and whose men destroyed Monte Cassino.

people.name: Istämi
people.summary: Ruler of the western wing of the Turkic khaganate, called Sizabul or Silziboulos by Menander, who destroyed the Hephthalites with Khosrow I and then allied with Justin II against Persia, receiving the embassy of Zemarchus (569).

people.name: Kubrat
people.summary: Bulgar ruler raised at Constantinople who threw off Avar rule around 635 and allied with Heraclius, who made him a patrician. His sons, according to Byzantine tradition, divided his people, one of them, Asparukh, founding the Danubian Bulgar state in 681.

people.name: Samo
people.summary: Frankish merchant who, according to Fredegar, led the Wends in revolt against the Avars and ruled them as king for 35 years, defeating Dagobert I at Wogastisburg (631).

people.name: Dengizich
people.summary: Son of Attila who tried to restore Hunnic power after the Nedao, demanding trade rights from Leo I, and invaded the empire across the Danube; he was killed by the general Anagast in 469.
people.death: killed in battle; head displayed in Constantinople, 469

people.name: Theodahad
people.summary: Nephew of Theodoric and wealthy Tuscan landowner with Platonic interests, made co-ruler by Amalasuntha in 534. He had her murdered, gave Justinian his casus belli, negotiated secretly to abdicate, and was deposed and killed after the fall of Naples.
people.death: killed while fleeing to Ravenna, December 536

people.name: Hilderic
people.summary: Son of Huneric and the Theodosian princess Eudocia, pro-Roman king of the Vandals who ended persecution of Catholics. Deposed by Gelimer in 530, he was killed in 533 as Belisarius approached Carthage.

people.name: Mermeroes
people.summary: Veteran Persian general of the Lazic war, who besieged Archaeopolis (551) and, though crippled by age and carried in a litter, kept the Persians in Lazica until his death.

people.name: Mesrop Mashtots
people.summary: Armenian former royal secretary and monk who invented the Armenian alphabet around 405 and, according to his pupil Koriwn, the Georgian and Albanian scripts, organising the translation of the Bible and Greek and Syriac texts.

people.name: Gerontius
people.summary: British-born general of Constantine III who cleared the Pyrenean passes, then rebelled in 409 with his own emperor Maximus. Deserted by his troops in 411, he died in a last stand with his Alan follower and his wife.
people.death: killed himself and his wife in his burning house in Spain, 411

people.name: Sabas
people.summary: Cappadocian monk who founded the Great Lavra (483) and other monasteries in the Judaean desert, led the Chalcedonian monks of Palestine against Anastasius, and petitioned Justinian for tax relief after the Samaritan revolt of 529.
people.death: died at the Great Lavra, 5 December 532

people.name: Musaylima
people.fullName: Maslama ibn Habib of the Banu Hanifa
people.summary: Prophet of the Banu Hanifa of Yamama, called by Muslim tradition the 'little Maslama' (Musaylima) and 'the Liar', who claimed revelation in Muhammad's lifetime and led the strongest resistance of the Ridda. He was killed at Aqraba by the spear of Wahshi, the slave who had killed Hamza at Uhud.
people.death: killed at the battle of Yamama, c. December 632

people.name: John of Biclaro
people.summary: Goth from Scallabis educated for seventeen years in Constantinople, exiled to Barcelona by Leovigild for his Catholicism, founder of the monastery of Biclaro and bishop of Gerona. His chronicle of 567-590 is the main source for Leovigild and Reccared.

people.name: Shirin
people.summary: Christian, probably Aramaean, wife of Khosrow II, patron of the Miaphysite church at court, whose pregnancy prompted Khosrow's votive gifts to St Sergius. Persian romance made her the heroine of Nizami's Khosrow and Shirin.

people.name: Theodoric II
people.summary: Visigothic king who murdered his brother Thorismund, made Avitus emperor (455), crushed the Suebi at the Órbigo (456) and expanded into Spain and Narbonensis. Sidonius Apollinaris left a celebrated portrait of his daily routine at Toulouse. His brother Euric murdered him in 466.

people.name: Iyad ibn Ghanm
people.summary: Arab commander who succeeded Abu Ubayda in northern Syria and conquered Roman Mesopotamia (Edessa, Harran, Amida, Dara and Callinicum) in 639-640, mostly by capitulation.

people.name: Egeria

roles.t: Pilgrim in the Holy Land, Sinai, Egypt and Mesopotamia

people.summary: A woman from the far west of the empire, probably Gallaecia, whose letters to her 'sisters' at home describe a three-year pilgrimage to Jerusalem, Sinai, Egypt, Edessa and Constantinople. The surviving text (the Itinerarium Egeriae) is the fullest early account of the Jerusalem liturgy and an important witness to spoken Latin.

people.name: Melania the Younger

roles.t: Ascetic; founder of monasteries on the Mount of Olives

people.summary: Granddaughter of Melania the Elder and heiress to one of the largest fortunes in the Roman West, she and her husband Pinianus liquidated estates across Italy, Sicily, Africa, Spain and Britain from c. 405, left Rome before Alaric's sack, lived at Thagaste near Augustine, and settled in Jerusalem, where she founded monasteries on the Mount of Olives.

people.name: Germanus of Auxerre
people.summary: Former provincial official turned bishop of Auxerre, sent to Britain in 429 (and perhaps again c. 445) to combat Pelagianism. His Life by Constantius of Lyon credits him with the 'Alleluia victory' over Picts and Saxons, one of the few narrative glimpses of sub-Roman Britain. He died at Ravenna while interceding for the rebel Armoricans.

wars.name: War with Lars Porsenna and the Tarquins
wars.outcome: Porsenna probably captured Rome but his power in Latium collapsed after his son's defeat at Aricia (c. 504); the Tarquins failed to return.
