list.note: 'Crowned in the womb'; 70-year reign; persecuted Christians from 340; besieged Amida (359); recovered Nisibis by Jovian's treaty (363).

list.name: Shapur III
list.note: Killed when nobles cut the ropes of his tent; partition of Armenia with Rome (c. 387).

list.name: Bahram IV
list.note: Killed by mutinous troops.

list.name: Yazdegerd I
list.note: Tolerant of Christians (synod of Seleucia-Ctesiphon 410); named guardian of Theodosius II by Arcadius (Procopius). Died in Hyrcania, by legend kicked by a magical horse; probably killed by nobles.

list.name: Shapur IV
list.note: Ex-king of Armenia; killed by nobles.

list.name: Bahram V Gur
list.note: Brief war with Rome (421-422); legendary hunter who disappeared into a swamp or quicksand while hunting.

list.name: Yazdegerd II
list.note: War with Rome (440); crushed the Armenian revolt at Avarayr (451).

list.name: Hormizd III
list.note: Killed by his brother Peroz.

list.name: Peroz I
list.note: Captured by the Hephthalites, ransomed; killed in a trench trap by them (484).

list.name: Balash
list.note: Blinded.

list.name: Kavad I
list.note: Deposed 496 (Mazdakite affair), escaped from the Fortress of Oblivion, restored 498/499 with Hephthalite help; wars with Rome 502-506 (took Amida) and 526-531.

list.name: Khosrow I Anushirvan
list.note: Fiscal and military reforms; Eternal Peace (532); sacked Antioch (540); Fifty Years' Peace (561/562); conquered Yemen (c. 570).

list.name: Hormizd IV
list.note: Deposed in a palace coup, blinded and killed.

list.name: Bahram VI Chobin
list.note: Mihranid general who took the throne; defeated by Khosrow II with Roman troops at the Blarathon (591).

list.name: Khosrow II Parviz
list.note: Restored by Maurice (591); used Maurice's murder as casus belli (603); conquered Syria, Jerusalem (614), Egypt (619); defeated by Heraclius (627). Deposed and executed 28 Feb 628.

list.name: Vistahm
list.note: Rebel king in the north-east (dates 591/595-596/600).

list.name: Kavad II (Sheroe)
list.note: Made peace with Heraclius; killed most of his brothers; died of plague.

list.name: Ardashir III
list.note: Child king killed by Shahrbaraz.

list.name: Shahrbaraz
list.note: General who had besieged Constantinople (626); usurped with Heraclius' backing; killed after 40 days.

list.name: Boran
list.note: Daughter of Khosrow II; first queen regnant; returned the True Cross. Second reign 631-632.

list.name: Azarmidokht
list.note: Sister of Boran.

list.name: Yazdegerd III
list.note: Lost al-Qadisiyya (636/637), Ctesiphon (637), Nahavand (642); killed by a miller near Merv (651).

list.name: Balamber
list.note: Named only by Jordanes; possibly legendary.

list.name: Uldin
list.note: Killed Gainas (400) and sent his head to Arcadius; ally of Stilicho against Radagaisus (406); defeated in Thrace 408.

list.name: Charaton
list.note: Visited by Olympiodorus.

list.name: Octar
list.note: Died of overeating on campaign against the Burgundians (Socrates).

list.name: Rua (Rugila)
list.note: Extracted 350 lb of gold a year from Constantinople; died, by Socrates' account, struck by lightning.

list.name: Bleda
list.note: Co-ruler with his brother; killed by Attila.

list.name: Attila
list.note: Treaty of Margus (435), Balkan campaigns (441-447, tribute raised to 2,100 lb a year), invasion of Gaul (Catalaunian Plains 451) and Italy (452). Died of a haemorrhage on his wedding night.

list.name: Ellac
list.note: Killed at the Nedao against the Gepids under Ardaric.

list.name: Dengizich
list.note: Killed by the Roman general Anagastes; his head was displayed in the Hippodrome in Constantinople.

list.name: Ernak
list.note: Settled in the Dobruja.

list.name: Athanaric
list.note: Iudex of the Thervingi; made peace with Valens on a boat in the Danube (369); persecuted Gothic Christians; died in Constantinople two weeks after being received by Theodosius.

list.name: Fritigern
list.note: Led the Goths across the Danube (376) and to victory at Adrianople (378); disappears from the sources c. 380.

list.name: Ermanaric
list.note: Ruled a large realm in the Pontic steppe; killed himself facing the Huns (Ammianus).

list.name: Vithimiris
list.note: Killed fighting the Huns and Alans.

list.name: Alatheus and Saphrax
list.note: Regents for Vithimiris' son Videric; their cavalry decided Adrianople.

list.name: Alaric I
list.note: Sacked Rome 24-27 Aug 410; died at Consentia and was buried in the bed of the Busento.

list.name: Athaulf
list.note: Married Galla Placidia at Narbo (414); murdered in a stable at Barcino.

list.name: Sigeric
list.note: Reigned seven days.

list.name: Wallia
list.note: Returned Placidia for 600,000 measures of grain; fought the Vandals and Alans in Spain for Rome; settled in Aquitaine (418).

list.name: Theodoric I
list.note: Killed at the Catalaunian Plains.

list.name: Thorismund
list.note: Killed by his brothers.

list.name: Theodoric II
list.note: Made Avitus emperor (455); described by Sidonius (Ep. 1.2); killed by his brother Euric.

list.name: Euric
list.note: Extended the kingdom to the Loire, Rhône and most of Spain; Code of Euric.

list.name: Alaric II
list.note: Breviary of Alaric (506); killed by Clovis at Vouillé.

list.name: Gesalec
list.note: Driven out by Ostrogothic forces.

list.name: Amalaric
list.note: Under Theodoric the Great's tutelage until 526; killed at Barcino after defeat by Childebert I.

list.name: Theudis
list.note: Ostrogothic general; failed attack on Septem (Ceuta).

list.name: Theudigisel
list.note: Killed at a banquet in Seville.

list.name: Agila I
list.note: Killed by his own men after Athanagild's revolt brought in Byzantine troops (Spania).

list.name: Athanagild
list.note: Moved the capital to Toledo; father of Brunhild and Galswintha.

list.name: Liuvigild
list.note: Reunified Spain, annexed the Suebic kingdom (585), executed his Catholic son Hermenegild (585).

list.name: Reccared I
list.note: Converted to Catholicism (587; Third Council of Toledo 589).

list.name: Liuva II
list.note: Hand cut off and killed by Witteric.

list.name: Witteric
list.note: Killed at a banquet.

list.name: Sisebut
list.note: Scholar-king, correspondent of Isidore; forced conversion of Jews; took most of Byzantine Spania. Death by illness or poison.

list.name: Suintila
list.note: Expelled the last Byzantine garrisons (c. 625).

list.name: Sisenand
list.note: Fourth Council of Toledo (633).

list.name: Tulga
list.note: Tonsured and sent to a monastery by Chindasuinth.

list.name: Valamir
list.note: Fought for Attila at the Catalaunian Plains; settled in Pannonia after Nedao; killed fighting the Sciri.

list.name: Theodemir
list.note: Father of Theodoric; moved the Goths into the Balkans (473).

list.name: Theodoric the Great (before Italy)
list.note: Hostage in Constantinople (461-471); consul 484; sent by Zeno against Odoacer (488).

list.name: Theodoric the Great
list.note: Killed Odoacer with his own hands (15 Mar 493); ruled Italy as king with a Roman administration (Cassiodorus, Boethius, executed 524). Mausoleum at Ravenna.

list.name: Athalaric
list.note: Grandson of Theodoric, under his mother's regency; died of drink aged 18.

list.name: Amalasuntha
list.note: Regent 526-534, queen 534; negotiated secretly with Justinian; strangled in her bath on Lake Bolsena, giving Justinian his casus belli.

list.name: Theodahad
list.note: Killed after failing to stop Belisarius taking Naples.

list.name: Witiges
list.note: Besieged Rome (537-538); surrendered at Ravenna (540).
list.death: natural, at Constantinople as a patrician

list.name: Ildibad
list.note: Killed by a Gepid bodyguard.

list.name: Eraric
list.note: Rugian king killed after five months.

list.name: Totila (Baduila)
list.note: Retook almost all Italy, took Rome twice (546, 550); mortally wounded at Busta Gallorum/Taginae against Narses.

list.name: Teia
list.note: Killed at Mons Lactarius near Vesuvius.

list.name: Odoacer
list.note: Scirian officer who deposed Romulus Augustulus and sent the regalia to Zeno; rex in Italy; killed by Theodoric at a banquet in Ravenna.

list.name: Godigisel
list.note: Killed by Franks before the Rhine crossing.

list.name: Gunderic
list.note: Led the Vandals across the Rhine (31 Dec 406) and into Spain (409); took Hispalis.

list.name: Gaiseric
list.note: Crossed to Africa (429) with c. 80,000 people; took Carthage 19 Oct 439; sacked Rome (455); destroyed Leo I's armada (468); treaty of 474 with Zeno.

list.name: Huneric
list.note: Married Eudocia, daughter of Valentinian III; persecuted Catholics.

list.name: Thrasamund
list.note: Married Theodoric's sister Amalafrida.

list.name: Hilderic
list.note: Pro-Roman, pro-Catholic grandson of Valentinian III.
list.death: executed by Gelimer when Belisarius landed

list.name: Gelimer
list.note: Defeated at Ad Decimum and Tricamarum (533); surrendered on Mount Papua (534); walked in Belisarius' triumph and retired to estates in Galatia.

list.name: Chlodio
list.note: Took Cambrai and the land to the Somme; defeated by Aetius at Vicus Helena.

list.name: Merovech
list.note: Eponym of the Merovingians; perhaps legendary.

list.name: Childeric I
list.note: Federate king at Tournai, fought alongside Aegidius and Count Paul; his grave (found 1653) held a signet ring and a crossbow brooch of a Roman official.

list.name: Clovis I
list.note: Defeated Syagrius at Soissons (486), the Alamanni (Tolbiac, c. 496/506), the Visigoths at Vouillé (507); Catholic baptism at Reims (496 or 508); honorary consul from Anastasius (508); Lex Salica.

list.name: Theuderic I
list.note: Reims/Metz.

list.name: Chlodomer
list.note: Orléans; killed at Vézeronce against the Burgundians.

list.name: Childebert I
list.note: Paris.

list.name: Chlothar I
list.note: Soissons; sole king 558-561.

list.name: Theudebert I
list.note: Invaded Italy (539); struck gold coins in his own name, outraging Procopius.

list.name: Charibert I
list.note: Paris.

list.name: Guntram
list.note: Burgundy; later venerated as a saint.

list.name: Sigebert I
list.note: Austrasia; husband of Brunhild; killed by assassins of Fredegund.

list.name: Chilperic I
list.note: Neustria; husband of Fredegund; stabbed returning from a hunt.

list.name: Chlothar II
list.note: Sole king 613 after executing Brunhild; Edict of Paris (614).

list.name: Theudebert II
list.note: Killed after defeat by his brother.

list.name: Theuderic II
list.note: Died of dysentery at Metz.

list.name: Sigebert II
list.note: Child king killed by Chlothar II.

list.name: Dagobert I
list.note: Austrasia 623, sole king 629-634; founded Saint-Denis; the last strong Merovingian.

list.name: Charibert II
list.note: Aquitaine; possibly murdered.

list.name: Sigebert III
list.note: Austrasia.

list.name: Clovis II
list.note: Neustria and Burgundy.

list.name: Wacho
list.note: Lething dynasty; marriage alliances with Thuringians, Gepids and Franks.

list.name: Audoin
list.note: Settled in Pannonia as Byzantine allies; sent 5,500 men to Narses (552).

list.name: Alboin
list.note: Destroyed the Gepids with the Avars (567), killing Cunimund and making a drinking cup of his skull; invaded Italy (568); killed at Verona at the instigation of his wife Rosamund, Cunimund's daughter.

list.name: Cleph
list.note: Killed by a slave; ten years of rule by the dukes followed (574-584).

list.name: Authari
list.note: Restored the monarchy; married Theodelinda. Possibly poisoned.

list.name: Agilulf
list.note: Catholic sympathies via Theodelinda; peace with the exarchate.

list.name: Arioald
list.note: Arian.

list.name: Rothari
list.note: Took Liguria and Opitergium from the exarchate; Edictum Rothari (643).

list.name: Gundahar
list.note: Settled on the Rhine (Worms) as foederati; with Goar backed Jovinus; destroyed by Aetius' Hunnic auxiliaries (436/437), the kernel of the Nibelungenlied.

list.name: Gundioc
list.note: Kingdom resettled in Sapaudia (443); magister militum.

list.name: Chilperic I (Burgundian)
list.note: Brother of Gundioc.

list.name: Gundobad
list.note: Killed Anthemius for Ricimer (472); briefly magister militum and kingmaker in Italy (Glycerius); Lex Burgundionum (Liber Constitutionum).

list.name: Godegisel
list.note: Killed at Vienne by Gundobad.

list.name: Sigismund
list.note: Converted to Catholicism; founded Saint-Maurice d'Agaune; captured and thrown down a well by Chlodomer.

list.name: Godomar
list.note: Defeated Chlodomer at Vézeronce (524); kingdom conquered by the Franks (534).

list.name: Hermeric
list.note: Led the Sueves into Gallaecia; abdicated in illness (438).

list.name: Rechila
list.note: Took Emerita (439) and Hispalis (441).

list.name: Rechiar
list.note: First Catholic Germanic king; defeated by Theodoric II at the Urbicus and executed.

list.name: Remismund
list.note: Turned Arian; the sources then fall silent until c. 550.

list.name: Theodemar
list.note: Catholic again (Martin of Braga); Councils of Braga (561, 572).

list.name: Andeca
list.note: Liuvigild annexed the kingdom (585).

list.name: Ardaric
list.note: Attila's favourite; led the revolt that destroyed the Huns at the Nedao (454).

list.name: Thurisind
list.note: Wars with the Lombards over Sirmium.

list.name: Cunimund
list.note: Killed by Alboin; the Gepid kingdom destroyed by Lombards and Avars.

list.name: Bayan I
list.note: Led the Avars into the Carpathian basin (568); took Sirmium (582); exacted rising tribute from Constantinople (80,000 to 120,000 solidi a year).

list.name: Son of Bayan (unnamed)
list.note: Ambush of Heraclius near Heraclea (617).

list.name: Khagan of the siege of 626 (unnamed)
list.note: Besieged Constantinople with Slavs and Persians (Jul-Aug 626); after the failure Avar hegemony over the Slavs and Bulgars collapsed (Samo, Kubrat).

list.name: Agron
list.note: Built the Illyrian navy; died celebrating a victory over the Aetolians.

list.name: Teuta
list.note: Regent for Pinnes; her piracy and the murder of a Roman envoy provoked the First Illyrian War (229); peace of 228.

list.name: Pleuratus
list.note: Roman ally.

list.name: Genthius
list.note: Sided with Perseus; captured by Anicius in 30 days (168); led in triumph.

list.name: Burebista
list.note: United Getae and Dacians; ally of Pompey; murdered c. 44, the same year as Caesar who planned to attack him.

list.name: Duras
list.note: Ceded power to Decebalus.

list.name: Decebalus
list.note: Defeated Cornelius Fuscus (86/87); fought Domitian and Trajan; cut his throat to avoid capture (106), scene shown on Trajan's Column; his head was brought to Rome by Tiberius Claudius Maximus (Philippi tombstone).

list.name: Odaenathus
list.note: Exarch of Palmyra; routed Shapur's army returning from Edessa (260), crushed Quietus, invaded Persia (262-263, 266); styled King of Kings and corrector totius Orientis; murdered at Emesa with his son Herodian.

list.name: Zenobia
list.note: Regent for Vaballathus; took Egypt (270) and Asia Minor; Augusta 272; defeated at Immae and Emesa; captured fleeing to the Euphrates.
list.death: lived at Tibur according to the HA; or died on the way to Rome (Zosimus)

list.name: Abu Bakr
list.note: Ridda wars; first raids on Roman Palestine (battle of Ajnadayn, Jul 634).

list.name: Umar ibn al-Khattab
list.note: Conquest of Syria (Damascus 635, Yarmuk Aug 636), Jerusalem (637/638), Iraq, Egypt (from 639); stabbed by the Persian slave Abu Lu'lu'a.

list.name: Uthman ibn Affan
list.note: Standardized the Quran; killed by rebels in Medina.

list.name: Ali ibn Abi Talib
list.note: Killed at Kufa by a Kharijite.

list.name: Titus Larcius Flavus
list.note: First dictator by Livy's preferred tradition (2.18); others named Manius Valerius. Threat from the Latins and Sabines. Dates of the earliest dictatorships are traditional.

list.name: Aulus Postumius Albus Regillensis
list.note: Victory over the Latins at Lake Regillus, where the Dioscuri reportedly fought for Rome (Livy dates it 499 or 496); vowed the temple of Castor.

list.name: Manius Valerius Volusus Maximus
list.note: Appointed during the debt crisis of the First Secession of the plebs; campaigned against the Sabines and resigned when the Senate rejected debt relief.

list.name: Gaius Aemilius Mamercus
list.note: Doubtful: inferred by Bendel from Lydus' 'dictator in the 48th year of the Republic' and the plague precedent invoked in 363; Broughton thinks Lydus confused an interrex.

list.name: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus
list.note: Called from his four-iugera farm across the Tiber to rescue the consul Minucius trapped by the Aequi on Mount Algidus; triumphed and resigned after 16 days (Livy 3.26-29).

list.name: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus
list.note: Second dictatorship, against the alleged regal ambitions of the grain-dealer Spurius Maelius, whom Ahala killed in the Forum. The story is probably an aetiology of the Aequimaelium.

list.name: Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus
list.note: War with Fidenae and Veii after the murder of Roman envoys by Lars Tolumnius; Aulus Cornelius Cossus won the spolia opima.

list.name: Quintus Servilius Priscus Fidenas
list.note: Capture of Fidenae.

list.name: Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus
list.note: Second dictatorship; reportedly carried a law limiting the censorship to 18 months.

list.name: Aulus Postumius Tubertus
list.note: Victory over Aequi and Volsci at Mount Algidus; said to have executed his son for leaving his post.

list.name: Mamercus Aemilius Mamercinus
list.note: Third dictatorship; final war with Fidenae, which was destroyed.

list.name: Quintus Servilius Priscus Fidenas
list.note: Second dictatorship; war with the Aequi; capture of Labici.

list.name: Publius Cornelius Rutilus Cossus
list.note: War with the Volsci and Aequi at Antium.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Captured Veii after the ten-year siege, reportedly by a tunnel under the temple of Juno; evocatio of Juno Regina to the Aventine.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Second dictatorship (Varronian 390 = c. 387/386): named in exile at Ardea after the Gallic sack; the tale of his rescuing the ransom gold ('non auro sed ferro') is later embroidery (Polybius knows the Gauls left with the gold).

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Third dictatorship; victories over Volsci, Aequi and Etruscans.

list.name: Aulus Cornelius Cossus
list.note: War with the Volsci; imprisonment of Marcus Manlius Capitolinus for agitation over debt.

list.name: Titus Quinctius Cincinnatus Capitolinus
list.note: Victory over the Praenestines at the Allia; captured nine towns.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Fourth dictatorship; used against the Licinio-Sextian agitation; abdicated.

list.name: Publius Manlius Capitolinus
list.causa: seditionis sedandae et rei gerundae causa
list.note: Named a plebeian as magister equitum, a concession to the Licinio-Sextian movement.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
list.note: Fifth dictatorship; defeated the Gauls near Alba; reconciled the orders and vowed the temple of Concord as the Licinio-Sextian laws opened the consulship to plebeians.

list.name: Lucius Manlius Capitolinus Imperiosus
list.note: Appointed to drive the nail in the Capitoline temple to end a plague; tried to wage war instead and was forced to resign.

list.name: Appius Claudius Crassus Regillensis
list.note: Victory over the Hernici. The magister's name is preserved in the Fasti only as SCA[.]VLA.

list.name: Titus Quinctius Pennus Capitolinus Crispinus
list.note: Gallic war: the single combat of Titus Manlius, who took the torque of a giant Gaul and the cognomen Torquatus.

list.name: Quintus Servilius Ahala
list.note: Defeated the Gauls at the Colline Gate.

list.name: Gaius Sulpicius Peticus
list.note: Victory over the Gauls.

list.name: Gaius Marcius Rutilus
list.note: First plebeian dictator; defeated the Etruscans and triumphed by vote of the people over the Senate's objection.

list.name: Titus Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus
list.note: War against Caere, which was granted a 100-year truce.

list.name: Gaius Julius Iulus
list.note: Rumoured Etruscan war; tried to secure two patrician consuls.

list.name: Marcus Fabius Ambustus
list.note: Held elections amid the patrician-plebeian struggle over the consulship.

list.name: Titus Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus
list.note: Second dictatorship.

list.name: Gaius Claudius Crassinus Regillensis (?)
list.note: Names missing from the Fasti and not stated by any ancient author.

list.name: Lucius Furius Camillus
list.note: Second dictatorship; war against the Aurunci; vowed the temple of Juno Moneta on the Arx.

list.name: Publius Valerius Poplicola
list.note: Appointed to institute a festival after prodigies (a rain of stones, darkness by day).

list.name: Marcus Valerius Corvus
list.note: Mutiny of the garrison of Campania; Corvus negotiated, and the leges Genuciae followed.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Crassus
list.note: Latin War; operations against Antium.

list.name: Quintus Publilius Philo
list.note: Carried the leges Publiliae: plebiscites binding on all, patrum auctoritas given in advance for centuriate laws, one censor to be plebeian.

list.name: Gaius Claudius Inregillensis
list.note: Abdicated, appointment found vitiated.

list.name: Publius Cornelius Rufinus
list.note: Abdicated on a religious flaw. The Fasti list 333 as the first of four 'dictator years' (333, 324, 309, 301) with a dictator and no consuls; Livy places these dictators under the preceding consuls. The dictator years are a later chronographic insertion.

list.name: Marcus Papirius Crassus
list.note: Gallic scare.

list.name: Gnaeus Quinctilius Varus
list.note: Nail-driving after the 'poisoning' scandal in which 170 matrons were condemned (Livy 8.18). Name possibly Gnaeus Quinctius Capitolinus.

list.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus
list.note: Abdicated, appointment declared vitiated by the augurs.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor
list.note: Second Samnite War. Papirius tried to execute his magister equitum Fabius for fighting (and winning) against orders; the people and Senate interceded (Livy 8.30-35). 324 is the second dictator year.

list.name: Aulus Cornelius Cossus Arvina
list.causa: rei gerundae or ludorum faciendorum causa
list.note: Sources conflict; most historians think he presided at the Ludi Romani when the praetor fell ill.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Ambustus
list.note: Abdicated on a flaw, in the year of the Caudine Forks.

list.name: Gaius Maenius
list.note: Livy describes an inquiry into conspiracies; causa disputed.

list.name: Titus Manlius Imperiosus Torquatus
list.note: Third dictatorship.

list.name: Lucius Aemilius Mamercinus Privernas
list.note: Second dictatorship; siege of Saticula.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus
list.magisterEquitum: Quintus Aulius Cerretanus; Gaius Fabius Ambustus
list.note: Defeat at Lautulae, where the magister equitum Aulius fell; replaced by Gaius Fabius.

list.name: Gaius Maenius
list.note: Second dictatorship; inquiry into Capuan conspiracy.

list.name: Gaius Poetelius Libo Visolus
list.note: Capture of Nola per Livy and the Fasti; an alternative tradition makes him dictator clavi figendi causa, and Diodorus credits the victories to Quintus Fabius.

list.name: Gaius Sulpicius Longus
list.note: Livy instead names Junius Bubulcus dictator.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor
list.note: Second dictatorship; great victory over the Samnites, whose gilded shields were displayed in the Forum (Livy 9.40). 309 is the third dictator year.

list.name: Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus
list.note: War with the Aequi, subdued in eight days (Livy 10.1).

list.name: Marcus Valerius Corvus
list.magisterEquitum: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus (?) or Marcus Aemilius Paullus (?)
list.note: Second dictatorship; Etruscans and Marsi. 301 is the fourth and last dictator year.

list.name: Quintus Hortensius
list.note: Appointed during the last secession of the plebs (to the Janiculum); carried the lex Hortensia making plebiscites binding on the whole people. Died in office.

list.name: Appius Claudius Caecus (?)
list.note: Possibly dictator suffectus after Hortensius' death (Mommsen); known only from the elogium of Appius, which credits him with a dictatorship.

list.name: Marcus Aemilius Barbula (?)
list.note: Known only from literary sources; Broughton dates him 292-285.

list.name: Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus Maximus
list.note: Also the first plebeian censor to close a lustrum (280).

list.name: Publius Cornelius Rufinus (?)
list.note: Date uncertain (Broughton 292-285; Niebuhr 280, after Heraclea).

list.name: Gnaeus Fulvius Maximus Centumalus
list.note: Nail-driving during the First Punic War.

list.name: Quintus Ogulnius Gallus
list.note: To celebrate the Latin Festival on the Alban Mount in the consuls' absence.

list.name: Marcus Claudius Glicia
list.note: Named in contempt by the consul Publius Claudius Pulcher after his defeat at Drepana; a freedman's son and scribe, he was forced to resign but kept the right to the toga praetexta.

list.name: Aulus Atilius Calatinus
list.note: First dictator to command an army outside Italy (Sicily).

list.name: Tiberius Coruncanius
list.note: First plebeian pontifex maximus.

list.name: Gaius Duilius
list.note: Victor of Mylae (260), the first Roman naval triumph.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus
list.note: Date inferred (Broughton): Livy calls 217 Fabius' second dictatorship, so a first must fall in the gap of 221-219. Plutarch (Marc. 5) tells of a dictator Minucius with Flaminius as magister who abdicated because a shrew squeaked, which may be the same episode.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus
list.note: Elected by the people after Trasimene (Livy calls him prodictator). His delaying strategy earned him the name Cunctator; a plebiscite of the tribune Metilius gave Minucius equal imperium, the only time two dictators served together.

list.name: Lucius Veturius Philo
list.note: Abdicated after 14 days on a flaw.

list.name: Marcus Junius Pera
list.note: After Cannae; enrolled 8,000 slaves (volones), debtors and convicts, and took arms from the temples.

list.name: Marcus Fabius Buteo
list.note: Unique causa: named, without a magister equitum, to fill the Senate's 177 vacancies after Cannae; resigned the same day (Livy 23.22-23). Two dictators held office simultaneously.

list.name: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus
list.note: Nominated by the consul Laevinus amid a quarrel over the right of nomination.

list.name: Titus Manlius Torquatus
list.causa: comitiorum habendorum et ludorum faciendorum causa
list.note: After the death of the consul Marcellus in an ambush near Venusia.

list.name: Marcus Livius Salinator
list.note: Victor of the Metaurus that year.

list.name: Gaius Servilius Geminus
list.note: Last traditional dictatorship; the office then lapsed for 120 years, replaced in emergencies by the senatus consultum ultimum.

list.name: Lucius Cornelius Sulla Felix
list.causa: legibus scribundis et rei publicae constituendae causa
list.note: Appointed under the lex Valeria proposed by the interrex Flaccus, without time limit. Used it for proscriptions and a constitutional overhaul (courts to senators, tribunate gutted, Senate doubled to c. 600, 20 quaestors). Resigned probably early 79 (or 81).

list.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
list.note: First dictatorship, 11 days, named by the praetor Lepidus under a special law to hold the consular elections; also passed debt and amnesty measures.

list.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
list.note: Second dictatorship (Oct 48 to late 47), voted after Pharsalus.

list.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
list.note: Third dictatorship, voted after Thapsus in April 46 for ten years, renewed annually.

list.name: Gaius Julius Caesar
list.magisterEquitum: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus (designated: Gaius Octavius; Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus, non iniit)
list.note: Perpetual dictator from c. Feb 44 (DICT PERPETVO on coins); assassinated 15 Mar 44. The lex Antonia then abolished the dictatorship for ever; Augustus refused it in 22 BC.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Mugillanus and Lucius Sempronius Atratinus
list.note: First censors, created to relieve the consuls (or consular tribunes) of the census (Livy 4.8). Both patrician.

list.name: Gaius Furius Paculus Fusus and Marcus Geganius Macerinus
list.note: Built the Villa Publica on the Campus Martius, where the census was taken.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Crassus (?) and Publius Pinarius Mamercinus (?)
list.note: Uncertain pair.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Mugillanus and unknown
list.note: Mugillanus' second censorship.

list.name: Marcus Furius Camillus and Marcus Postumius Albinus Regillensis
list.note: Imposed a tax on bachelors (aes uxorium) per Valerius Maximus and Plutarch.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor and Gaius Julius Iullus
list.note: Julius died in office and Marcus Cornelius Maluginensis was elected suffect; Rome was taken by the Gauls during that lustrum, after which a censor's death in office required both to resign.

list.name: Marcus Furius Fusus (?) and Lucius Papirius Mugillanus (?)
list.note: Uncertain.

list.name: Spurius Postumius Albinus Regillensis and Gaius Sulpicius Camerinus
list.note: Postumius died; no suffect appointed, the censors resigned and the census lapsed.

list.name: Spurius Servilius Priscus and Quintus Cloelius Siculus
list.note: Census impeded by war and debt agitation.

list.name: Gaius Sulpicius Peticus and Postumius Regillensis Albinus (?)
Marcus Fabius Ambustus and Lucius Furius Medullinus
Gnaeus Manlius Capitolinus Imperiosus and Gaius Marcius Rutilus
list.note: Marcius was the first plebeian censor.

list.name: Lucius Cornelius Scipio and Publius Cornelius Scipio (?)
Spurius Postumius Albinus Caudinus and Quintus Publilius Philo
list.note: Enrolled new citizens in two new tribes (Maecia and Scaptia).

list.name: Lucius Papirius Crassus and Gaius Maenius
list.note: Two new tribes (Oufentina and Falerna).

list.name: Appius Claudius Caecus and Gaius Plautius Venox
list.note: Built the Via Appia and the Aqua Appia; distributed the humiles across all tribes and enrolled freedmen's sons in the Senate; Appius held on beyond 18 months, allegedly for five years.

list.name: Marcus Valerius Maximus Corvinus and Gaius Junius Bubulcus Brutus
list.note: Built roads across the ager Romanus at public expense.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus and Publius Decius Mus
list.note: Confined freedmen and the urban poor to the four urban tribes; instituted the transvectio equitum (15 July parade of the equites).

list.name: Publius Sulpicius Saverrio and Publius Sempronius Sophus
list.note: Two new tribes (Aniensis and Terentina, 299).

list.name: Publius Cornelius Arvina and Gaius Marcius Rutilus Censorinus
list.note: Census of 262,321 citizens (Livy 10.47).

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Gurges (?) and Spurius Carvilius Maximus (?)
list.note: Uncertain.

list.name: Lucius Cornelius Scipio Barbatus and Gnaeus Domitius Calvinus Maximus
list.note: Domitius was the first plebeian censor to perform the lustrum.

list.name: Quintus Aemilius Papus and Gaius Fabricius Luscinus
list.note: Fabricius expelled the ex-consul and ex-dictator Publius Cornelius Rufinus from the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate.

list.name: Lucius Papirius Praetextatus and Manius Curius Dentatus
list.note: Curius began the Anio Vetus aqueduct from the spoils of Pyrrhus.

list.name: Lucius Aemilius Barbula and Quintus Marcius Philippus
Gnaeus Cornelius Blasio and Gaius Marcius Rutilus Censorinus
list.note: The only man censor twice; he then carried a law forbidding iteration, earning the cognomen Censorinus. Census 292,234.

list.name: Lucius Cornelius Scipio and Gaius Duilius
Lucius Postumius Megellus and Decimus Junius Pera
list.note: Postumius died in office; the censors resigned.

list.name: Manius Valerius Maximus Corvinus Messalla and Publius Sempronius Sophus
list.note: Demoted 400 equites who had disobeyed orders in Sicily to aerarii.

list.name: Aulus Manlius Torquatus Atticus and Aulus Atilius Calatinus
list.note: Census 241,712, showing First Punic War losses.

list.name: Marcus Fabius Buteo and Gaius Aurelius Cotta
list.note: Two last tribes (Velina and Quirina), bringing the total to 35.

list.name: Lucius Cornelius Lentulus Caudinus and Quintus Lutatius Cerco
list.note: Lutatius died in office.

list.name: Aulus Postumius Albinus and Gaius Atilius Bulbus
list.note: Census 270,713.

list.name: Titus Manlius Torquatus and Quintus Fulvius Flaccus
list.note: Resigned on a flaw in their election.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus and Marcus Sempronius Tuditanus
Gaius Claudius Centho and Marcus Junius Pera
list.note: Did not complete the lustrum.

list.name: Lucius Aemilius Papus and Gaius Flaminius
list.note: Flaminius built the Via Flaminia and the Circus Flaminius; freedmen restricted to four urban tribes.

list.name: Publius Furius Philus and Marcus Atilius Regulus
list.note: Punished Cannae survivors who planned to leave Italy and men who broke their oath to Hannibal; Furius died before the lustrum.

list.name: Lucius Veturius Philo and Publius Licinius Crassus Dives
list.note: Veturius died; Licinius resigned.

list.name: Marcus Cornelius Cethegus and Publius Sempronius Tuditanus
list.note: Census 137,108, the low point after Cannae (Livy 27.36).

list.name: Gaius Claudius Nero and Marcus Livius Salinator
list.note: The victors of the Metaurus degraded each other (each deprived the other of his public horse); introduced the salt tax.

list.name: Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus and Publius Aelius Paetus
list.note: Scipio named princeps senatus.

list.name: Gaius Cornelius Cethegus and Sextus Aelius Paetus Catus
list.note: Separate seats for senators at the Ludi Romani.

list.name: Titus Quinctius Flamininus and Marcus Claudius Marcellus
list.note: Census 258,318 after the enfranchisement of the Campanians as census-registered.

list.name: Lucius Valerius Flaccus and Marcus Porcius Cato
list.note: Cato's famously severe censorship: expelled Lucius Flamininus from the Senate, taxed luxury at ten times assessed value, built the Basilica Porcia, cut off private diversions of public water.

list.name: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Marcus Fulvius Nobilior
list.note: Reconciled at the Senate's urging; Basilica Aemilia (Fulvia) and the first stone piers of the Pons Aemilius; changed voting in the tribes by property and occupation.

list.name: Aulus Postumius Albinus Luscus and Quintus Fulvius Flaccus
list.note: Fulvius stripped the marble roof tiles of the temple of Juno Lacinia at Croton for his temple of Fortuna Equestris and was forced to return them; paved streets in Rome.

list.name: Gaius Claudius Pulcher and Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus
list.note: Clashed with the publicani and survived prosecution by a tribune; freedmen confined to one urban tribe (Esquilina); Basilica Sempronia.

list.name: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus and Quintus Marcius Philippus
list.note: Philippus set up a sundial; census 337,022 (Per. 46).

list.name: Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum and Marcus Popillius Laenas
list.note: Removed unauthorised statues from the Forum; Nasica set up the first water-clock in Rome.

list.name: Marcus Valerius Messalla and Gaius Cassius Longinus
list.note: Their stone theatre was demolished on Nasica's motion (151) as harmful to morals.

list.name: Lucius Cornelius Lentulus Lupus and Lucius Marcius Censorinus
Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus and Lucius Mummius Achaicus
list.note: Aemilianus reportedly changed the lustral prayer from asking the gods to increase Rome's possessions to preserving them (Val. Max. 4.1.10); Mummius was the lenient colleague.

list.name: Appius Claudius Pulcher and Quintus Fulvius Nobilior
list.note: Claudius, father-in-law of Tiberius Gracchus, was princeps senatus.

list.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus and Quintus Pompeius
list.note: First pair both plebeian. Metellus' speech urging marriage (de prole augenda) was later read out by Augustus.

list.name: Gnaeus Servilius Caepio and Lucius Cassius Longinus Ravilla
list.note: Censured Marcus Aemilius Lepidus Porcina for renting a house at 6,000 sesterces; census 394,736.

list.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Balearicus and Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi
Lucius Caecilius Metellus Diadematus and Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus
list.note: Expelled 32 senators.

list.name: Marcus Aemilius Scaurus and Marcus Livius Drusus
list.note: Drusus died in office; Scaurus refused to resign until forced; built the Via Aemilia Scauri and the Pons Mulvius in stone.

list.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Eburnus and Gaius Licinius Geta
Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus and Gaius Caecilius Metellus Caprarius
list.note: Metellus Numidicus tried to expel Saturninus and Glaucia from the Senate and refused to enrol the pretended son of Tiberius Gracchus.

list.name: Lucius Valerius Flaccus and Marcus Antonius
list.note: Antonius the orator; expelled the tribune Duronius from the Senate.

list.name: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Lucius Licinius Crassus
list.note: Edict against the Latin rhetoricians (Gellius 15.11); quarrelled bitterly (Crassus' lampreys); no lustrum.

list.name: Lucius Julius Caesar and Publius Licinius Crassus
list.note: Charged with enrolling the new citizens of the Social War in a limited number of tribes; no lustrum.

list.name: Lucius Marcius Philippus and Marcus Perperna
list.note: Under the Cinnan regime; census 463,000. No further censors until 70.

list.name: Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus Clodianus and Lucius Gellius Publicola
list.note: Restored the censorship after Sulla; expelled 64 senators; census 910,000 reflecting the post-Social War enfranchisement of Italy.

list.name: Marcus Licinius Crassus and Quintus Lutatius Catulus
list.note: Deadlocked over Crassus' plan to enrol the Transpadani and annex Egypt; both resigned.

list.name: unknown and Lucius Aurelius Cotta
list.note: Obstructed by tribunes; resigned.

list.name: Lucius Julius Caesar (?) and Gaius Scribonius Curio (?)
list.note: Names uncertain.

list.name: Marcus Valerius Messalla Niger and Publius Servilius Vatia Isauricus
list.note: No lustrum.

list.name: Appius Claudius Pulcher and Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus
list.note: Appius purged the Senate (expelling Sallust); the last Republican censorship before the civil war.

list.name: Publius Sulpicius Rufus and Gaius Antonius Hybrida
list.note: Appointed under the triumvirs; no lustrum.

list.name: Imperator Caesar (Octavian) and Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa
list.note: Not censors but consuls with censoria potestas; first lustrum in 41 years; revised the Senate from c. 1,000 to 800; census 4,063,000 (RG 8).

list.name: Paullus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Munatius Plancus
list.note: The last private pair of censors; quarrelled, achieved nothing (Velleius 2.95).

list.name: Augustus (consulari imperio, alone)
list.note: Second census of Augustus; 4,233,000 citizens.

list.name: Augustus and Tiberius
list.note: Census completed by consular imperium shortly before Augustus' death; 4,937,000 citizens.

list.name: Claudius and Lucius Vitellius
list.note: Emperor took the title censor; census of 5,984,072 citizens (Tac. Ann. 11.25); admitted Gallic notables (Aedui) to the Senate (Lyon tablet).

list.name: Vespasian and Titus
list.note: Last formal census of Roman citizens; adlected new senatorial and patrician families.

list.name: Domitian
list.note: Took the title censor perpetuus, which no later emperor used; censorial functions absorbed into imperial power.

fasti.note: First year of the Republic (Varronian). Brutus killed in battle with Arruns Tarquinius; Collatinus forced to resign as a Tarquin. Lucretius died in office. Horatius Pulvillus dedicated the Capitoline temple (13 Sept). Polybius 3.22 dates the first treaty with Carthage to the consulship of Brutus and Horatius. The college of five is widely regarded as a later elaboration.
War with Porsenna of Clusium (Horatius Cocles, Mucius Scaevola, Cloelia in the annalistic tradition).
Some ancient authorities place the Capitoline dedication in this year.
Aristodemus of Cumae and the Latins defeat Arruns Porsenna at Aricia (Greek-based date c. 504).
Migration of Attus Clausus (Appius Claudius) and his Sabine following to Rome.
Livy reports the first dictatorship (Titus Larcius) in this year or 498; the sources disagree.
Praenomen of Veturius given as Publius in some sources. Livy dates Lake Regillus here, Dionysius in 496.
Temple of Saturn dedicated (Livy 2.21).
Battle of Lake Regillus against the Latins, conventionally dated here; Postumius as dictator vowed the temple of Castor.
Death of Tarquinius Superbus at Cumae. Temple of Mercury dedicated. Debt crisis.
First secession of the plebs (to the Mons Sacer or Aventine); tribunes of the plebs created (traditionally 494/493). Manius Valerius dictator.
Foedus Cassianum with the Latins. Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera vowed (dedicated this year per Dionysius). Capture of Corioli attributed to Gnaeus Marcius (Coriolanus).
Famine; grain bought in Etruria and Sicily.
Trial and exile of Coriolanus in the annalistic tradition.
Coriolanus and the Volsci before Rome (488 in Livy). Furius' cognomen uncertain (Medullinus Fusus?).
Cognomina (Sabinus, Tuscus) are late and doubtful.
Treaty with the Hernici. Cassius proposes an agrarian law; executed 485 for aiming at kingship (adfectatio regni).
First of seven successive years with a Fabius as consul (485-479).
Temple of Castor dedicated (15 July).
Vestal Oppia buried alive.
Battle against Veii; Manlius and Quintus Fabius (cos. 485) killed.
The Fabii take up the war with Veii privately and fortify a post on the Cremera.
Servilius died in office.
Destruction of the 306 Fabii on the Cremera (Ovid, Fasti 2.193-196, gives 13 February; Livy and others assimilate it to the dies Alliensis, 18 July). Menenius later prosecuted.
Veientines occupy the Janiculum.
Forty-year truce with Veii. Hiero of Syracuse defeats the Etruscans off Cumae (synchronism).
Murder of the tribune Gnaeus Genucius.
Lex Publilia Voleronis: tribunes elected by an assembly voting by tribes (concilium plebis tributum).
Antium taken from the Volsci; colony at Antium 467.
Pestilence; both consuls die (Livy 3.6-7).
Tribune Gaius Terentilius Harsa proposes a commission to codify the law.
Trial of Caeso Quinctius, son of Cincinnatus.
Appius Herdonius seizes the Capitol with exiles and slaves; Valerius killed retaking it, replaced by Cincinnatus.
Minucius trapped by the Aequi on Mount Algidus; Cincinnatus named dictator from his plough, relieves him and resigns after sixteen days (Livy 3.26-29).
Tribunes of the plebs raised to ten.
Lex Icilia de Aventino publicando: the Aventine assigned to the plebs.
Lex Aternia Tarpeia on fines (in cattle and sheep). Embassy to Athens to study Solon's laws (traditional).
Quinctilius died of plague.
Embassy returns from Greece.
The consuls elect abdicated in favour of the first decemvirate (decemviri legibus scribundis), listed under 'tribunes'. Ten tables of law published.
Second decemvirate (half plebeian in Livy's list). Two further tables, including the ban on patrician-plebeian intermarriage. The 'tyranny' of Appius and the Verginia story belong to 450-449.

Fall of the decemvirs after the death of Verginia; second secession of the plebs. Leges Valeriae Horatiae: plebiscites binding (doubted as anachronistic), right of provocatio, sacrosanctity of tribunes reaffirmed. The decemvirs held office into this year.
Quaestors first elected by the people (Tacitus, Ann. 11.22).
Dispute of Ardea and Aricia over Corioli land awarded by the Roman people to itself.
Lex Canuleia permits intermarriage (conubium) between patricians and plebeians. Consular tribunate created as a compromise (Livy 4.1-6).

First consular tribunes; they abdicated after three months as vitio creati and were replaced by suffect consuls. The suffects are known from Licinius Macer's linen books (libri lintei) and are absent from some lists.
Censorship created; first censors Lucius Papirius Mugillanus and Lucius Sempronius Atratinus.
Colony at Ardea.
Famine; Lucius Minucius appointed praefectus annonae.
Spurius Maelius, a rich plebeian distributing grain, killed by Gaius Servilius Ahala, master of horse to the dictator Cincinnatus.

Consular tribunes (tribuni militum consulari potestate) in place of consuls. Names follow Livy and Broughton, MRR I; Livy, Diodorus and the Fasti Capitolini differ in number, order and identity for many of these colleges. Fidenae defects to Lars Tolumnius of Veii; Roman envoys murdered.
Aulus Cornelius Cossus kills Lars Tolumnius and wins the spolia opima; Livy (4.20) notes Augustus' claim that Cossus' linen corslet named him consul, i.e. 428.
Pestilence. Villa Publica built in the Campus Martius by the censors.

'Anarchy' (solitudo magistratuum): Livy (6.35) says Licinius and Sextius vetoed all curule elections for five years (375-371). Diodorus has only one year without magistrates. The five-year figure is probably an artefact of the Varronian chronology, which had to fill a gap relative to Greek synchronisms.

Consular tribunes (tribuni militum consulari potestate) in place of consuls. Names follow Livy and Broughton, MRR I; Livy, Diodorus and the Fasti Capitolini differ in number, order and identity for many of these colleges. Last consular tribunes. Leges Liciniae Sextiae: one consul may (or must) be plebeian; limit of 500 iugera on ager publicus (the figure possibly retrojected from the second century); debt relief. Camillus dictator (V) vows the temple of Concord.
Sextius the first plebeian consul. Praetorship created (first praetor Spurius Furius Camillus) and curule aedileship; ludi Romani extended by a day.
Pestilence; death of Camillus.
Ludi scaenici introduced with Etruscan performers to appease the gods during the plague (Livy 7.2). Some sources make the plebeian consul Gaius Licinius Stolo himself.
Lucius Manlius Capitolinus Imperiosus dictator clavi figendi causa; Marcus Curtius' leap into the chasm in the Forum (one version).
Genucius, the first plebeian consul to command an army under his own auspices, killed fighting the Hernici. Six military tribunes now elected by the people.
Titus Manlius wins the cognomen Torquatus by killing a Gallic champion at the Anio (Claudius Quadrigarius in Gellius 9.13; Livy dates the fight here).
Gauls near Rome; Gaius Poetelius triumphs over Gauls and Tiburtines.
Tribes Pomptina and Publilia created (27 tribes). Lex Poetelia de ambitu. Treaty with the Latins renewed.
Lex Manlia imposes a 5% tax on manumissions, passed by the army in camp at Sutrium. Lex Duilia Menenia caps interest at one-twelfth (unciarium faenus).
Gaius Marcius Rutilus the first plebeian dictator.
Two patrician consuls, in breach of the Licinian law; repeated in several years 355-343.
Treaty with the Samnites (Livy 7.19; Diodorus 16.45).
Caere granted a hundred-year truce.
Quinqueviri mensarii appointed to liquidate debts.
Gaius Marcius Rutilus the first plebeian censor.
Popillius defeats a Gallic army in Latium.
Claudius died before taking the field; Camillus sole consul. Marcus Valerius wins the cognomen Corvus in single combat with a Gaul aided by a raven.
Treaty with Carthage (Livy 7.27, Diodorus 16.69); probably the 'second treaty' of Polybius 3.24.
Interest reduced to one twenty-fourth (semunciarium) and debts rescheduled. Plautius' cognomen given as Hypsaeus or Venox.
Satricum destroyed.
Sora taken from the Volsci. Temple of Juno Moneta vowed (dedicated 344).
Temple of Juno Moneta dedicated on the Arx.
First Samnite War (343-341) after Capua's deditio. Battles of Mount Gaurus, Saticula and Suessula. Historicity of the war is debated; Carthage sends a gold crown.
Mutiny of the garrison in Campania. Leges Genuciae: ban on lending at interest; no one to hold the same magistracy within ten years; both consuls may be plebeian.
Peace with the Samnites; revolt of the Latins begins.
Latin War. Battle near Vesuvius (Veseris): Decius' devotio; Torquatus executes his son for fighting a duel against orders. Trifanum.
Leges Publiliae (Philo as dictator): plebiscites binding on all; patrum auctoritas given in advance for centuriate laws; one censor must be plebeian.

Latin settlement: League dissolved; some cities incorporated as municipia (Lanuvium, Aricia, Nomentum, Pedum), others with civitas sine suffragio (Capua, Fundi, Formiae, Cumae). Beaks of Antiate ships fixed to the speakers' platform (Rostra); column of Maenius.
Quintus Publilius Philo the first plebeian praetor.
Cales captured.
Latin colony of 2,500 at Cales. Postumius later called Caudinus. Alexander of Epirus campaigning in southern Italy; supposed treaty with Rome.

Dictator year: no consuls. The Fasti Capitolini insert a year in which a dictator (Publius Cornelius Rufinus, with master of horse Marcus Antonius) held office without consuls. Livy and the other literary sources ignore these four years (333, 324, 309, 301); they are a late-Republican chronographic device (associated with Atticus and Varro) to reconcile Roman and Greek chronology.
Tribes Maecia and Scaptia created (29). Treaty with Alexander of Epirus (Livy 8.17).
Poisoning scandal: 170 matronae condemned (Livy 8.18); dictator clavi figendi causa. Valerius' cognomen given as Flaccus or Potitus.
War with Privernum and Fundi.
Privernum taken. Colony at Tarracina (Anxur), citizen colony of 300.
Latin colony at Fregellae on the Liris, provoking the Samnites. Some lists have Gaius Plautius Decianus II.
War with Neapolis (Palaeopolis).
Philo's command prorogued: the first promagistracy. Neapolis becomes an ally (foedus aequum). Second Samnite War begins. Lex Poetelia Papiria abolishes nexum (debt bondage); Varro dates it to 313.
Vestini join the Samnites. Papirius Cursor dictator clashes with his master of horse Quintus Fabius Rullianus, who fought against orders.
Dictator year: Lucius Papirius Cursor continues as dictator without consuls (Fasti Capitolini only; ignored by Livy). See 333 BC.
Apulians allied.
Fulvius, from Tusculum, consul in the same year he was a magistrate there (Pliny NH 7.136).
Caudine Forks: both consuls' armies trapped by Gavius Pontius and sent under the yoke; the sponsio disowned by the Senate. Fregellae lost.
Livy's story of revenge at Luceria and Caudium in 320-319 is regarded as invented; the Romans more probably observed the Caudine peace until 316.
Some lists have Lucius Papirius Mugillanus instead of Cursor.
Tribes Oufentina and Falerna created (31). Praefecti sent to Capua. Two-year truce with the Samnites.
Apulia brought over; Teanum Apulum and Canusium.
War with the Samnites renewed; Lucius Aemilius dictator at Saticula.
Roman defeat at Lautulae (Fabius Rullianus dictator); Capua wavers. Saticula and Luceria taken.
Samnites defeated near Tarracina; Latin colony at Luceria (2,500). Campanian conspiracy suppressed.
Colonies at Suessa Aurunca, Pontiae, Saticula; Nola, Atina, Calatia captured.

Censorship of Appius Claudius Caecus (with Gaius Plautius): Via Appia to Capua and the Aqua Appia, Rome's first aqueduct; humiliores distributed through all tribes; freedmen's sons admitted to the Senate. Livy gives Valerius as Maximus.
Duoviri navales first elected; sixteen of the military tribunes elected by the people. Etruscan cities attack Sutrium. Temple of Salus vowed.
Fabius crosses the Ciminian Forest into Etruria and defeats the Etruscans near Perusia. Marcius (later Censorinus) wounded in Samnium.
Dictator year: Lucius Papirius Cursor dictator, said to have defeated the Samnites at Longula, without consuls (Fasti Capitolini only). See 333 BC.
Peace or truce with Tarquinii (40 years); Nuceria Alfaterna defects.
Agathocles-period treaty contacts. Volumnius campaigns among the Sallentini.

Revolt and defeat of the Hernici; Anagnia given civitas sine suffragio. Treaty renewed with Carthage (Livy 9.43), perhaps the 'Philinus treaty' denied by Polybius. Equestrian statue of Marcius in the Forum.
Bovianum captured; Minucius killed (or mortally wounded) and replaced by Fulvius.

Peace with the Samnites ends the Second Samnite War. Aequi crushed. Gnaeus Flavius, curule aedile and son of a freedman, publishes the legis actiones and the calendar; dedicates a shrine of Concord. Censors Quintus Fabius and Publius Decius confine the humiles to the four urban tribes; transvectio equitum instituted (15 July).
Latin colonies at Alba Fucens (6,000) and Sora (4,000). Arpinum and Trebula given civitas sine suffragio.

Cleonymus of Sparta raids the Italian coast; temple of Salus dedicated by Gaius Junius Bubulcus, with paintings by Fabius Pictor (the first Roman painter of note). Treaty with Tarentum barring Roman ships beyond the Lacinian promontory may belong here.

Dictator year: Marcus Valerius Corvus dictator without consuls (Fasti Capitolini only). Livy (10.3-5) has a dictatorship this year for war in Etruria (Arretium) and against the Marsi but treats it within a consular year. See 333 BC.
Lex Ogulnia opens the pontificate and augurate to plebeians (pontiffs raised to 8, augurs to 9). Lex Valeria de provocatione (the third such law in the tradition).
Manlius killed by a fall from his horse; Corvus suffect for his sixth consulship. Colony at Narnia; tribes Aniensis and Teretina created (33).
Third Samnite War begins. Barbatus' sarcophagus elogium (CIL I2 7) claims he took Taurasia and Cisauna in Samnium and subdued Lucania; Livy assigns him Etruria.
Victories near Tifernum and Maleventum.
Coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Gauls forms under Gellius Egnatius. Citizen colonies at Minturnae and Sinuessa.
Battle of Sentinum: Decius' devotio; Gellius Egnatius killed. Duris of Samos claimed 100,000 enemy dead (Diodorus 21.6). Temple of Jupiter Victor vowed by Fabius.
Temple of Victoria dedicated on the Palatine by Postumius. Peace with Volsinii, Perusia and Arretium for 40 years.

Battle of Aquilonia: linen legion of the Samnites destroyed; Papirius' triumph and the first sundial (from spoils) in Rome per Pliny's source. Plague leads to embassy to Epidaurus for Asclepius (arrives 292, temple on the Tiber island 291).
Gurges defeated, then victorious with his father as legate; Gavius Pontius captured and executed after the triumph (the tradition is suspect).
Latin colony at Venusia, reportedly 20,000 settlers (Dionysius 17/18.5). Postumius fined for using soldiers on his estate.
End of the Third Samnite War; Curius conquers the Sabines and Praetuttii, who receive civitas sine suffragio. Curius drains Lake Velinus (Cascata delle Marmore).
Colonies at Castrum Novum, Hadria and Sena Gallica in this period. Tresviri monetales possibly created c. 289 (Pomponius, Dig. 1.2.2.30), though the first Roman coinage is later.

Last secession of the plebs (to the Janiculum) over debt; Quintus Hortensius dictator passes the lex Hortensia making plebiscites binding on the whole people. Livy's books 11-20 are lost; the decade after 292 is known only from epitomes and fragments.
Lex Aquilia on damage to property is traditionally dated to a plebiscite around this time.
First Aemilius Lepidus in the fasti.
Senones besiege Arretium; Metellus (praetor or consul, now in 283) killed with seven military tribunes and 13,000 men (Polybius 2.19). Chronology of 284-283 disputed.
Senones expelled from the ager Gallicus; colony at Sena Gallica. Dolabella defeats Etruscans and Boii at Lake Vadimon.

Roman garrison installed at Thurii; Tarentum sinks a Roman squadron of ten ships in its harbour and expels the garrison. Further victory over Etruscans and Boii. Garrison of Campanian troops at Rhegium seizes the city (282 or 280).
War declared on Tarentum after the insult to the envoy Lucius Postumius; Tarentum invites Pyrrhus of Epirus.
Pyrrhus lands in Italy. Battle of Heraclea: Pyrrhus wins with elephants. He advances to within c. 60 km of Rome. Coruncanius later the first plebeian pontifex maximus (c. 254).
Battle of Asculum, Pyrrhus' costly victory (the 'Pyrrhic victory' quip in Plutarch, Pyrrhus 21). The Decius of this year is said to have made a third family devotio (doubted).
Treaty with Carthage against Pyrrhus (Polybius 3.25). Pyrrhus crosses to Sicily. Fabricius returns the traitorous physician who offered to poison Pyrrhus.
Croton recovered by Rufinus' stratagem.
Pestilence. Pyrrhus returns to Italy, losing ships to the Carthaginians in the Straits.
Battle of Beneventum (then Maleventum) against Pyrrhus, a Roman victory or draw; Pyrrhus leaves Italy. Curius' triumph displays the first elephants seen in Rome.
Curius and Merenda against the Lucanians and Samnites.
Embassy exchanged with Ptolemy II Philadelphus. Latin colonies at Cosa and Paestum.
Surrender of Tarentum, garrisoned by Pyrrhus' general Milo. Death of Pyrrhus at Argos. Censor Manius Curius begins the Anio Vetus aqueduct from the spoils.
War with the Brutti and Lucani concluded.
Rhegium retaken from the Campanian legion; survivors (300 in Polybius 1.7) scourged and beheaded in the Forum.
First Roman silver coinage traditionally dated to this year (Pliny NH 33.44); modern numismatics puts the Romano-Campanian didrachms earlier (c. 300-280) and the denarius c. 211.
Picentes conquered; Latin colonies at Ariminum and Beneventum. Sabines receive full citizenship (268 or 241). Temple of Tellus vowed during an earthquake.
Sallentini subdued; Brundisium taken. Quaestors increased to eight (Livy Per. 15), the new posts probably the Italian quaestores classici.
Triumphs over the Sarsinates and Sallentini; Apollonia's envoys insulted and the offenders surrendered.
Siege of Volsinii, where freedmen had seized power; Fabius killed. The city destroyed in 264 and 2,000 statues carried off; Volsinii Novi founded.

First Punic War begins: Rome accepts the alliance of the Mamertines of Messana; Claudius crosses to Sicily. Fulvius takes Volsinii. First gladiatorial show at Rome (Forum Boarium), given by Decimus and Marcus Junius Brutus at their father's funeral.

Hiero II of Syracuse makes peace and alliance (100 talents). Valerius takes the cognomen Messalla from the relief of Messana; brings a sundial from Catana, set up in the Forum though calibrated for a latitude 4 degrees south (Pliny NH 7.214).
Siege of Agrigentum (Akragas); city taken after seven months and 25,000 inhabitants sold.
Decision to build a fleet; 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes, modelled on a captured Carthaginian ship (Polybius 1.20).
Scipio captured at Lipara (hence 'Asina'). Duilius wins the first Roman naval victory at Mylae using the corvus; columna rostrata in the Forum (inscription a later restoration, CIL I2 25).
Scipio takes Aleria in Corsica; his elogium (CIL I2 9) records Corsica and a temple to the Tempestates.
Naval victory off Sulci (Sardinia); Hanno crucified by his own men. Camarina and Mytistratus taken.
Naval engagement off Tyndaris.
Caedicius died in office. Battle of Ecnomus, one of the largest naval battles in antiquity (Polybius: 330 Roman and 350 Carthaginian ships). Invasion of Africa; Regulus winters at Clupea/Aspis area.
Regulus defeated and captured by Xanthippus near Tunis (Bagradas valley). Roman fleet victorious off Cape Hermaeum, then wrecked off Camarina: 284 of 364 ships lost (Polybius 1.37).
Panormus taken; a new fleet of 220 ships built in three months.
Raid on the African coast; 150 ships lost in a storm off Cape Palinurus on the return.
Thermae Himeraeae and Lipara taken.
Metellus defeats Hasdrubal at Panormus (251 or 250) and captures his elephants (over 100), exhibited in the Circus.
Siege of Lilybaeum begins. The story of Regulus' embassy and return to torture in Carthage is first attested much later and is probably apocryphal.

Claudius defeated at Drepana after throwing the sacred chickens overboard; Pullus' fleet destroyed by storm off Camarina. Claudius named a freedman, Marcus Claudius Glicia, dictator and was forced to cancel it; Aulus Atilius Caiatinus the first dictator to lead an army outside Italy. Ludi Tarentini (later Saeculares) first held.
Treaty with Hiero renewed in perpetuity.
Hamilcar Barca takes command in Sicily and occupies Heircte near Panormus. Birth of Hannibal (247 or 246).
Latin colonies of this decade include Aesernia (263), Firmum (264), Alsium (247), Fregenae (245).
Colony at Fregenae. Livy's lost books make the 240s thin in detail.
Latin colony at Brundisium. Hamilcar moves to Mount Eryx.
Fleet of 200 quinqueremes funded by private loans from wealthy citizens, to be repaid after victory (Polybius 1.59).
Praetor peregrinus created (242 traditional date). Postumius, as flamen Martialis, forbidden by the pontifex maximus to leave Rome.

Battle of the Aegates Islands (10 March) won by Catulus as proconsul. Treaty of Lutatius: Carthage evacuates Sicily, pays 3,200 talents over ten years. Revolt of Falerii crushed in six days. Last two tribes, Velina and Quirina, created: 35 tribes in all. Reform of the comitia centuriata, linking centuries to tribes, often placed in this period.
Livius Andronicus stages the first Latin drama translated from Greek at the ludi Romani (Cicero, Brutus 72). Mercenary War in Africa (241-237).
Ennius born at Rudiae (239).
Rome seizes Sardinia from Carthage, which had invited intervention via mutinous mercenaries, and exacts 1,200 more talents. Floralia instituted (made annual 173).
Hamilcar Barca crosses to Spain with Hannibal (aged 9) after the oath at the altar.
Campaigns in Liguria and Corsica; Gaius Licinius' legate Claudius Clineas makes an unauthorised treaty with the Corsicans.
Temple of Janus closed for the first time since Numa (Livy 1.19.3), signifying peace.
Carvilius said to have divorced his wife for barrenness, the first Roman divorce (Gellius 4.3; the date is given as 231 or 230 by others).
Fabius triumphs over the Ligurians; dedicates a temple to Honos.
Tribune Gaius Flaminius carries the distribution of the ager Gallicus et Picenus to citizens viritim against Senate opposition (Polybius 2.21).
Papirius refused a triumph over Corsica; celebrates one on the Alban Mount, setting a precedent.
Illyrian queen Teuta's subjects murder a Roman envoy (one of the Coruncanii).
First Illyrian War: Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus enter Roman fides. Hamilcar drowns in Spain; Hasdrubal the Fair succeeds.

Peace with Teuta; Roman envoys to the Aetolian and Achaean Leagues and Corinth (admitted to the Isthmian Games). Human sacrifice of a Gallic and a Greek couple in the Forum Boarium (dated 228 or 216).
Praetors raised to four, the two new ones to govern Sicily and Sardinia-Corsica: the first provinces in the territorial sense.
Ebro treaty with Hasdrubal (226 or 225).

Great Gallic invasion (Boii, Insubres, Gaesatae): Battle of Telamon, Regulus killed; 40,000 Gauls reportedly slain. Polybius' (2.24) Roman manpower list, from Fabius Pictor, counts some 700,000 foot and 70,000 horse among Romans and allies.
Boii submit.
First Roman crossing of the Po; Flaminius defeats the Insubres and triumphs by popular vote against the Senate's wishes.
Marcellus kills the Gallic king Viridomarus at Clastidium and wins the spolia opima (the third and last time); Mediolanum taken.
Istrian campaign. Hasdrubal the Fair assassinated; Hannibal acclaimed commander in Spain. Circus Flaminius built by the censor Flaminius (220).
Marcus Valerius Laevinus and Quintus Mucius Scaevola, elected first, abdicated as vitio creati (Fasti Capitolini). Censorship of Flaminius: Via Flaminia to Ariminum.
Second Illyrian War against Demetrius of Pharos. Hannibal besieges and takes Saguntum (eight months).

Second Punic War. Hannibal crosses the Alps. Scipio wounded at the Ticinus; Sempronius defeated at the Trebia (December). Gnaeus Scipio lands at Emporion. Lex Claudia bars senators from owning sea-going ships over 300 amphorae. Latin colonies at Placentia and Cremona.

Flaminius killed at Lake Trasimene (21 June, per Ovid); Quintus Fabius Maximus elected prodictator, Marcus Minucius Rufus raised to co-dictator. Naval victory at the Ebro mouth. Lectisternium of twelve gods; ver sacrum vowed.
Battle of Cannae (2 August, Roman calendar); Paullus killed. Capua and much of the south defect. Two Gauls and two Greeks buried alive in the Forum Boarium. 8,000 slaves enlisted (volones).

Lucius Postumius Albinus, consul-elect in absentia (III), was ambushed and killed in the Silva Litana by the Boii before taking office; his skull was made into a cup. Marcellus elected in his place but abdicated after thunder (as two plebeians would have held office); Fabius replaced him. Lex Oppia limits women's display. Philip V's treaty with Hannibal.
First Macedonian War begins. Marcellus begins the siege of Syracuse; Archimedes' machines.
The Fabius of this year is the son of Verrucosus. Hannibal takes Tarentum (213/212) except the citadel.
Siege of Capua begins. Syracuse falls to Marcellus; Archimedes killed. Gracchus killed in Lucania. Publius and Gnaeus Scipio defeated and killed in Spain (211 or 212). Ludi Apollinares instituted.

Hannibal's march on Rome (Hannibal ad portas) fails to relieve Capua, which falls; its senators executed and its territory confiscated as ager Campanus. Treaty with the Aetolian League (Livy 26.24; inscription from Thyrrheion). The denarius system introduced around now (dated by the Morgantina excavations, 214-211).
Publius Cornelius Scipio (the future Africanus), a privatus aged about 25, given proconsular imperium in Spain. Agrigentum retaken; Sicily pacified.
Fabius retakes Tarentum by treachery. Scipio captures New Carthage. Twelve of the thirty Latin colonies refuse further contributions (Livy 27.9).
Both consuls ambushed near Venusia; Marcellus killed, Crispinus mortally wounded. Battle of Baecula; Hasdrubal Barca slips away towards Italy.

Battle of the Metaurus: Hasdrubal Barca defeated and killed after Nero's forced march from Apulia; his head thrown into Hannibal's camp. Hymn by Livius Andronicus to Juno; guild of writers and actors recognised.
Battle of Ilipa ends Carthaginian power in Spain. Mutiny at Sucro. Italica founded for wounded veterans. Peace of Phoenice negotiated 205.

Peace of Phoenice ends the First Macedonian War. Scipio prepares the invasion of Africa from Sicily; the Locri scandal (Pleminius). Sibylline oracle prompts the summoning of the Magna Mater from Pessinus (arrives April 204).

Scipio lands near Utica. Lex Cincia de donis et muneribus restricts gifts to advocates. Black stone of Cybele received by Publius Scipio Nasica, judged the best man in Rome. Censors Marcus Livius Salinator and Gaius Claudius Nero impose a salt tax.
Scipio burns the Numidian and Carthaginian camps and wins at the Great Plains; Syphax captured; Masinissa installed. Hannibal and Mago recalled; Mago dies at sea.
Battle of Zama (Naraggara), probably October: Hannibal defeated by Scipio and Masinissa.
Peace with Carthage: 10,000 talents over 50 years, fleet limited to ten triremes, no war without Roman permission. Scipio triumphs and takes the name Africanus.
Second Macedonian War: the comitia first reject, then approve the war. Battle of Cremona against the Gauls (Hamilcar). Lucius Furius Purpureo praetor.
Flamininus consul at about 30 without having held the praetorship; defeats Philip at the Aous gorge. Aelius Paetus' Tripertita, the first legal commentary.
Battle of Cynoscephalae: Flamininus defeats Philip V. Praetors raised to six; two Spanish provinces, Hispania Citerior and Ulterior, created. Revolt in Spain.
Flamininus proclaims the freedom of the Greeks at the Isthmian Games. Tresviri epulones created. Hannibal suffete at Carthage; reforms the finances.
Repeal of the lex Oppia despite Cato. Cato in Hispania Citerior: campaign around Emporion and the silver mines. War with Nabis of Sparta. Hannibal flees to Antiochus III.
Flamininus evacuates Greece. Citizen colonies at Puteoli, Volturnum, Liternum, Salernum, Buxentum, Sipontum, Croton, Tempsa. Senators given separate seats at the games.
Emporia built: Porticus Aemilia and the Emporium below the Aventine (193). Latin allies made subject to Roman debt law (lex Sempronia).
Antiochus III lands at Demetrias at the Aetolians' invitation. Nabis murdered.
Antiochus defeated at Thermopylae; Cato's flanking march. Temple of Magna Mater dedicated on the Palatine (Megalesia). Nasica crushes the Boii.
Lucius Scipio (later Asiaticus) with Africanus as legate crosses to Asia; naval victories at Side and Myonnesus. Battle of Magnesia ad Sipylum (December 190 or January 189 Julian).
Vulso's Galatian campaign; Fulvius besieges Ambracia, with Ennius in his retinue. Latin colony at Bononia.
Peace of Apamea: Antiochus cedes Asia Minor west of the Taurus, pays 15,000 talents, surrenders elephants and fleet; Pergamum and Rhodes enlarged. Formiae, Fundi and Arpinum receive full citizenship.

Via Aemilia (Ariminum-Placentia) and Via Flaminia minor (Bononia-Arretium) built. Trials of the Scipios over Antiochus' money begin (dating and details confused in the sources). 12,000 Latins expelled from Rome to their home cities.
Bacchanalian affair: senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus (bronze copy from Tiriolo, CIL I2 581); some 7,000 implicated (Livy 39.8-19). First athletic contests at Rome given by Fulvius Nobilior.
Campaigns in Liguria.
Censorship of Cato and Lucius Valerius Flaccus: severe review of the Senate and equites, luxury taxes, Basilica Porcia built. Plautus dies (184).
Deaths of Hannibal (in Bithynia), Philopoemen and (183 or 184) Scipio Africanus. Citizen colonies at Parma, Mutina, Potentia, Pisaurum.
Lex Orchia sumptuaria limits the number of dinner guests.
Latin colony at Aquileia (3,000 settlers). Lex Baebia de ambitu; perhaps alternation of four and six praetors. 'Books of Numa' found on the Janiculum and burned. First Celtiberian War (181-179).
Piso died, allegedly poisoned by his wife Quarta Hostilia to secure her son's election. Lex Villia annalis sets minimum ages for magistracies. 40,000 Apuan Ligurians deported to Samnium.
Two brothers by birth as consuls (Manlius adopted). Gracchus' settlement in Spain with fair treaty terms. Basilica Aemilia (Fulvia) begun by the censors; first stone pier of the Pons Aemilius.
Istrian War.

Gracchus (father of the tribunes) in Sardinia; claims 80,000 killed or captured; 'Sardi venales'. Citizen colony at Luna; Latin rights reduced in colonial allotments (the last Latin colony, Aquileia, 181).
Hispallus died in office (stroke); Petillius killed fighting the Ligurians.
Censors let contracts for paving streets in Rome with stone (silex) and roads outside with gravel.
Two Epicurean philosophers expelled (173 or 154). Ager Ligustinus et Gallicus distributed.
First year with two plebeian consuls (Fasti Capitolini note).
Third Macedonian War against Perseus. Roman defeat at Callinicus. Carteia founded in Spain, first Latin colony outside Italy, for sons of soldiers and local women.
Inconclusive campaigning; complaints from Greek allies (Chalcis, Abdera) about Roman commanders.
Lex Voconia limits women's inheritance. Censors Gracchus and Claudius restrict freedmen to one urban tribe. Basilica Sempronia. Ennius dies.

Battle of Pydna (22 June; lunar eclipse of 21 June 168 BC predicted by Sulpicius Galus): end of the Antigonid monarchy. Day of Eleusis: Gaius Popillius Laenas draws a circle round Antiochus IV and forces him out of Egypt. Genthius of Illyria defeated.

Tributum on Roman citizens suspended indefinitely from Macedonian booty. Macedon divided into four republics. 150,000 Epirotes enslaved. 1,000 Achaean hostages, including Polybius, taken to Italy. Delos made a free port, ruining Rhodes.
Terence's Andria produced.
Terence's Hecyra fails at its first performance.
Census of 337,022 citizens (Livy Per. 47 gives 337,452).
Thalna died in Corsica on hearing of a supplication voted in his honour (Valerius Maximus 9.12.3).
Both consuls abdicated after Gracchus confessed an error in taking the auspices (vitio creati).
Senatus consultum expelling philosophers and rhetors. Lex Fannia sumptuaria. Treaty of friendship with Judas Maccabaeus (1 Macc. 8). Terence's Eunuchus and Phormio.
Death of Aemilius Paullus; Terence's Adelphoe staged at his funeral games. Cethegus drains part of the Pomptine Marshes.
Lex Cornelia Fulvia de ambitu. Censor Scipio Nasica installs a water clock in the Basilica Aemilia.
Macedonian mines reopened.
First Julius Caesar in the consular fasti since the early Republic.
Dalmatian War.

Athenian embassy of the philosophers Carneades, Diogenes of Babylon and Critolaus; Carneades argues for and against justice on successive days; Cato has them sent home. Nasica blocks construction of a permanent stone theatre.
Postumius died (allegedly poisoned by his wife). Lusitanian war begins. Opimius campaigns for Massilia against the Ligurians, the first Roman army in Transalpine Gaul.
Consuls begin their year on 1 January from now (previously 15 March), because of the Celtiberian emergency. Nobilior defeated by the Celtiberians near Numantia (23 August).
Marcellus' conciliatory peace with the Celtiberians. Flaccus died in office. Law forbidding repeated consulships (c. 151) followed Marcellus' third tenure.
Levy resisted; consuls imprisoned by tribunes. Lucullus massacres the Caucaei at Intercatia; Scipio Aemilianus serves as military tribune. Carthage pays its final indemnity instalment.
Servius Sulpicius Galba massacres surrendered Lusitanians; Viriathus escapes. Carthage defeated by Masinissa, breaching the 201 treaty.

Third Punic War: Carthage surrenders arms then refuses to abandon the city. Lex Calpurnia de repetundis: first permanent quaestio (extortion court). Andriscus claims the Macedonian throne. Cato dies. Masinissa dies (148).
Andriscus defeated by Quintus Caecilius Metellus (Macedonicus). Via Postumia from Genua to Aquileia.
Aemilianus elected consul under age, without the praetorship, by popular pressure and a suspension of the lex Villia; given Africa by law.
Carthage destroyed by Aemilianus (spring); province of Africa. Mummius sacks Corinth after the Achaean War. Macedonia a province (148/146).
Fabius (Aemilianus' brother) against Viriathus. Gaius Laelius' proposal of land reform withdrawn.
Praetor Quintus Marcius Rex given funds to build the Aqua Marcia (completed 140).
Appius triumphs over the Salassi without authorisation, protected in his chariot by his Vestal daughter. Numantine War begins.
Censorship of Scipio Aemilianus and Lucius Mummius. Pons Aemilius completed with stone arches. Servilianus concedes a treaty recognising Viriathus as amicus (140).
Pompeius, a novus homo, makes a secret peace at Numantia and then disowns it.
Caepio procures the murder of Viriathus (139).
Lex Gabinia tabellaria: secret ballot in elections. Praetor Cornelius Hispalus expels astrologers (Chaldaei) and Jews (Valerius Maximus 1.3.3).
Consuls briefly imprisoned by tribunes over the levy. Brutus (later Callaicus) campaigns in Lusitania and Gallaecia; founds Valentia.

Mancinus' army trapped at Numantia; quaestor Tiberius Gracchus negotiates a treaty, later repudiated, and Mancinus is handed over naked to the Numantines (136), who refuse him. Lex Cassia tabellaria extends the ballot to trials (except perduellio).
Slave revolt in Sicily under Eunus begins (dated 136 or 135).
First Sicilian Slave War spreads; Eunus styles himself King Antiochus.
Aemilianus elected to a second consulship in breach of the law against iteration; given Numantia; raises volunteers and clients.

Tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus: lex Sempronia agraria, tresviri agris iudicandis adsignandis; deposition of the tribune Octavius; Gracchus killed by Scipio Nasica and senators. Numantia falls. Attalus III bequeaths Pergamum to Rome.
Special court punishes Gracchus' supporters. Rupilius ends the Sicilian slave war and issues the lex Rupilia for Sicily. Via Popillia. Aristonicus' revolt in Asia.
First two plebeian censors. Crassus, pontifex maximus, leaves Italy to fight Aristonicus; killed 130. Speech of the censor Metellus Macedonicus on compulsory marriage.
Lentulus died in office; whether a suffect was elected is uncertain. Perperna captures Aristonicus.
Death of Scipio Aemilianus (possibly murdered) after transferring the land commission's judicial powers. Aquillius organises the province of Asia (129-126).
Annius' cognomen also given as Luscus.
Ravilla the judge famous for asking 'cui bono?'.
Lex Iunia expels non-citizens from Rome. Gaius Gracchus quaestor in Sardinia.
Fulvius proposes citizenship for the allies; sent to help Massilia against the Saluvii. Revolt of Fregellae, destroyed by the praetor Lucius Opimius.
Sextius campaigns against the Saluvii; founds Aquae Sextiae (122).

First tribunate of Gaius Gracchus: lex frumentaria, lex iudiciaria (equites on the extortion juries), lex de provincia Asia (tithes auctioned at Rome), road building, colonies. Metellus conquers the Balearics (Balearicus), founds Palma and Pollentia.
Gaius Gracchus' second tribunate; colony Junonia at Carthage; citizenship bill defeated. Livius Drusus outbids him. Lex Acilia de repetundis (partly preserved on the Tabula Bembina) dated 123 or 122.

Senatus consultum ultimum: Gaius Gracchus and Fulvius Flaccus killed with some 3,000 followers. Opimius builds the temple of Concord. Fabius (Allobrogicus) and Domitius defeat the Arverni and Allobroges; the start of Gallia Transalpina. Via Domitia.
Opimius tried and acquitted. Carbo later defends him, apostatising from the Gracchans.
Gaius Marius tribune: law narrowing the voting bridges (pontes). Metellus (Delmaticus) campaigns in Dalmatia.
Citizen colony Narbo Martius founded (118). Micipsa of Numidia dies; kingdom divided between Adherbal, Hiempsal and Jugurtha. Cato (grandson of the Censor) died in Africa.
Sententia Minuciorum on the dispute between Genua and the Langenses Viturii (CIL I2 584). Scaevola the Augur, teacher of Cicero.
Senatorial commission under Lucius Opimius divides Numidia; Jugurtha gets the richer west.
Scaurus becomes princeps senatus. Sumptuary law of Scaurus.
Three Vestals tried for unchastity (114-113); Greek and Gallic couples buried alive again; temple to Venus Verticordia. Cato defeated by the Scordisci.
Cimbri and Teutones defeat Carbo at Noreia.
Jugurtha takes Cirta and massacres Italian traders; war declared. Lex agraria of 111 (Tabula Bembina) may be dated here or 111.
Nasica died in office. Bestia's peace with Jugurtha, suspected of bribery. Lex agraria privatises the Gracchan allotments (epigraphic law, 111).
Jugurtha in Rome murders Massiva; 'urbem venalem'. Aulus Postumius' army sent under the yoke at Suthul (early 109).
Metellus (Numidicus) in Africa, with Marius as legate; battle of the Muthul. Silanus defeated by the Cimbri. Mamilian commission condemns Opimius, Bestia and others.
Hortensius condemned before entering office (or during it); Scaurus suffect.
Marius, a novus homo, given the Numidian command by popular vote and enrols capite censi volunteers. Cassius killed by the Tigurini near Burdigala (Agen?), his army sent under the yoke.
Lex Servilia Caepionis restores senators to the juries (in part). Caepio seizes the 'gold of Tolosa', which vanishes. Births of Cicero (3 Jan) and Pompey (29 Sept).

Battle of Arausio (6 October): Caepio and Mallius destroyed by the Cimbri and Teutones; Livy's figure of 80,000 dead. Jugurtha betrayed to Sulla by Bocchus. Rutilius introduces arms drill by gladiatorial trainers.

Marius re-elected in absentia; army reforms traditionally attributed to 104-102 (eagle as sole standard, mules). Jugurtha executed after the triumph. Second Sicilian Slave War (104-100). Lex Domitia: priests elected by 17 tribes.
Orestes died in office. Saturninus' first tribunate: land for Marius' veterans in Africa; lex Appuleia de maiestate.
Marius destroys the Teutones and Ambrones at Aquae Sextiae. Marcus Antonius (Orator) given a command against Cilician pirates.
